root.text.Letter to R Joseph son of Juda:
My thought will guide you on the path of truth, and smooth the way.
Come, walk along its path, O all you who wander in the field of religion!
The impure and the ignorant shall not pass over it; it shall be called the sacred way.
[[t:0]]In the name of the Eternal[[t:1]] [[t:2]]God of the Universe[[fn:0]]
When[[fn:1]], my dear disciple Rabbi Joseph[[fn:2]], son of R. Yehuda [may he rest in paradise!],

you presented yourself before me, having come from a distant land[[fn:3]] to attend my lectures, you were already held in high esteem by me on account of your great passion for study, and because I had recognised in your poems a pronounced love for speculative matters, and this since your treatises and your [[t:0]]Makâmât[[t:1]][[fn:4]] had reached me from Alexandria, and before I could (personally) test your understanding. I said to myself (initially): Perhaps his desire is stronger than his comprehension; but when you had undertaken, under my guidance, your studies of astronomy and mathematical sciences which you had previously approached and which must necessarily serve as a preparation, I felt a far greater joy towards you on account of the excellence of your intellect and the promptitude of your understanding; and, seeing that you had a great love for mathematics, I allowed you the freedom to exercise yourself in them, knowing what your future would be[[fn:5]]. And when you had completed your studies of logic under me, my hope was attached to you and I judged you worthy of revealing to you the mysteries of the prophetic books, so that you might understand what perfect men ought to comprehend. I began, therefore, to give you glimpses of things and to provide you with certain indications; but I saw you asking for more, and you insisted that I explain to you subjects pertaining to metaphysics and that I make known to you, in this regard, what the [[t:2]]Motécallemîn[[t:3]][[fn:6]] aimed at, and whether their methods were based on demonstration, or, if not, to what art they belonged. I saw that you had already studied this matter somewhat under other (masters); but you were agitated and troubled[[fn:7]], and your noble soul stimulated you [[t:4]]to find the objects of your desire[[t:5]][[fn:8]]. I did not cease to dissuade you from this path and I advised you to take things in order; for my intention was (to ensure) that the truth would establish itself for you methodically and that certainty would not come to you by chance. As long as you were with me, I did not refuse, when a verse or one of the texts of the doctors was under discussion, to provide you with an explanation;

but when God decreed the separation and you departed to another side, these conferences revived within me an (ancient) resolution which had already waned, and your absence prompted me to compose this treatise which I have made for you and for your like, however few they may be. I have made of it detached chapters, and all that shall have been committed to writing shall reach you successively wherever thou shalt be. Fare you well.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.0: Show me the path that I shall follow, for it is unto thee that I have lifted up my soul (Ps. 143, [[t:0]]V[[t:1]]. 8).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.1: It is you, men, that I call, and my voice (is addressed) to the sons of Adam (Prov. 8, 4).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.2: Lend thine ear, and hearken unto the words of the wise, and apply thy heart unto my science (Prov. 22, 17).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.3: This treatise has as its primary objective to expound upon the meaning of certain names[[fn:9]] that appear in the prophetic books. Amongst these names, there are some that are homonymous, but which the ignorant take in one of the senses in which the homonym is employed; others are metaphorical, and are taken in the primitive sense from which the metaphor is derived; and others, finally, are amphibological, such that one sometimes believes they are employed as appellative names[[fn:10]] and at other times one imagines they are homonymous[[fn:11]]. The purpose of this treatise is not to render these names comprehensible to the common man or to those who are commencing their studies, nor to instruct one who studies only the science of the Law, that is to say, its traditional interpretation[[fn:12]];
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.4: for the purpose of this entire treatise and all that is of the same kind[[fn:13]] is the science of the Law in its reality, or rather its purpose is to awaken the religious man in whom the truth of our Law is established in the soul and has become an object of belief, who is perfect in his religion and in his morals, who has studied the sciences of the philosophers and is acquainted with their various subjects, and whom human reason has attracted and guided to enter into its domain, but who is perplexed by the external (literal) sense of the Law and by what he has always understood or been made to understand of the meaning of these homonymous, or metaphorical, or amphibological names, such that he remains in a state of agitation and turmoil. Will he permit himself to be guided by his reason and reject what he has learned regarding these names? He will then believe that he has rejected the foundations of the Law. Or will he adhere to what he has understood[[fn:14]] without allowing himself to be swayed by his reason? He will thus have turned his back on reason and will have distanced himself from it, believing nonetheless that he has suffered damage and loss in his religion, and persisting in these imaginary opinions by which he will feel troubled and oppressed, such that he will ceaselessly experience suffering in his heart and violent turmoil.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.5: This treatise has yet another purpose: it is to expound very obscure allegories found in the books of the prophets, which are not clearly recognisable as allegories, and are taken in their external sense by the ignorant and the foolish, without perceiving an esoteric meaning. Nevertheless, if a truly educated man examines them, he will also experience great turmoil when taking them in their external sense; but when we shall have expounded to him the meaning of the allegory, or warned him that it is an allegory, he will be set on the right path and saved from this turmoil. It is for this reason that I have entitled this treatise [[t:0]]Dalâlat al-'Hâyirîn[[t:1]] (the guide of those who are perplexed or erring).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.6: I do not say that this treatise will dispel, for one who has understood it, every kind of doubt, but I say that it will dispel most of the obscurities, and the most serious ones. The attentive man will not ask me, nor will he expect, when we have spoken of a certain subject, that we should exhaust it, or, when we have begun to expound the meaning of a certain allegory, that we should exhaust all that has been said on the subject of this allegory: this, an intelligent man could not do viva voce, in conversation[[fn:15]], and how could he commit it to writing in a book without exposing himself to be a target for every ignorant pretender to knowledge, who would launch at him the arrows of his ignorance.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.7: We have already given, in our Talmudic works[[fn:16]], several summary explanations of this kind, and drawn attention to many subjects, and we have noted that the [[t:0]]Ma'asé beréschîth[[t:1]] (account of the creation) is the physical science and the [[t:2]]Ma'asé mercabâ[[t:3]] (account of the celestial chariot) is the metaphysical science[[fn:17]], and we have expounded this sentence[[fn:18]]: 'Neither (shall one expound) the [[t:4]]mercabâ[[t:5]], even to a single (pupil), unless he be a wise man, understanding by his own intellect, (and in this case) one shall only impart to him the first principles.' You will therefore not ask me for anything else here but the first principles. These principles themselves are not found, in the present treatise, arranged in order and in a continuous manner, but, on the contrary, scattered and mixed with other subjects that one wished to expound; for my purpose is (to make it so) that the truths are glimpsed, and then they withdraw, in order not to be in opposition to the divine purpose, which, moreover, it would be impossible to oppose, and which has made the truths that have particularly for their object to make intellect comprehend God to be hidden from the common run of men, as has said (the psalmist): [[t:6]]The secret of the Lord is for those who fear Him[[t:7]] (Ps. 25, 14).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.8: With regard to the matters of physics, it is necessary to know that there are principles which cannot be clearly taught [[fn:19]] as they are in reality. You are aware of what the doctors [[fn:20]] say: 'Neither (shall one interpret) the [[t:0]]Ma'asé beréschîth[[t:1]] before two persons'; now, if someone were to explain all these things in a book, he would interpret them [[t:2]]to[[t:3]] thousands of people. This is why these subjects also present themselves in prophetic books through allegories, and the doctors have also spoken of them in enigmas and allegories, following the trace of the (sacred) books, because they are things which have an intimate relation to metaphysical science, and which also form part of the mysteries of metaphysics.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.9: One must not believe that there is a single one amongst us who knows these grave mysteries in all their extent [[fn:21]]. It is not so; but, on the contrary, truth sometimes appears to us in a manner that seems (clear as) the day, sometimes it is hidden by material and mundane things [[fn:22]], so that we fall back into a deep night, almost as we were before, and we are then like the man who, being in a deeply obscure night, sometimes sees a flash of lightning shine.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.10: There are amongst us those to whom the flash shines repeatedly [[fn:23]], so that, as it were, they are constantly and without interruption surrounded by light, and the night becomes for them like the day, and this is the degree of the greatest of prophets, to whom it was said: [[t:0]]And you, stay here with me[[t:1]] (Deuteronomy, 5:28), and of whom it has been said: [[t:2]]For the skin of his face shone[[t:3]], [[t:4]]etc.[[t:5]] (Exodus, 34:29) [[fn:24]]. There are others to whom (the flash) shines only once in their entire night, and this is the degree of those of whom it has been said: [[t:6]]And they prophesied and did not continue[[t:7]] (Numbers, 11:25). For others, finally, there are intervals, more or less long, between each flash.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.11: But there are also those who do not attain a degree (sufficiently elevated) for their darkness to be illuminated by a flash; (they are not,) on the contrary, except as by a polished body or something similar, such as gemstones, etc. which shine in the darkness of night. And even this small amount of light that shines for us[[fn:25]] is not continuous; but it appears and hides as if it were [[t:0]]the gleam of the sword that turns[[t:1]] (Genesis, 3, 24).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.12: It is therefore according to these circumstances that the degrees of perfect men vary. As for those who never see the light, but who err in the night, those of whom it has been said: [[t:0]]They know nothing and understand nothing, they walk in darkness[[t:1]] (Ps. 82, 5); those to whom truth is entirely hidden, however distinctly it may appear, as has been said of them: [[t:2]]And now they do not see the light that shines in the heavens[[t:3]] (Job, 37, 21), and this is the common lot of men; (as for those, I say,) there is no place to mention them here in this treatise.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.13: One must know that, when one of the perfect men desires, according to the degree of his perfection, to express himself, either verbally or in writing, on something he has understood concerning these mysteries, it is not possible for him to expound even what he has grasped with perfect clarity and in order, as he would for the other sciences whose teaching is widespread. On the contrary, the same thing will happen to him in the teaching of others as happened to him in his own studies; I mean that the thing will appear and become visible, and then it will withdraw; for one would say that such is the nature of this thing, whether it be much or little.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.14: It is for this reason that all learned metaphysicians and theologians[[fn:26]], friends of the truth, when they wished to teach something of this nature, spoke only through allegories and enigmas, and, multiplying the allegories, they employed different species and even different genres; they formed most of them in such a manner as to make the subject in question understood, either at the beginning of the allegory, or in the middle, or at the end, unless one could find an image that applied to the thing in question from beginning to end. (Sometimes) also the subject that one had as a goal to teach the student, although it was an essentially [[t:0]]one[[t:1]] subject, was divided, by putting it into several allegories distant from one another; but what is even more obscure, is when a single and same allegory is used for diverse subjects, in such a manner that the beginning of the allegory applies to one subject and the end to another. Sometimes also the entire allegory is used for two analogous subjects[[fn:27]] in this genre of science. Finally, when someone wished to teach without the use of allegories and enigmas, there was in their words an obscurity and brevity that took the place of the use of allegories and enigmas. It would seem that the learned and the doctors are guided in this regard by the divine will, just as their physical dispositions guide them (in other respects).
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.15: Do you not see, moreover, that God the Most High, wishing to perfect and improve the state of our societies through His practical laws — [which can only be done after (the establishment of) certain rational dogmas, the first condition of which is to understand the divinity according to our faculty, which can only be done through the science of metaphysics, which in turn can only come after the science of physics; for the latter is adjacent[[fn:28]] to metaphysics and precedes it in teaching, which is clear to one who has made these studies] — (do you not see, I say,) that He has placed at the opening of His book the account of creation, which is the science of physics, as we have explained? But because of the gravity and importance of this thing, and because our faculty is insufficient to understand the most serious of subjects in all its reality[[fn:29]], one has chosen, to speak to us of the profound subjects that divine wisdom judged necessary to discuss with us, allegories, enigmas, and extremely obscure words, as the doctors have said: 'To expose the power of the work of creation to mortals is impossible; this is why Scripture has spoken to you in an obscure manner: [[t:0]]In the beginning, God created, etc.[[t:1]].' They have thus warned you that the things mentioned are [[t:2]]obscure[[t:3]]. You are also familiar with these words of Solomon: [[t:4]]What exists is far[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]from our conception[[t:7]]); [[t:8]]this very profound thing, who can find it[[t:9]] (Ecclesiastes, 7, 25)? To speak of all these subjects, one has used homonymous words, so that common men could take them in a certain sense according to the measure of their intelligence and the weakness of their understanding, and so that the perfect man who has received instruction could take them in another sense.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.16: We had promised in the commentary on the Mischnâ[[fn:30]] to expound certain difficult subjects in (two works entitled): the [[t:0]]Book of Prophecy[[t:1]] and the [[t:2]]Book of Harmony;[[t:3]] the latter being a book in which we had promised to expound the obscurities of all the [[t:4]]Deraschôth[[t:5]][[fn:31]], whose external words are in great discord with truth and deviate from reason, and which are all allegories. But when, some years ago, we began these books and had written a part of them, the explanations to which we had committed ourselves, according to this method, did not please us; for it seemed to us that, proceeding ourselves by way of allegory and hiding what ought to remain hidden, we would not have deviated from the original purpose (of the [[t:6]]Deraschôth[[t:7]]), and we would have done, as it were, nothing but substitute one individual for another individual of the same species; but that, in expounding what needs expounding, this would not be suitable for the common man, and yet we desired nothing else but to expound to the common man the meaning of the [[t:8]]Deraschôth[[t:9]] and the external words of the prophecies. It also seemed to us that an ignorant man of the common sort of rabbis, in studying these [[t:10]]Deraschôth[[t:11]], would find no difficulty in them: for he who is ignorant, indolent, and devoid of knowledge concerning the nature of Being, does not find even impossible things implausible; that if, on the contrary, it were a perfect and distinguished man who studied them, he would necessarily arrive at one of two things: either he would take them in their external sense, and then he would have a bad opinion of the author and take him for an ignorant man, but there would be nothing in this that could undermine the foundations of faith; or he would attribute to them an esoteric meaning, and then he would fare well and have a good opinion of the author, no matter whether the (true) inner meaning of the words was clear to him or not. As for the significance of Prophecy, the exposition of its various degrees, and the interpretation of the allegories of its books, all this will be explained in a different manner in the present treatise. For all these reasons, therefore, we have renounced composing these two works as they had been conceived; and we have limited ourselves, — in speaking of the foundations of Faith and general truths with brevity and in giving a glimpse of (things) in a manner that approaches clear exposition —, to what we have said in the great Talmudic work [[t:12]]Mischné Torâ[[t:13]].
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.17: As for the present treatise, I address the word, as I have said, to one who has studied philosophy and acquired true sciences, but who, believing in religious matters, is troubled concerning their meaning, with regard to which obscure names and allegories[[fn:32]] leave uncertainty. We will also give in this treatise chapters in which no homonymous word will be mentioned. But one chapter will serve as preparation for another or will draw attention to one of the meanings of a homonymous word that I do not wish to speak of explicitly in this place; another chapter will expound some allegory or warn that a certain subject is an allegory; another will contain difficult subjects, concerning which one sometimes believes the contrary of what is true, either because of certain homonymies or because one confuses the image with the thing it is meant to represent or takes the represented thing for an image[[fn:33]].
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.18: And since I have spoken of allegories, we shall enunciate a proposition, which is this: 'It is necessary to know that the key to understanding all that the prophets have said and to knowing it in all its reality, is to understand allegories and their meaning and to know how to interpret their words.' You know what the Most High has said: [[t:0]]And by the prophets I make similitudes[[t:1]] (Hos., XII, 11); and you also know this other passage: [[t:2]]Propose an enigma and make a parable[[t:3]] (Ezek., 17, 2). You also know that it is because of the frequent use of allegories by the prophets that the prophet said: They say of me: [[t:4]]Is he not a maker of allegories[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]Ib[[t:7]]., XXI, 5)? You know, finally, how Solomon began (his book): [[t:8]]To understand the allegory and the eloquent discourse, the words of the wise and their enigmas[[t:9]] (Prov., 1, 6). And in the Midrash[[fn:34]] it is said: 'What did the words of the Torah resemble before Solomon appeared? A well whose cold water was situated in the depth, so that no one could drink from it. What did a wise man do then? He tied ropes together and threads together, and then he drew and drank. Thus Solomon passed[[fn:35]] from one allegory to another and from one discourse to another until he profoundized the words of the Torah.' Such are the textual words. I do not think that among men endowed with good sense there is one who imagines that the [[t:10]]words of the Torah[[t:11]] to which allusion is made here and which one has sought to understand by the (preliminary) intelligence of the meaning of allegories are the precepts concerning the making of cabins, the branches of palm trees, and the law relating to the four guardians[[fn:36]]; on the contrary, one undoubtedly had in view here the understanding of profound things. It is said in the same place (of the Midrash): 'The rabbis say: If someone loses a shekel or a pearl in his house, he only has to light a wick (worth) an obol to find the pearl; similarly, the allegory in itself is nothing, but by means of the allegory you understand the words of the Torah.' Such are their textual words again. And pay close attention that they clearly say that the interior of the words of the Torah is the pearl and that the external sense of every allegory is nothing, and that they compare the hidden and represented sense in the external words of the allegory to a pearl that someone has lost in his house, which is dark and full of furniture. This pearl exists, but he does not see it and does not know where it is: it is as if it had gone out of his possession, since he has no means of deriving any benefit from it until he lights the lamp as has been said; and it is to this that the understanding of the sense of the allegory resembles.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.19: The wise man has said: [[t:0]]Like apples of gold in nets[[t:1]] (Maskiyyôth) [[t:2]]of silver, such is a word spoken according to its different faces[[t:3]] (Prov., 21, II)[[fn:37]].
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.20: Hear the explanation of the subject of which he speaks: Maskiyyôth are reticular engravings, that is to say, where there are openings (formed) of extremely fine meshes, like the works of goldsmiths; they are called thus because the gaze penetrates them, for the Chaldaic version of [[t:0]]וַיַּשְׁקֵף[[t:1]] (he looked) is [[t:2]]we-istekhi[[t:3]][[fn:38]]. He says, therefore: As an apple of gold in a silver net with very fine openings, such is the word spoken according to its two faces. And behold[[fn:39]] how this sentence applies wonderfully to the allegory in rule; for he says that the discourse which has two faces, that is to say, which has an exterior and interior (sense), must have its exterior beautiful like silver, but its interior must be still more beautiful than its exterior, so that its interior will be, in comparison to its exterior, like gold is to silver. It is also necessary that there be in its exterior something which can indicate to the one examining it what is in its interior, like this apple of gold which has been covered with a silver net with extremely fine meshes: for, if one sees it from afar or without examining it attentively, one believes it to be a silver apple; but if the man with the penetrating eye examines it well attentively, what is within is shown to him, and he recognises that it is gold. And it is the same with the allegories of the prophets: their exterior words (contain) a wisdom useful for many things, and among others for the improvement of the state of human societies, as appears in the exterior words of the Proverbs (of Solomon) and other similar discourses; but their interior (sense) is a wisdom useful for beliefs having for object the true in all its reality.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.21: Know also that prophetic allegories are made in two ways: there are some in which each word of the allegory desires (that one finds) a particular sense; and there are others in which the entirety of the allegory reveals the entirety of the subject represented, but where it is also found that many words do not each add something to the subject represented, and which serve only to embellish the allegory and to the symmetry of the discourse, or to conceal with more care the subject represented, so that the discourse is constantly conceived as it must be according to the exterior sense of the allegory. It is necessary to understand this well.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.22: An example of the first species of prophetic allegories is found in this passage: [[t:0]]And behold, a ladder was set upon the earth, etc[[t:1]]. (Genesis, 28, 12); for the word [[t:2]]ladder[[t:3]] indicates a certain subject, the words [[t:4]]was set upon the earth[[t:5]] indicate a second, the words [[t:6]]and its head reached the heaven[[t:7]] indicate a third, the words [[t:8]]and behold, the angels of God[[t:9]] indicate a fourth, the word [[t:10]]went up[[t:11]] indicates a fifth, the words [[t:12]]and came down[[t:13]] indicate a sixth, and the words [[t:14]]and behold, the Lord stood above[[t:15]] indicate a seventh, so that each word which presents itself in this allegory adds something to the entirety of the subject represented.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.23: An example of the second species of prophetic allegories is found in the following passage (Prov., 7, 6 et seq.): [[t:0]]For through the window of my house, through my lattice I looked, and I saw among the simple, I discerned among the youths a child void of intellect, who, passing through the market near the corner, was advancing towards the house[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]where she dwelt[[t:3]]). [[t:4]]During the twilight, when the day was disappearing, in the darkness of the night and in the shadows. And behold, a woman comes forth to meet him in the attire of a courtesan and with a cunning heart. She is boisterous, unmanageable, etc. Now in the street, now in the squares, etc. She seizes him, etc. I had to offer peace sacrifices, etc. Therefore, I went forth to meet thee, etc. I covered my bed with tapestries, etc. I perfumed my couch, etc. Come, let us inebriate ourselves with love, etc. For the husband is not at home, etc. He has taken the purse containing the money, etc. She seduces him with the abundance of her words, she entices him with her fallacious lips[[t:5]].
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.24: The entire discourse is intended to warn that one ought not follow the pleasures and passions of the body; it therefore compares the matter which is the cause of all these corporeal passions to a courtesan who is at the same time a married woman, and it is upon this allegory that he has built his entire book. In several chapters of this treatise, we shall demonstrate the wisdom of comparing matter to an unfaithful married woman, and we shall note how he concludes his book with the praise of the woman who is not unfaithful, but rather occupies herself with the good order of her house and the position of her husband. (It will also be seen that) all the obstacles which prevent man from arriving at his final perfection, every vice and every sin which attaches itself to man, arise solely from the side of matter, as we shall explain in this treatise. It is therefore this general doctrine which forms the content of this entire allegory, namely that man ought not follow his sole animal nature, that is to say, his matter; for the immediate matter of man is also the immediate matter of other animals[[fn:40]]. After having given you this explanation and having revealed to you the mystery of this allegory, you will no longer[[fn:41]] hope to be able to ask me what is hidden beneath the words: [[t:0]]I had to offer peace sacrifices, today I have accomplished my vows;[[t:1]] what sense do the words convey: [[t:2]]I covered my bed with tapestries[[t:3]]; or what the words add to the general sense: [[t:4]]For the husband is not at home[[t:5]], as well as all that follows in this chapter. All of this is merely a series of phrases relating to the external sense of the allegory; for the details which he described are of the same species as those (which relate) to fornicators, and similarly these words and others like them are of the same species as those which adulterers address to one another.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.25: It is essential to comprehend my statements, for they are founded upon a principle of paramount importance to the explications I propose to furnish. Thus, should you perceive me elucidating the sense of a particular allégorie in a chapter of this treatise, and I direct your attention to the entirety of the thing represented, you shall not request (an explication of) every particular subject encountered within this allégorie, nor shall you endeavour to discover its analogue in the thing represented; for to do so would lead you to one of two consequences, either to lose sight of the subject which the allégorie was intended to convey, or to impose upon yourself the task of interpreting words not susceptible to interpretation and not written to be [[t:0]]interpreted[[t:1]]. And in imposing this task upon yourself, you would fall prey to that great folly which afflicts the majority of the world's schools in our era, as evidenced by their writings[[fn:42]]; for each of these individuals seeks to discern a meaning in words in which the author intended none of the significance they themselves wish to discern. You must, on the contrary, always direct your attention to comprehending the entirety of the thing intended to be conveyed in the majority of allégories, and in certain instances, it shall suffice for you to understand from my words that a particular subject is an allégorie, even if I do not expound further; for once you have ascertained that it is an allégorie, you shall immediately comprehend its object, and in stating that it is an allégorie, I shall, as it were, have removed the obstacle interposed between the viewer and the object viewed.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.26: [[t:0]]RECOMMENDATION REGARDING THIS TREATISE.[[t:1]] [[t:2]]If you wish to comprehend all that (this treatise) contains, in such a manner that nothing escapes you, it is necessary to combine its chapters with one another, and in reading a chapter, you must not only aim to understand the entirety of its subject, but also to grasp each word that presents itself in the sequence of the discourse, even if it does not pertain to the principal subject of the chapter. For in this treatise, I have never spoken fortuitously, but (all has been said) with great exactitude and with much precision, and with care to leave no explanation of any obscurity wanting; and if something has been said (here and there) that is not in its place, it has been only to explain something else in its true place. You must not approach it with your preconceived opinions, for you would do me an injustice without profiting yourself; but, on the contrary, you must first learn all that it is necessary to learn. You will make it the object of your continual studies, for it will explain to you the most grave obscurities of the Law, which are difficult even for every intelligent man. I implore, by God the Most High, all those who will have read the present treatise, not to comment on a single word of it, nor to explain anything of it to others, unless it be what is already clearly explained in the words of those who have preceded me among the celebrated doctors of our Law. But (the reader) who will have understood something of what others of our celebrated men have not said, must not explain it to others; nor must he hasten to refute me[[fn:43]]; for it may be that what he will have understood in my words was the contrary of what I intended to say, and then he would do me an injustice in return for what I intended to be useful to him, and [[t:3]]he would repay good with evil[[t:4]]. On the contrary, he to whom (this treatise) will have fallen into the hands, must study it with care, and if he finds in it something to satisfy his desire[[fn:44]], be it only on a single point of all that is obscure, he must thank God and be content with what he has understood. If he finds in it absolutely nothing that is useful to him, he must consider it as if it had never been composed; but if it seems to him to result in harm with regard to his opinions, he must interpret (my words) [[t:5]]in a manner that judges me favourably[[t:6]] ([[t:7]]ידין לכף זכות[[t:8]]), even by the most recherché interpretation, as it has been prescribed to us with regard to our common people, and all the more so with regard to our scholars and the supporters of our Law, who strive to teach us the truth according to their faculty.
root.text.Prefatory Remarks.27: I am aware that all beginners who have not yet undertaken any speculative study will derive benefit from certain chapters of this treatise; but perfect men, steeped in the study of the Law and who are troubled, as I have said, will benefit from all its chapters, and how joyful they will be and with what pleasure they will listen to (the reading) ! But as for those people who are perplexed, whose intellect is troubled by opinions contrary to truth and by false methods, and who nonetheless believe these to be true sciences and pretend to be men of speculative study, whilst they know absolutely nothing that can in reality be called science, — as for those, (I say,) they will turn away from a great number of its chapters, and they will experience a great repugnance, because they will not grasp the sense, and also because the falsity of the bad coin they hold in their hands and which is their treasure and the fortune set aside for their distress[[fn:45]] will be recognised. God, the Most High, knows that I have always felt a very great fear of committing to writing the things that I wish to deposit in this treatise; for these are hidden things, and on which no book has ever been composed among our coreligionists in this time of captivity, of which we still possess the works[[fn:46]]. And how, then, can I create something new and commit it to writing ! Nevertheless, I have relied on two principles: first, on what (the rabbis) have said concerning analogous matters: [[t:0]]When it is time to act for God, etc[[t:1]].[[fn:47]]; second, on what they have also said: [[t:2]]That all works be done in the name of heaven[[t:3]]. It is, therefore, on these two principles that I have relied for what I have written in certain chapters of this treatise. Finally, I am the man who, seeing himself confined in a narrow arena and not finding the means to teach a well-demonstrated truth, except in a manner that suits one distinguished man and displeases ten thousand ignorant men, prefers to speak for this single distinguished person, without paying attention to the blame of the great multitude, and claims to draw this single distinguished man out of the embarrassment in which he has fallen and to show him the way (to exit) from his error, in order to become perfect and to obtain rest.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.0: PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION. [[t:0]]The causes of the contradiction or opposition that one finds in a book or in any writing whatsoever are seven in number.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.1: FIRST CAUSE[[t:1]]: When the author has gathered the words of people of different opinions, omitting (to cite) the authorities and to attribute each word to its author. One then finds in his work contradictions or opposed assertions, because one of the two propositions is the opinion of one individual, and the other the opinion of another individual.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.2: S[[t:0]]ECOND CAUSE[[t:1]]: When the author of the book has initially professed a certain opinion from which he has subsequently recanted, and when both what he initially said and what he said afterwards have been recorded.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.3: T[[t:0]]HIRD CAUSE[[t:1]]: When the words (of the author) are not all (taken) in their external sense (literal); but some retain their literal sense and others are an image and have a figurative sense, or when the two contradictory propositions, according to their literal sense, are allegories, and when, taken in their literal sense, they appear contradictory or opposed to one another.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.4: F[[t:0]]OURTH CAUSE[[t:1]]: When there exists a certain condition[[fn:48]] which, for some reason, is not explicitly indicated in the very place, or when the two subjects are different[[fn:49]] and neither of the two is clearly designated in the very place, such that it appears there is a contradiction in the discourse without there actually being one.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.5: C[[t:0]]FOURTH CAUSE[[t:1]]: The necessity (to which one is sometimes reduced) for teaching and making understood (a certain thing); that is to say, when there is a certain obscure and difficult subject to conceive which one needs to mention or take as premises, in order to explain a subject easy to conceive and which in teaching should precede this first subject, because one always begins with the easiest [[fn:50]]. Then, the one who teaches must make himself comfortable to make this first subject understood, in any way, by examining it roughly without undertaking to expose exactly all its reality, and leaving it, on the contrary, to the reach of the listener's imagination, so that the latter may understand what one wants him to understand at this moment, reserving the right to expose more exactly this obscure subject which will manifest itself in its reality in the suitable place [[fn:51]].
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.6: S[[t:0]]SIXTH CAUSE[[t:1]]: When the contradiction hides and only manifests itself after several premises. The more premises are needed to manifest it, the more it will be hidden, in such a way as to escape the author, who will believe that there is no contradiction between the two first propositions. However, by taking each of the two propositions separately and joining a true premise to it, in such a way that a necessary conclusion is drawn from it, and doing the same with each conclusion, (I mean) by joining a true premise to it in such a way as to draw a necessary conclusion from it, one will arrive, after a series of syllogisms, at finding a contradiction or opposition between the two last conclusions. This is what happens even to learned authors; but if the two first propositions were manifestly contradictory and the author had only forgotten the first one when writing the other in another part of his work, this would be a very great inferiority, and such a man could not be counted among those whose words deserve attention.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.7: S[[t:0]]SEVENTH CAUSE[[t:1]]: The necessity of discourse, when it comes to very obscure things whose details must be partly hidden and partly revealed. For sometimes one is forced, when emitting an opinion, to express oneself in such a way as to affirm a certain proposition, while in another place one is forced to express oneself in such a way as to affirm a proposition which is in contradiction with the first. The common people should in no way perceive the place where the contradiction exists, and the author sometimes seeks all sorts of expedients to hide it [[fn:52]].
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.8: With regard to the contradictions found in the [[t:0]]Mischnâ[[t:1]] and in the [[t:2]]Baraïthôth[[t:3]], they emanate from the first cause. Thus you will continually find it said (in the Talmud): 'The beginning (of the chapter) is in contradiction with the end,' and this response is added: 'The beginning emanates from such-and-such a doctor and the end from another doctor.' You will also find these words: 'Rabbi[[fn:53]] approved the words of such-and-such a doctor in one case and simply reproduced his opinion (without naming him), and in another case he approved the words of another doctor and simply reproduced his opinion.' Often, too, you will find this formula: 'To whom does this anonymous assertion belong? It belongs to such-and-such a doctor. — To whom does our (paragraph of the) Mischnâ belong? It belongs to such-and-such a doctor.' These examples are innumerable.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.9: With regard to the contradictions and divergences found in the Talmud (or the [[t:0]]Guemarâ[[t:1]]), they emanate from the first and second cause. Thus you will always find these words: 'On such a subject he adopted the opinion of such-and-such a doctor and on another subject the opinion of another doctor.' It is also said: 'He adopted the opinion of one person in one case and deviated from it in another case.' It is said, finally: 'These are two [[t:2]]Amoraïm[[t:3]][[fn:54]] (who differ) on the opinion of such-and-such a doctor.' All examples of this kind conform to the first cause. With regard to the second cause, they (the Talmudists) explicitly say: [[t:4]]Râb recanted such an opinion[[t:5]], or [[t:6]]Rabâ recanted such an opinion[[t:7]][[fn:55]], and (in such a case) they discuss which of the two opinions is the later one. We may also quote the following words: 'According to the first redaction of Rabbi Asché[[fn:56]], he expressed himself in such a sense, and according to the second redaction he expressed himself in another sense.'
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.10: As for the contradiction or opposition that appears in the external sense of certain passages of all the prophetic books, it emanates from the third and fourth cause, and it is especially this subject that was the purpose of this entire preliminary observation. You know that (the doctors) often repeat these words: 'One text expresses itself in such a manner and another text in another manner.' They first establish the apparent contradiction, then they explain that there is a missing condition (in the text), or that it concerns two different subjects. Thus, for example, they say: 'Solomon, is it not enough that your words contradict those of your father? Must they also contradict each other, etc.?[[fn:57]]' The doctors often speak in this sense; but most of the time they deal with prophetic discourses related to (religious) precepts or morality. As for us, our only goal was to draw attention to verses that, taken in their literal sense, contain contradictions regarding certain opinions and beliefs; a part of this will be explained in various chapters of this treatise; for this subject is also part of the [[t:0]]Mysteries of the Law[[t:1]]. As for the question of whether there are contradictions in the books of the prophets emanating from the seventh cause, this is something that must be examined and discussed, and not decided upon hastily[[fn:58]].
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.11: With regard to the divergence found in the books of true philosophers, it emanates from the fifth cause.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.12: As for the contradictions found in most of the works of authors and commentators other than those we have mentioned, they emanate from the sixth cause. Likewise, in the [[t:0]]מִדְרָשוֹת[[t:1]] and in the [[t:2]]הַגָּדוֹת[[t:3]] there exist grave contradictions emanating from this same cause; this is why (the rabbis) say: 'One does not raise contradictions in the [[t:4]]הַגָּדוֹת[[t:5]].' There are also found contradictions emanating from the seventh cause.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.13: Lastly, the divergences that may exist in this treatise emanate from the fifth and seventh cause[[fn:59]]. It is necessary that you know this, that you penetrate it, and that you recall it well, in order not to be troubled regarding several of these chapters.
root.text.Part 1.Introduction.14: After these preliminary remarks, I commence to speak of the names from which it is necessary to extract the true meaning that was intended in each place according to the subject (which is being treated), and this shall be a key to enter into places whose doors are closed. And when these doors shall have been opened and one shall have entered into these places, the souls shall find rest there, the eyes shall delight, and the bodies shall be relieved of their pain and fatigue.
root.text.Part 1..0.0: Open the gates, that the righteous nation which keeps the truth may enter in.
root.text.Part 1..0.1: [[t:0]]Célem[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]צֶלֶם[[t:3]]) and [[t:4]]demouth[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]דְּמוּת[[t:7]]). — There have been people who believed that [[t:8]]célem[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]צלם[[t:11]]), in the Hebrew language, designated the form of a thing and its lineaments, and this led to pure corporification (of God), because it is said (in Scripture): [[t:12]]Let us make man in our image[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]בצלמנו[[t:15]]) [[t:16]]according to our likeness[[t:17]] (Genesis, 1, 26). They believed, therefore, that God had the form of a man, that is to say, his figure and lineaments, and it resulted in pure corporification for them, which they admitted as a belief, thinking that, if they deviated from this belief, they would deny the text (of Scripture), or even that they would deny the existence of God if He were not (for them) a body having a face and hands similar to theirs in form and lineaments; only, they admitted that He was greater and more resplendent (than they), and that His matter also was not blood and flesh, and this was all they could conceive of as more sublime with regard to God[[fn:60]].
root.text.Part 1..0.2: As for that which must be stated to remove corporeality and establish true unity, — which has no reality except by the exclusion[[fn:61]] of corporeality, — you shall know the demonstration of all this by the present treatise; here, in this chapter we only wish to draw attention to the explanation of the meaning of [[t:0]]célem[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]צלם[[t:3]]) and of [[t:4]]demouth[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]דמות[[t:7]]).
root.text.Part 1..0.3: I say, therefore, that the [[t:0]]form[[t:1]] as it is generally known to the common people[[fn:62]] [I mean the figure of the thing and its lineaments] bears in the Hebrew language the particular name of [[t:2]]toar[[t:3]] ([[t:4]]תאר[[t:5]]); one says, for example: [[t:6]]Beautiful in figure[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]תאר[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]and beautiful in countenance[[t:11]] (Genesis, 39, 6); [[t:12]]what is his figure[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]תארו[[t:15]]) (I Samuel, 28, 14)? [[t:16]]As the figure[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]כתאר[[t:19]]) [[t:20]]of the king's sons[[t:21]] (Judges, 13, 18). It has been said (in speaking) of the [[t:22]]artificial form[[t:23]]: He figures[[t:24]] ([[t:25]]יתארהו[[t:26]]) [[t:27]]with the burin[[t:28]]… and [[t:29]]he figures[[t:30]] ([[t:31]]יתארהו[[t:32]]) [[t:33]]with the circle[[t:34]] (Isaiah, 44, 13). This is a denomination that is never applied to God the Most High;—far be it from us (such a thought)!
root.text.Part 1..0.4: As for [[t:0]]célem[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]צלם[[t:3]]), it applies to the [[t:4]]natural form[[t:5]], I mean to that which constitutes the substance of the thing, whereby it becomes what it is and which forms its reality, inasmuch as it is such a being (determined). In man, this something is that from which comes the [[t:6]]understanding[[t:7]] of man, and it is because of this intellectual [[t:8]]compréhension[[t:9]] that it has been said of him: [[t:10]]He created him in the image[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]בצלם[[t:13]]) [[t:14]]of God[[t:15]] (Genesis, 1, 26).
root.text.Part 1..0.5: This is why it has been said (speaking of the impious): [[t:0]]You despise their image[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]צלמם[[t:3]]) (Ps. 73, 20); for contempt reaches the soul which is the [[t:4]]form specific[[t:5]][[fn:63]], and not the figures of the members and their lineaments. I say likewise that the reason why idols were called [[t:6]]celamîm[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]צלמים[[t:9]]), is that what was sought in them was something that was supposed in them[[fn:64]]; but it was in no way for their figure and lineaments. I shall say the same thing regarding the words: [[t:10]]the images[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]צלמי[[t:13]]) [[t:14]]of your[[t:15]] [[t:16]]TE’HORÎM[[t:17]] (I Sam., 6, 5)[[fn:65]]; for what was sought in them was the means of warding off evil from the [[t:18]]te’horîm[[t:19]], and it was in no way the figure of the [[t:20]]te’horîm.[[t:21]] If, however, it were absolutely necessary to admit that the name of [[t:22]]célem[[t:23]], applied to the images of the [[t:24]]te’horîm[[t:25]] and to idols, referred to the figure and lineaments, this name would be either homonymous or amphibological[[fn:66]], and would apply not only to the [[t:26]]form specific[[t:27]], but also to the [[t:28]]artificial form[[t:29]], as well as to the analogous figures of physical bodies and their lineaments.
root.text.Part 1..0.6: By the words: [[t:0]]Let us make man in our image[[t:1]], one would thus have wished to speak [[t:2]]of the specific form[[t:3]], that is to say, of the intellectual understanding, and not of the figure and lineaments. — Thus we have explained to you the difference between [[t:4]]célem[[t:5]] (image) and [[t:6]]toar[[t:7]] (figure), and we have also explained the meaning of [[t:8]]célem.[[t:9]]
root.text.Part 1..0.7: As for [[t:0]]demouth[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]דמות[[t:3]]), it is a name (derived) from [[t:4]]דמה[[t:5]] (to resemble), and which also indicates a resemblance with respect to some idea; for the words (of the psalmist): [[t:6]]I resemble[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]דמיתי[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]the pelican of the desert[[t:11]] (Ps. 102, 7), do not mean that it resembled it with respect to the wings and plumage, but that the sadness of the one resembled the sadness of the other. Similarly (in this passage): [[t:12]]No tree in the garden of God resembled[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]דמה[[t:15]]) [[t:16]]in beauty[[t:17]] (Ezek., 31, 8), it is a resemblance with respect to the idea of beauty; (likewise in these other passages): [[t:18]]They have poison similar[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]כדמות[[t:21]]) [[t:22]]to the poison of the serpent[[t:23]] (Ps. 58, 5); [[t:24]]He resembles[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]דמיונו[[t:27]]) [[t:28]]a lion eager for prey[[t:29]] (Ps. 17, 12). All (these passages indicate) a resemblance with respect to a certain idea, and not with respect to the figure and lineaments. Similarly: [[t:30]]The resemblance[[t:31]] ([[t:32]]דמות[[t:33]]) [[t:34]]of the throne[[t:35]] (Ezek., 1, 26) is a resemblance with respect to the idea of elevation and majesty, and not with respect to the square shape, the thickness, and the length of the feet, as the poor in spirit believe, and it is the same [[t:36]]with the resemblance[[t:37]] ([[t:38]]דמות[[t:39]]) [[t:40]]of the animals[[t:41]] (Ezek., 1, 13).
root.text.Part 1..0.8: Now, as man is distinguished by something very remarkable that exists within him and which is not found in any of the beings below the sphere of the moon, namely by intellectual comprehension, for which one employs neither senses, nor hands, nor arms[[fn:67]], (this faculty) has been compared to divine comprehension, which is not accomplished by means of an instrument; although the resemblance does not exist in reality, but only at first glance. And for this thing, I mean on account of the divine intellect that unites with man[[fn:68]], it has been said of him that he was made [[t:0]]in the image of God and in His likeness[[t:1]], (and this means) by no means that God the Most High is a body having any form whatsoever.
root.text.Part 1..1.0: A man of science posed to me, several years ago, a remarkable objection that merits consideration, as well as the response we provided to refute it.
root.text.Part 1..1.1: But before reporting the objection and the manner in which to refute it, here is what I have to say. Every Hebrew knows that the name of [[t:0]]Élohîm[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]אלהים[[t:3]]) is a homonym, applying to God, to angels, and to rulers governing states. Already Onkelos, the proselyte, has explained, — and his explanation is true, — that by the words: [[t:4]]And you shall be as [[t:5]]Élohîm [[t:6]]knowing good and evil[[t:7]] (Genesis, 3, 5), one intended the latter sense; for he says (in his Chaldaic translation): «And you shall be as the [[t:8]]great personages[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]כרברביא[[t:11]]).»
root.text.Part 1..1.2: After this preliminary observation on the homonymy of this name, we shall report the objection.
root.text.Part 1..1.3: It would appear, from the literal sense of the text, said the author of the objection, that the primitive intention in (the creation of) man was that he should be like the rest of the animals, without intellect and without reflection, and without the ability to distinguish between good and evil; but that, having disobeyed, his disobedience merited him this great particular perfection of man, namely to possess this discernment which is in us, which is the most noble thing of our existence and which constitutes our substance. But it is a remarkable thing that his punishment for his disobedience was to give him a perfection he had not previously had, namely, intellect. It is absolutely like the assertion of those who have said that a certain man, after having disobeyed (God) and committed excesses of injustice, was transformed and placed as a star in the heaven[[fn:69]].—Such was the purpose and thought of the objection, although it was not (presented) in the same terms.
root.text.Part 1..1.4.sub_0: Hear now in what manner we responded. O you, we said, who examine (things) with a superficial and unreflecting spirit[[fn:70]], and who believe you understand a book, a guide for the ancients and the moderns, by perusing it in a few moments of leisure (stolen from the pleasures) of drinking and cohabitation, as one would peruse some historical book or poem! Stop and examine; for the thing is not as you believed it to be at first glance, but as it shall manifest itself when one has considered what I am about to say. The reason that God has caused to emanate upon man, and which constitutes his final perfection, is that which Adam possessed before his disobedience; it is for this that he was said to be (made) [[t:0]]in the image of God and in His likeness[[t:1]], and it is on account of this that the word was addressed to him and he received commands, as it is said (in Scripture): [[t:2]]And the Lord God commanded[[t:3]], etc. (Genesis, 2, 16), for one cannot give commands to animals or to one who has no reason. By reason one distinguishes between the [[t:4]]true[[t:5]] and the [[t:6]]false[[t:7]], and this faculty he (Adam) possessed perfectly and completely; but the [[t:8]]ugly[[t:9]] and the [[t:10]]beautiful[[t:11]] exist in (matters of) [[t:12]]probable opinions[[t:13]], and not in (things that are) [[t:14]]intelligible[[t:15]][[fn:71]]; for one does not say that this proposition: [[t:16]]the heaven is spherical[[t:17]], is beautiful, nor that this other: [[t:18]]the earth is flat[[t:19]], is ugly; but one calls the one [[t:20]]true[[t:21]] and the other [[t:22]]false[[t:23]]. Thus in our language we employ (in speaking of) the [[t:24]]true[[t:25]] and the [[t:26]]false[[t:27]] (the words) [[t:28]]אמת[[t:29]] and [[t:30]]שקר[[t:31]], and for [[t:32]]beautiful[[t:33]] and [[t:34]]ugly[[t:35]] (we say) [[t:36]]טוב[[t:37]] and [[t:38]]רע[[t:39]]. By reason, therefore, man distinguishes the [[t:40]]true[[t:41]] from the [[t:42]]false[[t:43]], and this takes place in all (things that are) intelligible. When, therefore, he (Adam) was still in his most perfect and complete state, having only his primitive nature and his intelligible notions, on account of which it was said of him: [[t:44]]And You have made him a little lower than the angels[[t:45]] (Psalm),
root.text.Part 1..1.4.sub_1: 8, 6), there was in him no faculty that applied to the [[t:54]]probable opinions[[t:55]] in any way, and he did not even understand them; so that what is most manifestly base with regard to the [[t:56]]probable opinions[[t:57]], that is to say, to discover the shameful parts, was not base to him, and he did not even understand its baseness. But when, disobeying, he inclined towards his desires coming from the imaginative and towards the bodily pleasures of his senses, as it is said (in Scripture): … [[t:58]]That the tree was good to eat and that it was a pleasure for the eyes[[t:59]] (Genesis, 3, 6), he was punished by the privation of this intellectual understanding; that is why he transgressed[[fn:72]] the order that had been given to him because of his reason, and, having obtained the knowledge of the [[t:60]]probable opinions[[t:61]], he was absorbed by what he had to find base or beautiful, and he then knew what the thing was worth that had escaped him and of which he had been deprived, and in what state he had fallen. That is why it has been said: [[t:62]]And you will be like Élohîm knowing good and evil[[t:63]] ([[t:64]]Ibid.[[t:65]], 3, 5), and it has not been said: knowing the [[t:66]]false[[t:67]] and the [[t:68]]true[[t:69]], or: understanding the [[t:70]]false[[t:71]] and the [[t:72]]true;[[t:73]] whereas in the (domain of the) [[t:74]]necessary[[t:75]][[fn:73]] there is not at all good or evil, but false and true. — Consider also these words: [[t:76]]And the eyes of both of them were opened and they[[t:77]] [[t:78]]RECOGNIZED[[t:79]] [[t:80]]that they were naked[[t:81]] ([[t:82]]Ibid.[[t:83]], 3, 7). It is not said: And the eyes of both of them were opened and they [[t:84]]saw;[[t:85]] for what (man) had [[t:86]]seen[[t:87]] before, he also [[t:88]]saw[[t:89]] after. It is not that there was a veil on the eye that was then removed; but he underwent another state in which he found base what he had not found base before.
root.text.Part 1..1.5: Know that this word, that is to say [[t:0]]פקח[[t:1]], is used absolutely only in the sense of: [[t:2]]opening the moral view[[t:3]] (and not) of the rebirth of the sense of sight; for example: [[t:4]]And God opened his eyes[[t:5]] (Genesis, 21, 19); [[t:6]]Then the eyes of the blind will be opened[[t:7]] (Isaiah, 35, 5); [[t:8]]The ears opened they do not hear[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]Ibid.[[t:11]], 42, 20), which resembles these words: [[t:12]]Those who have eyes to see and do not see[[t:13]] (Ezekiel, 12, 2).
root.text.Part 1..1.6: As for what is said of Adam: [[t:0]]When he changed his[[t:1]] face [[t:2]]you sent him away[[t:3]] (Job, 14, 20)[[fn:74]], it must be interpreted and commented thus: "When he changed his [[t:4]]direction[[t:5]] he was expelled"; for [[t:6]]פנים[[t:7]] (face, visage) is a noun derived from [[t:8]]פנה[[t:9]] (to turn), because man directs himself with his face towards the thing he wishes to attain. It is said, therefore: When he changed his direction and turned towards the thing towards which he had been previously forbidden to turn, he was expelled from paradise. And this was a punishment similar to his disobedience, [[t:10]]measure for measure[[t:11]][[fn:75]]; for he had been permitted to eat pleasant things and to delight in rest and tranquillity; but having become avid, having followed his pleasures and his imagination, as we have said, and having eaten what had been forbidden to him, he was deprived of all and forced to eat the vilest of foods and that which had not previously served him as nourishment, (and this) with great toil and fatigue, as Scripture says: [[t:12]]It shall bring forth thorns and thistles, etc., by the sweat of thy brow, etc.[[t:13]] (Genesis, 3, 18, 19), and then it is clearly said: [[t:14]]And the Lord God sent him forth from the paradise to till the earth[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]Ibid.[[t:17]], [[t:18]]V[[t:19]]. 23). And He made him similar to the animals in his food and in most circumstances, as Scripture says: [[t:20]]And thou shalt eat the herb of the field[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]Ibid.[[t:23]], [[t:24]]V[[t:25]]. 18). And as if to explain this passage (the psalmist) has said: Man shall not abide in his dignity, and he was made similar to the dumb beasts (Ps. 49, 13).
root.text.Part 1..1.7: —Praise be to the Master of this will whose ultimate term and wisdom cannot be comprehended.
root.text.Part 1..2.0: One imagines that the meaning of [[t:0]]temounâ[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]תמונה[[t:3]]) and of [[t:4]]tabnîth[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]תבנית[[t:7]]) in the Hebrew language is the same; but such is not the case. [[t:8]]Tabnîth[[t:9]] is a noun derived from [[t:10]]בנה[[t:11]] (to build) and signifies the [[t:12]]structure[[t:13]] of a thing and its form, i.e., its figure, such as, for example, a square, circular, triangular figure, etc. It is said, for example: [[t:14]]The figure[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]תבנית[[t:17]]) [[t:18]]of the tabernacle and the figure[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]תבנית[[t:21]]) [[t:22]]of all its vessels[[t:23]] (Exod., 25, 9), and it is said again: [[t:24]]According to their figure[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]כתבניתם[[t:27]]) [[t:28]]which was shown thee on the mount[[t:29]] ([[t:30]]Ibid.[[t:31]], [[t:32]]V[[t:33]]. 40); [[t:34]]The figure[[t:35]] ([[t:36]]תבנית[[t:37]]) [[t:38]]of every bird[[t:39]] (Deut., 4, 17); [[t:40]]The figure[[t:41]] ([[t:42]]תבנית[[t:43]]) [[t:44]]of a hand[[t:45]] (Ezek., 8, 3); [[t:46]]The figure[[t:47]] ([[t:48]]תבנית[[t:49]]) [[t:50]]of the porch[[t:51]] (I Chron., 28, 11). All this is a [[t:52]]figure[[t:53]] ([[t:54]]visible[[t:55]]); this is why the Hebrew language does not employ this kind of expression in descriptions that relate to God,intellect and faculty being distinct from form and matter.
root.text.Part 1..2.1: As for [[t:0]]temounâ[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]תמונה[[t:3]]), it is a term employed amphibologically[[fn:76]] in three distinct senses. Firstly, it refers to the form of an object perceived by the senses independently of the mind—that is to say, its shape and its lineaments; and this is the sense of the words: [[t:4]]….. and that ye make a graven image of the figure[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]תמונת[[t:7]]) [[t:8]]of any thing whatsoever, etc.[[t:9]] (Deuteronomy, 4, 25); [[t:10]]For ye saw no manner of similitude[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]תמונה[[t:13]]) ([[t:14]]Ibid.[[t:15]], [[t:16]]v.[[t:17]] 15). Secondly, it denotes the imaginary figure which an object, having withdrawn from the senses, leaves in the imagination, as in this passage: [[t:18]]In thoughts[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]nées[[t:21]]) [[t:22]]from the visions of the night, etc.[[t:23]] (Job, 4, 13 et seq.), which concludes with these words: [[t:24]]It stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof: a figure[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]תמונה[[t:27]]) [[t:28]]was before mine eyes[[t:29]]; that is to say, there was a phantasm before mine eyes in slumber. Finally, thirdly, it signifies the true idea (of a thing) perceived by the intellect; and it is in this third sense that [[t:30]]temounâ[[t:31]] is employed when speaking of God; for example: [[t:32]]And he beholds the similitude[[t:33]] ([[t:34]]תמונת[[t:35]]) [[t:36]]of the LORD[[t:37]] (Numbers, 12, 8), which must be explicated in this wise: [[t:38]]And he comprehends God in His reality[[t:39]].
root.text.Part 1..3.0: Be aware that the three verbs [[t:0]]raâ[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]ראה[[t:3]]), [[t:4]]hibbît[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]הביט[[t:7]]), and [[t:8]]’[[t:9]]hazâ[[t:10]] ([[t:11]]הזה[[t:11]]) are applied to the vision of the eye; however, they are all employed metaphorically for the perception of the intellect.
root.text.Part 1..3.1: With regard to [[t:0]]raâ[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]ראה[[t:3]]), this is well-known to everyone. It is said, for example: [[t:4]]And he saw[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]וירא[[t:7]]), [[t:8]]and behold, there was a well in the field[[t:9]] (Genesis, 29, 2), where it concerns the vision of the eye; however, in these words: [[t:12]]And my heart saw[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]ראה[[t:15]]) [[t:16]]much wisdom and knowledge[[t:17]] (Ecclesiastes, 1, 16), it concerns an intellect perception.
root.text.Part 1..3.2: It is in this metaphorical sense that the verb [[t:0]]raâ[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]ראה[[t:3]]) must be understood whenever it is applied to God, as for example in these passages: [[t:4]]I[[t:5]] [[t:6]]saw[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]ראיתי[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]the Lord[[t:11]] (I Kings, 22, 19); [[t:12]]And the Lord appeared[[t:13]] [[t:14]]to him[[t:15]] (Genesis, 18, 1); [[t:16]]And God [[t:17]] [[t:18]]saw[[t:19]] [[t:20]]that it was good[[t:21]] (Genesis, 1, [[t:22]]passim[[t:23]]); [[t:24]]Show me[[t:25]] [[t:26]]thy glory[[t:27]] (Exodus, 33, 18); [[t:28]]And they [[t:29]] [[t:30]]saw[[t:31]] [[t:32]]the God of Israel[[t:33]] ([[t:34]]Ibid.[[t:35]], 24, 10). In all these instances, it is a matter of intellectual perception, and not at all of the vision of the eye; for the eyes only perceive (what is) corporeal and (only) from a certain side[[fn:77]], and with this, some accidents of the body, such as its colours, its geometric figure, etc., and God, on His part, does not perceive by means of an instrument, as will be explained (later).
root.text.Part 1..3.3: Similarly, [[t:0]]hibbît[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]הביט[[t:3]]) is used in the sense of: [[t:4]]looking[[t:5]] at a thing with the eye; for example: [[t:6]]Do not look[[t:7]] [[t:8]]אל תבט[[t:9]] [[t:10]]behind thee[[t:11]] (Genesis, 19, 17); [[t:12]]And his wife looked[[t:13]] [[t:14]]ותבט[[t:15]], [[t:16]]being behind him[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]Ibid.[[t:19]], [[t:20]]V[[t:21]]. 26); [[t:22]]And he shall look[[t:23]] [[t:24]]ונבט[[t:25]] [[t:26]]toward the earth[[t:27]] (Isaiah, 5, 30). But it is used metaphorically for theintuition of the mind approaching the consideration of a thing in order to understand it, as in this passage: [[t:28]]No iniquity is seen[[t:29]] [[t:30]]לא הביט[[t:31]] [[t:32]]in Jacob[[t:33]] (Numbers, 23, 21); for iniquity is not seen with the eye. It is the same with these words: [[t:34]]And they looked[[t:35]] [[t:36]]והביטו[[t:37]] [[t:38]]after Moses[[t:39]] (Exodus, 33, 8); for, according to what the doctors say, they express the same idea, and they state that they (the Israelites) were watching his actions and words and examining them[[fn:78]]. The words: [[t:40]]Look[[t:41]] [[t:42]]הבט[[t:43]] [[t:44]]toward the heaven[[t:45]] (Genesis, 15, 5), have the same meaning; for this took place in a prophetic vision. And (in general) the verb [[t:46]]הביט[[t:47]] (to look) has this metaphorical sense whenever it is applied to God; for example: … [[t:48]]to look[[t:49]] [[t:50]]מהביט[[t:51]] [[t:52]]toward God[[t:53]] (Exodus, 3, 6); [[t:54]]And he contemplates[[t:55]] [[t:56]]יביט[[t:57]] [[t:58]]the figure of God[[t:59]] (Numbers, 12, 8); [[t:60]]And thou canst not look[[t:61]] [[t:62]]והביט[[t:63]] [[t:64]]at iniquity[[t:65]] (Habakkuk, 1, 13).
root.text.Part 1..3.4: Similarly, ’[[t:0]]hazâ[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]חזה[[t:3]]) applies to the vision of the eye; for example: [[t:4]]And our eyes shall see[[t:5]] [[t:6]]ותחז[[t:7]] [[t:8]]the fall of Zion[[t:9]] (Micah, 4, 11); and it is used metaphorically for the perception of the heart, for example: … [[t:10]]he saw[[t:11]] [[t:12]]חזה[[t:13]] [[t:14]]upon Judah and Jerusalem[[t:15]] (Isaiah, 1, 1); … [[t:16]]the word of the Lord to Abram[[t:17]] [[t:18]]במחזה[[t:19]] [[t:20]]in a vision[[t:21]] (Genesis, 15, 1); and according to this metaphor it has been said: [[t:22]]And they saw[[t:23]] [[t:24]]ויחזו[[t:25]] [[t:26]]God[[t:27]] (Exodus, 24, 11). You must thoroughly understand this.
root.text.Part 1..4.0: The prince of philosophers[[fn:79]], in undertaking the investigation and demonstration of a most profound matter, expresses himself, by way of apology, in terms whose sense is: that the reader of his writings ought not to tax him with impudence or accuse him of speaking temerariously and precipitously on matters of which he is ignorant; but rather, he ought to perceive in him only the passion and zeal with which he is animated to produce and impart true opinions, in so far as this lies within the power of man.
root.text.Part 1..4.1: We say likewise that man ought not to approach this grave and important subject with precipitance, without having first exercised himself in the sciences and knowledge, and without having corrected his manners with the greatest care and slain his desires and passions dependent on the imaginativeimaginative faculty. It is only after having acquired the knowledge of true and certain axioms[[fn:80]], after having learned the rules of syllogism and demonstration, as well as the manner of preserving oneself from the errors of the intellect, that he will be able to undertake the investigation of this subject. He ought not to decide anything according to a first opinion that may occur to him, nor allow his thoughts to proceed directly, directing them resolutely towards the knowledge of God; but he ought to approach it with modesty and reserve, and pause occasionally, in order to advance gradually.
root.text.Part 1..4.2: It is in this sense that it was said: And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look upon God (Exodus 3:6)—where regard must also be had[[fn:81]] for what the literal sense indicates, namely, that he was afraid to look at the resplendent light (of the burning bush), not that the eyes could perceive the Divinity [may He be exalted and raised far above all imperfection!]. Moses earned praise for this, and the Most High bestowed His goodness and favor upon him to such an extent that it could later be said of him: And the figure of God he shall behold (Numbers 12:8); for the sages say that this was a reward for having initially hidden his face so as not to look upon God[[fn:82]].
root.text.Part 1..4.3: But as regards [[t:0]]the elect among the sons of Israel[[t:1]] (Exodus, 24, 11), they acted with precipitation, giving free rein to their thoughts; they perceived (the divinity), but in an imperfect manner. This is why it is said of them: [[t:2]]And they saw the God of Israel, and under His feet, etc.[[t:3]] ([[t:4]]Ibid.[[t:5]], [[t:6]]V[[t:7]]. 10), and one does not simply say: [[t:8]]And they saw the God of Israel;[[t:9]] for the entire phrase has no other purpose than to criticise their [[t:10]]vision[[t:11]], and not to describe how they had seen. Thus, one has only criticised the form under which they had perceived (God) and which was tainted with corporeality, which was the necessary result of the precipitation they had shown before perfecting themselves. They had deserved destruction[[fn:83]]; but Moses having interceded for them, they were granted a reprieve until they were burned at Tab’érâ and Nadab and Abihou were burned in the [[t:12]]tent of meeting[[t:13]], as reported by the true tradition[[fn:84]].
root.text.Part 1..4.4: If this was the case with them, all the more reason that inferior men like us and those below us should first strive to occupy themselves with the perfection of their preparatory knowledge and acquire preliminary principles that can purify the understanding of its stain, which consists in errors, and then they can advance[[fn:85]] to contemplate the holy divine majesty; for: [[t:0]]The priests also who approach the Lord shall sanctify themselves, lest the Lord break out among them[[t:1]] (Exodus, 19, 22). Already Solomon has recommended the greatest caution to the man who desires to attain the degree in question; and, using an image, he has given this warning: [[t:2]]Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God[[t:3]] (Ecclesiastes, 4, 17)..
root.text.Part 1..4.5: I now return to complete what I had begun to explain, and I say that, [[t:0]]the elect among the sons of Israel[[t:1]] having made mistakes in their perception, their actions also were troubled by it, and they inclined towards corporeal things, through the vice of their perception; this is why (the Scripture) says: [[t:2]]And they saw God, and they ate and drank[[t:3]] (Exodus, 24, 11)[[fn:86]].— As for the end of the verse (cited above)[[fn:87]], I mean the words: [[t:4]]And under His feet there was as it were a work of the splendour of the sapphire, etc.[[t:5]], it will be explained in a few chapters of this treatise[[fn:88]].
root.text.Part 1..4.6: In short, we have as our aim to establish that each time the verb [[t:0]]ראה[[t:1]], or [[t:2]]חזה[[t:3]], or [[t:4]]הביט[[t:5]], is employed in the sense in question, it pertains to an intellectual perception, and not to the vision of the eye; for the Most High is not a being that eyes can perceive.
root.text.Part 1..4.7: If, however, there be such a narrow-minded man who does not wish to attain to the degree to which we desire to ascend, and who admits that all these words, employed in the sense in question, indicate the sensible perception of certain created lights [[t:0]]créées[[t:1]], whether angels or something else, there is no harm in this.
root.text.Part 1..5.0: [[t:0]]Isch[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]איש[[t:3]]) and [[t:4]]ischâ[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]אשה[[t:7]]) are names originally employed to denoteman andwoman, and subsequently borrowed to signify the male and female of all other species of animals. It has been said, for example: [[t:12]]Of all the clean quadrupeds thou shalt take seven couples[[t:13]], [[t:14]]איש ואשתו[[t:15]], [[t:16]]themale and hisfemale [[t:17]] (Genesis, 7, 2); it is as if it had been said, the male and the female. Subsequently, the name of [[t:22]]ischâ[[t:23]] has been employed metaphorically for anything destined and ready to be joined to another thing; for example: [[t:24]]The five curtains shall be joined[[t:25]] [[t:26]]אשה אל אחותה[[t:27]] [[t:28]]one to another[[t:29]] (Exodus, 26, 3)[[fn:89]].
root.text.Part 1..5.1: It is clear from this that [[t:0]]אחות[[t:1]] (sister) and [[t:2]]אח[[t:3]] (brother) also, with regard to the figurative sense[[fn:90]], are employed as homonyms, similar to [[t:4]]איש[[t:5]] and [[t:6]]אשה[[t:7]].
root.text.Part 1..6.0: [[t:0]]Yalad[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]ילד[[t:3]]). — What is understood by this word is known; it signifies to beget; e.g.: [[t:4]]And they shall have begotten[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]וילדו[[t:7]]) [[t:8]]sons[[t:9]] (Deuteronomy, 21:15). Subsequently, this word was employed figuratively for the production of natural things; e.g.: [[t:10]]Before the mountains were brought forth[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]ילדו[[t:13]]) (Psalm 90:2), and it was also used in the sense of to cause to sprout, (speaking of) what the earth causes to sprout, by comparison with begetting; e.g.: … [[t:14]]that she has made it germinate[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]והולידה[[t:17]]) [[t:18]]and has caused it to sprout[[t:19]] (Isaiah, 55:10). It was also applied to the events of time, as if they were things that are born; e.g.: [[t:20]]For thou knowest not what the day shall bring forth[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]ילד[[t:23]]) [[t:24]]the day[[t:25]] (Proverbs, 17:1). Finally, it was applied to what occurs in thoughts and to what they produce in terms of ideas and opinions, as it was said: [[t:26]]And he shall bring forth[[t:27]] ([[t:28]]וילד[[t:29]]) [[t:30]]a lie[[t:31]] (Psalm 7:15), and it is in this sense that it was said: [[t:32]]And they are content with the children[[t:33]] ([[t:34]]בילדי[[t:35]]) [[t:36]]of strangers[[t:37]] (Isaiah, 2:6), that is to say, they are content[[fn:91]] with their opinions, as Jonathan ben-Usiel said in the version of this passage: [[t:38]]And they follow the laws of the nations.[[t:39]]
root.text.Part 1..6.1: It is in this same sense that one who has taught something to a person and has given him an idea can be considered as having begotten that person, being himself the author of that idea; and it is in this sense also that the disciples of the prophets were called [[t:0]]בני הנביאים[[t:1]], [[t:2]]sons of the prophets[[t:3]], as we shall explain when speaking of the homonymy of the substantive [[t:4]]בן[[t:5]], [[t:6]]son[[t:7]][[fn:92]].
root.text.Part 1..6.2: It is according to this metaphor that it has been said of Adam: [[t:0]]And Adam lived a hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image[[t:1]] (Genesis, 5, 3); for it has already been stated previously[[fn:93]] what is meant by [[t:2]]the image[[t:3]] of Adam and [[t:4]]his likeness[[t:5]]. This is because all the children he had previously did not possess (what constitutes) the human form in reality, which is called [[t:6]]the image[[t:7]] of Adam and [[t:8]]his likeness[[t:9]], and with regard to which it is said (that he was created) [[t:10]]in the image of God and after his likeness[[t:11]]. But with regard to [[t:12]]Seth[[t:13]], (Adam) having instructed him and given him understanding, so that he arrived at human perfection, it has been said of him: [[t:14]]And he[[t:15]] (Adam) [[t:16]]begat a son in his own likeness, after his image[[t:17]]. You know that whoever has not obtained this [[t:18]]form[[t:19]] which we have explained is not a man, but an animal having the figure of a man and his lineaments; but he has the faculty that other animals do not possess, of doing all sorts of harm and producing evils. For the reflection and thought which, in him, were intended to enable him to obtain a perfection he has not obtained, he employs in all sorts of cunning producing evils and giving rise to harm; he is, therefore, as it were, something that resembles a man or counterfeits him. Such were the sons of Adam prior to [[t:20]]Seth;[[t:21]] this is why it has been said in the [[t:22]]Midrash[[t:23]][[fn:94]]: 'Adam, during the hundred and thirty years he was reproved, begat [[t:24]]spirits[[t:25]]', that is to say, [[t:26]]demons;[[t:27]] but when he had obtained his grace, he begat his like, that is to say, [[t:28]]in his likeness, after his image[[t:29]]. This is what is expressed by these words: [[t:30]]And Adam lived a hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image[[t:31]].
root.text.Part 1..7.0: Makôm (מקום). — This name is applied primarily to a particular and common place[[fn:95]]; subsequently, the language extended its usage and made it a term designating the degree and rank of a person, I mean their perfection in any matter whatsoever, such that one says: So-and-so is in such a place (מקום) in such a thing (that is, having reached such a degree). You are familiar with the frequent usage made of it in our language when saying: To fill the place (מקום) of his fathers, e.g.: "He filled the place of his fathers in science or in piety," and further saying: "The discussion remains in the same place," that is, at the same degree. It is by this type of metaphor that it was said: Blessed be the glory of the Eternal from His place (Ezek. 3:12), that is to say, according to the elevated rank He occupies in the universe[[fn:96]]. Likewise, whenever the word מקום (place) is used in reference to God, it signifies nothing other than the rank of His existence, which has no equal or likeness, as will be demonstrated.
root.text.Part 1..7.1: Know that whenever we explain, in this treatise, the homonymy of a certain name, we do not have as our sole purpose to draw attention to what we mention in the chapter itself, but we wish to open a door and draw your attention to the various meanings of the name in question, which are useful with regard to our purpose, and not with regard to the purpose of those who speak any common language[[fn:97]]. It is for you to examine the prophetic books and the other books composed by the wise, to consider all the names that are employed in them, and to take each homonymous name in one of the senses that may suit it with regard to the discourse (in which it is found). What we have just said is the key to this treatise and others (of our writings).
