root.text.Part 1..7.2: Thus, e.g., (considering) the explanation we have given here of the meaning of [[t:0]]makôm[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]מקום[[t:3]]) in the passage: [[t:4]]Let the glory of the Eternal be praised in His place[[t:5]], you will know that this same meaning is that of [[t:6]]makôm[[t:7]] in the passage: [[t:8]]Behold, a place[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]מקום[[t:11]]) [[t:12]]beside me[[t:13]] (Exodus, 33, 21), that is to say, a degree of speculation, of penetration by means of the intellect, and not of penetration by means of the eye, having regard at the same time to [[t:14]]the spot[[t:15]] on the mountain to which allusion is made and where the isolation (of Moses) took place to attain perfection.
root.text.Part 1..8.0: [[t:0]]Kissé[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]כסא[[t:3]]) is primitively employed in the language (Hebrew) as the name of the [[t:4]]throne;[[t:5]] and, as the throne is occupied only by people of distinction and greatness, such as kings, and, consequently, it is a visible thing[[fn:98]], indicating the greatness of him who has been deemed worthy of it, his distinction and lofty position, the sanctuary has been called [[t:6]]Kissé[[t:7]] (throne), because it indicates the greatness of Him who has manifested Himself therein and who has caused His light and glory to descend upon it. Thus (the prophet) said: [[t:8]]A throne of glory, exalted, from the beginning, etc.[[t:9]] (Jeremiah, 17, 12). It is also in the same sense that the heaven has been called [[t:10]]Kissé[[t:11]] (throne); for him who knows[[fn:99]] and contemplates it, it indicates the greatness of Him who has brought it into existence, who sets it in motion, and who, by the good that emanates from it, governs the lower world. One reads, e.g.: [[t:12]]Thus says the Eternal, the heaven is my throne[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]כסאי[[t:15]]), [[t:16]]etc.[[t:17]] (Isaiah, 66, 1), that is to say, it indicates my existence, my greatness, and my power, just as the throne indicates the greatness of him who has been deemed worthy of it[[fn:100]].
root.text.Part 1..8.1: This is what those who seek the truth must believe, and not that there is a body upon which God rises; — how elevated (above such a thought) He is!—For it will be demonstrated to you that the Most High is incorporeal, and how could He take a place or rest upon a body? But the matter is as we have noted, namely, that every place which God has ennobled and distinguished by His light and radiance, such as the sanctuary or the heaven, is called [[t:0]]Kissé[[t:1]] (throne).
root.text.Part 1..8.2: If the language has extended the usage of this word by saying: [[t:0]]Car la main[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]est placée[[t:3]]) [[t:4]]sur le trône[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]כם[[t:7]]) [[t:8]]de Dieu[[t:9]] (Exodus, 17, 16)[[fn:101]], it is still a qualification of His grandeur and majesty, a thing that must not be represented as being outside of His essence, nor as one of His creatures, so that God would exist at one time without the throne and at another time with the throne. This would, without a doubt, be an impious belief; for (the prophet) has said clearly: [[t:10]]Toi, Éternel, tu résides éternellement, ton trône[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]reste[[t:13]]) [[t:14]]de génération en génération[[t:15]] (Lamentations, 5, 19), which indicates that (the throne) is a thing inseparable from Him. Thus, in this passage and in all the others similar to it, one wants to designate by [[t:16]]כםא[[t:17]] (throne) the majesty and grandeur of God, which are not something outside of His essence, as will be explained in a few chapters of this treatise[[fn:102]].
root.text.Part 1..9.0: We have already stated that every time we speak, in this treatise, of one of the homonymous names, our intention is not to mention all the senses in which this name is employed, — for this is not a treatise on language; — but we mention those of the various senses which we require for our purpose, nothing more.
root.text.Part 1..9.1: Among these words (homonyms) are [[t:0]]yarad[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]ירד[[t:3]]) and [[t:4]]’alâ[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]עלה[[t:7]]); for these two words are used in the Hebrew language in the sense ofdescendere andascendere. When a body is transported from one place to another lower, one says [[t:8]]ירד[[t:9]] (descendere), and when it is transported from one place to another higher than that one[[fn:103]], one says [[t:10]]עלה[[t:11]] (ascendere). Then these two words have been applied metaphorically to illustration and grandeur; so that, when a man's rank has been lowered, one says [[t:12]]ירד[[t:13]] (descendere), and when his rank has been elevated in illustration, one says [[t:14]]עלה[[t:15]] (ascendere). This is how the Most High has said: [[t:16]]The stranger who is in your midst willascendere[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]יעלה[[t:19]]) [[t:20]]higher and higher above you, and you willdescendere[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]תרד[[t:23]]) [[t:24]]lower and lower[[t:25]] (Deuteronomy, 28, 43). It has also been said (using derivatives of [[t:26]]עלה[[t:27]]): [[t:28]]And the Lord your God will place you above[[t:29]] ([[t:30]]עליון[[t:31]]) [[t:32]]all the nations of the earth[[t:33]] ([[t:34]]Ibid.[[t:35]], [[t:36]]V[[t:37]]. 1); and elsewhere: [[t:38]]And the Lord elevated Solomon very high[[t:39]] ([[t:40]]למעלה[[t:41]]) (I Chronicles, 29, 25). You also know that the doctors often use this expression: «One must makeascendere the sacred things, but not make themdescendere»[[fn:104]].
root.text.Part 1..9.2: One still expresses oneself in the same manner (when speaking of thought): when the reflection of man is lowered and his thought turns towards a very vile thing, one says that [[t:0]]he has descended[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]ירד[[t:3]]), and likewise when his thought turns towards something elevated and sublime, one says: [[t:4]]he has ascended[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]עלה[[t:7]]) [[t:8]][[fn:105]][[t:9]].
root.text.Part 1..9.3: Now, as we find ourselves, we men, in the most inferior place of creation and at the lowest degree in relation to the surrounding sphere[[fn:106]], whilst God is at the highest degree by the reality of existence, majesty, and grandeur, and not by an elevation of place, —the Most High, having wished to bring forth from Himself knowledge and to cause revelation to emanate upon some amongst us, employed, when speaking of the revelation descending upon the prophet and of the entrance of divine majesty into a place, the expression of [[t:0]]descending[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]ירד[[t:3]]); and, when speaking of the cessation of this state of prophetic inspiration in an individual or of the divine majesty withdrawing from a place, He employed the expression of [[t:4]]ascending[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]עלה[[t:7]]).
root.text.Part 1..9.4: Thus, whenever you find the expressions of [[t:0]]descending[[t:1]] and of [[t:2]]ascending[[t:3]] relating to the Creator, they can only be taken in the aforementioned signification.
root.text.Part 1..9.5: Similarly, when it comes to the arrival of a catastrophe in a nation or in a country, due to the eternal will of God,—where the prophetic books, before describing this calamity, first say that God, after having visited the actions of these people, sent down upon them the punishment,—the expressiondescendere to descend is also employed for this purpose;[[t:0]]descendre;[[t:1]] for man is too insignificant for his actions to be visited, so that he might suffer the penalty, were it not for the will (of God)[[fn:107]]. root.text.Part 1..9.6: Thus, (I say) the expressiondescendere to descend has been employed in this regard;[[t:0]]descendre;[[t:1]] e.g.: [[t:2]]Come, let us go down[[t:3]] ([[t:4]]נרדה[[t:5]]) [[t:6]]and confound their language[[t:7]] (Genesis, 11, 7); [[t:8]]And God went down[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]וירד[[t:11]]) [[t:12]]to see[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]Ibid.[[t:15]], [[t:16]]V[[t:17]]. 5); [[t:18]]I will go down[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]ארדה[[t:21]]) [[t:22]]and see[[t:23]] ([[t:24]]Ibid.[[t:25]], 18, 21). root.text.Part 1..10.1: It is in this latter sense that it has been said of God: [[t:0]]Thou, O Lord, dost reside[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]תשב[[t:3]]) [[t:4]]eternally[[t:5]] (Lament., 5, 19); [[t:6]]Thou who residest[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]היושבי[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]in heaven[[t:11]] (Ps. 123, 1); [[t:12]]He who resids[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]יושב[[t:15]]) [[t:16]]in heaven[[t:17]] (Ps. 2, 4), that is to say, He who is perpetual and stable, and who is not subject to any species of change, neither change of essence, nor change with respect to any state which would be outside of His essence, nor, finally, change with respect to His relation with anything else; for there is no relation between Him and other things such that He could suffer a change in this relation, as shall be explained[[fn:111]]. root.text.Part 1..10.2: But in the majority of passages, he is only associated with the heavens, because the heavens are a thing in which there is neither change nor variation, I mean to say that their individuals [[fn:113]] are not subject to change, as are the individuals in earthly things which are born and perish [[fn:114]].

root.text.Part 1..10.4: and it has been said again: [[t:0]]The Lord was seated[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]ישב[[t:3]]) [[t:4]]at the flood[[t:5]] (Ps. 29, 10), that is to say, when the things of the earth changed and perished, there was no change in God's relation, but this relation that He has with the thing[[fn:117]], whether it is born or perishes, is a single stable and fixed relation; for it is a relation to the species of beings, and not to their individuals. root.text.Part 1..13.0: As for the homonymy of the word Adam (אדם), it is primarily the name of the first man, a derived name[[fn:125]] which, according to the text (of Scripture), comes from adamâ (אדמה, earth)[[fn:126]]; subsequently, it is the name of the species; e.g.: My spirit shall not always strive with man (באדם) (Genesis 6:3); Who knows if the spirit of the sons of man (בני האדם), etc. (Ecclesiastes 3:21); The advantage of man (האדם) over the beast is nothing (Ibid., v. 19). root.text.Part 1..14.3: It is clear, furthermore, that, if I say here [[t:0]]above it[[t:1]], it is with respect to the allegory that has been employed [[fn:130]]. root.text.Part 1..16.0: One must not believe that it is of metaphysical science alone that one has been niggardly[[fn:138]] towards the common people, for it has been the same with the greater part of physical science[[fn:139]], and we have already cited on several occasions these words: 'Nor (shall one expound) the [[t:0]]Ma’asé beréschîth[[t:1]] before two persons'[[fn:140]]. This (was done) not only among theologians[[fn:141]], but also among philosophers; and the pagan sages of antiquity expressed themselves on the principles of things in an obscure and enigmatic manner. Thus,Plato et alii Plato and others before him called matter the [[t:2]]feminine[[t:3]], and form the [[t:4]]masculine[[t:5]][[fn:142]].
root.text.Part 1..16.1: [You know that the principles of beings that are born and perish are three in number:materia, forma, et privatio matter, form, and particular privation [[t:0]]particular[[t:1]][[fn:143]], which is always joined to matter; for, if the latter were not accompanied by privation, it would not be affected by form, and in this manner privation is one of the principles. When form arrives, this privation (particular), I mean the privation of this form that has arrived, ceases, and another privation is joined (to matter), and so on, as is explained in physics[[fn:144]].]
root.text.Part 1..16.2: If, therefore, those who had nothing to lose by explaining themselves clearly, made use, in their teaching, of figurative names and employed images, with greater reason must we, men of religion, avoid stating clearly things the intellect of which is difficult [[fn:145]] for the common people, or (with regard to which) they imagine the truth in a sense contrary to that which we have in view [[fn:146]]. One must also imbue oneself with this notion.

root.text.Part 1..17.1: — The second meaning of these three words expresses a union through knowledge, a drawing near through perception, and not a local drawing near. [[t:0]]Naga’[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]נגע[[t:3]]) was used in the sense of [[t:4]]union through knowledge[[t:5]] when it was said: [[t:6]]For his judgment has touched[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]נגע[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]up to heaven[[t:11]][[fn:147]] (Jeremiah, 51, 9). root.text.Part 1..17.2: Every time one encounters in prophetic books the expression of [[t:0]]karab[[t:1]] or of [[t:2]]nagasch[[t:3]] (applying to a relation) between God and any creature whatsoever, it is always in the latter sense; for God is not a body, as will be demonstrated in this treatise, and therefore the Most High does not approach anything, nor does He draw near to anything, and nothing draws near to Him nor does He approach anything; for, by excluding corporeality, one excludes space, and it is not a question of proximity, access, distance, union, separation, contact, or succession.
root.text.Part 1..17.3: I do not think thou hast any doubt (in this regard), and there shall be nothing obscure to thee in these passages: [[t:0]]The Lord is near to all who call upon Him[[t:1]] (Ps. 145, 18); [[t:2]]They desire to draw near to God[[t:3]] (Isaiah, 58, 2); [[t:4]]To draw near to God is my happiness[[t:5]] (Ps. 73, 28); for in all these passages it is a matter of drawing near through knowledge, that is to say, through scientific perception, and not through local approach. It is the same in these passages: ([[t:6]]God[[t:7]]) [[t:8]]near to Him[[t:9]] (Deuteronomy, 4, 7); [[t:10]]Draw near and hearken[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]Ibid.[[t:13]], 5, 27); [[t:14]]And Moses shall approach alone unto the Lord, but they shall not approach[[t:15]] (Exodus, 24, 2).
root.text.Part 1..17.4: However, if thou desirest to understand by the word [[t:0]]ונגש[[t:1]], [[t:2]]shall approach[[t:3]], applied to Moses, that he could approach that place on the mountain where the light descended, that is to say, [[t:4]]the glory of the Lord[[t:5]], thou art at liberty to do so; only thou must adhere to this principle, that no matter whether the individual be in the centre of the earth or at the summit of the ninth sphere[[fn:149]], — if this were possible, — he is not thereby farther from God, and there he is not nearer to Him; but one is near to God in perceiving Him, and he who ignores Him is far from Him. There is, in this regard, a great variety of gradations[[fn:150]] in approach and withdrawal; in one of the chapters of this treatise[[fn:151]] I shall explain what this relative superiority is in the perception (of the divinity).
root.text.Part 1..17.5: — As for these words: [[t:0]]Touche les montagnes, et qu’elles fument[[t:1]] (Ps. 144, 5), one intends to convey thereby; Cause thy command to reach them (which, in turn, is to be understood) metaphorically; likewise the words: [[t:2]]Et touche sa personne[[t:3]] (Job, 2, 5) signify: Cause thy affliction to descend upon him.
root.text.Part 1..17.6: Thus, in each passage, thou must consider the verb [[t:0]]נגע[[t:1]] (to touch), as well as its derived forms, in accordance with the entirety: one expresses by this verb, at times, the contact of one body with another, and, at times, the union through the science and perception of something; for he who perceives the thing he had not previously perceived, as it were, approaches a thing that was distant from him. This must be well understood.

root.text.Part 1..18.1: — It is in this sense that it has been said: [[t:0]]The whole earth is full of His glory[[t:1]] (Isaiah, 6, 3), which signifies: The whole earth bears witness to His perfection, that is to say, it shows Him (everywhere). root.text.Part 1..19.0: [[t:0]]Râm[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]רם[[t:3]]) is a homonym to designate the [[t:4]]elevation[[t:5]] of the place, as well as the elevation of rank, I mean the majesty, nobility, and power; one reads, for example: [[t:6]]And the ark[[t:7]][[fn:154]] [[t:8]]rose[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]ותרם[[t:11]]) [[t:12]]above the earth[[t:13]] (Genesis, 7, 17), which is in the first sense; in the second sense, one reads, for example: [[t:14]]I have exalted[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]הרימותי[[t:17]]) [[t:18]]the chosen one among the people[[t:19]] (Psalm 89, 20); [[t:20]]For I have exalted[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]הרימותיך[[t:23]]) [[t:24]]from the dust[[t:25]] (1 Kings, 16, 2)[[fn:155]]; [[t:26]]For I have exalted[[t:27]] ([[t:28]]הרימותיך[[t:29]]) [[t:30]]from the midst of the people[[t:31]] ([[t:32]]Ibid.[[t:33]], 14, 7).
root.text.Part 1..19.1: Every time the verb [[t:0]]râm[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]רם[[t:3]]) is applied to God, it is taken in this second sense; for example: [[t:4]]Rise[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]רומה[[t:7]]) [[t:8]]above the heavens, O God[[t:9]] (Psalm 57, 6).

root.text.Part 1..19.4: Perhaps thou shalt find a difficulty in what I say: [[t:0]]elevation of rank, majesty, and power[[t:1]]; how, thou wilt ask me, canst thou attach several ideas to one and the same sense[[fn:158]]? root.text.Part 1..19.5: You will have further chapters on the names and attributes (of God); the purpose of the present chapter is solely (to demonstrate) that the words [[t:0]]râm[[t:1]] ([Lat.: 'ram'] [[t:2]]רם[[t:3]]) and [[t:4]]nissa[[t:5]] ([Lat.: 'nasa'] [[t:6]]נשׂא[[t:7]]) (applied to God) must be understood in the sense, not of a [[t:8]]local elevation[[t:9]], but of a [[t:10]]elevation of rank[[t:11]].
root.text.Part 1..20.0: ’Abar (עבר) signifies primarily the same as the verb ’abara (عبر) in Arabic, and is predicated of a body which transports itself in space. It denots first[[fn:159]] the movement of a living creature at a certain direct distance; e.g.: And he passed over (עבר) before them (Genesis, 33, 3); Pass (עבֹר) before the people (Exodus, 17, 5); and such is frequent. Thenceforth it has been employed figuratively to express the propagation of sounds through the air; e.g.: They caused it to be proclaimed (ויעבירו קול) throughout the camp (Exodus, 36, 6); (The report) which I hear spreading (מעבירים) among the people of the Lord (I Sam., 2, 24).
root.text.Part 1..20.1: It has been further employed to designate the arrival of the light and the divine majesty which the prophets beheld in prophetic vision; e.g.: And behold a smoking furnace, and a burning lamp that passed (עבר) between those pieces (Genesis, 15, 17), which occurred in a prophetic vision; for it is said at the beginning of the narrative (v. 12): And a deep sleep fell upon Abram, etc. It is in accordance with this metaphor that we must understand these words: And I will pass (ועברתי) through the land of Egypt (Exodus, 12, 12), and all other similar passages.
root.text.Part 1..20.2: It is also used at times in speaking of one who, in performing any action, exceeds and overstepps the proper limit; e.g.: And like a man whom (עברו) wine has overcome[[fn:160]] (Jeremiah, 23, 9).
root.text.Part 1..20.3: Sometimes also it is employed in speaking of one who passes[[fn:161]] beyond a mark which he had in view, and directs himself toward another goal and another term; e.g.: And he shot the arrow to make it pass beyond (להעבירו) (I Sam., 20, 36). It is according to this figurative sense that one must, in my opinion, understand these words: And the Lord passed (ויעבר) before his face (Exodus, 34, 6), the pronoun in פניו, his face, referring to God. This is likewise what the Sages have admitted, to wit, that פניו (his face) referrs to God[[fn:162]]. Albeit they say this in a collection of haggadoth (or allegorical explanations) which would not be in their place here, there is nevertheless therein something which corroborats our opinion. Thus, the pronoun in פניו referring to God, the explanation of the passage in question is, as it seems to me, this: that Moses had requested a certain perception, namely, that which has been designated by the expression to see the face, in these words: But my face shall not be seen (Exodus, 34, 23), and that there was promised to him a perception inferior to that which he had requested, namely, that which has been designated by the expression to see the back, in these words: And thou shalt see my back (Ibid.). We have already called attention to this subject in the Mishneh Torah[[fn:163]]. It is intended here to be said[[fn:164]] that God veiled from him that perception designated by the word פנים, face, and caused him to pass toward another thing, I mean toward the knowledge of the actions attributed to God, which are taken for numerous attributes, as we shall explain[[fn:165]]. If I say: He veiled from him, I mean thereby that this perception is veiled and inaccessible by its very nature, and that every perfect man, whose intellect having attained that which it is in its nature to perceive, desirs thereafter another more profound perception[[fn:166]], ses his perception become blunted, or even lost[[fn:167]] [as shall be explained in one of the chapters of this treatise[[fn:168]]], unless he be assisted by divine aid, even as He has said: And I will cover thee with my hand until I have passed (Exodus, 33, 22).
root.text.Part 1..20.4: As for the Chaldaic paraphrase, it has here done what it habitually performs in such cases; for, whenever it encounters aught attributed to God which is tainted with corporality or with that which partakes of corporality, it presupposes the omission of [[t:0]]the annex[[t:1]][[fn:169]], and ascribes the relation to something understood as being [[t:2]]the annex[[t:3]] (of the name) of God[[fn:170]]. Thus, for instance, the paraphrast renders the words: [[t:4]]And, behold, the LORD standing above it[[t:5]] (Genesis, 28, 15) by these: "And, behold, [[t:6]]the glory of the LORD[[t:7]] standing ready above it;" the words: [[t:8]]The LORD watch between me and thee[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]Ibid.[[t:11]], 31, 49), he renders by these: "Let [[t:12]]the Word of the LORD[[t:13]] watch." Such is his constant method in his exposition; and he has done likewise in these words: [[t:14]]And the LORD passed before his face[[t:15]] (translating): "And the LORD [[t:16]]caused His Majesty to pass[[t:17]] before his face, and cried;" so that the thing which [[t:18]]passed[[t:19]] was, doubtless, in his estimation, something [[t:20]]created[[t:21]]. The pronoun in [[t:22]]פניו[[t:23]], [[t:24]]his face[[t:25]], is by him referred to Moses, our master, so that the words [[t:26]]על פניו[[t:27]] (before his face) signify [[t:28]]in his presence[[t:29]] (or [[t:30]]before him[[t:31]]), as in that passage: [[t:32]]And the present passed over before him[[t:33]] (Genesis, 32, 22), which is likewise a sound and plausible interpretation. That which confirms the explanation of Onkelos, the proselyte, are these words of Scripture: [[t:34]]And it shall come to pass, while My glory passes by[[t:35]], etc. (Exodus, 33, 22), where it is clearly stated that that which [[t:36]]passes by[[t:37]] is a thing [[t:38]]attributed[[t:39]] to God, and not [[t:40]]His essence[[t:41]] [glorified be His name!], and concerning this glory it might have been said by Him: [[t:42]]Until I be passed by[[t:43]] ([[t:44]]Ibid.[[t:45]]); [[t:46]]And the LORD passed before his face[[t:47]].
root.text.Part 1..20.5: But should it be deemed absolutely necessary to suppose an [[t:0]]adjunct[[t:1]] understood—as is ever the wont of Onkelos, who admitts as understood now [[t:2]]the Glory[[t:3]], now [[t:4]]the Shekhinâ[[t:5]] or [[t:6]]Majesty[[t:7]], and anon [[t:8]]the Word[[t:9]] (divine), according to that which befitts each passage—we likewise should admit here, as the adjunct understood, the word [[t:10]]קול[[t:11]], [[t:12]]voice[[t:13]], so that there would be virtually in the said passage: “And [[t:14]]the voice[[t:15]] of the Lord passed before him and cried.” We have already explained above that the Hebrew tongue employs the verb [[t:16]]עבר[[t:17]], [[t:18]]to pass[[t:19]], when speaking of the voice; as for example: They published (literally, [[t:20]]they caused a voice to pass[[t:21]]) [[t:22]]throughout the camp[[t:23]]. It would therefore be the [[t:24]]voice[[t:25]] which [[t:26]]cried;[[t:27]] nor shouldst thou find it improbable that the [[t:28]]cry[[t:29]] be attributed to the [[t:30]]voice[[t:31]], for the selfsame expressions are employed in speaking of the word of God addressed to Moses; e.g.: [[t:32]]And he heard the voice speaking unto him[[t:33]] (Numbers vii. 89); as therefore the verb [[t:34]]דבר[[t:35]], [[t:36]]to speak[[t:37]], has been attributed to the [[t:38]]voice[[t:39]], even so the verb [[t:40]]קרא[[t:41]], [[t:42]]to cry or call[[t:43]], is here attributed to the [[t:44]]voice[[t:45]]. Something similar is expressly found in Scripture, I mean to say, that the verbs [[t:46]]אמר[[t:47]], [[t:48]]to say[[t:49]], and [[t:50]]קרא[[t:51]], [[t:52]]to cry[[t:53]], are expressly attributed to the voice; e.g.: [[t:54]]A VOICE SAYS[[t:55]]: [[t:56]]Cry; and he said, What shall I cry[[t:57]] (Isaiah xl. 6)? According to this ellipsis, one must needs explain the passage in question thus: “And [[t:58]]a voice[[t:59]] from God passed before him and cried: The Lord! the Lord! etc.”; the repetition of the word [[t:60]]Lord[[t:61]] is to strengthen the vocative—God being He unto whom the call is addressed—even as we find elsewhere, Moses! Moses!—Abraham! Abraham! This is likewise a most excellent interpretation.
root.text.Part 1..20.6: Thou shalt not find it strange that a subject so profound and so difficult of apprehension should be susceptible of so many diverse interpretations, for this presents no inconvenience to our present purpose. Thou art therefore free to choose such opinion as thou wilt: thou mayest admit either that all this awful scene was indubitably a prophetic vision, and that all the efforts of Moses[[fn:171]] tended toward intellectual perceptions, so that what he sought, what was denied him, and what he perceived, were all alike intellectual, without the intervention of any sense, as we interpreted it at the beginning; or else, that there was simultaneously a perception by means of the sense of sight, but which had for its object a created thing, by the sight of which the perfection of the intellectual perception was obtained, as Onkelos has interpreted—provided that this perception by means of sight was not itself a prophetic vision[[fn:172]], like that which is read of Abraham: [[t:0]]And behold a smoking furnace, and a burning lamp that passed[[t:1]], etc.; or finally, that there was also therewith a perception by means of the sense of hearing, and that what passed before him was [[t:2]]the voice[[t:3]], which undoubtedly was also something [[t:4]]created[[t:5]]. Choose, therefore, whichever opinion thou pleasest; for my sole aim is that thou shouldst not believe that the verb [[t:6]]ויעבר[[t:7]], [[t:8]]He passed[[t:9]], has here the same sense as [[t:10]]עבֹר[[t:11]] in the passage: [[t:12]]Pass on before the people[[t:13]] (Exodus xvii. 5). For God (blessed be He!) is not a body, and one cannot attribute movement unto Him; it cannot therefore be said that He [[t:14]]passed[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]עבר[[t:17]]), according to the primary signification of that word in the language.
root.text.Part 1..21.0: The verb [[t:0]]bâ[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]בא[[t:3]]), in the Hebrew tongue, signifies [[t:4]]to come[[t:5]], being said of a living being moving toward any place or toward another individual; e.g.: [[t:6]]Thy brother came[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]בא[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]with subtilty[[t:11]] (Genesis xxvii. 35). It is also applied to the [[t:12]]entering[[t:13]] of a living being into a place; e.g.: [[t:14]]And Joseph came[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]ויבֹא[[t:17]]) [[t:18]]into the house[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]Ibid.[[t:21]], xliii. 26); [[t:22]]When ye be come[[t:23]] ([[t:24]]תבואו[[t:25]]) [[t:26]]to the land[[t:27]] (Exodus xii. 25). But this verb has also been employed metaphorically to denote [[t:28]]the arrival[[t:29]] of a thing which is not a body; e.g.: [[t:30]]That when [[t:31]] ([[t:32]]יבוא[[t:33]]) [[t:34]]thy sayings come to pass, we may do thee honour[[t:35]] (Judges xiii. 17); [[t:36]]Things that shall come[[t:37]] ([[t:38]]יבֹאו[[t:39]]) (Isaiah xlvii. 13); and men have gone so far as to employ it in speaking of certain [[t:40]]privations[[t:41]][[fn:173]]; e.g.: [[t:42]]There came[[t:43]] ([[t:44]]ויבא[[t:45]]) [[t:46]]evil[[t:47]] (Job xxx. 26); [[t:48]]Darkness came[[t:49]] ([[t:50]]Ibid.[[t:51]]). And, according to this metaphor by which it has been applied to something that is not a body, it has also been employed in speaking of the Creator (blessed be He!), whether to denote the arrival of His word or the arrival (the manifestation) of His Majesty. Conformably to this metaphor, it is said: [[t:52]]Lo, I come[[t:53]] ([[t:54]]בא[[t:55]]) [[t:56]]unto thee in a thick cloud[[t:57]] (Exodus xix. 9); [[t:58]]For the Lord, the God of Israel, enters[[t:59]] ([[t:60]]בא[[t:61]]) [[t:62]]by it[[t:63]] (Ezek. xliv. 2); and in all similar passages is signified [[t:64]]the arrival of His Majesty[[t:65]]. In the passage: [[t:66]]And the Lord my God shall come[[t:67]] ([[t:68]]ובא[[t:69]]), [[t:70]]and all the saints with thee[[t:71]] (Zechariah xiv. 5), is signified the arrival of His word, or[[fn:174]] the confirmation of the promises He has made through His prophets; and this is what he expresses by the words: [[t:72]]all the saints with thee[[t:73]]. It is as if he said: “Then shall come to pass the promise of the Lord my God, made through all the holy ones who are with thee,” addressing the words[[fn:175]] unto Israel.

root.text.Part 1..22.1: It is in this metaphorical sense that the verb [[t:0]]yaṣâ[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]יצא[[t:3]]) must be taken whenever it is attributed to God; e.g.: [[t:4]]For, behold, the Lord comes out[[t:5]] (literally, [[t:6]]goes forth[[t:7]]) [[t:8]]out of his place[[t:9]] (Isaiah xxvi. 21), that is to say, His word, which is now hidden from us, is about [[t:10]]to be manifested[[t:11]]. Herein is meant the coming into being of things which have not yet existed; for everything that happens from Him is attributed to His word; e.g.: [[t:12]]By the word of the Lord were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth[[t:13]] (Ps. xxxiii. 6), which is said by way of comparison with the acts emanating from kings, who, to transmit their will, employ speech as an instrument[[fn:177]]. But He, the Most High, has no need of an instrument for action; His action, on the contrary, is by His will alone, and there can be no question of literal speech[[fn:178]], as shall be explained[[fn:179]].
root.text.Part 1..22.2: — Now, as the verb יצא, to go forth, has been metaphorically employed to signify the manifestation of any act whatsoever proceeding from Him [as we have even now explained], and as it has been expressed: Behold, the Lord goes forth out of His place, one has likewise employed the verb שוב, to return, to denote the cessation, according to the Divine will, of the act in question; and it is said: I will go and return (אשובה) to my place (Hosea, v, 15), which signifies that the Divine Majesty, which was in the midst of us, shall withdraw from us, and, in consequence thereof[[fn:180]], Divine Providence shall fail us, as God has said in threatening us: And I will hide my face from them, and they shall be devoured (Deuter., xxxi, 17); for when Providence fails a man, he is abandoned to himself, and remains a mark for all that may occur by accident, so that his happiness and his misery depend upon chance. How terrible is this threat! It is that which has been expressed by these words: I will go and return to my place.
root.text.Part 1..23.0: The verb halakh (הלך, to go, to walk) is likewise among those which are applied to certain particular movements of living beings; e.g.: And Jacob went (הלך) on his way (Genesis, xxxii, 1); of which there are numerous examples. This word has been metaphorically employed to denote the expansion of bodies which are more subtle than the bodies of animals; e.g.: And the waters decreased (הלוך) continually (Genesis, viii, 5); And the fire ran along (ותהלך) upon the ground (Exodus, ix, 23). Subsequently, it was employed in a general sense to signify that a thing spreads and manifests itself, even though that thing be not a body; e.g.: The voice thereof shall go (ילך) like (the gliding of) a serpent (Jeremiah, xlvi, 22). Likewise in these words: The voice of the Lord God walking (מתהלך) in the garden (Genesis, iii, 8), it is to the voice that the word מתהלך (walking or spreading) is applied[[fn:181]].
root.text.Part 1..23.1: It is in this metaphorical sense that the verb halakh (הלך) must be understood whenever it relats to God, — I mean to say, having regard to the fact that it is said metaphorically of that which is not a body, — whether it be applied to the diffusion of the Divine word[[fn:182]] or to the withdrawal of Providence, analogous to that which, in a living being, is called turning away from a thing, which the animal performs by the act of walking[[fn:183]]. As therefore the withdrawal of Providence has been denoted by the expression hiding the face, in these words: And I will surely hide my face (Deuter., xxxi, 18), so has it been denoted by הלך (to walk, to go away), taken in the sense of turning away from a thing; e.g.: I will go and return to my place (Hosea, v, 15).
root.text.Part 1..23.2: As regards this passage: [[t:0]]And the wrath of the Eternal was kindled against them, and he[[t:1]] (or [[t:2]]she[[t:3]]) [[t:4]]went away[[t:5]] ([Lat.: Vayilach] (Nombr., XII, 9)), it contains at once both senses[[fn:184]], I mean the sense of the [[t:8]]retreat of Providence[[t:9]], designated by the expression of [[t:10]]turning away[[t:11]] ([Lat.: s'en aller] [[t:12]]), and that of the [[t:14]]dispersion[[t:15]] of the divine word which spreads and manifests itself, I mean that it is [[t:16]]the wrath[[t:17]] which [[t:18]]went away[[t:19]] and extended itself towards them both[[fn:185]], wherefore she (Miriam) became [[t:20]]leprous[[t:21]], ([Lat.: blanche] [[t:22]]as white as snow[[t:23]] [[t:24]]like the snow[[t:25]] ([Lat.: Ibid.] [[t:26]], [[t:27]]V[[t:28]]. 10).
root.text.Part 1..23.3: In like manner is the verb halakh (הלך) metaphorically used to signify walking in the right path (or possessing a goodly conduct), without there being any question of the movement of a body; e.g.: And thou shalt walk (והלכת) in His ways (Deuter., xxviii, 9); Ye shall walk (תלכו) after the Lord your God (Ibid., xiii, 4); Come ye, and let us walk (ונלכה) in the light of the Lord (Isaiah, ii, 5).
root.text.Part 1..24.0: Schakhan (שכן). — It is well known that the signification of this verb is to dwell; e.g.: And he dwelt (שוכן) in the plain of Mamre (Genesis, xiv, 13); And it came to pass, when Israel dwelt (בשכן)…(Ibid., xxxv, 22); and this is the generally accepted sense. To dwell signifies: to abide permanently in one and the same place[[fn:186]]; for, when a living creature prolongs its stay in a place, whether it be common or particular[[fn:187]], it is said of him that he dwells in that place, albeit, without doubt, he be there in motion.
root.text.Part 1..24.1: This verb is applied metaphorically to that which is inanimate or, to speak more precisely, to any thing which remains fixed and has attached itself to another thing; wherefore the verb שכן (to dwell) is likewise employed in this case, even though the object to which the thing in question has attached itself be not a place, nor the thing an animate being; e.g.: Let a cloud dwell (תשכן) upon it (Job, iii, 5); for the cloud, verily, is not an animate being, nor is the day a body, but a portion of time.
root.text.Part 1..24.2: It is in this metaphorical sense that (the verb in question) has been applied to God, I mean to the permanence of His Shekhinâ (Majesty)[[fn:188]], or of His Providence in any place whatsoever[[fn:189]], or to the Providence manifesting itself permanently[[fn:190]] in any thing. It has been said, e.g.: And the glory of the Lord abode (וישכן) (Exodus, xxiv, 17); And I will dwell (ושכניתי) among the children of Israel (Ibid., xxix, 45); And the good will of Him that dwelt (שכני) in the bush (Deuter., xxxiii, 16)[[fn:191]]. And, whenever this verb is found attributed to God, it signifies the permanence, in some place, of His Shekhinâ, I mean of His light (which is a) created thing, or the permanence of His Providence (manifesting itself) in any thing whatsoever, according as it befitts each passage.
root.text.Part 1..25.0: Thou art already acquainted with their dictum[[fn:192]] concerning all manner of interpretation relating to this subject[[fn:193]], to wit: that the Scripture has spoken according to the language of men. This signifies that whatever men in general[[fn:194]] are able to comprehend and to conceive at first sight has been applied to God, who, for this reason, has been described by epithets indicating corporeality, in order to signify that God exists; for the generality of men cannot conceive of existence, save in a body particularly, and whatever is not a body nor is found in a body has for them no existence.
root.text.Part 1..25.1: Likewise, all that is perfection for us has been attributed to God to indicate that He possesses all kinds of perfection without any admixture of imperfection; and whatever is conceived by the vulgar as being an imperfection or a lack, is not attributed unto Him. Wherefore, neither eating, nor drinking, nor sleep, nor sickness, nor injustice, nor any other such thing, is attributed to Him. But all that the vulgar believe to be a perfection has been attributed to Him, although it be a perfection only in relation to ourselves; for as regards Him[[fn:195]] all these things which we believe to be perfections are an extreme imperfection. The vulgar, however, would deem themselves to attribute an imperfection to God, were they to imagine that such human perfection might be wanting in Him[[fn:196]].
root.text.Part 1..25.2: Thou knowest that motion forms part of the perfection of the animal and is necessary unto it that it may be perfect; for, even as it has need to eat and to drink to replace that which has been dissolved[[fn:197]], so too it has need of motion to direct itself towards that which is suitable unto it and to flee from that which is contrary. There is no difference between attributing to God eating and drinking and attributing unto Him motion; nevertheless, [[t:0]]according to the language of men[[t:1]], that is to say, according to popular imagination, it would be to attribute an imperfection unto God to say that He eats and drinks, whereas motion would not denote an imperfection in Him[[fn:198]], albeit it is but necessity which compels to motion. It has been demonstrated that whatsoever moves is undoubtedly of a certain magnitude and divisible[[fn:199]]; now, it will be demonstrated that God possesses no magnitude, and consequently has no motion. Neither can repose be attributed unto Him; for repose can be attributed only unto him[[fn:200]] whose condition it is to move. Thus, therefore, all words indicating the different species of animal movements have been employed, in the aforesaid manner[[fn:201]], as attributes of God, even as [[t:2]]life;[[t:3]] for motion is an accident inherent in the animate being, and there is no doubt that by setting aside corporeality, one also sets aside all these notions of [[t:4]]descending[[t:5]], of [[t:6]]ascending[[t:7]], of [[t:8]]walking[[t:9]], of [[t:10]]standing[[t:11]], of [[t:12]]halting[[t:13]], of [[t:14]]going about[[t:15]], of [[t:16]]sitting[[t:17]], of [[t:18]]dwelling[[t:19]], of [[t:20]]going forth[[t:21]], of [[t:22]]entering[[t:23]], of [[t:24]]passing[[t:25]], and others similar.
root.text.Part 1..25.3: It would be superfluous to dwell at length upon this subject, were it not for that which has become familiar to the minds of the vulgar[[fn:202]]; wherefore it is necessary to provide an explanation thereof to those who have set themselves the task (of acquiring) human perfection and of ridding themselves of those errors, preconceived since the years of infancy[[fn:203]], (and to speak thereof) with some detail, even as we have done.
root.text.Part 1..26.0: Onkelos the proselyte, who possessed a perfect mastery of the Hebrew and Syriac tongues[[fn:204]], used his utmost endeavors to remove all corporification (of God); so that, whenever Scripture employs (concerning God) an epithet which might lead to corporality, he interprets it according to its (true) sense. Whenever he finds one of those words which indicate any of the diverse species of motion, he takes motion in the sense of manifestation, of the appearance of a created light, I mean of Divine Majesty, or else (in that) of Providence[[fn:205]]. He therefore translats ירד י״י (the Eternal shall descend, Exodus, 19, 11) by יתגלי י״י (the Eternal shall manifest Himself), וירד י״י (and the Eternal descended, ibid., v. 20) by ואתגלי י״י (and the Eternal manifested Himself), and he says not ונחת י״י (and the Eternal descended); likewise ארדה נא ואראה (I will now go down and see, Genesis, 18, 21) by אתגלי כען ואחזי (I will now manifest Myself and see[[fn:206]]); and this he does continually in his paraphrase.
root.text.Part 1..26.1: Nevertheless, the words אנכי ארד עמך מצרימה (I will go down with thee into Egypt, Genesis, 46, 4), he translats (literally): אנא איחות עמך למצריס, and this is a most remarkable thing which proves the perfect talent of this master, the excellence of his manner of interpretation, and how exactly he understood these matters; for by this translation (of the latter passage), he has likewise given us a glimpse[[fn:207]] of one of the principal points of Prophecy.
root.text.Part 1..26.2: This is how: In the beginning of this narrative (ibid., v. 2 and 3), it is said: And God spake unto Israel in the visions of the night, and said, Jacob, Jacob, etc. And He said, I am God, etc. (and God said in conclusion): I will go down with thee into Egypt. Now, as it follows from the beginning of the discourse that this occurred in the visions of the night, Onkelos saw no harm in rendering literally the words which had been spoken in these nocturnal visions. And this with reason[[fn:208]]: for it is the relation of something that had been said, and not the relation of a fact that had occurred, as (in the passage): And the Eternal descended upon mount Sinai (Exodus, 19, 20), which is the relation of a fact that came to pass in the real world[[fn:209]]; wherefore he has substituted the idea of manifestation and removed that which might indicate the existence of a motion. But (concerning) the things of the imagination, I mean the relation of that which had been said (to Jacob), he has left it intact[[fn:210]]. This is a remarkable thing.
root.text.Part 1..26.3: Thou art, in sooth, admonished thereby that the matter is right different, according as there be used the words [[t:0]]in a dream[[t:1]] or [[t:2]]in the visions of the night[[t:3]], or whether the words [[t:4]]in a vision[[t:5]] and [[t:6]]in an appearance[[t:7]] be employed, or whether it be simply said: [[t:8]]And the word of the Lord came unto me, saying[[t:9]], or: [[t:10]]The Lord said unto me[[t:11]][[fn:211]].
root.text.Part 1..26.4: It is also possible, in mine opinion, that Onkelos has interpreted here the word [[t:0]]Elohim[[t:1]] (God) in the sense [[t:2]]of angels[[t:3]], and that for this cause he felt no repugnance to say (in his version): “I will [[t:4]]go down[[t:5]] with thee into Egypt.” One must not deem it improper that Onkelos should have perceived in [[t:6]]Elohim[[t:7]] an [[t:8]]angel[[t:9]], albeit (the apparition) says unto him (to Jacob): [[t:10]]I am the[[t:11]] G[[t:12]]OD[[t:13]], [[t:14]]the God of thy father;[[t:15]] for the same terms are also sometimes employed by an angel. Dost thou not perceive that elsewhere, after it is said: [[t:16]]And the angel of God spake unto me in a dream, saying, Jacob: And I said, Here am I[[t:17]] (Genesis, xxxi, 11), it is expressed at the conclusion of the speech addressed unto Jacob: [[t:18]]I am the God of Beth-el, where thou anointedst the pillar, and where thou vowedst a vow unto me[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]Ibid.[[t:21]], [[t:22]]v[[t:23]]. 13)? Doubtless Jacob offered his vows unto God, and not unto the angel; but this occurs continually in the discourses of the prophets, I mean that in reporting the words which the angel spake unto them in the name of God, they express themselves as if it were God Himself who spake unto them. In all passages (of this kind) there is an ellipsis of a noun in the construct state[[fn:212]]; it is as if it were said: [[t:24]]I am[[t:25]] [[t:26]]THE MESSENGER[[t:27]] [[t:28]]of the God of thy father; I am[[t:29]] [[t:30]]THE MESSENGER[[t:31]] [[t:32]]of the God who appeared unto thee at Beth-el[[t:33]], and so forth.
root.text.Part 1..26.5: Concerning prophecy and its divers degrees, as also concerning the angels, there shall yet be spoken more at large, in accordance with the design of this treatise.
root.text.Part 1..27.0: [[t:0]]Reghel[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]רגל[[t:3]]) is an homonymous term. It is (primarily) the name of the [[t:4]]foot;[[t:5]] e.g., [[t:6]]רגל תחת רגל[[t:7]], [[t:8]]foot for foot[[t:9]] (Exodus, xxi, 24); but it is also found in the sense of [[t:10]]following;[[t:11]] e.g., [[t:12]]Get thee out[[t:13]], [[t:14]]and all the people that follow thee[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]ברגליך[[t:17]]) ([[t:18]]Ibid.[[t:19]], xi, 8), that is to say: who [[t:20]]follow[[t:21]] thee. It is likewise met with in a sense of [[t:22]]causality;[[t:23]] e.g., [[t:24]]And the Lord has blessed thee since my coming[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]לרגלי[[t:27]]) (Genesis, xxx, 30), that is to say, [[t:28]]by my cause[[t:29]] or [[t:30]]for my sake[[t:31]], for that which is done for the sake of a certain thing has the latter for its [[t:32]]cause[[t:33]]. It is often thus employed; e.g., [[t:34]]According to the pace[[t:35]] or [[t:36]]because[[t:37]] ([[t:38]]לרגל[[t:39]]) [[t:40]]of the cattle that goes before me and because[[t:41]] ([[t:42]]לרגל[[t:43]]) [[t:44]]of the children[[t:45]] (Genesis, xxxiii, 14).
root.text.Part 1..27.1: Thus, by these words: [[t:0]]And His feet[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]רגליו[[t:3]]) [[t:4]]shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives[[t:5]] (Zechariah, xiv, 4), it is meant that [[t:6]]His causes[[t:7]] shall subsist, to wit, the miracles which shall then be manifested in that place, and of which God is [[t:8]]the cause[[t:9]], I mean the author[[fn:213]]. It is this interpretation which Jonathan ben Uziel had in view when he said (in his Chaldee paraphrase): [[t:10]]He shall manifest Himself in His power, in that day, upon the mount of Olives;[[t:11]] and in like manner he translats by [[t:12]]גבורתיה[[t:13]], [[t:14]]His power[[t:15]], all (the words designating) the members[[fn:214]] (which are used) for [[t:16]]grasping[[t:17]] or for [[t:18]]moving from place to place[[t:19]], for they generally designate the acts which emanate from His will.
root.text.Part 1..27.2: As for these words: And under his feet (רגליו) there was as it were a work of the brilliance of sapphire (Exodus 24:10), Onkelos, as you know, interprets them in such a way as to consider the pronoun in רגליו (his feet) as referring to the word כסא, throne (which would be implied)[[fn:215]]; for he translates: ותחות כורסי יקריה, and under the throne of his glory. This must be understood, and you will be astonished (to see) how far Onkelos remains from the corporealization (of God) and from everything that can lead to it in even the most remote manner; for he does not say: and under his throne, because if one attributed the throne to (God) Himself, in the sense that would be seen at first glance, it would follow that God is established[[fn:216]] upon a body, and corporealization would result; he therefore attributes the throne to His glory, I mean to the Shekhinah, which is a created light[[fn:217]].
root.text.Part 1..27.3: He expresses himself after the same manner in the translation of the words: Because the hand (is placed) upon the Throne of God (Exodus, xvii. 16), where he says: «…from before God, whose Majesty rests upon the Throne of His Glory.» Thou findest likewise in the language of the whole Jewish nation the term כסא הכבוד, Throne of Glory.
root.text.Part 1..27.4: But we have digressed from the theme of this chapter to touch upon a matter which shall be explained in other chapters.
root.text.Part 1..27.5: I return, then, to the subject of the chapter. You know, I say, the manner in which Onkelos interprets (the passage in question); but the principal aim for him is to exclude corporealization, and he does not explain to us what they perceived[[fn:218]] nor what was intended by this allegory. Likewise, in all passages (of this nature), he does not address that question at all[[fn:219]]; rather, he limits himself to excluding corporealization, for that is a demonstrable thing, necessary in religious faith; he does so, therefore, in an absolute manner[[fn:220]], and expresses himself accordingly. As for the explanation of the meaning of the allegory, it is a matter of opinion; for the aim (of the allegory) could be this thing or another. These are also very obscure subjects, the understanding of which is not part of the foundations of the Faith, and which the vulgar do not easily grasp; that is why he does not engage in this question.
root.text.Part 1..27.6: But one, having regard to the object of this treatise, cannot forbear to offer some interpretation (of the passage in question). One therefore states that, by the words [[t:0]]under His feet[[t:1]], is signified [[t:2]]by its cause and by Him[[t:3]], as has been explained[[fn:221]]; what they perceived was the true condition of [[t:4]]prime matter[[t:5]], which proceeded from God, who is the cause of its existence. Observe carefully the words: [[t:6]]כמעשה לבנת הספיר[[t:7]], [[t:8]]as a work of the brightness of sapphire:[[t:9]] had [[t:10]]colour[[t:11]] been intended, it would have been said [[t:12]]כלבנת הספיר[[t:13]], [[t:14]]as the whiteness[[t:15]] or [[t:16]]the brightness of sapphire;[[t:17]] but [[t:18]]מעשה[[t:19]], [[t:20]]a work[[t:21]], was added, because matter, as is known, is ever [[t:22]]receptive[[t:23]] and [[t:24]]passive[[t:25]] in relation to its essence, and possesses action only accidentally, just as form is ever [[t:26]]active[[t:27]] by its essence and [[t:28]]passive[[t:29]] by accident, as is explained in the treatises of Physics; and it is on this account that [[t:30]]כמעשה[[t:31]], [[t:32]]as a work[[t:33]], has been said of the former[[fn:222]]. As to the words [[t:34]]לבנת הספיר[[t:35]] (which signify literally: [[t:36]]the whiteness of sapphire[[t:37]])[[fn:223]], they denote [[t:38]]transparency[[t:39]], and not [[t:40]]the white colour[[t:41]], for the whiteness of crystal is not a white colour, but a mere transparency; and transparency is not a colour, as has been demonstrated in the treatises of Physics[[fn:224]], for, were it a colour, it would not permit all colours to pass through[[fn:225]], and would not receive them. It is therefore because the transparent body is deprived of all colours that it receives them all successively; and this resembles [[t:42]]prime matter[[t:43]], which, in relation to its true condition, is deprived of all forms, and which, on that account, receives them all successively. Thus, therefore, what they perceived was prime matter and its relation to God[[fn:226]], (to wit) that it was[[fn:227]] the first of His creatures comprising [[t:44]]generation[[t:45]] and [[t:46]]corruption[[t:47]][[fn:228]], and that it was He who had produced it from nothingness[[fn:229]]. Further mention will be made of this subject (in another place)[[fn:230]].
root.text.Part 1..27.7: Know thou that thou hast need of such an interpretation, even beside that of Onkelos, who says: [[t:0]]and under the throne of His glory;[[t:1]] I mean that prime matter is also, in truth, beneath the heaven, which is called [[t:2]]throne[[t:3]], as has been said aforetime. That which suggested unto me this remarkable interpretation and caused me to find the subject in question, is solely an assertion which I found in the work of R. Eliezer, son of Hyrcanus, and which thou shalt learn in one of the chapters of this treatise[[fn:231]]. The aim, in sum, of every intelligent man, is to remove from God all that may lead to corporeality, and to regard all these perceptions of which we have spoken as appertaining to the intellect, and not unto the senses. This must be understood and pondered upon.
root.text.Part 1..28.0: [[t:0]]’Açab[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]עצב[[t:3]]) is a homonym which signifies (firstly) [[t:4]]pain[[t:5]] and [[t:6]]suffering;[[t:7]] e.g.: [[t:8]]In pain[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]בעצב[[t:11]]) [[t:12]]thou shalt bring forth children[[t:13]] (Genesis iii. 16). It signifies also the act of [[t:14]]provoking;[[t:15]] e.g.: [[t:16]]ולא עצבו אביו מימיו[[t:17]], [[t:18]]His father had not[[t:19]] [[t:20]]VEXED[[t:21]] [[t:22]]him at any time[[t:23]] (I Kings i. 6); [[t:24]]כי נעצב אל דוד[[t:25]], [[t:26]]For he was[[t:27]] [[t:28]]GRIEVED[[t:29]] [[t:30]]on account of David[[t:31]] (I Sam. xx. 34). It signifies finally [[t:32]]to oppose or to be rebellious;[[t:33]] e.g.: [[t:34]]They rebelled, and vexed[[t:35]] ([[t:36]]ועצבו[[t:37]]) [[t:38]]His holy spirit[[t:39]] (Isaiah lxiii. 10); [[t:40]]They provoked Him[[t:41]] ([[t:42]]יעציבוהו[[t:43]]) [[t:44]]in the wilderness[[t:45]] (Ps. lxxviii. 40); … [[t:46]]if there be in me a rebellious way[[t:47]] ([[t:48]]עצֶב[[t:49]]) (Ps. cxxxix. 24); [[t:50]]Every day they wrest[[t:51]] ([[t:52]]יעצבו[[t:53]]) [[t:54]]my words[[t:55]] (Ps. lvi. 6).
root.text.Part 1..28.1: It is according to the second or the third signification that it has been said (concerning God): [[t:0]]ויתעצב אל לבו[[t:1]], [[t:2]]And it[[t:3]] [[t:4]]GRIEVED[[t:5]] or [[t:6]]VEXED[[t:7]] [[t:8]]Him at His heart[[t:9]] (Genesis vi. 6). According to the second signification, the interpretation thereof would be: That God was wroth with them by reason of their evil deeds. As for the words [[t:10]]אל לבו[[t:11]], [[t:12]]in His heart[[t:13]], which are likewise employed in the history of Noah, saying: [[t:14]]And the Lord said in His heart[[t:15]] (Genesis viii. 21), hearken unto the meaning thereof: when it is said, in speaking of man, that he [[t:16]]said in his heart[[t:17]], [[t:18]]בלבו[[t:19]] or [[t:20]]אל לבו[[t:21]], it concerns something that man does not utter nor declare unto another; and in like manner, whenever it concerns something that God has willed, yet has not declared unto a prophet at the moment when the act was performed according to the Divine will, it is expressed: [[t:22]]And the Lord said in His heart[[t:23]], by assimilation to human things, and according to that constant rule, that [[t:24]]the Scripture speaks according to the language of men[[t:25]][[fn:232]]; and this is clear and manifest. Since, therefore, as touching the rebellion of the [[t:26]]generation of the flood[[t:27]], there is no mention in Scripture of any messenger sent unto them, nor of warning, nor of threat of destruction, it was said of them that God was vexed with them [[t:28]]in His heart[[t:29]]. Likewise, when God willed[[fn:233]] that there should be no more flood, He spake not unto any prophet: Go and announce unto them such a thing; wherefore it was said: [[t:30]]in His heart[[t:31]] (Genesis viii. 21).
root.text.Part 1..28.2: To interpret the words [[t:0]]ויתעצב אל לבו[[t:1]] according to the third signification, they must needs be explained in this sense: that [[t:2]]man opposed the will of God within him[[t:3]][[fn:234]]; for the will is also called [[t:4]]לב[[t:5]], [[t:6]]heart[[t:7]], even as we shall explain in treating of the homonymity of the word [[t:8]]leb[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]לב[[t:11]]) [[t:12]][[fn:235]][[t:13]].
root.text.Part 1..29.0: [[t:0]]Akhal[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]אכל[[t:3]], [[t:4]]to eat[[t:5]]). — This word, in the Hebrew tongue, is primarily applied, in speaking of animals, to the act of [[t:6]]taking food[[t:7]], and this requirs no citation of examples; subsequently, the language has considered in the act of eating two things: first, that the thing eaten is lost and perishes, I mean that its form is first corrupted; secondly, that the animal grows by the food it takes, whereby it continus to preserve itself, prolongs[[fn:236]] its existence, and restors all the powers of the body.
root.text.Part 1..29.1: With respect to the first consideration, the verb akhal (אכל) has been employed metaphorically for everything that perishes and is destroyed, and in general for every deprivation of form; as for instance: And the land of your enemies shall eat you up (ואכלה) (Levit. xxvi. 38); A land that eats up (אכלת) the inhabitants thereof (Numb. xiii. 32); Ye shall be devoured (תאֻכּלו) with the sword (Isa. i. 20); Shall the sword devour (תאכל) … (II Sam. ii. 26)? And the fire of the Lord burnt among them, and consumed (ותאכל) them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp (Numb. xi. 1); (God) is a consuming fire (אכׁלה) (Deut. iv. 24), that is to say, He destroys those who are rebellious against Him, even as fire destroys all that it seizes. This use (of the verb akhal) is frequent.
root.text.Part 1..29.2: With regard to the second consideration, the verb [[t:0]]akhal[[t:1]] has been employed metaphorically to signify [[t:2]]knowledge[[t:3]] and [[t:4]]instruction[[t:5]], and, in general, the intellectual perceptions whereby [[t:6]]the human form[[t:7]][[fn:237]] continues to be preserved in the most perfect state, just as, through nourishment, the body remains in its best condition; for example: [[t:8]]Come, buy and eat[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]ואכלו[[t:11]]), [[t:12]]etc.[[t:13]] (Isaïe, 55, 1); [[t:14]]Hear me, and you shall eat[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]ואכלו[[t:17]]) [[t:18]]that which is good[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]Ibid.[[t:21]], [[t:22]]V[[t:23]]. 2); [[t:24]]To eat[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]אכלׁ[[t:27]]) [[t:28]]too much honey is not good[[t:29]] (Prov., 25, 27); [[t:30]]Eat[[t:31]] ([[t:32]]אכל[[t:33]]) [[t:34]]honey, my son, for it is good; pure honey, sweet to thy palate. Such is for thy soul the knowledge of wisdom, etc.[[t:35]] ([[t:36]]Ibid.[[t:37]], 24, 13, 14).
root.text.Part 1..29.3: This usage is likewise frequent in the words of the Sages—I mean, the denoting of knowledge by the verb to eat; as for instance: “Come and eat fat meat at the house of Raba.”[[fn:238]] They say (elsewhere): “Wheresoever mention is made in this book of eating and drinking, nothing else is intended but wisdom,” or, according to some copies, “the Law.”[[fn:239]] In like manner, wisdom is frequently called water; as for instance: Ho, every one that thirsts, come ye to the waters (Isa. lv. 1)!
root.text.Part 1..29.4: This use (of the verb אכל) having become very frequent, and having received such extension that it has, in a manner, taken the place of the primitive signification, the words hunger and thirst have likewise been employed to denote the absence of knowledge and of intellectual perception; as for instance: I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord (Amos viii. 11); My soul thirsts for God, for the living God (Ps. xlii. 3). Of this there are numerous examples. The words, Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation (Isa. xii. 3), Jonathan ben Uziel (in his Chaldaic version) has rendered thus: And ye shall receive with joy a new doctrine from the chosen among the righteous. Observe well that, according to his interpretation, water denots the knowledge which shall be obtained in those days; the word מַעַיְנֵי (the wells), he assimilats to מֵעֵינֵי העדה (Numb. xv. 24), signifying the chiefs[[fn:240]], who are the learned. He says: from the chosen among the righteous, because righteousness (or piety) is the true salvation. Thou seest[[fn:241]] how he interprets every word of this verse in the sense of knowledge and instruction. Consider this well.
root.text.Part 1..30.0: Know[[fn:242]] that for the human intellect there are objects of perception which it is within its faculty and nature to perceive; but there are also, in that which exists, beings and things which it is not at all in its nature to perceive in any manner, nor by any cause whatsoever[[fn:243]], and the perception of which is absolutely inaccessible to it[[fn:244]]. Finally, there are things in existence of which it perceivs certain circumstances, whilst remaining in ignorance of others[[fn:245]]. Indeed, from the fact that it is a percipient thing, it does not necessarily follow that it must perceive all things; for the senses likewise have perceptions, yet they cannot perceive objects at every possible distance.
root.text.Part 1..30.1: The same holds true for other corporeal faculties; for, although man, for example, be capable of lifting two quintals, he is not thereby capable of lifting ten. The superiority which individuals of the (human) species possess one over another, in these [[t:0]]sensible[[t:1]] perceptions and in other corporeal faculties, is clear and manifest to all; yet it possesses a limit, and the matter does not extend to any distance whatsoever, nor to any measure whatsoever. It is precisely the same with regard to man's [[t:2]]intelligible[[t:3]] perceptions, in which individuals of the species enjoy a marked superiority one over another, a fact likewise exceedingly clear and manifest to men of science; insomuch that there is a subject which one individual draws forth by his own speculation, whilst another individual could never comprehend the same subject, and even were one to endeavour to make him comprehend it by every manner of phraseology and example and over a long period of time, his mind cannot penetrate thereto, but rather refuses to comprehend it. But the superiority in question extends not to infinity either, and human intelligence, on the contrary, undoubtedly possesses a limit whereat it ceases.
root.text.Part 1..30.2: For certain things, therefore, man acknowledgs the impossibility of grasping them, and feels no desire to know them, well knowing that this is impossible and that there is no gate whereby one may enter to attain thereunto. Thus, for example, we are ignorant of the number of the stars of heaven, and whether it be an even or an odd number; and we are likewise ignorant of the number of the species of animals, minerals, and plants, and other such-like things. But there be other things which man feels a great desire to grasp, and the efforts of the intelligence to seek the reality thereof and to scrutinize them thoroughly are met with among all the speculative sects of the world and in all ages[[fn:246]]. And concerning these things, opinions are numerous, disagreement reigns among thinkers, and doubts arise, because the intelligence strivs to grasp these things—I mean that it is thither drawn by desire—and because each one believs himself to have found a path whereby to know the reality of the thing, whilst it is not in the power of human intelligence to allege in this regard a demonstrative proof; for every thing whose reality is known by means of a demonstration cannot be the subject of a difference (of opinion), nor of a contention[[fn:247]], nor of a denial, unless it be on the part of an ignorant person who employs that manner of contradicting which is called the demonstrative contradiction[[fn:248]], as thou findest, for instance, folk who contest the sphericity of the earth and the circular motion of the celestial sphere and other like things. These latter find no place in the subject (which now occupies us).
root.text.Part 1..30.3: The points on which this confusion (in opinions) prevails are very numerous in metaphysical matters, few in physical matters, and none in mathematical matters.
root.text.Part 1..30.4: Alexander of Aphrodisias[[fn:249]] says that the causes of disagreement concerning certain things are three in number: 1st, ambitious and rival pretensions[[fn:250]] which prevent man from perceiving the truth as it is; 2nd, the subtlety of the perceptible thing in itself, its profundity and the difficulty of perceiving it; 3rd, the ignorance of him who perceivs, and his incapacity to grasp even that which it is possible to grasp. Thus says Alexander. In our own times there is a fourth cause which he mentioned not, because it existed not among them[[fn:251]]: namely, habit and education; for it is in the nature of man to love that which is familiar to him and to be attracted thereunto. Thus thou seest the Bedouins, unclean as they are, deprived of enjoyments and subsisting miserably, feel a repugnance for the cities, being insensible to the pleasures which they offer, and preferring the evil condition whereunto they are accustomed to a better condition whereunto they are not accustomed; so that they have no pleasure in dwelling in palaces, nor in clothing themselves in silk, nor in procuring the delights of the bath, of oils, and of perfumes.
root.text.Part 1..30.5: In like manner it happens that man loves the opinions which are familiar to him and in which he has been nurtured, that he takes them under his protection, and is affrighted by that which is outside them.
root.text.Part 1..30.6: And by the selfsame cause, man shutts his eyes to the perception of truths and inclins toward his habits, as befalls the vulgar in the question of corporeality and in many metaphysical matters, even as we shall set forth; all this by reason of habit and because one has been nurtured upon the words of Scripture, the constant object of respect and faith, the literal sense of which would indicate the corporeality of God and imaginary things void of truth, but which were spoken by way of allegory and enigma, and that for reasons of which I shall treat.
root.text.Part 1..30.7: It must not be supposed that what we have here said concerning the insufficiency of the human intellect, in maintaining that it has a limit at which it must needs stay its course, has been said from the standpoint of religion; it is, on the contrary, a thing which the philosophers have asserted and which they have perfectly understood, without regard to sect or opinion. And it is a true matter which cannot be called into doubt, save by him who is ignorant of things already demonstrated.
root.text.Part 1..30.8: This chapter we have placed here only to serve as a preparation for that which shall follow.
root.text.Part 1..31.0: Know, O reader of my treatise! that there occurrs in intelligible perceptions, in so far as they are linked to matter[[fn:252]], something similar to that which occurrs in sensible perceptions. Thus, when thou lookest with thine eye, thou perceivest that which it is within thy visual faculty to perceive. But, when thou strainest thine eyes and fixest thy gaze, endeavouring to see at a great distance, too remote for it to be within thy power to see so far, or when thou considerest a very fine script or a minute engraving, the perception of which is not within thy faculty, so as to strain thy gaze in order to examine it well, then thy sight becoms too weak, not only for that which thou couldst not easily see, but also for that which thy faculty permitted thee to perceive; thy gaze is blunted and thou seest no longer even that which thou wert able to perceive before having fixed thy gaze and fatigued it.
root.text.Part 1..31.1: In the same condition is he who studies any science whatsoever, when he gives himself over to meditation; for, if he makes efforts[[fn:253]] of meditation and fatigue his whole mind, he becoms hebetated, and then he no longer comprehends even that which it is within his power to comprehend, for all the corporeal faculties[[fn:254]] are, in this regard, in the same position.
root.text.Part 1..31.2: The like befalls thee in (purely) intelligible[[fn:255]] perceptions; for, if thou haltest before that which is obscure, if thou deceivest not thyself by believing that there is a demonstration for that which is indemonstrable, if thou art not in haste[[fn:256]] to reject and declare to be a lie aught whose contrary is not demonstrated, and if, finally, thou aspirest not to the perception of that which thou canst not perceive, then hast thou attained unto human perfection, and art in the rank of Rabbi Akiba, who entered in peace and went out in peace[[fn:257]] while studying these metaphysical things. But if thou aspirest to a perception beyond thy perceptive faculty, or art in haste to declare those things to be a lie whose contrary is not demonstrated, or which are possible, albeit in a most remote manner, thou joinest thyself unto Élischa’ A’her[[fn:258]], and not only shalt thou not be perfect, but thou shalt become the most imperfect of all; then shall it happen unto thee that thou shalt allow the imaginative faculties to prevail and be led into vice, depravity, and evil, because the intellect will be preoccupied and its light extinguished, even as all manner of vain phantoms present themselves to the sight when the visual spirit[[fn:259]] grows weak in the sick and in those who fix their gaze upon brilliant or very subtle objects.
root.text.Part 1..31.3: It is in this sense that it has been said: [[t:0]]If thou hast found honey, eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith[[t:1]], [[t:2]]and vomit it[[t:3]] (Prov., 25, 16). Indeed, the doctors have allegorically applied this passage to Élischa’ A’her[[fn:260]]. This allegory is indeed remarkable; for in comparing here knowledge to [[t:4]]eating[[t:5]], according to what we have already stated[[fn:261]], the sweetest of foods is mentioned, namely honey. Honey, by its nature, when taken in great quantity, excites the stomach and causes vomiting. This passage intimates that, whatsoever the importance and grandeur of this perception and the perfection found therein, it is in its nature — when one does not stop at a certain limit and does not advance therein with caution — to turn to imperfection, just as in eating honey one is nourished and delighted when partaking with moderation, but when too much is taken, all is lost; (which is why) it was not said: [[t:6]]Be not full thereof, for thou wouldst[[t:7]] [[t:8]]BECOME DISGUSTED[[t:9]], but it was said: [[t:10]]for thou wouldst[[t:11]] [[t:12]]VOMIT IT[[t:13]].
root.text.Part 1..31.4: Unto this same idea was allusion made in the words: It is not good to eat much honey, etc. (Prov. xxv. 27); likewise in saying: Be not wise over much; why shouldest thou destroy thyself (Ecclesiastes vii. 16)? Allusion was further made therein by these words: Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, etc. (Ibid., iv. 17); and David also alluded thereto, saying: Neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me (Ps. cxxxi. 1). It is this same idea which they (the Sages) had in view when they said[[fn:262]]: 'Search not out that which is too obscure for thee, and scrutinize not that which is too veiled for thee; study that which is permitted unto thee (to know), and occupy not thyself with obscure things'; which is to say that one must only engage one's intelligence in that which it is possible for man to perceive; but as for that which it is not in the nature of man to perceive, it is most perilous to occupy oneself therewith, even as we have explained. This is also what they had in view when they said: 'Whosoever examins four things, etc.[[fn:263]]', a passage which they concluded with these words: 'and whosoever has no regard for the glory of his Creator'; (which contains) an allusion to that which we have just explained, to wit: that man should not precipitately approach speculation with false imaginations, and that, if doubts arise within him, or if the matter in question be not demonstrated unto him, he must not abandon and reject it, nor hasten to declare it a lie, but, on the contrary, remain calm, respect the glory of his Creator, and abstain and halt. This is a matter sufficiently explained.
root.text.Part 1..31.5: But the aim of these sentences pronounced by the prophets and the Sages is not to close entirely the door of speculation, nor to despoil the intellect of the perception of that which it is possible to perceive, as believe the ignorant and the slothful, who are pleased to pass off their own imperfection and stupidity for perfection and wisdom, and the perfection of others and their science for imperfection and irreligion, that put darkness for light, and light for darkness (Isaiah v. 20); the whole intention is, on the contrary, to declare that the intellects of mortals have a limit at which they must halt.
root.text.Part 1..31.6: One must not cavil at certain words spoken concerning the intellect in this chapter and in others; for the aim has been to guide (the reader) toward the (particular) subject that was in view, and not to fathom the nature of the intellect, a matter which shall be examined in other chapters[[fn:264]].
root.text.Part 1..32.0: Know thou that it would be most perilous to commence one's studies with this science, I mean to say, with metaphysics; likewise would it be dangerous to explain at the outset the meaning of the prophetic allegories and to direct attention to the metaphors employed in discourse, with which the prophetic books are filled. It behooves us, on the contrary, to educate the youth and to strengthen those of lesser capacity according to the measure of their understanding; and as for him who manifests a perfect mind and is prepared for this lofty degree, that is to say, for the degree of demonstrative speculation and the true argumentations of the intellect, he shall be advanced little by little until he attains unto his perfection, whether by the guidance of another or by his own endeavor.
root.text.Part 1..32.1: But when one commencs with this metaphysical science, there results therefrom not only a disturbance in belief, but absolute irreligion[[fn:265]]. I can but compare this to one who should give to a suckling babe wheaten bread and meat to eat, and wine to drink; for verily he would slay him, not because these are evil nutriments and contrary to the nature of man, but because the recipient is too weak to digest them so as to derive profit therefrom. Likewise, if metaphysical truths[[fn:266]] have been presented in an obscure and enigmatical manner, and if the learned have employed all manner of devices to teach them without pronouncing clearly thereon, it is not because they contain inwardly aught that is evil, or because they overthrow the foundations of religion, as is believed by the ignorant who pretend to have reached the degree of speculation; rather have they been veiled because the intellects, in the beginning, are incapable of receiving them, and they have been shown but dimly, so that the perfect man might know them; wherefore they are called mysteries and secrets of the Law, as we shall hereafter explain.
root.text.Part 1..32.2: For this reason has Scripture spoken in the language of men, even as we have explained[[fn:267]]. For it is intended to serve as the initial study and to be learned by children, by women, and by the generality of men, who are not capable of understanding things in their reality; wherefore one has confined oneself for their sake to simple authority[[fn:268]] whenever it concerned a true opinion the truth of which it was desired to proclaim, and with regard to every ideal thing[[fn:269]] attention was directed to that which might indicate to the mind that it exists, and not to examine the true nature of its being[[fn:270]]. But when the individual has perfected himself, and the secrets of the Law are revealed unto him[[fn:271]], whether by another or by himself, through their mutual combination[[fn:272]], he attains to the point of recognizing the truth of these sound opinions by the true means of establishing the truth, either by demonstration, when such is possible, or by solid arguments, when this means is practicable; and likewise he represents to himself in their reality those ideal things, which were for him but matters of imagination and figures, and he comprehends their true being.
root.text.Part 1..32.3: We have already cited on several occasions, in our discourses, this passage: “Neither shall one interpret the Merkabah, even to one alone, unless he be a wise man, understanding by his own knowledge; and then one shall impart to him only the first elements thereof[[fn:273]].” None, therefore, ought to be initiated into this matter, save according to the measure of his capacity and under the two following conditions: first, that he be wise, that is to say, that he possess the knowledge from which are drawn the preliminary notions of speculation; secondly, that he be intelligent, discerning, and of a natural perspicacity, grasping a subject by the slightest indication; and such is the meaning of the words: understanding by his own knowledge.
root.text.Part 1..32.4: The reason why it is forbidden to instruct the masses according to the true method of speculation, and to enable them, at the very outset, to form a conception of the true nature of things[[fn:274]], and why it is absolutely necessary that it should be thus and not otherwise[[fn:275]], all this I desire to explain unto thee in the following chapter. I say, then:
root.text.Part 1..33.0: The causes which prevent the commencement of instruction with metaphysical subjects, and the awakening of attention unto that which merits attention, and the presentation thereof to the common people, are five in number.
root.text.Part 1..33.1: The FIRST CAUSE is the difficulty of the subject in itself, its subtlety and its depth; as it has been said: That which is far off (from our conception), and exceeding deep, who can find it out? (Ecclesiastes vii. 24); and as it is further said: But where shall wisdom be found? (Job xxviii. 12). Wherefore, one must not begin instruction with that which is most difficult of comprehension and most profound. One of the allegories current in (the traditions of) our nation is the comparison of science unto water;[[fn:276]] the doctors have explained this allegory in divers manners, and (they have said) amongst others: He who knows how to swim draws pearls from the bottom of the sea, but he who is ignorant of swimming is drowned; wherefore none venturs to swim save he who has exercised himself in the learning thereof.
root.text.Part 1..33.2: The [[t:0]]SECOND CAUSE[[t:1]] is: the incapacity inherent in the minds of men in general from the outset; for man is not endowed, primarily, with his ultimate perfection, but perfection resides within him [[t:2]]potentially[[t:3]], and in the beginning he is deprived of [[t:4]]actuality[[t:5]] (as Scripture states): [[t:6]]And man is born as a wild ass's colt[[t:7]] (Job, 11, 12). But when an individual possesses somewhat [[t:8]]potentially[[t:9]], it is not necessarily incumbent that this should pass [[t:10]]into actuality;[[t:11]] on the contrary, the individual sometimes remains in his imperfection, whether through certain impediments, or for want of exercising himself in that which would bring this [[t:12]]potency[[t:13]] into [[t:14]]actuality[[t:15]]. It is expressly stated: [[t:16]]There are not many who become wise[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]Ibid.[[t:19]], 32, 9); and the Doctors have said: «I have seen men of elevation, but they are few in number[[fn:277]];» for the obstacles to perfection are exceeding numerous, and the preoccupations which hinder it are manifold, and when, therefore, can one obtain that perfect disposition and that leisure (necessary) for study, so that what the individual possesses [[t:20]]potentially[[t:21]] may pass into [[t:22]]actuality[[t:23]]?
root.text.Part 1..33.3: The <small>THIRD CAUSE</small> is the length of the preparatory studies; for man naturally feels a desire to seek the highest points, and ofttimes he grows weary of preparatory studies or abandons them.
