But know thou well, that if one could arrive at any high point (of science) without the preparatory studies which must precede, these would not be preparatory studies at all, but rather useless occupations and mere superfluities. If thou shouldst awaken any man whatsoever, even the most stolid of men, as one awakens a sleeper, saying unto him: Wouldst thou not desire to know at this moment these heavens (and to know) what is their number, what is their form, and what they contain? What are the angels? How the world in its entirety was created, and what is its purpose according to the reciprocal arrangement of its parts? What is the soul, and how did it enter into the body? If the soul of man be separable (from the body), and if it be separable, how, by what means, and to what end it is so?[[fn:278]] and other such inquiries—this man would doubtless answer thee: “Yes,” and he would feel a natural desire to know these things in their reality; only he would wish to appease this desire and arrive at the knowledge of all this by a single word, or by two words which thou shouldst say unto him. Yet, if thou shouldst impose upon him (the obligation) to interrupt his business for a week, in order to comprehend all this, he would not do so, but would rather content himself with false imaginations wherewith his soul is quieted, and it would be unpleasing to him to be declared that there exists something which requirs a multitude of preliminary notions and very prolonged researches.
root.text.Part 1..33.4: As for thee, thou knowest that the subjects in question are linked one to another. In truth, there is in existence naught else than God and all His works; these latter being all that existence contains besides Him (God). There is no means of perceiving God save through His works; it is they which indicate His existence and what must be believed concerning Him, I mean, what must be affirmed or denied of Him. It is therefore necessary to examine all beings in their reality, so that from each branch (of science) we may draw true and certain principles to serve us in our metaphysical researches. How many principles are there not drawn, indeed, from the nature of numbers and from the properties of geometrical figures, (principles) by which we are led to (know) certain things which we must remove from the Divinity, and the negation of which leads us to divers (metaphysical) subjects![[fn:279]] As for the matters of astronomy and physics, there will be, I think, no doubt in thy mind that these are necessary things for understanding the relation of the universe to the government of God, such as it is in reality and not according to imaginations. There are also many speculative matters which, without furnishing principles for this (metaphysical) science, yet exercise the mind and cause it to acquire the art[[fn:280]] of demonstration and to know the truth in its essence,[[fn:281]] putting an end to the trouble which the confusion of accidental things with essential things generally brings forth in the minds of thinkers, as well as the false opinions resulting therefrom. Let us add to this (the advantage) of well conceiving these other subjects (of which we have just spoken), considered in themselves,[[fn:282]] even though they should not serve as a basis for metaphysical science. Finally, they fail not to have other advantages for certain things which lead to the attainment of this science.[[fn:283]] It is therefore necessary that he who desirs (to obtain) human perfection should first instruct himself in logic, then gradually in mathematics, then in the physical sciences, and after that in metaphysics.
root.text.Part 1..33.5: It is frequently observed that many individuals confine their intellectual pursuits to a particular branch of science, and even when their minds remain unrelaxed, it often happens that death intervenes whilst they are still engaged in preliminary studies.  If, therefore, we were never to receive an opinion through the channel of traditional authority, and were never guided by allegory in any respect, but were compelled to form a perfect conception of every subject by means of essential definitions, and to admit nothing as true except through demonstration, a condition which is only possible after these prolonged preliminary studies, it would necessarily follow that mankind, in general, would perish without even knowing whether a God exists for the universe or whether none exists, and still less would they attribute to Him a government or reject from Him an imperfection[[fn:284]].  No one would ever escape this calamity, except perhaps [[t:0]]one individual in a city or[[t:1]] (at most[[t:3]]) [[t:4]]two in a family[[t:5]][[fn:285]].
root.text.Part 1..33.6: As for those who are [[t:0]]the remnants which the Eternal One calls[[t:1]][[fn:286]], perfection, which is the ultimate goal, shall be truly acquired only after the preparatory studies. Solomon has already declared that the preparatory studies are absolutely necessary, and that it is impossible to attain true wisdom, unless one has exercised oneself; he said: [[t:2]]If the iron is dulled and has not been sharpened, shall it vanquish armies? but even more preparation is required to[[t:3]] ([[t:4]]acquire[[t:5]]) [[t:6]]wisdom[[t:7]] (Ecclesiastes, [Lat.: Chapter] 10, [Lat.: verse] 10)[[fn:287]]; and he said further: [[t:8]]Heed the counsel and receive instruction, that thou mayest become wise at the end[[t:9]] (Proverbs, [Lat.: Chapter] 19, [Lat.: verse] 20).
root.text.Part 1..33.7: That which further renders necessary the acquisition of preparatory knowledge is, that a multitude of doubts speedily present themselves to a man during his study, and that he perceivs with equal speed the objections—I mean, how certain assertions may be refuted (for it is in this as in the demolition of an edifice[[fn:288]])—whilst one cannot well establish assertions nor resolve doubts, save by means of many principles drawn from these preparatory branches of knowledge. He, therefore, who enters upon speculation without preparatory study, is like unto one who, running with all his might to reach a place, falls by the way into a deep pit whence he has no means of egress, so that he perishes; had he abstained from running and remained in his place, he would surely have done better.
root.text.Part 1..33.8: Solomon, in the Proverbs, has extensively delineated the habits of the slothful and their incapacity, all of which constitutes an allegory concerning the inability to pursue knowledge; speaking of him who desires to attain the ultimate principles (of science), and who, neglecting to acquire the preparatory knowledge conducive to these ultimate principles, does nought but desire, he expresses himself thus: [[t:0]]The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labour. All the day he covets greedily: but the righteous gives and spares not[[t:1]] (Prov., 21, 25 and 26). His meaning is that, if his desire proves fatal, the cause thereof lies in his neglect to undertake that which might assuage this desire; that, on the contrary, he does nought but ardently desire, and fixes his hopes upon that for the acquisition of which he possesses no instrument; it would, therefore, have been more expedient for him to relinquish this desire. Observe how well the conclusion of the allegory explains its commencement, by stating: [[t:2]]but the[[t:3]] [[t:4]]RIGHTEOUS[[t:5]] [[t:6]]gives and spares not;[[t:7]] for [[t:8]]righteous[[t:9]] (or [[t:10]]pious[[t:11]]) can only be opposed to [[t:12]]slothful[[t:13]] according to what we have expounded. He means, indeed, that the [[t:14]]righteous[[t:15]] amongst men is he who renders unto everything that which is due to it, that is to say (who dedicates) his entire time to study and reserves nothing for other pursuits; it is as if he had said: [[t:16]]but the righteous dedicates his days to science and reserves none thereof[[t:17]], an expression analogous to this: [[t:18]]Give not thy strength unto women[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]Ibid.[[t:21]], XXXI, 3).
root.text.Part 1..33.9: The greater part of the learned—I speak of those who possess a reputation for science—are afflicted with this malady, I mean that of seeking the ultimate ends (of science) and of discoursing thereon, without occupying themselves with preparatory studies. There are some in whom ignorance and the desire for dominion reach such a point as to make them blame those preparatory branches of knowledge which they are either incapable of grasping or too slothful to study, and who endeavour to show that they are injurious or (at the least) useless; but, when one reflects thereon, the truth is clear and manifest[[fn:289]].
root.text.Part 1..33.10: The FOURTH CAUSE is to be found in the natural dispositions; for it has been set forth and even demonstrated that the moral virtues are preparatory for the rational virtues[[fn:290]], and that the acquisition of true rational virtues—by which I mean perfect intelligible notions—is possible only unto a man who has well disciplined his morals and is calm and composed. There be many who possess, from their origin, a disposition of temperament wherewith no moral improvement is possible. He, for instance, who by nature has a heart of an exceedingly hot temperature[[fn:291]] cannot refrain from being violent, even though he should exert the greatest efforts upon himself[[fn:292]]; and he whose testicles are of a hot and moist temperament and strongly constituted, and whose seminal vessels produce much sperm, shall hardly be able to remain chaste, even though he should make extreme efforts upon himself. Likewise, thou shalt find certain men full of levity and thoughtlessness, whose very agitated and disordered movements indicate a vicious complexion and a bad temperament of which no account can be rendered[[fn:293]]. In such as these, perfection shall never be seen, and to occupy oneself with them in this matter[[fn:294]] would be pure folly on the part of him who should do so; for this science, as thou knowest, is neither medicine nor geometry, and, for the reasons we have stated, not everyone is prepared for it. It must therefore be preceded by moral preparations, so that man may attain to extreme rectitude and perfection; for the froward is abomination to the Lord: but His secret is with the righteous (Prov. iii. 32). This is why it is deemed ill to teach it to young men; for even these cannot receive it—having a boiling nature and a preoccupied mind, by reason of the flame of youth—until that flame which troubls them be extinguished, and they have obtained calm and tranquillity, and their heart has become humble and submissive by temperament. It is then that they will themselves desire to rise to that high degree[[fn:295]] which is the perception of God, I mean the science of metaphysics which has been designated by the name of Ma’asé mercabâ[[fn:296]], as Scripture says: The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart (Ps. xxxiv. 18) and elsewhere: I dwell (in the) high and holy place, and with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, etc. (Isaiah lvii. 15).
root.text.Part 1..33.11: It is for this reason that in the Talmud, concerning these words: the first elements thereof shall be transmitted to him, they (the Doctors) say[[fn:297]]: “They do not transmit even the first elements, save to a president of a tribunal, and only if he has a heart of affliction[[fn:298]];” and by this is meant humility, submission, and great piety joined to science.
root.text.Part 1..33.12: In the same place it is said: “They transmit the secrets of the Torah only to a man of counsel, a wise thinker, and one who expresses himself with intelligence[[fn:299]];” and these are qualities for which a natural disposition is indispensable. Knowest thou not that there are people very weak in giving an opinion, although very intelligent, whilst there is another who has a sound judgment and who knows well how to direct political affairs? It is such a one who is called יועץ, a man of counsel; nevertheless, he might not understand an intelligible thing[[fn:300]], even should it approach the first notions[[fn:301]], and he might even in this respect be very stupid and without any resource: Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he has no heart to it? (Prov. xvii. 16). There is another who is intelligent, of a natural penetration, and who masters the most obscure subjects, expressing himself with conciseness and accuracy[[fn:302]]—and it is he who is called נכון לחש, one who expresses himself with intelligence—but who has not laboured and has not acquired the sciences. But he who has acquired the sciences in act is he who is called חכם חרשים, a wise thinker. “When he speaks,” say the Doctors, “all become as if they were dumb[[fn:303]].”
root.text.Part 1..33.13: Observe well how they have laid down as a condition, making use of a sacred text[[fn:304]], that the person be perfectly versed in social government and in the speculative sciences, and possess, in addition thereto, natural penetration, intelligence, and a good elocution to present the subjects in such a manner as to afford a glimpse of them; and it is only then that they transmit to him the secrets of the Torah.
root.text.Part 1..33.14: In the same place it is said: “R. Johanan having said to R. Eleazar: Come, let me teach thee the Ma’asé mercabâ, the latter replied: אכתי לא קשאי,” which signifies: I am not yet old, and I find myself still of a boiling nature and with the levity of youth. Thou seest, therefore, that they have also made age a condition, joined to those virtues of which we have just spoken; and how then could one engage in this matter with the commonalty of men, children, and women?
root.text.Part 1..33.15: The FIFTH CAUSE is found in the occupations necessitated by the wants of the body, which constitute the first perfection[[fn:305]], especially when thereunto is joined the care for wife and children, and above all when there is added the pursuit of the superfluities of life, which, through custom and evil habits, become a potent natural necessity[[fn:306]]. Verily, even the perfect man, such as we have described, when he occupies himself much with these necessary things, and a fortiori when he concerns himself with things not necessary and desirs them with ardor, his speculative aspirations wax weak and are submerged; he seeks them no longer save with lukewarmness and slackness and with little solicitude; and then he perceivs not even that which he has the faculty to perceive, or else he has a confused perception, mingled of apprehension and incapacity.
root.text.Part 1..33.16: It is by reason of all these causes that the subjects in question befit but a very small number of the select few, and not the vulgar; wherefore they must be hidden from the beginner and he must be restrained from approaching them[[fn:307]], even as a young child is prevented from taking coarse food and from lifting heavy weights.
root.text.Part 1..34.0: It is not to be supposed that all which we have preliminarily stated, in the preceding chapters, concerning the importance of the subject, its obscurity, the difficulty of apprehending it, and the reserve to be observed regarding the vulgar, applies likewise to the negation of corporeality and that of the passions[[fn:308]]. Such is not the case; but, on the contrary, just as it is necessary to instruct children[[fn:309]] and promulgate among the masses that God [may He be glorified!] is [[t:0]]one[[t:1]] and that no other save Him is to be worshipped, so likewise must they learn, by tradition, that God is not a body, that there is no resemblance, in anywise, between Him and His creatures, that His existence resembles not theirs, that His life resembles not that of creatures endowed with life, nor His knowledge that of creatures endowed with knowledge[[fn:310]], and that the difference between Him and them consists not merely in degree, but rather in the very nature of existence. I mean, that it must be established for all that our knowledge and His, or our power and His, differ not by [[t:2]]more[[t:3]] and [[t:4]]less[[t:5]], or in that one is [[t:6]]stronger[[t:7]] and the other [[t:8]]weaker[[t:9]], or by other similar distinctions; for the strong and the weak are necessarily alike in kind, and a single definition comprehends them both; and likewise, all proportional relation obtains only between two things of the same kind, as has also been explained in the physical sciences[[fn:311]]. But all that is attributed to God is distinct from our attributes in every respect, such that the two things cannot be comprised within a single definition; just as His existence and the existence of that which is outside of Him are called, both alike, [[t:10]]existence[[t:11]] only by homonymy, as I shall explain.
root.text.Part 1..34.1: And this should suffice for children and for the vulgar to establish in their minds that there exists a perfect Being who is not a body, nor a faculty in a body; that this Being is God, that no kind of imperfection can reach Him, and that on this account He is in no wise subject to passivity.
root.text.Part 1..34.2: What is to be said concerning the attributes, how they are to be removed from Him (God), what is the meaning of the attributes applied to Him, likewise what is to be said concerning the manner in which He created all things and His manner of governing the world, how His providence extends over that which is outside of Him, what is to be understood by His will, His perception, His knowledge of all that He knows, likewise what is to be understood by Prophecy and what are its different degrees, and finally what is to be understood by the names of God, which, however numerous they be, designate a single Being—all these things are profound subjects; these are, in reality, the secrets of the Torah, and they are the mysteries which are constantly spoken of in the books of the prophets and in the discourses of the doctors. These are the things of which one must teach only the first elements, as we have said, and even then only to such a person as we have described.
root.text.Part 1..34.3: But if the matter concerns the removal of corporeity, and the exclusion from God of any likeness to creatures or of any passions, then is it a thing whereon one must speak clearly, which must be explained to every man according to his capacity[[fn:312]] and taught as a tradition unto children, unto women, unto simple folk, and unto those who lack natural aptitude; even as they learn by tradition that God is one, that He is eternal, and that none other but He must be worshipped. Verily, there is no unity save when corporeity is removed; for a body is not one, but rather composed of matter and form, which, by their definition, constitute two, and it is moreover divisible and susceptible of being parted. And if, having received this teaching, having become accustomed thereto, and having been nurtured and grown therein, they be troubled by certain texts of the prophetical books, one shall explain the sense thereof unto them, and initiate them into the manner of interpreting them, and call their attention to the homonymies and metaphors wherewith this treatise deals, until they be convinced of the truth of the belief in the unity of God and the veracity of the prophetical books.
root.text.Part 1..34.4: As for him whose mind refrains from understanding the allegorical interpretation of the texts, and from understanding that there may be a concordance in the name despite the difference in the sense[[fn:313]], thou shalt say unto him: “The interpretation of this text is understood by men of science; but as for thee, thou shalt know that God is not a body and that He is impassible, for passivity implies change, whereas God is not subject to change, resembls nothing of all that is outside of Him, and has absolutely no definition in common with any thing whatsoever[[fn:314]]; and thou shalt also know that such discourse of a prophet is true and must be interpreted allegorically.” There one shall stop with him; but one must not let the belief in corporeity, or the belief in any thing that pertains to bodies, establish itself in any man, any more than one should allow the belief in the non-existence of God, the notion of association[[fn:315]], or the worship of another than He, to take root.
root.text.Part 1..35.0: I shall explain unto thee, when I speak of the attributes, in what sense it has been said that such a thing pleass God, or provoks and movs Him to wrath; for it is in that sense that it is said of certain persons that God found pleasure in them, or that He was wroth, or that He was provoked against them. This is not the purpose of this chapter; but it has for its purpose that which I am about to say.
root.text.Part 1..35.1: Know that upon examining the entire Pentateuch and all the books of the prophets, one will find the expressions of [[t:0]]wrath[[t:1]], of [[t:2]]irritation[[t:3]], of [[t:4]]jealousy[[t:5]] only when the discourse pertains particularly to [[t:6]]idolatry[[t:7]]; and one will find that none is designated an [[t:8]]enemy[[t:9]] of God, or [[t:10]]hostile[[t:11]] to Him, or His [[t:12]]adversary[[t:13]], save the idolater in particular. We read, for example: … [[t:14]]and lest ye serve other gods, etc., so that the wrath of the Eternal be kindled against you[[t:15]] (Deuteronomy, 11, 16, 17); [[t:16]]Lest the wrath of the Eternal, thy God, be kindled[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]Ibid.[[t:19]], 6, 15); [[t:20]]To provoke Him to anger with the work of your hands[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]Ibid.[[t:23]], 31, 29); [[t:24]]They have moved Me to jealousy with that which is not God; they have provoked Me to anger with their vanities, etc.[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]Ibid.[[t:27]], 32, 21); [[t:28]]For a jealous God, etc.[[t:29]] ([[t:30]]Ibid.[[t:31]], 6, 15); [[t:32]]Why have they provoked Me to anger with their graven images?[[t:33]] (Jeremiah, 8, 19); [[t:34]]Because his sons and his daughters have provoked him[[t:35]] (Deuteronomy, 32, 19); [[t:36]]For a fire is kindled in My anger[[t:37]] ([[t:38]]Ibid.[[t:39]], [[t:40]]V[[t:41]]. 22); [[t:42]]The Eternal[[t:43]][[fn:316]] [[t:44]]takes vengeance on His adversaries, and He reserves wrath for His enemies[[t:45]] (Nahum, 1, 2; [[t:46]]And he repays His adversaries[[t:47]] (Deuteronomy, 7, 10); [[t:48]]Until he has cast out his enemies[[t:49]] (Numbers, 32, 21); … [[t:50]]which the Eternal, thy God, hates[[t:51]] (Deuteronomy, 16, 22); [[t:52]]All that is an abomination unto the Eternal[[t:53]], ([[t:54]]all that[[t:55]]) [[t:56]]He hates[[t:57]] ([[t:58]]Ibid.[[t:59]], 12, 31). Examples of this nature are too numerous for enumeration; but should one trace them through all the (holy) books, one will indeed discover them.
root.text.Part 1..35.2: If the prophetical books have so strongly insisted thereon, it is solely because it concerns a false opinion relating to God, I mean, idolatry. If any one believed that Zeid were standing at the moment when he is sitting, his deviation from the truth would not be so grave as the deviation of him who should believe that fire is below the air, or that water is below the earth[[fn:317]], or that the earth is a plane, and other like things; the deviation of this latter would not be as the deviation of him who should believe that the sun is composed of the element of fire, or that the heaven is a hemisphere, and other like things; the deviation of this third would not be as the deviation of him who should believe that angels eat and drink, and other like things; the deviation of this fourth would not be as the deviation of him who should believe that one must worship some other thing besides God. For in proportion as ignorance and false belief relate to a greater object, I mean to that which occupies a more important rank in Being, they possess more gravity than when they relate to that which occupies an inferior rank. By false belief, I mean: that one believs a thing to be the contrary of what it truly is; by ignorance, I mean: that one is ignorant of what it is possible to know. The ignorance of him who should be ignorant of the measure of the cone or the sphericity of the sun would not be so grave as the ignorance of him who should not know whether God exists or whether the universe has no God; and the false belief of him who should believe that the cone forms the half of the cylinder[[fn:318]] or that the sun is a disk[[fn:319]] would not be so grave as the false belief of him who should believe that God is more than one.
root.text.Part 1..35.3: Thou knowest that all those who devote themselves to the worship of idols do not adore them in the sense that there exists no divinity beside them; for never did any man of past generations imagine, nor will any man of future generations imagine, that the figure fashioned by him of metal, stone, or wood, has itself created heaven and earth, and that it is that which governs them. This latter, on the contrary, is worshipped only in the sense that it is the symbol of a thing that is intermediate between us and God, as (Scripture) clearly says: Who would not fear thee, O King of nations? etc. (Jeremiah, x. 7); and elsewhere: And in every place incense is offered unto my name, etc. (Malachi, i. 11), alluding to that which, according to them (the heathens), is the first cause. We have already expounded this in our great work[[fn:320]], and it is a matter which none among our co-religionists disputs.
root.text.Part 1..35.4: But, since these misbelievers, whilst believing in the existence of God, applied their false belief to something that is due unto God alone,—I mean, to the worship and veneration (due to the Divinity), as it is said: And ye shall serve the Lord, etc. (Exodus, xxiii. 25), to the end that His existence might be well established in the belief of the people,—and since they believed they (could render) this duty to that which is without Him [a thing which contributed to make the existence of God vanish from the belief of the people, the latter perceiving only the practices of worship, without (penetrating) the meaning, nor (knowing) the reality of Him to whom this worship is addressed], this must necessarily cause them to deserve death, as it is expressly said: Thou shalt save alive nothing that breaths (Deuter., xx. 16); and the reason thereof is expressly given, which is, to put an end to this false opinion, lest others be infected thereby, as it is added: That they teach you not to do etc. (Ibid., v. 18).
root.text.Part 1..35.5: These (the idolaters) have been called enemies, adversaries, hostile (to God), and it has been said that he who acts thus renders (God) jealous, provoks Him to anger, and incits His wrath; what then shall be the condition of him whose infidelity relats to the very essence of God, and whose belief[[fn:321]] is the reverse of what He (God) really is, I mean, who believs not in His existence, or who believs Him to be two, or who believs Him to be a body, or who believs Him subject to passions, or who attributs to Him any imperfection whatsoever? Such a man is indubitably worse than he who worshipps an idol, considering it as an intermediary, or because, in his opinion, it is beneficent or harmful.
root.text.Part 1..35.6: Thou must know that by believing in corporeality or (by attributing to God) any of the conditions of the body, thou renderest Him jealous, thou provokest Him to anger, thou enkindlest the fire of His wrath, thou art an adversary, an enemy, hostile, much more even than he who devots himself to idolatry. If it should occur to thy mind that he who believs in corporeality might be excused because he had been so reared, or because of his ignorance and the weakness of his intelligence, thou shouldst think the same with regard to him who devots himself to idolatry; for he does it only through ignorance or through education: they maintain the custom of their fathers[[fn:322]]. If thou shouldst say (regarding the former) that the literal sense of Scripture causs him to fall into this doubt, thou shouldst likewise know that he who worshipps idols is led to their worship only by imaginations and false ideas. There is therefore no excuse for him who, being himself incapable of meditation, follows not the authority of thinkers who seek the truth; for, verily, I do not declare him a misbeliever who does not remove corporeality (from God) by means of demonstration, but I declare him a misbeliever who believs not that it must be removed; the more so as we have the version of Onkelos and that of Jonathan ben-Uziel, who do their utmost to remove the idea of corporeality (from God). Such was the aim of this chapter.
root.text.Part 1..36.0: Panîm (פנים) is a homonym, and it is so chiefly in its metaphorical relation[[fn:323]]. It is, in the first place, the name of the face (or of the countenance) of any animal; e.g.: And all faces (פניס) are turned into paleness (Jeremiah, xxx. 6); Wherefore is your countenance (פניכס) sad (Genesis, xl. 7)? The examples thereof are numerous.
root.text.Part 1..36.1: It signifies also anger; e.g., And her countenance of wrath was no more (פניה) (I Sam. i. 18)[[fn:324]]; and, according to this signification, it has been oft employed to denote the wrath and the indignation of God; e.g., The anger (פני) of the Lord has divided them (Lament. iv. 16); The face (פני) of the Lord is against them that do evil (Ps. xxxiv. 17); My anger (פנַי) shall pass away, and I will give thee rest[[fn:325]] (Exodus xxxiii. 14); And I will set My face (פנַי) against that man, and against his family (Levit. xx. 5); there be many examples thereof.
root.text.Part 1..36.2: It signifies also the presence of a person and the place where he abids; e.g., He was established in the presence (על פני) of all his brethren (Genesis xxv. 18); Before the face (על פני) of all the people I will be glorified (Levit. x. 3), where the sense is: in their presence; .... if he will not curse Thee to Thy face (על פניך) (Job i. 11), that is to say, in Thy presence, Thou being there. It is according to this signification that it was said: And the Lord spake unto Moses face to face (פנים בפנים) (Exodus xxxiii. 11), which means: in the presence of one another, without intermediary, even as it is said elsewhere: Come, let us look one another in the face (II Kings xiv. 8); and as it has further been said: The Lord talked with you face to face (Deuter. v. 4), which, in another place, has been clearly expressed thus: Ye heard the voice of the words, but ye saw no similitude; only ye heard a voice (Ibid. iv. 12); and this it is which was called face to face; likewise by the words: And the Lord spake unto Moses face to face, naught else was expressed but what is said elsewhere concerning the manner in which God spake unto him[[fn:326]]: He heard the voice of one speaking unto him (Numbers vii. 89). Thus it is manifest unto thee that by face to face it is intended to indicate that he (Moses) heard the voice (divine) without the mediation of an angel. The words: And My face shall not be seen (Exodus xxxiii. 23) contain yet this same sense (of presence), that is to say: the reality of My existence as it truly is cannot be apprehended.
root.text.Part 1..36.3: Panîm (פנים) is likewise an adverb of place (signifying before), which is expressed in Arabic by imâm (أمام) or beîn yedei (بين يدى), and it is oft employed in this sense when speaking of God; e.g., לפני י״י, before the Lord (Genesis xviii. 22, and passim). It is in this sense also that the words ופני לא יראו (And My face shall not be seen) are taken in the interpretation of Onkelos, who says: ודקדמי לא יתחזון, and those that are before Me shall not be seen, to indicate that there be likewise sublime creatures which man cannot perceive in their reality, and which are the separate Intelligences[[fn:327]]; these have been brought into relation with God, as being constantly before Him and in His presence, because Providence cleavs strongly and constantly unto them[[fn:328]]. That which, according to him—I mean according to Onkelos—can be perceived in reality, are those things which occupy, in Being, a rank inferior to those others—I mean such as have matter and form[[fn:329]]; and it is with regard to these things that he says (in his paraphrase): ותחזי ית דבתראי And thou shalt see that which is behind Me, that is to say, the beings from which, as it were, I turn away and which I leave behind Me, (which is said) allegorically to indicate their remoteness from the Divine Being. Thou shalt hear later my interpretation of the request of Moses[[fn:330]].
root.text.Part 1..36.4: Panîm is also an adverb of time signifying before (aforetime) or of old; e.g., In former time (לפנים) in Israel, etc. (Ruth iv. 7); Of old (לפנים) hast Thou laid the foundation of the earth (Ps. cii. 26).
root.text.Part 1..36.5: Finally [[t:0]]panîm[[t:1]] signifies also [[t:2]]égard[[t:3]] and [[t:4]]attention[[t:5]] (or [[t:6]]soin[[t:7]]); for example: [[t:8]]לא תשא פני דל[[t:9]] [[t:10]]Thou shalt not regard the poor[[t:11]] (Leviticus, 19, 15); [[t:12]]ונשוא פנים[[t:13]] [[t:14]]And the respected man[[t:15]] (Isaiah, 3, 3); [[t:16]]אשר לא ישא פנים[[t:17]] [[t:18]]Who has no regard[[t:19]] (Deuteronomy, 10, 17), and many other passages. And it is also in this sense that it has been said: [[t:20]]That the Lord turns His face[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]פניו[[t:23]]) [[t:24]]toward thee and givs thee peace[[t:25]] (Numbers, 6, 25), which means that Providence[[t:26]] accompanies us.
root.text.Part 1..37.0: [[t:0]]A’hôr[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]אחור[[t:3]]) is a homonym which signifies [[t:4]]dos[[t:5]] (or [[t:6]]partie de derrière[[t:7]]); for example: [[t:8]]The derrière[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]אחורי[[t:11]]) [[t:12]]of the tabernacle[[t:13]] (Exodus, [Lat.: Chapter] 26, [Lat.: verse] 12); [[t:14]]And the lance issued forth from behind[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]מאחריו[[t:17]]) (II Samuel, [Lat.: Chapter] 2, [Lat.: verse] 23). It is also an adverb of time signifying [[t:18]]after;[[t:19]] for example: [[t:20]]And after him[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]ואחריו[[t:23]]) [[t:24]]he did not rise as he did[[t:25]] (II Kings, [Lat.: Chapter] 23, [Lat.: verse] 25); [[t:26]]After[[t:27]] ([[t:28]]אחר[[t:29]]) [[t:30]]these things[[t:31]] (Genesis, [Lat.: Chapter] 15, [Lat.: verse] 1); and numerous examples are to be found.
root.text.Part 1..37.1: It also conveys the sense of [[t:0]]following[[t:1]], [[t:2]]walking in the footsteps[[t:3]] of a person, by imitating their conduct; for example: [[t:4]]You shall walk after[[t:5]] ([Lat.: post], [[t:6]]אחרי[[t:7]]) [[t:8]]the Eternal, your God[[t:9]] (Deuteronomy, 13, 5); [[t:10]]They shall walk after[[t:11]] ([Lat.: post], [[t:12]]אחרי[[t:13]]) [[t:14]]the Eternal[[t:15]] (Hosea, 11, 10), which signifies [[t:16]]obeying God[[t:17]], of [[t:18]]walking in the footsteps of His actions[[t:19]] and of [[t:20]]imitating His conduct;[[t:21]] (similarly:) [[t:22]]He has walked after[[t:23]] ([Lat.: post], [[t:24]]אחרי[[t:25]]) [[t:26]]a[[t:27]] ([Lat.: vanus], [[t:28]]vain[[t:29]]) [[t:30]]command[[t:31]] ([Lat.: ius], [[t:32]]Ibid.[[t:33]], 5, 11).— It is in this sense that it has been said: [[t:34]]And thou shalt see me behind[[t:35]] ([Lat.: post], [[t:36]]אחורי[[t:37]]) (Exodus, 33, 23), (which signifies) thou shalt grasp that which follows me, that which is akin to me and that which results from my will, namely all my creatures, as I shall explain in one of the chapters of this treatise[[fn:331]].
root.text.Part 1..38.0: [[t:0]]Leb[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]לב[[t:3]]) is a homonym which denotes (originally) the [[t:4]]heart[[t:5]], I mean the member in which, for every being endowed with it, resides the principle of life[[fn:332]]; p. ex.: [[t:6]]And he thrust them into the heart[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]בלב[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]of Absalom[[t:11]] (II Sam., 18, 14).
root.text.Part 1..38.1: And as this organ is found in the midst of the body, the midst of any thing has been thus metaphorically so called; e.g.: Unto the heart or the midst (לב) of heaven (Deut. iv. 11); In the midst (לבת) of the fire (Exodus, iii. 2).
root.text.Part 1..38.2: This is also the name of the [[t:0]]thought[[t:1]]; p. e. g.: [[t:2]]My heart[[t:3]] ([[t:4]]לבי[[t:5]]) [[t:6]]has it not followed etc.[[t:7]] (II Kings, 5, 26); that is to say, I was present by my [[t:8]]thought[[t:9]] when such and such a thing occurred. In the same sense (it is said): [[t:10]]And you shall not incline after your heart[[t:11]] (Numbers, 15, 39), that is to say, you shall not follow your [[t:12]]thoughts[[t:13]] (and elsewhere:) [[t:14]]whose heart turns away today[[t:15]] (Deuteronomy, 29, 18), (that is to say) whose [[t:16]]thought[[t:17]] turns away.
root.text.Part 1..38.3: It signifies further opinion (or sentiment); e.g.: All the rest of Israel were of one heart (לב) to make David king (I Chron. xii. 38), that is to say, of the same sentiment; likewise: And fools die for want of heart (Prov. x. 21), which is to say: for want of good sense. The same obtains in this passage: My heart has never turned aside (Job xxvii. 6), which signifies: my sentiment has never turned away nor strayed from this thing; for the beginning of the verse says: My righteousness I hold fast, and will not let it go, (which well accords with these words:) and my heart has never turned aside[[fn:333]]. The sense which I give here to the word יחרף, I find likewise in שפחה נחרפת לאיש (Levit. xix. 20), — the word נחרפת being analogous to the Arabic word منحرفة , changed, turned aside, — that is to say, “a bondmaid whose bonds of servitude have been changed into bonds of marriage[[fn:334]]”.
root.text.Part 1..38.4: The term [[t:0]]Leb[[t:1]] (heart) also signifies [[t:2]]volonté[[t:3]] (or [[t:4]]intention[[t:5]]); for instance: [[t:6]]And I will give you shepherds according to my heart[[t:7]] (Jeremiah, 3, 15)[[fn:335]]; [[t:8]]Is thy heart upright as mine is[[t:9]] (II Kings, 10, 15)? that is to say, is thy [[t:10]]volonté[[t:11]] (thy [[t:12]]intention[[t:13]]) in uprightness as mine? In this sense, it is sometimes employed metaphorically when speaking of God; for example: [[t:14]]He will act according to what is in my heart and in my soul[[t:15]] (I Samuel, 2, 35), that is to say, he will act according to my [[t:16]]volonté; And my eyes and my heart shall be there always[[t:17]] (I Kings, 9, 3), that is to say, my providence and my [[t:18]]volonté[[t:19]].
root.text.Part 1..38.5: — It signifies moreover intellect; e.g.: Vain (hollow-minded) man shall be endowed with heart (ילבב) (Job xi. 12), that is to say, shall become intelligent; likewise: A wise man's heart is at his right hand (Eccles. x. 2), that is, his intellect (turns) towards perfect things. Numerous examples thereof are to be found. It is in this signification that it must be taken wheresoever it is metaphorically applied to God, I mean as designating the intellect, save for those rare exceptions where it designats the will, according to the context of each passage. Likewise the expressions: And thou shalt consider it in thine heart (Deuter. iv. 39), And none considers in his heart (Isaiah xliv. 19), and all other such expressions, have all the sense of intellectual consideration, as it is expressly said: Yet the Lord has not given you an heart to perceive, etc. (Deuter. xxix. 4), which is similar to this other expression: Unto thee it was shewed, that thou mightest know, etc. (Ibid., iv. 35)[[fn:336]].
root.text.Part 1..38.6: As for these words: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thine heart (Ibid., vi. 5), the sense is, in my opinion: with all the forces of thy heart, that is to say with all the faculties of the body; for they all take their origin in the heart. Hereby is meant: thou shalt have as thy goal, in all thy deeds, the perception of God, as we have set forth in the commentary upon the Mishnah[[fn:337]] and in the Mishneh Torah[[fn:338]].
root.text.Part 1..39.0: [[t:0]]Roua’h[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]רוח[[t:3]]) is a homonym which designates first of all the [[t:4]]air[[t:5]], I mean one of the four elements; for example: [[t:6]]And the [[t:7]]air[[t:8]] ([[t:9]]רוח[[t:10]]) [[t:11]]of God was hovering[[t:12]] (Genesis, 1, 2)[[fn:339]].
root.text.Part 1..39.1: It is then the name of the [[t:0]]wind[[t:1]] that blows; p. ex.: [[t:2]]And the wind[[t:3]] ([Lat.: 'ruach'] [[t:4]]רוח[[t:5]]) [[t:6]]of the East bore away the locusts[[t:7]] (Exodus, 10, 13); [[t:8]]A wind[[t:9]] ([Lat.: 'ruach'] [[t:10]]רוח[[t:11]]) [[t:12]]of the West[[t:13]] ([Lat.: 'ibid.'] [[t:14]], [[t:15]]V[[t:16]]. 19); examples of this kind are numerous.
root.text.Part 1..39.2: It is also the name of the [[t:0]]vital spirit[[t:1]][[fn:340]]; e.g.: [[t:2]]A spirit[[t:3]] ([[t:4]]רוח[[t:5]]) [[t:6]]which departs and returns not[[t:7]] (Ps. 78, 39); [[t:8]]Who has within him a spirit[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]רוח[[t:11]]) [[t:12]]of life[[t:13]] (Genesis, 7, 15).
root.text.Part 1..39.3: This is still the name of the thing that remains of man after death, and which is not subject to perishing; e.g.: [[t:0]]And the spirit[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]והרוח[[t:3]]) [[t:4]]returns to God who gave it[[t:5]] (Eccl., XII, 7).
root.text.Part 1..39.4: It denots, moreover, the inspiration of divine intellect which emanats (from God) upon the prophets, and wherewith they prophesy [as we shall explain unto thee when we treat of prophecy in such wise as is meet for this treatise]; for example: And I will take of the spirit (מן הרוח) which is upon thee and I will put it upon them (Numbers xi. 17); And when the spirit (הרוח) rested upon them (Ibid., V. 25); The spirit (רוח) of the Lord spake by me (II Sam. xxiii. 2); of this there be numerous examples.
root.text.Part 1..39.5: Finally, this word signifies intention and will (or design); for example: A fool utters all (that which is in) his spirit (רוחו) (Prov. xxix. 11), that is to say, his intention and his purpose. Likewise: The spirit (רוח) of Egypt shall fail in the midst thereof, and I will destroy the counsel thereof (Isaiah xix. 3), which is to say: her designs shall be confounded and the art of governance shall be hidden from her; likewise: Who has measured the spirit (את־רוח) of the Lord, or where is the man who might make known unto us[[fn:341]] that which He purposs (Ibid., xl. 13)? which signifies: “Who is he that knows the order of His will or grasps the manner of His governance of the universe, that he might make it known unto us?”—a subject which we shall set forth in certain chapters concerning the governance (of the universe)[[fn:342]].
root.text.Part 1..39.6: Whenever the word ruaḥ (רוח) is attributed to God, it is according to the fifth signification[[fn:343]], and sometimes it is in the last sense, which is that of will, as we have set forth; it must therefore be explained in every passage according to that which the context of the discourse indicats.
root.text.Part 1..40.0: [[t:0]]Néphesch[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]נפש[[t:3]]) is a homonym which designates, in the first instance, the [[t:4]]animal soul[[t:5]] common to all beings endowed with sensibility[[fn:344]]; e.g.: … [[t:6]]having a soul[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]נפש[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]living[[t:11]] (Genesis, 1, 30). Then it denotes the [[t:12]]blood;[[t:13]] e.g.: [[t:14]]And thou shalt not eat the soul[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]הנפש[[t:17]]) [[t:18]]with the flesh[[t:19]] (Deuteronomy, 12, 23). Next, it is the name of the [[t:20]]rational soul[[t:21]], that is to say, of (that which constitutes) the [[t:22]]form of man;[[t:23]] e.g.: [[t:24]]By the living God who has made us this soul[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]את־הנפש הזאת[[t:27]]) (Jeremiah, 38, 16). It is, moreover, the name of that which remains of man after death[[fn:345]]; e.g.: [[t:28]]The soul[[t:29]] ([[t:30]]נפש[[t:31]]) [[t:32]]of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life[[t:33]] (I Samuel, 25, 29). Lastly, this word signifies [[t:34]]will;[[t:35]] e.g.: [[t:36]]To bind his princes at his pleasure[[t:37]] ([[t:38]]בנפשו[[t:39]]) (Psalm 105, 22), that is to say, at his [[t:40]]will;[[t:41]] likewise: [[t:42]]And deliver him not unto the will[[t:43]] ([[t:44]]בנפש[[t:45]]) [[t:46]]of his enemies[[t:47]] (Psalm 41, 3)[[fn:346]], that is to say, deliver him not unto their [[t:48]]will[[t:49]]. One takes in the same sense (the words): [[t:50]]If it be in your soul[[t:51]] ([[t:52]]את־נפשכם[[t:53]]) [[t:54]]to bury my dead[[t:55]] (Genesis, 23, 8), that is to say, if it be in your [[t:56]]intention[[t:57]] and in your [[t:58]]will;[[t:59]] likewise: [[t:60]]Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my soul[[t:61]] ([[t:62]]נפשי[[t:63]]) [[t:64]]could not be toward this people[[t:65]] (Jeremiah, 15, 1), where the sense is: my [[t:66]]will[[t:67]] would not be for them, that is to say, I would not desire to preserve them. Whenever the word [[t:68]]néphesch[[t:69]] ([[t:70]]נפש[[t:71]]) is attributed to God, it bears the sense of [[t:72]]will[[t:73]], as one has stated previously concerning the words: [[t:74]]He shall do according to that which is in mine heart and in my soul[[t:75]] (I Samuel, 2, 35)[[fn:347]], the meaning of which is: in my [[t:76]]will[[t:77]] and in my [[t:78]]intention[[t:79]].
root.text.Part 1..40.1: According to this signification the words ותקצר נפשו בעמל ישראל (Judges, x. 16) must be explained thus: and His will ceased from afflicting Israel. Jonathan ben-Uziel has not translated this passage; for having understood it according to the first signification (of the word nephesh), there resulted for him a passivity (attributed to God), and for that reason he abstained from translating it[[fn:348]]. But if one takes (the word nephesh) in the last signification, the explanation (of our passage) is right clear; for it is said previously that Divine Providence had forsaken them, so that they perished, and that they had implored His succour, but He succoured them not. When, therefore, they showed an exceeding repentance, being in a profound humiliation and under the dominion of the enemy[[fn:349]], He had pity upon them, and His will ceased from causing their affliction and their humiliation to endure. Thou must well consider this, for it is a remarkable (explanation). The ב in בעמל ישראל is in the place of מן, from; it is as if one had said מן עמל ישראל. The grammarians have enumerated many such examples, as: והנותר בבשר ובלחם and that which remains OF the flesh and OF the bread (Levit., viii. 32); נשאר בשנים that which remains OF the years (Ibid., xxv. 52); בגר ובאזרח הארץ (whether he be) OF strangers or OF those born in the land (Exodus, xii. 19)[[fn:350]]. This is frequently found.
root.text.Part 1..41.0: Hay [[t:0]] (['living', 'alive'] [[t:1]] ([[t:2]]חי[[t:3]] [[t:4]]vivant, vivre[[t:5]]) is said of that which has growth and sensibility[[fn:351]]; p. ex.: [[t:6]]All that moves which is living [[t:7]] ([[t:8]]חי[[t:9]]) (Genesis, 9, 3). It also signifies [[t:10]]to recover[[t:11]] from a very violent disease; p. ex.: [[t:12]]When he was recovered [[t:13]] ([[t:14]]ויחי[[t:15]]) [[t:16]]from his disease [[t:17]] (Isaiah, 38, 9); ([[t:18]]Iis remained[[t:19]]) [[t:20]]in the camp until they were recovered [[t:21]] ([[t:22]]עד חיותם[[t:23]]) (Joshua, 5, 8); similarly: [[t:24]]of sound flesh [[t:25]] ([[t:26]]חי[[t:27]]) (Leviticus, 13, 10).
root.text.Part 1..41.1: Similarly the word muth (מות), which signifies to die, denots also a violent sickness; e.g.: And his heart died (וימת) within him, and he became as a stone (I Sam., xxv. 37), which denots the violence of the sickness (of Nabal). Wherefore it was explicitly said of the son of the woman of Zarephath: And his sickness was so sore, that there was no breath (of life) left in him (I Kings, xvii. 17); for had it been simply said, and he died ([[t:22]]וימת[[t:23]]), one might have thought that it concerned only a violent sickness bordering upon death, like unto that of Nabal when he heard the news[[fn:352]].
root.text.Part 1..41.2: In fact, someone from Andalusia said (concerning the son of the woman of Sarepta) that he ceased to breathe, so that no breath was visible in him, as sometimes occurs in cases of apoplexy and [[t:0]]hysterical suffocation[[t:1]][[fn:353]], to such an extent that one does not know if (the patient) is dead or alive, a doubt that may last for one or two days.
root.text.Part 1..41.3: This word ([[t:0]]חי[[t:1]]) is also frequently employed when treating of the acquisition of knowledge; e. g.: [[t:2]]And they shall be life[[t:3]] ([[t:4]]חיים[[t:5]]) [[t:6]]unto thy soul[[t:7]] (Prov., 3, 22); [[t:8]]For whoso finds me finds life[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]Ibid.[[t:11]], 9, 35); [[t:12]]For they are life unto those that find them[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]Ibid.[[t:15]], 4, 22), and many other passages. In conformity with this, sound opinions have been denominated [[t:16]]life[[t:17]], and corrupt opinions, [[t:18]]death;[[t:19]] the Most High has said: [[t:20]]See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil[[t:21]] (Deuteronomy, 30, 15), where the two words are clearly explained by declaring that good is [[t:22]]life[[t:23]], and evil, [[t:24]]death[[t:25]]. I interpret in like manner the words: [[t:26]]That ye may live, etc.[[t:27]] ([[t:28]]Ibid.[[t:29]], 5, 30); and this in accordance with the traditional explanation of this passage: [[t:30]]That thou mayest be happy, etc.[[t:31]] ([[t:32]]Ibid.[[t:33]], 22, 7)[[fn:354]]. It is in conformity with this metaphorical sense (of the word [[t:34]]חי[[t:35]]), so prevalent in the (Hebrew) language, that the doctors have said: “Pious men, even after their death, are called [[t:36]]living[[t:37]]; and the wicked, even during their life, are called [[t:38]]dead[[t:39]][[fn:355]].” It is essential that thou impress this upon thy mind.
root.text.Part 1..42.0: [[t:0]]Canaph[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]כנף[[t:3]]) is an homonym, and it is so especially in relation to metaphorical usage. It originally denotes the [[t:4]]wing[[t:5]] of birds; e.g.: … [[t:6]]of every bird having wings[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]כנף[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]which soars in the heavens[[t:11]] (Deutér., 4, 17).
root.text.Part 1..42.1: Subsequently, we have employed it metaphorically to signify the extremities and the angles of garments; for example: [[t:0]]Aux quatre coins[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]כנפות[[t:3]]) [[t:4]]of thy garment[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]Ibid.[[t:7]], 22, 12).
root.text.Part 1..42.2: It has furthermore been employed metaphorically to denote the extremities and borders of the inhabited part of the earth, remote from our countries; e.g.: That it might take hold of the ends (בכנפות) of the earth (Job xxxviii. 13); From the uttermost part (מכנף) of the earth have we heard songs (Isaiah xxiv. 16).
root.text.Part 1..42.3: Ibn Janah[[fn:356]] says that this word is also found in the sense of [[t:0]]to veil[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]to hide, to conceal[[t:3]]), after the manner of the Arabic, in which it is said[[fn:357]] [[t:4]]kanaftu al-shei[[t:5]] [[t:6]](كَنَفْتُ الشَّيْءَ)[[t:7]] in the sense of: [[t:8]]I have concealed the thing[[t:9]]; and he explains [[t:10]]ולא יכנף עוד מוריך[[t:11]] (Isaiah xxx. 20): [[t:12]]and he that enlightens thee[[t:13]][[fn:358]] [[t:14]]shall no longer hide himself from thee, nor be veiled[[t:15]], which is a right good interpretation. Thence comes, in my judgment, the expression [[t:16]]ולא יגלה כנף אביו[[t:17]] (Deut. xxiii. 1), that is to say: [[t:18]]he shall not lift the veil of his father[[t:19]][[fn:359]]. Likewise the words [[t:20]]ופרשת כנפך על אמתך[[t:21]] (Ruth iii. 9) must be explained, according to my view: [[t:22]]spread thy veil over thy handmaid[[t:23]].
root.text.Part 1..42.4: It is in this latter sense, as I deem, that the word [[t:0]]kanaph[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]כנף[[t:3]]) has been metaphorically applied to the Creator, and likewise to the angels; for the angels, in our opinion, possess no body, even as I shall hereafter set forth[[fn:360]]. Thus the words [[t:4]]אשר באת לחסות תחת כנפיו[[t:5]] (Ruth ii. 12) must be rendered: [[t:6]]under whose veil thou art come to trust[[t:7]][[fn:361]]. Likewise, whenever the word [[t:8]]kanaph[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]כנף[[t:11]]) relats to angels, it has the signification of [[t:12]]veil[[t:13]]. Hast thou not observed these words: [[t:14]]With twain[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]wings[[t:17]]) [[t:18]]he[[t:19]] [[t:20]]COVERED[[t:21]] [[t:22]]his face, and with twain he[[t:23]] [[t:24]]COVERED[[t:25]] [[t:26]]his feet[[t:27]] (Isaiah vi. 2)? Verily, the cause of its existence—I speak of that of the angel—is enshrouded in obscurity[[fn:362]], and this is what is called [[t:28]]his face[[t:29]]. In like manner, those things of which the angel is the cause, and which are denoted by [[t:30]]his feet[[t:31]] [as we have explained in treating of the homonym [[t:32]]regel[[t:33]][[fn:363]]], are likewise obscure; for the action of the [[t:34]]Intelligences[[t:35]][[fn:364]] is obscure, and their influence[[fn:365]] is not manifest unto us save when we have devoted ourselves to study, and this for two reasons, of which one resids in them and the other in us—I mean the weakness of our understanding and the difficulty of comprehending the [[t:36]]Separate Intelligence[[t:37]] in its reality. As for the words: [[t:38]]and with twain he did fly[[t:39]] ([[t:40]]ibid.[[t:41]]), I shall explain in a separate chapter the reason wherefore the motion of flight has been attributed to angels[[fn:366]].

It signifies also [[t:20]]care[[t:21]] (or [[t:22]]regard[[t:23]]), as it is said in reference to Jeremiah: [[t:24]]Take him and look well[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]עיניך[[t:27]]) [[t:28]]to him[[t:29]] (Jeremiah xxxix. 12), which is to say: have a care for him. And it is according to this metaphor that it must be understood wherever it is applied to God; e.g.: [[t:30]]Mine eyes[[t:31]] ([[t:32]]עיני[[t:33]]) [[t:34]]and mine heart shall be there perpetually[[t:35]] (1 Kings ix. 3), that is to say, my [[t:36]]Providence[[t:37]] and my purpose, even as we have formerly stated[[fn:368]]; ... [[t:38]]whereon the eyes[[t:39]] ([[t:40]]עיני[[t:41]]) [[t:42]]of the Lord thy God are always[[t:43]] (Deut. xi. 12), that is to say, upon which (watches) His [[t:44]]Providence; The eyes[[t:45]] ([[t:46]]עיני[[t:47]]) [[t:48]]of the Lord which run to and fro, etc.[[t:49]] (Zechariah iv. 10)[[fn:369]], that is, His [[t:50]]Providence[[t:51]] encompasses all that is upon the earth, as shall be declared in other chapters treating of [[t:52]]Providence[[t:53]][[fn:370]].
root.text.Part 1..43.1: If there be joined, in speaking of the [[t:0]]eyes[[t:1]] (of God), the verb [[t:2]]ראה[[t:3]] or [[t:4]]חזה[[t:5]], [[t:6]]to see[[t:7]], as, for instance: [[t:8]]Open thine eyes and see[[t:9]] (2 Kings xix. 16); [[t:10]]His eyes behold[[t:11]] (Ps. xi. 4), there is ever denoted thereby an [[t:12]]intellectual[[t:13]] perception, and not a [[t:14]]sensory[[t:15]] one; for [[t:16]]to perceive by the senses[[t:17]] is ever to be passive, to be affected[[fn:371]], as thou knowest, whereas God is [[t:18]]active[[t:19]], and not subject to [[t:20]]passivity[[t:21]], even as I shall demonstrate.
root.text.Part 1..44.0: [[t:0]]Shama’[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]שמע[[t:3]]) is an homonym signifying [[t:4]]to hear[[t:5]] (to hearken) and also [[t:6]]to accept[[t:7]] (to listen, to obey). For the signification of [[t:8]]to hear[[t:9]], one may cite: [[t:10]]It shall not be heard[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]לא ישמע[[t:13]]) [[t:14]]out of thy mouth[[t:15]] (Exodus xxiii. 13); [[t:16]]And the fame thereof was heard[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]נשמע[[t:19]]) [[t:20]]in Pharaoh’s house[[t:21]] (Genesis xlv. 16), and many other examples.
root.text.Part 1..44.1: Examples are also numerous for the employment of [[t:0]]schama’[[t:1]] in the sense of [[t:2]]accueillir[[t:3]] or of [[t:4]]écouter[[t:5]], such as: [[t:6]]But they heeded not[[t:7]] ([Lat.: they did not hear] [[t:8]]ולא שמעו[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]Moses[[t:11]] (Exodus, 6, 9); [[t:12]]If they obey Him[[t:13]] ([Lat.: they will hear] [[t:14]]ישמעו[[t:15]]) [[t:16]]and that they may adore Him[[t:17]] (Job, 36, 11); [[t:18]]Will you then hearken unto us[[t:19]] ([Lat.: will you listen] [[t:20]]הנשמע[[t:21]]) (Nehemiah, 13, 27)? … [[t:22]]and who will not obey[[t:23]] ([Lat.: and will not hear] [[t:24]]ולא ישמע[[t:25]]) thy words (Joshua, 1, 18).
root.text.Part 1..44.2: —It is also said (for [[t:0]]to understand[[t:1]]) in the sense of [[t:2]]to know[[t:3]] and of [[t:4]]to know[[t:5]]; p. ex.: [[t:6]]A nation of which thou shalt not hear[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]לא תשמע[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]the language[[t:11]] (Deutér., 28, 49), that is to say, of which thou shalt not [[t:12]]know[[t:13]] the language.
root.text.Part 1..44.3: Whenever the verb shama’ is applied to God, and when, according to the literal sense, it would be taken in the first signification, it denots perception, which appertains to the third signification; e.g.: And the Lord heard it (וישמע) (Numbers, 11, 1), For that He hears (בשמעו) your murmurings (Exodus, 16, 7), in which it everywhere concerns a perception of knowledge[[fn:372]]. But when, according to the literal sense, it would be taken in the second signification[[fn:373]], it signifies that God has or has not granted the prayer of him that prayed; e.g.: I will surely hear (אשמע) his cry (Ibid., 22, 23); I will hear it (ושמעתי), for I am gracious (Ibid., v. 27); Incline Thine ear, O Lord, and hear (ושמע) (II Kings, 19, 16); And the Lord would not hearken (ולא שמע) to your voice, nor give ear unto you (Deuter., 1, 45); Yea, when ye make many prayers, I will not hear (Isaiah, 1, 15); For I will not hear thee (Jeremiah, 7, 16), and many other examples.
root.text.Part 1..44.4: Thou shalt find yet further on, concerning these metaphors and anthropomorphisms, that which shall quench thy thirst[[fn:374]] and resolve thy doubts, and all their significations shall be explained unto thee, so that naught shall remain obscure in any respect[[fn:375]].
root.text.Part 1..45.0: We have already stated, in one of the chapters of this treatise[[fn:376]], that there is a great difference between leading one to the (mere notion of the) existence of a thing, and searching into its essence and substance. Verily, one may direct the mind toward the existence of a thing, even by means of its accidents or its actions, or indeed by means of very remote relations which may exist between that thing and others.
root.text.Part 1..45.1: If, for example, thou shouldst desire to make known the sovereign of a realm to some inhabitant of his country who knew him not, thou mightest, in order to make him known and to draw attention to his existence, proceed in manifold ways. Thou wouldst say, for instance: He is a person of lofty stature, white of hue and with grey hair; and thou wouldst thus make him known by his accidents. Or else thou wouldst say: He is that one around whom is seen a great multitude of men on horse and on foot, who is environed by naked swords, above whose head banners are raised, and before whom trumpets are sounded; or again: He is he who dwells in the palace existing in such a city of this realm; or again: He is he who has commanded the raising of this wall or the construction of this bridge; or finally (thou wouldst designate him) by others of his actions and of his relations with certain things. Thou mightest also indicate his existence by circumstances less manifest than these. Someone, for example, might ask thee: Has this country a sovereign? and thou wouldst answer: Yea, without doubt; but (he would rejoin) what is the proof thereof? “The money-changer here present,” thou wouldst reply, “is, as thou seest, a weak man of a puny body, and has before him this great quantity of gold pieces, and that other individual, portly and strong, but poor, standing before him, asks of him the charity of a mite[[fn:377]], a thing which he does not, treating him, on the contrary, with abruptness, and repulsing him with his words; yet (the poor man), were it not for the fear of the sovereign (which restrains him), would hasten to slay him or to thrust him back, and would take the money which he has in his hands: here then is a proof that this state possesses a king.” Thou wouldst thus demonstrate his existence by the good order which reigns in the state, and which has for its cause the fear inspired by the sovereign and the expectation of being punished by him. In all that we have just cited as an example, there is naught which indicats the essence of the sovereign and his true substance in so far as he is sovereign.
root.text.Part 1..45.2: Such is that which has come to pass in all the books of the prophets, and likewise in the Pentateuch, when it was a question of making God known; for, as there was a necessity to direct all men towards (the knowledge of) the existence of God and (to make them understand) that He possesses all perfections,—that is to say, that He exists not solely as the earth exists and as the heaven exists, but that He exists as a living being possessing knowledge, power, action, and other things which must be believed regarding His existence and which shall be set forth further on,—the minds of men were led by the idea[[fn:378]] of corporeity to (understand) that He exists, and by the idea of motion to (understand) that He is living. In effect, the vulgar consider only the body as a thing of solid, true, and indubitable existence: everything which is not itself a body, but is found within a body, is (considered as) existing, yet of an existence lesser than that of the body, needing the body in order to exist; but that which is in no wise a body nor is found within a body is not, according to what man conceivs at first and especially according to the imagination, a thing that has existence. Likewise, the vulgar form of life no other idea than motion, and everything which movs not with a spontaneous motion in space is not living (in their eyes), although motion be not in the substance of that which lives, but be only an accident inherent therein[[fn:379]].
root.text.Part 1..45.3: In like manner, the perception which is most familiar unto us is effected by the senses, notably by hearing and sight; we obtain not the knowledge of anything, nor can we figure to ourselves the transmission of an idea from the soul of one individual to that of another, save by means of language[[fn:380]], that is to say, of the sound articulated by the lips and the tongue, and the other organs of speech. When, therefore, it was desired also to lead our mind to (understand) that God perceivs and that certain things are communicated by Him to the prophets, in order that these might communicate them unto us, He was presented unto us (on the one hand) as if He heard and saw,—which is to say that He perceivs those things which are seen and heard and that He knows them,—and He was presented unto us (on the other hand) as if He spake,—which is to say that certain things are communicated by Him to the prophets—; and therein lies the sense of prophecy, a matter which shall be set forth with particular care[[fn:381]]. Furthermore, as we understand not that we can produce any object otherwise than by making it by manual operation, God was presented as acting (or making things). Likewise again, as the vulgar understand by that which is living naught else but that which is endowed with a soul, God was also presented as having a soul, which [although the name of the soul (נפשׁ) be homonymous, as has been explained[[fn:382]]] signifies that He is living.
root.text.Part 1..45.4: Now, as it would not be conceived that we ourselves could accomplish all these actions otherwise than by means of corporeal organs[[fn:383]], there have been metaphorically attributed unto God all the organs: those by which local motion is effected, that is to say, the feet and the soles of the feet; those by which hearing, sight, and smell take place, that is to say, the ear, the eye, and the nose; those by means of which one speaks, as well as the matter of speech[[fn:384]], that is to say, the mouth, the tongue, and the voice; those, finally, by which each of us operats whilst working, that is to say, the hands, the fingers, the palm, and the arm. It results from all this, in sum, that there have been metaphorically attributed unto God [may He be exalted above all imperfection!] corporeal organs, in order to indicate thereby His actions, and that these actions themselves have been metaphorically attributed unto Him, in order to indicate thereby some perfection which consists not in the action itself. Thus, for example, there have been attributed unto Him the eye, the ear, the hand, the mouth, and the tongue, in order to indicate thereby sight, hearing, action, and speech. But sight and hearing have been attributed unto Him to indicate perception in general. [Wherefore thou shalt find that the Hebrew tongue putts the perception of one sense in the place of the perception of another sense; e.g.: Behold the word of the Lord (Jeremiah ii. 31) for: hearken, for what was intended to be said thereby was: apprehend the sense of His word; likewise: See the smell of my son (Genesis xxvii. 27) for: smell the odour of my son, for it concerns the perception of his smell. It is in accordance with this that it has been said: And all the people SAW the thunderings (Exodus xx. 15),—although, moreover, this scene was a prophetic vision, which is a thing known, proclaimed by national traditions[[fn:385]].] Action and speech have been attributed unto Him to indicate some influence emanating from Him, as shall be set forth[[fn:386]].
root.text.Part 1..45.5: Thus, every corporeal organ which thou findest (attributed unto God) in all the prophetic books, is either an organ of locomotion to indicate life, or an organ of sensation to indicate perception, or an organ of touch to indicate action, or an organ of speech to indicate the influence of the Intelligences[[fn:387]] upon the prophets, even as shall be set forth.
root.text.Part 1..45.6: All these metaphors serve, then, to direct us in such wise as to confirm within us the conviction that there exists a living Being who works all that is external to Himself, and who likewise perceivs His own handiwork. We shall explain, when we come to treat of the negation of attributes, how all this is reduced to a single thing, to wit, the sole essence of God; for the aim of this chapter is none other than to explain the meaning of those corporeal organs ascribed unto God [exalted be He above all imperfection!], and to show that they do but indicate the actions pertaining unto them—actions which, for us, constitute a perfection—in order to manifest unto us[[fn:388]] that He possesses all manner of perfections, even as we have been taught by that maxim: The Torah speaks according to the language of the sons of men[[fn:389]].
root.text.Part 1..45.7.sub_0: As touching the organs of locomotion ascribed unto God, it is said, for example: The footstool of my feet (Isaiah lxvi. 1); And the place of the soles of my feet (Ezek. xliii. 7). As for the organs of touch ascribed unto God, there is said: The hand of the Lord (Exod. ix. 3 et passim); With the finger of God (Ibid. xxxi. 18); The work of thy fingers (Ps. viii. 4); And thou hast laid thine hand upon me (Ibid. cxxxix. 5); And to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed (Isaiah liii. 1); Thy right hand, O Lord (Exod. xv. 6). Unto Him have been ascribed the organs of speech, it being said: The mouth of the Lord has spoken (Isaiah i. 20 et passim); … and that he would open his lips against thee (Job xi. 5); The voice of the Lord is powerful (Ps. xxix. 4); And his tongue as a devouring fire (Isaiah xxx. 27). Finally, there are ascribed unto Him the organs of sensation, it being said: His eyes behold, his eyelids try the children of men (Ps. xi. 4); The eyes of the Lord run to and fro (Zechariah iv. 10)[[fn:390]]; Incline thine ear, O Lord, and hear (2 Kings xix. 16); Ye have kindled a fire in mine anger (Jeremiah xvii. 4). Of the inward members, none have been ascribed unto Him save the heart, because the name of the heart is a homonym signifying also intellect[[fn:391]], and because the heart is the principle of life in the living being. Verily, by these expressions: My bowels are troubled for him (Jeremiah xxxi. 20); The sounding of thy bowels (Isaiah lxiii. 15), it was likewise intended to designate the heart; for bowels[[fn:392]] is a term employed in both a general and a particular sense, signifying in particular the intestines, and in general any inward member, and consequently the heart also. The proof of which is that the expression has been used: And thy Law is WITHIN MY BOWELS (Ps. xl. 9) as equivalent to: in my heart.
root.text.Part 1..45.7.sub_1: Wherefore it was said in the verses aforesaid[[fn:393]]: My bowels are troubled, the sounding of thy bowels, for the verb המה, to sound, is said rather of the heart than of other members; as for example: My heart makes a noise (הומה) in me (Jeremiah iv. 19). In like manner, the shoulder has not been ascribed unto Him, because it is commonly regarded as an instrument of burden, and because that which is carried is in contact therewith[[fn:394]]. With yet greater reason have the organs of nutrition not been ascribed unto Him, because they betoken, at the first glance, a manifest imperfection[[fn:395]].
root.text.Part 1..45.8: In verity, the condition of all organs, whether external or internal, is the same; they are all instruments for the diverse actions of the soul. Some serve for the preservation of the individual for a certain season, and such are all the internal members; others serve for the preservation of the species, such as the organs of generation; others yet serve to improve the condition of the individual and to accomplish his actions, and such are the hands, the feet, and the eyes, all of which serve for the fulfillment of motion, labor, and perception. As for motion, it is necessary unto the animal that it may go towards that which is convenient for it and flee from that which is contrary. Sensation is necessary for it to distinguish that which is contrary from that which is convenient. Man has need of the handicrafts to prepare his food, his raiment, and his habitation; for all these are necessary to his nature, by which I mean that he has need to prepare that which is convenient for him. There be certain arts found also among divers animals, because they have need of this or that art.
root.text.Part 1..45.9: — Now, methinks no man doubts that God has no need of anything for the prolongation of His existence, nor that He in any wise improvs His condition; consequently He has no organ, that is to say, He is no body, and His actions proceed solely from His essence, and not by means of an organ. The faculties, it cannot be doubted, are parts of the organs, and consequently He possesses no faculty, I mean that there is in Him[[fn:396]], external to His essence, no thing whereby He acts, He knows or He wills; for the attributes are but faculties, in which the name alone has been changed and nothing more[[fn:397]]. But this is not the purpose of the present chapter.
root.text.Part 1..45.10.sub_0: The Sages have delivered a maxim of great import[[fn:398]], which refuts all those false notions that might be engendered by the corporeal attributes mentioned by the prophets (when speaking of God); and this maxim shows thee that the corporeality (of God) never entered the minds of the Sages, and that there is naught in their words which could give rise to error or doubt[[fn:399]]. Wherefore thou shalt find that everywhere, in the [[t:0]]Talmud[[t:1]] and in the [[t:2]]Midrashoth[[t:3]], they constantly imitate these expressions of the prophets[[fn:400]], knowing full well that this is a matter in which one is secure from doubt and in which there is no fear of falling into error, and that everything therein is spoken rather by way of allegory and to direct the mind toward a (Supreme) Being. Now, as this allegory has been constantly employed, in which God is compared[[fn:401]] unto a king who commands and forbidds, who punishes and rewards the people of his land, and who has servants and ministers to transmit his orders and to execute that which he wills to be done, they also—I mean the Sages—have everywhere persevered in this comparison, and have expressed themselves according to what this allegory required (by attributing unto God the action) of [[t:4]]speaking[[t:5]], of [[t:6]]answering[[t:7]], of [[t:8]]enjoining commands[[t:9]][[fn:402]], and other similar actions (emanating) from kings; and they did all this with security, being certain that neither confusion nor doubt would result therefrom. The [[t:10]]maxim of great import[[t:11]] unto which we have alluded is contained in these words of [[t:12]]Bereshith Rabba[[t:13]][[fn:403]]: «Great was the boldness of the prophets in comparing the creature to its Creator; as, for example, in saying: [[t:14]]And upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness as the appearance of a man[[t:15]] (Ezek. i. 26)[[fn:404]].» Thus they (the Sages) have expressly declared that, in general, those figures which all the prophets perceived in the prophetic vision were [[t:16]]created[[t:17]] figures, of which God was the Creator[[fn:405]]. And this is true; for every figure that is in the imagination is [[t:18]]created[[t:19]][[fn:406]].
root.text.Part 1..45.10.sub_1: This expression «[[t:20]]had great boldness[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]גדול כחן[[t:23]])» is passing remarkable; (the Sages speak) as if this thing had appeared to them exceeding grave.— [In sooth, they ever express themselves thus to indicate that which they find grave in a word spoken or an act performed, which has, in appearance, something unseemly; as, for instance, in the following passage[[fn:407]]: «Rabbi Such-a-one caused the act to be performed with a shoe, in private, and during the night[[fn:408]]; great was his boldness ([[t:24]]רב גובריה[[t:25]]), says another Sage, to do it [[t:26]]in private[[t:27]].» [[t:28]]רב גובריה[[t:29]] (in Aramaic) is the same as [[t:30]]גדול כחו[[t:31]] (in Hebrew).] — It is therefore as if they had said: How grave is that which the prophets were led to do in indicating God Himself by the creations which He has produced. Thou must well consider this; for they (the Sages) have thus expressly declared that they themselves were free from the belief in the corporeality (of God), and that every figure and circumscribed thing seen in the prophetic vision were created things, but that they (the prophets) [[t:32]]compared the creature to its Creator[[t:33]], as the Sages express it. If, however, it should please any one to think ill of them, after these declarations, out of mere malice and to detract from men whom he has not seen and of whose circumstances he knows naught[[fn:409]], no harm would result unto them therefrom[[fn:410]].
root.text.Part 1..46.0: We have already observed divers times[[fn:411]] that whatsoever the vulgar imagins to be an imperfection, or which cannot be conceived as compatible with God, the prophetic books have in no wise metaphorically attributed unto Him, although it be in the same condition as the things which have been attributed unto Him: the reason is that those things which have been given Him as attributes are deemed, after a fashion, perfections, or, at the least, they may be conceived (as belonging unto God).
root.text.Part 1..46.1: This being established[[fn:412]], it behoves us to explain wherefore hearing, sight, and smell have been metaphorically attributed unto God, whilst neither taste nor touch have been so attributed; for He stands in the same condition of exaltation with regard to all the five senses: all of them constitute an imperfection with regard to perception, even for (that being) which perceivs only by the senses[[fn:413]], because they are passively affected, impressed (by another thing), interrupted and subject to suffering, like other organs. When we say that God [[t:0]]ses[[t:1]], the sense is that He perceivs visible things, and (when we say) that He [[t:2]]hears[[t:3]], it signifies that He perceivs the objects of hearing; one might therefore likewise attribute unto Him taste and touch, interpreting it in the sense that He perceivs the objects of taste and those of feeling. In sooth, the condition of perception is the same for all (the senses), and if one removs from God the perception which belongs unto one (of the senses), one must remove the perception of all, I mean of the five senses; but as soon as one affirms of Him the perception of one of them, I mean (as soon as one affirms) that He perceivs what one of the senses perceivs, He must needs perceive the objects of perception of all five. Nevertheless, we find that our (holy) books say: [[t:4]]the Lord saw, the Lord heard, the Lord smelled[[t:5]], and that they say not: [[t:6]]the Lord tasted[[t:7]] nor [[t:8]]the Lord touched[[t:9]]. The cause thereof is that it is established in the imagination of all that God cannot be in contact with bodies as one body is with another, since (men) cannot see Him; now, these two senses, I mean taste and touch, perceive the objects of their sensation only by touching them, whereas sight, hearing, and smell perceive the objects of their sensation even when the bodies endowed with (perceptible) qualities[[fn:414]] are far removed from them; wherefore, according to the imagination of the vulgar, it was permissible (to attribute them unto God)[[fn:415]]. Furthermore, in metaphorically attributing these senses unto Him, the object and aim were to indicate that He perceivs our actions; now, hearing and sight sufficed for this, I mean that it is by means of these senses[[fn:416]] that one perceivs all that another does or says. It is thus that the Sages, in a collection of exhortations, have said, by way of admonition and warning: «Know what is above thee: an eye that ses and an ear that hears[[fn:417]].»
root.text.Part 1..46.2: Thou shalt therefore know, upon examining (the matter) closely, that all (the senses) stand in the same condition, and that, even as the perception of touch and taste has been removed from God, so must we, for the same reason, remove therefrom that of sight, hearing, and smell; for all these be corporeal perceptions, [[t:0]]passions[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]πάθη[[t:3]]), and mutable conditions, save that some appear as an imperfection, whilst others pass for a perfection. Likewise, the imagination appears as an imperfection, whereas in thought and in understanding the imperfection is not manifest (unto all)[[fn:418]]; wherefore the word [[t:4]]ra’ayon[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]רעיון[[t:7]]), which signifies [[t:8]]imagination[[t:9]], has not been metaphorically employed when speaking of God, whilst the words [[t:10]]ma’hashabah[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]מחשבה[[t:13]]) and [[t:14]]tebunah[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]תבונה[[t:17]]), which signify [[t:18]]thought[[t:19]] and [[t:20]]understanding[[t:21]], have been so employed; e.g.: [[t:22]]And the thoughts[[t:23]] (purposes) [[t:24]]that the Lord has meditated[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]חשב[[t:27]]) [[t:28]]the Lord[[t:29]] (Jeremiah xlix. 20); [[t:30]]And by His understanding[[t:31]], or [[t:32]]His intelligence[[t:33]] ([[t:34]]בתבונתו[[t:35]]), [[t:36]]He has stretched out the heavens[[t:37]] ([[t:38]]Ibid.[[t:39]] x. 12). It has therefore happened likewise for the inner perceptions as it happened for the sensible and external perceptions, that is to say, that some are metaphorically attributed (unto God), whilst others are not. And all this [[t:40]]in accordance with the language of men[[t:41]][[fn:419]]: that which they (men) believe to be a perfection has been attributed unto Him; but that which is a manifest imperfection has in no wise been attributed unto Him. Nevertheless, if one goes to the root of the matter, He has no essential and real attribute[[fn:420]] joined unto His essence, even as shall be demonstrated.
