root.text.Part 1..47.0: Whenever the idea of [[t:0]]hearing[[t:1]] is found ascribed unto God, thou shalt find that Onkelos the proselyte has departed therefrom and has explained it in the sense that the matter reached God—that is to say, that He [[t:2]]perceived[[t:3]] it; and when a prayer is concerned, he explains (the verb [[t:4]]to hear[[t:5]]) in the sense that God [[t:6]]accepted[[t:7]] or [[t:8]]did not accept[[t:9]] (the prayer). He thus ever expresses himself, in rendering the words [[t:10]]the Lord heard[[t:11]], by [[t:12]]שמיע קדם יי[[t:13]], [[t:14]]it was heard before the Lord;[[t:15]] and where a prayer is concerned, he translats, e.g.: [[t:16]]I will surely hear his cry[[t:17]] (Exodus, xxii. 22) by [[t:18]]קבלא אקבל[[t:19]], [[t:20]]I will surely accept;[[t:21]] this he does continually in his paraphrase, without departing therefrom in a single passage. But as touching the passages where [[t:22]]sight[[t:23]] is ascribed unto God, Onkelos has therein shown an astonishing versatility[[fn:421]], the aim and intention of which are not clear unto me; for in certain passages he translats [[t:24]]וירא יי[[t:25]] by [[t:26]]וחזא יי[[t:27]], [[t:28]]and the Lord saw[[t:29]], and in other passages he translats these words by [[t:30]]וגלי קדם יי[[t:31]], [[t:32]]and it was manifest before the Lord[[t:33]]. Since he translats by [[t:34]]וחזא יי[[t:35]], [[t:36]]and the Lord saw[[t:37]], it proves with evidence that the verb [[t:38]]חזא[[t:39]], [[t:40]]to see[[t:41]], in the Syriac tongue, is homonymous, and that it signifies the perception of the intellect as well as that of the senses; but if such were his opinion, I would fain know why he has avoided (this verb) in certain passages, translating: [[t:42]]and it was manifest before the Lord[[t:43]].
root.text.Part 1..47.1: Nevertheless, a perusal of the copies which I have found of the [[t:0]]Targum[[t:1]] (of Onkelos), conjoined with that which I had heard during the period of my studies, has shown me[[fn:422]] that whenever he found the verb [[t:2]]ראה[[t:3]] (to see) relating to an injustice, or to aught that is hurtful, or to an act of violence, he rendered it by: [[t:4]]to be manifest before the Lord[[t:5]]. The verb [[t:6]]חזא[[t:7]] (to see), in that (Aramaic) tongue, indubitably implies the idea of [[t:8]]perceiving[[t:9]] and of [[t:10]]acknowledging the thing perceived even as it has been perceived[[t:11]][[fn:423]]; wherefore, when he (Onkelos) found the verb [[t:12]]to see[[t:13]] relating to an injustice, he did not say [[t:14]]וחזא יי[[t:15]], [[t:16]]and the Lord saw[[t:17]], but [[t:18]]וגלי קדם יי[[t:19]], [[t:20]]and it was manifest before the Lord[[t:21]].
root.text.Part 1..47.2.sub_0: I have thus found that throughout the Pentateuch, wheresoever the verb [[t:0]]ראה[[t:1]] (to see) is applied unto God, he translats it (literally) by [[t:2]]חזא[[t:3]] (to see), save in the passages which I am about to cite: For [[t:4]]For God saw[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]ראה[[t:7]]) [[t:8]]my affliction[[t:9]] (Genesis, xxix. 32) he putts: [[t:10]]ארי גלי קדם יי עולבני[[t:11]] [[t:12]]For my ignominy is manifest before God;[[t:13]] for [[t:14]]For I have seen[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]ראיתי[[t:17]]) [[t:18]]all that Laban does unto thee[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]Ibid.[[t:21]], xxxi. 12): [[t:22]]ארי גלי קדמי[[t:23]] [[t:24]]For ... is manifest before me;[[t:25]] and although he who speaks here is an angel, he has not ascribed unto him the perception signifying the [[t:26]]acknowledgment[[t:27]] (or [[t:28]]approbation[[t:29]]) of the thing, because it concerns an injustice; for [[t:30]]And God saw[[t:31]] ([[t:32]]וירא[[t:33]]) [[t:34]]the children of Israel[[t:35]] (Exodus, ii. 25) he putts: [[t:36]]וגלי קדם יי שעבודא דבני ישראל[[t:37]] [[t:38]]And the servitude of the children of Israel was manifest before God;[[t:39]] for [[t:40]]I have surely seen[[t:41]] ([[t:42]]ראה ראיתי[[t:43]]) [[t:44]]the affliction of my people[[t:45]] ([[t:46]]Ibid.[[t:47]], iii. 7): [[t:48]]מגלא גלי קדמי ית שעבודא דעמי[[t:49]], [[t:50]]The servitude of my people is manifest before me;[[t:51]] for [[t:52]]And I have also seen[[t:53]] ([[t:54]]ראיתי[[t:55]]) [[t:56]]the oppression[[t:57]] ([[t:58]]Ibid.[[t:59]], [[t:60]]v[[t:61]].
root.text.Part 1..47.2.sub_1: 9): [[t:62]]ואף גלי קדמי דחקא[[t:63]] [[t:64]]And also is manifest before me the oppression, etc.[[t:65]]; for [[t:66]]And that he had seen[[t:67]] ([[t:68]]ראה[[t:69]]) [[t:70]]their affliction[[t:71]] ([[t:72]]Ibid.[[t:73]], iv. 31): [[t:74]]וארי גלי קדמוהי שעבודהון[[t:75]] [[t:76]]And that their servitude was manifest before him;[[t:77]] for [[t:78]]I have seen[[t:79]] ([[t:80]]ראיתי[[t:81]]) [[t:82]]this people[[t:83]] ([[t:84]]Ibid.[[t:85]], xxxii. 9): [[t:86]]גלי קדמי עמא הדין[[t:87]] [[t:88]]This people is manifest before me[[t:89]], for the meaning is: [[t:90]]I have seen their rebellion[[t:91]], even as in (the words): [[t:92]]And God saw the children of Israel[[t:93]], the meaning is: [[t:94]]He saw their affliction[[t:95]][[fn:424]]; for [[t:96]]The Lord saw[[t:97]] ([[t:98]]וירא[[t:99]]) [[t:100]]and was provoked to anger[[t:101]] (Deuter., xxxii. 19): [[t:102]]וגלי קדם יי[[t:103]] [[t:104]]And it was manifest before God, etc.[[t:105]]; for [[t:106]]For he ses[[t:107]] ([[t:108]]יראה[[t:109]]) [[t:110]]that power is gone[[t:111]] ([[t:112]]Ibid.[[t:113]], [[t:114]]v[[t:115]]. 36): [[t:116]]ארי גלי קדמוהי[[t:117]] [[t:118]]For it is manifest before him[[t:119]], for here also it concerns an [[t:120]]injustice[[t:121]] committed against them and the victory of the enemy. In all these instances he has been consistent, and has had regard unto (those words): [[t:122]]And thou canst not look on iniquity[[t:123]] (Habakkuk, i. 13); wherefore, whenever servitude or rebellion is the matter, he translats by [[t:124]]גלי קדמוהי[[t:125]] [[t:126]]it was manifest before him[[t:127]], or by [[t:128]]גלי קדמי[[t:129]] [[t:130]]it was manifest before me[[t:131]].
root.text.Part 1..47.3: Nevertheless, this excellent and useful interpretation, which is in no wise doubtful, fails in three passages[[fn:425]] which, according to the rule in question, he ought to have translated by [[t:0]]וגלי קדם יי[[t:1]] [[t:2]]and it was manifest before the Lord[[t:3]], whereas we find therein, in the copies: [[t:4]]וחזא יי[[t:5]] [[t:6]]and the Lord saw[[t:7]]. They are the following: [[t:8]]And the Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great[[t:9]] (Genesis, vi. 5); [[t:10]]And God looked upon the earth, and behold, it was corrupt[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]Ibid.[[t:13]], [[t:14]]v[[t:15]]. 12); [[t:16]]And the Lord saw that Leah was hated[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]Ibid.[[t:19]], xxix. 31). It seems probable unto me that this is an error which has crept into the copies[[fn:426]]; for we possess not the autograph of Onkelos, wherefore we might say that he perchance had a (particular) interpretation for these passages[[fn:427]].
root.text.Part 1..47.4: If, on the other hand, he has rendered the words: God will provide (choose) for Himself a lamb (Ibid., xxii, 8) by קדם י״י גלי אמרא Before God the lamb is manifest, it was lest this passage (literally translated) might give occasion to believe that God had need to seek the lamb in order to bring it into His presence[[fn:428]]; or else, because he deemed it unbefitting likewise, in that language (the Aramaic), to associate the Divine perception with an individual[[fn:429]] from among the irrational animals.
root.text.Part 1..47.5: One must diligently seek in this regard the true reading of the manuscripts; and should these passages be found even as we have stated, I know not his intention[[fn:430]] in this matter.
root.text.Part 1..48.0: Neither have the angels bodies; they are, on the contrary, Intelligences separate from all matter. Nevertheless, they are created beings, and it is God who has brought them into existence, as shall be set forth hereafter. In Bereshith Rabba[[fn:431]] it is said: «This expression, The flame of the turning sword (Genesis, iii, 24), corresponds to this other: His ministers a flaming fire (Ps. civ, 4)[[fn:432]]; the term turning (המתהפכת) is used because they (the angels) transform themselves (מתהפכים): now they are called men, now women, now winds (or spirits), now angels[[fn:433]].» By this passage it is declared that they are by no means material, and that they possess no stable and corporeal form external to the mind[[fn:434]], but that, on the contrary, all this exists only in the prophetic vision and according to the action of the imaginative faculty, as we shall state when treating of the true nature of prophecy. If it be said (in this passage): «now women», it is because the prophets also at times beheld angels in the form of women, and this is an allusion to that passage of Zechariah (chap. v, v. 9): And, behold, there came out two women, and the wind (was) in their wings, etc.
root.text.Part 1..48.1: Thou knowest that the perception of that which is exempt from matter and entirely devoid of corporeality is passing difficult for man,— save it be after great exercise, — and particularly for him who distinguishes not between the intelligible and the imaginary, and who, for the most part, relies only upon the perception of the imagination; so that, in his view, everything imagined exists or may exist, whilst that which cannot be grasped by the imagination[[fn:435]] exists not and cannot exist[[fn:436]]. Such men, — and they comprise the majority of those who study, — never possess a precise idea of any subject, and no obscure matter is ever made clear unto them.
root.text.Part 1..48.2: It is likewise by reason of the difficulty of this matter that the prophetic books present words which, in their literal sense, would lead one to understand that angels are corporeal and possess certain movements; that they have a human form, receive the commands of God, transmit them (unto men), and perform His will by His decree; all this being intended to bring the mind to a knowledge of their existence, and that they are living and perfect, even as we have set forth concerning God. Nevertheless, had they been represented only thus[[fn:437]], their true essence[[fn:438]] would have been, in the imagination of the vulgar, similar to the essence of God; for there have likewise been employed regarding God words whose literal sense would seem to indicate that He is a body possessed of life and motion and of a human form. It is therefore to signify to the mind that the rank of their existence is below the rank of the Deity, that there has been mingled with their form something of the form of irrational animals, in order to make it understood that the existence of the Creator is more perfect than theirs, just as man is more perfect than the irrational animal. But, as regards the animal form[[fn:439]], naught has been attributed unto them save wings; for one cannot imagine flight without wings, even as one cannot imagine walking without feet, and the very existence of the said faculties can only be imagined as residing in the said subjects[[fn:440]]. And if flight has been chosen (as an attribute of angels) to indicate that they are living, it is because this is the most perfect and noble of the local movements of animals, and man perceivs therein a great perfection, desiring himself to be able to fly, that he might easily flee from all that is harmful to him and promptly reach that which is suitable, at whatsoever distance it may be.
root.text.Part 1..48.3: It is therefore for this reason that such motion has been attributed unto them, and furthermore because the bird, within a right brief space of time, now appears and now conceals itself, now draws nigh and now withdraws; for these be generally the circumstances which must be admitted concerning the angels, as shall hereafter be set forth.
root.text.Part 1..48.4: This alleged perfection, I mean the motion of flight, is in no wise attributed unto God, forasmuch as it is a motion pertaining unto an irrational animal. Thou must not be misled by these words: And he rode upon a cherub and did fly (Ps. xviii. 11); for herein it is the cherub which flew[[fn:441]]. It was intended by this allegory that the matter in question comes to pass swiftly; even as it has been said elsewhere: Behold, the Lord rids upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt (Isaiah xix. 1), where it is signified that the calamity in question shall fall rapidly upon them.
root.text.Part 1..48.5: Neither must thou suffer thyself to be led into error by the expressions which thou findest particularly in Ezekiel, such as: the face of an ox, the face of a lion, the face of an eagle (Ezek. i. 10), the sole of a calf's foot (Ibid., v. 7)[[fn:442]]; for there is for all this another interpretation which thou shalt hear later[[fn:443]], and moreover this is but the description of the hayyôth[[fn:444]]. These subjects shall be explained by means of indications which will suffice to awaken the attention[[fn:445]].
root.text.Part 1..48.6: As for the motion of flight (ascribed unto angels), it is found everywhere in the (sacred) texts, and (as we have said) it cannot be conceived save by means of wings; wherefore wings have been assigned unto them to indicate a circumstance of their existence, and not to designate their true being.
root.text.Part 1..48.7: It must be known that unto whatsoever movs with a rapid motion, the action of flying is attributed to indicate the swiftness of the movement; it has been said, for example: … as the eagle flies (Deut. xxviii. 49), because the eagle is, among all birds, that which flies and darts most swiftly, so that it has passed into a proverb. It must also be known that wings are the (efficient) causes of flight; wherefore the wings which appear (in prophetic visions) are of the same number as the causes of the motion of that which movs[[fn:446]]. But this is not the purpose of the present chapter.
root.text.Part 1..49.0: Know[[fn:447]], O reader of this my present treatise, that belief is not a thing which is merely uttered, but a thing which is conceived in the soul, whilst it is believed that the object is even as it is conceived. If, therefore, in the matter of true opinions or those deemed to be such, thou art content to express them in words, without conceiving them or believing them, and, with even greater reason, without seeking therein a certainty, this is a thing right easy; and thus it is that thou findest many foolish men who retain in their memory beliefs of which they conceive absolutely no idea.
root.text.Part 1..49.1: But if thou art of those whose thought does rise to ascend unto that exalted degree, which is the degree of speculation, and to possess the certainty that God is one, with a real unity, so that there be found in Him naught composite nor aught that is virtually divisible in any manner whatsoever, it behoovs thee to know that God has no essential attribute, under any condition, and that even as it cannot be admitted that He is a body, so is it inadmissible that He should possess an essential attribute[[fn:448]].
root.text.Part 1..49.2: Whosoever should believe that He is one, yet possessing manifold attributes, would indeed declare by his speech that He is one, but in his thought he would believe Him to be manifold. This would resemble that which the Christians say: «He is one, yet He is three, and the three are one»; for it would be the same thing if one said: «He is one, but He possesses many attributes, and He with His attributes are one», whilst setting aside corporeality and believing in the absolute simplicity (of God), as though our purpose were merely to seek how we should express ourselves, and not what we ought to believe[[fn:449]]. There can be no belief except where there has been conception; for belief consists in admitting as true that which has been conceived, and in believing that the thing exists outside the mind even as it has been conceived in the mind. If there be joined unto this belief the conviction that the contrary of that which is believed is absolutely impossible, and that there exists in the mind no means of refuting this belief, nor of thinking that the contrary might be possible, that is certainty.
root.text.Part 1..49.3: If thou divestest thyself of desires and habits, if thou art intelligent and ponderest well what I shall say in these following chapters concerning the negation of attributes[[fn:450]], thou shalt necessarily have certainty in this regard, and then shalt thou be of those who conceive the unity of God, and not of those who merely pronounce it with their mouth, without conceiving an idea thereof, and who belong unto that class of whom it has been said: Thou art near in their mouth, and far from their reins (Jeremiah, xii. 2). For it behoovs man to be of those who conceive the truth and understand it, even though they should not utter it, as it has been commanded unto virtuous men, saying unto them: Commune (think) with your own heart upon your bed, and be still (Ps. iv. 4).
root.text.Part 1..50.0: There are, in existence, many things clear and manifest, of which some are first notions[[fn:451]] and sensible things, and others are such as approach unto these; so that man, even were he left as he is[[fn:452]], would stand in no need of proof for these matters. Such are, for example, the existence of motion, the freedom of action belonging unto man, the evidence of generation and corruption[[fn:453]], and the natural properties of things which strike the senses, as the heat of fire and the coldness of water; many similar things might be cited. But when there arose extraordinary opinions on the part of those who were in error or who had therein some purpose, and who, by these opinions, set themselves in opposition to the nature of existence, denying that which is perceived by the senses or wishing to make believe in the existence of that which exists not, the men of science had need to establish the existence of these manifest things and the non-existence of things of mere supposition[[fn:454]]. Thus we find that Aristotle established motion, because it had been denied[[fn:455]], and demonstrated the non-existence of atoms, because their existence had been affirmed[[fn:456]].
root.text.Part 1..50.1: Of this same category is the requirement to remove from God all essential attributes;
root.text.Part 1..50.2: for it is a [[t:0]]primary notion[[t:1]] that the attribute is distinct from the [[t:2]]essence[[t:3]] of the qualified subject, that it is a certain circumstance of the essence, and, consequently, an [[t:4]]accident[[t:5]]. When the attribute is the very essence of the qualified subject, it is naught else than a tautology, as, for instance, if one were to say: [[t:6]]man is a man;[[t:7]] or else it is the explanation of a name, as, for instance, if one were to say: [[t:8]]man is a living being[[t:9]] (or [[t:10]]animal[[t:11]]) [[t:12]]rational[[t:13]] [for [[t:14]]living and rational[[t:15]] expresses the essence of man and his reality, and there is no third idea beyond those of [[t:16]]living[[t:17]] and [[t:18]]rational[[t:19]], which constitute man, who is qualified by [[t:20]]life[[t:21]] and [[t:22]]reason[[t:23]], or, to speak more precisely, this attribute is the explanation of a name and nothing else, and it is as if one were to say: that the thing whose name is [[t:24]]man[[t:25]] is that which is composed of [[t:26]]life[[t:27]] and [[t:28]]reason[[t:29]]].
root.text.Part 1..50.3: It is therefore clear that the attribute must necessarily be one of two things: either it is the very essence of the subject, such that it is the explanation of a name—a thing which, in this respect[[fn:457]], we do not reject regarding God, but rather in another respect, as shall be explained[[fn:458]]; or the attribute is something other than the subject, or rather, it adds something to the subject, which would result in making the attribute an accident of said essence. But by excluding the denomination of accident from the Creator's attributes, one does not exclude the idea; for whatever is added to the essence is accessory to it and is not the complement of its true idea, and this is precisely the meaning of accident[[fn:459]]. Add to this that, if there were many attributes, it would follow that there are many eternal things; but there is unity only on the condition of admitting a one and simple essence, in which there is neither composition nor multiplicity of ideas, but, on the contrary, a single idea, which is found to be one from whatever side one envisions it and from whatever point of view one considers it, which in no way nor by any cause could be divided into two ideas, and in which no multiplicity exists, neither outside the mind nor within the mind (of the thinker)[[fn:460]], as will be demonstrated in this treatise.
root.text.Part 1..50.4: Certain thinkers[[fn:461]] have even proceeded so far as to affirm that the attributes of God are neither His essence, nor aught external to His essence[[fn:462]]; but this resembles what certain others have averred: «The [[t:0]]conditions[[t:1]] — for thus do they designate the [[t:2]]general ideas[[t:3]] — are neither existent, nor non-existent[[fn:463]]»; and what others again have stated: «The simple substance (the atom) is not in space, yet it occupies a circumscribed position[[fn:464]]», and: «Man possesses no [[t:4]]action[[t:5]], but he possesses [[t:6]]acquisition[[t:7]][[fn:465]]». These are assertions which are all merely [[t:8]]spoken[[t:9]], which exist in words but not in minds, and which, à fortiori, can have no existence external to the mind[[fn:466]]. Nevertheless, as thou knowest, and as is known to all who do not deceive themselves, they are shielded by a superabundance of words and by images of spurious brilliance, and upheld by declamations, by invectives[[fn:467]], and by numerous means (of discussion) borrowed alike from dialectics and from sophistry[[fn:468]]. But if, after having enunciated them and supported them by such means[[fn:469]], one recurs within oneself to one's own conviction[[fn:470]], one discovers naught save perplexity and mental impotence, because one strives to impart existence to that which exists not, and to create a middle term between two opposites where none subsists; for is there a middle term between that which exists and that which exists not, or is there one between the identity and the non-identity of two things[[fn:471]] ?
root.text.Part 1..50.5: What prompted this was, as we have said, that they abandoned themselves to imaginations and always figured that all existing bodies are essences, each of which necessarily has attributes, and that we never find an essence of a body existing alone and without an attribute; persisting thus in this imagination, they believed that God, likewise, is composed of diverse things, (namely) of His essence[[fn:472]] and of the ideas added to the essence. Some, pushing anthropomorphism further, believed Him to be a body having attributes, while others, rising above this lowest degree[[fn:473]], removed the body (from God) and let the attributes remain. What brought all this about was that they followed the literal sense of the books of revelation, as I shall explain in chapters dealing with these subjects[[fn:474]].
root.text.Part 1..51.0: Whenever a subject has an affirmative attribute[[fn:475]] and it be said that it is such, this attribute cannot fail to be of one of the following five classes.
root.text.Part 1..51.1: I. The FIRST CLASS is that in which the thing has for its attribute its own definition, as, for example, when man is designated by saying that he is a rational animal. Such an attribute indicats the true essence of a thing[[fn:476]], and we have already set forth that it is the explanation of a name and naught else[[fn:477]]. This kind of attribute must, by the consent of all, be removed from God, for God has no prior causes which have caused His existence, so that they might serve to define Him[[fn:478]]. Wherefore it is generally admitted by all thinkers who express themselves with precision[[fn:479]] that God cannot be defined.
root.text.Part 1..51.2: II. The SECOND CLASS is that in which the thing has for its attribute a part of its definition[[fn:480]], as, for example, when one designats man by the quality of animality or by reason. Herein is the idea of inherence[[fn:481]]; for, if we say: every man is rational, it signifies that in everything possessing the quality of man, reason is found. This kind of attribute must, by the consent of all, be removed from God; for, were He to possess a part of a quiddity, His quiddity would be a composite thing. This class of attributes is therefore as inadmissible in His regard as was the former.
root.text.Part 1..51.3: III. The [[t:0]]THIRD CLASS[[t:1]] is that in which the thing possesses as an attribute something exterior to its reality and its essence, so that it forms no part of that which completes and constitutes the essence[[fn:482]], and consequently, it forms therein (merely) a [[t:2]]quality[[t:3]]. But [[t:4]]quality[[t:5]], as a [[t:6]]higher genus[[t:7]], is one of the accidents[[fn:483]]; if therefore God possessed an attribute of this class, He would be the [[t:8]]substratum[[t:9]] of accidents, and this alone suffices to demonstrate that to affirm He possesses a quality would be to depart from His reality and His essence[[fn:484]]. Yet one must marvel that those who admit attributes nonetheless avert from God assimilation (to creatures) and [[t:10]]qualification[[t:11]][[fn:485]]; for, when they state He cannot be [[t:12]]qualified[[t:13]], this signifies nothing other than that He possesses no [[t:14]]quality[[t:15]]; and yet, every attribute which is ascribed to an essence in an affirmative and essential sense[[fn:486]] either constitutes the essence, — and in that case it is (the essence) itself, — or else is a quality of that essence.
root.text.Part 1..51.4: The species of quality are four in number[[fn:487]], as thou knowest; I shall give thee an example of each of these species in the form of an attribute, in order to show thee the impossibility of admitting for God this kind of attribute.
root.text.Part 1..51.5: [[t:0]]First example:[[t:1]] when one characteriss man by one of his [[t:2]]capacities[[t:3]][[fn:488]] speculative or moral, or by the dispositions which he possesses as a living being[[fn:489]], as, e.g., when one says: such an one, a carpenter, or chaste, or sick. There is no difference (in this regard) between the denomination of [[t:4]]carpenter[[t:5]] and that of [[t:6]]learned[[t:7]], or of [[t:8]]wise[[t:9]][[fn:490]], all of which (designate) [[t:10]]dispositions in the soul[[t:11]], and likewise there is no difference between saying [[t:12]]chaste[[t:13]] and saying [[t:14]]merciful;[[t:15]] for every art, every science, and every permanent moral quality[[fn:491]] is a disposition in the soul. All this is manifest to him who has in any wise occupied himself with Logic.
root.text.Part 1..51.6: [[t:0]]Second example:[[t:1]] when one characteriss a thing by a natural power or incapacity which is found therein, as, e.g., when one says: the soft and the hard. There is no difference between saying [[t:2]]soft[[t:3]] and [[t:4]]hard[[t:5]] and saying [[t:6]]strong[[t:7]] and [[t:8]]weak[[t:9]][[fn:492]]; all these (signify) natural aptitudes.
root.text.Part 1..51.7: [[t:0]]Third example:[[t:1]] when one qualifies a man by an affective quality or by affections, as, p. ex., when one says: such a person is in a rage, or irritated, or afraid, or compassionate, without, however, this signifying a permanent moral quality[[fn:493]]. Of the same kind is the qualification by colour[[fn:494]], taste, smell, heat, cold, dryness, and moisture.
root.text.Part 1..51.8: [[t:0]]Fourth example:[[t:1]] when one characteriss a thing by what it is in respect of quantity as such[[fn:495]], as, e.g., when one says: the long, the short, the curved, the straight, and other such things.
root.text.Part 1..51.9: Considering all these attributes and others of like nature, thou shalt find them inadmissible with regard to God: for He has no quantity, that there might be in Him such a quality as exists in [[t:0]]quantity as such;[[t:1]] He is neither impressed nor passively affected, that there might be in Him a quality of [[t:2]]affections;[[t:3]] He has no [[t:4]]aptitudes[[t:5]], that there might be in Him [[t:6]]powers[[t:7]] (faculties)[[fn:496]] or aught of a similar kind; finally, God has no soul, that He might have a [[t:8]]disposition[[t:9]] and that there might be in Him [[t:10]]capacities[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]ἕξεις[[t:13]]), such as meekness, shame, and others of a like nature, or that which pertains to the [[t:14]]living being[[t:15]] as such[[fn:497]], e.g.: health and sickness. It is therefore manifest that every attribute which belongs to the higher genus of [[t:16]]quality[[t:17]][[fn:498]] cannot be found in God.
root.text.Part 1..51.10: Thus it is demonstrated that these three classes of attributes—to wit, all that signifies a quiddity[[fn:499]], or a part of a quiddity, or any quality whatsoever that is found within the quiddity—are inadmissible in respect of God; for they all betoken composition, which, as we shall demonstrate[[fn:500]], is inadmissible in respect of God[[fn:501]].
root.text.Part 1..51.11: IV. The <small>FOURTH CLASS</small> of attributes is that in which one designats the thing by its relation to another thing, by relating it, for instance, to a certain time, to a place, or to another individual, as, for example, when one designats Zeid (by saying) that he is the father of such a one, or the associate of such a one, or an inhabitant of such a place, or he who existed in such a time. This kind of attributes implies neither multiplicity nor change in the essence of the subject; for the Zeid in question is (at once) the associate of ‘Amr, the father of Becr, the master of Khalid, the friend of (the other) Zeid, the inhabitant of such a house, and he who was born in such a year. These notions of relation are neither his essence nor, like qualities, aught within his essence; and it appears at first glance that one might ascribe to God this kind of attributes; nevertheless, upon verifying the matter and examining it with care, it will be manifest that this cannot be.
root.text.Part 1..51.12: Firstly, it is evident that God is not related to time and space: for time is an accident that pertains to movement, when, in the latter, one considers the notion of antecedence and posteriority, so that it is numbered (by time), — as is explained in the particular places dedicated to this subject[[fn:502]] —; now, movement being a property of bodies, and God not being a body, it follows that there is no relation between Him and time. Similarly, there is no relation between Him and space[[fn:503]].
root.text.Part 1..51.13.sub_0: But that which it behoves one to investigate and examine is whether there exists between God and any of the substances created by Him a certain veritable relation, in such wise that it may serve as an attribute unto Him. That there can be no [[t:0]]relation[[t:1]] (properly so called)[[fn:504]] between Him and any of the things created by Him, this is manifest at first glance: for one of the properties of two correlatives is perfect reciprocity[[fn:505]]; now, God is of a [[t:2]]necessary[[t:3]] existence, and that which is external to Him is of a [[t:4]]possible[[t:5]] existence, as shall be expounded[[fn:506]], and, consequently, there can exist no [[t:6]]relation[[t:7]] (between God and the creature). But that any sort of relation should subsist between them, this is a thing which has been deemed admissible, albeit such is not the case. Indeed, one could not conceive of a relation between intelligence and colour, even though, according to our view, one and the same existence embraces them both[[fn:507]]; and how then could one conceive of a relation between two beings, one of which possesses absolutely nothing in common with that which is external to it[[fn:508]]? — for, in our opinion, it is only by simple homonymy that (the word) [[t:8]]to exist[[t:9]] is predicated simultaneously of God and of that which is external to Him. There is, therefore, absolutely no relation in reality between Him (God) and any whatsoever of His creatures: for relation necessarily subsists solely between two things which fall under one and the same [[t:10]]proximate species[[t:11]][[fn:509]], but, when they are (merely) under one and the same [[t:12]]genus[[t:13]], no relation exists between them[[fn:510]]; hence it is not said: "This red is stronger or weaker than this green, or equal thereto," albeit both[[fn:511]] are comprised under one and the same [[t:14]]genus[[t:15]], which is colour. If, however, the two things should fall under diverse genera[[fn:512]], then it is clear, even to simple common sense, that no relation subsists between them, even though they might ultimately revert to a single [[t:16]]genus[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]superior[[t:19]]). Thus, for example, there is no relation between [[t:20]]a hundred cubits[[t:21]] and the [[t:22]]heat of pepper;[[t:23]] for one of the two things pertains to the genus[[fn:513]] of [[t:24]]quality[[t:25]], whilst the other pertains to that of [[t:26]]quantity[[t:27]].
root.text.Part 1..51.13.sub_1: But neither is there any relation[[fn:514]] between science and sweetness, nor between mildness and bitterness, although all these be under the higher genus of quality. How then could there be a relation between God and aught of His creatures, given the great distance in the reality of being, a distance so great that there is none more marked? If there were a relation between them[[fn:515]], it would also follow that the accident of relation appertains unto God; for, though it be true that this would not be an accident in the very essence of God, it is yet, in short, a kind of accident. There is therefore, in reality, no means[[fn:516]] of ascribing to God an affirmative attribute, even were it (by qualifying Him) by a relation[[fn:517]]. But these attributes of relation are those which one must show oneself more ready to admit with regard to God[[fn:518]]; for they imply no multiplicity in the Eternal Being[[fn:519]], and they imply no change in the essence of God by reason of the change of things wherewith He is placed in relation.
root.text.Part 1..51.14: V. The FIFTH CLASS of affirmative attributes is that in which a thing has for its attribute its action. By its action, I mean not the artistic capacity which resids therein [as, for instance, when one says the carpenter[[fn:520]] or the blacksmith], for this belongs unto the species of quality, as we have formerly stated[[fn:521]]; but I mean thereby the action (in general) which one has accomplished, as, for example, when it is said: Zeid is he who has fashioned this door, builded this wall, and woven this fabric. Attributes of this sort are far removed from the essence of the subject[[fn:522]]; wherefore it is permissible to attribute them unto God, provided it be well understood that these diverse actions do not necessarily proceed from diverse conditions existing within the essence of their author[[fn:523]], as shall be set forth hereafter[[fn:524]]. On the contrary, the diverse actions of God are all performed by His very essence, and not by anything superadded thereto[[fn:525]], even as we have declared.
root.text.Part 1..51.15: In summary, then, it has been set forth in this chapter[[fn:526]] that God is one in every respect, that there is in Him no multiplicity nor anything superadded to His essence, and that the many attributes of diverse significations employed in the (sacred) books to designate God denote the multiplicity of His actions, and not a multiplicity in His essence[[fn:527]]. Some (are employed) to indicate His perfection in relation to that which we believe to be a perfection, even as we have explained[[fn:528]]. As for knowing whether it be possible that the essence, one and simple, in which there is no multiplicity, may perform varied actions, this shall presently be demonstrated by examples.
root.text.Part 1..52.0: Men have been led to believe that God has attributes in much the same manner as they were led to believe in (God's) corporeality[[fn:529]]. Verily, he who believs in corporeality was not led thereto by intellectual speculation, but by following the literal sense of the Scriptural texts; and it is likewise with regard to the attributes: finding that the books of the Prophets and those of the Pentateuch[[fn:530]] ascribed attributes unto God, they took the matter literally, and believed that He possessed attributes. They have, so to speak, exalted Him above corporeality, yet without exalting Him above the circumstances of corporeality, which are accidents—I mean, the dispositions of the soul, all of which are qualities[[fn:531]]. In every attribute which, in the opinion of him who believs in attributes, is essential in God, thou shalt find the notion of quality, although they (the Prophets) do not express themselves clearly in this regard, simply assimilating (the attributes of God) unto those conditions familiar to them in every body endowed with a vital soul[[fn:532]]; and concerning all this it has been said: «The Law speaks according to the language of the sons of men.» The aim of all (the attributes of God) is none other than to ascribe unto Him perfection (in general), and not that very thing which is a perfection for such creatures as are endowed with a soul. Most of them are attributes (arising) from His diverse actions;
root.text.Part 1..52.1: for the diversity of actions does not presuppose the existence of diverse ideas within the agent[[fn:533]]. One shall, in this regard, be presented with an example drawn from those things which exist near unto us, (to demonstrate) that, the agent being [[t:0]]one[[t:1]], there nevertheless result diverse actions, even when it possesses no will, and, *a fortiori*, when it acts with will. Thus, for example, fire liquefies certain substances, coagulates others, cooks, burns, whitens, and blackens; and, if one were to ascribe to fire the attributes of [[t:2]]whitening[[t:3]], of [[t:4]]blackening[[t:5]], of [[t:6]]burning[[t:7]], of [[t:8]]cooking[[t:9]], of [[t:10]]coagulating[[t:11]], and of [[t:12]]liquefying[[t:13]], one would speak truly. Now, he who comprehends not the nature of fire believes that there exist within it six distinct virtues: one virtue by which it blackens, another by which it whitens, a third by which it cooks, a fourth by which it burns, a fifth by which it liquefies, and a sixth by which it coagulates, notwithstanding that these are all actions opposed one to another, and that the idea of the one excludes that of the others[[fn:534]]; but he who comprehends the nature of fire well knows that it is by a single active quality that it produces all these actions, to wit, by heat. Now, if this holds true in that which acts by nature, (the same must apply) *a fortiori*, with regard to that which acts with will, and, with yet greater force, *a fortiori*, with regard to God, Who is elevated above all description; and, when one perceives within Him diverse relations of meaning[[fn:535]], because, within ourselves, the idea of [[t:14]]knowledge[[t:15]] is distinct from that of [[t:16]]power[[t:17]], and that of power distinct from that of [[t:18]]will[[t:19]][[fn:536]], how might one thence conclude that there exist within Him diverse things which are [[t:20]]essential[[t:21]] to Him, so that there be in Him something by which He [[t:22]]knows[[t:23]], something by which He [[t:24]]wills[[t:25]], and something by which He [[t:26]]can[[t:27]]? Such, nevertheless, is the purport of the attributes which are proclaimed. Some pronounce this clearly, by enumerating the things superadded to the essence; others, without pronouncing it clearly, evidently profess the same opinion, albeit they do not express themselves in this regard by intelligible words, saying, for example, (that God is) [[t:28]]powerful by His essence, knowing by His essence, living by His essence, willing by His essence[[t:29]][[fn:537]].
root.text.Part 1..52.2: I shall further cite for thee as an example the rational faculty which exists in man; for, by this faculty which is one, without multiplicity, man comprehends the sciences and the arts, and by it at once he sews, carpents, weavs, builds, knows geometry, and governs the state[[fn:538]]. Here, then, are diverse actions resulting from a single simple faculty, in which there is no multiplicity; and they are very varied actions, for there is an infinite number of these arts which the rational faculty produces[[fn:539]]. It is therefore not inadmissible, in regard to God, that these diverse actions (which are attributed unto Him) should emanate from a single simple essence[[fn:540]], in which there is neither multiplicity, nor absolutely anything accessory, so that every attribute found in the divine books designats His action, and not His essence[[fn:541]], or indicats an absolute perfection; (and it by no means follows) that there is there an essence composed of diverse things — [for it suffices not to refrain from speaking expressly of composition, for the essence endowed with attributes not to imply the notion thereof[[fn:542]]].
root.text.Part 1..52.3: Yet there remains here somewhat of obscurity which has given rise to error[[fn:543]], and which I shall lay before thee: to wit, that they who admit attributes do not admit them (solely) by reason of the multiplicity of actions; for verily, say they, a single essence may produce divers actions, but the essential attributes of God are not of (those which proceed from) His actions, since one cannot conceive, (for example), that God should have created Himself[[fn:544]].
root.text.Part 1..52.4: They differ, furthermore, concerning these attributes which they term essential, I mean as to their number, each following some text of Scripture[[fn:545]]. But I desire to record (only) those which all admit by common consent, claiming that they are dictated by reason, without needing to depend upon the word of a prophet; these are four attributes, namely: living, powerful, knowing, willing. These, say they, are ideas distinct one from another, and perfections of which not one can be wanting in God, and which cannot be numbered among His actions[[fn:546]]. Such is the summary of their opinion.
root.text.Part 1..52.5: But thou knowest well[[fn:547]] that, in God, knowing signifies the same thing as living; for every (being) that perceivs itself is endowed with life and knowledge, (taken here) in one and the same sense—[provided, of course, that by knowledge we mean self-perception][[fn:548]]. The essence which perceivs is indubitably that very same which is perceived[[fn:549]]; for, according to our opinion, He (God) is not composed of two things, that is to say, of a thing which perceivs and of another which perceivs not, as man, who is composed of a soul which perceivs and a body which perceivs not[[fn:550]]. If, therefore, by knowledge one understands self-perception, life and knowledge (in God) are one and the same thing. But those (who profess the attributes) have not in view this sense (of divine knowledge); on the contrary, they have in view that perception (of God) which has for its object His creatures.
root.text.Part 1..52.6: Likewise, power and will exist neither the one nor the other in the Creator in relation to His essence; for He exerciss no power over Himself, nor can one attribute unto Him a will having Himself for its object, a thing which no man could imagine. These attributes, on the contrary, they have admitted only with respect to divers relations existing between God and His creatures, that is to say, that He has the power to create that which He creats, the will to bring into existence that which is such as He has produced it, and the knowledge of that which He has produced. It is therefore manifest that these attributes also[[fn:551]] are (ascribed to God), not with regard to His essence, but with regard to created things;
root.text.Part 1..52.7: Wherefore this is what we affirm, we who truly profess the [[t:0]]Unity:[[t:1]] even as we do not admit that there is in His essence aught accessory by which He created the heavens, aught else by which He created the elements, and, in the third place, aught by which He created the (separate) Intelligences, so likewise do we not admit that there is in Him aught accessory by which He [[t:2]]can[[t:3]], aught else by which He [[t:4]]wills[[t:5]], and, in the third place, aught by which He possesses the [[t:6]]science[[t:7]] of the things created by Him; but His essence is one and simple, and there is in it nothing accessory in any wise. It is this essence[[fn:552]] which created all that it created, and which [[t:8]]knows[[t:9]] (things), without it being by aught accessory; and it matters little whether these diverse attributes relate to actions or to diverse relations existing between Him and the things made (by Him)[[fn:553]], to say naught of what we have expounded concerning the true meaning of [[t:10]]relation[[t:11]], for it has been admitted only by error[[fn:554]].
root.text.Part 1..52.8: Such is that which it behoves one to believe concerning the attributes mentioned in the books of the prophets[[fn:555]]; or else, one shall admit for some amongst them that they are attributes serving to indicate a perfection, by way of assimilation unto our own perfections, in such manner as they are understood amongst us, even as we shall hereafter expound.
root.text.Part 1..53.0: Know that the prince of the learned, our master Moses [peace be upon him!], addressed unto God two petitions, and obtained an answer unto these two prayers[[fn:556]]: by the one, he besought God to make known unto him His true essence; by the other [which is that which he addressed unto Him first[[fn:557]]], to make known unto him His attributes. God answered him concerning these two demands, promising to make known unto him all His attributes, which are His actions, and signifying unto him that His essence could not be apprehended in its whole reality; nevertheless He awakened his attention unto a speculative point of view whence he might perceive all that which it is possible for man at last to perceive. That which he himself perceived, no man has perceived either before him or after him.
root.text.Part 1..53.1: As for his request to know the attributes of God, it is contained in these words: Shew me now Thy ways, that I may know Thee, etc. (Exodus, xxxiii, 13). Consider well what these words contain of remarkable: the words Shew me now Thy ways, that I may know Thee, indicate that one knows God by means of His attributes, for it was after having recognized the ways (quoth Moses) that he should know Him; the words that I may find grace in Thy sight (Ibid.) indicate that he alone who knows God finds grace in His sight, and not he who merely limits himself to fasting and to prayer. Verily, whosoever knows Him is an object of favour, brought nigh unto Him, and whosoever is ignorant of Him is an object of wrath, removed from Him; and it is by reason of knowledge or of ignorance that favour or wrath, approximation or distance, takes place. But we have departed from the subject of the chapter; I shall therefore return thereto.
root.text.Part 1..53.2: Having then requested to know the attributes, while imploring at the same time pardon for the nation, and having thereafter, upon obtaining this pardon, requested to perceive the essence of God, saying: I beseech Thee, shew me Thy glory (Ibid., V. 18), there was granted unto him that which he had first requested in these words: Shew me now Thy ways, and it was answered him: I will make all my goodness pass before thee (Ibid., V. 19); but unto the second request he received this answer: Thou canst not see my face, etc. (Ibid., V. 20). As for the words all my goodness, they contain an allusion unto the presentation before him (Moses) of all beings, concerning which it has been said: And God saw every thing that He had made, and, behold, it was very good (Genesis, i, 31); by their presentation before him, I mean that (according to the divine promise) he was to understand their nature, their connection one with another, and to know how God governs them in their whole and in their details. It is also unto this idea that allusion was made by these words: He is faithful in all mine house (Numbers, xii, 7)[[fn:558]], that is־to-say: he has of all My universe a true and firm intelligence; for opinions which are not true have no firmness. The matter here, then, is the perception of the actions (of God), which are His attributes[[fn:559]] by means of which He is known; and the proof that the actions of God were the thing of which the perception was promised unto him, is that he was made to know naught but simple attributes of action, such as: merciful, gracious, long-suffering, etc. (Exodus, xxxiv, 6 and 7). It is therefore clear that the ways of which he requested the knowledge, and which were made known unto him, were the actions which emanate from God. The doctors call them middôth (מדות), and speak of thirteen middôth (of God); this word, in their usage, applies unto moral qualities[[fn:560]]), e.g.: There are four MIDDÔTH (qualities, or manners of acting) amongst those who give alms; There are four MIDDÔTH amongst those who frequent the school[[fn:561]], and yet more frequently. It is not intended here (in speaking of the middôth of God) to say that He possesses moral qualities, but that He produces actions similar unto those which, amongst us, emanate from moral qualities, I mean from dispositions of the soul, not that God has any such dispositions of the soul.
root.text.Part 1..53.3: If one has limited himself to mentioning these thirteen middôth, although he (Moses) perceived all His goodness, I mean, all His actions, it is only because these are the actions proceeding from God to bring men into existence and to govern them; and that was the ultimate end of his request, for he concluds by saying: that I may know Thee, that I may find grace in Thy sight, and consider that this nation is Thy people (Exodus, xxxiii, 13), that which I must govern by actions imitating those wherewith Thou dost govern it[[fn:562]].
root.text.Part 1..53.4: It is thenceforth manifest that the derakhīm (ways) and the middôth (attributes) are one and the same: they be those actions which proceed from God and are displayed within the universe.
root.text.Part 1..53.5.sub_0: In proportion, then, as any of His actions were perceived, there was attributed unto Him the quality whence that action proceeds, and there was applied unto Him the name derived from that action. Perceiving, for example, the tender care He bestows upon the fashioning of the embryo[[fn:563]] of animals, and the production, within it and within the parent that must rear it after birth, of faculties which may prevent it from perishing or being lost, and preserve it from harm and aid it in its necessary functions—a manner of acting which, among us, would proceed only from a passion[[fn:564]] and a sentiment of tenderness designated by the term mercy—God has been called רחום, merciful, according to that which has been said: Like as a father pities his children, etc. (Ps. 103:13); And I will spare them, as a man spars his own son (Malachi, III, 17); not that God is passively affected or moved to tenderness, but an action similar to that which proceeds from a father toward his child, and which is the result of tenderness, commiseration, and pure passion, proceeds also from God toward His favoured ones, yet without it being by reason of any passion or any sentiment involving a change[[fn:565]]. Likewise, since among us, when we bestow something upon one who has no claim upon us, it is called in our tongue חנינה, grace—e.g., Be favourable (חנונו) unto them (Judges, 21:22)[[fn:566]]; … which God has graciously given (Genesis, 33:5); because God has dealt graciously with me (Ibid., v. 11), and many other passages—and since God calls into existence and governs those whom He is under no obligation to create or govern, He has for this reason been called חנון, gracious (clement). Likewise, we find among His actions manifested toward men great calamities which fall upon certain individuals to annihilate them, or which involve in their destruction[[fn:567]] whole families, and even an entire region, causing many generations to perish at once[[fn:568]] and leaving neither tillage nor progeny, as, for
root.text.Part 1..53.5.sub_1: example, floods, earthquakes, destructive tempests, the expedition of one people against another to destroy them by the sword and to blot out their trace, and many other similar actions, which, among us, are not undertaken by one against another[[fn:569]] save as a consequence of fierce wrath, or great hatred, or with the intent of taking vengeance; He has therefore been called, in respect of these actions: jealous, revengeful, keeping rancour, and irascible (Nahum, 1:2), signifying that actions such as those which, among us, proceed from a disposition of the soul, to wit, from jealousy, vengeance, hatred, or wrath, are manifested also on the part of God by reason of the demerit of those who are punished, yet they proceed in no wise from any passion [exalted be He above all imperfection!]. Thus it is that all actions attributed unto God are actions similar to those which, among men, proceed from passions and dispositions of the soul; but on the part of God, they proceed in no wise from anything accidental to His essence.
root.text.Part 1..53.6: It behoves him who governs the state, if he be a prophet[[fn:570]], to take these divine attributes for a pattern, so that the said actions may proceed from him by just appreciation and according to what is deserved, and not by the mere impulse of passion. He must not give rein to anger, nor suffer himself to be dominated by passions; for every passion is an evil. He must, on the contrary, guard himself therefrom as much as a man is able, so as to be at one time, toward some, clement and gracious, not out of mere tenderness and commiseration, but according to what is due; and at another time, toward others, revengeful, keeping rancour, and irascible, by reason of what they have deserved, and not out of mere wrath, even to the point that he must command the burning of an individual without feeling against him either indignation, or wrath, or hatred, having regard, on the contrary, only to that which he shall appear to have deserved, and considering how the accomplishment of this act is of sovereign utility for the great multitude.
root.text.Part 1..53.7: Dost thou not perceive that, in the texts of the Law, after having commanded the destruction of the seven nations and having said: Thou shalt save alive nothing that breaths (Deut., 20:16), these words are immediately followed by: That they teach you not to do after all their abominations, which they have done unto their gods; so should ye sin against the Lord your God (Ibid., v. 18)? This signifies: Believe not that this is cruelty or a desire for vengeance; it is, on the contrary, an act required by human reason, namely, to cause the disappearance of all those who turn aside from the ways of truth, and to remove all obstacles which prevent the attainment of perfection, that is to say, the perception of God.
root.text.Part 1..53.8: Notwithstanding all this, it behoovs that acts of mercy, of pardon, of commiseration and of benevolence, should proceed from him who ruls the state far more frequently than acts of punishment; for the thirteen middôth are all attributes of mercy, with the exception of one alone, to wit: Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children (Exodus, xxxiv, 7); for the words ונקה לא ינקה (Ibid.) signify: and He does not utterly root out (destroy) altogether[[fn:571]], (a sense derived) from the word ונקתה (Isaiah, iii, 26), and she shall be destroyed.
root.text.Part 1..53.9: It must be known that the words visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children relate only to the sin of idolatry in particular, and not to other sins; of which the proof lies in these words of the Decalogue: … upon the third and fourth generation of them that hate me (Exodus, xx, 5), for by him that hats (God), none is designated save the idolater[[fn:572]], (who is likewise presented as the object of God’s hatred): For every abomination to the Lord (and all) which He hats, etc. (Deuteron., xii, 31). One has limited it to four generations, because a man can see of his posterity at most but the fourth generation. Thus, when the population of a city given over to idolatry is put to death[[fn:573]], the aged idolater is slain together with his race even unto the great-grandson, who is the child of the fourth generation. It has therefore been, as it were, indicated[[fn:574]] that among the commandments of God, which indubitably form part of His actions, is that of slaying the descendants of idolaters, though they be young children, [[fn:575]]indiscriminately with their fathers and their grandsires. This command we find everywhere repeated in the Pentateuch, as, for instance, it was ordained concerning the seduced city: to devote it to destruction, it and all that is therein (Deut., xiii, 16); all this to the end that every trace of that which produces so great a perdition might be blotted out, even as we have set forth.
root.text.Part 1..53.10: We have digressed from the subject of the chapter; yet it behoved us to explain wherefore, in speaking here of the actions of God, one has confined oneself to these alone[[fn:576]]. The reason is that they are necessary for the governance of states; for the supreme virtue of man is to render himself like unto God as far as he is able, that is to say, that we ought to make our actions like unto His, even as the (Sages) have set forth, in commenting upon the words be ye holy, etc. (Levit., xix, 2): «Even,» say they, «as He is gracious, so also must thou be gracious; even as He is merciful, so also must thou be merciful[[fn:577]].»
root.text.Part 1..53.11: Our design, in sum, is (to show) that the attributes ascribed unto Him are attributes (derived) from His actions, and in no wise signify that He possesses any quality.
root.text.Part 1..54.0: We have already observed, in divers places of this treatise, that whatsoever implies corporeality must necessarily be removed from God. Likewise, all passion must be removed from Him; for all passions imply change, and the agent of these passions is indubitably distinct from that which is passively affected. Now, if God were, in any manner, passively affected, there would be somewhat other than He which would act upon Him and change Him. In like manner, one must necessarily remove from Him all privation[[fn:578]] and (not admit) that any perfection whatsoever should at one time be wanting to Him, and at another exist (in Him); for if this were admitted, He would be perfect (only) potentially, but all potentiality is necessarily accompanied by a privation, and everything that passes from potentiality to actuality has absolute need of somewhat else existing actually, which causs it to pass thither. Wherefore it is necessary that all His perfections should exist actually and that He should have nothing whatsoever potentially. Furthermore, that which must necessarily be removed from Him is resemblance to any of the beings that exist; this is a matter known to all, and already in the books of the prophets has assimilation been expressly removed, when it is said: To whom then will ye liken me, or (to whom) shall I be equal? (Isaiah, xl, 25.) To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto Him? (Ibid., v. 18.) There is none like unto Thee, O Lord! (Jeremiah, x, 6.) — There are of this many examples.
root.text.Part 1..54.1: In sum, therefore, everything that tends toward one of these four species must necessarily be excluded from Him by means of clear demonstration; namely, all that tends toward corporeality, or that tends toward a [[t:0]]passion[[t:1]] and a change, or that tends toward a [[t:2]]privation[[t:3]], as, for example, (to admit) that a thing might not exist in Him [[t:4]]in act[[t:5]][[fn:579]] and thereafter be [[t:6]]in act[[t:7]], or finally that which tends toward assimilating Him to one of His creatures. These matters are among those in which physical science proves useful for the knowledge of God; for, whoever does not possess these (physical) sciences does not apprehend what is defective in the [[t:8]]passions[[t:9]], nor does he comprehend what is meant by [[t:10]]being in potentiality[[t:11]] and [[t:12]]being in act[[t:13]], and remains ignorant that [[t:14]]privation[[t:15]] is inherent in all that is [[t:16]]in potentiality[[t:17]][[fn:580]], that which is [[t:18]]in potentiality[[t:19]] being more imperfect than that which moves in order that this [[t:20]]potentiality[[t:21]] may pass into [[t:22]]act[[t:23]], and that which moves being likewise imperfect in comparison to that towards which it moves in order to arrive at [[t:24]]act[[t:25]][[fn:581]]. But, if one comprehends these things without also knowing their demonstrations, one does not apprehend the particularities which necessarily result from these general propositions; hence, one possesses no demonstration for the existence of God, nor for the necessity of excluding from Him these (four) species (of things).
root.text.Part 1..54.2: Having made these preliminary observations, I proceed to another chapter, in which I shall demonstrate the falsity of that which those who admit in Him [[t:0]]essential attributes[[t:1]] believe. However, this can only be comprehended by one who has first acquired knowledge of logic and the nature of being.
root.text.Part 1..55.0: Know thou that similitude is a certain relation between two things; and whenever no relation can be admitted between two things, neither can a similitude be conceived between them. Likewise, whenever there is no similitude between two things, there is also no relation between them. Thus, for example, it is not said: "Such a heat is similar to such a color", nor: "such a sound is similar to such a sweetness"; and this is a matter manifest in itself[[fn:582]]. Now, as the relation between us and God—I mean, between Him and that which is outside of Him—is (a thing) inadmissible, it follows that similitude is likewise inadmissible. It must be known that, whenever two things come under the same species—I mean, that their quiddity is one—and they differ only in greatness and smallness, or in strength and weakness, or in other things of this kind, they are necessarily similar to each other, although they differ in the said kind of difference. Thus, for example, the mustard seed and the sphere of the fixed stars are similar in having the three dimensions; and although the latter be exceedingly great[[fn:583]] and the other exceedingly small, the notion of the existence of dimensions is the same in both. Likewise, the wax which melts in the sun and the element of fire are similar in having heat; and although the heat of the latter be exceedingly strong and that of the former exceedingly weak, the notion of the manifestation of this quality is nevertheless the same in both.
root.text.Part 1..55.1: Thus, then, those who posit that there exist [[t:0]]essential[[t:1]] attributes applicable to the Creator, namely, that He possesses [[t:2]]existence[[t:3]], [[t:4]]life[[t:5]], [[t:6]]power[[t:7]], [[t:8]]knowledge[[t:9]][[fn:584]], and [[t:10]]will[[t:11]], ought to apprehend that these qualities cannot be ascribed, in the identical sense, to Him and to us, with the sole distinction that these attributes (of God) would be greater, or more perfect, or more enduring, or more stable than our own[[fn:585]], such that His existence would be more stable than ours, His life more durable than ours, His power greater than ours, His knowledge more perfect than ours, and His will more extensive than ours, and that a single definition would encompass both; as indeed those proponents contend[[fn:586]]. This is by no means the case: for the comparative degree is employed solely (when a comparison is drawn) between those things to which the adjective in question applies as a [[t:12]]common noun[[t:13]][[fn:587]], and, this being so, there must exist similitude (between these things); but, according to the persuasion of those who believe in [[t:14]]essential attributes[[t:15]], it would be necessary to concede that, just as the essence of God cannot resemble other essences, so too the essential attributes they ascribe to Him bear no resemblance to the attributes (of other beings), and that (consequently) the same definition cannot apply to both. Nevertheless, they do not proceed thus, believing, on the contrary, that a single definition encompasses both, notwithstanding the absence of similitude between them[[fn:588]].
root.text.Part 1..55.2: It is, in truth, evident to him who comprehends the signification of the [[t:0]]similitude[[t:1]], that, if the term [[t:2]]existing[[t:3]] is simultaneously applied to God and to all that lies beyond Him, it is merely a matter of simple homonymy; and similarly, if the [[t:4]]science[[t:5]], the [[t:6]]power[[t:7]], the [[t:8]]will[[t:9]], and the [[t:10]]life[[t:11]] are attributed simultaneously to God and to all that is endowed with science, power, will, and life, it is merely a matter of simple homonymy, whereby there is no resemblance of signification between the two (kinds of attributes).
root.text.Part 1..55.3: It must not be believed that they are employed by amphiboly; for the names which are predicated by amphiboly are those which apply to two things between which there is a resemblance in some respect[[fn:589]]. This sense is an accident in them and does not constitute the essence of each of them; but these things attributed to God cannot be accidents, according to any of the thinkers[[fn:590]], whilst the attributes which belong unto us are all accidents, according to the opinion of the Mutakallimīn[[fn:591]]. I would fain know, then, whence the similitude should arise, so that a single definition might embrace both (kinds of attributes) and that they might be designated by a common name[[fn:592]], as they do maintain!—Thus, it is demonstrated in a decisive manner that between these attributes which are ascribed to God and those known to us, there is absolutely no species of community of meaning, and that the community exists only in the name, and naught else. This being so, thou must not admit ideas added to the divine essence and similar to those attributes which are added to our own essence, because there is between the two (sorts of attributes) a community of name.
root.text.Part 1..55.4: This subject is of great importance amongst those who are conversant with these matters; it behoves thee, therefore, to penetrate into it and to render an account thereof unto thyself as best thou mayest, so that it may serve as a preparation for that which we desire to make thee understand.
root.text.Part 1..56.0:
UPON THE ATTRIBUTES.
MORE PROFOUND THAN THE FOREGOING[[fn:593]].
root.text.Part 1..56.1: It is known that existence is an accident supervening upon that which exists; wherefore it is something accessory to the [[t:0]]quiddity[[t:1]] of that which exists[[fn:594]]. This is an evident and necessary truth in all that of which the existence has a cause; for its existence is a thing superadded to its [[t:2]]quiddity.[[t:3]] But as for that of which the existence has no cause, and this is God alone, the Most High, [for this is what is signified by saying that God is of a [[t:4]]necessary existence[[t:5]],] His existence is His true essence; His essence is His existence, and it is not an essence to which it has [[t:6]]happened[[t:7]] to exist, so that His existence therein should be something accessory; for He is always of a [[t:8]]necessary existence[[t:9]], and (His existence) is not something new in Him, nor an accident which has supervened upon Him[[fn:595]]. Thus, therefore, He [[t:10]]exists[[t:11]], but not by [[t:12]]existence[[t:13]], and likewise, He [[t:14]]lives[[t:15]], but not by [[t:16]]life[[t:17]], He [[t:18]]can[[t:19]], but not by [[t:20]]power[[t:21]], and He [[t:22]]knows[[t:23]], but not by [[t:24]]knowledge[[t:25]][[fn:596]]; the whole, on the contrary, reverts to a single idea, in which there is no multiplicity, as shall be explained.
root.text.Part 1..56.2: It is also essential to note that unity and multiplicity are accidents that have befallen that which exists, inasmuch as it is [[t:0]]multiple[[t:1]] or [[t:2]]a unit[[t:3]], a concept that has been elucidated in the [[t:4]]Metaphysics[[t:5]][[fn:597]]. And, just as number is not the very things that are enumerated, so too is unity not the very thing that is [[t:6]]one[[t:7]]; for these are all (two) accidents of the sort of discrete quantity [[t:8]]discrète[[t:9]][[fn:598]], which attain to beings capable of receiving analogous accidents.
root.text.Part 1..56.3: As touching the Necessary Being[t:1] (God), who is verily simple and altogether exempt from composition, even as one could not attribute unto Him the accident of multiplicity[t:3], so likewise were it false to attribute unto Him the accident of unity;[t:5] I mean to say that unity is in no wise a thing added unto His essence, but that He is one, yet not by unity.[t:7]
root.text.Part 1..56.4: These subtle subjects, which almost escape the minds, cannot be expressed by the usual language, which is one of the great causes of error; for, in every language, we are (in this regard) extremely limited in expression, so that such a subject, we cannot represent it (by words) except by relaxing ourselves for expression[[fn:599]]. Therefore, when we wish to indicate that God [[t:0]]is not multiple[[t:1]], this cannot be said except by (the word) [[t:2]]un[[t:3]], although the [[t:4]]un[[t:5]] and the [[t:6]]multiple[[t:7]] both belong to the [[t:8]]quantity;[Lat.: quantitas] c'est pourquoi, résumant l'idée, nous amenons l'esprit à (comprendre) la réalité de la chose, en disant: [[t:10]]un, non par l'unité.[[t:11]]
root.text.Part 1..56.5: It is thus that we express [[t:0]]Eternal[[t:1]] to signify that God is not something which is [[t:2]]born[[t:3]][[fn:600]]. But to say [[t:4]]Eternal[[t:5]], is, doubtless, to place ourselves at ease (with the expression); for the word [[t:6]]eternal[[t:7]] denotes something which is in relation to time, which is an accident of the movement that is inherent in the body[[fn:601]]. Furthermore, this word expresses a [[t:8]]relation[[t:9]][[fn:602]]; for one says [[t:10]]eternal[[t:11]] with regard to time as one says [[t:12]]long[[t:13]] and [[t:14]]short[[t:15]] with regard to the line[[fn:603]]. All that does not touch the accident of time cannot, in reality, be said to be either [[t:16]]eternal[[t:17]], or [[t:18]]born[[t:19]] (or [[t:20]]created[[t:21]]), any more than sweetness can be said to be [[t:22]]curved[[t:23]] or [[t:24]]straight[[t:25]], or sound, [[t:26]]salty[[t:27]] or [[t:28]]insipid[[t:29]].
root.text.Part 1..56.6: These matters are not obscure to one who has diligently trained himself to apprehend subjects in their veritable reality, and who examines them in such a manner that the intellect grasps them in their abstraction, and not according to the collective sense which the words denote[[fn:604]]. Whenever, therefore, in the (sacred) books, one discovers that the attributes of [[t:0]]first[[t:1]] and [[t:2]]last[[t:3]][[fn:605]] are ascribed to God, it is as when the [[t:4]]eye[[t:5]] and the [[t:6]]ear[[t:7]][[fn:606]] are attributed to Him; by this is signified that God is not susceptible to change, and that absolutely nothing new accrues to Him, but not that God falls under the dominion of time, such that there should be any analogy between Him and other things existing in time, and that He should thus be [[t:8]]first[[t:9]] and [[t:10]]last.[[t:11]] All these words are employed solely [[t:12]]in accordance with the language of men;[[t:13]]
root.text.Part 1..56.7: so likewise, when we say (that He is) one[t:1], the meaning is that there is naught like unto Him, but not that the idea of unity[t:3] is added unto His essence.
root.text.Part 1..57.0: <small>OF A DEEPER NATURE THAN THE FOREGOING.</small>
root.text.Part 1..57.1: Know thou that the true attributes of God are those in which the attribution is effected by means of negations, which requirs no improper expression, nor gives occasion, in any wise, to ascribe unto God any imperfection whatsoever[[fn:607]]; but an attribution enunciated affirmatively involvs the notion of association and of imperfection, even as we have set forth[[fn:608]].
root.text.Part 1..57.2: It behoves me first to explain unto thee how negations are, in a certain manner, attributes, and in what wise they are distinguished from affirmative attributes; thereafter shall I explain unto thee how we have no means of assigning an attribute unto God, save by negations, and not otherwise.
root.text.Part 1..57.3: I say, then: an attribute is not only that which particularizes the subject in such wise that it shars not this attribute with aught else, but an attribute is also at times the attribute of a subject, even though the latter should share it with another and no particularization should result therefrom. If, for example, beholding a man from afar, thou askest what is the object seen, and it be answered thee (that it is) an animal, this is indubitably an attribute of the object seen; for, although it distinguishes it not particularly from all other things, there nevertheless results therefrom a certain particularisation, in the sense that the object seen is a body which belongs neither to the species of plants, nor to that of minerals. Likewise again: if, a man being in a certain house, thou knowest that there is therein a certain body, without knowing what it is, and, having asked what is in that house, someone answers thee that there is therein neither mineral nor vegetable body, there results (from this answer) a certain particularisation, and thou knowest that there is therein an animal, although thou knowest not what animal it be. In this respect, therefore, negative attributes have something in common with affirmative attributes; for they necessarily produce a certain particularisation, although this be limited to the removing, by negation, of all that which we did not at first believe ought to be denied[[fn:609]]. But here is the respect in which negative attributes are distinguished from affirmative attributes: it is that affirmative attributes, even when they do not particularize (the subject), always indicate a part of the thing which one desirs to know, whether it be a part of its substance, or one of its accidents, whilst negative attributes do in no wise make us to know what is in reality the essence that we desire to know[[fn:610]], unless it be accidentally, as we have given examples thereof.
root.text.Part 1..57.4: Upon this preliminary observation, it is said: It is a thing demonstrated that God, the Most High, is the [[t:0]]necessary[[t:1]] being, in which, as we shall demonstrate, there is no composition. We apprehend nothing of him, save that [[t:2]]he is[[t:3]], but not [[t:4]]what he is[[t:5]][[fn:611]]. It is therefore impossible to admit that he has an affirmative attribute: for he has no [[t:6]]being[[t:7]] outside of his [[t:8]]quiddity[[t:9]], whereby the attribute might indicate one of the two things[[fn:612]]; nay, his quiddity cannot be [[t:10]]composed[[t:11]], whereby the attribute might indicate its two parts[[fn:613]]; and, a fortiori, he cannot have accidents that might be indicated by the attribute. There is therefore, in any manner, no affirmative attribute of God.
root.text.Part 1..57.5: Negatory attributes are those which must be employed to guide the mind toward that which it behoovs us to believe concerning God; for there results from their part no multiplicity, and they lead the mind to the term of that which is possible for man to apprehend of God. Since it is demonstrated unto us, for example, that there exists necessarily somewhat beyond these essences perceived by the senses and of which we embrace the knowledge by means of the intellect, we say of this somewhat that it exists, which signifies that its non-existence is inadmissible. Perceiving thereafter that it is not with this Being as it is, for example, with the existence of the elements, which are inanimate bodies, we say that He is living, which signifies that God is not without life. Perceiving thereafter that it is also not with this Being as with the existence of the heaven, which is a body (albeit) living, we say that He is by no means a body. Perceiving thereafter that it is not with this Being as with the existence of the intellect, which, although it be neither a body nor without life, is nevertheless the product of a cause, we say that God is eternal, which signifies that He has no cause which has brought Him into existence. Then we perceive that the existence of this Being, which is His essence[[fn:614]], does not suffice Him in such wise as to exist only (Himself), but that, on the contrary, there emanate from Him many existences; and this, not as heat emanats from fire, nor as light proceeds from the sun, but by a divine action which gives them duration and harmony by governing them well[[fn:615]], as we shall set forth. And it is because of all this that we attribute unto God power, knowledge, and will, meaning by these attributes that He is neither impotent, nor ignorant, nor heedless, nor negligent. If we say that He is not impotent, it signifies that His existence suffices to bring into existence things other than Himself; not ignorant signifies that He perceivs, that is to say, that He lives, for everything that perceivs has life[[fn:616]]; by neither heedless nor negligent, we mean to say that all these beings follow a certain order and a regime, that they are not neglected and delivered unto chance, but that they are as everything which is conducted, with an intention and a will, by Him who wills it[[fn:617]]. Finally, we perceive that this Being has no fellow; if therefore we say[[fn:618]]: He is one, it signifies that there are not many[[fn:619]].
root.text.Part 1..57.6: It is therefore manifest that every attribute wherewith we invest Him, is either an attribute of action, or else [if its purpose be to make understood the essence of God, and not His action] it must be regarded as the negation of its privative[[fn:620]]. But these negations themselves must not be employed, to apply them unto God, save in the manner that thou knowest; (I mean) that one sometimes denies of a thing that which it is not in its condition to possess, as when we say of the wall that it ses not[[fn:621]].
root.text.Part 1..57.7: — Thou knowest, O reader of this treatise! that this very heaven — [which yet is a moved body[[fn:622]], and which we have measured by spans and by cubits, even to embracing with our science the measures of certain of its parts and the greater part of its movements[[fn:623]]] —, our intellects are much too weak to comprehend its quiddity, although we know that it has necessarily[[fn:624]] matter and form, save that it is not there a matter such as that which is in us; wherefore we can only qualify it by words without precision[[fn:625]], and not by a precise affirmation.
