In fact, we say that the heaven is neither light nor heavy, that it is impassible, and that because of this it receivs no impression; that it has neither taste nor smell, and other such negations[[fn:626]]; all this because of our ignorance concerning the said matter. And what shall it be of our intellects, if they seek to apprehend Him who is exempt from matter, who is of an extreme simplicity, the necessary Being, who has no cause and who is affected by nothing which might be added to His perfect essence, whose perfection signifies (for us) negation of imperfections, as we have set it forth? for we apprehend of Him naught else save that He is, that there is a Being whom none of the beings He has produced resembls, who has absolutely naught in common with these latter, that there is in Him neither multiplicity, nor impotence to produce that which is outside of Him, and that His relation to the world is that of the captain to the vessel; not that this be the true relation, nor that the comparison be just, but it serves as a guide to the mind (to understand) that God governs the beings, that is to say, that He perpetuats them and maintains them in order, as is behoovful. This subject shall yet be more amply set forth.
root.text.Part 1..57.8: Praise be unto Him who (is so highly exalted that), when intellects contemplate His essence, their comprehension is changed into incapacity, and when they examine how His actions result from His will, their knowledge is changed into ignorance, and when tongues desire to glorify Him by attributes, all eloquence becoms a feeble stammering[[fn:627]]!
root.text.Part 1..58.0: One might here pose the following question: If, in truth, there be no means to perceive the true essence of God, if one can demonstrate the impossibility of perceiving aught else save that He is[[fn:628]], and if affirmative attributes be impossible, as has been demonstrated, in which then consists the relative superiority amongst those who perceive? for then, that which our master Moses and Solomon perceived is the same thing as that which every individual amongst the students perceivs, and it is impossible to add aught thereto. And yet it is generally admitted by the theologians[[fn:629]], or rather by the philosophers, that there are in this regard many gradations[[fn:630]]. Know then that verily it is so, and that there are most great nuances of superiority among those who perceive. In fact, in proportion as one augments the attributes of a subject, the latter is better determined and one apprehends better and better its true nature[[fn:631]]; and likewise, in proportion as thou augmentest the negations in regard to God, thou drawest nigh unto perception and art nearer thereto than he who denies not that which is demonstrated unto thee as behooving to be denied.
root.text.Part 1..58.1: Wherefore one man may weary himself for many years to understand a science and to verify the principles thereof, so that he may attain unto certitude[[fn:632]]; and then all this science produces no other result than (to teach us) that we must deny of God a certain thing which is known, by demonstration, to be inadmissible in respect of Him[[fn:633]]; whilst for another, among those who are weak in speculation, this is not demonstrated, and it remains doubtful for him whether this thing exists or exists not in God; and another yet, among those who are utterly bereft of vision, affirms of Him this thing whose negation is demonstrated (as indispensable). I, for example, shall demonstrate that He is in no wise a body; another will doubt, and will not know whether He be a body or whether He be not; and yet another will decide that He is a body, and will approach God with such a belief[[fn:634]]. How great shall be the difference between these three persons! The first shall indubitably be the nearest unto God, the second shall be far from Him, and the third, the farthest. Likewise, if we should suppose a fourth, for whom it was demonstrated that passions are inadmissible in respect of God, whereas for the first, who only denies corporeity, this was not demonstrated, this fourth person would indubitably be nearer unto God than the first, and so forth; so that, if there were found a person for whom it was demonstrated that it is impossible (to admit), in respect of God, many things which, according to us, might exist in Him, or emanate from Him, — and with all the more reason, if we went so far as to believe this necessary, — this person would indubitably be more perfect than we.
root.text.Part 1..58.2: Thus, it is manifest unto thee that, as often as it shall be demonstrated unto thee that a certain thing must be denied of God, thou shalt thereby be more perfect, and that as often as thou shalt affirmatively attribute unto Him a thing added (to His essence), thou shalt liken Him (unto the creatures), and thou shalt be far from knowing His reality. It is in this manner that one must draw near to the perception of God, by means of inquiry[[fn:635]] and study, in order to know the falsity of all that is inadmissible in respect of Him, and not by affirmatively attributing to Him a thing as being added to His essence, or as if this thing were a perfection in respect of Him, because it is found to be one in respect of ourselves; for all perfections are but certain capacities[[fn:636]], and no capacity exists in every (being) endowed with capacity[[fn:637]].
root.text.Part 1..58.3: Thou shalt know, therefore, that if thou affirmatively attributest unto Him a thing other (than Himself), thou removest thyself from Him in two respects: first, because all that thou attributest unto Him is a perfection (only) for us, and, secondly, because He possesses no thing other (than Himself), but on the contrary, it is His essence itself which forms His perfections, as we have set forth.
root.text.Part 1..58.4: Now, everyone having perceived that, even as to that which we have the faculty to perceive (of God), there is no means to perceive it otherwise than by negation, and negation making us know absolutely nothing of the reality of the thing to which it is applied[[fn:638]], all, both ancients and moderns, have declared that the intellects cannot perceive God, that He alone perceivs what He is, and that to perceive Him is (to recognize) that one is powerless to perceive Him fully[[fn:639]]. All the philosophers say: We are dazzled by His beauty, and He hids Himself from us by the very force of His manifestation, even as the sun hids itself from the eyes, which are too weak to perceive it. Men have enlarged upon this in (discourses) which it would be useless to repeat here[[fn:640]]; but that which has been said most eloquently in this regard are these words of the Psalmist: לך דמיה תהלה (Ps. 65, 2), the sense of which is: unto Thee silence is praise. This is a most eloquent expression upon this subject; for, whatsoever we may say with the intent of exalting and glorifying (God), we shall find therein something offensive[[fn:641]] in respect of God, and we shall see (expressed) therein a certain imperfection. It is therefore better to be silent and to limit oneself[[fn:642]] to the perceptions of the intellect, as perfect men have recommended, saying: Commune (meditate) with your own heart upon your bed, and be still (Ps. 4, 5).
root.text.Part 1..58.5: Thou knowest also a celebrated passage of the Sages to which I would that all their words were similar; although it be a passage which is known by heart, I shall cite it to thee textually, in order to call thy attention to the ideas it contains. Behold what they say[[fn:643]]: "A certain man, coming into the presence of Rabbi Hanina, expressed himself thus (whilst making his prayer): O God, the great, the mighty, the terrible, the magnificent, the strong, the feared, the imposing!... The Rabbi said unto him (interrupting him): Hast thou finished all the praises of thy Lord? Verily, even the first three (attributes), had Moses not pronounced them in the Law[[fn:644]] and had the men of the Great Assembly[[fn:645]] not come to fix them in the prayer, we should not dare to utter them; and thou, thou utterest so great a number! To make a comparison: a mortal king, for example, who should possess millions of pieces of gold, and whom one should praise for (possessing pieces) of silver, would this not be an offense unto him?" Behold how this good man expressed himself.
root.text.Part 1..58.6: Observe first how great was his reluctance and his aversion to the accumulation of affirmative attributes[[fn:646]], and observe likewise that he says clearly that, were we left to our own intelligence alone[[fn:647]], we should never utter[[fn:648]] any attributes nor pronounce any of them; but since, by the necessity of speaking unto men in such wise as to give them some idea (of God), one was forced to describe[[fn:649]] God by their (own) perfections — [in accordance with these words: the Law has spoken according to the language of men[[fn:650]]] —, we ought, in the last resort, to confine ourselves to the (three) words in question[[fn:651]], and even then we should never employ them as names of God, save when we read them in the Pentateuch. If, however, the men of the Great Synod, who were (in part) prophets, came afterwards to sanction their use in prayer, we ought ever to restrict ourselves to these words alone[[fn:652]]. In substance, then, he (R. ’Hanînâ) setts forth that two necessities must meet for us to employ them in prayer: the first, that they be found in the Pentateuch; the second, that the prophets should have established them in prayer. Without the first necessity, we should not pronounce them (at all); without the second, we should not have taken them from their (primitive) place to use them in prayer; and thou (added he), dost thou accumulate attributes[[fn:653]]?
root.text.Part 1..58.7: It is manifest unto thee also by these words (of R. ’Hanînâ) that it is not permitted us to employ in prayer, nor to pronounce, all the epithets which thou findest attributed to God in the books of the prophets; for he says not (merely): “Had not Moses said them, we should not dare to say them”, but (he adds as) another condition: “and had not the men of the Great Synod come to establish them in prayer”, and since then only has it been permitted us to employ them in prayer. But not as have done those men verily inept, who have striven to dwell at length (upon the attributes), in prayers of their own composition and orations of their own fashion, whereby they thought to draw nigh unto God, and in which they have given Him attributes which, even were they given to a human being, would imply an imperfection[[fn:654]]. It is because, not understanding these sublime subjects, which are too foreign to the intelligences of the vulgar, they approached God with their rash tongues, and used toward Him all the attributes and all the addresses which they thought they might permit themselves[[fn:655]], and dwelt thereon, in order to move Him, as they imagined, in such wise that He might be affected (by their words). Especially when they found in this regard some text of a prophetic discourse, they believed themselves permitted to employ these same terms, which, in any case, have need of being allegorically interpreted; they took them in their literal sense, derived therefrom (other terms), formed ramifications thereof, and built discourses thereupon. This species of license is frequent among poets and orators, or among those who pretend to make verses; so that there have been composed discourses which, in part, are pure irreligion, and in part betray a weakness of mind and a corruption of the imagination such as would naturally cause a man to laugh when he listens to them, and to weep when he considers that such language has been held toward God. Were it not painful for me to disparage the authors, I should cite to thee somewhat thereof to draw thy attention to what is there impious[[fn:656]]; but these are discourses whose vice is too evident to him who knows how to understand,
root.text.Part 1..58.8: and thou must say to thyself in pondering thereon: if it be a grievous sin to speak evil and to slander the reputation of another[[fn:657]], how much more so (is one guilty) in giving free rein to his tongue when it concerns God, and in giving Him attributes above which He is exalted? I should not call this a sin, but an offence, and a blasphemy rashly committed by the multitude that listens and by that fool who utters (such words). But as for him who understands what there is of vice in such discourses, and who (notwithstanding this) pronouncs them, he is, in my judgment, of the number of those of whom it was said: and the children of Israel imagined concerning God words that were not right (II Kings, xvii, 9)[[fn:658]], and elsewhere: and to utter error against the Lord (Isaiah, xxxii, 6). If then thou art of those who respect the glory of their Creator[[fn:659]], thou must by no means lend an ear thereto; and how then wouldst thou dare to pronounce them, and how (much more so) wouldst thou dare to compose the like? For thou knowest how great is the sin of him who hurls words toward heaven[[fn:660]]. One must by no means engage in attributes of God (expressed) by affirmation, believing thereby to glorify Him, and one must not depart from that which the men of the Great Synod have established in prayers and benedictions; there is therein enough for the need, and more than enough, as R. ’Hanînâ has said. As for what is further found (in the way of attributes) in the books of the prophets, one may read it in passing, provided one admit, as we have set forth, that these are attributes of action, or that they indicate the negation of their privation[[fn:661]]. And this, moreover, must not be divulged to the multitude; on the contrary, this kind of study belongs to the select few who do not believe they glorify God by saying that which is not seemly, but by understanding aright.
root.text.Part 1..58.9: I return now to complete my remarks upon the words of R. ’Hanînâ and their wise arrangement[[fn:662]]. He says not: “To make a comparison, a mortal king, for example, who should possess millions of pieces of gold, and whom one should praise for (possessing) a hundred pieces”; for this comparison (so conceived) would indicate that the perfections of God are greater than those attributed to Him, but that they are nevertheless of the same species, whereas, as we have demonstrated, it is not so. But the wisdom of this comparison consists in these words: “... pieces of gold, and whom one should praise for (possessing pieces) of silver”, which indicate that God has nothing which is of the same species as those perfections which are found in us, and that these, on the contrary, are imperfections in respect to Him, as he explains by saying: “Would this not be an offence unto him?”
root.text.Part 1..58.10: Thus, I have made known to thee that all those attributes which thou believest to be a perfection[[fn:663]] constitute an imperfection in respect to God, if they be of the same species as those which we possess. Solomon has already sufficiently instructed us in this regard, saying: For God is in heaven, and thou upon earth; therefore let thy words be few (Ecclesiastes, v, 1).
root.text.Part 1..59.0: In this chapter, I desire to set before thee certain illustrations, by which thou mayest better conceive how necessary it is to ascribe unto God numerous negative attributes, and whereby thou shalt more and more avoid the admission of affirmative attributes in respect of Him. Suppose a man has the notion that there exists (something which is called) a ship, yet knows not whether the thing to which this name appertains be a substance or an accident; thereafter another individual has recognized that it is by no means an accident; another again, that it is not a mineral; another, that it is neither an animal; another, that it is not a vegetable still attached to the earth; another, that it is not a single body forming a natural whole; another, that it is not something having a flat form, such as planks and doors; another, that it is not a sphere; another, that it is not something of a conical form; another, that it is neither something circular, nor something having plane sides[[fn:664]]; and lastly, another, that it is not a solid body; — it is manifest that this last person will have arrived, by means of these negative attributes, almost at the point of figuring to himself the ship as it is, and will find himself, as it were, on a level with him who figurs it unto himself as a wooden body, hollow, oblong, and composed of many pieces of wood, and who represents it by means of affirmative attributes. As for the preceding persons of whom we have spoken in our illustration, each of them is further from forming an idea of the ship than he who follows him, so that the first, in our example, knows naught thereof but the name alone.
root.text.Part 1..59.1: In such wise do negative attributes bring thee closer unto the knowledge of God and the perception of Him; but thou must above all endeavour that every new negation which thou addest be demonstrated, and thou must not be content merely to pronounce it[[fn:665]]; for, in proportion as it shall be manifested unto thee by a demonstration that a thing which was believed to exist in God must be denied of Him, thou shalt indubitably have drawn closer unto Him by one degree more.
root.text.Part 1..59.2: It is in this manner that certain men are found very near unto Him, whilst others are extremely remote from Him; yet not that there is herein any local proximity[[fn:666]], so that one might (materially) draw near to or depart from Him, as they believe who are destitute of sight. Comprehend this well, know it, and thou shalt find thyself happy therein. Thou knowest now the path in which thou must walk to draw near unto God, and it depends upon thy will to walk therein[[fn:667]].
root.text.Part 1..59.3: As for the attributes of God (expressed) by affirmations, they involve a great peril; for it has already been demonstrated that whatsoever we might take for a perfection [even though this perfection should exist in God, according to the opinion of those who admit the attributes], would not be the same kind of perfection that we should imagine, but would only be so called by homonymy, as we have explained[[fn:668]]. This would necessarily lead thee to a negative idea: for, in saying that He knows by a sole knowledge, and that, by this immutable and not multiple knowledge, He knows the multiple and variable things which are incessantly renewed, without there occurring in Him any new knowledge, and that it is by a single immutable knowledge that He knows a thing before it is born, after it has come into existence, and after it has ceased to exist, thou declarest that He knows with a knowledge which is not like ours; and likewise, there must be attached to His existence another idea than unto ours[[fn:669]]. Thou producest therefore necessarily negations, and, far from succeeding in establishing an essential attribute, thou comest to (establish) multiplicity and to admit that God is an essence having unknown attributes; for those which thou pretendest to lend Him affirmatively, thou thyself refusest to assimilate unto the attributes known amongst us, and, consequently, they are not of the same kind. Thus, then, to admit affirmative attributes[[fn:670]] would, as it were, only amount to saying: that God is a subject affected by certain attributes, and that this subject is not the same thing as these attributes[[fn:671]], so that the final result which we should obtain by this belief would be naught else than association[[fn:672]]. Indeed, every subject indubitably possesses attributes, and, although one by existence, it is (divided into) two by definition, the idea of the subject being other than that of the attribute[[fn:673]]. In several chapters of this treatise it shall be clearly demonstrated unto thee that composition is impossible in God, but that He is pure simplicity, in the highest degree.
root.text.Part 1..59.4: I will not say, moreover, that he who ascribs affirmative attributes unto God apprehends Him imperfectly, or associats (other beings) with Him, or apprehends Him contrary to what He is; but I will rather say that, without perceiving it, he eliminats from his belief the existence of God[[fn:674]]. I explain myself: he who apprehends imperfectly the reality of a thing, is he who apprehends one part thereof and is ignorant of another, as, for example, he who, in the idea of man, apprehends that which pertains to the animal nature, without apprehending that which pertains to reason; now, in the real being of God there is no multiplicity, so that one might understand such a thing thereof and be ignorant of such another. Likewise, he who associats (another thing) with a thing, is he who, whilst representing to himself a certain essence according to its real nature, ascribs a similar nature to another essence; now, the attributes in question, according to the opinion of those who admit them, are not the essence of God, but ideas added to the essence[[fn:675]]. Finally, he who apprehends a thing contrary to what it is must necessarily apprehend something of what it really is[[fn:676]]; for, if any one should figure to himself that savour were a quantity, I should not say that he figurs the thing contrary to what it is, but I should say that he is ignorant even of the existence of savour and that he knows not to what this name appertains. These are very subtle considerations, which must be well understood.
root.text.Part 1..59.5: By this explanation thou shalt know that he alone apprehends God [[t:0]]imperfectly[[t:1]], and is far from knowing Him, who does not recognize the non-existence (in God) of certain things which others have demonstrated must be denied of Him; so that in proportion as one admitts fewer negations, he apprehends Him less perfectly, as we have set forth at the beginning of this chapter. As for him who assigns unto God an affirmative attribute, he knows of Him naught but the mere name, but the object to which, in his imagination, this name applies, is something that has no existence; it is rather an invention and a falsehood, and it is as though he applied this name to a non-entity, for there is in existence nothing like unto it. It is as one who, having heard the name of the elephant and having known that it is an animal, should desire to know its form and true nature, and to whom another, deceived or deceiving, should say: «It is an animal with but one foot and three wings, dwelling in the depths of the sea; it has a transparent body, and a face as broad and of the same form and figure as the human face; it speaks like a man, and now flies in the air and now swimms like a fish.» Verily, I would not say that this man conceivs the elephant [[t:2]]contrary[[t:3]] to what it is in reality, nor that he has of the elephant an [[t:4]]imperfect[[t:5]] knowledge; but I would say that the thing which he imagins to be in this fashion is an invention and a falsehood, that naught like it exists, and that, on the contrary, it is a non-entity to which the name of a being has been applied, such as the [[t:6]]griffin[[t:7]][[fn:677]], the [[t:8]]man-horse[[t:9]] (centaur), and other imaginary figures to which the name of some real being has been applied, whether it be a simple or a compound name. It is absolutely the same here: for indeed, God — may He be glorified! — is a Being whose existence has been demonstrated to be necessary, and from [[t:10]]necessary[[t:11]] existence results (as a consequence) pure simplicity, even as I shall demonstrate; but that this simple essence, of a necessary existence, should have attributes and be affected by other things, as has been pretended, is that which can in no wise take place, as has been demonstrated. If therefore we should say that this essence, for example, which is called [[t:12]]God[[t:13]], is an essence containing numerous ideas which serve as its attributes, we should apply this name to a pure non-entity. Consider, consequently, how perilous it is to assign unto God affirmative attributes.
root.text.Part 1..59.6: Thus, then, that which must be believed regarding the attributes which are encountered in the Pentateuch and in the books of the Prophets, is that they all have no other purpose than to lead us to (recognize) the perfection of God, or else they designate actions emanating from Him, as we have already set forth[[fn:678]].
root.text.Part 1..60.0.sub_0: All the names of God found in the (sacred) books are generally derived from actions[[fn:679]], which thing is not unknown. One name alone must be excepted, namely (that which is written by) [[t:0]]yod, he, waw, he;[[t:1]] for it is a name [[t:2]]distinctively assigned[[t:3]][[fn:680]] to God, and which, for that reason, is called [[t:4]]Shem ha-Meforash[[t:5]][[fn:681]], signifying that it indicats expressly the essence of God, and that therein is no homonymy. As for His other glorious names, they designate Him by homonymy; for they are derived from certain actions of which the like are found amongst us, as we have set forth[[fn:682]]. The name itself (of [[t:6]]Adonai[[t:7]]), which is substituted for that of [[t:8]]yod, he, waw, he[[t:9]][[fn:683]], is likewise [[t:10]]derivative[[t:11]], (containing the idea) of [[t:12]]lordship;[[t:13]] (one reads for example:) [[t:14]]The man, the Lord[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]אדני[[t:17]]) [[t:18]]of the country[[t:19]], [[t:20]]spake[[t:21]], etc. (Genesis, 42, 30). The difference between [[t:22]]Adoni[[t:23]] ([[t:24]]אֲדׂנִי[[t:25]], [[t:26]]my lord[[t:27]]), the [[t:28]]nun[[t:29]] having the vowel [[t:30]]i[[t:31]], and [[t:32]]Adonai[[t:33]] ([[t:34]]אֲדׂנָי[[t:35]]), the [[t:36]]nun[[t:37]] having a long [[t:38]]a[[t:39]], is the same as that which exists between [[t:40]]Sari[[t:41]] ([[t:42]]שָׂרִי[[t:43]]), signifying [[t:44]]my prince[[t:45]], and [[t:46]]Sarai[[t:47]]([[t:48]]שָׂרַי[[t:49]]), the name of the [[t:50]]wife of Abram[[t:51]] ([[t:52]]Ibid.[[t:53]], 12, 17; XVI, 1); for these are [[t:54]]emphatic[[t:55]] names which embrace also other beings[[fn:684]], and it has also been said (in speaking) to an angel: [[t:56]]Adonai[[t:57]] (my lord)... [[t:58]]pass not away[[t:59]] ([[t:60]]Ibid.[[t:61]], 18, 3). If I have given thee this explanation, particularly regarding (the name) [[t:62]]Adonai[[t:63]], employed by substitution, it is because, of all the names of God most widely spread, it is that one which is most proper unto Him. As for the others, such as [[t:64]]Dayyan[[t:65]] (judge), [[t:66]]Tzaddik[[t:67]] (just), [[t:68]]Hannun[[t:69]] (gracious, clement), [[t:70]]Rahum[[t:71]] (merciful), [[t:72]]Elohim[[t:73]][[fn:685]], they are evidently names [[t:74]]common[[t:75]] and [[t:76]]derivative.[[t:77]] But the name which is spelled [[t:78]]yod, he, waw, he[[t:79]], has no known etymology[[fn:686]], and is applied to no other being[[fn:687]].
root.text.Part 1..60.0.sub_1: It is not doubtful that this glorious name, which, as thou knowest, was to be pronounced only in the Sanctuary, and particularly by the [[t:80]]priests sanctified unto the Lord[[t:81]][[fn:688]], in the sacerdotal blessing[[fn:689]], and by the High Priest on the Day of Fasting[[fn:690]], indicats a certain idea in respect of which there is naught in common between God and that which is outside of Him; perchance it indicats — according to the (Hebrew) tongue, of which there remains[[fn:691]] unto us to-day but very little, and according to the manner in which it was pronounced — the idea of [[t:82]]necessary existence.[[t:83]] In sum, that which causs this name to have so high an importance and that men refrain from pronouncing it, is that it indicats the very essence of God, so that no created being participats in what it indicats[[fn:692]], as the Doctors have said concerning this name: [[t:84]]My name, which is peculiar to Me[[t:85]][[fn:693]].
root.text.Part 1..60.1: As for the other names, they all indicate attributes, (I mean that they indicate) not only an essence, but an essence having attributes[[fn:694]], for they are [[t:0]]derivative;[[t:1]] and by that very fact they lead to the belief in multiplicity (in God), I mean, they lead to the belief that there exist attributes and that there is an essence and something added to the essence. In effect, such is the significance of every [[t:2]]derivative[[t:3]] name; for it indicats a certain idea and an unexpressed subject to which this idea is joined[[fn:695]]. Now, as it has been demonstrated that God is not a subject to which certain ideas have come to be joined, it is known that the derivative names are (given to God), either to attribute unto Him [[t:4]]action[[t:5]], or to lead us to (recognize) His perfection.
root.text.Part 1..60.2: Wherefore Rabbi Hanina would have felt a reluctance to say: “The great, mighty, and awful (God),” had there not been the two necessities of which he speaks[[fn:696]]; for these words might lead to the belief in essential attributes, I mean to say, perfections existing in God. These names of God, being derived from His actions, having multiplied, led certain men to believe that He possessed numerous attributes, as many as the actions wherefrom they are derived; therefore was it predicted that men should attain to a perception which shall cause this error to cease for them, and it is said: In that day shall the Lord be ONE and His name ONE (Zechariah xiv. 9); that is to say: even as He is one, so shall He then be invoked by one name only, that which uniquely indicats the essence (of God), and it shall by no means be a derivative name. In the Pirke Rabbi Eliezer (chap. iii.), we read: “Before the world was created, there was none but the Holy One and His name alone.” Observe well how clearly he stats that all these derivative names were born only after the birth of the world; and this is true, for they are all names established in relation to the actions (of God) found in the universe; but if we consider His essence, void and stripped of all action, He has absolutely no derivative name, but a single name properly applied to indicate His essence. We possess no Shem (name) which is not derivative, save that one, to wit, Yod, He, Vav, He, which is the absolute Shem ha-mephorash[[fn:697]];
root.text.Part 1..60.3: thou must believe naught else, nor give admission in thy mind to the folly of those who write kami’oth[[fn:698]] and to that which thou shalt hear from them or read in their senseless writings, concerning the names they forge[[fn:699]] without offering any sense whatsoever, calling them Shemoth (sacred names), and pretending that they require holiness and purity, and that they work miracles. All these things are fables[[fn:700]] which a perfect man should not so much as listen to; and how then could he believe in them?
root.text.Part 1..60.4: The term Shem ha-mephorash is therefore applied only to this Tetragrammaton name alone, which is written, but is not read according to its letters. It is clearly stated in the Sifre (upon this verse): Thus (כּהׁ) ye shall bless the children of Israel (Numbers vi. 23): “Thus, that is to say, in these words; thus, that is to say, by the Shem ha-mephorash[[fn:701]].” It is likewise said there: “In the Holy City, (this name is pronounced) even as it is written; in the province, by the substituted name[[fn:702]].” And in the Talmud it is said[[fn:703]]: “Thus (כּהׁ) signifies, by the Shem ha-mephorash; if (doubting still) thou shouldst ask: Is it truly by the Shem ha-mephorash, or only by the name substituted for it? there are, to inform thee, these words: And they shall put MY NAME (Ibid., v. 27), that is to say, the name which is peculiar unto Me.”
root.text.Part 1..60.5: It is therefore clear that the [[t:0]]schem ha-mephorasch[[t:1]] is this name [[t:2]]tétragrammate[[t:3]], and that it is he alone who indicates the essence (of God) without association of any other idea; it is for this reason that one has said of him: [[t:4]]he who is mine.[[t:5]]
root.text.Part 1..60.6: In the following chapter, I shall set forth unto thee that which has led men to this belief concerning the Shemoth (or mysterious names); I shall explain unto thee the depth of this question and shall lift the veil therefrom for thee, so that there may remain no obscurity in this regard, unless thou shouldst desire to deceive thyself.
root.text.Part 1..61.0: The [[t:0]]sacerdotal benediction[[t:1]] has been enjoined upon us, in which the Name of the Eternal (is pronounced) as it is written, and this is the [[t:2]]schem ha-mephorasch.[[t:3]] It was not universally known how it ought to be pronounced, nor by what vowel each of its letters should be actuated, nor whether any of its letters, amongst those susceptible of it, should be doubled[[fn:704]]; the learned men transmitted this amongst themselves, that is to say, the manner of pronouncing this Name, which they taught to none, save [[t:4]]to the elect disciple, once a week[[t:5]][[fn:705]]. I believe that when the doctors say[[fn:706]]: “the Name of four letters, the sages transmit it to their sons and to their disciples once a week,” it refers not solely to the manner of its pronunciation, but also to the instruction concerning the idea for the sake of which this Name was [[t:6]]devised[[t:7]][[fn:707]], and within which there is likewise a divine mystery.
root.text.Part 1..61.1: There was also possessed a name which comprised twelve letters[[fn:708]], and which was inferior in sanctity to the name of four letters; that which is most probable, in my judgment, is that it was not a single name, but two or three, which being joined together had twelve letters. It was that which was substituted whenever the name of four letters occurred in reading, even as we substitute this day that which commencs with aleph, daleth. This name of twelve letters had doubtless also a more particular sense than that indicated by the name of Adonai; it was by no means forbidden to teach it, nor was a mystery made thereof[[fn:709]] unto any man of science, but on the contrary, it was taught unto whomsoever desired to learn it. It was not so with the tetragrammaton name; for none of those who knew it ever taught it save unto his son and his disciple once in a week. But since certain lawless men, having learned this name of twelve letters, professed in consequence thereof evil beliefs[[fn:710]],—as it happens unto every man who is not perfect, when he learns that the thing is not such as he had at first imagined,—this name was also hidden, and was taught only unto the most pious of the sacerdotal order, to be used in blessing the people in the sanctuary; for already, by reason of the corruption of men, they had ceased to pronounce the shem ha-mephorash, even in the sanctuary: “After the death of Simon the Just,” say the doctors, “the priests, his brethren, ceased to bless by the Name (tetragrammaton)[[fn:711]]”; but they blessed by this name of twelve letters. “At first,” they say elsewhere[[fn:712]], “it was transmitted unto every man; but since temerarious men multiplied, it was transmitted only unto the most pious of the sacerdotal order, and these caused it to be swallowed up in the melodies of the priests, their brethren. Rabbi Tarphon said: One day I followed my maternal grandfather[[fn:713]] upon the dais, and, inclining mine ear toward a priest, I heard that he caused the name in question to be swallowed up in the melodies of the priests his brethren.”
root.text.Part 1..61.2: There was likewise possessed a name of two-and-forty letters. Now, every man capable of an idea knows well that it is absolutely impossible for two-and-forty letters to form a single word; they could therefore be naught but several words, which formed a total of two-and-forty letters. These words, it cannot be doubted, necessarily indicated certain ideas which were intended to bring man near unto the true conception of the divine essence, by the process of which we have spoken[[fn:714]]. If these words, composed of numerous letters, have been designated as a single name, it is only because they indicate a single thing, as do all improvised proper names; and, to make this thing understood, several words were employed, for at times many words are used to make a single thing understood.
root.text.Part 1..61.3: Thou must well penetrate this, and know also that what was taught were the ideas indicated by these two names, and not the mere pronunciation of the letters, devoid[[fn:715]] of all idea. Never was the appellation shem ha-mephorash applied unto the said name of twelve letters, nor unto that of two-and-forty;[[fn:716]] this designation denots only the particular name (tetragrammaton), as we have set forth. As for these two other names, they necessarily contained a certain metaphysical instruction, and the proof that one of them contained an instruction of this kind is that the doctors say in this regard[[fn:717]]: “The name of two-and-forty letters is most holy, and is transmitted only unto the pious man who is in his middle age, who is not prone to anger, nor to drunkenness, nor persists in his evil ways, and who speaks gently with all creatures. Whosoever knows this name and guards it with heed and purity is beloved above and cherished here below; he is an object of respect for all creatures, his learning endurs within him, and he has for his portion two worlds, this world and the world to come.” Such is the text of the Talmud; but how far is the sense which men attach to these words from the intention of their author! Indeed, the most part believe that there is naught there but letters which one pronouncs, but whereunto no idea is attached, so that it would be by these letters that one should obtain the said sublime things, and that it would be for their sake that one would have need of those moral dispositions and that great preparation of which mention was made; whereas it is manifest that the matter in all this is only to make known metaphysical subjects, of those subjects which form part of the mysteries of the Torah, as we have set forth[[fn:718]]. In the books which have been composed[[fn:719]] upon the science of metaphysics, it has been explained that it is impossible to forget this science, I mean the perception of the Active Intellect[[fn:720]]; and that is the sense of these words: his learning endurs within him.
root.text.Part 1..61.4: But perverse and ignorant men, having found these talmudic texts, saw therein a vast field for falsehood, saying unto themselves[[fn:721]] that they might gather together such letters as they pleased and say that it was a shem (or sacred name) which would act and operate if it were written or pronounced in such or such a manner. Afterward these lies, invented[[fn:722]] by an initial perverse and ignorant man, were committed to writing; the writings having been transmitted into the hands of good men, pious but narrow-minded, and who lacked judgment[[fn:723]] to discern the true from the false, these latter made a mystery of them, and when these writings were found in their succession, they were taken for pure truth. In short, the simple believs every word (Prov. xiv. 15).
root.text.Part 1..61.5: We have departed from our sublime subject and our subtle speculation to apply ourselves to the refutation of a folly whose absurdity is manifest to any one who has but commenced his studies; yet were we necessarily led thereto whilst treating of the names (of God), of their signification, and of the opinions prevalent regarding them among the vulgar. I return, therefore, to my subject,
root.text.Part 1..61.6: and, having observed that all the names of God are derived, with the exception of the schem ha-mephorasch, it behoves us to speak, in a special chapter, of the name (contained in these words:) אהיה אשר אהיה, I am that I am (Exodus, iii, 14); for this relats to the subtle subject wherewith we are here occupied, I mean the negation of attributes.
root.text.Part 1..62.0: We shall first make a preliminary observation. Concerning those words (of Moses): If they shall say to me: What is His name? what shall I say unto them? (Exodus, iii, 13); (one might first inquire:) how could the matter in hand lead to such a question (on the part of the Hebrews), that Moses should find it necessary to ask what answer he should return? [As for those words: But, behold, they will not believe me, nor hearken unto my voice: for they will say, The Lord has not appeared unto thee (Ibid., iv, 1), they are right clear; for such is that which must be said to any one who claims to be a prophet, until he produce proof thereof.] Furthermore[[fn:724]], if, as it seems (at first sight), it be simply a matter of a name to be pronounced, it must needs be admitted, either that the Israelites already knew this name, or that they had never heard it. Now, if it were known to them, the utterance thereof could not serve Moses as an argument, since he knew naught of it save what they themselves knew; if, on the contrary, they had never heard tell of it, what then would prove that this was indeed the name of God, even supposing that the mere knowledge of the name could serve as a proof (in favour of Moses)? Finally, God, after having taught him the name in question, said unto him: Go, and gather the elders of Israel together..... and they shall hearken to thy voice (Ibid., iii, 16 and 18); then Moses answered Him, saying: But, behold, they will not believe me, nor hearken unto my voice, although God had already said unto him: and they shall hearken to thy voice. And thereupon God said unto him: What is that in thine hand? and he said: A rod (Ibid., 4, 2).
root.text.Part 1..62.1: That which must be known, so that all these obscurities may be enlightened for thee, is what I am about to tell thee. Thou knowest how prevalent in those times were the opinions of the Sabians[[fn:725]], and that all men then, with the exception of a few, were given over to idolatry, I mean that they believed in the spirits (of the stars) and in incantations, and that they fashioned talismans[[fn:726]]. The pretension[[fn:727]] of whosoever arrogated to himself (a divine mission) had from all time been limited to this: either he maintained that by meditating and seeking for proofs it had been demonstrated to him that one single God presided over the whole universe,—and thus did Abraham,—or he claimed that the spirit of a star, or an angel, or some other similar being, had revealed itself unto him. But that any one should claim to be a prophet, (saying) that God had spoken to him and had sent him, is a thing which had never been heard of before Moses, our master. Thou must not let thyself be led into error by what is related of the patriarchs, saying that God addressed His word to them and that He manifested Himself unto them; for thou wilt not find this kind of prophetic mission (which consists) in making an appeal to men or in guiding others, so that Abraham, or Isaac, or Jacob, or those who preceded them, should have said to men: “God has told me that ye must do or not do (such a thing)”, or else: “He has sent me unto you”. Never did such a thing occur; on the contrary, there was spoken to them naught else but what concerned them personally, I mean, (that it was a matter) of making them perfect, of directing them in what they should do, and of announcing to them what would be the future of their race, but naught besides; and they themselves called men by means of study and instruction[[fn:728]], which, according to us, is clearly indicated in these words: and the souls that they had gotten in Haran (Genesis, xii, 5)[[fn:729]].
root.text.Part 1..62.2: When, therefore, God manifested Himself to Moses, our master, and commanded him to call these men (to the faith) and to bring them the message in question: “But,” he replied, “that which they will first ask of me is to establish for them that there exists a God for the universe, and then I may maintain that He has sent me.” In truth, all men then, with the exception of a few, were ignorant of the existence of God, and their highest meditation went not beyond the celestial sphere, its forces and its effects; for they detached not themselves from sensible things and possessed no intellectual perfection. God, therefore, gave him then a knowledge which he was to communicate to them, in order to establish for them the existence of God, and that is (what is expressed by the words) EHYE asher EHYE (I am that I am); this is a name derived from HAYA (היה), which denots existence, for HAYA signifies he was, and, in the Hebrew tongue, no distinction is made between being and existing. The whole mystery lies in the repetition, in the form of an attribute, of this very word which denots existence; for the word asher (אשר, which), being an incomplete noun which requirs an adjunct and having the sense of the words alladhī (الذى) and allatī (التي) in Arabic, requirs that the attribute which is conjoined[[fn:730]] to it be expressed; and, by expressing the first noun, which is the subject, by EHYE, and the second noun, which serves as its attribute, by this same word EHYE, it has been, as it were, declared that the subject is identically the same thing as the attribute. This is, therefore, an explanation of this idea: that God exists, but not by existence[[fn:731]]; so that this idea is thus summed up and interpreted: the Being who is the Being, that is to say, the Necessary Being. And it is indeed that which can be rigorously established by the demonstrative way[[fn:732]], (to wit) that there is something whose existence is necessary, which has never been non-existent and which shall never be so, even as I shall set forth the demonstration thereof (elsewhere).
root.text.Part 1..62.3: God therefore having made known unto Moses the proofs whereby His existence might be established for their learned men [for it is said further on: Go, and gather the ELDERS of Israel together], and having promised him that they would apprehend that which He had taught him[[fn:733]] and would accept it [which is expressed by these words: and they shall hearken to thy voice]: "If it be true," Moses replied, "that, by these demonstrations proceeding from the intellect, they shall admit that there is a God, by what means shall I prove that this God who exists has sent me?" Thereupon he was put in possession of a miracle[[fn:734]].—It is therefore manifest that the words what is his name signify naught else but: who is he by whom thou claimest to be sent? If he said: what is his name? 'twas but to express himself in a respectful manner when addressing the Deity[[fn:735]]; 'tis as though he had said: Thine actual essence, no man can be ignorant thereof, but if I be asked[[fn:736]] Thy name, what is the idea signified by that name? For, deeming it unseemly to say, when speaking (to God), that there might be any one to whom that Being was unknown, he attributed their ignorance to His name, and not to Him who was designated by that name.
root.text.Part 1..62.4: Similarly, the name [[t:0]]YAH[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]יה[[t:3]]) implies the idea of eternal existence[[fn:737]]. — S[[t:4]]CHADDAY[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]שדי[[t:7]]) is derived from [[t:8]]DAY[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]די[[t:11]]), which signifies [[t:12]]sufficiency[[t:13]], — e.g.: [[t:14]]the matter was[[t:15]] [[t:16]]דיס[[t:17]] [[t:18]]sufficient for them[[t:19]] (Exodus, 26, 7)—; the shin has the meaning of [[t:20]]asher[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]אשר[[t:23]]), as, e.g., in [[t:24]]she-kebar[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]שכבר[[t:27]], [[t:28]]who already[[t:29]], Ecclesiastes, IV, 2), so that the meaning (of the said name) is [[t:30]]אשר די[[t:31]], [[t:32]]who is sufficient[[t:33]], which signifies that He requires no (being) outside of Himself for that which He produces to come into existence and to continue to exist[[fn:738]], but that the mere existence of God [[t:34]]suffices[[t:35]] for this. ’H[[t:36]]ASÎN[[t:37]] ([[t:38]]חםין[[t:39]]), likewise, is a derived name, (having the meaning) of [[t:40]]strength[[t:41]], e.g., [[t:42]]and He is strong[[t:43]] ([[t:44]]חםׂן[[t:45]]) [[t:46]]like the oaks[[t:47]] (Amos, 2, 9). Similarly [[t:48]]ÇOUR[[t:49]] ([[t:50]]צור[[t:51]]) [[t:52]][[fn:739]][[t:53]] is a homonym, as we have explained.
root.text.Part 1..62.5: It is therefore clear that all the names (of God) are either [[t:0]]derived[[t:1]], or else are pronounced by [[t:2]]homonymy[[t:3]] like [[t:4]]ÇOUR[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]צור[[t:7]]) and its counterparts[[fn:740]]. Finally, there is no name of God that is not [[t:8]]derived[[t:9]], with the exception of the tetragrammaton, which is the [[t:10]]schem ha-mephorasch;[[t:11]] for this name does not signify an attribute, but a simple [[t:12]]existence[[t:13]], and nothing else. Absolute existence encompasses the idea of that [[t:14]]which is always[[t:15]], I mean of the [[t:16]]necessary Being.[[t:17]]
root.text.Part 1..62.6: Imprint well upon thy mind all that we have said hitherto.
root.text.Part 1..63.0: Know that by [[t:0]]schem[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]שם[[t:3]]) or [[t:4]]NAME[[t:5]] [[t:6]]of the Eternal[[t:7]] is often designated (in Scripture) the simple [[t:8]]name[[t:9]], as, for example, in these words: [[t:10]]Thou shalt not take the[[t:11]] [[t:12]]NAME[[t:13]] [[t:14]]of the Eternal, thy God, in vain[[t:15]] (Exodus, 20, 6); [[t:16]]And he that blasphems the[[t:17]] [[t:18]]NAME[[t:19]] [[t:20]]of the Eternal[[t:21]] (Leviticus, 24, 16)[[fn:741]]. The examples thereof are innumerable. Sometimes is designated thereby the essence of God and His true being, e. g.: [[t:22]]If they say unto me, What is His[[t:23]] [[t:24]]NAME[[t:25]] (Exodus, 3, 13)? At other times is designated thereby the [[t:26]]ordinance of God[[t:27]], so that, if we say [[t:28]]NAME[[t:29]] [[t:30]]of the Eternal[[t:31]], it is as though we said [[t:32]]WORD OR ORDINANCE[[t:33]] [[t:34]]of the Eternal;[[t:35]] thus, e. g., the words [[t:36]]for my[[t:37]] [[t:38]]NAME[[t:39]] [[t:40]]is in him[[t:41]] ([[t:42]]Ibid.[[t:43]], 23, 21) signify: [[t:44]]my[[t:45]] [[t:46]]WORD[[t:47]] or [[t:48]]my[[t:49]] [[t:50]]ORDINANCE[[t:51]] [[t:52]]is in him[[t:53]], which means that he (the messenger) is the instrument of My will and of My desire. I shall explain these words when discussing the homonymy of the word Malakh ([[t:54]]מלאך[[t:55]]) [[t:56]][[fn:742]][[t:57]].
root.text.Part 1..63.1.sub_0: In like manner, by cabôd (כבוד) or glory of the Lord is sometimes denoted the created light which God, in a miraculous manner, causs to descend into a place to glorify it[[fn:743]]; e.g.: And the glory (כבור) of the Lord abode upon mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it, etc. (Ibid., XXIV, 16); And the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle (Ibid., 40, 35).—At other times, there is denoted thereby the essence of God and His very being; e.g.: I beseech thee, shew me thy glory (Ibid., 33, 18), whereunto it was replied: …for there shall no man see me, and live (v. 20), which indicats that the glory of which mention is here made is His essence. If he said thy glory, it was out of reverence (for the Divinity), according to that which we have set forth regarding these words: if they say to me, What is his name[[fn:744]]? — Finally, there is sometimes denoted by cabôd (כבוד) the magnification of which God is the object on the part of all men, or rather on the part of all things besides Him, for all things serve to glorify Him[[fn:745]]. Verily, His true magnification consists in the comprehension of His greatness, and whosoever comprehends His greatness and His perfection glorifies Him according to the measure of his comprehension. Man, in particular, glorifies Him[[fn:746]] by words, to indicate that which he has comprehended by his intellect and to make it known unto others; but those beings which have no perception, such as inanimate things, glorify Him also, after a fashion, by manifesting through their nature the power and wisdom of Him who produced them, and thereby he who contemplats them is led to glorify Him, whether by his tongue, or even without speech, if it be a being unto whom speech is not granted[[fn:747]]. The Hebrew language has taken unto itself some latitude in this respect, so that the verb אמר, to say, is applied to the idea in question, and it is even said of that which has no perception that it praiss God; it is said, for example[[fn:748]]: All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like unto thee (Ps. 35, 10)? which signifies that they give rise to this conviction, as though they did pronounce it[[fn:749]], for it is by them also that this is known.
root.text.Part 1..63.1.sub_1: It is in this sense (of magnification) attributed to the word cabôd (glory) that it was said: The whole earth is full of his GLORY (Isaiah, 6, 3), which is similar to these words: And the earth was full of his PRAISE (Habakkuk, 3, 3); for praise is called cabôd (glory), even as it has been said: Give glory (כבור) to the Lord your God (Jeremiah, 13, 16); And in his temple does every one speak of GLORY (Ps. 29, 9)! There are numerous examples thereof. Thou must also possess thyself of this homonymity of the word cabôd (glory) and construe it in each passage according to that which is fitting, and thou shalt thereby escape from great difficulties.
root.text.Part 1..64.0: I do not think that, having arrived at this point and having recognized that God exists, but not through existence, and that He is one, but not through unity[[fn:750]], thou still hast need that there be set forth unto thee the necessity of removing from God the attribute of speech; especially since our nation admitts by common consent that the Law is a created thing[[fn:751]], which signifies that the speech attributed to God is a created thing[[fn:752]], and that, if it has been attributed to God, it is only because the discourse heard by Moses was created and produced by God like all the works of creation[[fn:753]]. Prophecy shall be spoken of more fully hereafter; here it is only intended to show that, if speech be attributed to God, it is as when there are attributed to Him, in general, actions similar to our own. Thus, in order to lead minds to recognize that there is a divine knowledge which the prophets obtain, it was said that God had spoken to them and had said to them such a thing[[fn:754]], so that we might know that those things which they reported to us on behalf of God did not proceed simply from their own thought and reflection, as shall be set forth elsewhere. We have already touched upon this subject previously[[fn:755]].
root.text.Part 1..64.1: This chapter has for its sole object (to demonstrate) that the verbs [[t:0]]dibber[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]דבר[[t:3]], [[t:4]]to speak[[t:5]]) and [[t:6]]amar[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]אמר[[t:9]], [[t:10]]to say[[t:11]]) are homonyms. They apply, first, to [[t:12]]language[[t:13]] properly so called[[fn:756]]; for example: [[t:14]]משה ידבר[[t:15]], [[t:16]]Moses spoke[[t:17]] (Exodus, 19, 19); [[t:18]]ויאמר פרעה[[t:19]], [[t:20]]And Pharaoh said[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]Ibid.[[t:23]], 5, 5). Next, they apply to the [[t:24]]thought[[t:25]] which one forms in the intellect, without expressing it; for example: [[t:26]]And I[[t:27]] [[t:28]]SAID[[t:29]] [[t:30]]in my heart[[t:31]] (Eccles., II, 15); [[t:32]]And I[[t:33]] [[t:34]]SPOKE[[t:35]] [[t:36]]in my heart[[t:37]] ([[t:38]]Ibid[[t:39]].); [[t:40]]And thy heart[[t:41]] [[t:42]]SHALL SPEAK[[t:43]] (Prov., 23, 33); [[t:44]]My heart[[t:45]] [[t:46]]said unto me[[t:47]] [[t:48]]of thee[[t:49]] (Ps. 27, 8); [[t:50]]And Esau[[t:51]] [[t:52]]SAID[[t:53]] [[t:54]]in his heart[[t:55]] (Genesis, XXVII. 41); there are numerous examples thereof. Finally, they apply to the [[t:56]]will;[[t:57]] for example: [[t:58]]And he[[t:59]] [[t:60]]SAID[[t:61]] [[t:62]]to smite David[[t:63]] (II Sam., 21, 16), — which signifies, [[t:64]]and he[[t:65]] [[t:66]]WISHED[[t:67]] [[t:68]]to smite him[[t:69]], that is to say, [[t:70]]he purposed it;[[t:71]] — [[t:72]]Do you[[t:73]] [[t:74]]say to slay me[[t:75]] (Exodus, 2, 14), — which must be explained in the sense of, [[t:76]]Do you[[t:77]] [[t:78]]wish to slay me?[[t:79]] — [[t:80]]And all the congregation[[t:81]] [[t:82]]SAID[[t:83]] [[t:84]]to stone them[[t:85]] (Numbers, 14, 10); there are likewise numerous examples thereof.
root.text.Part 1..64.2: Whenever the verbs [[t:0]]amar[[t:1]] (to say) and [[t:2]]dibber[[t:3]] (to speak) are attributed to God, they possess both latter significations, I mean to say that they signify either the [[t:4]]will[[t:5]] and the [[t:6]]intention[[t:7]], or some thing that is understood (being reported) from God, be it that one has learned it through a [[t:8]]created voice[[t:9]] or through one of the prophetic means that we shall expound; and (they signify) in no wise that God has spoken by letters and sounds, nor that He has a soul, so that things might be impressed upon His soul[[fn:757]] in such a manner as to be within Him something that is added to His essence. But these things have been attributed to God, and they have been attributed to Him as have all His other actions.
root.text.Part 1..64.3: However, if the intention and the will (of God) have been designated by the verbs amar and dibber, it is not only because of that which we have set forth concerning the homonymy of these words, but also by way of assimilation to ourselves, as we have previously observed[[fn:758]]. In sooth, man understands not at the first how that which one wills to be done can be executed by the simple will; he rather thinks at the outset that he who wills a thing to be must of necessity either do it himself or command another to do it. Therefore there has been metaphorically attributed unto God a command, to express that what He willed was accomplished, and it was said: «He commanded that such a thing should be, and it was»; and this by way of assimilation to our actions, and having regard also to the fact that this verb (to say or to command) likewise signifies the sense of willing, even as we have set it forth. Thus, whenever there is found, in the narrative of the creation, ויאמר; and (God) said, it signifies He willed or it pleased Him; this is what others have already said before us[[fn:759]], and it is very well known. The proof thereof—I mean (that which proves) that everywhere here the verb amar (to say) designats the will, and not speech—is that speech can be addressed only to a being that is capable of receiving a command[[fn:760]]. Thus these words: By the word of the Lord were the heavens made (Ps. 33, 6), are parallel to these: and all the host of them by the breath of His mouth (ibid.); even as His mouth and the breath of His mouth are a metaphor, so His word and His saying are a metaphor, and the meaning is that they (the heavens) were produced by His intention and His will. This is a thing of which none of our renowned sages was ignorant. I need not set forth that the verbs amar and dibber, in the Hebrew tongue, are also synonymous (which results from this passage): For it has heard all the words (אמרי) of the Lord which He spake unto us (דבר) (Joshua, 24, 27)[[fn:761]].
root.text.Part 1..65.0: It is said that the Tables (thus the Scripture) were the work of God (Exodus, 32, 16): this signifies that they were a production of nature, and not of art[[fn:762]]; for all natural things are called the work of God; for example: They have seen the works of the Eternal (Ps. 107, 24); and in like manner, after having mentioned all natural things, such as plants, animals, winds, rains, etc., (the poet) exclaims: How great are thy works, O Eternal (Ps. 104, 24)! But what is even more expressive than this attribution[[fn:763]], are these words: The cedars of Lebanon, which He has planted (Ps. 104, 16); for, as they are a production of nature, and not of art, it is said that God has planted them.
root.text.Part 1..65.1: In like manner, when it is said a writing of God (Exodus, 32, 16), it is evident that the writing is attributed unto God; and indeed it is said (that the Tables were) written with the finger of God (Ibid., 31, 18). It is here said with the finger of God, even as it is said, in speaking of the heaven: the work of Thy fingers (Ps. 8, 4), although it is expressly said that it was made by the word: By the word of the Lord were the heavens made (Ps. 33, 6). It is therefore clear that the (sacred) texts express metaphorically by the verbs amar (to say) and dibber (to speak) that a thing has been produced (by God), and that this very thing which is said to have been made by the word, is also called the work of the finger (of God); thus the expression written with the finger of God is equivalent to (written) by the word of God, and if, indeed, it had been said בדבר אלהים, by the word of God, it would be equivalent to בחפץ אלהים, that is to say, by the will and the intention of God.
root.text.Part 1..65.2: As for Onkelos, he has adopted concerning this matter a strange interpretation[[fn:764]], for he has said (in his version): כתיבין באצבעא די״י, written with the finger of the Lord, regarding the word finger as something which is placed in relation with God, and interpreting finger of God as (he interprets) mountain of God and rod of God; he means thereby that it was a created instrument which engraved the Tables by the will of God[[fn:765]]. I know not what moved him to this; for it were simpler to translate: כתיבין במימרא די״י, written by the WORD of the Lord, conformably to these words: By the word of the Lord were the heavens made. Can one, in sooth, find the existence of the writing upon the Tables more extraordinary than that of the stars within the spheres? Even as the latter is the effect of a primitive will (of God), and not of an instrument that should have fashioned (the stars), so this writing was traced by a primitive will, and not by an instrument. Thou knowest the terms of the Mishnah in (this passage): «Ten things were created (on the eve of the Sabbath) at twilight, etc.»; of their number were the Writing (holy) and the writing (engraved upon the Tables)[[fn:766]], which proves that a thing whereon there has been general agreement is that it is with the writing of the Tables as with all the other works of creation, as we have set forth in the Commentary on the Mishnah.
root.text.Part 1..66.0: Since the verb [[t:0]]amar[[t:1]] (to say) has been employed metaphorically to signify the [[t:2]]volonté[[t:3]] (manifesting itself) in all that was produced during the six days of creation, so that it was said each time: [[t:4]]ויאמר[[t:5]], [[t:6]]and God said[[t:7]], the verb [[t:8]]schabath[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]שבת[[t:11]]. [Lat.: to cease, to repose[[t:12]]), in speaking of the Sabbath day, during which there was no new creation, and it was said: [[t:14]]And he ceased[[t:15]] or [[t:16]]reposed[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]וישבת[[t:19]]) [[t:20]]on the seventh day[[t:21]] (Genesis, 2, 2); for the verb [[t:22]]schabath[[t:23]] is also employed in the sense of [[t:24]]ceasing to speak;[[t:25]] for example: [[t:26]]And these three men ceased[[t:27]] ([[t:28]]וישבתו[[t:29]]) [[t:30]]to respond to Job[[t:31]] (Job, 32, 1).
root.text.Part 1..66.1: In like manner, one finds the verb noua’h (נוח, to be quiet, to rest) employed in the sense of ceasing to speak, as, for example, in this passage: And they spake to Nabal in the name of David all those words, then THEY REMAINED QUIET (וינוחו) (I Sam., 25, 9); which signifies, in my judgment: they ceased to speak in order to hear the response. Verily, it has not been related previously that they were fatigued; so that, even had they been truly weary, the word וינוחו (in the sense of they rested) would still be right improper[[fn:767]] in this narrative. But naught is here recounted save that, after having skilfully set forth[[fn:768]] all this discourse, in which there was much affability, they held their peace, that is to say, they added naught else to this discourse, nor any action which might merit the response he made them; for the aim of this narrative is to describe his meanness[[fn:769]], because he was of an exceeding meanness.
root.text.Part 1..66.2: — It is also in this sense (of [[t:0]]cesser[[t:1]] or [[t:2]]s’arrêter[[t:3]]) that it has been said [[t:4]]וַיָּנַח ביום השביעי[[t:5]] (Exodus, 20, 11)[[fn:770]].
root.text.Part 1..66.3: However, the Doctors and other commentators have taken this word (וַיָּנַח) in the sense of rest and have rendered it a transitive verb; the Doctors say: “He caused to rest His universe on the seventh day[[fn:771]]”, that is to say, the creation was stayed[[fn:772]] on that day.
root.text.Part 1..66.4: It is possible that it be a verb having for its first or for its third radical a weak letter[[fn:773]], and that the sense be: “He established, or He made to endure[[fn:774]] the universe such as it was on the seventh day”; which would signify that on each of the six days there occurred events (which were) outside (the law) of nature[[fn:775]] such as it is established and as it now exists in the whole of the universe, but that on the seventh day everything was consolidated and took on its present stability[[fn:776]]. One cannot object against us[[fn:777]] that the word in question is not conjugated as are verbs having for their first or for their third radical a weak letter[[fn:778]]; for there be sometimes verbal forms which deviate (from the rule) and which follow not analogy, and especially in these weak verbs. And moreover, when it concerns the removal of such a cause of error, one cannot oppose a rule of conjugation[[fn:779]], especially whilst we know that we do not today encompass the (complete) knowledge of our tongue, and that (furthermore) the rules of every language are a matter of plurality[[fn:780]]. We find, moreover, in this root, even by giving it a weak letter for its second radical[[fn:781]], the sense of placing and of establishing; for example: וְהֻנִּיחָה שׁם, and it shall be PLACED there (Zechariah, 5, 11); in like manner: And she suffered not the birds of the air to REST (לנוח) upon them (II Sam., 21, 10). Such is also, in my view, the sense (of this verb) in: אשר אָנוּחַ ליום צרה, for I wait STEADFASTLY (or QUIETLY) for the day of trouble (Habakkuk, 3, 16)[[fn:782]].
root.text.Part 1..66.5: As for the word wayyinnaphasch (וינפש, Exodus, 31, 17), it is a niphal of nephesh (נֶפֶש) [[fn:783]]. We have already set forth that nephesh is a homonym, and that it is (employed) in the sense of intention and of will[[fn:784]]; consequently (the verb וינפש) signifies that His intention was accomplished and that all His will was executed.
root.text.Part 1..67.0: Thou art acquainted with that celebrated proposition which the philosophers have propounded concerning God, to wit, that He is the Intellect, the Intellector, and the Intelligible[[fn:785]], and that these three things, in God, are but one and the same thing, in which there is no multiplicity. We also have already spoken thereof in our great work[[fn:786]]; for this is the foundation of our religion, as we have there set forth—I mean to say, that He is one only, and that no other thing is in relation with Him[[fn:787]], that is to say, that there is nothing eternal save Him. For this reason is it said חי י״י (As the Lord lives!), and it is not said חֵי י״י (By the life of the Lord!)[[fn:788]]; for His life is naught else than His essence, as we have already explained in the rejection of the attributes[[fn:789]].
root.text.Part 1..67.1: Doubtless, he who has not studied the books treating of the intellect, who has not apprehended the essence of the intellect, who knows not its true being, and who understands it only so far as he understands the notion of white and black, will find great difficulty in comprehending this subject; and when we say that God is the Intellect, the Intellector, and the Intelligible, it will be to him as though we said that whiteness, the thing whitened, and that which whitens are one and the same thing[[fn:790]]. And indeed, how many ignorant persons will there be who shall hasten[[fn:791]] to refute us by this example and others of a like nature! and how many even of those who, while laying claim to science, will find this matter difficult and will believe it to be beyond our mind to acknowledge its absolute truth[[fn:792]]! Nevertheless, this is a subject demonstrable and manifest, according to what the metaphysical philosophers have expounded, and I shall make thee to understand what they have established by demonstration.
root.text.Part 1..67.2: Know that man, before he thinks a thing, is intelligent in potentiality[[fn:793]]; but when he has thought a certain thing, as, for example, when he has thought the form of this wood in question, having abstracted that which is its form from that which is its matter, and has represented to himself the abstract form [for it is in this that the action of the intellect consists], he has become intelligent in act. The intellect which has passed into act is itself the form of the wood abstracted in the mind of man; for the intellect is naught else but the intelligible object. Thou shalt understand, therefore, that the intelligible thing is the abstract form of the wood, which is itself the intellect passed into act; there are not there two things, to wit, the intellect and the thought form of the wood; for the intellect in act is naught else but that which has been thought, and the thing by which the form of the wood has been thought and abstracted, and which is the Intellector[[fn:794]], is itself indubitably the intellect passed into act. In truth, the essence of every intellect consists in its action, and it cannot be that the intellect in act be one thing and its action another; for the true being of the intellect[[fn:795]] is perception. It must not, therefore, be believed that the intellect in act is something which exists on its own part, separate from perception, and that perception is some other thing (existing) within it; but (that which constituts) the intellect in itself and its reality is perception, and consequently, when thou posest an intellect existing in act, (thou posest) thereby the perception of a thought object. This is very clear to him who has occupied himself with these manner of speculations.
root.text.Part 1..67.3: Since, therefore, it is manifest that the action of the intellect, which consists in its perception, is (that which constituts) its true essence, it follows that that by which the form of this wood has been abstracted and perceived, to wit, the intellect, is itself the Intellector; for it is this intellect itself which has abstracted the form and which has perceived it, and this is its action for the sake of which it is called Intellector. But its action being itself its essence, there is, in that which has been posited as intellect in act, naught but the form of the wood in question[[fn:796]]. It is therefore clear (on the one hand) that, whenever the intellect exists in act, this intellect is itself the intelligible thing, and (on the other hand) it has been expounded that the action which constituts the essence of every intellect is to be intelligent[[fn:797]]; whence it follows that the intellect, the Intellector and the Intelligible are always one and the same thing whenever there is question of a thought in act[[fn:798]].
root.text.Part 1..67.4: But when one poss (a thought) in potentiality, there are necessarily two things: the intellect in potentiality and the intelligible in potentiality. If, for instance, thou speakest of that hylic intellect which is in Zeid[[fn:799]], it is an intellect in potentiality, and likewise this wood is intelligible in potentiality[[fn:800]], and there are indubitably two things there. But when (the thought) has passed into act, and the form of the wood has become intelligible in act, then the intelligible form is identical with the intellect, and it is by this intellect itself[[fn:801]], which is intellect in act, that it has been abstracted and thought; (I say intellect in act,) because everything of which there exists a (real) action exists in act.
root.text.Part 1..67.5: Thus, therefore, the intellect in potency and the intelligible in potency are ever twain. But all that which is in potency must needs have a substratum which sustains that potency, as, for example, man; so that there shall be three things: the man who sustains the said potency and who is the intelligent being in potency, the potency itself, which is the intellect in potency, and the thing apt to be thought, which is the intelligible in potency; or rather, to speak according to our example: man, the hylic intellect, and the form of wood, which are three distinct things. But when the intellect has attained unto actuality, the three things become but one alone, and there shall never be found in the intellect and the intelligible two different things[[fn:802]], save when they are taken in potency.
root.text.Part 1..67.6: Now, as it is demonstrated that God [exalted be He!] is intellect in act[[fn:803]], and as there is in Him absolutely naught that is in potency — which is manifest in itself and shall yet be demonstrated — so that it cannot be that at one time He perceivs and at another He perceivs not, but on the contrary He is ever intellect in act, it follows that He and the thing perceived are one and the same thing, which is His essence[[fn:804]]; and moreover this same act of perceiving, wherefor He is called intelligent, is the very intellect which is His essence. Consequently, He is perpetually intellect, intelligent, and intelligible.
root.text.Part 1..67.7: It is clear also that, if it be said that the intellect, the intelligent, and the intelligible form but [[t:0]]one[[t:1]] in number, this applies not only to the Creator, but to every intellect. In us also, the intelligent, the intellect, and the intelligible are one and the same thing whenever we possess the intellect [[t:2]]in act;[[t:3]] but it is only by intervals that we pass from potentiality to act[[fn:805]]. Similarly, the [[t:4]]separated intellect[[t:5]], by which I mean the active (universal) intellect[[fn:806]], sometimes experiences an impediment to its action; and, although this impediment proceeds not from itself, but from without, it is a certain perturbation which supervenes accidentally upon this intellect[[fn:807]]. But our present purpose is not to explain this subject; our aim is rather to expound that the attribute which belongs to God alone and is peculiar to Him, is to be always [[t:6]]intellect in act[[t:7]] and to experience no impediment to perception, neither from Himself, nor from any other quarter. Thence it follows that He is always and perpetually intelligent, intellect, and intelligible; it is His very essence which is [[t:8]]intelligent[[t:9]], it is that which is the [[t:10]]intelligible[[t:11]], and it is also that which is the [[t:12]]intellect[[t:13]][[fn:808]], as must be the case in every [[t:14]]intellect in act.[[t:15]]
root.text.Part 1..67.8: If we have frequently iterated ourselves in this chapter, it is because it concerns a matter which minds conceive with exceeding difficulty[[fn:809]]. I deem not that in thee the intellectual conception can be troubled by the imagination, nor that thou mightest, in thy faculty of phantasy, establish in this regard a comparison with sensible things[[fn:810]]; for this treatise was composed only for those who have studied philosophy and who know that which has been set forth concerning the soul and all its faculties.
root.text.Part 1..68.0: Philosophers, as you are aware, designate God the [[t:0]]First Cause[[t:1]][[fn:811]]; but those known by the appellation of [[t:2]]Motecallemin[[t:3]][[fn:812]] scrupulously avoid this designation and term God the [[t:4]]Agent[[t:5]]. They maintain that a significant distinction obtains between affirming [[t:6]]cause[[t:7]] and affirming [[t:8]]agent[[t:9]]: for, they assert, were we to declare Him (God) to be a [[t:10]]cause[[t:11]], it would necessarily follow that the [[t:12]]effect[[t:13]] exists concurrently, which would lead to the [[t:14]]eternity of the world[[t:15]] and (to the admission) that the world is (coexistent with) Him in a necessary manner[[fn:813]]; but if we designate Him an [[t:16]]Agent[[t:17]], it does not necessarily follow that the [[t:18]]object of the action[[t:19]] exists concomitantly with Him, for the [[t:20]]agent[[t:21]] may precede his [[t:22]]action;[[t:23]] and they even proceed so far as to imagine that an agent can only be termed an [[t:24]]agent[[t:25]] on the condition of being prior to his action[[fn:814]].
root.text.Part 1..68.1: But this is the reasoning of one who knows not how to distinguish between that which is [[t:0]]in potentiality[[t:1]] and that which is [[t:2]]in actuality[[t:3]]; for it must be understood that there is no difference in this regard between the terms [[t:4]]cause[[t:5]] and [[t:6]]agent[[t:7]]. Indeed, the [[t:8]]cause[[t:9]] also, if one considers it [[t:10]]in potentiality[[t:11]], precedes its [[t:12]]effect[[t:13]] in time; whereas, if it be a cause [[t:14]]in actuality[[t:15]], the effect necessarily coexists with this [[t:16]]cause in actuality[[t:17]][[fn:815]]. Similarly, if one considers the [[t:18]]agent[[t:19]] as an agent [[t:20]]in actuality[[t:21]], it necessarily follows that the object of its action exists; for the architect, before constructing the house, is not an architect [[t:22]]in actuality[[t:23]], but an architect [[t:24]]in potentiality[[t:25]][[fn:816]] [just as the material of the house, before its construction, is a house [[t:26]]in potentiality[[t:27]]]; but when he builds, he becomes an architect[[fn:817]] [[t:28]]in actuality[[t:29]], and it then necessarily follows that something constructed exists (simultaneously). We would therefore gain naught by preferring the denomination of [[t:30]]agent[[t:31]] to that of [[t:32]]cause[[t:33]]. And (indeed) the sole purpose here is to establish the equality between these two denominations, and (to show) that, just as we term God [[t:34]]agent[[t:35]], even though the object of His action might not yet exist, — and this because there is nothing that can restrain Him or prevent Him from acting when He wills, — so also is it permissible for us to term Him [[t:36]]cause[[t:37]], absolutely in the same sense, even though the [[t:38]]effect[[t:39]] might not yet exist.
root.text.Part 1..68.2: That which led the philosophers to designate God as [[t:0]]cause[[t:1]] and not as [[t:2]]agent[[t:3]], was not their well-known opinion concerning the eternity of the world; rather, they held other reasons for this, which I shall now recapitulate. It has been set forth in the [[t:4]]Physics[[t:5]] that there exist diverse [[t:6]]causes[[t:7]] for everything that possesses a cause[[fn:818]], four in number, namely: matter, form, the agent (or efficient cause), and the final cause[[fn:819]], and that there are both [[t:8]]proximate[[t:9]] and [[t:10]]remote[[t:11]] causes[[fn:820]]; each of these four is termed a [[t:12]]cause[[t:13]]. Among their tenets, one which I do not dispute is this: that God is simultaneously the [[t:14]]efficient cause[[t:15]], the [[t:16]]form[[t:17]], and the [[t:18]]final cause;[[t:19]] it is in this sense that they declare God to be the [[t:20]]cause[[t:21]], a designation which encompasses these three causes conjointly, signifying that God is the efficient cause of the world, its form, and its final cause[[fn:821]].
