My purpose, therefore, in this chapter, is to elucidate to you in what sense it has been affirmed of God that He is the [[t:22]]efficient cause[[t:23]] (or the [[t:24]]agent[[t:25]]), and that He is likewise the [[t:26]]form[[t:27]] of the world and its [[t:28]]final cause[[t:29]]. Herein, you need not concern yourself with the question of whether God freely produced the world, or whether, as they (the philosophers) conceive, it necessarily coexists with Him[[fn:822]]; for upon this matter, we shall enter into extensive detail, as befits so weighty a subject[[fn:823]].
root.text.Part 1..68.3: Here the sole purpose is (to establish) that God is the efficient of the particular facts which occur in the world, even as He is the efficient of the world in its entirety. This, then, is what I say: It has been set forth in the Physics that, for each of these four kinds of causes, another cause must be sought, so that one will first find, for the thing that is born, its four immediate causes, and thereafter one will find for these other causes, and, for those (secondary) causes, yet other causes, until one arrivs at the first causes; thus, for example, a certain thing is the effect produced by a certain efficient, which, in its turn, shall have its efficient, and so forth, until one arrivs at a first mover who shall be the true efficient of all these intermediate things[[fn:824]]. Verily, let A be moved by B, B by C, C by D, and D by E; since this cannot extend to infinity, let us stop, for example, at E, and there will be no doubt that E is the mover of A, B, C, and D, and it is with justice that one may say of the movement of A that it is E who has wrought it. It is in this manner that every fact in the universe, whatever be the immediate efficient that has produced it[[fn:825]], is attributed unto God, as we shall set forth (elsewhere); He is therefore the most remote cause thereof, in the capacity of efficient.
root.text.Part 1..68.4: Likewise, if we pursue the physical forms, which are born and perish, we shall find that they must necessarily be preceded (each) by another form which prepars such matter to receive such (immediate) form; this second form, in its turn, shall be preceded by another, (and so forth,) until we arrive at the last form which is necessary for the existence of these intermediate forms, which are the cause of the said immediate form. This ultimate form of all being is God. If we say of Him that He is the ultimate form of the whole universe, it must not be believed that this is an allusion to that ultimate form[[fn:826]] of which Aristotle says, in the Metaphysics, that it is neither born nor does it perish; for the form there spoken of is physical, and not a separate intelligence[[fn:827]]. Indeed, when we say of God that He is the ultimate form of the world, it is not as the form having matter is a form for that matter, so that God should be a form for a body[[fn:828]]. It is not in this wise that it must be understood, but in the following manner: even as the form is that which constituts the true being of everything that has form, so that, the form perishing, the being likewise perishes, so God is found to be in an absolutely similar relation with all the most remote principles of being[[fn:829]]; for it is by the existence of the Creator that everything exists, and it is He who perpetuats its duration by something which is named the emanation, as we shall set forth in one of the chapters of this treatise[[fn:830]]. If, therefore, the non-existence of the Creator were admissible, the entire universe would no longer exist, for that which constituts its remote causes would vanish, as would the last effects and that which is intermediate; and, consequently, God is to the universe what the form is to the thing that has form and which thereby is what it is, the form constituting its true being. Such then is the relation of God to the world, and it is from this point of view that it has been said of Him that He is the ultimate form and the Form of forms; which is to say that He is the one upon whom leans, in the last resort, the existence and maintenance of all forms in the world, and that it is through Him they subsist, even as things endowed with forms subsist by their forms. And it is because of this that He has been called, in our tongue, חי העולמים, which signifies that He is the Life of the Universe, as shall be set forth (hereafter)[[fn:831]].
root.text.Part 1..68.5: It is even so with every end[[fn:832]], for when a thing has a certain end, thou must seek for that end another end. If, for example, thou sayest that the matter of this throne is wood, its efficient the joiner, its form square and of such or such a figure, and its end to sit upon it, thou must thereafter ask: To what end does one sit upon the throne? It shall be answered, that he who sitts thereon may be raised above the ground. But, thou wilt ask again, to what end must he be raised above the ground? and it shall be answered: It is in order that, being thus seated, he may appear great in the eyes of those who behold him. And to what end, thou wilt pursue, must he appear great to those who behold him? It shall be answered, that he may be feared and respected. But, thou wilt ask once more, to what end must he be feared? It shall be said, that his command may be obeyed. And to what end, thou wilt yet pursue, must his command be obeyed? It shall be answered, that he may prevent men from doing harm to one another. And if thou askest yet: To what end? it shall be answered: It is that their existence may continue in good order. It must necessarily be the same with each new end, until one arrivs at last—according to a certain opinion which shall be set forth (elsewhere)—at the simple will of God, so that one shall answer for the end: Thus has God willed it; or else (one shall reach)—according to another opinion—the requirement of the Divine Wisdom, as I shall set forth, so that one shall answer for the end: Thus has His wisdom required it[[fn:833]]. The series of all ends shall therefore, according to these two opinions, terminate at the will and the wisdom of God. But these, according to our opinion, are His essence; for it has been set forth that the intention, the will, and the wisdom of God are not things outside His essence, I mean to say, other than His essence[[fn:834]]. Consequently, God is the ultimate end of all things; everything likewise has for its end to become like unto Him in perfection, as much as that may be, and it is this which must be understood by His will, which is His essence, as shall be set forth[[fn:835]]. It is therefore from this point of view that He has been called the End of ends.
root.text.Part 1..68.6: Thus I have explained in what sense it has been said of God that He is [[t:0]]efficient, form[[t:1]] and [[t:2]]end;[[t:3]] it is for this reason that they (the philosophers) have called Him [[t:4]]cause[[t:5]], and not merely [[t:6]]agent[[t:7]] (or efficient).
root.text.Part 1..68.7: Know thou that certain thinkers[[fn:836]] among these Mutakallimūn have carried their ignorance and boldness so far as to maintain that, even were it admitted that the Creator could cease to exist, it would by no means follow that the thing which the Creator has produced, to wit, the world, should likewise cease to exist; for (say they) it follows not necessarily that what has been made must perish because the author, after having made it, has ceased to be. What they have therein asserted would be true if God were solely efficient, and if this thing made had no need of Him to prolong[[fn:837]] its duration; even as, when the carpenter dies, the chest (which he has made) does not perish for that reason, for it is not he who prolongs its duration. But, since God is at the same time the form of the world, as we have expounded, and since it is He who prolongs its permanence and duration, it is impossible (to suppose) that He who gives duration should disappear, and that nevertheless the thing which has no duration save through Him should continue to exist[[fn:838]].
root.text.Part 1..68.8: Thus, this assertion would lead to a great error: that God is merely [[t:0]]efficient[[t:1]], and is neither [[t:2]]end[[t:3]] nor [[t:4]]form[[t:5]].
root.text.Part 1..69.0: Rakhab (רכב) [[fn:839]]. — This word is a homonym which, in its primary signification[[fn:840]], denots the habitual manner of riding upon a beast[[fn:841]]; e.g.: And he was riding (רכב) upon his ass (Numbers, xxii. 22). Subsequently it was metaphorically employed in the sense of having dominion over a thing, because the rider dominats and governs his mount, and it is in this sense that it has been said: He made him to ride (ירכיבהו) on the high places of the earth (Deut. xxxii. 13); And I will cause thee to ride (והרכבתיך) upon the high places of the earth (Isaiah, lviii. 14), which signifies: ye shall have dominion over the heights of the earth; (likewise:) I will make (ארכיב) Ephraim to ride (Hosea, x. 11), that is to say, I will make him to reign and to dominate. It is in this sense that it has been said of God: Who rids (רכב) upon the heaven, in thy help (Deut. xxxiii. 26), which signifies: He who dominats over the heaven. Likewise the words לרוכב בערבות, To Him that rids upon ‘Arabōth (Ps. lxviii. 5), signify: He who dominats over ‘Arabōth; for that is the uppermost sphere which encompasses all[[fn:842]], even as the Sages repeat in several places, saying[[fn:843]] that there be seven heavens and that ‘Arabōth is the highest of them, which encompasses them all. Thou shalt not blame them for counting (only) seven heavens, although there be more; for sometimes one counts but as a single globe that which nevertheless contains several spheres, as is manifest to those who study this matter, and as I shall expound (elsewhere)[[fn:844]]. Here the sole intent is (to show) that they always clearly declare that ‘Arabōth is the highest of all (the heavens), and that it is of ‘Arabōth they (speak when it) is said: Him that rids upon the HEAVEN in thy help.
root.text.Part 1..69.1: There is a passage in [[t:0]]’Haghîgâ[[t:1]] where it is stated[[fn:845]]: «Upon ’[[t:2]]Arabôth[[t:3]] dwells the Most High, for it is said: [[t:4]]Extol Him that rids upon[[t:5]] ’A[[t:6]]RABÔTH[[t:7]] (Ps. 68, 5). And whence know we that this is the appellation for heaven? It is because here it is written: [[t:8]]He that rids upon[[t:9]] ’A[[t:10]]RABÔTH[[t:11]], and elsewhere: [[t:12]]He that rids upon the[[t:13]] [[t:14]]HEAVEN[[t:15]].» It is therefore clear that allusion is made everywhere to a single sphere, that which encircles the universe, and concerning which thou shalt yet learn further particulars. Observe well that they say: ([[t:16]]the Most[[t:17]]-[[t:18]]High[[t:19]]) [[t:20]]dwells[[t:21]] [[t:22]]UPON[[t:23]] [[t:24]]it[[t:25]], and that they do not say: [[t:26]]dwells[[t:27]] [[t:28]]WITHIN[[t:29]] [[t:30]]it;[[t:31]] for, had they said [[t:32]]within it[[t:33]], it would have been to assign a place to God, or to assert that God is a faculty therein, as the sects of the Sabians[[fn:846]] imagined, namely, that God is the spirit of the celestial sphere. By thus saying [[t:34]]dwells[[t:35]] [[t:36]]UPON[[t:37]] [[t:38]]it[[t:39]], they declared that God is separate from the [[t:40]]sphere[[t:41]], and that He is by no means a faculty within it[[fn:847]].
root.text.Part 1..69.2: Know thou also that the metaphorical expression whereby God rids upon the heaven, contains a most remarkable comparison. Verily, the rider is superior to the mount [the term superior is here but improperly used[[fn:848]], for the rider is not of the same species as the mount], and moreover, it is the rider who putts the beast into motion and leads it wheresoever he wills; the latter is unto him an instrument which he disposs at his pleasure, whilst he himself is independent of it, and, far from being joined thereto, he remains without it. In like manner, God [blessed be His name!] is the Mover of the highest sphere, by the motion of which all that is moved within it is set in motion; but God is separate from it and is in no wise a faculty within it.
root.text.Part 1..69.3.sub_0: In the Berēshīth Rabbā, the doctors, in expounding this divine word: A dwelling-place, the eternal God (Deut. xxxiii. 27), express themselves thus[[fn:849]]: «God is the dwelling-place of the world, but the world is not His dwelling-place;» and they thereafter add (comparing God to a warrior mounted on horseback): «The horse is secondary to the rider, but the rider is not secondary to the horse; it is this which is written: When thou didst ride upon thine horses (Habakkuk iii. 8).» Behold their own terms; pay thou diligent heed thereto, and thou shalt understand[[fn:850]] that they have thereby set forth what is the relation of God to the sphere, to wit, that the latter is His instrument whereby He governs[[fn:851]] the universe. Verily, when thou findest among the doctors the assertion that in such a heaven there is such a thing, and in such a heaven such another thing[[fn:852]], it must not be understood in the sense that there are in the heaven bodies other than the heaven itself, but the sense is that the faculties (of nature) which bring forth such or such a thing and maintain the regularity thereof derive from such or such a heaven. The proof of what I have just said is that the doctors say: «’Arābōth, in which are justice, virtue, right, treasures of life, treasures of peace, treasures of blessing, the souls of the righteous, the souls and the spirits of those yet to be born, and the dew wherewith the Holy One shall restore the dead to life.» It is manifest that naught of all they here enumerate is a body so as to be in a place; for the dew is not here a dew[[fn:853]] in the proper sense of the word. Thou shalt also remark that here they say in which (שֶׁבּוֹ), that is to say, that these things are in ’Arābōth, and that they do not say they are upon it; they have in a manner declared thereby that the things in question, which exist in the world, exist therein only by faculties emanated from ’Arābōth, and that it is God who has made the latter the principle of these things and has fixed them therein. Amongst their number are the treasures of life, which is exactly true; for all life found in any living being whatsoever comes only from that life, as I shall set forth further on[[fn:854]].
root.text.Part 1..69.3.sub_1: Remark also that they include in the number the souls of the righteous, as well as the souls and the spirits of those yet to be born; and this is a subject of high importance for him who knows how to understand it. Indeed, the souls which survive after death are not the same thing as the soul which is born in man at the moment of his birth; for that which is born at the same time with him is only a thing in potentiality and a disposition[[fn:855]], whilst the thing which remains separately after death is that which has become (intellect) in act[[fn:856]]. The soul which is born (with man) is not the same thing as the spirit which is born (with him); wherefore they count separately, as things to be born, the souls and the spirits[[fn:857]], whilst the separate soul is but a single thing[[fn:858]]. We have already set forth the homonymy of the word רוח (spirit)[[fn:859]], and we have also explained, at the end of the book Madda’, concerning these various homonyms[[fn:860]].
root.text.Part 1..69.4: Thou seest thereby how these sublime truths, the object of the speculation of the greatest philosophers[[fn:861]], are scattered throughout the Midrashōth, which the inequitable scholar, in reading them superficially, finds ridiculous, because he ses the literal sense to be in contrast with the reality of being; but the cause of all this is that they have expressed themselves in an enigmatic manner, because these subjects were too profound for vulgar intelligences, as we have already said many a time.
root.text.Part 1..69.5: To conclude the subject of which I have approached the explanation, I add[[fn:862]] that the doctors have undertaken to prove by passages from Scripture[[fn:863]] that the things enumerated exist in ’Arābōth, saying: «As for justice and right, it is written: justice and right are the foundation of thy throne (Ps. lxxxix. 15).» And in like manner, they prove that the other things which they have enumerated likewise exist there, by showing that they are brought into relation with God[[fn:864]]. This must be well understood. — In the Pirkē Rabbi Eliʻēzer (chap. 18), it is said: «The Holy One created seven heavens, and among them all He chose none, for the glorious throne of His kingdom, save ’Arābōth alone; for it is said: Extol Him that rids upon ’Arābōth (Ps. lxviii. 5).» Such is the textual passage; thou must likewise be thoroughly imbued therewith.
root.text.Part 1..69.6: Know also that a collection of beasts of burden is called mercabâ (מרבבה, chariot or car), a word which is frequently employed; e.g.: And Joseph made ready his MERCABA or his chariot (Genesis, xlvi, 29); in the chariot (מרבבת) of the second-in-command (Ibid., xli, 43); the chariots or the cars (מרבבות) of Pharaoh (Exodus, xv, 4). The proof that this name signifies a number of beasts is that it has been said: A MERCABA (or a chariot) came up and went out of Egypt for six hundred pieces of silver, and a horse for an hundred and fifty (I Kings, X, 29), and this proves that mercabâ signifies four horses. Now, I say, as it has been affirmed by tradition[[fn:865]] that the glorious throne (of God) is borne by four living creatures, the doctors have for this reason called it mercabâ, by comparison with the chariot which consists of four individuals.
root.text.Part 1..69.7: But behold, we have been led far from the subject of this chapter[[fn:866]]. There must necessarily yet be many other observations to be made upon this matter; but we must return to the aim of this chapter, which was to show[[fn:867]] that the words He that rids upon the heaven (Deut., XXXIII, 26) signify: He who, by His power and His will, causs the surrounding sphere to revolve and move[[fn:868]]. Likewise, at the end of the verse, the words and in His excellency, the skies, signify: He who by His excellency causs the heavens to revolve. Thus the first [which, as we have explained, is ’Arabôth] has been distinguished by the verb to ride (רכב), whilst for the others[[fn:869]] (there has been employed) the word excellency (גאוה); for it is in consequence of the diurnal motion, accomplished by the superior sphere, that all the (other) spheres move, as the part movs in the whole, and that is the great power which movs all and which, for that reason, is called excellency (גאוה).
root.text.Part 1..69.8: Let this subject be ever present to thy mind for (comprehending) what I shall say hereafter; for it contains the most important proof by which one may know the existence of God [I mean to speak of the convolution of the celestial sphere], as I shall demonstrate it[[fn:870]]. Thou must well weigh this.
root.text.Part 1..70.0: Know that the many sciences which our nation possessed to fathom these subjects[[fn:871]] have been lost, as well by the length of time as by the dominion which barbarous nations exercised over us, and also because these subjects, even as we have explained[[fn:872]], were not delivered to everyone, the texts of the Scriptures being the only thing that was accessible unto all. Thou knowest that even the traditional Law[[fn:873]] was not formerly committed to writing, because of that saying so widespread in our communion: “The words which I have spoken to thee orally, thou art not permitted to transmit in writing[[fn:874]].” And this was an exceeding wise measure with regard to the Law; for thereby were avoided the inconveniences into which men fell later[[fn:875]], I mean, the manifold ways of seeing, the division of opinions, the obscurities which reigned in the expression of the redactor, the error to which he was subject[[fn:876]], the disunion occurring among men, who divided themselves into sects, and lastly the uncertainty concerning practices. Far from that, the matter remained entrusted in all respects to the Great Tribunal, as we have explained in our Talmudic works and as the text of the Law indicats[[fn:877]].
root.text.Part 1..70.1: Now, if with regard to the traditional Law so much reserve has been used[[fn:878]], so as not to perpetuate it in a collection lavished upon everyone, (and that) because of the inconveniences that might result therefrom, with much greater reason could nothing be put in writing of these secrets of the Law to be delivered to everyone; these latter, on the contrary, were only transmitted by some few select men to some other select men, even as I have explained to thee by quoting this passage: “One only delivers the secrets of the Law to a counsellor, a wise craftsman, etc.[[fn:879]].” And this is the cause which made to disappear in our nation those fundamental principles so important, concerning which one finds only some few slight remarks and some indications which present themselves in the Talmud and in the Midrashôth, and which are but a small number of kernels surrounded by many husks; so that men have occupied themselves with these husks, not suspecting that there was any kernel hidden beneath.
root.text.Part 1..70.2: As for those few matters which thou findest of the Kalām[[fn:880]] in the writings of some of the Gaonim and the Karaites[[fn:881]], concerning the unity of God and that which pertains thereto, they are things which they borrowed from the Mutakallimūn of the Mohammedans, and it is very little in comparison with what the Mohammedans have written thereupon. It also came to pass that, as soon as the Mohammedans had begun to adopt this method, a certain sect was formed, namely that of the Mu'tazilah[[fn:882]], and our coreligionists borrowed much from them and followed their method. Much later, there arose among the Mohammedans another sect, that of the Ash'ariyyah[[fn:883]], professing other opinions, of which nothing is to be found among our coreligionists; not that the latter chose by preference the first opinion rather than the second, but because it had chanced that they received the first opinion and had adopted it, believing it to be founded upon demonstrative proofs[[fn:884]]. As for the Andalusians of our communion, they are all attached to the words of the philosophers and incline towards their opinions, in so far as they are not in contradiction with a fundamental article of religion; and thou shalt not find them walking, in any respect, in the ways of the Mutakallimūn. For this reason, in the few works which remain to us from their modern authors, they follow, in many respects, nearly our system adopted in this treatise[[fn:885]].
root.text.Part 1..70.3: Thou must know that all which the Mohammedans, both Mu'tazilites and Ash'arites, have said upon the subjects in question, consists of opinions based upon certain propositions, which are borrowed from the writings of the Greeks and the Syrians, who sought to contradict the opinions of the philosophers and to criticize their words[[fn:886]]. And this for the following reason: When the Christian Church, whose profession of faith is known, had received into its bosom those nations[[fn:887]] among whom the opinions of the philosophers were spread—for from them did philosophy emanate—and when there had arisen kings who protected the religion, the learned men of those ages, among the Greeks and the Syrians, saw that there were therein assertions with which the philosophical opinions were in great and manifest contradiction. Then arose among them this science of Kalām, and they began to establish propositions profitable for their belief, and to refute those opinions which subverted the foundations of their religion.
root.text.Part 1..70.4: And when the followers of Islam appeared and the writings of the philosophers were transmitted to them, there were also transmitted to them those refutations which had been written against the books of the philosophers. They found, therefore, the discourses of John the Grammarian[[fn:888]], of Ibn-'Adi[[fn:889]] and of others besides, treating of these matters; and they laid hold of them in the belief that they had made a momentous discovery. They chose also from the opinions of the ancient philosophers all that they deemed to be useful unto them[[fn:890]], although the more recent philosophers had demonstrated the falsity thereof, as, for example, the hypothesis of atoms and of the vacuum[[fn:891]]; and they imagined that these were matters of common interest and propositions needed by all who professed a positive religion. Afterwards the Kalām was extended, and they entered into other extraordinary paths, in which the Greek and other Mutakallimūn had never engaged[[fn:892]]; for these latter were more nearly approached to the philosophers[[fn:893]]. Then there arose again, among the Mohammedans, religious doctrines which were peculiar to them and of which it was necessary to take up the defense; and division having further broken out among them in this regard, each sect established hypotheses which might serve it to defend its opinion.
root.text.Part 1..70.5: There is no doubt that there be matters therein which equally interest the three communions, I mean, the Jews, the Christians, and the Mohammedans, as, for example[[fn:894]], the dogma of the novelty of the world, [upon the truth of which depends that of miracles,] and others besides[[fn:895]]. But the other questions in which the followers of the two religions (the Christian and the Mohammedan) have seen fit to engage, as, for example, the former in the question of the Trinity and certain sects of the latter in that of the Word[[fn:896]] [so that they felt the need to establish certain hypotheses of their own choosing, in order to sustain the questions in which they were engaged[[fn:897]]], as well as all that is peculiar to each of the two communions and has been laid down as a principle by it[[fn:898]], (of all this, I say,) we have no need in any wise.
root.text.Part 1..70.6: In sum, all the ancient[[fn:899]] Mutakallimūn, as well among the Greeks who became Christians as among the Mohammedans, did not at first adhere, in their propositions, to that which is manifest in existence, but they considered how existence ought to exist in order that it might serve as a proof of the truth of their opinion, or at least not subvert it. This imaginary existence once established, they declared that existence is in such a manner; they set themselves to argue to confirm these hypotheses whence they were to take the propositions by which their system might be confirmed or be sheltered from attack. Thus did even the intelligent men who first followed this procedure; they committed this to books and pretended that pure speculation alone had led them thereto without their having had regard to any system or opinion of the past. Those who later read these books knew nothing of what had transpired; so that, finding in these ancient books weighty arguments and great efforts to establish or to deny a certain thing, they imagined that it was by no means in the interest of the fundamental principles of religion that one had need to establish or deny that thing[[fn:900]], and that the ancients had only done so to show what was confused in the opinions of the philosophers and to raise doubts concerning what the latter had taken for a demonstration. Those who thus reasoned did not suspect that the matter was quite otherwise[[fn:901]]; for, on the contrary, if the ancients took such pains to seek to establish one thing and deny another[[fn:902]], it was only because of the danger which might result therefrom, were it even at the end of a series of an hundred premises, for the opinion which they desired to verify, so that these ancient Mutakallimūn cut off the malady at its very source[[fn:903]]. But I shall tell thee as a general thesis that the matter is even as Themistius has said, to wit: that existence does not accommodate itself to opinions, but that true opinions accommodate themselves to existence[[fn:904]].
root.text.Part 1..70.7: Having studied the writings of these Mutakallimūn, so far as I had the facility, even as I have also studied, according to my power, the writings of the philosophers, I have found that the method of all the Mutakallimūn is of one and the same kind, albeit presenting diverse varieties. In sooth, they all hold as a principle that one must have no regard for being as it is, for that is naught but a habit, the contrary of which is ever possible in our reason. Also, in many places, they follow imagination, which they deck with the name of reason. Having thus established the propositions which we shall make known unto thee, they have peremptorily decided, by means of their demonstrations, that the world is created; now, so soon as it is established that the world is created, it is indubitably established that there is an Artificer who created it. They then demonstrate that this Artificer is one, and finally they establish that, being one, He is not a body. Such is the method of every Mutakallim among the Muslims in this kind of questions; and it is the same with those who have imitated them among our coreligionists and who have walked in their ways. As for their modes of argument and the propositions whereby they establish the novelty of the world or deny the eternity thereof, there are various kinds; but the thing which is common to them all is to establish first of all the novelty of the world, by means of which it is proved that God exists.
root.text.Part 1..70.8: When, therefore, I examined this method, my soul felt a very great repugnance thereat, and it deservs in truth to be rejected; for all that is claimed to be a proof of the novelty of the world is subject to doubt, and these are decisive proofs only for him who knows not how to distinguish between demonstration, dialectics, and sophistry[[fn:905]]. But for him who is acquainted with these different arts, it is clear and manifest that all these demonstrations are doubtful, and that there have been employed therein premises which are not demonstrated.
root.text.Part 1..70.9: The furthest point to which, in my judgment, the theologian[[fn:906]] who seeks the truth could go, would be to show the nullity of the demonstrations alleged by the philosophers for the eternity of the world; and how magnificent would it be if success were therein achieved! Indeed, every penetrating thinker who seeks the truth and does not deceive himself knows well that this question, I mean that of whether the world be eternal or created, cannot be resolved by a decisive demonstration, and that it is a point whereat the intellect stays. We shall speak thereof at length; but let it suffice thee now, concerning this question, that for three thousand years, and even unto our time, the philosophers of all ages have been divided thereupon, as may be seen in what we find of their works and of their history[[fn:907]].
root.text.Part 1..70.10: Now, since it is thus with this question, how then should we take it as a premise whereon to construct the proof of the existence of God? This latter would then be doubtful: If the world be created, one would say, there is a God; but if it be eternal, there is no God. Such would be our plight, unless we should pretend to have a proof for the novelty of the world and should impose it by main force[[fn:908]], in order that we might claim to know God by means of demonstration. But all this would be far from the truth;
root.text.Part 1..70.11: to my mind, on the contrary, the true manner, that is to say, the demonstrative method in which there is no doubt, consists in establishing the existence of God, His unity, and His incorporeality by the methods of the philosophers, which methods are based upon the eternity of the world. Not that I believe in the eternity of the world, or that I make a concession unto them in this regard; but it is because, by this method, the demonstration becoms sure and one obtains a perfect certainty concerning these three things, namely, that God exists, that He is one, and that He is incorporeal, without it being of any moment to decide aught regarding the world, to wit, whether it be eternal or created. These three grave and important questions being resolved by a true demonstration, we shall thereafter return to the novelty of the world and we shall produce in this regard all possible arguments[[fn:909]].
root.text.Part 1..70.12: If then thou art of those who rest content with that which the Motécallemīn have declared, and believest that there exists a solid demonstration for the novelty of the world, verily it is well; and if the matter seems not demonstrated unto thee, yet thou acceptest by tradition from the prophets that the world was created, there is no harm therein. Nevertheless, thou must not inquire (at this present): How can prophecy subsist, if the world be eternal? (and thou must wait) until thou hast heard what we shall say concerning prophecy in the present treatise; for we occupy not ourselves now with that subject. But what must be known is that in the propositions which the men of the roots[[fn:910]]—I mean the Motécallemīn—have established to affirm the novelty of the world, there is a subversion of the world and an alteration of the laws of nature[[fn:911]], as thou art about to hear; for I cannot dispense with speaking unto thee of their propositions and of their manner of arguing.
root.text.Part 1..70.13: As for my method, it is such as I shall summarily describe unto thee. The world, I say, is necessarily either eternal or created. Now, if it be created, it has indubitably a creator; for it is a primary notion that what is brought into being has not brought itself into being, but that which has brought it into being is other than itself; wherefore (it is said), He who brought the world into being is God. If (on the contrary) the world be eternal, it follows necessarily, by virtue of such and such proof, that there exists a being, other than all the bodies of the universe, who is neither a body nor a faculty in a body, who is one, permanent, eternal, who has no cause and who is immutable; this being is God. It is therefore manifest that the proofs of the existence of God, of His unity and of His incorporeality, must be obtained solely by the hypothesis of the eternity (of the world), and it is only thus that the demonstration shall be perfect, whether (in reality) the world be eternal or whether it be created[[fn:912]]. Wherefore thou shalt find that whenever, in my Talmudic works, I chance to speak of the fundamental dogmas[[fn:913]] and undertake to establish the existence of God, I do so in terms leaning towards the eternity (of matter). It is not that I profess eternity; but I desire to confirm the existence of God in our belief by a demonstrative method whereon there can be no dispute, so as not to support this true dogma, of so great importance, upon a basis which every man might shake and seek to demolish, and which another might even regard as null and void[[fn:914]]. And the more so[[fn:915]] as the philosophical proofs upon these three questions[[fn:916]] are taken from the visible nature of being, which cannot be denied save by favor of certain preconceived opinions, whereas the proofs of the Motécallemīn are drawn from propositions contrary to the visible nature of being, so that they are constrained[[fn:917]] to establish that no thing has a (fixed) nature.
root.text.Part 1..70.14: I shall give thee in this treatise, whilst speaking of the novelty of the world, a particular chapter in which I shall set forth a certain demonstration upon this question[[fn:918]], and I shall attain the end unto which every Motécallem has aspired, without thereby denying the nature of being, nor contradicting Aristotle in aught that he has demonstrated. For, whereas the proof which certain Motécallemīn have alleged for the novelty of the world, and which is the strongest of their proofs[[fn:919]], could not be established by them without their having denied the nature of all being and contradicted all that the philosophers have set forth, I myself shall arrive at an analogous proof, without being in contradiction with the nature of being, nor having need to contest sensible things[[fn:920]].
root.text.Part 1..70.15: I deem it my duty to report unto thee the general propositions by means of which the Motécallemīn establish the novelty of the world, as well as the existence, the unity, and the incorporeality of God; I shall show thee what is their method in this regard, and I shall set forth that which results from each of the said propositions. Thereafter I shall report unto thee the propositions of the philosophers directly relating to this subject, and I shall show thee the method of the latter.
root.text.Part 1..70.16: Thou shalt not require of me that, in this treatise, I demonstrate the truth of those philosophical propositions which I shall summarily report unto thee; for therein lies the greater part of physics and metaphysics. Likewise, thou shalt not desire that I make thee hear, in this treatise, the arguments alleged by the Motécallemīn to demonstrate the truth of their propositions; for they have spent their lives therein, as will also spend theirs those who are to come, and their books have multiplied. For each of these propositions, with the exception of a small number, is refuted by that which is seen in the nature of being, and doubts arise; so that they have need of making books and controversies to confirm each proposition, to resolve the doubts that arise therein, and even to reject the evidence which refuts it, if there be no other possible means[[fn:921]]. But, as for the philosophical propositions which I shall summarily report unto thee to serve for the demonstration of the said three questions—I mean, of the existence, the unity, and the incorporeality of God—they are, for the most part, propositions which will give thee certainty as soon as thou shalt have heard them and understood their meaning. Some will indicate unto thee in themselves the places in the books of Physics or Metaphysics where they are demonstrated; thou mayest therefore seek the place thereof and verify that which may have need of being verified.
root.text.Part 1..70.17: I have already made known unto thee that there exists naught else but God and this universe. God can only be demonstrated by this universe (considered) in its entirety and in its details; it is therefore necessary to examine this universe as it is, and to derive the premises (of the proofs) from its visible nature. Consequently, one must be acquainted with its visible form and nature, and only then may one induce therefrom proofs concerning that which lies outside it. I have therefore deemed it necessary to provide first a chapter in which I set forth the whole of the universe, in the form of a simple relation of that which has been demonstrated (elsewhere) and whose truth is beyond doubt. Thereafter I shall provide other chapters, in which I shall report the propositions of the Mutakallimūn and set forth the methods of which they make use to resolve the four questions at issue[[fn:922]]. Then, in yet other chapters, I shall expound to thee the propositions of the philosophers and their methods of argumentation regarding the said questions. Finally, I shall set forth the method which I myself follow, as I have announced unto thee, regarding these four questions.
root.text.Part 1..71.0: Know that this universe in its entirety forms but a single individual; I mean to say: the globe of the extreme heaven with all that it contains is indubitably a single individual, under the same title of individuality as Zayd and ‘Amr[[fn:923]]. It is with its different substances—I mean the substances of this globe with all it contains—as it is, for example, with the different substances of the members of the human individual. Even as Zayd, for example, is a single individual, though composed of different parts, such as flesh and bones, different humours and spirits[[fn:924]], so this globe in its entirety embraces the spheres and the four elements with that which is composed of them. It has absolutely no void, but is a solid plenum having for its centre the terrestrial globe; the earth is environed by water, this by air, this by fire[[fn:925]], and this last finally is environed by the fifth body[[fn:926]]. This latter[[fn:927]] is composed of numerous spheres, contained one within the other, between which there is no hollow nor void, but which exactly encompass each other, being applied one to the other. They all possess an equal circular motion, and in none of them is there any precipitation or slackening; I mean that none of these spheres movs now rapidly, now slowly, but each, as to its velocity and manner of moving, remains subject to its natural law. Nevertheless, these spheres move more rapidly than one another, and that which among them all has the most rapid motion is the sphere which environs everything, that is to say, that which has the diurnal motion and which causs them all to move with it as the part movs in the whole, for all of them form parts within it. These spheres have different centres; some have for their centre the centre of the world[[fn:928]], others have their centre outside that of the world[[fn:929]]. There be some which perpetually follow their particular motion from East to West, whilst others move continually from West to East[[fn:930]]. Every star within these spheres is part of the sphere in which it remains fixed in its place; it has no motion peculiar to itself, and appears moved only by the motion of the body of which it is a part. The matter of this entire fifth body, which has the circular motion, is in no wise similar to that of the bodies of the four elements which are found in the interior.
root.text.Part 1..71.1: The number of these spheres which environ the world cannot in any wise be less than eighteen[[fn:931]]; it is possible, however, that there be more, and it is a matter to be examined. As for knowing whether there be spheres of revolution which do not environ the world, this likewise is to be examined[[fn:932]].
root.text.Part 1..71.2: In the interior of the inferior sphere which is nearest unto us[[fn:933]], there is a matter different from that of the fifth body, and which has received four primitive forms whereby four bodies have been formed, (which are) earth, water, air, and fire. Each of these four (bodies) has a natural place which is peculiar to it, and is found in no other (place) so long as it remains left to its nature. These are inanimate bodies, having neither life nor perception, and which do not move by themselves, but remain at rest in their natural places. If, however, one of them has been forced to depart from its natural place, then, as soon as the cause which forced it thereto ceass, it movs to return to that natural place; for it has within it the principle by virtue of which it movs in a straight line to return to its place, but it has within it no principle by virtue of which it must (always) remain at rest or move otherwise than in a straight line. The motions in a straight line made by these four elements, when they move to return to their places, are of two kinds: a motion toward the circumference, which belongs to fire and air, and a motion toward the centre, which belongs to water and earth; and each, after arriving at its natural place, remains at rest[[fn:934]]. As for these (celestial) bodies which have circular motion, they are living and possess a soul whereby they move; there is in them absolutely no principle of rest, and they undergo no change save in position, having circular motion. As for knowing whether they have also an intelligence whereby they conceive, this cannot be elucidated save by means of subtle speculation[[fn:935]].
root.text.Part 1..71.3: The entire fifth body accomplishing its circular motion, there ariss therefrom continually in the elements a forced motion whereby they depart from their regions—I mean (there ariss a motion) in the fire and the air, which are driven back toward the water, and all of them penetrate into the body of the earth even into its depths, so that there results therefrom a mixture of the elements. Thereafter they begin to move to return to their (respective) regions, and, in consequence thereof, particles of earth likewise quit their places, joining themselves to water, air, and fire. In all this, the elements act upon one another and receive impressions from one another, and the mixture undergoes a transformation, so that there ariss therefrom[[fn:936]] first the different species of vapours[[fn:937]], then the different species of minerals, all the species of plants, and numerous species of animals, according to what the complexion of the mixture requirs. All that which is born and perishes is born only of the elements and returns thereto in perishing. Likewise, the elements are born of one another and are lost in one another; for all has but a single matter, and matter cannot exist without form, even as no physical form of these things which are born and perish can exist without matter. Therefore, the birth and destruction of the elements, as well as of all that which is born of the latter and is resolved therein in perishing, follow (as it were) a circular motion, similar to that of the heaven; so that the motion which this formed matter[[fn:938]] makes, through the forms which successively come upon it, may be compared to the motion which the heaven makes in place[[fn:939]], the same positions being repeated[[fn:940]] for each of its parts.
root.text.Part 1..71.4: Even as in the human body there be (on the one hand) dominant members, and (on the other hand) subordinate members which require, for their preservation, the governance of the principal member that ruls them, even so there be, in the whole of the universe, dominant parts, such as the fifth body which encompasses (all), and subordinate parts which require a guide, as the elements and that which is composed thereof.
root.text.Part 1..71.5: Even as the principal member, which is the heart, movs ever[[fn:941]] and is the principle of all movement existing in the body, whilst the other members of the body are governed by it, and it is that which, by its movement, sends unto them the faculties of which they have need for their actions, even so it is the celestial sphere which, by its movement, governs the other parts of the universe, and it is that which sends unto all that is brought into being the faculties found therein; so that every movement existing in the universe has for its first principle the movement of the celestial sphere, and every soul of that which, in the universe, is endowed with a soul, has its principle in the soul of the celestial sphere.
root.text.Part 1..71.6: It behoves to know that the faculties which proceed from the celestial sphere unto this world are, as has been set forth, four in number, namely: a faculty which produces mixture and composition, and which suffices indubitably for the production[[fn:942]] of minerals; another faculty, which bestows the vegetative soul upon every plant; another, which bestows the vital soul upon all that lives; and finally another, which bestows the rational faculty upon every reasonable being; and all this is accomplished by the mediation of the light and the darkness resulting from the light of the stars and from their revolution about the earth[[fn:943]].
root.text.Part 1..71.7: Even as, furthermore, when the heart stays its motion for a single instant, the individual dies and all his movements and faculties cease, even so, if the celestial spheres should stay their motion, it would be the death of the whole universe and the annihilation of all that is found therein.
root.text.Part 1..71.8: Even as, finally, the animal lives in its entirety solely by the effect of the movement of its heart, although it possesses members void of movement and sensation, as, for example, the bones, the cartilages, and such like, even so this whole universe is a single individual, living by the movement of the celestial sphere which occupies therein the same rank as that held by the heart in that which has a heart, although it contains many bodies without movement and inanimate.
root.text.Part 1..71.9: Thus must thou represent to thyself the whole of this sphere as a single individual, living, moving, and endowed with a soul; for this manner of representation is highly necessary, or at the least[[fn:944]] most profitable, for the demonstration of the unity of God, even as it shall be set forth[[fn:945]], and in this wise it shall also be manifest that the One has created but a single being[[fn:946]].
root.text.Part 1..71.10: In like manner as it is impossible that the members of a man should exist separately as true members of man—I mean, that the liver or the heart should be isolated, or that flesh should exist in isolation—so would it be impossible that the parts of the universe should exist the one without the other, in this well-constituted being of which we speak[[fn:947]], so that fire should exist without earth, or earth without heaven, or heaven without earth.
root.text.Part 1..71.11: Even as there exists in this human individual a certain faculty which binds his members one to another, governs them, bestows upon each member what is requisite for its preservation in a goodly state, and wards off that which is harmful to it—to wit, that which physicians expressly designate as the directing faculty of the animal body, and which they often term nature[[fn:948]]—so likewise there is in the whole of the universe a faculty which binds the parts thereof together, which prevents the species from perishing and preservs also the individuals of these species so long as it is possible so to do, and which likewise preservs a portion of the individuals of the universe[[fn:949]]. It remains, however, to be considered whether this faculty acts, or no, by the mediation of the celestial sphere[[fn:950]].
root.text.Part 1..71.12: Within the body of the human individual there are, on the one hand, things which have a particular purpose: some, like the organs of nutrition, have for their end the preservation of the individual; others, like the organs of generation, have for their end the preservation of the species; yet others, as for example the hands and eyes, are destined to provide for those things of which man has need in the way of nourishment[[fn:951]] and other like matters. And, on the other hand, there exist[[fn:952]] also things which have no end in themselves, but which are attached as accessories to the complexion of certain members, which particular complexion is necessary for these latter to obtain their proper form, that they may fulfill the functions for which they are destined. Thus, to that which is formed for a certain purpose[[fn:953]], there are joined, according to the exigency of matter, certain other things, as, for example, the hair and the colour of the body; wherefore[[fn:954]] these things possess no regularity, and there are even some which oftentimes are wholly wanting, and there exists in this regard a very great difference between individuals[[fn:955]], which is not the case with the members. Verily, thou shalt not find an individual whose liver is ten times as great as that of another individual, whilst thou shalt find such a man void of a beard, or who has no hair in certain parts of his body, or whose beard is ten or twenty times greater than that of another individual; and this is very frequent[[fn:956]] in this order of things—I mean the difference which exists between individuals as to hair and colour. In like manner[[fn:957]], in the whole of the universe, there are, on the one hand, species whose generation has a determined end, which follow with constancy a certain rule and in which there are but small anomalies remaining within the limits of the species in respect of quality and quantity[[fn:958]]; and, on the other hand, species which have no end in themselves, but are a necessary consequence of the general laws of generation and corruption[[fn:959]], such as, for example, the diverse species of worms which are born in dung, the diverse species of animalcules which are born in fruits when they decay, that which springs from the corruption of moist things, the worms which are born in the intestines, and so forth. In general, it seems to me that all that has not the faculty of procreating its like is of this category; wherefore thou shalt find that these things observe no rule, albeit they must of necessity exist, even as it is necessary that human individuals should be of different colours and have different kinds of hair.
root.text.Part 1..71.13: In like manner as there are in man bodies of an individual permanence[[fn:960]], such as the principal members, and bodies permanent as a species, and not as an individual, like the four humours[[fn:961]], so there are in the whole of the universe stable bodies, of an individual permanence, like the fifth body with all its parts[[fn:962]], and bodies permanent as a species, such as the elements and that which is composed thereof[[fn:963]].
root.text.Part 1..71.14: Even as the faculties whereby man is brought into being and is preserved for a certain season[[fn:964]] are the very same that cause his destruction and ruin, so likewise, in the whole of the world of generation and corruption[[fn:965]], the causes of birth are themselves the causes of destruction. Of this is an example: If those four faculties which exist in the body of every living thing that is nourished, to wit, the attractive, the retentive, the digestive, and the expulsive[[fn:966]], could resemble the intellectual faculties, so as to perform only what is requisite, at the time when it is requisite and in the measure that is requisite, man would be preserved from the greatest calamities and from many diseases; but, since this is not possible, and since, on the contrary, they perform physical functions without reflection or discernment, and without in any wise understanding what they do, it follows that they give rise to grievous maladies and calamities, though they be the instruments by which the animal is born and is preserved for a certain season. Thus, to explain my meaning, if the attractive faculty, for example, did attract only that which is suitable in every respect, and only in the measure of need, man would be preserved from many diseases and calamities. But, as it is not so, and as, on the contrary, it attracts every matter that presents itself, provided it be of the kind of its attraction[[fn:967]], even though this matter should deviate somewhat from the just measure in respect of quantity and quality, it results that it also attracts matter which is hotter, or colder, or thicker, or subtler, or in greater quantity than is needful; whereby the veins are gorged, and there occurrs obstruction and putrefaction, the quality of the humours is corrupted and their quantity is altered, and there arise diseases, such as the itch, the scab, and warts, or great calamities, such as cancerous tumours, elephantiasis, and gangrene, so that the form of one or more members is destroyed. And it is the same with the other of the four faculties. — Now, it is precisely the same thing that occurrs in the whole of the universe: the thing which causs to be born that which is born, and prolongs its existence for a certain season, — to wit, the mixture of the elements produced by the faculties of the celestial sphere which set them in motion and are diffused therein, — is itself the cause which brings into the universe harmful things, such as floods, heavy rains, snow, hail, hurricanes, thunder, lightning, and the corruption of the air, or terrible catastrophes which destroy one or more cities or a whole country, such as the sinkings of the earth[[fn:968]], earthquakes, violent storms, and the waters which overflow from the seas and the depths[[fn:969]].
root.text.Part 1..71.15.sub_0: It behoves us to know that, notwithstanding all that we have said concerning the similitude which exists between the whole of the universe and the human individual, it is nevertheless not on account of all this that man has been called a little world (microcosm); for all this comparison might be pursued in respect of every individual among the animals of a complete organism, and yet thou hast never heard that any of the ancients said that the ass or the horse was a little world. If this has been said of man, it is solely because of that which particularly distinguishes him; and that is the rational faculty, I mean that intelligence which is the hylian intellect[[fn:970]], a thing which is found in no other species of animals. Of this is the explanation: Every individual among the animals has need neither of thought, nor of reflection, nor of a regime, to prolong its existence; but it goes and comes according to its nature, eats what it finds suitable for itself, shelters itself in the first place it meets, and coupls with the first female it encounters when it is in heat, if indeed it has a season of heat. Thereby the individual endurs for such time as it can endure, and the existence of its species is perpetuated; it has in no wise need of another individual of its species to succour it and help it to preserve itself, in such manner that the latter should do for it things which it cannot do itself. But it is otherwise with man; for, if one were to suppose a human individual[[fn:971]] existing alone, deprived of all regime and become like unto the animals, such an individual would perish straightway and could not even subsist for a single day, unless it were by accident, I mean, that he should by chance find something wherewith to nourish himself. In truth, the foods whereby man subsists require art and long preparations which can only be accomplished by dint of thought and reflection, with the help of many instruments and with the concurrence of a great number of persons, of which each one takes upon himself a particular function. Wherefore it is necessary for men to have someone to guide and unite them, so that their society may be organized and perpetuated, and that they may afford one another mutual succour.
root.text.Part 1..71.15.sub_1: Likewise, to preserve himself from the heat in the time of heat and from the cold in the cold season, and to guard himself against rains, snows, and winds, man is obliged to make many preparations, all of which can only be accomplished by means of thought and reflection. It is therefore on this account that he has been endowed with this rational faculty whereby he thinks, reflects, acts, and, by the aid of diverse arts, prepars his food and that wherewith to shelter and clothe himself; and it is by it also that he governs all the members of his body, so that the ruling member may do what it ought to do, and that that which is subjected may be governed as it ought to be. Wherefore, if thou shouldst suppose a human individual deprived of this faculty and abandoned to his animal nature alone, he would be lost and would perish at that very instant. This faculty is most noble, more noble than any of the faculties of the animal; it is also most occult, and its true nature cannot be understood at first sight by simple common sense, as are the other natural faculties.
root.text.Part 1..71.16: — Likewise, there is in the universe something which governs the whole thereof, and which setts in motion the ruling and principal member, unto which it communicats the motive faculty in such manner as to govern thereby the other members[[fn:972]]; and, were it to be supposed that the thing in question could disappear, this entire sphere of the universe, both the ruling part and the subjected part, would cease to exist. It is by this thing that the existence of the sphere and of each of its parts is perpetuated; and this thing is God [exalted be His name!]. — It is in this sense alone that man in particular has been called a microcosm, that is to say, because there is in him a principle which governs his whole being; and it is because of this idea that God has been called, in our language, the life of the universe, and that it has been said: And he sware by the life of the universe (Daniel, 12:7)[[fn:973]].
root.text.Part 1..71.17: It behoves us to know that the comparison which we have established between the whole of the universe and the human individual admitts of no contradiction in anything that we have said, save only in three points:
root.text.Part 1..71.18: The dominant member (or the heart), in every animal that has a heart, derivs benefit from the subjected members, from which utility returns unto it. But naught of the like occurrs in the universal being; on the contrary, every thing which (in the universe) exercs a directing influence or imparts a faculty[[fn:974]] derivs on its own part no benefit from the subject part, but its manner of giving is like that of the beneficent and liberal man, who does good through generosity of character and by an innate goodness, and not in the hope (of a reward)[[fn:975]]; nay, more[[fn:976]], it is to render himself like unto God [may His name be exalted!].
root.text.Part 1..71.19: In all animals that possess a heart, the same is found in the midst, and all the subjected members environ it to be generally profitable thereto, by guarding and protecting it, lest any mishap from without should befall it. But in the whole of the universe, the matter is the reverse: the more noble part environns that which is less noble, because it is in no wise exposed to receive an impression from that which is without it; and even were it susceptible of impression, it would find no other body outside itself that could act upon it, for it influencs that which is within it, and there reaches it no impression nor any faculty (coming) from another body.—There is, however, herein some resemblance: for whatsoever among the members of the animal is more remote from the dominant member is less noble than that which is nearer thereto; and likewise, in the whole of the universe, according as bodies approach the centre, they become dull, their substance becoms more gross and their movement more difficult, and they lose their lustre and their transparency, by reason of their distance from the noble, luminous, transparent, mobile, subtle and simple body, I mean, the celestial sphere; but, according as a body approaches it, it acquirs something of these qualities, by reason of its proximity, and enjoys a certain superiority over that which is beneath it.
root.text.Part 1..71.20: This rational faculty (of which we have spoken) is a faculty in a body and inseparable therefrom, whilst God is in no wise a faculty in the body of the universe, but is separate from all the parts of the universe. The governance of God and His providence are joined unto the whole world by a bond the true nature of which is unknown to us, and which the faculties of mortals cannot comprehend; for it can be demonstrated (on the one hand) that God is separate from the world and that He is independent thereof[[fn:977]], and (on the other hand) it can also be demonstrated that the influence of His governance and of His providence extends over each of the parts of the world, however feeble and insignificant it may be[[fn:978]]. Praise be unto Him whose perfection fills us with admiration!
root.text.Part 1..71.21: Know that we ought to have compared the relation between God and the universe to that which exists between the acquired intellect and man; for this intellect also is not a faculty in a body, being in reality separate from the body upon which it is poured forth[[fn:979]]. As for the rational faculty, one might compare it to the intelligences of the spheres, which are found in bodies. But the question of the intelligences of the spheres, the existence of separate intelligences, and the idea of the acquired intellect, which is likewise separate, are matters which need to be studied and examined, and the demonstrations of which are obscure albeit true; they are subject to many doubts and exposed to the attacks of him who seeks to criticise and cavil[[fn:980]]. We have therefore preferred that one should first be able to represent the universe by its manifest form; and indeed[[fn:981]] naught of what we have advanced in an absolute manner can be denied save by two sorts of persons: either by him who is ignorant even of that which is most evident, as (for example) he who is no geometrician denies mathematical things which are demonstrated; or by him who preferrs to cling to a preconceived opinion and to deceive himself. As for him who wishes to engage in true speculation, he must apply himself to study, so that the truth of all that we have related may become evident to him, and that he may know, without having the least doubt in this regard, that such is (indeed) the form of this being whose existence is (invariably) constituted. If any one wills to accept it from him to whom all has been rigorously demonstrated, let him accept it and let him build thereon his syllogisms and his proofs[[fn:982]]; but if he loves not simple tradition, even for these principles (of things)[[fn:983]], then let him study, and it shall become manifest to him that the matter is so. Lo, this we have searched it, so it is; hear it, and know it for thy good (Job, v, 27).
root.text.Part 1..71.22: After this preparation, I approach the subject which I promised to set forth[[fn:984]].
root.text.Part 1..72.0: The general propositions which the Motécallemîn have established, notwithstanding[[fn:985]] their diverse opinions and their manifold methods, [propositions which are necessary for them to affirm that which they desire to affirm concerning the four questions in point,] are twelve in number. I shall first state them unto thee (summarily); thereafter I shall expound unto thee the meaning of each of these propositions and that which results therefrom:
root.text.Part 1..72.1: The Ist proposition affirms (the existence of) the simple substance[[fn:986]];
root.text.Part 1..72.2: the IInd, the existence of the vacuum;
root.text.Part 1..72.3: the III<sup>rd</sup>, that time is composed of instants[[fn:987]];
root.text.Part 1..72.4: the IV<sup>th</sup>, that substance is inseparable from manifold accidents;
root.text.Part 1..72.5: the V[[t:0]]e[[t:1]], which in the [[t:2]]substance simple[[t:3]] (or the [[t:4]]atome[[t:5]]) reside the accidents on which I shall explain myself, and which are inseparable from it;
root.text.Part 1..72.6: the VI[[t:0]]th[[t:1]], that the accident does not endure two [[t:2]]times[[t:3]] (or [[t:4]]instants[[t:5]]);
root.text.Part 1..72.7: the VIIth proposition, that the reason for being is the same for the [[t:2]]capacities[[t:3]] and for their [[t:4]]privations[[t:5]][[fn:988]], and that all of them are real accidents which require an efficient cause;
root.text.Part 1..72.8: the VIIIth proposition, that there is nothing in the entire being [that is to say, in all created things,] other than substance and accident, and that the [[t:2]]form physical[[t:3]] is also an accident;
root.text.Part 1..72.9: the IX[[t:0]]th[[t:1]], in which accidents do not affect one another;
root.text.Part 1..72.10: the Xth is, that the possible is not to be considered from the point of view of the conformity of being with any given idea[[fn:989]];
root.text.Part 1..72.11: the XIth is, that, as touching the inadmissibility of the infinite, it matters little[[fn:990]] whether it be so in act or in potentiality, or accidentally; I mean to say, that it matters little whether infinite things exist simultaneously, or whether they be deemed (to be composed) of that which is and that which is no more[[fn:991]] [and this is that which is accidentally]; all this, say they, is (equally) inadmissible;
root.text.Part 1..72.12: the XII<sup>th</sup> finally, is their assertion: that the senses lead into error, since many things escape their perception[[fn:992]], and that consequently their judgment cannot be admitted, nor can they be taken absolutely as the principles of a demonstration.
root.text.Part 1..72.13: Having thus enumerated them, I shall proceed to explain their sense and set forth that which results therefrom, (approaching them) one by one.
root.text.Part 1..72.14: The FIRST PROPOSITION has the following meaning: They maintained that the whole universe, that is to say, every body which it contains, is composed of very small particles, which, by reason of their subtilty, admit of no division[[fn:993]]. Each of these particles is absolutely without quantity; but when they are joined to one another, the whole has quantity and is then a body. According to the opinion of some, as soon as two of these particles join together, each of them becoms a body, thus making two bodies[[fn:994]]. All these particles are similar and alike to one another, and there is no kind of difference between them. It is not possible, say they, that there should exist any body whatsoever that is not composed of these similar particles, by juxtaposition[[fn:995]]; so that, for them, generation is the union (of atoms), and destruction is their separation. Nevertheless, they do not bestow upon the latter the name of destruction, but they say: generations[[fn:996]] are union, separation, motion, and rest. They say also that these particles are not of a limited number[[fn:997]] in the universe, as Epicurus and others who professed the doctrine of atoms believed; they maintain, on the contrary, that God perpetually creats these substances when He wills, and that they may likewise not exist. I shall make known unto thee their opinions concerning the privation of substance[[fn:998]].
root.text.Part 1..72.15: The SECOND PROPOSITION is the assertion of the vacuum: — The men of the roots[[fn:999]] likewise believe that the vacuum exists, that is to say, (that there exist) one or more spaces in which there is absolutely nothing, but which are void of all body and deprived of all substance. This proposition is necessary unto them so soon as they admit the first proposition. Indeed, if the universe were full[[fn:1000]] of these atoms, how then could that which movs be moved? for one cannot imagine that bodies enter into one another, and these atoms can neither unite nor separate save by motion. They are therefore of necessity obliged[[fn:1001]] to admit the vacuum, in order that it may be possible for these atoms to unite and to separate, and that motion may take place in this vacuum, in which there is no body nor any of these (simple) substances.
root.text.Part 1..72.16: The THIRD PROPOSITION says: “that time is composed of instants;” that is to say, that it is composed of many small times which, by reason of their brief duration, admit of no division. This proposition is likewise necessary unto them because of the first proposition; for, having doubtless seen the demonstrations whereby Aristotle has proved that extension, time, and local motion are three corresponding things in being [that is to say, that they stand in the same mutual relation to one another, and that, when one of these things is divided, the other is divided likewise and in the same proportion], they were constrained to acknowledge[[fn:1002]] that if time were continuous and susceptible of division unto infinity, it would follow that this atom which they posited as indivisible is of necessity divisible, and that likewise, if one admitted that extension is continuous, one would be forced to admit the divisibility of that instant of time which was posited as indivisible, even as Aristotle has set forth in the Acroasis[[fn:1003]]. Wherefore they have laid down as a principle that extension is in no wise continuous, but composed of atoms whereat divisibility stays, and that likewise time results in instants which admit of no division. Thus, for example, an hour having sixty minutes, the minute sixty seconds, the second sixty thirds, the matter shall result for them in particles such as, for instance, tenths, or others yet smaller, which can in no wise be subdivided and which, like (the atoms of) extension, shall no longer admit of division. According to this, time would be a thing of position and order[[fn:1004]]; and verily they have in no wise fathomed the true nature of time.
root.text.Part 1..72.17: And this was as it should be; for if the most skilful philosophers have been perplexed regarding time and several have not comprehended the notion thereof,—insomuch that Galen says it is a thing divine, the true nature of which cannot be grasped,—how much more should this be true of those who have no regard for the nature of any thing?
root.text.Part 1..72.18: Hearken now unto that which they were compelled to admit as a consequence of these three (initial) propositions: Motion, they said, consists in this, that each of these indivisible particles transports itself from one atom (of extension) to the adjacent atom[[fn:1005]], and it follows from this hypothesis that motions are not swifter one than another. Indeed, they say, when thou seest that two things in motion traverse two different distances in the same time, the cause thereof is not that the motion of that which traverss the longer distance is swifter, but the cause is that into that motion which we call slow, there enter more intervals of rest, whilst into that which we call swift, there enter fewer intervals of rest. When there was opposed to them (the example of) the arrow shot from a bow strongly bent[[fn:1006]], they replied: verily, it also has its motions interrupted by intervals of rest, and if thou believest that it movs with a continuous motion, it is by an error of the senses; for many things escape the perception of the senses, even as they have laid down as a principle in the twelfth proposition. It was then said to them: Have ye not seen that when the millstone performs a perfect circular motion, the part which is at its circumference traverss the extent of the largest circle in precisely the same time during which the part which is near the centre traverss the smallest circle? the motion of the circumference is therefore swifter than that of the inner circle; and it is not permitted you to say that in the motion of this latter part there enter more intervals of rest, since the whole body—I mean, the body of the millstone—is one and continuous. And hereupon they replied that in the revolution its parts become separated, and that the intervals of rest which enter into each part turning near the centre are more numerous than those which enter into the part far from the centre. But then, it was said to them, how comes it to pass that the millstone, in which we recognize a single body which cannot be broken with hammers, should break asunder whilst turning and then rejoin itself as soon as it is at rest, and become again as it was? and how is it not perceived that its parts have separated? And in answer thereto, they availed themselves precisely of this twelfth proposition, which says that one must not have regard to the perception of the senses, but to the testimony of the intellect.
root.text.Part 1..72.19: One must not believe, moreover, that what I have just said is the most absurd consequence of these three propositions; for, certes, that which results from the belief in the existence of the vacuum is yet more extraordinary and more absurd; and what I have related to thee concerning motion[[fn:1007]] is no greater absurdity than to admit, as is necessary according to this system, that the diagonal of the square is equal to its side[[fn:1008]], so that there were some among them who maintained that the square is a thing which has no existence. In short, by reason of the 1st proposition, all the demonstrations of the whole of geometry are found to be destroyed. These may be divided in this regard into two categories[[fn:1009]]: one part shall be entirely annulled, as, for example, the properties of incommensurability and commensurability[[fn:1010]] in lines and planes, the existence of rational and irrational lines[[fn:1011]], and (in general) all that is contained in the 10th book of Euclid, as well as other similar things. For another part, the demonstrations shall not be absolute, as, for instance, in the problem of the division of a line into two equal parts[[fn:1012]]; for if the atoms of the line be an odd number, it shall not be possible, according to their hypothesis, to effect the division[[fn:1013]]. — Know also that the celebrated Book of Artifices, by the Banu Shakir[[fn:1014]], contains above an hundred artifices, all of which are supported by demonstrations and have been put into practice; now, if the vacuum could exist, not a single one (of these devices) could be carried out, and many hydraulic operations could not take place. Nevertheless, men have spent their lives arguing to confirm these propositions and others like unto them. — I return now to the explanation of the other propositions which I have recorded.
root.text.Part 1..72.20: The FOURTH PROPOSITION says: “that accidents exist, that they are notions added to the notion of substance, and that there is no body whatsoever entirely exempt therefrom[[fn:1015]].” Were this proposition confined to these terms, it would be a true, clear, and manifest proposition, containing naught of doubt or obscurity[[fn:1016]]. But they say that, if a (simple) substance possesses not within itself the accident of life, it must perforce possess the accident of death; for, of two opposite (accidents), that which receivs (accidents) must of necessity possess one of them[[fn:1017]]. Thus, say they, it has (for example) colour and taste, and (moreover) motion or rest, union or separation[[fn:1018]]. If it possess the accident of life, it must likewise perforce possess certain other kinds of accidents, such as knowledge or ignorance, will or its opposite, power or impotence, perception or one of its opposites[[fn:1019]]; in short, every (accident) which may exist in a living being, it must of necessity possess itself, or else possess one of its opposites.
root.text.Part 1..72.21: The <small>FIFTH PROPOSITION</small> says: “that it is in the atom itself that these accidents reside[[fn:1020]] and that from it they are inseparable.” Behold the explanation and the meaning of this proposition: They say that each of these atoms which God creats has accidents wherefrom it is inseparable, as, for example, colour and odour, motion or rest; excepting however quantity, for each atom apart has no quantity, and indeed, they do not call quantity an accident, nor do they recognize therein the notion of an accident[[fn:1021]]. According to this proposition, they deem that one cannot say of any of the accidents existing in any body whatsoever that it is proper to the whole of that body; on the contrary, this accident exists, according to them, in each of the atoms of which the body is composed. In this heap of snow, for instance, whiteness exists not alone in the whole mass, but it is each of the atoms of this snow which is white, and it is for this reason that whiteness is found in their whole.
