Likewise, they maintain, with regard to a body in motion, that it is each of its atoms which movs, and that for this reason its whole movs. Even so does life also exist, according to them, in each of the atoms of the living body, and likewise, as touching sensibility, each atom in this sensitive whole is, according to them, endowed with sensibility; for life, sensibility, intelligence, and knowledge are, in their view, accidents like unto blackness and whiteness, even as we shall show by the exposition of their opinions.
root.text.Part 1..72.22: As touching the soul, they are divided: according to the prevailing opinion, it is an accident existing in but one of all the atoms of which man, for example, is composed; and if the whole be called animated, it is because this atom forms part thereof. There be some who say that the soul is a body[[fn:1022]] composed of subtle atoms, which atoms are doubtless endowed with a certain accident peculiar to them and whereby it becoms a soul, and these atoms, say they, mingle with the atoms of the body; consequently, they do not renounce the view of the soul as an accident. As for the intelligence, I see them to be in common accord that it is an accident (existing) in one of the atoms of the intelligent whole.
root.text.Part 1..72.23: Concerning the science, there exists amongst them a state of indecision (with regard to the question of) whether it exists as an accident in each of the atoms of the aggregate endowed with science, or (whether it exists only in) a single atom; but both opinions have absurd consequences.
root.text.Part 1..72.24: When it was objected unto them that metals and stones are for the most part found endowed with an intense colour, which nevertheless departs as soon as they are reduced to powder — [for, when we reduce to powder the emerald, which is of a deep green, it is transformed into a white dust, which proves that this accident pertains to the whole[[fn:1023]], and not to each of its parts; and, what is yet more manifest, when parts of a living being are cut off, they are in no wise living, which proves that this notion (of life) pertains to the whole, and not to each of its parts] — they replied thereto that the accident has no duration, but that it is perpetually created; and it is this opinion which I shall set forth in the following proposition.
root.text.Part 1..72.25: The SIXTH PROPOSITION says: “that an accident endurs not for two times.” The meaning of this proposition is as follows: They maintain that God, in creating the (simple) substance, creats simultaneously therein whatever accident He wills, and that one cannot attribute unto God the power to create a substance without an accident, for that is impossible[[fn:1024]]. The true conception of an accident is that it endurs not, and subsists not for two times, that is to say, two instants[[fn:1025]]; the accident, therefore, as soon as it is created, perishes and remains not, and God creats another accident of the same kind. This latter likewise perishes, and God creats a third of the same kind; and thus it continus so long as God wills this kind of accident to endure. If God wills to create another kind of accident in this substance, He does so; but if He abstains from creating, and creats no further accident, this substance ceass to be. Such is the opinion of a portion of the (Mutakallemîn), and it is the majority; and this is the creation of accidents of which they speak[[fn:1026]]. Nevertheless, several amongst the Mu‘tazilites maintain that there be accidents which endure for a certain time, and that there be others which endure not for two instants; yet have they no rule in this regard for their guidance, whereby they might say: Such a kind of accidents endurs, and such another kind endurs not.
root.text.Part 1..72.26: That which has led them to adopt this opinion is that they do not admit (amongst them) that there be a nature (of things)[[fn:1027]], and that, for example, the nature of a certain body requirs that it be affected by this or that accident; for, on the contrary, they will maintain that God has created these accidents instantaneously, without the mediation of a natural law or of any other thing whatsoever. Now, in professing this opinion, they were necessarily driven to this conclusion: that the accident endurs not. Verily, if it were admitted that it endurs for a certain time and thereafter ceass to be, this would give rise to the question, what thing has caused it to cease to be? and if it were answered that it is God who causs it to cease to be when He wills, that could not be true according to their opinion[[fn:1028]]; for the efficient cause works not non-existence, which has no need of an efficient cause, but it is when the efficient cause abstains from acting that the effect ceass to be [which is true in a certain respect[[fn:1029]]]. Wherefore, having desired to maintain that there is no natural law which necessitats the existence or non-existence of anything whatsoever, they have been led thereby to say[[fn:1030]] that accidents are created successively. According to some, therefore, when God wills that the substance should cease to be, He creats no accident therein, and thereby it ceass to be; others, however, say that if God willed to destroy the world, He would create the accident of destruction without the latter having a substratum[[fn:1031]], and this destruction would neutralize[[fn:1032]] the existence of the world.
root.text.Part 1..72.27: By virtue of this proposition, they have maintained that this cloth which we believe to have been dyed red, it is not we who have dyed it, but it is God who has caused this colour to arise in the cloth at the moment when the latter was joined with the red colour; for, say they, although we believe that this colour has (perforce) penetrated the cloth, it is not so[[fn:1033]]. On the contrary (they add)[[fn:1034]], it is God who has established as a customary thing[[fn:1035]] that this black colour, for example, should only arise at the moment when the cloth is joined with the indigo[[fn:1036]]; yet this black, which God has created at the moment when the thing to be blackened was joined with the black colour, remains not, but perishes at that very instant, and God creats another black. In like manner, God has made it His custom to create, after the disappearance of this black, not a red or yellow colour, but a similar black.
root.text.Part 1..72.28: In accordance with this hypothesis, they have maintained that the cognitions which we now possess of a certain thing cannot be the same as those which we possessed yesterday; that these latter, on the contrary, have vanished, and that others like unto them have been created; and if it be so, say they, it is because science is an accident. And likewise, he who believs that the soul is an accident must necessarily admit that there be created in every living being an hundred thousand souls, for example, in every minute; for, according to them, as thou knowest, time is composed of indivisible instants.
root.text.Part 1..72.29: They maintain further, by virtue of this proposition, that when a man movs the pen[[fn:1037]], it is not the man who movs it; for this movement which ariss in the pen is an accident which God has created therein. Likewise, the movement of the hand, which in our opinion movs the pen, is an accident which God has created in the hand which movs[[fn:1038]]; God has only established it as a custom that the movement of the hand joins itself to the movement of the pen, without the hand having for all that any influence whatsoever or any causality in the movement of the pen, for, say they, the accident passes not beyond its substratum[[fn:1039]]. They admit therefore by common consent that this white cloth which has been lowered into the indigo-vat and which has been dyed, it is not the indigo that has rendered it black; for blackness is an accident in the body of the indigo and cannot pass to another body. There is absolutely no body which exerts an action; the ultimate efficient cause is none other than God, and it is He[[fn:1040]] who has caused the blackness to arise in the body of the cloth when it was joined with the indigo, for such is the custom which He has established. In short, one can in no wise say: Such a thing is the cause of such another; that is the opinion of the great majority of the Mutakallemîn. There be some amongst them who have admitted causality, but they have been blamed for it.
root.text.Part 1..72.30: — Nevertheless, touching the actions of men, they are divided. The greater part of them, and (notably) the Asch’ariyya en masse, hold the opinion that, for the movement[[fn:1041]] of this pen, God has created four accidents which are in no wise causes one unto another, and which do but co-exist together. The first accident is my will to move the pen; the second accident is the faculty wherewith I move it; the third accident is the human movement itself, I mean, the movement of the hand; finally, the fourth accident is the movement of the pen. Indeed, they pretend that when a man wills a thing and thereafter performs it [at least, according to his belief], there has been created in him first the will, then the faculty to do that which he willed to do, and finally the action itself; for he acts not by means of the faculty created within him, which has no influence upon the action.— Nevertheless, the Mo’tazales say that he acts by means of the faculty created within him[[fn:1042]]; and a portion of the Asch’ariyya maintain that the created faculty exerts a certain influence upon the action and participats therein[[fn:1043]], an opinion which has been censured[[fn:1044]]. This created will, according to the opinion of all, and likewise the created faculty and the created action, according to the opinion of some, are all accidents without duration; and it is God who creats in this pen movements one after another, which continus so long as the pen movs. That it may rest, it is necessary that God should likewise create therein rest[[fn:1045]], and He ceass not to create rest successively therein, so long as the pen remains at rest.
root.text.Part 1..72.31: Thus it is that in each of these instants, I mean (in each) of these atoms of time, God creats an accident in every individual being[[fn:1046]], whether it be angel, or celestial sphere, etc., and this continus thus perpetually. This, say they, is what is truly called believing that God is efficient; and he who believs not that God acts thus denies, according to them, that God is efficient. But, in my judgment and in that of every intelligent man, it is concerning such beliefs that one may say: Will ye mock Him (God) as one mocks a mortal (Job, xiii. 9)? For this is verily naught but pure mockery.
root.text.Part 1..72.32: The SEVENTH PROPOSITION is that they believe the privations of capacities[[fn:1047]] to be (real) things existing in the body and added to its substance, that they are accidents likewise having a (real) existence and which, consequently, are perpetually created, so that, when one disappears, another is created. Here follows the explanation: They admit not that rest is the privation of movement, nor that death is the privation of life, nor that blindness is the privation of sight, nor (in general) that there be such privations of capacities[[fn:1048]]. On the contrary, according to them, it is with movement and rest as with heat and cold[[fn:1049]]; and even as heat and cold are two accidents existing in two subjects, that which is hot and that which is cold, so movement is an accident created in that which movs and rest an accident which God creats in that which is at rest. This latter likewise[[fn:1050]] endurs not for two times, as has been already seen in the preceding proposition; wherefore, in this body at rest, God, according to them, creats rest for each of its atoms, and one rest having vanished, He creats another, so long as this thing is at rest. It is exactly the same, according to them, with knowledge and ignorance; for ignorance, according to them, is a positive accident, and it ceass not to vanish and to be created anew so long as he who is ignorant of a certain thing remains in his ignorance[[fn:1051]]. It is furthermore exactly the same with life and death. Verily, both the one and the other, according to them, are accidents (in the same right), and they say plainly that, so long as the living being remains alive, there is always an (instantaneous) life which disappears and another which is created; but when God wills that he should die, He creats in him the accident of death, following upon the (final) disappearance of the accident of life, which endurs not for two times. All this they say expressly;
root.text.Part 1..72.33: and it follows necessarily from this hypothesis that the accident of death created by God disappears likewise at the same instant, and that God creats (forthwith) another death, for otherwise death would not endure. Even as, therefore, life is created upon life, so is death created upon death[[fn:1052]]. Nevertheless, I would fain know how long God shall create the accident of death in the dead! Is it so long as he retains his outward form, or so long as there remains one of his atoms? For the accident of death which God creats, He creats it, as they suppose, in each of these atoms. Now, we find molar teeth of the dead which have been there for thousands of years, which proves that God has not reduced this substance to naught, and that, consequently, He creats therein the accident of death during those thousands of years, so that, one death disappearing, He creats another. And such indeed is the opinion of the greater number (of the Mutakallimūn).
root.text.Part 1..72.34: Notwithstanding, a portion of the [[t:0]]Mo’tazales[[t:1]] concede that certain [[t:2]]privations of faculties[[t:3]][[fn:1053]] are not positive things; they assert, to the contrary, that impotence is (truly) the [[t:4]]privation[[t:5]] of power and ignorance the [[t:6]]privation[[t:7]] of knowledge. However, they do not thus judge[[fn:1054]] in regard to all privations, and they do not admit that darkness is the privation of light, nor that rest is the privation of movement. Far from it, they behold in these privations, in part, positive things and, in part, true privations, according to what suits their creed, as they have also done in the case of the duration of accidents, (saying) that some endure for a certain time, and that others endure not two instants; for their purpose, in general, is to suppose a Being whose nature is in conformity with our opinions and our beliefs.
root.text.Part 1..72.35: The EIGHTH PROPOSITION stats: «that there exists (everywhere) naught but substance and accident, and that physical forms are likewise accidents[[fn:1055]].» Here follows the explanation of this proposition: All bodies, according to them, are composed of similar atoms, as we have set forth in their first proposition, and they differ from one another only by accidents. Wherefore, in their view, the quality of being an animal, that of being a man, sensation, reason, and so forth, are accidents in the same manner as whiteness, blackness, bitterness, and sweetness; so that individuals of diverse species differ among themselves only as do individuals of the self-same species[[fn:1056]]. They perceive, consequently, in the body of the heavens, and even in that of the angels, and even unto that of the so-called[[fn:1057]] celestial throne, the same substance as in any insect of the earth or in any plant whatsoever; all these things differ from each other only by accidents, and all have for their substance the atoms.
root.text.Part 1..72.36: The NINTH PROPOSITION stats: «that accidents do not support one another.» One cannot therefore say, according to them, that a certain accident is supported by another[[fn:1058]], and that other by the substance; but all accidents are supported, immediately and in like manner, by the substance itself. That which they desire to avoid thereby is the necessity of admitting that a second accident could not exist in the substance save with the first which had preceded it; for they deny that such an occurrence takes place for certain accidents[[fn:1059]], and they strive to devise for these certain accidents the possibility of existing in any substance whatsoever, without the latter being determined by another accident, (and this) in accordance with their opinion, to wit, that all accidents are something which determins (the substance). Furthermore, it is necessary that the subject which bears the attribute should remain stable for a certain duration; now, since according to them an accident endurs not for two times, that is to say, two instants, how could it be, upon this supposition[[fn:1060]], that it should serve as a substratum for another thing?
root.text.Part 1..72.37: The TENTH PROPOSITION concerns that admissibility[[fn:1061]] of which they speak, and which is the foundation of the science of Kalam. Hearken unto its significance: They are of the opinion that whatsoever is imaginable is likewise admissible to the reason, (and they say) for example, that the terrestrial globe might become a sphere revolving in a circle[[fn:1062]] and the sphere be transformed into a terrestrial globe, and that it is admissible to the reason that such might happen; that the sphere of fire might move towards the centre and the terrestrial globe towards the circumference[[fn:1063]], and that, according to this principle of rational admissibility, one of the two places suits each of these bodies as much as the other[[fn:1064]]. Likewise, they say, every thing amongst these beings which we behold might be greater or smaller than it is[[fn:1065]], or might be found, in respect of its figure and place, in a state contrary to its own. Thus, for example, there might be a human individual of the dimension of a great mountain, having several heads and swimming[[fn:1066]] in the air; or there might exist an elephant of the dimension of a gnat and a gnat of the dimension of an elephant; all this, they say, is admissible to the reason. This principle of admissibility is applied consistently to the whole universe, and, for all that they thus suppose, they say: «One may admit that it be so, and it is possible that it be so, and it must not be that such a thing be rather in one manner than in another», without considering whether reality corresponds to their supposition[[fn:1067]]; for, they say, if this being has known forms, determinate dimensions, and fixed conditions, which undergo neither alteration nor change, this is but a mere habit[[fn:1068]]. Thus, for example, it is the habit of the sovereign not to traverse the streets of the city save upon a mount, and he is never seen otherwise, although it be not inadmissible to the reason that he might traverse the city on foot; on the contrary, no one doubts that this be possible, and it is admitted that it may happen. In like manner, they say, it is the course of habit that the terrestrial element should move towards the centre and fire upwards, or that fire should burn and water cool; but it is not inadmissible to the reason that this habit might change, so that fire might cool and move downwards, while yet being fire, and that likewise water might produce heat and move upwards, while yet being water. Such is the basis of all their reasoning[[fn:1069]].
root.text.Part 1..72.38: Nevertheless, they agree by common consent that the conjunction of contraries in the same subject and at the same instant is an absurd and impossible thing which reason cannot admit. Likewise, they say that the existence of a substance without any accident, or that of an accident without a substratum [admitted by some[[fn:1070]]], is an impossible thing which reason cannot admit. Finally, they say likewise that substance cannot be transformed into accident, nor accident into substance, nor one body penetrate into another body; and they even assert that these are things rationally impossible.
root.text.Part 1..72.39: Verily, (in saying) that all these things enumerated as impossible cannot be conceived in the mind, and that what they have called possible can be conceived, there is some truth therein. Yet the philosophers say (unto them): If ye call such a thing impossible because it cannot be imagined, and another thing ye call possible because it can be imagined, then that which seems possible to you is so only in the imagination, but not for the reason; consequently, in this proposition, ye consider the necessary, the admissible, and the absurd, sometimes from the point of view of the imagination and not of the reason, and sometimes from that of mere common sense, as Abu-Nasr (Al-Farabi) has said, in speaking of that which the Mutakallimun call reason.
root.text.Part 1..72.40: It is therefore manifest that, unto them, whatsoever may be imagined is possible [whether reality conforms thereto or not], and that whatsoever cannot be imagined is impossible. But this proposition cannot be sustained save by means of the nine preceding propositions, and it was doubtless for the sake of this one that they were constrained to establish those others first. This shall result more clearly from that which I am about to set forth unto thee, by revealing what lies at the foundation of these matters, in the form of a discussion which took place between a Mutakallim and a philosopher:
root.text.Part 1..72.41: Wherefore, inquired the Mutakallim of the philosopher, do we find the body of this iron to be exceedingly solid and hard and of a black colour, and the body of this butter to be exceedingly tender and soft and of a white colour?
root.text.Part 1..72.42: It is, the philosopher replied unto him, because every natural body has two species of accidents: some betide it by reason of its matter, as, for example, health and sickness in man; others betide it by reason of its form, as, for example, astonishment and laughter in man[[fn:1071]]. Now, the matters of bodies of a perfected composition[[fn:1072]] vary greatly according to the forms peculiar to those matters, so that the substance of iron becoms the opposite of the substance of butter, and both are accompanied by the different accidents which thou seest therein; the hardness of the one and the softness of the other are therefore accidents which hold to the diversity of their respective forms[[fn:1073]], whilst blackness and whiteness are accidents which hold to the diversity of their ultimate matter[[fn:1074]].
root.text.Part 1..72.43: But the Mutakallim overthrew the whole of this reply by means of his aforementioned propositions, even as I shall expound unto thee: There exists no form, said he, which, as ye believe, constituts the substance in such wise as to make of it varied substances, but there are everywhere naught but accidents [according to their opinion, which we have set forth in the VIIIth proposition[[fn:1075]]]. There is no difference, he continued, between the substance of iron and that of butter; for all is composed of atoms similar to one another. And this is their opinion which we have set forth in the Ist proposition, from which, as we have explained, the IInd and IIIrd propositions necessarily flow; and likewise one has need of the XIIth proposition to establish the existence of atoms. Neither can it be admitted, according to the Mutakallim, that a certain substance possesses certain accidents which are peculiar to it and by which it is disposed and prepared to receive secondary accidents; for, according to him, an accident cannot bear another accident, as we have set forth in the IXth proposition. Neither has the accident any duration, as we have set forth in the VIth proposition. — The Mutakallim having thus arrived, by means of his propositions, at the affirmation of all that he desired[[fn:1076]], and having obtained this result: “that the substances of butter and of iron are similar and identical, that there is one and the selfsame relation between every substance and every accident[[fn:1077]], that one substance is no more apt than another to (receive) a certain accident, and that, even as one atom is no more susceptible of motion than of rest, so the atoms are no more apt than one another to receive the accident of life or that of intelligence or that of sensibility [it matters not whether the number of atoms (united) be greater or less[[fn:1078]], for, according to the opinion set forth in the Vth proposition, the accident exists in each of the atoms]”, it follows from all these propositions that man is no more apt to think than the beetle[[fn:1079]]; and they were forced to arrive at this admissibility of which they treat in the present proposition. It was toward this proposition that all their efforts tended; for it lends itself marvelously to all the hypotheses which one wishes to establish[[fn:1080]], as shall presently be set forth.
root.text.Part 1..72.44: ANNOTATION. Know, O reader of this treatise! that if thou art of those who know the soul and its faculties, and if thou dost penetrate into each thing in all the reality of its being, thou shalt know that imagination belongs to most animals; that, at least as regards the perfect animals, I mean those which have a heart, it is evident that they all possess imagination[[fn:1081]], and that it is not by this that man is distinguished (from other animals). The action of the imagination is not the same as that of the intellect, but is opposed to it. Indeed, the intellect analyss composite things, distinguishes their parts, abstracts them, represents them in their reality and with their causes, and thus perceivs in a single object numerous things, as distinct for the intellect as two human individuals are distinct beings for the imagination[[fn:1082]]. It is by the intellect that one distinguishes that which is general from that which is individual, and no demonstration can take place save by means of that which is general[[fn:1083]]; finally, it is by the intellect that one knows (how to distinguish) the essential attribute from the accidental. But the imagination can accomplish none of these actions; for it perceivs only the individual and the composite in its entirety, even as the senses perceive it, or else it composs things which in reality are separate and which it combins one with another, and this aggregate[[fn:1084]] becoms a body or one of the faculties of the body. Thus, for example, one may conceive in the imagination a human individual having the head of a horse and wings, and other similar (creations); and this is what is called a falsified invention, for there is absolutely no being that conforms thereto. The imagination cannot, in its perception[[fn:1085]], rid itself in any wise of matter, even though it should make every effort to abstract a form; wherefore no heed must be paid unto the imagination.
root.text.Part 1..72.45: —Hearken, however the mathematical sciences are instructive for us (in this regard), and how weighty are the propositions which we derive therefrom.
root.text.Part 1..72.46: Know that there are certain things which man, when he considers them by his imagination, can in no wise conceive, and which on the contrary he finds as impossible for the imagination as would be the conjunction of opposites; and yet, such a thing as it is impossible to imagine, one may establish by demonstration that it exists and bring to light the reality thereof[[fn:1086]]. If, for example, thou shouldst imagine a great globe of such dimension as thou wilt, even shouldst thou imagine it as great as the globe of the encompassing sphere, and that then thou shouldst imagine therein an axis which traverss the centre, and finally thou shouldst figure to thyself two men standing upon the two extremities of the axis, in such manner that their feet be placed in the direction of the axis and that the latter form, as it were, with the feet one single straight line, it must necessarily be that this axis be parallel to the horizon or be not so[[fn:1087]]; now, if it be parallel (to the horizon), the two men shall fall, and, if it be not parallel, one of them, he who is below, shall fall, and the other shall remain standing[[fn:1088]]. Such at least is that which the imagination figurs to itself. Now, it is demonstrated that the earth is of a spherical figure, and that at the two extremities of its axis there are inhabited lands[[fn:1089]]. Each of the inhabitants of the two extremities has his head toward heaven and his feet toward those of his antipode[[fn:1090]]; and yet it is neither possible nor imaginable that either of the two should fall, for they are not one above and the other below, but each of the two is above or below in relation to the other.—Likewise (to cite another example), it has been demonstrated, in the IInd book of the Conic Sections, that there are two lines proceeding (from certain points) and between which there is, at their point of departure, a certain distance which diminishes as they are prolonged; so that they ever approach one another without ever being able to meet, even should they be extended to infinity, although nevertheless they draw ever nearer as they are prolonged[[fn:1091]]. Behold a thing which one could not figure to oneself and which the imagination could in no wise conceive[[fn:1092]]. These two lines are, the one straight, the other curved, even as it is set forth in the place cited. It is therefore demonstrated that there exist things which one cannot imagine, and which (not only) could not be comprehended by the imagination, but even appear unto it impossible. Likewise, it is demonstrated (on the other hand) that certain things which the imagination would affirm are (in reality) impossible, as, for example, that God be a body or a faculty in a body; for, unto the imagination, naught has existence, save it be a body or something within a body.
root.text.Part 1..72.47: It is therefore manifest that there exists another faculty whereby one judges the necessary, the possible, and the impossible, and that this is not the imagination. And how excellent and of what great profit is this study for him who desirs to avoid the calamity of suffering himself to be guided by the imagination[[fn:1093]]!
root.text.Part 1..72.48: It must not be believed that the Mutakallimūn perceive nothing of all this; on the contrary, they have indeed some sentiment thereof and know it so well that they call presumption and chimera[[fn:1094]] that which, albeit impossible, is admitted by the imagination, as, for example, that God be a body, and oftentimes they say clearly that these presumptions are mendacious. This is why they have had recourse to the nine propositions which we have reported, in order to be able to affirm this tenth proposition, which enunciats the admissibility of all imaginable things which they wished to declare admissible, and that by favour (of the hypotheses) of the parity of atoms and of the equal nature of all accidents[[fn:1095]], even as we have set it forth.
root.text.Part 1..72.49: Reflecting well thereon, one shall see that this may give rise to a difficult discussion[[fn:1096]]. For indeed, there are certain ideas which one may set forth as conceptions of the intellect, whilst another will maintain that they belong to the domain of the imagination; and, in this case, we should desire to find a criterion for distinguishing intelligible things from the conceptions of the imagination. Now, if the philosopher should say: “I have for witness Being[[fn:1097]] [as he expresses himself] and it is thereby that we examine the necessary, the possible, and the impossible”, the theologian would answer him: “But this is precisely the point in dispute; for I maintain[[fn:1098]] that this Being has been made by the (divine) Will, and that it is not the result of necessity; and, although it be made in such a manner, it is admissible that it might have been made differently, unless the conception of the intellect decide that it could not be otherwise than it is, even as thou dost pretend.”
root.text.Part 1..72.50: Such is this principle of admissibility, concerning which I reserve to myself to return in other passages of this treatise; nor is it a matter that one ought to be in haste to reject altogether and lightly[[fn:1099]].
root.text.Part 1..72.51: The ELEVENTH PROPOSITION says: “that the existence of the infinite (in the universe) is inadmissible, in whatsoever manner it may be.” Here is the explanation thereof: It has been demonstrated that it is impossible that there should exist an infinite magnitude, or that there should exist magnitudes whose number is infinite [even though each of them were a finite magnitude], provided always that these infinite things exist simultaneously[[fn:1100]]. Likewise, it is inadmissible that there should exist causes in infinitum; I mean, that a thing serving as a cause to another should in its turn have another cause, and this latter yet another cause, and so forth in infinitum, so that there would be there things infinite in number existing in act[[fn:1101]]. And it matters not whether they be bodies or separated substances[[fn:1102]], provided they serve as causes one to another. This is the essential physical order[[fn:1103]], regarding which it has been demonstrated that the infinite is therein impossible[[fn:1104]].
root.text.Part 1..72.52: As for the infinite existing [[t:0]]in potentiality[[t:1]] or [[t:2]]accidentally[[t:3]], we have in part demonstrated its existence; thus, for example, we have demonstrated that a magnitude is [[t:4]]virtually[[t:5]] divisible to infinity, and that time is so as well[[fn:1105]]. But in part, this gives rise to speculation[[fn:1106]], as, for instance, the existence of the [[t:6]]infinite by succession[[t:7]], which is also called the [[t:8]]infinite by accident[[t:9]], that is to say, when one thing exists after another has ceased to exist, and this other after a third has ceased to exist, and so on (ascending) to infinity. This is a very difficult subject for speculation.
root.text.Part 1..72.53: Those who claim to have demonstrated the eternity of the world maintain that time is infinite, and for them naught inadmissible follows therefrom, for, as one part of time is produced, another which preceded it has vanished; and it is the same, according to them, with the succession of accidents that happen to matter in infinitum, without anything inadmissible following therefrom, since they do not all exist simultaneously, but successively, the impossibility of which has in no wise been demonstrated[[fn:1107]]. But, according to the Mutakallimūn, it is indifferent whether one says that an infinite magnitude exists, or whether one says that body and time are divisible in infinitum[[fn:1108]]. It is likewise indifferent, according to them, (to suppose) the simultaneous existence of a series of things infinite in number[[fn:1109]], speaking, for example, of the human individuals existing at this moment, or to say that there happen in the universe things infinite in number, although vanishing successively, as one might say, for instance: Zeid and the son of ’Amr, this one the son of Khaled, this one the son of Becr, and so forth (ascending) in infinitum; for this is, according to them, as inadmissible as the first case[[fn:1110]]. These four classes of the infinite are therefore equal, according to them[[fn:1111]]. As for the last class[[fn:1112]], there be some among them who think it their duty to prove the truth thereof, I mean (that they think they must) demonstrate its impossibility, by a method which I shall set forth to thee in this treatise[[fn:1113]]. Others say that this is self-evident[[fn:1114]], and that it is something known from the first, requiring no demonstration. Now, if it were manifestly inadmissible that there should be things infinite by succession, even though that which now exists thereof be finite, the eternity of the world would appear inadmissible at the first, without the need of any other proposition[[fn:1115]]. But this is not the place to examine this subject.
root.text.Part 1..72.54: The TWELFTH PROPOSITION says: “that the senses do not always yield certainty.” In fact, the Mutakallimūn suspected[[fn:1116]] the perception of the senses in two respects. Firstly, they say, many sensible objects escape them, either by reason of the subtilty of the perceptible body [as they say concerning (the hypothesis of) atoms and that which follows therefrom[[fn:1117]], as we have explained], or because they are too far removed from him who would perceive them; thus man can neither see, nor hear, nor smell, at the distance of several leagues, and likewise the motion of the heavens is in no wise perceptible. Secondly, they say, the senses are deceived in their perceptions. Thus, for example, a thing which is large, man ses as small when it is remote from him; a small thing, he ses as large when it is in the water; finally, he ses as a broken line that which is straight[[fn:1118]], when one part is in the water and the other without. Likewise, he who is afflicted with jaundice ses things yellow, and he whose tongue is imbued with yellow bile[[fn:1119]] finds sweet things to have a bitter taste. They enumerate yet many things of this kind; wherefore, they say, one cannot trust the senses so as to take them for a principle of demonstration.
root.text.Part 1..72.55: It must not be supposed that it was in vain that the Mutakallemim insisted upon this proposition[[fn:1120]], even as the majority of these modern (Mutakallemim) believe that it was without necessity that their predecessors strove to maintain (the hypothesis of) the atom. On the contrary, all that we have hitherto reported on their part is necessary; and, when one assails even a single one of these propositions, the entire object is frustrated. As for this last proposition, it is right necessary; for, when the perception of our senses is in contradiction with what they have established[[fn:1121]], they say that one must pay no heed to the senses so soon as a thing is demonstrated by means of what they call the testimony of reason[[fn:1122]]. It is thus they pretend concerning motion, which nevertheless is continuous, that there enter therein intervals of rest, and that the millstone is sundered whilst turning[[fn:1123]]; and they further pretend that the (previous) whiteness of this cloth has now vanished, and that this is another whiteness[[fn:1124]]. These are things in opposition to what is seen; and (likewise) there results from the existence of the void many things which are all belied by the senses. To all this they answer: “It is a thing which escaps the senses”, whenever, indeed, it is possible so to answer; for other matters[[fn:1125]], they reply that it is one of the many errors of the senses.
root.text.Part 1..72.56: Thou knowest that these are all ancient opinions professed by the Sophists[[fn:1126]], even as Galen reports in his book On Natural Faculties (speaking) of those who say that the senses are deceptive; he has related therein (on this subject) all that thou knowest[[fn:1127]].
root.text.Part 1..72.57: Having first spoken of these propositions (of the Mutakallemim), I shall set forth their methods concerning the four questions at issue[[fn:1128]].
root.text.Part 1..73.0: In this chapter I shall relate unto thee in summary the proofs of the Mutakallemim (establishing) that the world is created. Thou shalt not ask of me to give the exposition thereof in their own terms and with their prolixity; but I shall make known unto thee what each of them had in view[[fn:1129]] and his method of argumentation for affirming the creation of the world or for denying its eternity, and I shall briefly point out to thee the propositions employed for each method[[fn:1130]]. If thou readest their prolix books and their most celebrated works, thou shalt find therein absolutely nothing more than what my words shall make thee understand of their argumentation on this subject; but thou shalt find therein a more abundant language and fair and brilliant expressions. Sometimes they have employed rhyme and symmetrical periods, and have made choice of the most elegant expressions[[fn:1131]]; and sometimes also they have employed an obscure style, with the intent to astound the hearer and to affright him who approaches the contemplation thereof. Thou shalt also find, in their works, repetitions, doubtful questions which they propose and which they pretend to have resolved, and frequent sallies against their adversaries.
root.text.Part 1..73.1: FIRST METHOD[[fn:1132]]: There are some among them who maintain that by admitting a single produced thing[[fn:1133]], one may demonstrate that the world is created. Thus, for example, it is inadmissible that this individual Zeid, who at first was a molecule[[fn:1134]] and who thereafter was transformed successively until he attained his perfection, should have thus changed himself, and that it should be he who produced in himself these diverse metamorphoses. On the contrary, there was outside of him something which changed him; and, consequently, it is demonstrated that he had need of an artificer who should organize his structure and cause him to undergo diverse transformations. It is the same, by analogy, with this palm-tree and with every other thing; and it is the same also, it has been said[[fn:1135]], with the whole of the universe. Thou seest, consequently, that this one[[fn:1136]] believs that, from what is found to take place in one body, conclusions must be drawn for every other body[[fn:1137]].
root.text.Part 1..73.2: SECOND MSOD: They further assert that by admitting the creation of even a single individual among those propagated by generation, it may be demonstrated that the whole universe is created. Here is the explanation thereof: This Zeid, who at first existed not, subsequently came into existence; yet, he could only have been born through ’Amr, his father, and the latter, being likewise born, could only have been born through Khaled, the grandfather. Now, the latter being also born[[fn:1138]], this would proceed thus unto infinity; but they have laid down as a principle that the existence of an infinite, even in this manner[[fn:1139]], is inadmissible, as we have set forth in the XIth of their propositions. Likewise, if thou shouldst arrive, for example, at a first individual without a father, who were Adam, there would yet follow the question: “whence was this Adam born?” If thou shouldst answer, for example: “from the dust,” it would necessarily be asked: “but whence was this dust produced?” If, for example, one should answer: “from water,” it would again be asked: “but whence was this water produced?” It is therefore absolutely necessary, they say, that this should continue thus unto infinity, which is inadmissible; or else thou shalt arrive at the existence of a thing brought forth out of absolute non-existence. Therein lies the truth[[fn:1140]] and there the questions shall cease. This, therefore, is a proof, they say, that the world was brought forth out of absolute non-existence[[fn:1141]].
root.text.Part 1..73.3: THIRD MSOD: The atoms of the universe, say they, must perforce be either joined or separated[[fn:1142]], and there be some which at one time unite and at another separate. Now, it is manifest and evident that, in respect of their essence, neither union alone nor separation alone appertains unto them; for, if their essence and nature required that they should be only separated, they would never unite, and likewise, if their essence and their true character required that they should be only joined, they would never separate. Thus, then, separation suits them no more than union, nor union more than separation; and consequently, if they be in part joined and in part separated, and if in part they further change their condition, being at one time united and at another separated, this is a proof that these atoms stand in need of one who shall unite that which is to be united and separate that which is to be separated. Consequently, they say, this is a proof that the world is created.—It is clear that the author of this method has availed himself of the Ist of their propositions and of all that follows therefrom.
root.text.Part 1..73.4: F[[t:0]]OURTH METHOD[[t:1]]: The entire universe, they affirm, is composed of substance and accident, and no substance is exempt from one or several accidents[[fn:1143]]; now, as all accidents [[t:2]]originate[[t:3]], it follows that the substance which supports them must likewise have [[t:4]]originated[[t:5]], for everything that attaches itself to things [[t:6]]originated[[t:7]] and is inseparable from them is likewise [[t:8]]originated[[t:9]][[fn:1144]]. Consequently, the entire world is [[t:10]]originated[[t:11]] (or [[t:12]]created[[t:13]]). Should anyone contend: “perchance the substance has not [[t:14]]originated[[t:15]], and perchance it is only the accidents which [[t:16]]originate[[t:17]] by succeeding one another thereupon unto infinity,” they would reply that in such case there must needs be an infinite number of things [[t:18]]originated[[t:19]] (successively), which they have posited as inadmissible[[fn:1145]].— This method is regarded by them as the most ingenious and the best, such that many have perceived in it a (veritable) demonstration.
root.text.Part 1..73.5: Three hypotheses have been admitted for this method, the necessity of which shall escape no thinker[[fn:1146]]: 1st, That an infinite by succession is inadmissible; 2nd, That every accident is produced[[fn:1147]]. But our adversary, who maintains the eternity of the world, contradicts us concerning one of the accidents, which is circular motion. Verily, Aristotle maintains that circular motion is neither produced nor perishes; wherefore, according to him, the mobile which has this motion is neither produced nor perishes[[fn:1148]]. We gain nothing, therefore, by establishing the production of other accidents; for our adversary does not contest that these latter are produced, and he maintains that they succeed one another in that which is not produced[[fn:1149]]. Likewise he maintains that this single accident, to wit, circular motion [I mean, the motion of the celestial sphere], is not produced and that it belongs to none of the species of produced accidents[[fn:1150]]. It is therefore this accident alone which it would be necessary to examine, in order to demonstrate that it is (likewise) produced. Finally, the 3rd hypothesis which the author of this method has admitted is this: that there is no sensible being other than substance and accident; I mean, the simple substance (or the atom) with the accidents attributed thereto[[fn:1151]]. Nevertheless, if the body were composed of matter and form, as our adversary has demonstrated, it would be necessary to demonstrate that prime matter and prime form are produced and perish, and only then could one establish a demonstration for the newness of the world[[fn:1152]].
root.text.Part 1..73.6: A FIFTH METHOD is that of determination[[fn:1153]]. They have a very great predilection for this method, the sense of which returns to that which I have set forth unto thee concerning their Xth proposition. Fixing the mind[[fn:1154]] upon the whole of the world or upon any one of its parts whatsoever, one says: It is admissible that this thing should be such as it is, in respect of figure and measure, with the accidents found therein and in the time and place where it is found; but it is admissible also that it might have been either larger or smaller, or of a different figure, or (accompanied) by such accidents, or exist before or after the time of its existence, or in some other place. Now, as it is determined by a certain figure, or by a measure, or by a place, or by a certain accident and by a particular time, although it be admissible that all this might have been otherwise, this is a proof that there is (a Being) who determins freely (all things) and who has preferred one of these two admissible cases[[fn:1155]]. Consequently, the whole of the world or one of its parts standing in need of a Being who determins, this proves that the world is created; for it matters little whether thou sayest determining, or efficient, or creator, or producer, or innovator, or acting with intention, all these have but one and the same meaning.
root.text.Part 1..73.7: Entering upon this method with many general and special details, they say, for example: “It is no more meet for the earth to be beneath the water than to be above it[[fn:1156]]; who then was it that assigned to it this place? It is no more meet for the sun to be round than to be square or triangular, for all figures are equally suited to bodies endowed with figure; who then has particularized the sun with this figure?” And in this manner they contemplate the details of the whole universe; so that when they behold flowers of diverse colours, they are astonished thereat and find therein wherewith to fortify their argument[[fn:1157]]. For, say they, this earth being one and this water one, wherefore then is this flower yellow and that other red? Can this come to pass otherwise than through a determining being? and this determining being is God; wherefore, the whole world has need of a being who determins the whole, as well as each of its parts, by some [[fn:1158]]particularity.
root.text.Part 1..73.8: All this results (solely) from the acceptance of the Xth proposition; and it must be added thereto that, among those very ones who maintain the eternity of the world, there are some who do not contest determination with us, as we shall set forth[[fn:1159]]. But, in short, this method seems unto me the best, and I have thereupon an opinion which thou shalt hear (further on)[[fn:1160]].
root.text.Part 1..73.9.sub_0: SIXTH METHOD: One of the moderns has pretended to have lighted upon a very good method, better than all those which precede, and which is (drawn from) the preference[[fn:1161]] accorded to being over non-being. Every man, says he, grants that the existence of the world is but possible, for if it had a necessary existence, it would be God; now we speak here only to him who, whilst professing the eternity of the world, nevertheless affirms the existence of God. That which is possible is that which may exist or may not exist, and being is no more meet for it than non-being. Now, since that whose existence is but possible does (actually) exist, although there be for it an equal reason for being and for not being, this is a proof that there is something which has preferred its existence to its non-existence[[fn:1162]]. This is a method (which may seem) very satisfactory, yet it is but a branch of that of determination, which preceded it, save that this author has changed the word determine into prefer, and that for the conditions of being he has substituted the very existence of being[[fn:1163]]. But, either he has sought to deceive us, or he has himself been deceived as to the sense of this thesis which says: that the world is of a possible existence; for our adversary, who admitts the eternity of the world, when he says: “the world is of a possible existence,” employs the word possible in a sense other than that given to it by the Mutakallim, as we shall set forth[[fn:1164]]. Furthermore, when it is said that the world has need of something which preferrs its existence to its non-existence, there is therein something very erroneous; for preference and determination can only be applied to some being capable of receiving equally one of two opposite or different qualities[[fn:1165]], so that one might say: since we find it in such a condition and not in another, this proves that there is therein an artificer acting with intention.
root.text.Part 1..73.9.sub_1: Thus, for example, one would say: This copper is no more apt to receive the form of an ewer than to receive that of a candlestick; if, therefore, we find it a candlestick or an ewer, we know thereby of necessity that a determining (artificer) acting with intention has had in view one of these two admissible forms. Now, it is evident that the copper existed, and that before the action of him who gave preference to one of the two admissible forms attributed to it, there was naught non-existent there save these very forms[[fn:1166]]. But, as for that being concerning which there is no agreement whether its existence has always been and shall always be such as it is, or whether it began to exist after (absolute) non-being, it can in no wise give rise to this thought[[fn:1167]]; and one could not ask: “Who is he that has preferred its existence to its non-existence?” save after having recognized[[fn:1168]] that it came into existence after not having existed, which is precisely the matter whereon there is no agreement. For if we took its existence and its non-existence for something ideal[[fn:1169]], we should simply return to the Xth proposition, which says that regard must be had only to imaginations and ideas, and not to real and intelligible things[[fn:1170]]; for the adversary, who admitts the eternity of the world, thinks that the imaginary supposition of the non-existence of the world is like unto the supposition of any other impossible thing that might come to our imagination. — But it is not the purpose here to refute their opinions[[fn:1171]]; I have desired only to set forth unto thee that it is not true, as has been pretended, that this method[[fn:1172]] is different from the preceding one, and that on the contrary it is with this as with the former, in that it supposs[[fn:1173]] that admissibility which is known[[fn:1174]].
root.text.Part 1..73.10: <small>SEVENTH METHOD</small>: Another among the moderns has maintained that the creation of the world can be established by means of the permanence of souls admitted by the philosophers. If the world, says he, were eternal, the men who have died in the boundless past would be infinite in number; there would therefore be souls infinite in number and existing simultaneously. Now, it has been indubitably demonstrated that this is false; I speak of the simultaneous existence of things infinite in number[[fn:1175]].—This is a most singular method, which demonstrats an obscure thing by means of that which is yet more obscure; and it is to this that one may rightly apply that proverb current among the Syrians[[fn:1176]]: “Thy surety himself stands in need of a surety.” It would seem that for such a one the permanence of souls is a demonstrated thing and that he knows in what manner they survive (the bodies) and what is the thing that survivs[[fn:1177]], so that he may draw arguments therefrom. If, however, he has had no other aim than to raise an objection against the adversary[[fn:1178]] who admitts the eternity of the world whilst admitting the permanence of souls, his objection would be founded only on the condition that the adversary also confessed the idea attributed to him concerning the permanence of souls[[fn:1179]].
root.text.Part 1..73.11: Certain modern philosophers have resolved this difficulty, saying: The souls which survive are in no wise bodies, so that they should possess a place and a situation, or that infinity should be incompatible with their manner of existence[[fn:1180]]. But thou[[fn:1181]], thou knowest that those separated things[[fn:1182]], I mean those which are neither bodies nor a faculty within a body, but pure intelligences, do in no wise admit of multiplicity, save (in this sense) that some among them are the cause of the existence of others, so that they are distinguished one from another only in that the one is cause and the other effect[[fn:1183]]. Now, that which survivs of Zeid is neither the cause nor the effect of that which survivs of ‘Amr; wherefore the whole is one in number[[fn:1184]], as has been shewn by Abu-Bekr ibn al-Çâyig, both he and others who have applied themselves[[fn:1185]] to speak of these profound matters. In fine, it is not from things so obscure, which the minds of men are incapable of conceiving, that one must take premises to demonstrate other things.
root.text.Part 1..73.12: It must be known that all those who strive to establish the creation of the world, or to contest its eternity, by means of these methods of the Kalâm, must of necessity employ therein either one of these two propositions or both at once; to wit, the Xth proposition [that is to say, rational admissibility], in order to establish that there is a determining Being, or else the XIth proposition, which proclaims the inadmissibility of an infinite by succession. This latter proposition they seek to verify in diverse manners. First, the disputant attaches himself to any species whatsoever (of creatures) whose individuals are born and perish, and, ascending in his mind to the time past, he obtains this result: that, according to the opinion which admitts the eternity (of the world), the individuals of the said species (which have existed) from a certain epoch and anteriorly in the eternal past are infinite (in number), and that (on the other hand) the individuals of this same species (which have existed) from a later epoch, for example, a thousand years after that which was first adopted, and ascending into the eternal past, are likewise infinite[[fn:1186]]; now, this latter totality exceeding the former totality by the whole number of those who were born during those thousand years, they pretend, by this consideration, to arrive at this result: that there would be therein one infinite greater than another infinite[[fn:1187]]. They do the like with the revolutions of the celestial sphere[[fn:1188]], and they pretend to obtain this result: that there would be infinite revolutions more numerous than other infinite revolutions. Sometimes also they compare the revolutions of one sphere with those of another which are slower and which are all infinite[[fn:1189]]. They do the same for every kind of accidents that supervene[[fn:1190]]. They count, therefore, (everywhere) the individualities which exist no more, and represent them to themselves as though they existed and as though they were delimited things[[fn:1191]]; thereafter they add to this ideal thing or subtract from it[[fn:1192]]. But these are things purely ideal and not real. Already Abu-Naçr al-Farâbi has destroyed[[fn:1193]] this (eleventh) proposition, shewing the error it presented in all its particular applications; even as, with an impartial examination, thou shalt find it clearly set forth[[fn:1194]] in his celebrated work On Variable Beings[[fn:1195]].
root.text.Part 1..73.13: These are the principal methods of the Mutakallimūn for establishing the creation of the world. As soon as they have established by these proofs that the world is created, it necessarily follows that it has an Artificer who created it with intention, with will, and of His own free choice[[fn:1196]]. Thereafter they have demonstrated, by (various) methods which we shall set forth unto thee in the following chapter, that He (the Creator) is one.
root.text.Part 1..74.0: I shall also set forth unto thee, in this chapter, the proofs of the Unity (of God) according to the system of the Mutakallimūn. This Being, say they, whom the universe indicats as being its Artificer and Producer, is one; and their principal methods for establishing the Unity are two in number: the method of mutual hindrance and that of reciprocal diversity[[fn:1197]].
root.text.Part 1..74.1: The FIRST METHOD, to wit, that of mutual hindrance, is that which is preferred by the great majority. This is the sense thereof: If, it is said, the universe had two gods, it would be necessary that the atom—which (in principle) cannot be exempt from one of two opposite (accidents)[[fn:1198]]—should be devoid of both at once, which is inadmissible, or else that the two opposites should be joined together at the same time and in the same substratum, which is likewise inadmissible. If, for example, the atom or the atoms which the one (of the two gods) wished now to make hot, the other wished to make cold, it would follow either that they would be neither hot nor cold, because the two actions would mutually hinder each other—[which is inadmissible, every body receiving one of the two opposite accidents]—or else that the body in question would be at once hot and cold (which is impossible). Likewise, if one of the two wished to set in motion a certain body, it might be that the other wished to place it at rest; and it would follow that it would be neither in motion nor at rest, or that it would be at once in motion and at rest. This species of argumentation is based upon the question of the atom, which is (the object of) their Ist proposition, upon the hypothesis of the (perpetual) creation of accidents[[fn:1199]] and upon the proposition which says that the privations of capacities are positive things which require an efficient cause[[fn:1200]]. Verily, if any one should say that the inferior matter, in which, according to the opinion of the philosophers, generation and corruption succeed each other, is other than the superior matter [that is to say, that which serves as a substratum[[fn:1201]] to the celestial spheres], as has been demonstrated[[fn:1202]], and if it were maintained that there are two gods, the one governing the inferior matter and whose action extends not to the spheres, the other governing the spheres and whose action extends not to the elementary matter[[fn:1203]], as the Dualists[[fn:1204]] did pretend, such an opinion would in no wise lead to mutual hindrance[[fn:1205]]. And if it were objected that this would be to attribute an imperfection to each of the two, because the one would not dispose of that which the other disposs of, one might reply that this constituts no imperfection in respect of either of them; for that thing to which his action extends not is in respect of him impossible, and to be unable to do the impossible constituts no imperfection in the artificer[[fn:1206]], even as, for us unitarians, there is no imperfection in the one God in that He cannot join contraries in the same subject, and that His power extends neither to that, nor to other like impossibilities.
root.text.Part 1..74.2: Having perceived the weakness of this method, although there was something that drew them to it[[fn:1207]], they have passed to another method.
root.text.Part 1..74.3: SECOND METHOD: If there were two gods, say they, it would behoove them to possess something in common and something else which should belong to the one and not the other, whereby their reciprocal diversity[[fn:1208]] might be established. This is a philosophical and (verily) demonstrative method, provided it be pursued[[fn:1209]] and its premises be set forth. I myself shall set it forth when I relate the opinions of the philosophers upon this matter. Yet this method cannot be followed according to the system of those who admit the attributes[[fn:1210]]; for, according to them, there be in the eternal Being[[fn:1211]] many things distinct from one another[[fn:1212]], the idea of knowledge being for them distinct from the idea of power, and likewise the idea of power distinct from the idea of will[[fn:1213]]. It would not, therefore, be impossible, under this system, that each of the two gods should contain several ideas, so that some he might have in common with the other (god), and by others he might differ therefrom.
root.text.Part 1..74.4: THIRD METHOD: There is yet another method which requirs one of the hypotheses admitted by the partisans of this system[[fn:1214]]. It is that several among them (the Motécallemîn) — and these are the most ancient — believe that God wills by a will, which is not an idea superadded to the essence of the Creator, but is a will without a substratum. According to this hypothesis[[fn:1215]] which we have just stated, but of which it is difficult, as thou seest, to form a conception[[fn:1216]], they say: The single will which is not in a substratum could not belong to two; for, they add, a single cause cannot produce two results for two (different) essences[[fn:1217]]. This is, as I have already remarked to thee, to explain an obscure thing by that which is yet more obscure[[fn:1218]]. Of this will of which they speak, one cannot form a conception; there be some among them who deem it impossible, and even they who admit it recognize therein innumerable difficulties[[fn:1219]]. And yet they take it for a proof of the unity (of God).
root.text.Part 1..74.5: FOURTH METHOD: The existence of an action, say they, proves of necessity that there is an agent, but proves not unto us that there be several agents, no matter whether it be claimed that God is two, or three, or twenty, or any number whatsoever[[fn:1220]]; which thing is clear and manifest. Now, if it were objected that this proof does not demonstrate that plurality in God is impossible, but only that it demonstrats that the number thereof is unknown, and that consequently it may equally be that there is one God or that there be several[[fn:1221]], such an one[[fn:1222]] would complete his demonstration by saying: “In the existence of God there is no possibility, but He is a necessary Being, and consequently the possibility of plurality (in God) is inadmissible.” — Such is the manner in which the author of this demonstration reasons; but the error therein is altogether evident. In sooth, it is in the very existence of God that there is no possibility; but, in the knowledge which we have of Him, there is indeed possibility; for to be possible unto science is a different thing from being possible in reality[[fn:1223]]. It might therefore be that God were neither three, as the Christians believe, nor one, as we ourselves believe[[fn:1224]]. — This is clear unto him who has learned to know in what manner conclusions result from premises[[fn:1225]].
root.text.Part 1..74.6: FIFTH METHOD: One of the moderns has claimed to have found a demonstrative method to (establish) unity; it is that which is called the method of need, of which this is the explanation: Either, says he, it was an easy thing for a single (god) to produce all that exists, and then a second would be superfluous and there would be no need of him; or else this universe could not be completed and ordered save by the two together, and then each of the two, having need of the other, would be affected with impotence and would not be self-sufficient. This is naught else than a branch (of the method) of mutual hindrance[[fn:1226]],
root.text.Part 1..74.7: And here is what one might object to this genre of argumentation: One is by no means called powerless who does not that which it is not in his nature to do; for we say not of a human individual that he is weak because he cannot move a thousand quintals, and we attribute no impotence unto God for not being able to become corporeal, nor to create His like, nor to create a square of which the side is equal[[fn:1227]] to the diagonal. Likewise, we cannot say that He is powerless because He should not create alone; for (according to the hypothesis) it would be within the conditions of the divine being that there should be two gods[[fn:1228]], and there would be no (mutual) need therein, but rather a necessity, and the contrary would be impossible[[fn:1229]]. Thus even as, according to their system, we cannot say that God is powerless for being unable to produce a body save by first creating atoms and uniting them by accidents which He creats therein, — a thing which we call neither need nor impotence, the contrary being impossible, — so likewise will the dualist[[fn:1230]] say: It is impossible that the one (of the two gods) should act alone, and this constituts no impotence in respect of either of the two, for unto their being it is an essential condition to be two[[fn:1231]].
root.text.Part 1..74.8: There were some among them who, being weary of inventing artifices, said that the unity of God must be accepted as a religious dogma[[fn:1232]]; but the Motécallemîn have strongly censured this and have shown contempt for him who said it. I, however, believe that he among them who said this was a man of a very upright mind, to whom it was repugnant to accept sophisms[[fn:1233]]; having therefore heard nothing in their words which was truly a demonstration, and his mind being in no wise tranquillised by that which they pretended to be one, he said that this was a thing which must be accepted as religious tradition. Verily, these people have recognised in nature no fixed law[[fn:1234]] whence a true argument might be drawn, nor have they conceded to the intelligence any innate rectitude[[fn:1235]] by means of which true conclusions might be formed. All this has been done with intention, so as to suppose a universe which allows us to demonstrate that which is not demonstrable; the result of which has been to render us incapable of demonstrating that which can be demonstrated. It remains only to appeal unto God and unto men of justice and intelligence[[fn:1236]].
root.text.Part 1..75.0:
OF INCORPOREALITY, ACCORDING TO THE SYSTEM OF THE MOTÉCALLEMÎN.
The methods of the Motécallemîn and their argumentations to set aside corporeity (from God) are very weak, weaker than their proofs of unity; for, unto them, incorporeality is as a branch which is necessarily attached to unity as the stem: “The body,” say they, “is not one[[fn:1237]].” — As for him who rejects corporeity for the reason that the body is necessarily composed of matter and form [for that is a (veritable) composition, and it is evident that composition is impossible in the essence of God[[fn:1238]]], I consider him not as a Motécallem; for this proof is not based upon the principles of the Motécallemîn, but it is a true demonstration, based upon the doctrine of matter and form and upon the conception of these two ideas[[fn:1239]]. This is a philosophical doctrine of which I shall speak further on, and which I shall set forth whilst relating the demonstrations of the philosophers upon this matter. In this chapter, our sole purpose is to relate the proofs of the Motécallemîn upon incorporeality, according to their propositions and their methods of argumentation.
root.text.Part 1..75.1: FIRST METHOD: If God, they say, were a body, it would necessarily follow, either that the true idea of divinity resided in all the (simple) substances of that body, I mean in each of its atoms, or else that it resided in but one of the atoms of that body[[fn:1240]]. Now, if it resided in a single atom, of what use would the other atoms be? The existence of that body would be without meaning. If (on the contrary) it resided in each of the atoms of that body, there would be many gods, and not one god alone; but it has already been set forth that there is but one. If thou examinest this demonstration, thou shalt find it based upon the Ist and the Vth of their propositions. But one might object to them[[fn:1241]]: that the body of God is not composed of indivisible parts, that is to say, that it is not composed of (small) substances similar to those which He creats, as ye say, but that it is a single and continuous body which is susceptible of division only in thought, and that one must not have regard unto false ideas[[fn:1242]]. It is thus, indeed, that thou imaginest that the body of the heaven is susceptible of being rent and parcelled, whilst the philosopher says that this is but the effect of the imagination and (that it is) judging by that which is visible [i.e., by the bodies which exist near us] of that which is invisible[[fn:1243]].
root.text.Part 1..75.2: THE SECOND METHOD, which they consider very important, is (taken from) the impossibility of similitude. God (say they) cannot resemble any of His creatures; but, if He were a body, He would resemble other bodies. They enlarge much upon this subject, and they say (among other things): “If we said (that He is) a body, yet not like other bodies, it would be a contradiction[[fn:1244]]; for every body is similar to every other body in respect of corporeity, and bodies differ among themselves only in other respects, that is to say, in accidents.” It would follow further, according to them, that God would have created His like[[fn:1245]].
root.text.Part 1..75.3: This proof may be refuted[[fn:1246]] in two manners. First, one might object: «I do not grant the non-similitude, for how shall you demonstrate that God can in no wise resemble any of His creatures? Unless, by God[[fn:1247]]! you rely in this regard [I mean, concerning the negation of similitude] upon some text of a prophetic book; but then the incorporeality of God would be a thing received by tradition, and not an object of the intellect.» And if it were said that God, if He resembled aught among His creatures, would have created His like, the adversary might reply: «But it is not His like in every aspect; for I deny not that the divinity contains many ideas and presents itself under several aspects.» And indeed, he who believs in the corporeality of God contests not this.
root.text.Part 1..75.4: — A second manner, which is more profound[[fn:1248]], is this: It is established and proven for whosoever has studied philosophy and has immersed himself in the systems of the philosophers that, if the word body has been applied (at once) to the celestial spheres and to these hylic[[fn:1249]] bodies, it is but by simple homonymy; for there is therein identity neither of matter nor of form[[fn:1250]], but, on the contrary, it is likewise by homonymy that the words matter and form are applied to that which is here below and to the celestial spheres. If it be true that the celestial sphere has indubitably dimensions, it is not dimensions in themselves which constitute the body, but the latter is something composed of matter and form. Now, if this be said regarding the celestial sphere, how much more may he who admitts corporeality say it regarding God. He will say, in effect: God is a body having dimensions; but His essence, His true nature and His substance resemble naught among His creatures, and it is only by homonymy that the word body is applied to Him and to them, even as it is by homonymy that, according to true thinkers, the word being is applied to Him and to them. He who maintains corporeality grants not either that all bodies are composed of like atoms, but he says that God is the creator of all these bodies, which vary in substance and in nature; and even as for him the body of dung[[fn:1251]] is not (the same thing as) the body of the solar globe, even so he says that the body of the created light, I mean, of the schekhînâ[[fn:1252]], is not the body of the spheres and stars; nor is the body of the schekhînâ, or of the created pillar of cloud, according to him, the body of God. This body, he says on the contrary, is the perfect and sublime essence which was never composed, which never changed, and of which change is impossible; for, on the contrary, this body has ever necessarily existed such as it is, and it is He who does all that is outside of Him, according to His intention and His will. — I would fain know how this system, however infirm it may be, could be refuted by means of their astonishing methods which I have made known unto thee!
root.text.Part 1..75.5.sub_0: THE THIRD METHOD is this: If God, say they, were a body, He would be finite [which is true], and if He were finite, He would have a certain measure and a certain determinate figure [which is likewise a true consequence]. Now, say they, whatever be the measure and the figure (one supposs), God, inasmuch as He is a body, could be greater or smaller than that measure and have a figure different from that one; if therefore He be determined by a certain measure and a certain figure, there was required for this a determining being[[fn:1253]]. — This demonstration also I have heard extolled by them, although it be weaker than all that preceds, being based upon the Xth proposition, of which we have already exposed all the difficulties that it presents even with regard to other beings [since it is supposed they might have a nature different from that which they have[[fn:1254]]], and how much more so with regard to God. There is no difference between this reasoning and what they say concerning the preference accorded to the existence of the world over its non-existence, and which (according to them) would prove that there is an agent who has preferred its existence over its non-existence, both being possible[[fn:1255]]. Now, if one were to ask them: why does this not apply to God, and why say we not that, since He exists, there must be a being who has preferred His existence to His non-existence? they would doubtless answer: it is because that would lead to an (infinite) chain, and that it would be necessary to stop at a necessary being, in whom there is no possibility and who has no need of another being to bring Him into existence. But this same answer may be applied to figure and to measure. In effect, that figures and measures should be of but possible existence, they must apply to a being who exists after not having existed, and of such a being only can it be said[[fn:1256]]: it was possible that he were greater or smaller than he really is and that he had a figure different from that which he has, so that he had absolute need of a determining being.
root.text.Part 1..75.5.sub_1: But as touching the figure and the measure of God [far from Him be all imperfection and assimilation!], the partisan of corporeality will say: «It was not after not having existed that He arrived at existence, so that He should have had need of a determining being. On the contrary, His essence with the measure and the figure which it has is thus of a necessary existence; it has had no need of a being who should determine it nor who should prefer[[fn:1257]] its existence over its non-existence, for there is in it no possibility of non-existence; and likewise it has had no need of a being who should give it a determinate figure and measure, for its existence was necessary in this manner[[fn:1258]].»
root.text.Part 1..75.6: And now, O reader! if thou preferrest the quest of truth, if thou castest far from thee passion, belief upon authority, and prejudice for that which thou wast wont to respect, and if thou wilt not deceive thyself, behold to what these thinkers are reduced, what has befallen them, and what has proceeded from them[[fn:1259]]; for they are[[fn:1260]] as one who escaps from burning ashes (only to fall) into the fire[[fn:1261]]. Indeed, they have effaced every natural law[[fn:1262]] and altered the nature of heaven and earth, by pretending that by these propositions one can demonstrate that the world is created. But, far from having demonstrated the creation of the world, they have destroyed for us the demonstrations of the existence, the unity, and the incorporeality of God; for the demonstrations by which all this becoms clear can be taken only from the nature of being, such as it is established, visible, and perceived by the senses and the intellect.
root.text.Part 1..75.7: Having fully summarized their discourses[[fn:1263]], we shall likewise report the propositions of the philosophers and their demonstrations establishing that God exists, that He is one, and that it is impossible for Him to be a body; and this, by granting them first the hypothesis of the eternity of the universe, albeit we ourselves admit it not[[fn:1264]].
