Thereafter, I shall show thee the method which, guided by true speculation, I have myself adopted to complete the demonstration of these three questions[[fn:1265]]; and finally, by the help of the Almighty, I shall return to engage with the philosophers concerning what they have said of the eternity of the universe[[fn:1266]].
root.text.Part 1..75.8:
END OF THE FIRST PART
OF THE GUIDE FOR THE PERPLEXED.
root.text.Part 2..0.0: [[fn:1342]]It follows from the twenty-fifth proposition that there is a motor which has set in motion the matter of that which is generated and perishes[[fn:1343]], that it might receive form; and, if one seeks what has set in motion this proximate motor, it must needs be that another motor be found for it in its turn, whether of its own kind or of another: for motion is found in the four categories unto which the term motion is generally applied, even as we have stated in the fourth proposition. Yet this cannot continue ad infinitum, as we have said in the third proposition. Now, we find that all motion here below leads to the motion of the fifth body, whereat it stays[[fn:1344]]. It is from this last motion that all which in the whole inferior world imparts motion and disposs unto the reception of form is derived, and unto it, by a chain of sequence, it returns[[fn:1345]]. The celestial sphere has the motion of translation, which is antecedent to all motions, as has been said in the fourteenth proposition. Likewise, all locomotion here below leads to the motion of the celestial sphere. One may say, for example, that as for this stone which movs, it is the staff which has set it in motion; the staff was moved by the hand, the hand by the tendons, the tendons were moved[[fn:1346]] by the muscles, the muscles by the nerves, the nerves by the natural heat, and this last finally was moved by the form within it[[fn:1347]], which, undoubtedly, is the prime motor. That which has moved this motor to act would have been, for instance, an opinion[[fn:1348]], to wit, to cause this stone, by thrusting it with the staff, to reach a skylight, so as to stop it up, that the wind which blows might not penetrate thereby unto him. Now, that which movs this wind and produces[[fn:1349]] its breath is the motion of the celestial sphere; and thus shalt thou find that every cause of generation and corruption returns to the motion of the celestial sphere[[fn:1350]].
root.text.Part 2..0.1: When, by our contemplation, we have at last arrived at this sphere, which is likewise moved, it behoves, say we, that it should have in its turn a motor, according to what has been said in the seventeenth proposition. Its motor can only be either within it or without it; and this is a necessary alternative. If it be without it, it must necessarily be either corporeal or incorporeal; in the latter case, however, one would not say that it is without it, but rather that it is separate from it: for of that which is incorporeal, it is only by extension that it is said to be without the body[[fn:1351]]. If its motor, I mean that of the sphere, be within it, it can only be either a force diffused throughout its whole body and divisible together with the latter, like heat in fire, or else a force situated within it but indivisible, like the soul and the intellect, as has been said in the tenth proposition[[fn:1352]]. Consequently, the motor of the celestial sphere shall necessarily be one of these four things: either another body without it, or a separate being, or a force diffused within it, or an indivisible force.
root.text.Part 2..0.2: The first case, which assums as the motor of the celestial sphere another body without it, is untenable, as I shall presently show. Inasmuch as, being a body, it shall itself be moved whilst imparting motion, as has been said in the ninth proposition; now, as this sixth body[[fn:1353]] shall likewise be moved in communicating motion, it will be necessary that a seventh body move it, and this one again shall be moved in its turn. It would follow, therefore, that there exist bodies of an infinite number, and that it is thereby that the celestial sphere movs. But this is untenable, as has been said in the second proposition.
root.text.Part 2..0.3: The third case, which supposs as the motor of the celestial sphere a force diffused within it, is likewise inadmissible, as I shall show. For the sphere, being a body, is necessarily finite, as results from the first proposition; its force will therefore likewise be finite, as the twelfth says, and it shall be divided by the division of the body, as the eleventh says[[fn:1354]]. It cannot therefore impart a motion which, as we have laid down in the twenty-sixth proposition, would be infinite[[fn:1355]].
root.text.Part 2..0.4: As for the fourth case, which supposs as the motor of the celestial sphere an indivisible force which should be within it, as for example the human soul is within man, it is likewise inadmissible that this motor alone be the cause of perpetual motion, albeit it be an indivisible force[[fn:1356]]. For, were it the first motor thereof, this motor nevertheless would be moved itself accidentally[[fn:1357]], as has been said in the sixth proposition; but I add here an explanation[[fn:1358]]. When, for example, man is moved by his soul, which is his form, to ascend from the house to the upper chamber[[fn:1359]], it is his body which is moved essentially, and the soul is the first essential motor. But the latter is moved accidentally: for when the body transports itself from the house to the chamber, the soul, which was in the house, likewise transports itself and is found thereafter in the chamber[[fn:1360]]. Nevertheless, when the soul ceass to move, that which is moved by it, to wit, the body, is likewise found at rest, and (in its turn), by the rest of the body, the accidental motion which had happened unto the soul ceass[[fn:1361]]. Now, all that is moved accidentally will necessarily be at rest, as has been said in the eighth (proposition); and when it shall be at rest, that which is moved by it shall likewise be so. It is therefore necessary that this first motor have another cause, outside of the whole composed of a motor and a thing moved; if this cause, which is the principle of motion, be present, the first motor which is in this whole will set in motion the moved part; but if it be absent, the latter will be at rest. Wherefore the bodies of animals do not move continually, although there be in each of them an indivisible first motor: for their motor does not move continually by its essence, but on the contrary, that which leads it to produce motion are things outside of it, whether (the desire) of seeking what is fitting for it or of fleeing what is contrary to it, or an imagination, or a conception, in (those beings) which have conception[[fn:1362]]. It is by this alone that it movs, and, in giving motion[[fn:1363]], it is itself moved accidentally; it will therefore necessarily return to rest, as we have said. — Consequently, if the motor of the celestial sphere were found within it in this manner, it would not be possible for it to have a perpetual motion[[fn:1364]].
root.text.Part 2..0.5: If therefore this motion be continual and eternal, as our adversary has said[[fn:1365]], — which is possible, as has been said in the thirteenth proposition, — it will be necessary, according to this opinion, to admit for the first cause of the motion of the celestial sphere the second case, to wit, that it is separate from the sphere, and even so does the (previous) division require[[fn:1366]].
root.text.Part 2..0.6: It is therefore demonstrated that the first motor of the celestial sphere, if the latter have an eternal and continual motion, can in no wise be either a body or a force in a body; so that this motor has no motion, neither essential nor accidental[[fn:1367]], and that by reason thereof it is also not susceptible either of division or of change, as has been said in the seventh and in the fifth propositions. And this is God — glorified be His name! — I mean, (that He is) the first cause which setts in motion the celestial sphere.
root.text.Part 2..0.7: It is inadmissible that it should be [[t:0]]two[[t:1]] or more: for separated [[t:2]]things[[t:3]], which are not corporeal, do not admit of numeration, unless (in this sense) they are causes and effects one of the other, as was said in the sixteenth (proposition). It is also clear that, since movement is not applicable to it, it does not fall under time, as was said in the fifteenth.
root.text.Part 2..0.8: This speculation has therefore led us to establish, by a demonstration, that the celestial sphere[[fn:1368]] cannot give unto itself perpetual motion[[fn:1369]]; that the First Cause which imparts motion thereto is neither a body nor a force residing in a body; and that it is one and not subject to change, for its existence is not bound by time. These be the three questions which the most excellent among the philosophers have determined by way of demonstration.
root.text.Part 2..0.9: <small>SECOND SPECULATION</small> of these same philosophers. — Aristotle has first laid down as a principle that if a thing be found composed of two distinct elements, and one of these elements exists separately without the composite thing, it is necessary that the other also exists separately without that composite thing; for, if it were a necessary condition of their existence that they exist only together[[fn:1370]], as is the case with matter and physical form, neither of the two could in any wise exist without the other. Thus, therefore, the separate existence of one of the two being a proof of their mutual independence[[fn:1371]], it necessarily follows that the other likewise shall exist separately. If, for example, oxymel exists, and at the same time honey exists alone, it necessarily follows that vinegar also exists alone. — After having set forth this proposition, he says: We find many things composed of a mover and of that which is moved—that is to say, which move another thing and, while imparting motion, are themselves moved by something else; this is manifest in all things intermediate in motion[[fn:1372]]. But we find also a thing moved which movs not at all, and this is the last moved thing[[fn:1373]]; consequently, it is necessary that there should also exist a mover that is not moved, and this is the First Mover[[fn:1374]]. — Since, then, motion in Him is impossible, He is neither divisible, nor a body, nor does He fall under the category of time, as has been explained in the preceding demonstration.
root.text.Part 2..0.10: THIRD PHILOSOPHICAL SPECULATION upon this subject, borrowed from the words of Aristotle, albeit he produced it for another purpose[[fn:1375]]. — Here is the sequence of the reasoning: it cannot be doubted that there be things which exist, and these are the beings perceived by the senses. One can admit concerning beings only three cases, and this is a necessary division: either that all beings neither come into existence nor perish; or that all of them come into existence and perish[[fn:1376]]; or that in part they come into existence and perish, and in part they neither come into existence nor perish. The first case is evidently inadmissible; for we see many beings which come into existence and perish. The second case is likewise inadmissible, as I shall explain: Indeed, if every being were subject to generation and corruption, each and every being would have the possibility of perishing; but what is possible for the species cannot but necessarily happen, as thou knowest[[fn:1377]]. It would thence follow that all of them would have necessarily perished, I mean all beings. Now, after they had all perished, it would have been impossible that anything should exist; for there would have remained nothing that could bring anything into existence; whence it would follow that, in effect, there exists absolutely nothing. Nevertheless, we see things which exist, and we ourselves exist. — It follows therefore necessarily from this speculation that, if there be beings which come into existence and perish, as we perceive, there must also be some being which neither comes into existence nor perishes. In this being which neither comes into existence nor perishes, there shall be absolutely no possibility of perishing; on the contrary, it shall be of a necessary existence, and not of a possible existence[[fn:1378]].
root.text.Part 2..0.11: — It has been further said[[fn:1379]]: The necessary being can be such only in respect of itself, or else in respect of its cause; so that in this latter case it might, in respect of itself, exist or not exist, whilst it will be of a necessary existence in respect of its cause, and its cause, consequently, will be the true necessary being, as was stated in the nineteenth proposition. It is therefore demonstrated that there must necessarily exist a being whose existence is necessary in respect of itself, and that without it there would exist absolutely nothing, neither that which would be subject to generation and corruption, nor that which would not be so—if indeed there be anything that exists in this latter manner, as Aristotle maintains[[fn:1380]], I mean something not subject to generation and corruption, being the effect of a cause whose existence is necessary. — This is a demonstration which admitts neither doubt, nor refutation[[fn:1381]], nor contradiction, save for him who is ignorant of the demonstrative method.
root.text.Part 2..0.12: We say further: The existence of every being necessary in itself must necessarily have no cause, as was stated in the twentieth[[fn:1382]] proposition; there will be in it absolutely no multiplicity of ideas, as was stated in the twenty-first proposition, whence it follows that it will be neither a body nor a force residing in a body, as was stated in the twenty-second. It is therefore demonstrated, by this speculation, that there is a being which, by its own very essence, is of a necessary existence, and it is that whose existence has no cause, in which there is no composition, and which, for that reason, is neither a body nor a force in a body; this being is God [may His name be glorified!].
root.text.Part 2..0.13: In like manner, it may be readily demonstrated that it is inadmissible for [[t:0]]necessary[[t:1]] existence, in relation to the essence itself, to appertain to two (beings): for the [[t:2]]species[[t:3]] of necessary being would then be an idea superadded to the essence of each of the two, and neither of the two would any longer be a necessary being solely by its own essence; but rather by that singular idea which constitutes the [[t:4]]species[[t:5]] of being and which would appertain to both[[fn:1383]]. — It may be demonstrated by various means that in the necessary being there can exist no [[t:6]]duality[[t:7]] whatsoever, neither by similitude nor by contrariety[[fn:1384]]; the rationale for all this resides in the pure simplicity and absolute perfection (of this being), — which permits no room outside of its essence for anything whatsoever of its species[[fn:1385]], — as well as in the total absence of any [[t:8]]cause[[t:9]][[fn:1386]]. There is consequently no association (within it).
root.text.Part 2..0.14: FOURTH SPECULATION, likewise philosophical[[fn:1387]]. — It is well known that we continually behold things which are (at first) in potentiality and pass into actuality. Now, whatsoever passes from potentiality into actuality has outside itself some thing which causs it so to pass, as has been said in the eighteenth proposition. It is likewise manifest that this agent was at first an agent in potentiality before being such in actuality[[fn:1388]]; and the reason why it was at first but in potentiality is either in an obstacle (proceeding) from itself, or in (the absence of) a certain relation initially lacking between it and the thing which it has caused to pass (into actuality), so that, when this relation existed, it did verily cause it to pass (into actuality). Each of these two cases necessarily required (in its turn) an agent, or something which might cause the obstacle to cease; and the same must be said of the second agent, or of that which caused the obstacle to cease. But, as this cannot extend to infinity, it is necessary to arrive at something which causs to pass from potentiality into actuality, whilst always existing in the same state, and without there being in it any potentiality whatsoever, I mean without its having in its very essence any thing (which is) in potentiality: for, if there were in its essence any possibility, it might cease to exist, as has been said in the twenty-third (proposition). It is likewise inadmissible that this being should have matter; but, on the contrary, it shall be separate[[fn:1389]], as has been said in the twenty-fourth (proposition). This separate being, in which there is absolutely no possibility, but which exists (in actuality) by its essence, is God[[fn:1390]]. Finally, it is manifest that, being in no wise a body, He is one, as has been said in the sixteenth proposition.
root.text.Part 2..0.15: These are all demonstrative methods for (establishing) the existence of one God, who is neither a body nor a force in a body, (and this) while yet admitting the eternity of the world.
root.text.Part 2..0.16: There is yet another demonstrative method for removing corporeity and establishing the unity (of God)[[fn:1391]]: it is that, if there were two gods, it would necessarily follow that they should have somewhat in common, — to wit, that thing by which each of the two deserved to be (called) God, — and some other thing likewise necessary, whereby their reciprocal distinction might take place and whereby they should be two. But then, if each of the two had somewhat which the other had not, each would be composed of two notions, neither of the two would be either first cause or a being necessary by itself, and each would have causes, as has been set forth in the nineteenth (proposition). If, on the contrary, the distinguishing thing were found only in one of the two, he that possessed these two things would by no means be a being necessary by himself.
root.text.Part 2..0.17.sub_0: Another method for (establishing) the unity. — It has been established by demonstration that the whole universe is as a single individual, whose parts are linked one to another, and that the forces of the celestial sphere are diffused throughout this inferior matter and dispose it[[fn:1392]]. This being established, it is inadmissible that one god should isolate himself with one of the parts of this being, and that a second god should isolate himself with another part: for they are linked one to the other. There remains, therefore, no other partition to be made, unless it be that one (of the two gods) should act at one time and the other at another time, or else that they should always both act together, so that no action could be accomplished save by both together. — To suppose that one acts at one time and the other at another time is impossible for several reasons. Indeed, if it were possible that, during the time when one of the two acts, the other should act likewise, what would be the cause which would make one to act and the other to be idle? If, on the contrary, it were impossible for one of the two to act at the same time as the other acts, this would suppose another cause which would have made it possible for the one to act, while for the other it was impossible: for in time itself there is no difference, and the substratum of the action also is one alone whose parts are linked one to another, as we have set forth. Furthermore, each of the two would fall under time: for his action would be bound to time. Thence, each of the two would pass from potentiality into actuality at the moment when he should act, so that each would stand in need of somewhat to make him pass from potentiality into actuality. Finally, there would be in the essence of each a possibility. — But to suppose that they always both operate together everything that is done in the universe, so that one acts not without the other, is likewise an impossible thing, as I shall explain. In effect, whenever a certain action cannot be accomplished save by a collective (of individuals), no individual of that collective is an absolute agent by his essence, and none is the first cause for the action in question; but, on the contrary, the first cause is the union of the whole. But it has been demonstrated that the Necessary Being must be absolutely devoid of cause.
root.text.Part 2..0.17.sub_1: Furthermore, the unification of the whole is (in itself) an act which, in its turn, requirs another cause; and it is this cause which units the whole. Now, if that which has unified this whole, without which the action cannot be accomplished, be a unique (being), it is undoubtedly God. If, on the contrary, that which has unified this whole be in its turn another whole, it will be necessary for this second whole that which was required for the first. One must perforce arrive at a unique being, who shall be the cause of the existence of this unique universe, in whatever manner the latter exists: whether it be by a creation ex nihilo, or by necessity[[fn:1393]]. — It is therefore likewise manifest, by this method, that the unity of the entire universe proves unto us that its author is one.
root.text.Part 2..0.18: Another method for (establishing) incorporeity[[fn:1394]]. — 1° Every body is composite, as has been said in the twenty-second (proposition), and every composite necessarily presupposs an efficient cause, which is the cause of the existence of its form within its matter. 2° It is also perfectly manifest that every body is divisible and has dimensions, and that, consequently, it is indubitably a substratum for accidents. Thus, therefore, a body cannot be one, on the one hand, because it is divisible, and on the other, because it is composite—I mean, because there is a duality in the very term (of body)[[fn:1395]]: for every body is only such a determined body by an idea added to the idea of body in general, and, consequently, there are necessarily in it two ideas. But it has already been demonstrated that in the Necessary Being, there is composition in no wise.
root.text.Part 2..0.19: Having first recounted these demonstrations, we shall begin to set forth our own method[[fn:1396]], even as we have promised.
root.text.Part 2..1.0: This fifth body, which is the celestial sphere, must perforce be either something which is generated and perishes [and it shall be the same with motion], or else something which is neither generated nor perishes, as the adversary says[[fn:1397]]. Now, if the celestial sphere be a thing which is generated and perishes, that which has caused it to exist after non-existence is God [glorified be His name!]; this is a primary notion, for whatsoever exists after not having existed necessarily presupposs something that has called it into existence, and it is inadmissible that it should have brought itself into existence. If, on the contrary, this sphere has never ceased and shall never cease to move thus by a perpetual and eternal motion, it must needs be, by virtue of the preceding propositions, that that which imparts unto it eternal motion be neither a body nor a force within a body; and this shall still be God [glorified be His name!]. It is therefore manifest that the existence of God [a Necessary Being, without cause, and whose existence is in itself exempt from all possibility] is demonstrated by decisive and certain proofs[[fn:1398]], no matter whether the world be a creation ex nihilo, or whether it be not. Likewise, it is established by demonstrations that He (God) is one and incorporeal, as we have previously stated: for the demonstration of His unity and His incorporeity remains established, whether the world be, or be not, a creation ex nihilo, as we have set forth in the third of the philosophical methods[[fn:1399]], and as we have (afterwards) separately set forth the incorporeity and the unity by philosophical methods[[fn:1400]].
root.text.Part 2..1.1: It has seemed good unto me to complete the theories of the philosophers by setting forth their proofs for the existence of the separate intelligences, and to show that they are in agreement, in this matter[[fn:1401]], with the principles of our religion: I mean to speak of the existence of the angels. After having concluded this subject, I shall return to the argument which I promised concerning the novelty of the world: for our principal proofs thereupon shall only be solid and clear after one shall have known the existence of the separate intelligences and the proofs upon which it rests[[fn:1402]]. But, before all this, I must make a preliminary observation, which shall be a beacon to enlighten the obscurities of this entire treatise, as well of the chapters which have preceded as of those which shall follow, and this observation is as follows:
root.text.Part 2..1.2:
PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION.
Know that, in this treatise, I have not had for my purpose to compose (a work) upon physical science, any more than to analyse according to certain systems the subjects of metaphysical science, or to reproduce the demonstrations of which they have been the object[[fn:1403]]. Neither have I aimed therein to summarise and abridge (the science of) the disposition of the celestial spheres, nor to make known the number of the latter; for the books which have been composed upon all these matters are sufficient, and should they be insufficient for any subject whatsoever, that which I might say myself upon such a subject would be of no more worth than all that has been said. My purpose in this treatise has been none other than that which I made known unto thee in the introduction thereof[[fn:1404]]; namely, to explain the obscurities of the Law and to manifest the true meanings of its allegories, which are above the reach of common understandings. Wherefore, when thou shalt see me speak of the existence[[fn:1405]] and the number of the Separate Intelligences, or of the number of the spheres and the causes of their motions, or of the true notion of matter and form, or of what is to be understood by the divine emanation[[fn:1406]], or of other similar matters, thou must not believe for a single moment[[fn:1407]] that my sole aim has been to examine this philosophical subject; for these subjects have been treated in many books, and the truth thereof has, for the most part, been demonstrated. But my aim is only to report that the understanding of which may serve to clear up certain obscurities of the Law, and to set forth briefly such a subject by the knowledge of which many difficulties may be resolved[[fn:1408]].
root.text.Part 2..1.3: Thou knowest already, from the introduction to this treatise, that it turns principally[[fn:1409]] upon the explanation of what it is possible to understand of the Ma’asé beréshîth (Account of the Creation) and of the Ma’asé mercabâ (Account of the Chariot)[[fn:1410]], and upon the elucidation of the obscurities inherent in prophecy and in the knowledge of God. Whenever, in any chapter whatsoever, thou shalt see me approach the explanation of a subject which has already been demonstrated either in physical science or in metaphysical science, or which has only been presented as that which is most admissible, or a subject which is connected with what has been set forth in mathematics, — thou shalt know that this subject is necessarily a key for the understanding of some certain thing in the prophetic books, I mean of their allegories and their mysteries, and that it is for this reason that I have mentioned and clearly set it forth, as being useful either for the knowledge of the Ma’asé mercabâ and the Ma’asé beréshîth, or for the explanation of a principle relating to prophecy or to any true opinion whatsoever which one ought to admit in religious beliefs.
root.text.Part 2..1.4: After this preliminary observation, I return to fulfil the task which I had imposed upon myself[[fn:1411]].
root.text.Part 2..2.0: Know that the opinions which Aristotle propounds concerning the causes of the motion of the spheres, and from which he has concluded that there exist Separate Intelligences, although they be hypotheses not susceptible of a demonstration, are nevertheless, among the opinions that may be uttered, those which are least subject to doubt and which present themselves with the greatest method[[fn:1412]], as Alexander says in (his treatise) The Principles of All Things[[fn:1413]]. These are also statements which, as I shall set forth, are in accord with many of those of the Law, especially according to the explanation of the most celebrated Midrashim, which, without doubt, belong to our Sages. Wherefore, I shall cite his opinions[[fn:1414]] and his proofs, in order to choose from them that which is in accord with the Law and conformable to the statements of the Sages [may their memory be blessed!].
root.text.Part 2..3.0.sub_0: That the celestial sphere is endowed with a soul, is what becoms clear when one well examins (the matter)[[fn:1415]]. That which causs him who hears this to believe it a thing difficult to understand, or to reject it utterly, is that he imagins that, when we say endowed with a soul, it concerns a soul like that of man, or like that of the ass and the ox. But such is not the meaning of these words, by which it is intended only to say that its local motion[[fn:1416]] proves that it has indubitably within it a principle by which it movs, and this principle, without any doubt, is a soul. In truth, — to explain myself more clearly, — it is inadmissible that its circular motion should be like the straight motion of a stone downwards, or of fire upwards, so that the principle of this motion should be a nature[[fn:1417]], and not a soul; for that which has this natural motion, the principle which is within it movs it solely to seek its (natural) place, when it finds itself in another place, so that it remains at rest as soon as it has arrived at its place[[fn:1418]], whilst this celestial sphere movs circularly (remaining ever) in the same place. But it suffices not that it be endowed with a soul, that it should necessarily move thus; for everything which is endowed with a soul movs only by a nature, or by a conception. — By nature I mean here (that which leads the animal) to direct itself towards that which suits it and to flee that which is contrary to it, no matter whether that which thus setts it in motion be without it, — as, for example, when the animal fles the heat of the sun, and, being thirsty, seeks the place of water, — or whether its mover be the imagination [for the animal movs also by the mere imagination of that which is contrary to it and that which suits it]. — Now, this sphere movs not at all for the purpose of fleeing that which is contrary to it or of seeking that which suits it; for the point towards which it movs is also its point of departure, and every point of departure is also the point towards which it movs. Furthermore, if its motion had that purpose, it would be necessary that, having arrived at the point towards which it movs, it should remain at rest; for if it moved to seek or to flee something, without ever attaining it, the motion would be in vain.
root.text.Part 2..3.0.sub_1: Its circular motion cannot, therefore, take place save by virtue of a certain conception[[fn:1419]], which constrains it to move in such a manner. Now, conception takes not place save by means of an intellect; the celestial sphere, consequently, is endowed with an intellect[[fn:1420]]. But everything that possesses an intellect, whereby it conceivs a certain idea, and a soul, whereby it becoms possible for it to move, does not (necessarily) move when it conceivs (an idea); for conception alone does not necessitate motion. This has been set forth in the First Philosophy (or in the Metaphysics), and it is also manifest (in itself). Verily, thou shalt find of thyself that thou conceivest many things toward which thou art likewise able to move, and yet thou movest not toward them until there necessarily supervens a desire (which impells thee) toward that thing which thou hast conceived, and then only dost thou move to obtain what thou hast conceived. It is therefore clear that neither the soul whereby the motion is effected, nor the intellect whereby the thing is conceived, suffices to produce the motion in question until there be joined thereto a desire for the thing conceived. It follows thence that the celestial sphere has the desire (to approach) that which it has conceived, to wit, the beloved object, which is God [exalted be His name!]. It is from this point of view that it has been said that God setts the celestial sphere in motion, that is to say, that the sphere desirs to assimilate itself unto the object of its perception[[fn:1421]], and this is that thing conceived (by it), which is of an extreme simplicity, in which there occurrs absolutely no change, nor any new situation, and from which goodness continually flows. But the celestial sphere, inasmuch as it is a body, cannot accomplish this except because its action is circular motion, and not otherwise [for the highest point of perfection that a body can attain is to have a perpetual action]. This is the simplest motion that a body can possess, and (this being so) there occurrs no change, neither in its essence, nor in the outpouring of the benefits which result from its motion[[fn:1422]].
root.text.Part 2..3.1: Aristotle, having recognized all this, applied himself to a new investigation, whereby he found demonstratively (that there are) numerous spheres, whose respective motions differ one from another in velocity, in slowness, and in direction[[fn:1423]], albeit they all have circular motion in common. This physical study led him to believe that the thing which such a sphere conceivs, so as to accomplish its rapid motion in one day, must necessarily differ from that which another sphere conceivs, which accomplishes a single motion in thirty years[[fn:1424]]. He has therefore decidedly concluded that there are Separate Intelligences, equal in number to that of the spheres, that each of the spheres feels a desire for that intelligence which is its principle, and that the latter imparts to it the motion which is peculiar to it, so that a (certain) determined intelligence setts a certain sphere in motion. Neither Aristotle, nor any other[[fn:1425]], has decided that the intelligences are ten or a hundred in number; but he has said that they are of the same number as the spheres. Now, as it was believed in his time that the spheres were fifty in number, Aristotle says: “If it be so, the Separate Intelligences are fifty in number[[fn:1426]].” For mathematical knowledge was rare in his time and had not yet reached perfection; it was believed that for every motion a sphere was required, and it was not known that the inclination of a single sphere gave rise to several visible motions, as, for example, the motion in longitude, the motion in declination, and also the (apparent) motion seen upon the circle of the horizon, in the amplitude of the risings and settings[[fn:1427]]. But this is not our aim, and we return to our subject[[fn:1428]].
root.text.Part 2..3.2: If the modern philosophers have said that the Intelligences are ten in number, it is because they have counted the globes containing stars and the surrounding sphere, although some of these globes contain several spheres. Now, they have counted nine globes, (to wit) the sphere which surrounds all, that of the fixed stars, and the spheres of the seven planets. As for the tenth Intelligence, it is the Active Intellect, the existence of which is proved by our intellects passing from potentiality to actuality, and by the forms supervening upon beings that are born and perish, after they have been in their matter only in potentiality[[fn:1429]]. For everything that passes from potentiality to actuality necessarily has outside of itself something which causs it so to pass; and it behoves that this agent be of the same species as the thing upon which it acts[[fn:1430]]. Indeed, the carpenter fashions not the chest because he is an artisan, but because he has in his mind the form of the chest; and it is the form of the chest, in the mind of the carpenter, which has caused the (objective) form of the chest to pass into actuality and to supervene upon the wood. Likewise, without any doubt, that which gives the form is a separate form, and that which gives existence to the intellect is an intellect, to wit, the Active Intellect; so that the Active Intellect is to the elements and to that which is composed thereof, what each separate intelligence, belonging to any sphere whatever, is to that sphere[[fn:1431]], and the role of the intellect in act existing within us, which is emanated from the Active Intellect and whereby we perceive the latter, is the same as that of the intellect existing in each sphere, which is emanated from the separate intelligence, and whereby it (the sphere) perceivs the separate intelligence, conceivs it, desirs to assimilate itself thereto, and thus arrivs at motion.
root.text.Part 2..3.3: It follows also for him[[fn:1432]] that which has already been demonstrated, to wit: that God does not do things by contact; when (for example) He burns[[fn:1433]], it is by the mediation of fire, and the latter is moved by the mediation of the motion of the celestial sphere, which in its turn is moved by the mediation of a Separate Intelligence. The Intelligences are therefore the angels that draw near (unto God)[[fn:1434]], and by whose mediation the spheres are set in motion. Now, as separate Intelligences are not susceptible of being numbered in respect of the diversity of their essences,—for they are incorporeal,—it follows that, according to him (Aristotle), it is God who produced the first Intelligence, which setts the first sphere in motion, in the manner we have set forth; the Intelligence which setts the second sphere in motion has for its cause and principle only the first Intelligence, and so forth[[fn:1435]]; so that the Intelligence which setts in motion the sphere nigh unto us[[fn:1436]] is the cause and principle of the Active Intellect. The latter is the last of the separate Intelligences[[fn:1437]], even as bodies also, beginning with the superior sphere, end with the elements and with that which is composed of them. It could not be admitted that the Intelligence which setts the superior sphere in motion is itself the (absolute) Necessary Being; for, as it has one thing in common with the other Intelligences, to wit, the setting in motion of the (respective) bodies, and as they all are distinguished one from another by another thing, each of the ten is (composed) of two things[[fn:1438]], and, consequently, there must be a first cause for the whole.
root.text.Part 2..3.4: Such are the words of Aristotle and his opinion. His proofs[[fn:1439]] concerning these things have been set forth, as far as they can be[[fn:1440]], in the books of his successors. That which results from all his words is that all the celestial spheres are living bodies, possessing a soul and an intellect; that they conceive and perceive God, and that they also perceive their principles[[fn:1441]]; finally, that there exist Separate Intelligences, absolutely incorporeal, which all are emanated from God, and which are the intermediaries between God and all these (celestial) bodies.
root.text.Part 2..3.5: — And now I will set forth unto thee, in the ensuing chapters, that which our Law contains, whether in conformity with or in opposition to these opinions.
root.text.Part 2..4.0: That the celestial spheres are living and [[t:0]]rational[[t:1]], that is to say, (beings) which [[t:2]]perceive[[t:3]], is that which is also proclaimed by the Law a thing true and certain; (that is to say) that they are not dead bodies, like fire and earth, as the ignorant suppose, but that they are, as the philosophers assert, animated beings, obeying their master, praising and glorifying Him in the most signal manner[[fn:1442]]. It has been stated: [[t:4]]The heavens declare the glory of God[[t:5]], [[t:6]]etc.[[t:7]]. (Ps. [[t:8]]XIX[[t:9]], 2); and how far would he be removed from the apprehension of truth, who should believe this to be a mere metaphor[[fn:1443]]! for the Hebrew tongue could not have employed simultaneously the verbs [[t:10]]הגּיד[[t:11]] (to announce) and [[t:12]]ספּר[[t:13]] (to relate) save when speaking of a Being endowed with intelligence. That which proves with evidence that (the Psalmist) here speaks of something inherent in themselves, that is to say, in the spheres, and not of something which men attribute unto them[[fn:1444]], is that he says: [[t:14]]There is no speech[[t:15]], [[t:16]]nor language; their voice is not heard[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]Ibid.[[t:19]], v. 4); he therefore clearly expresses that he speaks of them themselves, (by stating) that they praise God and relate His wonders without the language of lips and of tongue. And this is the truth; for he who praises by speech merely announces that which he has conceived, but it is in this conception itself that true praise consists, and, if one expresses it, it is to impart knowledge thereof to others, or to manifest that one has oneself attained a certain perception. It has been said (in this regard): [[t:20]]Commune[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]meditate[[t:23]]) [[t:24]]with your own heart[[t:25]] [[t:26]]upon your bed[[t:27]], [[t:28]]and be still[[t:29]] (Ps. [[t:30]]IV[[t:31]], 5), as one has already expounded[[fn:1445]]. This proof, drawn from Holy Writ, will be gainsaid only by an ignorant man or one who delights in contradiction.
root.text.Part 2..4.1: As for the opinion of the Doctors in this regard, it requires, I apprehend, neither explanation nor proof. One has but to consider their formulation of the [[t:0]]benediction of the moon[[t:1]][[fn:1446]], and that which is frequently reiterated in the prayers[[fn:1447]], as well as the texts of the [[t:2]]Midrashim[[t:3]] concerning these passages: [[t:4]]And the host of heaven worshipps Thee[[t:5]] (Nehemiah, [[t:6]]IX[[t:7]], 6)[[fn:1448]]; [[t:8]]When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy[[t:9]] (Job, [[t:10]]XXXVIII[[t:11]], 7)[[fn:1449]]. They often revert to this theme in their discourses. Thus do they express themselves, in the [[t:12]]Berêshîth Rabbâ[[t:13]], concerning this word of God: [[t:14]]And the earth was[[t:15]] [[t:16]]TOHU[[t:17]] [[t:18]]and[[t:19]] [[t:20]]BOHU[[t:21]] (Gen. [[t:22]]I[[t:23]], 2): «It was [[t:24]]toha[[t:25]] and [[t:26]]boha[[t:27]] [that is to say, the earth lamented and despaired of its unfortunate fate]; I and they, it said, were created together [that is, the earth and the heavens]; but the superior things are living, whilst the inferior things are dead[[fn:1450]].» They therefore also clearly state that the heavens[[fn:1451]] are living bodies, and not dead bodies, like the elements.
root.text.Part 2..4.2: Thus it is manifest that, if Aristotle has said that the celestial sphere possesses perception and conception, this is in accord with the words of our prophets and the pillars of our Law[[fn:1452]], who are the Sages.
root.text.Part 2..4.3: It is also necessary to understand that all philosophers concur that the governance of this terrestrial world is accomplished by the force which emanates from the celestial sphere upon it, as we have stated[[fn:1453]], and that the spheres perceive and comprehend the matters which they govern. And this is what the Law has likewise expressed by saying (concerning the celestial hosts): [[t:0]]that God has allotted them unto all the peoples[[t:1]] (Deut. [[t:2]]IV[[t:3]], 19), which signifies that He made them intermediaries for governing creatures, and not for their adoration. It has further been plainly stated: [[t:4]]And to rule[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]ולמשל[[t:7]]) [[t:8]]over the day and over the night[[t:9]], [[t:10]]and to divide[[t:11]], [[t:12]]etc.[[t:13]] (Gen. [[t:14]]I[[t:15]]. 18); for the verb [[t:16]]משל[[t:17]] signifies [[t:18]]to rule by governing[[t:19]]. This is an idea superadded to that of [[t:20]]light[[t:21]] and [[t:22]]darkness[[t:23]], which are the proximate cause of generation and corruption[[fn:1454]]; for concerning the idea of light and darkness (produced by the celestial bodies) it has been said: [[t:24]]and to divide the light from the darkness[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]Ibid.[[t:27]]). Now, it is inadmissible that he who [[t:28]]governs[[t:29]] a thing should lack knowledge of that thing, once one has apprehended the true meaning which the word [[t:30]]to govern[[t:31]] bears in this context.
root.text.Part 2..4.4: We shall enlarge further upon this subject in another place.
root.text.Part 2..5.0: As touching the existence of angels, it is a matter whereon it is not necessary to adduce any proof from Scripture; for the Law declars itself in this regard in many a passage. Thou knowest already that ÉLOHIM is the name of judges (or of governors)[[fn:1455]]; e.g., before the Elohîm (judges) shall come the cause of both (Exod. XXII, 9). Wherefore this name has been metaphorically employed for (designating) the angels, and also for God, because He is the judge (or the ruler) of the angels; and for this reason also it was said (Deut. X, 17): For the Lord your God, which is an address to all mankind; and thereafter: He is the God of gods, that is to say, the God of angels, and the Lord of lords, that is to say, the Master of the spheres and the stars, which are the lords of all other bodies. This is the true sense, and the words elohîm (gods) and adonîm (lords) cannot here designate human beings[[fn:1456]]; for these would be too insignificant for such a purpose[[fn:1457]]; and furthermore, the words your God[[fn:1458]] already encompass the whole human species, the ruling part as well as the ruled. — Neither is it possible that it was intended thereby that God is the Master of all that which, in the form of (statues of) stone and wood, is reputed a divinity; for it would not be to glorify and magnify God to make Him the Master of stone, wood, and a piece of metal. But what was intended is that God is the Ruler of rulers, that is to say, of the angels, and the Master of the celestial spheres.
root.text.Part 2..5.1: We have already, in an earlier section of this treatise, presented a chapter expounding that angels are not corporeal[[fn:1459]]. This is also the assertion of Aristotle; only, a difference of nomenclature obtains here: he, for his part, speaks of [[t:0]]Separate Intelligences[[t:1]], whereas we speak of [[t:2]]angels[[t:3]][[fn:1460]]. As for his dictum that these Separate Intelligences also serve as intermediaries between God and other beings, and that it is through their agency that the spheres are moved — which constitutes the efficient cause of the genesis of all that comes into being[[fn:1461]] — this, too, is proclaimed by all sacred books; for one shall never find therein that God accomplishes aught save through the mediation of an angel. One is aware that the term [[t:4]]מַלְאָךְ[[t:5]] (angel) signifies [[t:6]]messenger;[[t:7]] whosoever, therefore, executes a command is a [[t:8]]מַלְאָךְ[[t:9]], such that the movements of even the irrational animal are accomplished, according to the text of Scripture, through the instrumentality of a [[t:10]]מַלְאָךְ[[t:11]], when this movement conforms to the purpose of God, who has implanted in the animal a force by which it performs this movement. One reads, for example: [[t:12]]My God has sent his angel[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]מַלְאָכֵהּ[[t:15]]) [[t:16]]and has shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me[[t:17]] (Daniel, [[t:18]]VI[[t:19]], 22); and similarly all the movements of Balaam’s ass occurred through the agency of a [[t:20]]מַלְאָךְ[[t:21]]. The very elements are designated [[t:22]]מַלְאָכִים[[t:23]] ([[t:24]]angels[[t:25]] or [[t:26]]messengers[[t:27]]); for instance: [[t:28]]He maks his angels winds[[t:29]] ([[t:30]]מַלְאָכָיו[[t:31]]) [[t:32]]and his ministers a flaming fire[[t:33]] (Ps. [[t:34]]CIV[[t:35]], 4). It is thus clear that the term [[t:36]]מַלְאָךְ[[t:37]] applies: 1° to the [[t:38]]messenger[[t:39]] among men, for example: [[t:40]]And Jacob sent[[t:41]] [[t:42]]מַלְאָכִים[[t:43]] or [[t:44]]messengers[[t:45]] (Gen. [[t:46]]XXXII[[t:47]], 3); 2° to the [[t:48]]prophet[[t:49]], for instance: [[t:50]]And an[[t:51]] [[t:52]]מַלְאָךְ[[t:53]] [[t:54]]of the Lord came up from Gilgal to Bochim[[t:55]] (Judges [[t:56]]II[[t:57]], 1); [[t:58]]He sent a[[t:59]] [[t:60]]מַלְאָךְ[[t:61]] [[t:62]]and brought us forth out of Egypt[[t:63]] (Num. [[t:64]]XX[[t:65]], 16); 3° to the [[t:66]]Separate Intelligences[[t:67]] which manifest themselves to the prophets in prophetic vision; and finally, 4° to the animal faculties, as we shall further expound.
root.text.Part 2..5.2: In this place, we speak only of angels, which are Separate Intelligences; and verily our Law does not deny that God governs this world by the mediation of angels. Behold how the Sages express themselves upon the words of the Law: Let us make man in our image (Gen. I, 26), Go to, let us go down (Ibid. XI, 7), where the plural is employed: "If," say they, "it be permitted thus to speak, the Holy One does nothing without having looked upon the celestial family[[fn:1462]]." The word looked is right remarkable[[fn:1463]]; for Plato has said, in these same terms, that God having looked upon the world of intelligences, it was from this that being emanated[[fn:1464]]. In some places, they say simply: "the Holy One does nothing without having consulted the celestial family[[fn:1465]]." The word פמליא (familia) signifies army in the Greek tongue[[fn:1466]]. It is said again in the Bereshith Rabba, as also in the Midrash Koheleth, (on the words) that which they have already done (Ecclesiastes II, 12): "It is not said here עשהו, he has done it, but עשדהו they have done it; for, if it be permitted thus to speak, He (God) and His court have consulted together upon each of thy members and have set it upon its base, as it is said: He has made thee, and established thee (Deut. XXXII, 6)[[fn:1467]]." It is further said in the Bereshith Rabba: "Wherever it is said: AND the Lord, it is He and His court[[fn:1468]]."
root.text.Part 2..5.3.sub_0: All these texts do not aim, as the ignorant believe, (to affirm) that the Most High speaks, or reflects, or examines, or consults to assist Himself with the opinion of others[[fn:1469]]; for how would the Creator seek help from what He has created? On the contrary, all of this clearly expresses that even the (smallest) details of the universe, down to the creation of animal limbs as they are, all of this (I say) was done through the mediation of angels; for all faculties are angels. How powerful[[fn:1470]] is the blindness of ignorance, and how dangerous it is! If you were to say to someone who claims to be among the sages of Israel that God sends an angel who enters the woman's womb and forms the fetus there, this would please him greatly; he would accept it and believe that it attributes greatness and power to God, and recognizes His high wisdom[[fn:1471]]. At the same time, he would also admit that the angel is a body (formed) of a burning fire, and that its size is about a third of the entire universe; and all this would seem possible to him regarding God. But if you told him that God has placed in the semen a formative power that shapes and outlines these limbs, and that this is the angel, or that all forms come from the action of the active intellect and that it is this which is the angel and the prince of the world of whom the doctors always speak, he would reject such an opinion[[fn:1472]]; for he would not understand the meaning of this true greatness and power, which consists in bringing into being within a thing active forces imperceptible to the senses. The doctors have therefore clearly explained, for one who is truly a sage, that each of the corporeal forces is an angel, and all the more so the forces spread throughout the universe, and that each force has a certain determined action, and not two actions. In the Bereshith Rabba we read: 'It has been taught: a single angel does not fulfill two missions, and two angels do not fulfill the same mission[[fn:1473]]'; — and this is indeed a condition of all (physical) forces.
root.text.Part 2..5.3.sub_1: That which shall further confirm unto thee that all individual forces, whether physical or psychical, are termed angels, is that which they have observed in several places, and primarily in the Berēshīth Rabbā: “Every day the Holy One creats a class of angels, who recite a song before Him and depart thence[[fn:1474]].” Inasmuch as there has been objected to these words a passage indicating that the angels are stable, — and indeed it has been set forth many a time that the angels are living and stable, — this answer was made, that there be some among them who are stable, whilst there be others who are perishable[[fn:1475]]. And so it is in truth; for these individual forces are born and perish continually, whilst the species of these forces are permanent and suffer no decay[[fn:1476]]. — It is further stated therein[[fn:1477]], concerning the history of Judah and Tamar: “Rabbi Jo’hanan said: He (Judah) wished to pass by; but God sent unto him an angel appointed over concupiscence,” that is to say, over the venereal faculty. This faculty, therefore, has likewise been called an angel. And thus shalt thou find that they ever say: An angel appointed over such or such a thing; for every faculty wherewith God has charged any matter whatsoever[[fn:1478]] is (accounted as) an angel appointed over that thing. A passage in the Midrash Koheleth says: “Whilst man sleeps, his soul speaks to the angel, and the angel to the cherubim[[fn:1479]];” here then, for him who understands and reflects, they have clearly declared that the imaginative faculty is likewise called an angel and that the intellect is called a cherub[[fn:1480]]. This shall appear passing fair to the man of learning, but shall greatly displease the ignorant[[fn:1481]].
root.text.Part 2..5.4: We have already stated elsewhere that whenever an angel manifests himself in any form whatsoever, it is in a prophetic vision[[fn:1482]]. Thou findest[[fn:1483]] prophets who behold the angel[[fn:1484]] as though he were a mere human individual; e.g.: And, lo, three men (Gen. XVIII, 2). To others, he appears as a man redoubtable and fearful; e.g.: And his countenance was like the countenance of an angel of God, very terrible (Judges, XIII, 6). To yet others he appears as fire; e.g.: And the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a flame of fire (Exodus, III, 2). It has further been remarked in the same place[[fn:1485]]: “To Abraham, who possessed an excellent faculty, they appeared in the likeness of men; but to Lot, who had but a meaner faculty, they appeared in the likeness of angels.” Herein is a great mystery concerning prophecy, of which we shall speak in due season hereafter[[fn:1486]]. — It is further said therein: “Before they had accomplished their mission, (they showed themselves as) men; after they had accomplished it, they resumed their angelic nature[[fn:1487]].” — Observe well that on every hand it is clearly indicated that by angel one must understand some action or other, and that every vision of an angel occurrs only in prophetic vision and according to the state of him who perceivs.
root.text.Part 2..5.5: In that which Aristotle has said upon this subject, there is likewise naught which stands in contradiction to the Law. But that which is contrary to us[[fn:1488]] in all this is that he (Aristotle) believs all these things to be eternal, and that they proceed from God by necessity; whereas we believe that all this is created, that God has created the separate Intelligences and has placed in the celestial sphere a faculty of desire which draws it towards them; that it is He (in a word) who has created the Intelligences and the spheres, and who has endowed them with these governing faculties[[fn:1489]]. It is in this that we differ from him.
root.text.Part 2..5.6: Thou shalt hear hereafter his opinion, as also the opinion of the true Law, concerning the newness of the world.
root.text.Part 2..6.0: We have therefore explained that the word mal’ākh (angel) is a homonymous term, and that it compriss the Intelligences, the spheres, and the elements; for they all execute a command (of God). Yet it must not be believed that the spheres or the Intelligences are in the same rank as other forces purely corporeal, which are a mere nature[[fn:1490]] and possess no consciousness of their action; on the contrary, the spheres and the Intelligences have consciousness of their actions, and exercise liberty in their governance[[fn:1491]]. Albeit, this is not a liberty like unto ours, nor a rule like unto ours, in which everything depends upon things accidental and newly arisen. The Law contains several passages which awaken our attention thereto. Thus, for example, the angel says unto Lot: For I cannot do anything, etc. (Gen. XIX, 22); and he says unto him in saving him: “Behold, I have accepted thee concerning this thing also” (ibid., v. 21); and elsewhere it is said: “Beware of him (the angel), and obey his voice, provoke him not; for he will not pardon your transgressions: for My name is in him” (Exodus, XXIII, 21). All these passages indicate unto thee that they act with full consciousness[[fn:1492]] and that they possess will and liberty in the governance committed unto them[[fn:1493]], even as we possess a will in that which has been committed unto us, and the power of which has been given us from our birth. We, however, do sometimes the least possible; our rule and our action are preceded by privation[[fn:1494]], whereas it is not so with the Intelligences and the spheres. These, on the contrary, ever perform that which is good, and in them there is naught but good, as we shall set forth in other chapters; all that pertains unto them is found perfect and ever in actu, from the moment they have existed.
root.text.Part 2..7.0: It is one of the ancient opinions prevalent[[fn:1495]] amongst the philosophers and the generality of men, that the motion of the celestial spheres produces a great and right fearful sound[[fn:1496]]. To provide proof thereof, they allege that, since the small bodies here below[[fn:1497]], when they be moved with a rapid motion, cause a great noise and a terrifying clangour to be heard, by a much stronger reason must the bodies of the sun, the moon, and the stars, which be so great and so swift, do likewise. The whole Pythagorean sect believed that they possess harmonious sounds, which, notwithstanding their power, are proportioned among themselves, even as musical modulations are; and they bring forward[[fn:1498]] causes why we hear not these sounds so fearful and so loud. This opinion is likewise prevalent within our nation[[fn:1499]]. Perceivest thou not that the Doctors describe the great noise made by the sun whilst daily traversing the celestial sphere[[fn:1500]]? And the same follows for all (the other stars). Nevertheless, Aristotle refuss (to admit) this and shows that they have no sounds. Thou shalt find this in his book On the Heavens, and there mayest thou be instructed upon this subject. Be not offended that the opinion of Aristotle is here in opposition to that of the Doctors; for this opinion—to wit, that they (the stars) have sounds—does but follow the belief (which admitts) "that the sphere remains fixed and that the stars revolve[[fn:1501]]". But thou knowest that in these astronomical matters, they acknowledge the preponderance of the opinion of the sages of the nations of the world over their own: for thus they say plainly: "And the sages of the nations of the world prevailed[[fn:1502]]". And this is true; for all those who have spoken upon these speculative matters have done so only according to the result to which speculation had led them; wherefore one must believe that which has been established by demonstration[[fn:1503]].
root.text.Part 2..8.0: We have already expounded unto thee that the number of the spheres had not been determined in the time of Aristotle[[fn:1504]], and that those who, in our time, have reckoned nine spheres, have but considered as a single globe that which embraces several spheres[[fn:1505]], as is manifest unto him who has studied astronomy. Wherefore also one must not find fault with what one of the Doctors has said: "There are two firmaments, as it is said: Behold, the heaven and the heaven of heavens belong to the Lord thy God (Deut. X, 14)[[fn:1506]]." For he who said this has reckoned but a single globe for all the stars[[fn:1507]]—I mean, for the spheres containing stars—and has reckoned as the second globe the surrounding sphere, in which there is no star; wherefore he said: there are two firmaments.
root.text.Part 2..8.1: I shall make unto thee a preliminary observation which is necessary for the purpose which I have proposed to myself in this chapter; it is as follows:
root.text.Part 2..8.2: Know that concerning the two spheres[[fn:1508]] of Venus and Mercury, there is a divergence of opinion amongst the ancient mathematicians (as to whether) they be above or below the sun; for the order in which these two spheres are placed cannot be rigorously demonstrated[[fn:1509]]. The opinion of all the ancients was that the two spheres of Venus and Mercury are above the sun, which thing must be known and well understood[[fn:1510]]. Thereafter came Ptolemy, who preferred to admit that they are below, saying that it is more natural for the sun to be in the midst and that there be three planets above him and three below[[fn:1511]]. Subsequently there appeared in Andalusia, in these latter times, men[[fn:1512]] right well versed in mathematics, who showed, according to the principles of Ptolemy, that Venus and Mars are above the sun. Ibn-Aflah of Seville, with whose son I was connected, composed a famous book thereupon[[fn:1513]]; then the excellent philosopher Abu-Bekr ibn-al-Sa’igh[[fn:1514]], under one of whose disciples I have taken lessons, examined this subject, and produced certain arguments [which we have copied from him[[fn:1515]]], by which he represented it as improbable that Venus and Mercury be above the sun; but that which Abu-Bekr has said is an argument to show the improbability thereof, and proves not its impossibility. In short, whether it be so or not, (the fact remains that) all the ancients placed Venus and Mercury above the sun, and by reason of this, they reckoned the spheres[[fn:1516]] (to the number of) five: that of the moon, which, indubitably, is near unto us[[fn:1517]], that of the sun, which is necessarily above it, that of the five (other) planets, that of the fixed stars, and lastly the sphere which surrounds the whole, and in which there are no stars. Thus then, the figured spheres—I mean the spheres with figures, in which there are stars, for it is thus that the ancients called the stars figures, as is known from their writings—these spheres (say I) would be four in number[[fn:1518]]: the sphere of the fixed stars, that of the five planets, that of the sun, and that of the moon; and above all is a naked sphere, in which there are no stars. This number (of four) is for me an important principle for a subject which has come to my mind, and which I have not seen clearly (expounded) in any of the philosophers; but I have found in the discourses of the philosophers and in the words of the Doctors that which has awakened my attention thereto. I shall speak of it in the following chapter, and I shall expound the matter.
root.text.Part 2..9.0: It is known, and it is a thing widespread in all the books of the philosophers, that when they speak of the governance (of the world), they say that the governance of this inferior world—I mean of the world of generation and corruption—takes place only by means of the forces which flow from the celestial spheres. We have already said this several times, and thou shalt find that the Doctors say likewise[[fn:1519]]: "There is not even the smallest plant here below which has not in the firmament its mazzâl (that is to say, its star), which striks it and bidds it to grow, as it is said (Job, XXXVIII, 33): Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven, or canst thou set its dominion (its influence) upon the earth?— [By mazzâl, one designats also a star[[fn:1520]], as thou findest clearly at the beginning of Bereshith Rabba, where they say: ‘There is such a mazzâl (i.e., such a star or such a planet) which complets its course in thirty days, and another which complets its course in thirty years[[fn:1521]].’] — They have therefore clearly indicated by this passage that even the individuals of nature[[fn:1522]] are under the particular influence of the forces of certain stars; for, although all the forces of the celestial sphere together be diffused through all beings, each species nevertheless finds itself also under the particular influence of some star whatsoever[[fn:1523]]. It is as with the forces of a single body[[fn:1524]]; for the entire universe is a single individual, as we have said.—Thus it is that the philosophers have said that the moon has an augmentative force which is exercised particularly upon the element of water; that which proves it is that the seas and the rivers increase in measure as the moon waxes and decrease as it wans, and that the flood-tide, in the seas, is (in relation) with the advancement of the moon and the ebb-tide with its retrogradation—I mean its ascent and its descent in the quadrants of the orbit—as is clear and manifest unto him who has observed it[[fn:1525]]. That, on the other hand, the rays of the sun set in motion the element of fire, is a thing most evident, as thou seest by the heat which is diffused in the world in the presence of the sun, and by the cold which prevails as soon as it (the sun) withdraws from a place, or is hidden from it. This is too evident to be expounded at length.
root.text.Part 2..9.1: Knowing this, it has occurred to me that, albeit from the whole of these four figured spheres there emanate forces (which spread) into all beings that come into existence and of which they are the causes, yet each sphere may have (under its governance) one of the four elements, in such wise that a particular sphere be the principle of force for a particular element, to which, by its own motion, it gives the movement of generation[[fn:1526]]. Thus, the sphere of the moon would be that which movs the water; the sphere of the sun, that which movs the fire; the sphere of the other planets, that which movs the air [and their manifold motion, their inequality, their retrogradation, their directness and their station[[fn:1527]] produce the numerous configurations of the air, its variation and its prompt contraction and expansion]; finally, the sphere of the fixed stars, that which movs the earth; and it is perhaps for this cause that the latter movs with difficulty to receive impression and mixture[[fn:1528]], (I mean) because the fixed stars have a slow motion. To this relation of the fixed stars with the earth, allusion has been made in saying that the number of the species of plants corresponds to that of the individuals of the whole of the stars[[fn:1529]].
root.text.Part 2..9.2: In this manner, therefore, it is possible that the order (in nature) be this: four spheres, four elements moved by them, and four forces emanated from them (and acting) in nature in general, as we have set forth.
root.text.Part 2..9.3: Likewise, the causes of all movement of the spheres are four in number, to wit: the figure of the sphere,—I mean its sphericity,—its soul, its intellect whereby it conceivs, as we have explained, and the separate Intelligence, the object of its desire[[fn:1530]]. Thou must well possess thyself of this. Here is the explanation thereof: if it had not this (spherical) figure, it would by no means be possible for it to have a circular and continuous motion; for the continuity of motion ever repeated is possible only in circular motion alone. Rectilinear motion, on the contrary, even should the thing moved return several times over one and the same extent, could not be continuous; for, between two opposite motions, there is always a rest, as has been demonstrated in its place[[fn:1531]]. It is therefore manifest that it is a necessary condition of the continuity of motion ever returning over the same extent, that the thing moved should move circularly[[fn:1532]]. But naught save a living being can move; there must needs, therefore, exist a soul (in the sphere). It is indispensable also that there be something which invits to motion; this is a conception and the desire for that which has been conceived, as we have said. But this cannot take place here save by means of an intellect; for it is a question here neither of fleeing what is contrary, nor of seeking what is convenient. Finally, it is necessary that there be a being which has been conceived and which is the object of desire, as we have set forth. Thus there are four causes for the motion of the celestial sphere; and (there are also) four species of general forces descended from it towards us, which are: the force which brings minerals into being, that of the vegetative soul, that of the vital soul, and that of the rational soul, as we have set forth[[fn:1533]]. Then, if thou considerest the actions of these forces, thou shalt find that they are of two species, (to wit) to bring into being all that is born and to preserve this thing born, I mean to preserve its species perpetually and to preserve the individuals for a certain time. And this is what is meant by nature, of which it is said that it is wise, that it governs, that it takes care to produce the animal by an art similar to the artistic faculty (of man)[[fn:1534]], and that it takes care to preserve and perpetuate it, producing (first) formative forces which are the cause of its existence, and (afterward) nutritive faculties which are the cause whereby it endurs and is preserved as long as possible; in a word, this is that divine thing whence come the two actions in question, through the mediation of the celestial sphere.
root.text.Part 2..9.4: This number four is noteworthy and gives occasion for reflection. In the Midrash of Rabbi Tanhuma it is said: «How many steps had the ladder? four[[fn:1535]].» Here the passage is concerned and behold, a ladder was set up on the earth (Gen. XXVIII, 12). In all the Midrashim it is related «that there are four legions of angels,» and this is frequently repeated[[fn:1536]]. In some copies I have seen: «How many steps had the ladder? seven»; but all copies (of Midrash Tanhuma) and all Midrashim agree in saying that the angels of God whom he (Jacob) saw ascending and descending were but four, no more, «two ascending and two descending,» that the four stood together upon one of the steps of the ladder and that all four were upon one and the same rank, the two that ascended as well as the two that descended. They have therefore learned thence that the breadth of the ladder in the prophetic vision was like the universe and a third (of the universe); for the space of a single angel, in this prophetic vision, being as the third of the universe,—since it is said: And his body was like a TARSHISH (Daniel, x, 6)[[fn:1537]],—it follows that the space occupied by the four was like the universe and a third (of the universe). — In the allegories of Zechariah, after having described (ch. VI, v. 1) the four chariots coming out from between two mountains; and the mountains were mountains of brass (NE’HOSCHES), he adds to give the explanation thereof (Ibid, v. 5): These are the four spirits of the heavens, which go forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth, and which are the cause of all that is born[[fn:1538]]. In the mention of brass (NE’HOSCHES), as in the words burnished brass (NE’HOSCHES KALAL, Ezek., I, 7), naught was intended but a certain homonymy, and thou shalt hear later an observation thereupon[[fn:1539]].
root.text.Part 2..9.5: — As to what they say that the angel is the third part of the universe, — which they express textually in the Bereshith Rabbah by the words שהלמלאך שלישו של עולם, — it is very clear, and we have already set it forth in our great work on the traditional law[[fn:1540]]. For indeed, the whole of created things is divided into three parts: 1st, the separate Intelligences, which are the angels; 2nd, the bodies of the celestial spheres; 3rd, prime matter, I mean the continually changeable bodies, which are beneath the celestial sphere.
root.text.Part 2..9.6: Thus must he understand who desirs to comprehend the prophetic enigmas, to awaken from the slumber of sloth, to be rescued from the sea of ignorance, and to ascend unto things sublime[[fn:1541]]. As for him who delights in swimming in the seas of his own ignorance and in descending ever lower[[fn:1542]], he shall have no need to weary his body; yet shall his heart not be free from agitation[[fn:1543]], and he shall naturally sink to the lowest degree.
root.text.Part 2..9.7: It behoovs one well to understand all that has been said and to reflect thereupon.
root.text.Part 2..10.0: Know thou that if a mere mathematician read and understand those astronomical subjects of which mention has been made, he may believe that there is herein a decisive proof (demonstrating) that such are the form and the number of the spheres. However, it is not so, and such is not the quest of astronomical science[[fn:1544]]. Verily, there be some of these matters which are susceptible of demonstration[[fn:1545]]: thus, for example, it is demonstrated that the orbit of the sun declins from the equator, and there is no doubt thereof. But that it has an eccentric sphere, or an epicycle[[fn:1546]], is that which has not been demonstrated, and the astronomer does not trouble himself therewith; for the aim of this science is to establish a system whereby the motion of the star may be uniform and circular, being never accelerated, nor retarded, nor altered, and that the result thereof may accord with that which is observed[[fn:1547]]. Withal, the intent is[[fn:1548]] to diminish the motions and the number of the spheres as much as possible; for if, for instance, we can establish a system whereby the visible motions of a certain star can be justified by (the hypothesis of) three spheres, and another system whereby the same may be justified by four spheres, it is better to abide by the system in which the number of motions is less. Wherefore do we prefer, for the sun, eccentricity unto the epicycle, even as Ptolemy has said[[fn:1549]].—In this view therefore, since we perceive the motions of all the fixed stars as a single invariable motion, and as they change not their positions one toward another, we maintain (5[[fn:1550]]) that they are all in one single sphere; but it would not be impossible that each of these stars should be in a (particular) sphere, in such wise that they all had a uniform motion and that all these spheres (revolved) upon the same poles. There would then be Intelligences according to the number of the spheres, even as it is said: Can his armies be numbered? (Job, xxv, 3)? that is to say, by reason of their great number; for the Intelligences, the celestial bodies, and all the forces, all these together form his armies, and their species must of necessity be limited by a certain number. But, should it be so, this would in no wise prejudice our classification[[fn:1551]], in that we have counted as one the sphere of the fixed stars, even as we have counted as one the five spheres of the planets with the numerous spheres which they contain; for thou hast well understood that we have had no other aim than to count (as one) the totality of each force which we perceive in nature as a single whole[[fn:1552]], without concerning ourselves with rendering an exact account of the true state of the intelligences and the spheres[[fn:1553]].
root.text.Part 2..10.1: But our intent, in brief, is (to show): 1st, That all beings besides the Creator are divided into three classes: the first (compriss) the separate intelligences; the second, the bodies of the celestial spheres, which are substrata for stable forms, in which the form passes not from one substratum to another, nor is the substratum itself subject to change; the third, those bodies which are subject to generation and corruption and which are embraced by a single matter. 2nd, That the governance descends[[fn:1554]] from God upon the intelligences, according to their (successive) order, that the Intelligences, from what they have themselves received, pour forth benefits and lights upon the bodies of the celestial spheres, and that the spheres finally pour forth forces and benefits upon this (lower) body which is generated and perishes, (communicating unto it) that which they have received in greatest measure from their principles[[fn:1555]].
root.text.Part 2..10.2: It must be known that everything which, in this classification, communicats any good, has not for the sole final cause of its existence—though it be a giver[[fn:1556]]—the giving unto that which receivs; for (were it so), there would follow therefrom a manifest absurdity. Verily, the end is more noble than the things which exist for the sake of that end; now, it would follow (from the said supposition) that what is higher, more perfect, and more noble exists for the sake of that which is inferior to it, a thing which no intelligent man could imagine.
root.text.Part 2..10.3: But the matter is as I shall state: When a thing possesses a certain kind of perfection, sometimes this perfection occupies therein an extent (sufficient) for the thing itself to be perfect, without any perfection being communicated therefrom to another thing; sometimes the perfection has such an extent that there is a surplus wherewith to perfect another thing. Thus, to cite an example, thou wouldst say that there is a certain man who possesses a fortune sufficient only for his needs, and there remains naught in excess of which another may profit, and another who possesses a fortune of which there remains unto him a surplus[[fn:1557]] wherewith to enrich many people, so that he may give unto another person sufficiently for that person to be likewise rich and have enough remaining to enrich a third person. It is the same in the universe: the efflux, which comes from God to produce separate Intelligences, is also communicated from these intelligences so that they produce one another, even unto the Active Intellect, wherewith the production of separate (intelligences) ceass. From each separate (intelligence) there likewise emanats another production[[fn:1558]], until the spheres terminate at that of the moon. After this last comes this (lower) body which is generated and perishes, I mean prime matter and that which is composed thereof. From each sphere there come forces (which are communicated) unto the elements, until their efflux stays at the term of (the world of) generation and corruption.
