We have already set forth that all these things do in no wise subvert the words of our prophets and the pillars of our Law[[fn:1559]]; for our nation was a learned and perfect nation, even as God has proclaimed by the hand of the Master who perfected us, saying: Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people (Deut. IV, 6). But when the wicked among the ignorant nations had brought to nought our fair qualities, destroyed our sciences[[fn:1560]] and our books, and put to the sword our wise men,—so that we became ignorant, even as it had been threatened us on account of our sins, saying: The wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid (Isaiah, 29, 14),—we mingled with these nations[[fn:1561]], and their opinions passed unto us, as also did their manners and their actions. Even as it was said, concerning the assimilation of actions: They were mingled among the heathen and learned their works (Ps. 106, 35), so likewise was it said, concerning the opinions of the ignorant nations transmitted unto us: And they please themselves in the children of strangers (Isaiah, 2, 6)[[fn:1562]], which Jonathan ben-Uzziel translats: And they follow the laws of the nations. Since, therefore, we were nurtured in the habit of the opinions of the ignorant peoples, these philosophical matters appeared to be as foreign to our Law as they were to the opinions of the ignorant peoples, though in truth it be not so.
root.text.Part 2..10.4: Forasmuch as in our discourse mention has been made several times of the emanation (proceeding) from God and from the Intelligences, it behoovs us to set forth the true meaning thereof, I mean the idea designated by the word emanation. Thereafter, I shall begin to treat of the novelty of the world.
root.text.Part 2..11.0: It is manifest that everything which is produced[[fn:1563]] must of necessity have an efficient cause which caused it to be after it had not been. This proximate efficient cause can be naught else than either corporeal or incorporeal; nevertheless, a body, whatsoever it be, acts not in its capacity as a body, but it exerciss such an action because it is such a body, I mean to say (that it acts) by its form. I shall speak of this further on. This proximate efficient, producer of the thing produced, may itself be produced (of another thing); but this cannot continue unto infinity, and on the contrary, so soon as there is a thing produced, it is necessary that we arrive at last at a primitive, uncreated producer, who has produced the thing. But then there remains the question (to wit) why he has produced now and why he did it not sooner, since he existed. It must needs be, therefore, that this new act was impossible beforetime[[fn:1564]]: either because, the agent being corporeal, there lacked a certain relation between the agent and the object of the action; or because, the agent being incorporeal, there lacked the disposition of the matter[[fn:1565]].
root.text.Part 2..11.1: The entire exposition is the result of physical speculation[[t:0]]physique[[t:1]], without our presently concerning ourselves with the eternity or novelty of the world; for this is not the purpose of this chapter.
root.text.Part 2..11.2.sub_0: It has been set forth in physical science that every body which exerciss a certain action upon another body acts upon the latter only by approaching it, or by approaching something which approaches it, if this action be exercised by intermediaries. Thus, for example, this body which has now been heated, was so either because the fire itself approached it, or because the fire heated the air and the air surrounding the body heated it, so that it was the mass of hot air which was the proximate agent for heating this body. Thus it is that the loadstone attracts iron from afar by means of a force which proceeds from it into the air which approaches the iron. Wherefore it exerciss not attraction at any distance whatsoever, even as fire heats not at any distance whatsoever, but only at a distance which permitts the modification of the air that is between it and the thing heated by its force; but when the heat of the air coming from this fire is cut off (or removed) from beneath the wax, the latter can no longer be melted thereby; the same holds true concerning attraction. Now, for a thing which was not hot to become so thereafter, it was necessary that there should supervene a cause to heat it, whether a fire was kindled, or whether there were one at a certain distance which was changed. This is the relation which was lacking at first and which thereafter supervened. Likewise, (if we seek) the causes of all that occurrs in this world in the way of new creations, we shall find that the cause thereof is the mixture of the elements, bodies which act upon one another and receive action from one another, I mean that the cause of what is born is the drawing near or the withdrawal of the (elementary) bodies from one another. — As for that which we see brought into being without its being the simple consequence of the mixture[[fn:1566]], — and these are all the forms, — there is required for this also an efficient, I mean something which bestows the form. And this is by no means a body; for the efficient of the form is a form without matter, as has been set forth in its proper place[[fn:1567]], and we have previously indicated the proof thereof[[fn:1568]].
root.text.Part 2..11.2.sub_1: That which may further serve to explain this unto thee is that every mixture is susceptible of increase and decrease, and comes about by degrees; whereas it is not so with forms, for these do not arrive by degrees, and for this reason they have no motion, but they appear and disappear in an instant[[fn:1569]]. They are not, therefore, the effect of the mixture; rather, the mixture does but dispose matter to receive the form. The efficient cause of the form is a thing not susceptible of division, for its action is of the same kind as itself[[fn:1570]]; wherefore it is evident that the efficient cause of the form—I mean that which bestows it—is necessarily a form, and this is a separate (form)[[fn:1571]]. It is inadmissible that this efficient cause, which is incorporeal, should produce its impression by reason of a certain relation. For, being in no wise a body, it can neither draw nigh nor depart, nor can any body draw nigh unto it or depart from it; for there exists no relation of distance between the corporeal and the incorporeal. It follows thence by necessity that the absence of this action[[fn:1572]] is caused by the lack of disposition in such matter to receive the action of the Separate Being.
root.text.Part 2..11.3.sub_0: It is therefore manifest that the action which the (elementary) bodies, by virtue of their (particular) forms, exert one upon another, results in disposing the (various) matters to receive the action of that which is incorporeal, that is to say, those actions which are the forms[[fn:1573]]. Now, since the impressions of the Separate Intelligence[[fn:1574]] are manifest and evident in this world—I speak of all those novelties (of nature) which arise not from the mere mixture in itself—it must perforce be acknowledged that this efficient cause acts not by contact, nor at a fixed distance, since it is incorporeal. This action of the Separate Intelligence is ever designated by the word emanation (FÉIDH), by comparison with a fountain of water which overflows on all sides, and which has no fixed sides, neither whence it flows forth, nor whither it spreads itself elsewhere, but it gushes from every part and continually waters all sides around, both what is near and what is far. For it is even so with this Intelligence: no force comes unto it from a certain side nor from a certain distance, nor does its force reach elsewhere by a determined side, nor at a determined distance, nor at one time rather than another; on the contrary, its action is perpetual, and whenever a thing has been disposed[[fn:1575]], it receivs this ever-existing action which has been designated by the word emanation. Likewise, as the incorporeity of the Creator has been demonstrated, and it has been established that the universe is His work and that He is its efficient cause—as we have set forth and shall further set forth—it has been said that the world comes from the emanation of God, and that God has poured forth upon it all that therein occurrs[[fn:1576]]. In like manner it has been said that God has poured forth His knowledge upon the prophets. All this signifies that these actions are the work of an incorporeal Being; and it is the action of such a Being that is called emanation. The Hebrew tongue likewise has employed this word—I mean (the word) emanation—in speaking of God, by comparison with a fountain of water which overflows[[fn:1577]], as we have said.
root.text.Part 2..11.3.sub_1: Verily, no better expression could be found than that—I mean fÉidh (emanation)—to designate by comparison the action of the Separate Being; for we could not find a word truly corresponding to the real idea, the conception of the action of the Separate Being being a thing most difficult, even as difficult as the conception of the very existence of the Separate Being. Even as the imagination cannot conceive a being otherwise than as a body or as a force in a body, so it cannot conceive that an action can be exerted otherwise than by the contact of an agent, or at least at a certain (limited) distance and from a determined side. Now, as for certain men, even of the vulgar, it is an established thing that God is incorporeal, or even that He draws not nigh unto the thing which He makes, they have imagined that He gives His commands unto the angels, and that these perform the actions by contact and by a corporeal approach, as we ourselves act upon what we make; they have therefore imagined that the angels also are bodies. Some there be who believe that God commands the thing by speaking even as we speak—I mean by letters and sounds—and that then the thing is made[[fn:1578]]. All this is to follow the imagination, which is also, in truth, the yécer ha-ra’ (the evil imagination)[[fn:1579]]; for every rational or moral vice is the work of the imagination or the consequence of its action. But this is not the purpose of this chapter. We rather intend to make understood what is meant by emanation, in speaking either of God, or of the Intelligences or the angels, who are incorporeal[[fn:1580]]. It is also said of the forces of the celestial spheres that they emanate upon the (lower) world, and it is said: 'the emanation of the celestial sphere,' although the effects produced by the latter come from a body, and for that reason the stars act at a determined distance—to wit, according as they are near to or far from the centre (of the world) and according to their mutual relation[[fn:1581]]. Herein is the first starting-point of judicial astrology[[fn:1582]].
root.text.Part 2..11.4: As to what we have stated, that the prophets likewise metaphorically presented the action of God through the idea of [[t:0]]efflux[[t:1]], it is, for instance, in this passage: [[t:2]]They have forsaken Me[[t:3]], [[t:4]]the Fount of living waters[[t:5]] (Jeremiah, 2, 13), which signifies [[t:6]]efflux of life[[t:7]], that is to say, of [[t:8]]existence[[t:9]], which, indubitably, is life. Similarly it has been stated: [[t:10]]For with Thee is the Fount of life[[t:11]] (Ps. 36, 10), which signifies the [[t:12]]efflux of existence;[[t:13]] and it is again the same idea which is expressed at the close of that passage by the words: [[t:14]]in Thy light we see light[[t:15]] (which signifies) that, through the efflux of the [[t:16]]intellect[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]active[[t:19]]) which has emanated from Thee, we cogitate, and thereby are we directed and guided[[fn:1583]] and apprehend the (active) intellect. Thou must impress this deeply upon thy mind.
root.text.Part 2..12.0: Touching the question whether the world be eternal or created, those who admit the existence of God have professed three different opinions[[fn:1584]]:
root.text.Part 2..12.1: I. The first opinion, embraced by all those who admit the Law of Moses our Master, is this: That the universe in its totality, I mean every being except God, was produced by God from pure and absolute non-existence; that there had existed at first only God alone, and naught beside Him, neither angel, nor sphere, nor that which is within the celestial sphere; that subsequently He produced all these beings, such as they are, by His free will and not out of any thing; finally, that time itself is likewise part of the created things, since it accompanies motion, which is an accident of the thing moved, and that this thing itself, whose motion time accompanies, was created and has come into being after having not existed. For if it be said, “God was before He created the world,”—where the word was denots a time,—and likewise if it follows thence for the mind[[fn:1585]] that His existence before the creation of the world was prolonged unto infinity, there is in all this naught but a supposition or imagination of time, and not the reality of time; for time is indubitably an accident, and it belongs, in our view, to the created accidents as much as blackness and whiteness. Although it be not of the species of quality[[fn:1586]], it is yet, in short, an accident inherent in motion, as is clear unto him who has understood what Aristotle says to explain time and its true being[[fn:1587]].
root.text.Part 2..12.2: We shall here give an explanation, which will be profitable for the subject we treat, albeit it does not relate thereto directly. That which (say we) has caused time to remain an obscure matter for the most part of the men of science, so that they have been undecided[[fn:1588]] — as for example Galen[[fn:1589]] and others — upon the question of whether it has, or has not, a real existence, is that it is an accident within another accident. Verily, the accidents which exist in bodies in an immediate manner, such as colours and tastes, are understood at first sight and the idea thereof is conceived. But the accidents whose substrata are other accidents, as, for example, the brightness in colour, or curvature and roundness in a line, are a very obscure thing, especially when there is joined thereto this circumstance, that the accident which serves as a substratum is not in a fixed state, but changs its condition[[fn:1590]]; for then the matter is more obscure. Now, in time, both things are united; for at first it is an accident inherent in motion, which is an accident in the thing moved; and subsequently motion is not in the condition of blackness or whiteness, which are somewhat fixed, but on the contrary, it is of the very essence of motion not to remain a single twinkling of an eye in the same state. It is this, therefore, which has caused time to remain an obscure thing.
root.text.Part 2..12.3: Our purpose is to establish that, for us, it is a thing created and brought into existence, like other accidents and like the substances which bear these accidents. Consequently, the production of the world by God could not have had a temporal beginning, time being itself part of the created things.
root.text.Part 2..12.4: Thou must meditate deeply upon this subject, so that thou be not exposed to the objections from which he who is ignorant of this cannot escape. Indeed, as soon as thou affirmest that there existed a time before the world, thou art obliged to admit eternity; for time being an accident, for which a substratum is necessarily required, it would follow thence that something existed before the existence of this world which now exists, and it is precisely that which we wish to avoid.
root.text.Part 2..12.5: Such then is one of the three opinions, which forms indubitably a fundamental principle of the Law of Moses our Master, the second principle after that of the Unity of God; and it must by no means occur to thy mind that it could be otherwise. It was our father Abraham who began to publish this opinion, unto which he had been led by speculation; wherefore he proclaimed the name of the Lord, the Everlasting God[[fn:1591]]. He clearly expressed this opinion in saying: Possessor of heaven and earth (Genesis, xiv, 22).
root.text.Part 2..12.6: II. The second opinion is that of all the philosophers of whom we have heard tell, or whose words we have seen. It is inadmissible, say they, that God should produce aught from nothing; nor is it possible, according to their view, that a thing be reduced to (absolute) non-existence; I mean to say, that it is not possible that any being whatsoever, having matter and form, should be born without matter having ever existed, nor that it should perish in such wise that matter itself be reduced to absolute non-existence[[fn:1592]]. To attribute unto God the power of (doing) such a thing would be, in their sight, as though one attributed unto Him the power of joining together at the same instant[[fn:1593]] two contraries, or of creating His like, or of becoming corporeal, or of creating a square whose diagonal should be equal to its side, or similar impossible things. What is implied in their words is that they mean to say that, even as He cannot be charged with impotence for not producing impossible things—for the impossible has a stable nature, which is not the work of an agent, and which, because of this, is invariable[[fn:1594]]—likewise one cannot attribute impotence unto Him because He should not be capable of producing aught from (absolute) non-existence; for that belongs to the category of all impossible things. They believe, therefore, that there exists a matter which is eternal even as God is eternal; that He exists not without it, nor it without Him. Nevertheless, they do not believe for all that that it occupies in being the same rank as God; but, on the contrary, God is (according to them) the cause wherefore it exists, and it is unto Him as the clay is unto the potter, or as the iron is unto the smith. He creats therein what He wills: now He forms of it heaven and earth, and now He forms of it somewhat else.
root.text.Part 2..12.7: The partisans of this opinion believe that the heaven also was born and is perishable, but that it was not born of nothing, nor is it to perish (in such wise as to return) to nothing. On the contrary, even as the individuals among animals are born and perish (issuing) from a matter which exists and (returning) to a matter which exists, likewise the heaven was born and must perish, and it is with its birth and its corruption even as with those of the other beings which are beneath it. Those who belong to this sect are divided into several classes, the divisions and opinions of which it is useless to mention in this treatise; but[[fn:1595]] the universal principle of this sect is that which I have told thee. Plato also professes this opinion; thou shalt find that Aristotle relats of him in the Acroasis (or the Physics) that he believed—that is to say, Plato—that the heaven was born and is perishable[[fn:1596]], and likewise thou shalt find his opinion clearly expressed in his book to Timaeus[[fn:1597]]. Nevertheless, he believs not that which we believe, as is thought by those who scrutinize not opinions and study not with care, and who imagine that our opinion and his are similar. It is not so at all; for we believe that the heaven was born, not of something, but of absolute non-existence, whilst he believs that it existed (virtually) and was formed of something[[fn:1598]]. Such is the second opinion.
root.text.Part 2..12.8: III. The third opinion is that of Aristotle, of his followers, and of the commentators of his works. He maintains, with the adepts of the sect of which mention has just been made, that no material thing can be produced without a (pre-existing) matter; but he maintains further that the heaven is in no wise subject to generation and corruption. Here is the summary of his opinion: He claims that this entire universe, even as it is, has always been and shall always be thus[[fn:1599]]; that the stable thing which is not subject to generation and corruption, that is to say, the heaven, never ceass to be such (as it is); that time and motion are eternal and permanent, without beginning or end; that that which is born and perishes, to wit, that which is beneath the sphere of the moon, continus ever thus [that is to say, that this prime matter in itself was not born and shall not perish, but that forms succeed one another therein, so that, being despoiled of one form, it invests itself with another]; finally, that this whole order (of the universe), the superior as well as the inferior, shall not be altered and shall not cease, that nothing new shall be produced therein which is not in its nature, and that there shall happen absolutely nothing[[fn:1600]] which departs from the rule.
root.text.Part 2..12.9: He says [for, although he expresses himself not in these terms, it is yet that which results from his opinion] that it is, in his view, of the category of the impossible that God should change His will or that there should come upon Him a new volition, and that this whole universe, even as it is, God has made to exist by His will, without however having made aught from nothing. Even as, he thinks, it is of the category of the impossible that God should cease to exist or that His essence should change, so is it of the category of the impossible that He should change His will or that there should come upon Him a new desire. It follows consequently that this whole universe, as it is now, even so has it been from all eternity and even so shall it be for evermore.
root.text.Part 2..12.10: Such is the summary of these opinions and their true sense; and these are the opinions of those for whom it is a thing demonstrated that there exists a God for this universe. As for those who have not acknowledged the existence of God, but who have thought that things are born and perish[[fn:1601]] by aggregation and separation[[fn:1602]], according to chance, and that there is no being who governs and orders the universe—and these are Epicurus, his sect, and those like unto him, as Alexander relats—it is of no utility for us to speak of these sects; for the existence of God has been demonstrated, and it would be useless to mention the opinions of people who have built their system upon a foundation which has already been overthrown by demonstration[[fn:1603]]. It would be equally useless for us to make efforts to establish the truth of what is said by the partisans of the second opinion, namely, that the heaven is born and that it is perishable; for those men admit the eternity (of matter), and there is no difference, in our view, between those who believe that the heaven was necessarily born of something and that it shall return thither in perishing, and the opinion of Aristotle, who believs that it was not born and that it shall not perish. In truth, all who follow the Law of Moses and of our father Abraham, or who walk in their footsteps, tend to naught else but this belief: that there exists absolutely no eternal thing beside God, and that to produce being from (absolute) non-existence is not for God of the category of the impossible; nay, in the opinion of certain thinkers, it is even a necessary thing[[fn:1604]].
root.text.Part 2..12.11: Having set forth the divers opinions, I proceed to expound in brief[[fn:1605]] the proofs of Aristotle which he adducs for his own opinion, and the manner in which he was led thereto.
root.text.Part 2..13.0: I need not reiterate in every chapter that I have composed this treatise for thee only because I am mindful of thy attainments[[fn:1606]]; it is therefore not necessary that I should everywhere cite the words of the philosophers verbatim, but it suffices to indicate the subjects thereof, without prolixity, and merely calling thy attention to the methods of demonstration which they had in view, even as I have done regarding the opinions of the Mutakallimūn. I shall pay no regard to those who, besides Aristotle, have reasoned upon these matters; for his opinions alone are those which demand examination, and if that which we object against him, or the doubt which we raise against him upon any point whatsoever, be well-founded[[fn:1607]], it will be yet more so and will have greater force with respect to all others who contradict the fundamental principles of the Law. — I say then[[fn:1608]]:
root.text.Part 2..13.1: I. Aristotle says that motion had no beginning, neither shall it perish — that is to say, motion par excellence[[fn:1609]] —; for, says he, if motion were newly come into existence, then, every newly-occurred thing being preceded by a motion, which is its transition from potentiality to actuality and its becoming after not having been, it would follow that there had already existed a motion, to wit, that by virtue of which this later motion exists. Therefore, the first motion is necessarily eternal; otherwise, the matter would regress to infinity[[fn:1610]]. Proceeding from this principle, he further says that time had no beginning, neither shall it perish; for time accompanies motion and is inherent therein, so that motion occurrs only in time, and time cannot be conceived save with motion, as has been demonstrated[[fn:1611]]. — This is a first method of his, from which one may conclude the eternity of the world.
root.text.Part 2..13.2: II. A second method of his is this: Prime matter, says he, common to the four elements, had no beginning, neither shall it perish; for, if prime matter had come into being, it would in its turn have a matter from which it was produced, whence it would follow that this produced matter would be endowed with form, which is the true condition of becoming. Now, as we have supposed it to be a matter not endowed with form, it necessarily follows that it is not born of anything; it is therefore eternal and shall not perish[[fn:1612]]. And this likewise leads to the eternity of the world[[fn:1613]].
root.text.Part 2..13.3: III. His [[t:0]]Third Method[[t:1]]: In the substance of the entire celestial sphere, he states, no species of [[t:2]]contrariety[[t:3]] exists, circular motion having no [[t:4]]contrary[[t:5]], as has been expounded; contrariety, as has been demonstrated, occurs only in rectilinear motion[[fn:1614]]. Now, he continues, everything that perishes has for the cause of its perdition only the contrariety inherent within it; but, as there is no contrariety in the celestial sphere, the latter does not perish[[fn:1615]], and that which does not perish is likewise not [[t:6]]generated[[t:7]]. For he enunciates absolutely the following propositions: all that is generated is perishable; all that is perishable is generated; all that is not generated is not perishable; all that is not perishable is not generated[[fn:1616]]. This, then, is yet another method by which he arrives, as is his object, at establishing the eternity of the world[[fn:1617]].
root.text.Part 2..13.4: IV. Fourth method: In everything that comes into being (or is born), says he, the possibility of its coming into being temporally preceds that which comes into being; and likewise, in all that changs, the possibility of changing temporally preceds the change. From this proposition he concluds that circular motion is perpetual and has neither end nor beginning; and it is also by this proposition that his modern followers have explained the eternity of the world[[fn:1618]]. Ere the world was, say they, its birth must needs have been either possible, or necessary, or impossible; now, if its birth were necessary, it has always existed; if its birth were impossible, it could never have existed; finally, if it were possible, what then would be the substratum of this possibility? It was therefore necessary that there should exist something which should be the substratum of the possibility, and whereby the thing in question might be said to be possible. — This is a most puissant method for establishing the eternity of the world.
root.text.Part 2..13.5: Some of the most discerning among the modern Mutakallemīn have sought to resolve the difficulty by saying: possibility resids in the agent and not in the object of the action. But this is void of significance; for there be two distinct possibilities. Verily, in everything that is born, the possibility of being born is anterior to the birth; and likewise, in the agent who has caused it to be born, the possibility of bringing such a thing into being existed before he brought it into being; there be therefore, indubitably, two possibilities: a possibility in the matter, (that) of becoming such a thing, and a possibility in the agent, (that) of doing such a thing.
root.text.Part 2..13.6: Such are the principal methods followed by Aristotle to establish the eternity of the world, by taking the world itself as his starting-point.
root.text.Part 2..13.7: But there be certain other methods, mentioned by his successors, who have derived them from his philosophy, and in which they establish the eternity of the world by taking God as their starting-point.
root.text.Part 2..13.8: V. One of these (is as follows): If, say they, God had produced the world out of nothing, God would have been, before creating the world, an agent in potentiality, and by creating it, He would have become an agent in actuality. God would therefore have passed from potentiality to actuality, and, consequently, there would have been in Him a possibility and He would have required an efficient cause to have made Him pass from potentiality to actuality[[fn:1619]]. — This is again a great difficulty, upon which every intelligent man must meditate, in order to resolve it and to fathom its mystery[[fn:1620]].
root.text.Part 2..13.9: VI. Another method: If an agent, say they, at one time acts and at another time acts not, this can only be by reason of obstacles or wants[[fn:1621]] which supervene unto him or which are within him; for obstacles constrain him to desist from doing that which he would have willed, and wants[[fn:1622]] constrain him to will that which he had not willed before. Now, whereas the Creator has no wants that might bring about a change of will, and as there are for Him neither hindrances nor obstacles that might supervene or cease, there is no reason why He should act at one time and act not at another time; on the contrary, His action must perpetually exist in actuality, even as He is Himself perpetual.
root.text.Part 2..13.10: VII. [[t:0]]Another method:[[t:1]] The works of God, they say, are very perfect, and there is nothing defective, useless, or superfluous in them. This is what Aristotle continually repeats, saying: [Lat.: natura est sapientia] the nature is wise and does nothing in vain, but makes each thing in the most perfect manner possible[[fn:1623]]. From this, they say, it follows that this universe is the most perfect of all, and there is nothing that surpasses it[[fn:1624]]; therefore, it must be eternal, for the wisdom of God is eternal as His essence, or rather His essence is (itself) His wisdom which has required the existence of this universe.
root.text.Part 2..13.11: All that thou shalt find, in the way of argumentations (proceeding) from those who admit the eternity of the world, derivs from these methods and may be reduced to one of them.
root.text.Part 2..13.12: They say further, as if to reduce the matter to an absurdity: How could it be that God had been idle, doing absolutely naught and producing naught throughout all past eternity[[fn:1625]], and that after having done naught during the whole duration of His eternal existence which is without end, He should since yesterday have commenced (to create) the universe? For, even shouldst thou say, for example, that before this world God created many others, as numerous as the grains of mustard-seed which the globe of the utmost sphere might contain, and that each of these worlds has existed for as many years as that same content of grains of mustard-seed, all this would still be, in comparison with the infinite existence of God, as though thou saidst that it was but yesterday that God created the world. Verily, so soon as we affirm that the universe commenced after absolute non-existence, it matters little whether thou admittest that this took place hundreds of thousands of years ago[[fn:1626]] or from a time most nigh; for they who admit the eternity (of the world) find this equally absurd.
root.text.Part 2..13.13: Argument has been made also from that which has at all times been generally received[[fn:1627]] by all peoples, and whence it results that the thing is natural and not (merely) hypothetical; so that men have come to an agreement in this regard. All men, says Aristotle, openly acknowledge the perpetuity and the stability of the heaven, and, as they have perceived that it is not born and that it is likewise not perishable, they have made of it the dwelling-place of God and of spiritual beings, that is to say, of the angels; they have attributed it to God to indicate His perpetuity[[fn:1628]]. He allegs, in the same chapter, other things of this kind, in order to strengthen, by probable opinions[[fn:1629]], the opinion which speculation had caused him to recognize as true.
root.text.Part 2..14.0: My aim, in this chapter, is to set forth that Aristotle possesses no demonstration touching the eternity of the world according to his opinion.
root.text.Part 2..14.1: He does not even deceive himself in this matter; I mean that he himself knows that he has no demonstration thereof, and that those argumentations and those proofs which he adducs are but those which possess the greatest semblance of truth and toward which the soul most strongly inclins. They are indeed, as Alexander maintains, those which offer the fewest doubts; yet it must by no means be believed that an Aristotle could have taken these reasonings for a demonstration, since it was Aristotle himself who taught unto men the methods of true demonstration, its rules and its conditions.
root.text.Part 2..14.2: — That which has induced me to speak of this is that the moderns among the followers of Aristotle claim that he has demonstrated the eternity of the world. Most of those who profess to be philosophers do therefore follow, in this question, the authority of Aristotle, believing that all which he has said is a decisive demonstration in which there is naught of doubt; and they even deem it absurd to gainsay him, or to suppose that anything could have remained hidden[[fn:1630]] from him, or that he could have erred in any matter whatsoever.
root.text.Part 2..14.3: Wherefore I have deemed it my duty to proceed with them according to their own opinion, and to show them that Aristotle himself does not pretend to give a demonstration upon this question. Thus, for example, he says in the Acroasis: “All the physicists who have preceded us believed that motion had no beginning and is imperishable, with the exception of Plato, who believed that motion had a beginning and is perishable; and likewise the heavens, according to him, had a beginning and are perishable.” Such are his expressions[[fn:1631]]. Now, it is clear that if this question had been demonstrated by rigorous demonstrations, Aristotle would have had no need to support it by the concordant opinion of the ancient physicists[[fn:1632]], nor would he have had need to say all that he has said in the same place to show the absurdity of those who gainsay him and to render their opinion contemptible; for, as soon as a thing is demonstrated, its truth cannot increase, nor can its certainty be strengthened by the common consent of all the learned, and on the other hand, its truth cannot diminish, nor its certainty be weakened, by the contradiction of all the inhabitants of the earth. Thou shalt also find that Aristotle, in the treatise On the Heavens and the World, where he beginns to set forth that the heavens had no beginning and are imperishable, expresses himself thus: “We wish therefore, after this[[fn:1633]], further to make researches concerning the heavens, and we say: dost thou believe they were created from something, or that they were not? that they are subject to corruption, or that they shall never perish[[fn:1634]]?” After having posed this question, desiring (as he says) to report the arguments of those who say that the heavens had a beginning[[fn:1635]], he continus in the following terms: “When we shall have done this, our words will be received with more benevolence by those who excel in speculation; especially when they shall first have heard the arguments of the adversaries. For if, without reporting the arguments of our adversaries, we were to state only our own opinion and our arguments, these would appear to the hearers too weak to be accepted. It is worthy of him who wishes to judge with truth not to be hostile toward him who contradicts him; he ought, on the contrary, to be benevolent and impartial toward him, rendering justice to his arguments as to his own[[fn:1636]].” Such are the textual words of this man.
root.text.Part 2..14.4: And now, O all ye who are thinkers! is there yet, after this preliminary declaration, aught for which to blame this man? Shall it still be believed, after such words, that he possessed a demonstration upon this question? Can any man whatsoever, and much more so Aristotle, imagine that a thing which has been demonstrated could be feebly received if one has not heard the arguments of those who gainsay it? — Furthermore, Aristotle declaring that this is an opinion[[fn:1637]] of his own and that his proofs thereupon are but dialectical argumentations, — is it an Aristotle who could be ignorant of the difference between argumentations and demonstrations, between opinions which appear to the mind strong or weak and demonstrative things? Finally, this oratorical expression of impartiality toward the adversary, which he adds as if to strengthen his opinion! is there need of all this in a demonstration? Certes, no; but all that he has in view is to show that his opinion is truer than that of his adversaries, or of those who claim that philosophical speculation leads to the admission that the heavens are subject to birth and corruption, but that nevertheless they were never absolutely non-existent, — or that they were formed from something, — and that they shall not absolutely perish[[fn:1638]]; and other similar things which he reports of these opinions. And this is indubitably true; for indeed his opinion is nearer to the truth than theirs, when one seeks to argue from the nature of being. But we do not think thus[[fn:1639]], as I shall set forth. Nevertheless, all the sects, and even the philosophers, have suffered themselves to be led away by passions, so that they have wished to establish that Aristotle has demonstrated this question. Perchance, according to their opinion, Aristotle made a demonstration upon this question without perceiving it himself[[fn:1640]], so that it was only after him that the remark was made! — As for me, it seems to me beyond doubt that all the opinions which Aristotle expresses upon these subjects, — I mean the eternity of the world, the cause of the varied motions of the spheres, and the order of the Intelligences, — that all this, I say, is not susceptible of a demonstration. Thus Aristotle never had the thought that these reasonings could be considered a demonstration; on the contrary, as he himself says, we have no means of approaching these things by demonstrative methods[[fn:1641]], and they possess for us no principle from which we might argue[[fn:1642]].
root.text.Part 2..14.5: Thou art acquainted with the text of his words, which run thus: 'And there are (problems) concerning which we have no argument, or which appear grave unto us; for it is difficult for us to declare the why thereof, as for instance the question whether the world be eternal or not.'[[fn:1643]] Such are his expressions. But thou knowest how Abu-Naçr (al-Farâbi) interpreted this example, what explanation he gave thereof, and how he repelled (the notion) that Aristotle could have doubted the eternity of the world.[[fn:1644]] He speaks of Galen with sovereign contempt, because the latter had said that this is an obscure question for which no demonstration is known.[[fn:1645]] Abu-Naçr thinks that it is a clear and evident thing, susceptible of a (rigorous) demonstration, that the heaven is eternal, and that what is within it is subject to birth and corruption.
root.text.Part 2..14.6: In sum, it is not by any of the manners which we have related in this chapter that an opinion may be confirmed, or destroyed, or called into doubt.[[fn:1646]]
root.text.Part 2..14.7: We have made these citations only because we know that most of those who pretend to be geniuses, albeit they understand no science, pronounce upon the eternity of the world by following the authority of the celebrated scholars who have proclaimed its eternity, and reject the words of all the prophets, because these are not conceived in the didactic style,[[fn:1647]] but in that of a proclamation on the part of God. In this path (of the prophets) are guided only a few whom intelligence has favoured.
root.text.Part 2..14.8: That which we desire (to establish), for our part, relative to the creation of the world, according to the opinion of our Law, I shall declare in the following chapters.
root.text.Part 2..15.0: Behold a chapter in which I shall set forth unto thee my thoughts upon this question, and thereafter I shall allege proofs for that which we desire (to establish). I say, therefore, concerning all that is uttered by those of the Mutakallimun who claim to have demonstrated the creation of the world, that I accept not those proofs, and that I will not deceive myself by decorating sophistical methods with the name of demonstrations. If a man claims to demonstrate a certain question by sophisms, he does not, in my judgment, strengthen the belief in that thing which is sought, but, on the contrary, he weakens it and gives occasion to contest the matter; for the nullity of these proofs having become manifest, the soul refuss to believe[[fn:1648]] what one has sought to prove. It were better that the thing upon which there is no demonstration should remain simply in the state of a question, or that one should accept (by tradition)[[fn:1649]] one of the two terms of the contradiction. I have already related the methods whereby the Mutakallimun establish the creation of the world,[[fn:1650]] and I have called thy attention to the criticism to which they give rise. Likewise, all that Aristotle and his successors have said to prove the eternity of the world is not, in my judgment, a rigorous demonstration; they are, on the contrary, but argumentations subject to grave doubts, as thou shalt hear (hereafter).
root.text.Part 2..15.1: What I desire to effect, for my part, is to demonstrate that the creation of the world ex nihilo, in accordance with the opinion of our Law which I have already set forth, is by no means impossible, and that all those philosophical disputations, wherefrom it seems to follow that the matter is not as we have stated[[fn:1651]],—that all these reasonings (I say) have a side whereby one may demolish them and prevent their being employed as arguments against us. This being ascertained by me, and this question,—to wit, whether the world be eternal or created,—remaining undetermined[[fn:1652]], I accept the solution afforded by prophecy[[fn:1653]], which explains things whereunto the speculative faculty could not attain; for we shall set forth that prophecy is no vain thing, even according to the opinion of him who admitts the eternity (of the world).
root.text.Part 2..15.2: Having set forth that what we maintain is possible, I shall likewise endeavour, by speculative proof, to make it prevail[[fn:1654]] over the other (opinion); I mean, to make the opinion of creation prevail over that of eternity. I shall show that, if we be led to some absurd consequence by admitting creation, one is driven to a yet more grievous absurdity by admitting eternity.
root.text.Part 2..15.3: And now I shall attempt to present a method for demolishing the proofs of all those who argue in favour of the eternity of the world.
root.text.Part 2..16.0: Every new thing that comes into being after having not existed,—albeit its matter existed and the latter did but divest itself of one form and invest itself with another,—possesses, after it is born, perfected, and arrived at its final state, a nature other than that which it had at the moment when it was being born and began to pass from potentiality into actuality, and different also from that which it had before moving to pass into actuality[[fn:1655]]. Thus, for example, the female semen, whilst it is as yet but blood in the vessels, has a nature different from that which it has at the moment of conception, when it has been touched by the male semen and beginns to move; and the nature which it has in that moment is likewise different from that of the perfect animal after its birth. One cannot in any wise argue from the nature which a thing has, after it is born, perfected, and arrived finally at its most perfect state, concerning the state in which that thing was at the moment when it was moving towards birth. Nor can one argue from the state in which it was at the moment of moving concerning that in which it was before it began to move. So soon as thou errest therein and persistest in arguing from the nature of a thing arrived at actuality concerning that which it had whilst being in potentiality, grave doubts arise within thee; things which must be appear unto thee absurd[[fn:1656]], and absurd things seem unto thee as though they must be.
root.text.Part 2..16.1.sub_0: Let there be made, touching the example which we have alleged, the following supposition[[fn:1657]]: A man was born with a most perfect disposition[[fn:1658]]; his mother having died after having suckled him for some months, the husband[[fn:1659]] alone occupied himself, in a retired island, with completing the education of this child, until he had grown up and become intelligent and instructed. Having never seen either woman or any female of the animals, he asked one day of one of the men who were with him: “How comes it that we exist, and in what manner were we formed?” He to whom he had addressed the question replied: “Every one of us was formed in the womb of an individual of our species, like unto ourselves, and who was a woman having such and such a form; every one of us was a small body in the interior of the womb, moving, feeding, growing little by little, living, until, arrived at such a limit of greatness, there opened for him, in the lower part of the body (of the woman), a door through which he appeared and came forth, and after that he ceased not to grow until he became such as thou seest us.” This orphan child will necessarily inquire anew and say: “This individual among us, whilst he was small in the womb, living, moving, and growing, did he eat? did he drink? did he breathe by the mouth and the nose? did he void excrements?” — Nay, it will be answered him. — But he will undoubtedly hasten to deny this, and will demonstrate the impossibility of all these things, which nevertheless are true[[fn:1660]], by arguing from the perfect being arrived at its final state. “If one of us,” he will say, “were for some moments deprived of breath, he would die, and his movements would cease; and how then can one figure to oneself that any of us could remain for months within a thick membrane[[fn:1661]], enclosed in the interior of a body, and withal live and move? If one of us could swallow a sparrow, verily, that sparrow would die instantaneously as soon as it arrived in the stomach, and much more so in the lower belly. Every one of us, if he took no food by the mouth and if he drank not, would undoubtedly die at the end of a few days; and how then could an individual remain for months without eating or drinking?”
root.text.Part 2..16.1.sub_1: “If any one of us, after having taken food, were not to void the excrements, he would perish in a few days in the most grievous pains; how then could that being remain for months without voiding any excrement? If one were to pierce the belly of any of us, he would die within a few days; how then can it be believed that this foetus has the umbilicus open? how, finally, does it come to pass that he opens not his eyes, nor extends his hands, nor stretches forth his feet, as ye assert, seeing that all his members are in good condition and suffer no malady?” — And thus he will pursue his reasonings, to prove that it is impossible for man to be formed in such a manner.
root.text.Part 2..16.2: Examine well this example and reflect thereon, O thou who seekest to think! and thou shalt find that such is likewise our condition in respect of Aristotle. Indeed, all we, the followers of Moses our Master and of Abraham our Father, believe that the world was formed in such and such a manner, that it developed in such a manner[[fn:1662]], and that one thing was created after another; but Aristotle setts himself to contradict us, arguing against us from the nature of being as it has attained its final state, perfect and existing in act, whilst we, on our part, affirm unto him that after having attained its final state and become perfect, it resembls in no wise that which it was at the moment of its birth, and that it was produced out of absolute non-existence. What argument, therefore, can be drawn against us from all that he says? for these arguments strike only him who claims that it is the nature of this being, having reached its final state, which proves of itself that it was created, whereas I have already made known unto thee that, for my part, I do not maintain this.
root.text.Part 2..16.3: I shall now resume the principles of his methods[[fn:1663]], and I will show thee how there follows therefrom absolutely nothing against us, who maintain that God produced the whole world out of nothing, and formed it (successively) until it became perfect, even as thou seest it.
root.text.Part 2..16.4: The First Matter, says he, has neither been born nor shall it perish; and, arguing from things born and perishable, he shows that it is impossible it should have been born[[fn:1664]]. And this is true[[fn:1665]]. For we do not maintain that the first matter was formed as man is formed from the semen, nor that it must perish as man perishes by becoming dust; but we maintain, on the contrary, that God produced it out of nothing, and that after its production it is such as it is[[fn:1666]],—I mean to say, that all things are formed therefrom, and that all which is formed therefrom returns thereto in perishing. It exists not divested of form[[fn:1667]], and it is the term of generation and of corruption. As for itself, it was not born (of anything), as everything is born which is formed from it, and it shall not perish (into anything), as that perishes which perishes within it; but on the contrary, it is a thing created, and whenever its Creator shall will it, He shall reduce it to pure and absolute non-existence. We shall say precisely the same thing concerning motion; for arguments have been drawn from the nature of motion to prove that it was not born and shall not perish[[fn:1668]]. And this is likewise true[[fn:1669]]; for we maintain that it is inconceivable that, since motion has existed with its invariable and fixed nature, it could, in its universality, be subject to birth and corruption, even as are the partial motions which are born and perish[[fn:1670]]. The same reasoning applies to all that is inherent in the nature of motion[[fn:1671]].
root.text.Part 2..16.5: Likewise, when he says of circular motion that it has no beginning, this is true (in the sense) that after the production of the spherical body, which movs circularly, one could not imagine in its motion any beginning whatsoever[[fn:1672]].
root.text.Part 2..16.6: We shall say the like concerning the possibility which must precede all things brought into existence[[fn:1673]]; for this is necessary only in this (completely) established universe, in which everything that is born proceeds from some being or other. But a thing produced from nothingness does not indicate, whether to the senses or to the intellect, any (anterior) thing, such as would require it to be preceded by a possibility.
root.text.Part 2..16.7: Finally, we shall reason in the same manner concerning (that which he says) that in the heavens there is no contrariety[[fn:1674]]. This is likewise true; only (it must be noted) that we do not maintain that the heavens were formed as the horse and the palm-tree are formed, and (consequently) we do not maintain that, being composite, they must perish like plants and animals, by reason of the contrariety which would exist therein[[fn:1675]].
root.text.Part 2..16.8: The essence of the matter is that which we have stated, (namely) that a being being in its perfect and completed state, one cannot reason from its actual state to the state (in which it was)[[fn:1676]] before its perfection.
root.text.Part 2..16.9: Neither do we find aught of absurdity in that which has been said, that the heavens were formed before the earth, or the earth before the heavens[[fn:1677]], or that the heavens were at first without stars, or (that there existed) such a species of animals without another; for all this applies to the period when this whole (of the universe) was being formed. It is even as with the animal during its formation, the heart being formed before the testicles, as is manifest to the sight, and the veins before the bones, although, in its perfect state, none of its members exists independently of all the others, without which the preservation of the individual were impossible. All this must also (be admitted), if one takes the text (of Scripture) in its literal sense, although it be not so, as shall be explained when we treat thereof more at length[[fn:1678]].
root.text.Part 2..16.10: — Thou must give good heed to this subject[[fn:1679]]; for it is a great wall that I have built around the Law, and which encompasses it to protect it against the stones cast at it. If Aristotle, — I mean he who adopts his opinion, — should argue against us, saying: Since no proof can be drawn from this (finished) universe, how then do ye yourselves know that it was created and that there was another nature[[fn:1680]] which created it? we should reply: This does not affect us in respect of our present purpose[[fn:1681]]. Verily, we do not seek now to establish that the world was created; but what we desire is (to show) that it is possible it should have been created; and the falsehood of this assertion cannot be demonstrated by arguing from the nature of the universe, with which we do not place ourselves in opposition[[fn:1682]]. The possibility of this assertion being established, as we have set forth, we shall afterwards endeavour to make the opinion of creation prevail. There would then remain in this regard (no other means of refuting us) than to demonstrate to us the impossibility of the creation of the world, not by the nature of the universe, but by that which the intellect judges to be necessary in respect of God; and these are the three methods of which I have spoken to thee previously, and by which men seek to demonstrate the eternity of the world by taking God as the point of departure[[fn:1683]]. I shall therefore show thee, in the following chapter, in what manner they may be called into doubt, so that no proof may result therefrom.
root.text.Part 2..17.0: The first method of which they speak is that in which they pretend to establish that, according to our view[[fn:1684]], God must have passed from potentiality to actuality, since He would have acted at one certain moment and not at another[[fn:1685]]. — It shall be very easy to refute this objection[[fn:1686]]: For, in truth, one can only reason in this wise[[fn:1687]] concerning that which is composed of matter in a state of possibility and of a form. Without any doubt, if such a body acts by its form after having been inactive, there has been in it something in potentiality which has passed into actuality, and, consequently, it has stood in need of an efficient cause; for, as touching things endowed with matter, this is a demonstrated proposition. But that which is incorporeal and immaterial has in its essence no possibility, and all that is within it is perpetually in act. One cannot, therefore, apply to it the reasoning in question, and for it, it is by no means impossible that at one time it acts and at another it acts not. For the separate being, this is neither a change nor a passage from potentiality to actuality.
root.text.Part 2..17.1: We have a proof thereof in the Active Intellect, which, according to the opinion of Aristotle and his followers, is separate, and which, nevertheless, at one time acts and at another acts not, as Abu-Naṣr has set forth in his treatise on the Intellect[[fn:1688]]. He expresses himself therein in these terms: “It is evident that the Active Intellect does not act perpetually; but, on the contrary, at one time it acts and at another it acts not.” These be his very words, and it is evidently the truth. But, although it be thus, it is not said, however, that the Active Intellect is subject to change, nor that after having been an agent in potentiality, it has become so in act, because it might have done at a certain moment what it had not done before; for there is no relation between bodies and that which is incorporeal, and there is no similitude between them, neither at the moment of action, nor at the moment when they abstain from acting. If the action of material forms and that of the separate being are both called action, it is only by homonymy; wherefore, if the separate being performs not at a certain moment the action which it will perform later, it does not follow therefrom that it will have passed from potentiality to actuality, as we find it to be in material forms.
root.text.Part 2..17.2: Perchance it may be believed that in what I have just said there resids some sophistry: If, it will be said, the Active Intellect necessarily acts at one certain moment and acts not at another, this is not because of aught inherent in its essence, but because of the disposition of the materials; on its part, the action is perpetually exercised upon all that is disposed, and if there be aught that hinders the action, that proceeds from the disposition of the matter, and not from the Intellect in itself[[fn:1689]].— Let him therefore who thus thinks[[fn:1690]] well know that our purpose is not to make known the cause for which God acted at one certain moment and not at another; and, in citing this example, we have not concluded therefrom that, since the Active Intellect, which is separate, acts at one time and acts not at another, it must be the same with God[[fn:1691]]. We have not said that, nor have we made such a conclusion; and had we done so, it would indeed have been a sophistry. But what we have concluded therefrom—and it is a true conclusion—is that, although the Active Intellect, which is neither a body nor a force in a body, acts at one certain moment and performs not the same action at another moment, no matter what the cause thereof may be, it is not said on that account that it has passed from potentiality to actuality, nor that there has been in its essence any possibility, nor finally that it has need of an efficient cause to make it pass from potentiality to actuality[[fn:1692]]. Thus is set aside from us that grave objection which has been made against us by those who maintain the eternity of the world; for, as we believe that God is neither a body, nor a force in a body, He is in no wise affected by change in acting after having not acted.
root.text.Part 2..17.3: The second method is that in which the eternity of the world is concluded from the fact that for God there are neither needs, nor aught that supervens, nor obstacles[[fn:1693]]. The solution of this objection is difficult and withal subtle; hearken thou unto it.
root.text.Part 2..17.4: Know thou that every agent who possesses a will and who acts for any reason whatsoever must needs act at one time and not act at another, by reason of certain obstacles or needs that supervene. Thus, for example, a certain man who would desire to possess a house will nevertheless not build one, by reason of hindrances, whether it be that he has not the materials at hand, or that these, prepared though they be, are not ready[[fn:1694]] to receive the form, by reason of a lack of instruments. It may also be that the materials and the instruments are ready, and that nevertheless the man builds not, because, having no need of a dwelling, he wills not to build; but when there shall supervene accidents, such as heat or cold, which shall constrain him to seek a shelter, then will he desire to build. It is therefore clear that supervening accidents change the will, and that obstacles oppose the will in such wise that one cannot act. Nevertheless, all this only takes place when actions have for their reason something outside the will itself. But when the action has absolutely no other end than that of obeying a will, that will has no need of an invitation from without; and in such a case it is not necessary either that he who possesses the will, whilst having no obstacles, should always act; for he has no external end which causs him to act, in such a manner that he should be forced to act so soon as there were no obstacles to reaching the end, since the action, in this case, obeys the will alone.
root.text.Part 2..17.5: It might be objected against us: All this is true; but is there not a change in this very fact, that at one time He wills and at another He wills not[[fn:1695]]? To this we shall reply: Nay; for that which constituts the true idea of the will is to will and not to will. Now, if this will belongs to a material being, and that which is sought thereby be an external end, it shall be a will subject to change, by reason of obstacles and of that which may betide; but the will of the separate being, which is in no wise determined by aught else, is not subject to change; and, if He wills now one thing and on the morrow another thing, that constituts no change in His essence, nor does it require another cause (outside of Him), even as there is no change in that He at one time acts and at another time acts not, as we have already set forth. It shall be shown (further on)[[fn:1696]] that it is only by homonymy that the name will is applied both to our will and to that of the separate being, and that there is no similitude between the two wills. — Thus, then, this objection is likewise destroyed, and it is manifest that naught results for us from this method which is inadmissible[[fn:1697]]. This is what we desired (to obtain), as thou knowest.
root.text.Part 2..17.6: The third method is that whereby the eternity of the world is proved (by reasoning) thus: When the (Divine) wisdom decids that a thing must appear, it has appeared[[fn:1698]]; now, the wisdom of God being eternal as His essence, that which results therefrom is (likewise) eternal[[fn:1699]]. — But this is a very feeble reasoning; for, even as we are ignorant why His wisdom required that the spheres should be nine (in number), neither more nor less, that the stars should be as numerous as they are, neither more nor less, and (that they should be) neither greater nor smaller, even so we are ignorant why the wisdom, at a (relatively) recent epoch, caused the universe to exist after having not existed[[fn:1700]]. All things conform to His perpetual and invariable wisdom; but we, for our part, are utterly ignorant of the law of this wisdom and of what it requirs[[fn:1701]]. For, according to our opinion, the will likewise conforms to the wisdom; all (in God) is one and the same thing, I mean to say that His wisdom is His essence, for we admit not attributes[[fn:1702]]. Thou shalt hear much upon this subject when we speak of Providence[[fn:1703]]. — By this consideration, therefore, this absurdity (attributed to us) likewise falls[[fn:1704]].
root.text.Part 2..17.7: As for what Aristotle says, that the peoples, in ancient times, believed with one accord that the angels dwelt in heaven, and that God also was in heaven[[fn:1705]], — a thing which the literal sense of the (sacred) texts also says, — this cannot serve as a proof for the eternity of the world, as he himself wills; but it was said to prove that the heaven indicats to us the existence of the separate Intelligences, which are the spiritual beings and the angels, and that it indicats to us also the existence of God, who setts it in motion and who governs it, as we shall set forth. We shall show that there is no proof which better demonstrats to us the existence of the Creator, according to our opinion[[fn:1706]], than that drawn from the heaven; and the latter, as we have already said, proves also, according to the opinion of the philosophers, that there exists (a Being) who setts it in motion, and that this latter is neither a body nor a force in a body.
root.text.Part 2..17.8: After having shown thee that what we affirm is admissible, and that (at the least) it is not an impossible thing, as is pretended by those who maintain the eternity (of the world), I shall show, in the following chapters, that our opinion is preferable from the speculative point of view, and I shall reveal the absurd consequences which the other opinion has[[fn:1707]].
root.text.Part 2..18.0: [[fn:1708]]It follows evidently from the system of Aristotle, as from the system of all those who profess the eternity of the world, that according to him this universe is emanated from the Creator by necessity, that God is the cause and this world the effect, and that, consequently, the latter is necessary[[fn:1709]]. Even as one could not say of God why He exists, nor how He exists thus, I mean one and incorporeal, so one could not say of the universe in its entirety why it exists nor how it exists thus (as we see it); for it is necessary that all this exist thus, (I mean) the cause and its effect; and it is impossible for both not to exist or to become other than they are. It follows then from this opinion that every thing must necessarily preserve always the nature which it has, and that no thing can, in any wise, change its nature. According to this opinion, the change of nature of any being whatsoever is an impossible thing, and, consequently, all these things could not have been born by the design of a being having an intention and who would have freely willed that they should be thus; for, if they had been born by such a design, they would not have existed thus before the design was determined[[fn:1710]].
root.text.Part 2..18.1: But, according to our own opinion, it is manifest that things exist by virtue of a design, and not by necessity. It might therefore be that He who formed the design should change it and form another design. Nevertheless, this could not be, in an absolute sense, any design whatsoever; for there is a nature of the impossible which is stable and which cannot be destroyed[[fn:1711]], as we shall set forth. — My purpose, in this chapter, is to show thee, by proofs which approach demonstration, that this universe necessarily indicates to us a Creator acting with intention[[fn:1712]], without my wishing for all that to undertake what the Mutakallimūn have attempted, by destroying the nature of being and by proclaiming the atom, the perpetual creation of accidents, and all that I have exposed to thee of their principles, whose sole aim is to establish determination[[fn:1713]]. One must not believe that they have also said what I am about to say; but what cannot be doubted is that they have aimed at the same goal as I. They speak also, then, of the things of which I shall speak, having in view determination; but for them, if such a plant be rather red than white, rather sweet than bitter, it is a particularization on the same ground as that of the heaven having by preference that figure which it has, and not a square or triangular figure[[fn:1714]]. They, verily, have established determination by means of their propositions which thou already knowest[[fn:1715]], whilst I shall establish determination, where it is necessary, by means of philosophical propositions drawn from the nature of being.
root.text.Part 2..18.2: I shall set forth this method, after having first laid down as a principle what follows: whenever a matter[[fn:1716]] is common to things which differ among themselves in any manner whatsoever, there must necessarily have been, apart from this common matter, a cause which brought it to pass that these things should have, some such quality, and others such another, or rather (there must have been) as many causes as there are different things. This is a proposition upon which the partisans of the eternity (of the world) and those of creation do agree.
root.text.Part 2..18.3: Having laid down this principle, I enter upon the exposition of that which I had in view, (discussing) in the form of question and answer, concerning the opinion of Aristotle.
root.text.Part 2..18.4: We first address to Aristotle the following question: Thou hast demonstrated to us that all sublunary things have one and the same matter, common to all; what then is the cause of the diversity of species which exist here below, and what is the cause of the diversity of individuals of each of these species? — Thereupon, he will answer us: That which causs the diversity is that the things composed of this matter differ in mixture. This common matter first received four forms, each of which is accompanied by two qualities[[fn:1717]], and by these four qualities it becoms the elements of that which is composed thereof[[fn:1718]]; for they (the elements) commingle first in consequence of the motion of the celestial sphere, and thereafter, having formed a tempered mixture[[fn:1719]], diversity ariss in the mixed things, which are composed (of the elements) in different degrees of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. Through these diverse mixtures, it (the matter) acquirs diverse dispositions for receiving diverse forms, and these forms, in their turn, dispose it for the reception of other forms, and so forth. The matter (substratum) of a single specific form possesses a great latitude of quantity and quality, and it is by reason of this latitude that there is a variety of individuals of the same species, even as has been set forth in physical science. — All this is true and manifest for him who is equitable towards himself and who desirs not to deceive himself.
root.text.Part 2..18.5: Next, we shall address once more to Aristotle this other question: If it be true that the mixture of the elements is the cause which disposs the matters to receive the diverse forms, what was it then that disposed this first matter in such wise that one part should receive the form of fire, and another part the form of earth, and that that which is between the two (should become apt) to receive the form of water and of air? Since the whole has a common matter, what was it then that rendered the matter of the earth more fit for the form of earth, and the matter of fire more fit for the form of fire?
root.text.Part 2..18.6: — To this Aristotle would make the following reply: That which has effected this is the difference of positions[[fn:1720]]; for it is these which have produced in the single matter diverse dispositions. The portion which is nigher to the circumference has received from it an impression of subtilty and rapid motion, and approaches its nature, so that, being thus prepared, it has received the form of fire; but, in proportion as the matter receds from the circumference and is nigher unto the centre, it becoms thicker, more consistent, and less luminous; it then becoms earth, and, for the same reason, water and air. This must necessarily be so; for it would be absurd to say that this matter is in no place, or that the circumference itself is the centre, and vice versa. It is this, therefore, which has caused it to be particularised by diverse forms; I mean to say, that which has disposed it to receive diverse forms.
root.text.Part 2..18.7: Finally, we shall further ask of him: Is the matter of the circumference, that is to say, of the heaven, the same as that of the elements?
root.text.Part 2..18.8: — Nay, he will answer; but, on the contrary, that is another matter, and it has other forms[[fn:1721]]. If one gives at the same time to the bodies here below and to those above the name of body, it is but by homonymy, as the moderns have set forth[[fn:1722]]. All this has been demonstrated.
root.text.Part 2..18.9: Hearken now, O reader of this treatise, unto that which I myself say.
root.text.Part 2..18.10: — Thou knowest it has been demonstrated by Aristotle that from the difference of actions one may infer the difference of forms[[fn:1723]]. Now, as the motions of the four elements are rectilinear, whilst the motion of the celestial sphere is circular, it is perceived, in the first place, that the matter of the former is not the same as that of the latter, which is a truth resulting from physical speculation; but, as it is also found that those elements which have rectilinear motions differ in direction, some moving upwards and others downwards, and that even those which tend toward the same side have motion more or less rapid or slow, it is recognised that they differ in forms. Thus has it been recognised that the elements are four in number[[fn:1724]]. It is by an argument altogether similar that one comes to the conclusion that all the celestial spheres have one and the same matter; for they all move circularly. But, in respect of form, the spheres differ one from another[[fn:1725]]; for one movs from east to west, and another from west to east[[fn:1726]], and, furthermore, the motions differ in rapidity and slowness. One must therefore yet address to him (that is, to Aristotle) the following question: Since all the spheres have a common matter, and in each of them the substratum has a particular form which is not that of the others, who is it then that has particularised these substrata and has disposed them to receive diverse forms? Is there, beyond the sphere, any other thing to which one may attribute this particularisation, if it be not God, the Most High?
root.text.Part 2..18.11: I must here call thy attention to the great profundity of Aristotle and to his extraordinary comprehension, and (remark to thee) how much, without doubt, this objection has embarrassed him, and how he has endeavoured to extricate himself by means in which (the nature of) existence afforded him no succour. For, although he has not mentioned this objection, it is nevertheless evident from his words that he desirs to present to us systematically the existence of the spheres, as he has done for that which is beneath the celestial sphere[[fn:1727]], in such wise that all things take place by a physical necessity and not by the intention of a being who pursus the end which he wills and who determins (things)[[fn:1728]], in whatever manner it pleass him. But in this he has not succeeded, nor shall any man ever succeed therein. He endeavours to give the reason: 1st, why the motion of the sphere proceeds from the East and not from the West[[fn:1729]]; 2nd, why (the spheres) possess motions, some rapid, others slow, which depends upon the order of their position over against the superior sphere[[fn:1730]]; 3rd, why each of the seven planets has several spheres, whilst this great multitude (of fixed stars) is in a single sphere[[fn:1731]]. He endeavours to indicate the causes of all this, in order to present the matter unto us according to a physical order (existing) by necessity. Nevertheless, he has succeeded in none of these things; for, if all that he has set forth unto us regarding sublunary things be systematic and conformable to that which (actually) exists and the causes of which are manifest, and if it may be said that everything therein takes place by a necessity (resulting) from the motion and the forces of the celestial sphere, he has been unable to give any evident reason for all that he has said regarding the celestial sphere, and the matter does not present itself in a systematic form, so that one might maintain the necessity thereof. For, as touching the spheres, we perceive that sometimes those which possess the more rapid motion are above those which possess the slower motion, sometimes those which have the slower motion are above those which have the more rapid motion, and sometimes, finally, they have equal motions, although they be one above the other[[fn:1732]]. There are yet other things (which become) very difficult, as soon as one adopts the point of view of necessity[[fn:1733]], and I shall devote to them a particular chapter of this treatise[[fn:1734]].
root.text.Part 2..18.12: In short, Aristotle, recognizing doubtless the weakness of that which he says to justify these things and to indicate their causes, has prefixed, when entering upon these researches, words of which this is the text: «We wish now to examine carefully two questions which it is necessary to examine, and we shall say thereof what our intelligence[[fn:1735]], our science and our opinion permit; but no one should for this reason charge us with presumption and audacity. We should, on the contrary, admire our passion and our zeal for philosophy; and when we examine great and noble questions[[fn:1736]] and succeed in giving them a solution even slightly solid, the hearer ought to experience a great pleasure and be in joy[[fn:1737]].» Such are his own terms. It is therefore clear that he indubitably recognized the weakness of what he said in this regard; all the more so since the science of mathematics was yet imperfect in his time, and that which we know today regarding the motions of the celestial sphere was not then known. It seems to me that if Aristotle says, in the Metaphysics, that one must suppose a Separate Intelligence for each sphere, it is likewise because of the subject in question, (that is to say) in order that there may be a thing which gives a particular motion to each sphere[[fn:1738]]. But we shall show that he gains nothing thereby.
root.text.Part 2..18.13: As for that which he says in the text I have cited: «what our intelligence, our science and our opinion permit,» I shall explain to thee the sense thereof; for I have seen it (set forth) by none of the commentators. By the words our opinion, he indicats the point of view of necessity, that is to say, the opinion of the eternity of the world. The words our science indicate that evident thing upon which there is agreement, (to wit) that each of these (celestial) things necessarily has a cause and does not occur by simple chance. The words our intelligence signify: our inability to indicate, in a completely perfect manner, the causes of such things; nevertheless, he claims to be able to say somewhat thereof. And this is indeed what he has done; for what he says concerning the rapidity of the universal motion and the slowness of the sphere of the fixed stars, (its motion) taking an opposite direction, is a strange and astonishing argument[[fn:1739]].
