Likewise he says that as a sphere is more distant from the eighth, its motion must be more rapid; and yet it is not always so, as I have set forth to thee[[fn:1740]]. And what is even more serious than this, is that there are also spheres beneath the eighth which move from East to West; it would therefore be necessary that those which move from East to West should be (each of them) more rapid than those which are beneath them, and that (generally) those whose motion proceeds from the East should be more rapid in proportion as they are nearer to the (diurnal) motion of the ninth[[fn:1741]]. But, as I have already informed thee, the science of astronomy was not in his time what it is today.
root.text.Part 2..18.14: Know that, according to the opinion of all of us who profess the creation of the world, all this is easy and proceeds well (in accord) with our principles; for we say that there is a Determining Being, who, for each sphere, has determined as He willed the direction and the rapidity of the motion, but that we are ignorant of the mode of that wisdom which has caused such a thing to arise in such a manner. If Aristotle had been able to give us the reason for the diversity of the motion of the spheres, in such wise that all were in harmony with their reciprocal position, as he believed, it would have been marvellous; and then it would have been with the cause of that which is peculiar (to each sphere) in this diversity of motions, as it is with the cause of the diversity of the elements in regard to their (respective) position between the circumference and the centre (of the universe)[[fn:1742]]. But the matter is not so regulated, as I have set forth to thee.
root.text.Part 2..18.16: But, as soon as it is admitted that all is due to the design of a Being acting with intention, who has fashioned it thus, there remains naught at which one need marvel[[fn:1748]], nor aught that is improbable;
root.text.Part 2..18.17: and there is no further room for enquiry, unless thou shouldst ask: what is the cause of this design? In essence, all that is known is that this occurs for a reason unknown to us, yet it is not an idle work, nor the result of chance. For it is well known that the veins and nerves of the canine or equine individual are not the product of chance, nor do they possess such measure fortuitously, and that it is not merely by chance that one vein is large and another thin, that one nerve branches out into many, while another does not, that one descends straight, while another folds back upon itself; for none of this occurs without certain advantages whose necessity is well understood. And how, then, could an intelligent man imagine that the positions of these stars, their measurements, their number, and the movements of their various spheres are without reason, or the work of chance? There can be no doubt that each of these things is necessary in relation to the design of the one who acted with intention, and it is very difficult to conceive that this order of things comes from an (blind) necessity, rather than from a [[t:0]]design[[t:1]].
root.text.Part 2..18.18: There is not, in my judgment, a greater proof of design than the variety of the movements of the spheres and the stars fixed within them; wherefore thou shalt find that all the prophets have taken the stars and the spheres as proof that there necessarily exists a God. That which the tradition concerning Abraham relats of his observation of the stars is well known[[fn:1749]]. Isaiah says, to call attention to the proofs to be drawn therefrom: Lift up your eyes on high, and behold; who has created these things? etc. (Is., XL, 26). Likewise Jeremiah says: He who has made the heavens[[fn:1750]]. Abraham said: the Lord, the God of heaven (Genesis, 24, 7), and the prince of prophets: He who rids upon the heavens (Deuter., 33, 26), which we have explained[[fn:1751]]. And this is indeed the true proof, in which there is nothing doubtful. I shall explain myself: If there be beneath the celestial sphere so many diverse things, although their matter be one, as we have set forth, thou mayest say that what has particularized them are the forces of the spheres and the different positions of matter with respect to the celestial sphere, even as Aristotle has taught us. But, as touching the diversities which exist in the spheres and the stars, who could have particularized them, save God? for, should any one say (that they are) the separate intelligences, he would have gained naught by this assertion. For the intelligences are not bodies, such that they might have a position in respect to the sphere; why then should this movement of desire (which attracts each sphere) toward its separate intelligence[[fn:1752]], be directed by one sphere toward the east and by another toward the west? Believest thou that one intelligence is on the side of the west and another on the side of the east? Why, again, should one (sphere) be slower and another swifter, without there even being in this a (regular) sequence in relation to their (respective) distance from one another[[fn:1753]], as thou knowest? It must then necessarily be said that it is the very nature of such a sphere and its substance which required it to move toward such a side and with such a degree of speed, and that the result of its desire was such a thing (obtained) in such a manner. And this is indeed what Aristotle says and what he clearly proclaims[[fn:1754]]. We are thus returned to our point of departure, and we say: Since all (the spheres) have one and the same matter, what then can cause them to be distinguished from one another by a particular nature[[fn:1755]], and that some should have a certain desire producing such a species of motion and opposed to the desire of others producing another species of motion? Is there not necessarily required something which particularizes them? — This consideration has led us to examine two questions. The one (is this): can one, or not, conclude from the existence of this diversity that all is necessarily wrought by the design of a Being having an intention, and not by necessity? The second question (is this): Supposing that all this be due to the design of a Being having an intention, who has thus particularized things, can it be concluded therefrom that all has been created after not having existed? or rather, must one not draw this conclusion, and admit on the contrary that this particularization has taken place from all eternity[[fn:1756]]? — for this opinion[[fn:1757]] has been held also by some of those who admit the eternity (of the world). I shall, therefore, in the following chapters, approach these two questions and set forth what is necessary concerning them.
root.text.Part 2..19.0: Aristotle demonstrats that physical things in general do not happen by chance, and the demonstration which he gives thereof is this: things of chance happen neither continually, nor even most frequently[[fn:1758]]; but all these (physical) things happen either continually or (at least) most frequently. As for the heaven, with all that it contains, it remains continually in certain situations, without undergoing any change, as we have set forth, neither in its very essence, nor by changing its place. But the physical things which are beneath the sphere of the moon take place, some continually, others most frequently: continually, as, for example, fire which heats and the stone which descends downwards; most frequently, as, for example, the forms of the individuals of each species and its actions[[fn:1759]]. All this is manifest. Now, since the partial things (of the world)[[fn:1760]] are not due to chance, how could the whole be so? It is therefore demonstrated that these beings are in no wise the work of chance.
root.text.Part 2..19.1: Thus speaks Aristotle, whilst refuting those among the ancients who alleged that this world has arisen from chance and that it was born spontaneously, without a cause: “Others,” says he, “have assigned as the cause of this heaven and of all the worlds spontaneity[[fn:1761]]; for, say they, it is spontaneously that the revolution ariss, as well as the movement which has distinguished and constituted all things in this order. But there is in this something passing strange: they say (on the one hand), of animals and plants, that they neither are nor are born by chance, but that they have for their cause either a nature, or an intellect, or some other similar thing; for every thing whatsoever is not born from every seed or from every sperm (at random), but from such a seed an olive-tree is born, and from such sperm a man is born. And (on the other hand), they say of the heaven and of the bodies which (alone) among all visible bodies are (verily) divine[[fn:1762]], that they are born only spontaneously and that they have absolutely no cause, such as animals and plants possess.” Such are his expressions, and he enters into long details to show the falsity of what they have presumed.
root.text.Part 2..19.2: It is therefore manifest that Aristotle believs and demonstrats that all these beings exist not by chance; that which refuts (the opinion admitting) that they are the work of chance, is that they exist essentially, that is to say, they have (evidently) a cause which wills that they be necessarily thus, and by this cause they exist even as they are. This is what has been demonstrated and what Aristotle believs. But (as to the question of knowing) if, from the fact that they are not born spontaneously, it necessarily follows that they are the work of a design and of a free will[[fn:1763]], it is not proven unto me that Aristotle believs this; for, to unite together existence by necessity and birth by a design and a will, so as to make of them one and the same thing, this appears to me well-nigh the union of two opposite things. Indeed, the idea of necessity admitted by Aristotle is (this): that all among beings that are not the product of art necessarily have a cause which produced and formed them as they are; this cause has a second cause, this latter a third, and so forth, until one arrivs at a first cause from which all has emanated; for one could not admit a chain (of causes) unto infinity. But he does not believe for all that that the existence of the world results necessarily from the Creator, I mean from the first cause, as the shadow results from the body, or as heat results from fire, or as light results from the sun, as is maintained of him by those who understand not his words. He believs, on the contrary, that it is with this necessity much as (when we say that) the intelligible results necessarily from the intellect, the intellect being the efficient of the intelligible in as much as it is intelligible[[fn:1764]]; for, even according to him (Aristotle), this first cause is an intellect in the highest and most perfect degree of being. But, although he says that God wills that which emanats from Him, that He has joy and pleasure therein[[fn:1765]] and that He could not will the contrary, one could not call this design[[fn:1766]], and there is not therein the idea of design. Indeed, man desirs to have two eyes and two hands, he feels joy and pleasure therein, and he could not will the contrary; but if such an individual has two eyes and two hands, it is not by a design (proceeding from him), nor because he particularly wills such a figure and such actions. The idea of design and that of determination apply only to a thing which exists not yet and which may exist or not exist even as it has been projected or determined.
root.text.Part 2..19.3: I know not (moreover) whether the moderns[[fn:1767]] have understood the words of Aristotle, saying that things have necessarily a cause[[fn:1768]], in the sense of design and of determination; or else, if they have contradicted him on this point and if it be they who have preferred the opinion of design and of determination, believing that it is not in contradiction with the eternity (of the world).
root.text.Part 2..19.4: — After this exposition, I approach the opinion of these moderns.
root.text.Part 2..20.0: Know thou that, among the modern philosophers who profess the eternity of the world, there be some who say that God is the efficient cause of the world, whose existence He has preferred (to non-existence), that He has made it with design and has determined it even as it is, but that it is inadmissible that this should have taken place in one time rather than in another, and that, on the contrary, it has always been and shall always be thus. That which causes, say they, that we could not figure to ourselves that an agent has made something without this agent having preceded his action in time, is that in what we ourselves do, it is necessarily thus; for, in every agent of this sort[[fn:1769]], there is a certain privation: he is (first) an agent in potentiality, and, after having acted, he has passed into actuality. But God, in whom there is no privation, nor absolutely anything that is in potentiality, does not precede His action; on the contrary, He has never ceased to act, and even as there is an immense difference between His essence and ours, so also the relation which exists between His action and Himself differs from that which exists between our action and ourselves. They follow the same reasoning concerning determination and will; for, it matters little whether thou sayest agent, or willing, or acting with design, or preferring, or determining, (all these words) having the same sense[[fn:1770]]. It is inadmissible, say they further, that His action or His will should be subject to change, as we have already set forth[[fn:1771]].
root.text.Part 2..20.1: It is therefore manifest unto thee, O reader of this my present treatise, that those persons have indeed changed the word necessity, yet have allowed the idea thereof to remain. Perchance they intended to choose a more excellent expression, or (at least) to avoid something ill-sounding[[fn:1772]]; for (if it be said) that the universe is intimately bound to its cause, — which is God, as Aristotle says, — and that it participats in His perpetuity, it is absolutely the same idea as when they say that the world proceeds from the action of God, or (that it was made) by His design, His will, His choice, and His determination, but that it has never ceased and shall never cease to be as it is, even as the rising of the sun is indubitably the efficient of the day, without the one preceding the other in time. Yet this is not the conception of design[[fn:1773]] as we understand it; on the contrary, we mean thereby that the world did not necessarily emanate from God, as an effect emanats from its cause, from which it is so inseparable that it cannot change unless the cause itself undergo a change, or at least change in respect of one of its conditions. When thou shalt have thus understood the idea (of design), thou wilt recognize how false it is to say that the world is a necessary consequence of the existence of God, as the effect is of the cause, and (thou shalt know) that it has come from the (free) action of God or (that it exists) by His determination.
root.text.Part 2..20.2: Having thus set forth the subject, we proceed to examine the question of that diversity which exists in the heavens and which, as has been demonstrated, must necessarily have a cause; (and we ask) whether this cause, by its very existence, has motivated and rendered necessary this diversity[[fn:1774]], or whether it be the efficient of this diversity which has determined[[fn:1775]] it in the manner that we believe, we the followers of Moses, our teacher? We shall answer this, after having first made a preliminary observation to explain the sense of the necessity admitted by Aristotle, in order that thou mayest conceive the idea thereof; and thereafter I shall set forth to thee the preference which I give to the opinion of the creation of the world, (supported) by speculative and philosophical proofs, pure from all false reasoning.
root.text.Part 2..20.3: If he says that the first Intelligence necessarily emanated from God, the second Intelligence from the first, and the third from the second, and likewise, if he thinks that the spheres emanated from the Intelligences and (if he proclaims) that well-known order which thou hast been able to study in the passages relating thereto and which we have here set forth in summary[[fn:1776]], it is clear that he means not thereby that one thing existed first, and that subsequently there was born from it that other thing which is its necessary consequence; for he admitts not the birth of any of these things. In saying necessary consequence, he means to speak only of causality, as if he were to say: the first Intelligence is the cause of the existence of the second Intelligence, this latter is the cause of the existence of the third, and so forth; and it is the same with what he says of the spheres and of prime matter[[fn:1777]], for all these things do in no wise precede one another and exist not, according to him, the one without the other[[fn:1778]]. It is, for example, as if one were to say that, from the primary qualities[[fn:1779]], there result necessarily roughness, smoothness, hardness, softness, thickness, and sponginess[[fn:1780]]; for no one doubts that it is those (the primary qualities), I mean heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, which have given birth to roughness, smoothness, hardness, softness, thickness, sponginess, and other such things, and that these latter have necessarily emanated from the primary qualities, although it be impossible that there should exist a body which, possessing the primary qualities, should be devoid of these secondary qualities[[fn:1781]]. It is therefore in absolutely the same manner that Aristotle says[[fn:1782]], of the universe in general, that such a thing has necessarily emanated from such another, until one arrivs at the First Cause, as he expresses it, or the First Intelligence, or[[fn:1783]] by whatever name thou mayest wish to call it. We all have in view one and the same Principle; but he thinks that all that which is outside (of this Principle) emanated from it by necessity, as I have said, whilst we say that it is God who has made all these things with design and by willing this universe, which existed not at first and which has now been called into existence by the will of God. I shall now, in the following chapters, produce the proofs which lead me to give preference to (the opinion which admitts) that the world was created.
root.text.Part 2..21.0: It is a proposition whereon Aristotle and all the philosophers are agreed, that from a simple thing there can emanate (directly) but a single simple thing[[fn:1784]]. If the thing be composite, there may emanate from it several things, according to the number of simple elements which it contains and of which it is composed. Fire, for example, being a composite of two (primary) qualities, heat and dryness, it follows that it heats by its heat and dries by its dryness[[fn:1785]]. Likewise, a thing being composed of matter and form, there may emanate from it, if it be of manifold composition, several things on the side of its matter and several others on the side of its form. — Conformably to this proposition, Aristotle says that there was no primitive emanation from God but a single simple intelligence, and naught else.
root.text.Part 2..21.1: [[t:0]]The Second Proposition[[t:1]][[fn:1786]][[t:2]]:[[t:3]] No thing whatsoever can arise fortuitously from any thing whatsoever, but it is always necessary that there be a certain relation between the cause and its effect. Even accidents themselves cannot arise by chance from one another, as for example, quantity from quality, or quality from quantity. In like manner, a form cannot arise from matter, nor matter from form.
root.text.Part 2..21.2: Third proposition: Every agent that acts with design and will, and not by its nature, may perform diverse and numerous actions.
root.text.Part 2..21.3: [[t:0]]Fourth Proposition:[[t:1]] A whole composed of diverse substances [[t:2]]juxtaposed[[t:3]] forms a [[t:4]]composition[[t:5]] more truly than a whole composed of diverse substances [[t:6]]mingled together.[[t:7]] Thus, for instance, bones, or flesh, or veins, or nerves, are more simple than the entire hand or foot, composed of nerves, flesh, veins, and bones. — This is too clear to require further explanation.
root.text.Part 2..21.4: After these preliminary remarks, I shall say that, if Aristotle asserts[[fn:1787]] that the first Intelligence serves as the cause of the second, the second of the third, and so forth, even were there thousands of degrees, the last[[fn:1788]] of these Intelligences shall ever indubitably be simple. Whence, then, should proceed the composition, which, according to the opinion of Aristotle, would exist by necessity in these beings (of this lower world)? We are well pleased to agree with him when he says that, in proportion as the Intelligences depart (from the First Cause), there is found in them a greater composition of (diverse) ideas, their intelligibles becoming more and more numerous; but, whilst admitting with him this conjectural opinion, (we would ask him) how could the Intelligences become the cause of the spheres emanating from them? What relation is there between the matter (of the spheres) and the separate Intelligence, which is absolutely immaterial? Even should we grant that each sphere has for its cause an Intelligence, as has been said, because that Intelligence is composed in that it thinks itself and (thinks also) that which is outside of it, — so that it is, after a manner, composed of two things, of which one produces the other Intelligence which is below it, and the other produces the sphere[[fn:1789]], — one might yet ask him: This one and simple thing from which (according to you) the sphere emanats, how could it produce the sphere, since the latter is composed of two matters and two forms, which are (on the one hand) the matter and the form of the sphere, and (on the other hand) the matter and the form of the star fixed within the sphere[[fn:1790]]? If, therefore, all proceeded by way of necessity, we should necessarily have to suppose in that composed Intelligence a cause likewise composed of two parts, one of which might produce the body of the sphere and the other the body of the star[[fn:1791]]. And furthermore, it would be necessary that the matter of all the stars be one and the same[[fn:1792]]; yet it may be that the brilliant stars are of one distinct substance, and the nebulae[[fn:1793]] of another substance. Finally, it is known that every body is composed of its matter and its form[[fn:1794]].
root.text.Part 2..21.5: It is therefore manifest that these things proceed not by way of necessity, as he says. Likewise, the diversity of the motion of the spheres is not in relation to their successive order[[fn:1795]], one below the other, in such wise that one might maintain in this regard the system of necessity, of which we have already spoken[[fn:1796]].
root.text.Part 2..21.6: There is yet (in this system) another thing which overthrows all that has been established regarding physical things, if one considers the state of the celestial sphere: If the matter of all the spheres be one, how comes it that the form of such a sphere is not necessarily transferred to the matter of another, as happens in sublunary things, by reason of the aptitude of matter[[fn:1797]]? Why does such a form remain ever in such (determined) matter, since all have a common matter? — Unless, by God, one would maintain that each sphere has a matter different from that of the others, so that then the form of motion would no longer be a proof for (the unity of) the matter[[fn:1798]]; but that would be the subversion of all principles.
root.text.Part 2..21.7: Furthermore, if the matter of all the stars be one, by what means (one might inquire) are their individualities distinguished? Is it by forms or by accidents? However, in either of these two hypotheses, it would be necessary that either these forms or these accidents should of necessity be transferred unto each of the stars, unless one would deny the aptitude of matter[[fn:1799]].
root.text.Part 2..21.8: Thou shalt therefore understand thereby that, if we speak of the matter of the spheres, or the matter of the stars, this must in no wise be taken in the same sense as that sublunary matter, and that there is therein but a mere homonymy; for each of these celestial bodies has an existence peculiar unto itself, in which the others do not participate. But if it be so, how comes it nevertheless that there is a community touching the circular motion of the spheres or the fixedness of the stars? — However, if we admit that all this takes place by the design of a Being acting with intention, who has made and determined all things as His incomprehensible wisdom has required[[fn:1800]], none of these questions can be addressed unto us, which one has a right to put only to him who maintains that all things come to pass by necessity and not by a free will[[fn:1801]]. But this latter opinion accords not with the order of the universe, and no one has been able to support it by any reason or sufficient proof. Moreover, there follow therefrom things passingly improbable; for God, whom every intelligent man affirms to be endowed with all manner of perfections, would find Himself, with respect to all beings, powerless to innovate aught[[fn:1802]], and if He willed to lengthen the wing of a fly or shorten the foot of an insect, He could not do so. But Aristotle will say to this that God wills it not, and that it would even be inadmissible that He should will it to be otherwise; that (he would say) would not be to attribute unto Him greater perfection, and perhaps it would rather be an imperfection in certain respects[[fn:1803]].
root.text.Part 2..21.9: I shall tell thee as a general thesis—for although I know that many passionate men[[fn:1804]] will reproach me for understanding their words but little or for departing from them by design, I shall not for that reason abstain from saying what I have perceived and understood according to my feeble intelligence—and this thesis is as follows: All that Aristotle has said concerning all that exists beneath the sphere of the moon, unto the centre of the earth, is indubitably true; and no one could depart therefrom, save him who understands it not, or he who has preconceived opinions which he desirs to defend at any cost[[fn:1805]], or which lead him to deny an evident thing. But, from the sphere of the moon upwards, all that Aristotle says thereof resembls, well-nigh, mere conjectures; and with greater reason, what he says of the order of the Intelligences, as well as some of those metaphysical opinions which he adopts, without being able to demonstrate them, but which contain great improbabilities, evident and manifest errors prevalent among the nations, and evil doctrines which have been divulged[[fn:1806]].
root.text.Part 2..21.10: One must not criticize me for having brought to light the doubts[[fn:1807]] which attach unto his opinion. Is it indeed by doubts, thou wilt say to me, that one can destroy an opinion, or establish the opposite opinion? Verily, it is not so; but we act with this philosopher as his followers have recommended us to act with him. Indeed, Alexander has already set forth that, whenever a thing is not susceptible of being demonstrated, one must needs pose the two contrary hypotheses[[fn:1808]] in succession, see what doubts attach unto each of the two opposite cases, and admit that which offers the fewest doubts. Thus it is, says Alexander, with all that Aristotle says touching certain metaphysical opinions for which one has no demonstration; for all those who have come after Aristotle affirm that what Aristotle has said thereof offers fewer doubts than all that might else be said[[fn:1809]].
root.text.Part 2..21.11: And this is what we have done: after it has been verified unto us that, in the question of knowing whether the heaven be created or eternal, neither of the two opposite hypotheses can be demonstrated, and after having set forth the doubts inherent in each of the two opinions, we have shown thee[[fn:1810]] that the opinion of the eternity of the world offers the most doubts and that it is right dangerous for the belief which one must profess concerning God. Let us add thereto that the creation of the world is the opinion of our father Abraham and of Moses, our prophet.
root.text.Part 2..21.12: Since we have affirmed that opinions must needs be examined by means of the doubts which they contain, I deem it my duty to enter into some details thereupon.
root.text.Part 2..22.0: Know that, in the comparison to be established between the doubts which attach to a certain opinion and those which attach to the contrary opinion, in order to give preference to that which offers the fewest doubts, it is not a matter of taking into consideration the mere number of doubts, but rather the gravity of the improbability which they reveal and of the difficulties encountered in the nature of existence[[fn:1811]]. For it may be that a single doubt possesses in itself more importance than a thousand other doubts.
root.text.Part 2..22.1: Furthermore, this comparison can only be profitably established by one who should accord an equal value to the two contrary hypotheses; but if any man, whether by reason of his education or through some interest whatsoever, should prefer beforehand one of the two opinions, he would remain blind to the truth. Verily, a man moved by passion cannot persist in his obstinacy against a thing demonstrable; but, when it concerns such hypothetical matters, it is but too possible to show oneself rebellious.
root.text.Part 2..22.2: Thou mayest sometimes, if thou wilt, divest thyself of passion, rid thyself of habit, rely solely upon speculation, and choose by preference that which merits to be preferred; but for this, several conditions must be fulfilled: Firstly, to know how to measure the capacity of thy mind and the perfection of thy natural talent; and thou shalt enlighten thyself hereupon by studying all the mathematical sciences[[fn:1812]] and by seeking to understand the rules of logic. Secondly, to know the physical sciences and to fathom them, so as to render unto thyself an exact account of the doubtful points[[fn:1813]]. Thirdly, to watch over thy morals; for as soon as a man, whether by his nature or by acquired habit, finds himself drawn towards appetites and pleasures, or allows himself to yield to violence and anger, letting his irascible faculty prevail and giving it the rein, he will ever stumble and trip whithersoever he goes, seeking opinions that may serve to support his natural inclination.
root.text.Part 2..22.3: I have directed thy attention thereto, lest thou be seduced; for it may be that someone, some day, shall lead thee into error by raising doubts against the creation of the world, and that thou be too ready to let thyself be deceived by adopting an opinion which undermins religion at its foundation and proclaims a heresy regarding God[[fn:1814]]. Thy mind must therefore be ever on its guard in this respect[[fn:1815]], and thou must follow the two prophets[[fn:1816]] who are the pillar of the improvement of the human race in its beliefs and its social life. Thou shalt not depart from the opinion of the creation of the world save by reason of a true demonstration; but such a thing exists not in nature.
root.text.Part 2..22.4: Let not the reader of this treatise find fault with me for having here employed rhetorical arguments to support the opinion of the creation of the world; for the prince of philosophers, Aristotle, in his principal writings, has likewise employed rhetorical arguments to support his opinion of the eternity of the universe; and it is in such a case that one may say in truth: “Does not our perfect law excel their frivolous discourses[[fn:1817]]?” If he supports his opinion by the follies of the Sabeans[[fn:1818]], how should we not support ours by the words of Moses and Abraham, and by all that follows therefrom?
root.text.Part 2..22.5: I have promised thee a chapter[[fn:1819]] in which I should speak to thee of the grave doubts which may be opposed to him who believs that human science can account[[fn:1820]] for the order of the motions of the heavenly sphere, and that these are physical matters which occur by a necessary law, the order and connection of which are clear. I now, therefore, approach the exposition thereof.
root.text.Part 2..23.0: Thou knowest of astronomy that which, in my lessons, thou hast read and understood of the contents of the book of the Almagest; but time was not sufficient to cause thee to commence another study[[fn:1821]].
root.text.Part 2..23.1: What thou already knowest is that, in order to account for the regularity of the motions, and that the course of the stars may accord with visible phenomena, one must admit (one of these) two hypotheses[[fn:1822]], either an epicycle or an eccentric sphere, or even both together[[fn:1823]]. But I shall point out to thee that each of these two hypotheses is entirely[[fn:1824]] outside of all rule and contrary to all that has been expounded in physical science. Firstly, to establish an epicycle which revolvs upon a certain sphere, without revolving around the center of that sphere which bears it, as has been supposed for the moon and for the five planets[[fn:1825]], is a thing wherefrom it would necessarily follow that there is a rolling, that is to say, that the epicycle rolls and entirely changs its place, an inadmissible thing which they sought to escape, (to wit) that there should be (in the heavens) anything whatsoever that changs its place[[fn:1826]]. It is for this reason that Abu Bekr ibn al-Sa’igh, in a discourse of his which exists upon astronomy, has said that the existence of the epicycle is inadmissible; and, after having spoken of the said consequence (of rolling), he says that besides this inadmissible thing which would result from the existence of the epicycle, there would follow yet other inadmissible things. I shall expound them to thee: 1st, There would be a revolution around a center which would not be that of the world; and yet it is a fundamental principle of all this universe, that motions are three in number: a motion (proceeding) from the middle, another (tending) toward the middle, and another around the middle[[fn:1827]]. But, if there were an epicycle, its motion would be neither from the middle, nor toward it, nor around it. 2nd, It is one of the principles laid down by Aristotle, in physical science, that there must necessarily be something fixed around which the motion occurrs, and this is why it is necessary that the earth remain fixed; but, if the epicycle existed, it would be a circular motion around naught that is fixed.
root.text.Part 2..23.2: I have heard it said that Abu Bekr mentioned having found an astronomical system in which there was no epicycle, but (where all was explained) solely by eccentric spheres; yet, I have not heard this (from the mouth) of his disciples[[fn:1828]]. But, even had he succeeded therein, he would not have gained much; for, in (the hypothesis of) eccentricity, one likewise departs from the principles laid down by Aristotle, to which naught can be added. And this is an observation which belongs to me. For, in eccentricity also, we find a circular motion of the spheres which occurrs not around the middle (of the universe), but around an imaginary point which departs from the center of the world; and this is likewise a motion which occurrs not around something fixed. It is true that those who have no knowledge of astronomy pretend that, since these (imaginary) points are within the sphere of the moon, as it appears at first sight, eccentricity also admitts a motion around the middle (of the universe); and we should wish to be able to grant them that it (the motion) occurrs around a point in the fire or in the air, although that be not a motion around something fixed[[fn:1829]]. But we shall expound to them that the measures of the eccentricities have been demonstrated in the Almagest, according to the hypotheses adopted therein; and the moderns having established by a true demonstration, in which there is naught doubtful, what is the measure of these eccentricities relative to the semi-diameter of the earth[[fn:1830]], even as they have expounded all the distances and magnitudes (of the stars), it has been proved that the center of the eccentric of the sun[[fn:1831]] is necessarily outside the concavity of the sphere of the moon and below the convexity of the sphere of Mercury[[fn:1832]]. Likewise, the point around which Mars revolvs, I mean the center of its eccentric, is outside the concavity of the sphere of Mercury and below the convexity of the sphere of Venus. Likewise again, the center of the eccentric of Jupiter is found at this same distance[[fn:1833]], I mean between the spheres[[fn:1834]] of Mercury and Venus. As for Saturn, the center of its eccentric falls between Mars and Jupiter. Behold[[fn:1835]], consequently, how far all these things depart from physical speculation! All this shall become clear to thee, when thou shalt have studied the distances and magnitudes known for each sphere and for each star; and the evaluation of all this is made by the semi-diameter of the earth, so that all (is calculated) according to one and the same ratio, without establishing any between the eccentricity and the respective sphere.
root.text.Part 2..23.3: But there is something stranger still and far more obscure: it is that, whenever there be two spheres placed one within the other, closely applied on all sides to each other, but having different centres[[fn:1836]], it may happen that the smaller movs within the larger without the latter moving also; but it is impossible that the larger should move upon any axis whatsoever, without the smaller moving also; for whenever the larger movs, it necessarily carries the smaller along by its motion, save only when the motion occurrs upon the axis which passes through the two centres[[fn:1837]]. Now, by reason of this demonstrative proposition, by reason of that which has been demonstrated, that a vacuum exists not[[fn:1838]], and finally, by reason of the hypothesis of eccentricity[[fn:1839]], it would follow that, the superior (sphere) being in motion, it should carry the inferior along, by its motion, around its (own) centre; and yet we find not that it is so, but on the contrary we find that neither of the two spheres, the one containing and the other contained, movs either by the motion of the other, nor around the centre of the latter, nor around its poles, and that each has a motion which is peculiar to itself. Wherefore men have been constrained to admit (that there exist), between the spheres taken in pairs, bodies other than those of the spheres (of the planets)[[fn:1840]]. But, how many obscurities would yet remain there, if it were truly thus! where would one suppose the centres of these bodies to be, which would exist between each couple of spheres? And it would be necessary that these bodies also should have a peculiar motion. — Already Thâbit[[fn:1841]] has set this forth in a special treatise, and he has demonstrated, according to what we have said, that one must necessarily (admit) a spherical body between each couple of spheres. — I did not explain all this unto thee when thou didst follow my lessons, lest I should confuse thee in that which I intended to make thee understand.
root.text.Part 2..23.4: Regarding the inclination and the obliquity which are spoken of concerning the latitude of Venus and Mercury[[fn:1842]], I have set forth unto thee viva voce and (clearly) shown that it is impossible to conceive how such a thing can exist in the (celestial) bodies[[fn:1843]]. Ptolemy has clearly acknowledged the difficulty thereof[[fn:1844]], as thou hast seen; for he expresses himself in these terms: «Let no man believe that these principles and the like can with difficulty take place, considering what we have presented here as things obtained by artifice and by the subtlety of art, and which can with difficulty take place; for it is not meet to compare human things with things divine[[fn:1845]].» Such are his own words, as thou knowest.
root.text.Part 2..23.5: I have indicated unto thee the places wherefrom thou mayest verify all that I have told thee, save only what I told thee[[fn:1846]] concerning the observation of those points which are the centres of the eccentrics, (to wit) where they fall; for I have never met with any (author) who has occupied himself therewith. But this shall become clear unto thee, when thou shalt know the measure of the diameter of each sphere, and what is the distance between the two centres, relatively to the semi-diameter of the earth, as Al-Kabîçî has demonstrated in the treatise on Distances[[fn:1847]]; for, when thou shalt examine these distances, thou shalt acknowledge the truth of that which I have remarked unto thee.
root.text.Part 2..23.6: Observe, therefore, how obscure all this is; if that which Aristotle says in physical science be the truth, there is[[fn:1848]] neither epicycle nor eccentric, and all revolvs around the centre of the earth. But whence then would come to the planets all these diverse movements? Is it possible, in any manner, that the motion should be perfectly circular and uniform, and that it should correspond (at the same time) to the visible phenomena, if it be not (explained) by one of the two hypotheses[[fn:1849]] or by both at once? The more so as, in admitting all that Ptolemy says of the epicycle of the moon and of its deviation toward a point without the centre of the world and also without the centre of the eccentric[[fn:1850]], the calculations made according to these hypotheses are not found wanting by so much as a single minute, and the truth thereof is attested by the reality of eclipses, ever calculated according to these hypotheses and for which one fixes so exactly the epochs, as well as the times and the measurements[[fn:1851]] of the obscuration. — How further can one conceive the (apparent) retrogradation of a planet, with its other movements, without (the hypothesis of) the epicycle[[fn:1852]]? How, finally, can it be imagined that there is there (in the heavens) a rolling or motion around a non-fixed centre? And this is a real perplexity.
root.text.Part 2..23.7: I have already explained unto thee viva voce that all this concerns not the astronomer; for he has not for his aim to make us know in what form the spheres exist, but his aim is to establish a system whereby it may be possible to admit circular motions, uniform and conformable to that which is perceived by the sight, regardless of whether the matter be (really) thus, or not[[fn:1853]].
root.text.Part 2..23.8: Thou art aware that Abu-Bekr ibn-al-Çâyeg, in his discourse upon Physics, expresses this doubt: whether Aristotle was cognizant of the eccentricity of the sun, and if, passing it over in silence, he occupied himself only with that which results from inclination, — the effect of eccentricity being in no wise distinct from that of inclination[[fn:1854]], — or whether, perchance, he knew it not at all. The truth is that he knew it not, and had never heard thereof; for the mathematical sciences were imperfect in his time. Had he heard of it, he would most certainly have rejected it with vehemence; and had it been proven unto him, he would have found himself in great perplexity regarding all that he had established upon this matter.
root.text.Part 2..23.9: That which I have already declared above[[fn:1855]], I shall here repeat: to wit, that all which Aristotle has said concerning sublunary things follows a logical sequence; these are matters of which the cause is known and which are deduced one from another, and the place therein held by the wisdom and providence of nature is evident and manifest. As for all that is in the heavens, man knows naught thereof, save only this small portion of mathematical theories[[fn:1856]]; and thou seest how it stands. I shall say, employing a poetical phrase: The heavens are the Lord's; but the earth has He given to the children of Adam (Ps. cxv. 16), which is to say, that God alone perfectly knows the true nature of the heavens, their substance, their form, their movements, and their causes; but as for that which is beneath the heavens, He has given unto man the power to know it, for that is his world and the habitation in which he has been placed, and of which he himself forms a part. And this is the truth; for it is impossible for us to possess the elements necessary to reason upon the heavens, which are far from us and too exalted[[fn:1857]] by their place and rank; and even the general proof that may be drawn therefrom, saying that they prove unto us the existence of their Mover, is a matter unto the knowledge of which human intelligences cannot attain[[fn:1858]]. But to weary the mind with that which it cannot grasp, having not even the instruments to reach thereto, would be naught but a lack of understanding and a species of folly. Let us therefore stop at that which is within our power; but that which cannot be grasped by reasoning, let us abandon it unto him who was the object of the great divine inspiration, so that he merited that it should be said of him: With him will I speak mouth to mouth (Num. xii. 8).
root.text.Part 2..23.10: This is all that I am able to say upon this question; but it is possible that another may possess a demonstration which shall render evident the truth of that which has been obscure unto me. The greatest tribute I could pay unto the truth is to have openly declared how much these matters cast me into perplexity[[fn:1859]], and that I have neither heard nor known of any demonstration for any of them.
root.text.Part 2..24.0: Know thou that, if we refrain from professing the eternity of the universe, it is not because the text of the Law proclaims the world to be created; for the texts which indicate the novelty of the world are not more numerous than those which indicate the corporeality of God. Concerning the novelty of the world likewise, the means of an allegorical interpretation would not be wanting unto us, nor would they be forbidden us[[fn:1860]]; on the contrary, we might employ this mode of interpretation here, even as we have done to do away with the corporeality of God. Perchance it might even be much easier, and we should be well able to interpret the texts in question and establish the eternity of the universe, even as we have interpreted the other texts and rejected the corporeality of God. But two reasons have induced us not to do this and not to admit it. One is this: the incorporeality of God has been demonstrated, and it is necessary to have recourse to allegorical interpretation whenever the literal sense, being refuted by a demonstration, is known beforehand to be necessarily subject to interpretation[[fn:1861]]. But the eternity of the universe has not been demonstrated, and, consequently, it is not fitting to do violence to the texts and to interpret them allegorically, in order to make prevail an opinion of which one might just as well make the contrary prevail by reasoning in another manner[[fn:1862]]. Such, then, is one reason.
root.text.Part 2..24.1: — The second reason is this: our belief in the incorporeality of God does not subvert any of the foundations of our religion, nor does it give the lie to anything that the prophets have proclaimed. There is in this no inconvenience, save that, according to the ignorant, it would be contrary to the texts of Scripture; but, as we have shown, there is naught therein contrary to it, and it is rather the aim of Scripture. But to admit eternity as Aristotle believs it, that is to say, as a necessity, so that no law of nature can be changed and nothing can depart from its habitual course, would be to undermine religion at its foundation, necessarily to brand all miracles as falsehoods, and to deny[[fn:1863]] all that religion has caused to be hoped or feared, unless, by God! one would also interpret the miracles allegorically, as have done the Bâtenis (or allegorists)[[fn:1864]] among the Muslims, which would lead to a species of madness. — Nevertheless, if one admitts eternity according to the second opinion we have set forth[[fn:1865]], which is that of Plato, and according to which the heavens also are perishable[[fn:1866]], this opinion does not subvert the foundations of religion, and there follows not the negation of the miracle, but, on the contrary, its admissibility. One might interpret the texts in its sense[[fn:1867]] and find[[fn:1868]], in the texts of the Pentateuch and elsewhere, many analogous expressions to which it might be attached and which might even serve as proof for it. However, no necessity compells us thereto, unless this opinion could be demonstrated; but, since it has not been demonstrated, we incline not toward this opinion, nor do we pay any heed thereto[[fn:1869]]. We rather take the texts in their literal sense, and we say that religion has made known to us a thing which we are incapable of conceiving, and the miracle bears witness to the truth of that which we maintain.
root.text.Part 2..24.2: It must be known that, so soon as one admitts the novelty of the world, all miracles becoming possible, the (revelation of the) Law becoms possible also, and all the questions that might be asked on this subject vanish. If, therefore, it were asked: Why did God reveal Himself to such a man and not to another? why did God give this Law to a particular nation, without giving one to others? why did He give it at such an epoch and give it neither before nor after? why did He command certain things to be done and forbid others? why did He signalize the prophet by such miracles as are related, without there being others? what was God's purpose in this legislation? why, finally, did He not inspire our nature with the sentiment of these things commanded or forbidden, if such were His purpose[[fn:1870]]? — the answer to all these questions would be this: “Even so has He willed it,” or else: “Even so has His wisdom required it.” Just as He caused the world to be born in this form at the moment He willed it, without our being able to account for His will in this respect, nor for the wisdom which caused Him particularly to choose such forms[[fn:1871]] and such an epoch, even so we cannot account for His will, nor for what His wisdom demanded, when He determined all that is the subject of the preceding questions. But, if it were maintained that the world is thus by necessity, it would necessarily be required to ask all these questions, and one could only escape them by sorry answers, which would contain the denial and negation of all those texts of the Law of which a man of understanding could not doubt the literal sense[[fn:1872]]. It is for this reason that men have avoided (professing) this opinion, and for this reason pious men have passed and will pass their lives meditating upon this question; for, if the novelty (of the world) were demonstrated, were it even according to the opinion of Plato, all that the philosophers have said to refute us would fall; and likewise, if they had succeeded in demonstrating the eternity (of the world)[[fn:1873]] according to the opinion of Aristotle, the whole of religion would fall, and one would be led toward other opinions.
root.text.Part 2..24.3: I have already set forth unto thee that all depends upon this question; mark it well.
root.text.Part 2..25.0: In the celebrated Aphorisms of Rabbi Eliezer the Great, known by the title of Pirke Rabbi Eliezer, I have seen a passage such as I have never seen more strange in the discourses of any who follow the law of Moses, our master. Hearken in what terms he expresses himself[[fn:1874]]; “From whence were the heavens created? He (God) took of the light of His garment and spread it like a cloth; and thence the heavens went forth unfolding, even as it has been said: Who coverest thyself with light as with a garment, who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain (Ps. civ. 2). — From whence was the earth created? He took of the snow from beneath the throne of His glory and cast it, even as it has been said: For He says to the snow, Be thou on the earth (Job xxxvii. 6).”
root.text.Part 2..25.1: — Such are the terms of the passage in question. Would that I knew what this sage believed! Did he perhaps believe that it is inadmissible for a thing to be produced from nothing, and that there must necessarily be a matter from which everything that is born is formed? And is it for this reason that he sought for the heaven and the earth (the matter) from whence they had been created? But, in whatever manner his answer be understood, one must necessarily ask him: “From whence was created the light of His garment? From whence was created the snow which is under the throne of glory? From whence was created this throne itself?” — For if, by the light of His garment, he had intended to indicate something uncreated, and if likewise (according to him) the throne of glory were uncreated, this would be (an opinion) most reprehensible[[fn:1875]]; for he would then have affirmed the eternity of the world[[fn:1876]], at the very least in the sense of the opinion of Plato[[fn:1877]].
root.text.Part 2..25.2: As touching the throne of glory, the doctors say expressly that it is one of the created things, although they express themselves in a singular manner (saying) that it was created before the creation of the world[[fn:1878]]. As for the texts of the (sacred) books, they speak not at all of creation in its regard, with the exception of these words of David: The Lord has prepared His throne in the heavens (Ps. ciii. 19); but this is a passage which lends itself much to allegorical interpretation[[fn:1879]]. What the text declars expressly is its eternal duration: Thou, O Lord, remainest for ever; Thy throne (endurs) from generation to generation (Lam. v. 19).
root.text.Part 2..25.3: — If, therefore, R. Eliezer had admitted the eternity of the Throne, the same could designate naught but an attribute of God and not a created body[[fn:1880]]; but how then would it be possible for anything to have been born of an attribute? — Yet that which is most marvelous is the expression the light of His garment.
root.text.Part 2..25.4: In sum, this is a passage which greatly perplexes the theologian, who is a man of science, in his faith[[fn:1881]]. I could not give a sufficient interpretation thereof, and I have only spoken of it to thee so that thou shouldst not allow thyself to be led into error;
root.text.Part 2..25.5: but, be that as it may, he (the author) has rendered us a great service therein, by stating clearly that the matter of the heavens is other than that of the earth, and that they are two right distinct matters. The one, by reason of its elevation and majesty, is attributed to God and proceeds from the light of His garment[[fn:1882]]; the other, remote from the light and splendor of God, is the inferior matter, which is made to proceed from the snow which is under the throne of glory[[fn:1883]]. — This is what led me to interpret the words of the Pentateuch, And under His feet there was as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone (Exodus, xxiv. 10), in this sense: that they perceived, in that prophetic vision, the true condition of the inferior prime matter; for Onkelos, as I have explained to thee, considers the words His feet as referring to the throne, which clearly indicats that this whiteness, which was under the throne, is the terrestrial matter[[fn:1884]].
root.text.Part 2..25.6: Rabbi Eliezer has therefore repeated the same thing, expressing himself more clearly, to wit, that there are two matters, one superior and one inferior, and that the matter of all things is by no means one and the same. This is a great mystery, and one must not disdain what the greatest doctors of Israel have revealed concerning it; for it is one of the mysteries of Being, and one of the secrets of the Torah. In the Bereshith Rabba we read: “R. Eliezer says: the creation of all that is in the heavens proceeds from the heavens, and the creation of all that belongs to the earth proceeds from the earth[[fn:1885]].” Remark well how this doctor says clearly that all which belongs to the earth, that is to say, all that is beneath the sphere of the moon, has one common matter, and that the matter of the heavens and of all that is found therein is another, distinct from the former[[fn:1886]]. In his Aphorisms, he adds this new trait concerning the majesty of one of these matters, nigh unto God, as also the defectiveness of the other and its circumscribed space. Thou must fully possess thyself of this.
root.text.Part 2..26.0: I have already expounded to thee that the belief in the creation of the world is necessarily the basis of the whole religion; but that this world, a new creation, must also one day perish[[fn:1887]], is not, in our view, an article of faith, and in believing in its perpetuity, one would offend none of our creeds. Perchance thou wilt say: “Has it not been demonstrated that everything which is born is perishable? Therefore, since it was born, it must perish.” But know thou well that we are not bound to reason thus[[fn:1888]]; for we have not maintained that it was born as physical things are born, subject to a natural law[[fn:1889]]. In truth, that which is born according to the natural course of things must needs perish according to the course of nature; for just as its nature required that it should not at first exist such as it is[[fn:1890]] and that afterwards it should become so, even so does it necessarily require that it should not perpetually exist thus[[fn:1891]], since it is proved that, by its very nature, this manner of existence does not suit it perpetually. But according to our religious thesis, which attributs the existence of things and their loss to the will of God, and not to necessity, according to this opinion (I say), naught constrains us to admit that God, after having produced a thing which had not existed, must necessarily destroy that thing. On the contrary, it shall depend either upon His will, which shall be free to destroy it or to preserve it, or[[fn:1892]] upon what His wisdom shall require; it will therefore be possible that He should preserve it eternally and grant it a permanence similar to His own.
root.text.Part 2..26.1: Thou knowest (for example) that the Sages have expressly declared that the Throne of Glory is a created thing, and yet they have never affirmed that it must cease to be; it has never been heard, in the discourse of any prophet or any sage, that the Throne of Glory must perish or cease to be, and the text of Scripture has even proclaimed its eternal duration[[fn:1893]]. In like manner, the souls of the righteous, according to our opinion, though created, do never cease to exist[[fn:1894]]. According to certain opinions of those who adhere to the literal sense of the Midrashim, their bodies also shall enjoy perpetual delights throughout all eternity, which resembls the well-known belief that certain folk profess concerning the denizens of Paradise[[fn:1895]].
root.text.Part 2..26.2: In sum, (philosophical) speculation leads to this conclusion: that the world is not necessarily subject to destruction. There remains, therefore, (to be examined) only the point of view of the prediction of the prophets and sages: has it been foretold, or not, that the world shall infallibly be reduced to naught? Verily, the vulgar among us believe, for the most part, that this has been foretold and that this whole world must perish; but I shall manifest unto thee that it is not so, but on the contrary, a great number of texts proclaim its perpetuity, and that everything which, taken in the literal sense[[fn:1896]], seems to indicate that it must perish, is most evidently an allegory, as I shall explain. If any partisan of the literal sense refuss this, saying that he must necessarily believe in the (future) destruction of the world, one must not cavil with him on that account[[fn:1897]]. However, he must be made to know that, if the destruction of the world be necessary, it is not because it is created, and that, if according to him it must be admitted, it is rather by a sincere faith in that which has been foretold by that allegorical expression which he himself has taken in its literal sense. There is in this no kind of danger to religion.
root.text.Part 2..27.0: Many of our coreligionists believe that Solomon admitted the eternity (of the world). But it is marvelous that one could have imagined that a man who professed the religion of Moses our Master could have admitted eternity. If any one believed—from which may God preserve us!—that he had deserted therein religious opinions[[fn:1898]], how then would all the prophets and sages have accepted him? how would they not have attacked him upon this point and blamed him after his death, as was necessary to be done[[fn:1899]] for the strange women and for other things? That which gave rise to the suspicion concerning him in this regard is that the sages say: “They sought to suppress the Book of Ecclesiastes, because its words lean toward the words of heretics[[fn:1900]].” Such is the case, doubtless; I mean to say that this book, taken in its literal sense, contains things which lean toward heterodox opinions[[fn:1901]] and which stand in need of interpretation. But the eternity (of the world) is not among them; there is (in this book) no passage which indicats it, and still less finds one there a text which manifestly declars the eternity of the world. However, it contains passages which indicate its perpetual duration, which is true; now, having seen therein passages which indicate its perpetuity, it was thought that Solomon believed it uncreated, whereas it is not so.
root.text.Part 2..27.1.sub_0: The passage concerning perpetuity is this: and the earth abids for ever, לעלם (Ecclesiastes, i. 4); and those who have not bestowed their attention upon this curious point have been obliged to have recourse to this explanation: during the time which has been appointed unto it[[fn:1902]]. They have likewise said, concerning these words of God: While the earth remains (Genesis, viii. 22), that it referrs to the duration of the time appointed unto it. But I would fain know what shall be said of the words of David: He laid the foundations of the earth, that it should not be removed, for ever (Ps. civ. 5); for if the words עולם ועד, in sœculum, did not also indicate perpetual duration, God also would have a certain limited duration, since His perpetuity is expressed in these terms: the Lord shall reign for ever and ever, לעלם ועד (Exodus, xv. 18)[[fn:1903]]. But what must be known is that עולם, sœculum, indicats perpetual duration only when the particle עד is joined thereto, whether after, as, for example, עולם ועד, or before, as, for example, עד עולם; thus therefore, the expression of Solomon, לעלם עמדת abids for ever, would even say less than that of David, בל תמוט עולם ועד, that it should not be removed for ever. David, in effect, has clearly set forth the perpetuity of the heaven and (declared) that its laws, as well as all that it contains, shall remain invariably in the same state. He said: Praise ye the Lord from the heavens, etc., for He commanded, and they were created; He has also established them for ever and ever; He has made a decree which shall not pass (Ps. cxlviii. 1, 5, 6), which means that those laws which He has fixed shall never be changed; for the word חֹק (law) is an allusion to the ordinances of heaven and earth, of which mention was previously made[[fn:1904]].
root.text.Part 2..27.1.sub_1: But at the same time he declars that they were created, saying: for He commanded, and they[[fn:1905]] were created. Jeremiah said: Thus says the Lord, which gives the sun for a light by day, (who has prescribed) the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night, etc., if those ordinances depart from before me, says the Lord, then the seed of Israel also shall cease from being a nation. (Jeremiah, xxxi. 35); he has therefore likewise declared that although they were created, namely these laws, they shall not depart. If then one pursus the research, one shall find (also this doctrine) elsewhere than in the words of Solomon. But Solomon (himself) has said further that these works of God, that is to say the world and that which it contains, shall remain perpetually stable in their nature, although they were made: I know that, whatsoever God does, says he, it shall be for ever; nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it (Ecclesiastes, iii. 14). He has thus made known by this verse that the world is the work of God and that it is of perpetual duration, and he has also given the cause of its perpetuity, saying: nothing can be put to it, nor any thing taken from it; for this is the cause why it shall be for ever. It is as if he had said that the thing which is subject to change is only so because of that which is defective in it and which must be completed, or (because) of that which is superfluous and useless in it, so that this superfluity must be retrenched; whereas the works of God, being exceedingly perfect, so that it is impossible to add thereto or to take away therefrom, remain necessarily as they are, naught within them being able to bring about change[[fn:1906]]. It would seem that he wished also to indicate the end of creation, or to justify the changes that occur[[fn:1907]], saying at the end of the verse: And God does it, that men should fear before Him, which is an allusion to the miracles that occur. When he says subsequently (v. 15): That which has been is now, and that which is to be has already been, and God seeks that which is (continual); he means thereby that God wills the perpetuity of the universe and that all things therein follow each other by a mutual concatenation.
root.text.Part 2..27.2: That which he has said concerning the perfection of the works of God, and the impossibility of adding anything thereto or diminishing anything therefrom, the prince of the learned[[fn:1908]] has already declared in saying: The Rock (the Creator), His work is perfect (Deut. xxxii. 4); which signifies that all His works, to wit, His creatures, are exceedingly perfect, that no defect is mingled therein, and that they contain nothing superfluous nor anything useless. In like manner, all that is accomplished for these creatures and through them is perfectly just and conformable to the requirements of (divine) wisdom, as shall be set forth in certain chapters of this treatise.
root.text.Part 2..28.0: Know that he who understands not the language of a man whom he hears speaking, knows doubtless that this man speaks, but he is ignorant of his meaning. But, what is yet more serious, is that one sometimes hears in the discourse (of a man) words which, in the language of him who speaks, indicate a certain sense, while by chance, in the language of the listener, such a word has a sense contrary to that which the speaker intended (to express); and yet the listener believs that the word has, for him who speaks, the significance which it has for himself. If, for example, an Arab should hear a Hebrew say abâ, the Arab would believe that the other means to speak of one who rejects a thing and wills it not, whereas the Hebrew means, on the contrary, that the thing pleass him and that he wills it. Such likewise is that which befalls the vulgar with the language of the prophets; in part, they understand it not at all, but it is as (the prophet) has said: The vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed (Isaiah xxix. 11); in part, they take it backward or in a contrary sense, as (another prophet) has said: And ye have perverted the words of the living God (Jeremiah xxiii. 36). Know also that each prophet has a language peculiar to himself, which is as it were the (particular) tongue of that person; and it is in the same manner that the revelation, which is personal to him, makes him speak to those who can understand him.
root.text.Part 2..28.1: After this preamble, it must be known that that which frequently occurrs in the discourse of Isaiah,—but rarely in that of other (prophets),—is that when he wills to speak of the fall of a dynasty[[fn:1909]] or the ruin of a great nation, he employs such expressions as: The stars have fallen, the heavens have been troubled[[fn:1910]], the sun is darkened, the earth has been devastated and shaken, and many other similar metaphors.
root.text.Part 2..28.2: It is even as they say among the Arabs (speaking) of him whom a great misfortune has smitten: His heaven has been turned upside down upon his earth[[fn:1911]]. Likewise, when he describs the prosperity of a dynasty and a renewal of fortune, he employs metaphors such as the increase of the light of the sun and of the moon, the renewal of the heaven and the earth, and other analogous expressions. Thus it is that (the other prophets), when they describe the ruin of an individual, of a nation, or of a city, attribute unto God dispositions of wrath and great indignation against them; but when they describe the prosperity of a people, they attribute unto God dispositions of joy and gladness. They say (speaking) of His dispositions of wrath against men: He has gone forth, He has come down, He has roared, He has thundered, He has caused His voice to be heard, and many other similar words; they say also: He has commanded, He has said, He has acted, He has made, and so forth, as I shall set forth. Furthermore, when the prophet relats the ruin of the inhabitants of a certain place, he sometimes substituts the whole (human) species for the inhabitants of that place; thus Isaiah says: And the Lord have removed men far away (vi. 12), meaning the ruin of Israel[[fn:1912]]. Zephaniah says in the same sense: I will utterly consume man from off the land, and I will stretch out mine hand upon Judah (i. 3 and 4). Thou must be thoroughly impressed with this.
root.text.Part 2..28.3: Having explained this language (of the prophets) to thee in general, I shall now show that what I say is true and give thee proof thereof[[fn:1913]]. Isaiah,—when God charged him to announce the fall of the Babylonian empire, the destruction of Sennacherib, that of Nebuchadnezzar who appeared after him, and the cessation of his reign, and when (the prophet) beginns to depict the calamities (which were to smite them) at the end of their reign, their routs and that which was to reach them in the way of misfortunes that reach whosoever is routed and fles before the victorious sword,—(Isaiah, I say,) expresses himself thus: For the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light, the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine (Isaiah xiii. 10). He says again in the same description: Therefore I will shake the heavens, and the earth shall remove out of her place, in the wrath of the Lord of hosts, and in the day of His fierce anger (ibid., v. 13). I do not think there is a single man in whom ignorance, blindness, and adherence to the literal sense of metaphors and rhetorical expressions, have reached such a point that he would think the stars of heaven and the light of the sun and of the moon were altered when the kingdom of Babylon perished, or that the earth departed from its centre, as the (prophet) expresses it. But all this is the description of the state of a man put to flight, who, without doubt, beholds all light as darkness, finds all sweetness bitter, and imagins that the earth is too narrow for him and that the heaven has been darkened[[fn:1914]] over him.
root.text.Part 2..28.4: In like manner, when he portrays the state of abasement and humiliation into which the Israelites were to fall during the days of the impious Sennacherib, when he should seize all the fenced cities of Judah (ibid., XXXVI, 1), how they were to be led captive and put to rout, what calamities were successively to descend upon them from the hand of that king, and how the land of Israel was then to perish by his power, — he expresses himself thus: Fear, and the pit, and the snare, are upon thee, O inhabitant of the earth. And it shall come to pass, that he who fles from the noise of the fear shall fall into the pit; and he that comes up out of the midst of the pit shall be taken in the snare; for the windows from on high (celestial) are open, and the foundations of the earth do shake. The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly. The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, etc. (ibid., XXIV, 17-20). At the conclusion of this discourse, in describing what God will do unto Sennacherib, the loss of his haughty dominion in his expedition against Jerusalem, and the shame wherewith God shall confound him before that city, he says allegorically[[fn:1915]]: Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of hosts shall reign, etc. (ibid., v. 23). Jonathan ben Uziel has right well interpreted these words; for he says that, when that which is to happen unto Sennacherib shall befall him in his expedition against Jerusalem, the worshippers of the stars shall know that it is a divine act, and they shall be stupified and troubled: Those, says he, who pay worship to the moon shall be confounded, and those who bow down before the sun shall be humiliated, for the kingdom of God shall be revealed, etc[[fn:1916]].
root.text.Part 2..28.5: Furthermore, in depicting the tranquillity which the Israelites should enjoy when Sennacherib had perished, the fertility and the repeopling of their lands, and the prosperity of their empire under Hezekiah, he says allegorically that the light of the sun and the moon shall be increased; for, even as it has been said concerning the vanquished, that the light of the sun and moon departs and is changed into darkness in respect of the vanquished, so likewise the light of both luminaries increass for the victor. Thou shalt ever find that, when a great calamity befalls a man, his eyes wax dim, and the light of his vision is not clear, because the visual spirit[[fn:1917]] is troubled by the abundance of vapours, and at the same time it is weakened and diminished by great sorrow and by the contraction of the soul. In joy, on the contrary, when the soul expands and the spirit (visual) becoms bright, man beholds the light, as it were, more powerful than heretofore. — After having said: For the people shall dwell in Zion at Jerusalem: thou shalt weep no more, etc. (the prophet adds), at the end of the discourse: Moreover the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day that the Lord binds up the breach of his people, and heals the stroke of their wound (ibid., XXX, 19 and 26); he means thereby: when He shall raise them up from their fall[[fn:1918]] which they shall have suffered at the hand of the impious Sennacherib. As for these words: as the light of seven days, the commentators say that he means to indicate thereby a great quantity of light; for the Hebrews employ seven for a great number. But it seems unto me that he alludes unto the seven days of the dedication of the Temple which took place in the days of Solomon; for never had the nation enjoyed such happiness, prosperity, and general joy as in those days. He says, therefore, that their happiness and prosperity shall then be as great as in those seven days.
root.text.Part 2..28.6: When he describs the ruin of the impious Edomites, who oppressed the Israelites, he says: Their slain also shall be cast out, and their stink shall come up out of their carcases, and the mountains shall be melted with their blood. And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll: and all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falls off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree. For my sword shall be bathed in heaven: behold, it shall come down upon Idumea, etc. (ibid., XXXIV, 3–5). Now, consider, ye who have eyes to see, if there be in these texts aught that is obscure, or that might lead one to suppose that he describs an event which shall happen in the heavens, and if this be aught else than a metaphor to signify that their kingdom shall be destroyed, that the protection of God shall be withdrawn from them, that their fortune shall be cast down, and that the dignities of their great ones shall vanish away[[fn:1919]] with the utmost speed and extreme rapidity. It is as though he said that those personages who were comparable unto the stars for their stability, for their elevation of rank, and for their distance from vicissitudes, shall fall, in the briefest space, as the leaf falls off from the vine, etc. This is too manifest to be discussed in a treatise such as this, and, with even greater reason, to be dwelt upon. Yet necessity has called us thereto; for the vulgar, and even those who are accounted men of distinction, draw proofs from this verse, without paying heed to what preceds or follows, and without reflecting upon what subject it was spoken, regarding it only as a narrative by which the Scripture intended to announce unto us the end of heaven, even as it has related its birth.
root.text.Part 2..28.7: Furthermore, when Isaiah announcs unto the Israelites the ruin of Sennacherib and of all the nations and kings that were with him [as is well known] and the victory they shall gain through the help of God alone, he says unto them allegorically: see how this heaven dissolvs, how this earth waxes old; they that dwell therein die, and ye, ye are succoured. It is as though he said that they who have encompassed the whole earth and who were thought as firm as heaven, — by way of hyperbole[[fn:1920]], — shall perish swiftly and vanish away like smoke, and their monuments which were in sight[[fn:1921]] and appeared as stable as the earth, these monuments shall perish as a garment that is worn out. At the beginning of this discourse, he says: For the Lord shall comfort Zion: he will comfort all her waste places; etc. Hearken unto me, my people, etc. My righteousness is near; my salvation is gone forth, etc. Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look upon the earth beneath: for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment, and they that dwell therein shall die in like manner: but my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished (ibid., LI, 3-6).
root.text.Part 2..28.8: In speaking of the restoration of the kingdom of the Israelites, of its stability and duration, he says that God will produce anew a heaven and an earth; for, in his language, he ever speaks concerning the reign of a king as if it were a world peculiar unto himself, to wit: a heaven and an earth. After having commenced the consolations with the words: I, even I, am he that comforts you (ibid., v. 12), and what follows, he expresses himself thus: And I have put my words in thy mouth, and I have covered thee in the shadow of mine hand, that I may plant the heavens, and lay the foundations of the earth, and say unto Zion, Thou art my people (ibid., v. 16).
