To signify that dominion shall remain with the Israelites and that it shall depart from the celebrated mighty ones, he says: For the mountains shall depart, etc. (ibid., LIV, 10). In speaking of the perpetuity of the reign of the Messiah, and to signify that the kingdom of Israel shall thenceforth no more be destroyed, he says: Thy sun shall no more go down, etc. (ibid., LX, 20). — In fine, for him who comprehends the sense of this language, these are similar metaphors, oftentimes repeated, which Isaiah employs in his discourse. It is thus that, describing the circumstances of the exile and their particularities, and thereafter the return of power and the disappearance of all those mournings, he says allegorically: I shall create another heaven and another earth; those of the present[[fn:1922]] shall be forgotten and their trace shall be blotted out. Then he explains this in the sequel of the discourse, saying: If I employ the words I create etc., I mean thereby that I will form for you a state of continual joy and gladness in place of these mournings and this affliction, and no more shall men think upon those former mournings.
root.text.Part 2..28.9.sub_0: Hearken unto the concatenation of ideas and the manner in which the verses relating thereto follow one another: first, in commencing this subject, he says: I will mention the lovingkindnesses of the Lord, and the praises of the Lord, etc. (ibid., LXIII, 7). After this, he depicts first of all the bounties of God toward us (saying): He bare them, and carried them all the days of old, and the whole of the passage (ibid., v. 9). Then he describs our rebellion: But they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit, and that which follows (ibid., v. 10). Next he describs how the enemy became master over us: Our adversaries have trodden down thy sanctuary; we are (as those) over whom thou never barest rule, and that which follows (ibid., v. 18 and 19). Then he prays for us, and says: Be not wroth very sore, O Lord, and that which follows (ibid., LXIV, 8). After this he calls to mind in what manner we have deserved the grievous chastisement wherewith we have been tried, since we were called unto the truth and we answered not; and he says: I am sought of them that asked not for me, etc. (ibid., LXV, 1). Then he promiss pardon and mercy, and says: Thus says the Lord, As the new wine is found in the cluster, and that which follows (ibid., v. 8). He then threatens those who have oppressed us, and says: Behold, my servants shall eat, but ye shall be hungry, etc. (ibid., v. 13). Finally, he adds thereto that the beliefs of this nation shall be amended, that she shall become an object of blessing upon the earth, and that she shall forget all previous vicissitudes; and he expresses himself in these terms: And he shall call his servants by another name; that he who blesses himself in the earth shall bless himself in the God of truth; and he that swears in the earth shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten, and because they are hid from mine eyes. For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind. But be ye glad and rejoice for ever in that which I create: for, behold, I create Jerusalem a rejoicing, and her people a joy.
root.text.Part 2..28.9.sub_1: And I will rejoice in Jerusalem, etc. (ibid., v. 15-19). — Thou hast therefore now a clear explanation of the whole subject. It is that, after having said: For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, he explains it immediately, saying: For, behold, I create Jerusalem a rejoicing, and her people a joy. After this preamble, he says: Even as these circumstances of faith and the exultation thereunto attached, circumstances which I have promised to create[[fn:1923]], shall ever subsist, — for faith in God and the exultation caused by that faith are two circumstances which can never cease nor be altered in him to whom they have come[[fn:1924]]; — he says therefore: Even as this state of faith and exultation, which I announce as destined to be universal upon the earth, shall be perpetual and stable, so shall your seed and your name endure. It is this which he says afterward: For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me, says the Lord, so shall your seed and your name remain (ibid., LXVI, 22). For it happens sometimes that the seed remains, whilst the name remains not; thou findest, for example, many peoples who indubitably are of the seed of the Persians or of the Greeks, and who nevertheless are no longer known by a particular name, but whom another nation has absorbed. There is therein further, according to my view, an allusion to the perpetuity of the Law (of Moses), by reason of which we have a particular name.
root.text.Part 2..28.10: Since these metaphors are frequently encountered in Isaiah, I have been obliged, for that reason, to traverse them all; but they are also found sometimes in the discourse of other prophets.
root.text.Part 2..28.11: J[[t:0]]EREMIAH[[t:1]] says, in describing the destruction of Jerusalem, occasioned by the crimes of our ancestors: [[t:2]]I have seen the land[[t:3]], [[t:4]]and there was only void and chaos[[t:5]] (IV, 23).
root.text.Part 2..28.12: EZEKIEL says, in describing the ruin of the kingdom of Egypt and the fall of Pharaoh by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar: I will cover the heaven when I extinguish thee, and make the stars thereof dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give her light. All the bright lights of heaven will I make dark over thee, and set darkness upon thy land, says the Lord God (XXXII, 7–8).
root.text.Part 2..28.13: J[[t:0]]OEL,[[t:1]] son of Pethouel, said (in speaking) of the multitude of locusts which arrived in his time: [[t:2]]Before them the earth trembls[[t:3]], [[t:4]]the heavens are shaken[[t:5]], [[t:6]]the sun and the moon are darkened[[t:7]], [[t:8]]and the stars withdraw their light[[t:9]] (II, 10).
root.text.Part 2..28.14: AMOS says, in describing the destruction of Samaria: I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day; I will turn your feasts into mourning, etc. (VIII, 9 and 10).
root.text.Part 2..28.15: MICAH says, concerning the destruction of Samaria, whilst ever adhering to those oratorical figures generally known: For, behold, the Lord comes forth out of His place, and will come down, and tread upon the high places of the earth; the mountains shall be molten, etc. (I, 3-4).
root.text.Part 2..28.16: ’HAGGAI says (speaking) of the destruction of the kingdom of the Persians and the Medes: I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land; I will shake all nations, etc. (II, 6-7).
root.text.Part 2..28.17: Concerning the expedition of Joab against the Syrians, when he (David) depicts how weak and abased the nation was aforetime, and how (the Israelites) were vanquished and put to flight, and when he prays that they may be victorious at this season, he expresses himself thus: Thou hast made the earth to tremble; Thou hast broken it: heal the breaches thereof, for it shaks (Ps. 60, 4). Likewise, to admonish us that we ought to fear nothing when nations perish and pass away,—forasmuch as we rely upon the help of the Most High and not upon our own combat and upon our own strength, as (Moses) has said: A people saved by the Lord (Deut., XXXIII, 29),—he says: Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea (Ps. 46, 3).
root.text.Part 2..28.18: Concerning the drowning of the Egyptians, one finds (the following expressions): The waters saw thee and they trembled, and the depths were moved. The voice of thy thunder was in the whirlwind etc., the earth trembled and shook (Ps. lxxvii. 17 and 19). Is the Lord angry against the rivers (Habakkuk iii. 8)? There went up a smoke out of his nostrils etc. (Ps. xviii. 9). Likewise, in the song of Deborah: the earth trembled, etc. (Judges v. 4). Many (other passages) of this kind are met with; that which I have not cited, thou shalt explain in an analogous manner[[fn:1925]].
root.text.Part 2..28.19: As for these words of Joel (iii. 3-5): I will shew wonders in the heavens and in the earth, blood, and fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the Lord come. And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered; for in mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be a refuge etc., — I should be much inclined to believe that he intends to describe the ruin of Sennacherib (in his expedition) against Jerusalem. But if thou wilt not (admit) this, it may be the description of the ruin of Gog (which shall take place) before Jerusalem, in the days of the King-Messiah, albeit there is question, in this passage, only of great carnage, the ravage of flames, and the eclipse of the two luminaries. Perhaps thou wilt say: how is it that, according to our explanation, he calls the day of the ruin of Sennacherib the great and terrible day of the Lord? But it must be known that every day whereon there occurrs a great victory or a great calamity is called the great and terrible day of the Lord. Joel has likewise said (speaking) of the day when those locusts came against them[[fn:1926]] (ii. 11): For the day of the Lord is great and very terrible; and who can abide it?
root.text.Part 2..28.20: The aim at which we point is already known; it is (to prove) that a (future) destruction of this world, a change in the state in which it is, or even any change whatsoever in its nature, such that it must thenceforth remain in that altered state[[fn:1927]], is a thing which no prophetic text, nor even any discourse of the Sages, does support; for when these latter say: "The world endurs six thousand years and for one millennium it remains devastated[[fn:1928]]," it is not (in this sense) that all which exists must return unto nothingness, since those very words: and for one millennium it remains devastated, indicate that time shall remain[[fn:1929]]. For the rest, this is an individual opinion and (conceived) according to a certain way of viewing things[[fn:1930]]. But that which thou findest continually among all the Sages, and which is a fundamental principle whence each of the doctors of the Mishnâ and the Talmud draws arguments, is that, according to this word: There is no new thing under the sun (Ecclesiastes i. 9), no renewal shall take place in any manner or by any cause whatsoever. This is so true, that even he who takes the words (of Isaiah) new heavens and new earth in the sense attributed to them (by error)[[fn:1931]], says nevertheless: "Even the heavens and the earth that shall be produced one day are already created and subsist, since it is said: they remain before me; it is not said therefore they shall remain, but they remain"; and he takes for an argument these words, there is no new thing under the sun[[fn:1932]]. Do not believe (moreover) that this be in opposition to what I have set forth; it is possible, on the contrary, that he meant thereby that the physical disposition which must then produce those promised circumstances (by the prophet) has been created since the six days of creation; which is true.
root.text.Part 2..28.21: If I have said that nothing shall change its nature, so as to remain in that altered state, it was solely to make my reservations concerning miracles; for, albeit the rod (of Moses) was changed into a serpent and the water into blood, and the pure and glorious hand became white (with leprosy), without this being the result of a natural cause, these circumstances nevertheless and others like them did not endure and did not become another nature; and it was said on the contrary: The world follows its habitual course[[fn:1933]]. Such is my opinion, and this is what must be believed. Verily, the Sages have expressed themselves concerning miracles in a most extraordinary manner, in a passage which thou shalt find in the Bereshith Rabbah and in the Midrash Koheleth. But the idea they wished to express is this[[fn:1934]]: that miracles also are, in some sort, in nature; for, they say, when God created this universe and placed therein those physical dispositions, He also placed in those dispositions (the faculty) of bringing forth all the miracles that occurred at the very moment when they actually occurred[[fn:1935]]. The sign of the prophet (according to this opinion) consists in God making known to him the time when he must announce such an event[[fn:1936]] and when such a thing shall receive such an action, according to what was placed in its nature from the principle of its creation.
root.text.Part 2..28.22: If it be truly thus, it gives a high idea of the author of this passage and shews us that he found it extremely difficult (to admit)[[fn:1937]] that any physical disposition could be changed after the work of creation[[fn:1938]], or that there could occur another (divine) will after everything had been thus fixed[[fn:1939]]. His opinion seems to be, for example, that it was placed in the nature of water to be continuous and to flow always from above to below, except at the epoch when the Egyptians should be drowned; then only was the water to divide[[fn:1940]]. Thus have I pointed out to thee what is the veritable spirit of the passage in question, and that all this was said to avoid the admission of an innovation in any thing whatsoever in nature. This is what is there related[[fn:1941]]: «Rabbi Jonathan said: God made conditions with the sea, that it should divide before the Israelites; this is what is written: וישב … לאיתנו, the sea returned, toward the morning, to its former CONDITION (Exodus, xiv, 27). R. Jeremiah, son of Eleazar, said: It was not with the sea alone that God made conditions, but with all that was created in the six days of Creation; such is the sense of these words: It was my hands that stretched out the heavens, and all their host have I commanded (Isaiah, xlv, 12). I commanded the sea to divide, the fire not to harm Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, the lions not to hurt Daniel, and the whale to vomit up Jonah.» And in a like manner must the other miracles be explained.
root.text.Part 2..28.23: Now is the matter clear unto thee, and the opinion which I profess is plainly set forth. It is that we agree with Aristotle in one half of his opinion: we believe that this universe shall exist for ever and perpetually with that nature which God willed to bestow upon it, and that naught thereof shall be changed in any manner whatsoever, save in some particularity and by way of miracle, though God has the power to change it totally or to reduce it to non-existence, or to cause any of its physical dispositions to cease as it may please Him; nevertheless, it had a beginning, and at first there was absolutely nothing in existence save God. His wisdom required that He should produce the creation at the moment when He did produce it, that what He had produced should not be reduced to naught, and that its nature should be changed in nothing, save in some particularities which it might please God to change, which we already know in part, but which, in part, are yet unknown to us and belong to the future.
root.text.Part 2..28.24: Such is our opinion and such is the fundamental principle of our Law. But Aristotle thinks that, even as the universe is perpetual and imperishable, so it is eternal and has not been created. Now, we have already stated and clearly shown that this can only well accord with the law of necessity; but to proclaim necessity would be to profess a heresy[[fn:1942]] regarding God, as we have already demonstrated.
root.text.Part 2..28.25: The discussion having arrived at this point, we shall provide a chapter in which we shall also make some observations upon certain texts found in the account of creation [for the principal object in this treatise is none other than to explain what is possible to be explained in the Ma’aseh Bereshith and the Ma’aseh Mercabah[[fn:1943]]]; but we shall precede it by two general propositions.
root.text.Part 2..28.26: ONE OF THESE is the following proposition: «All that is related in the Pentateuch concerning the Work of Creation must not always be taken in its literal sense, as the vulgar imagine;» for if it were so, the men of science would not have been so reserved[[fn:1944]] in this regard, and the Doctors would not have so greatly recommended the concealment of this subject and the withholding of it from the multitude. In truth, these texts, taken literally, lead to a great corruption of ideas and give currency to evil opinions concerning the Divinity; or even lead to pure irreligion[[fn:1945]] and the denial of the foundations of the Law. The truth is, that one must refrain from considering them with the imagination alone and void[[fn:1946]] of science; and one must not act as those poor Darshanim (preachers) and commentators, who imagine that science consists in knowing the explanation of words, and in whose eyes it is a very great perfection to speak with abundance and prolixity; but to meditate thereon with a true intelligence, after having perfected oneself in the demonstrative sciences and in the knowledge of the prophetic mysteries, is verily a duty. Nevertheless[[fn:1947]], whosoever shall have acquired any knowledge of this subject must not divulge it, as I have set forth several times in the Commentary on the Mishnah[[fn:1948]]. It has been expressly said: «From the beginning of the book (of Genesis) until here, the majesty of God requirs to conceal the thing[[fn:1949]];» this is what was said in the Midrash at the end of the account of the sixth day of creation.
root.text.Part 2..28.27: Thus, what we have said is clearly demonstrated. Nevertheless, as the divine precept necessarily obligs every one who has acquired a certain perfection to bestow it upon others [as we shall explain hereafter in the chapters on prophecy], every learned man who has come to understand aught of these mysteries, whether by his own speculation or by a guide who has led him thereto, cannot refrain from speaking thereof; but, as it is forbidden to speak of them clearly, he shall make only simple allusions[[fn:1950]]. Such allusions, observations, and indications are often found also in the discourses of some of the Doctors; but they are mingled with the words of others and with other subjects[[fn:1951]]. Wherefore thou wilt find that, in speaking of these mysteries, I ever mention only the word which is the basis of the subject, and I leave the rest to those who are worthy thereof.
root.text.Part 2..28.28: A SECOND PROPOSITION[[t:1]] is the following: "The prophets, as we have stated, employ, in their discourses, homonyms and names by which they have not in view what these names signify in their first acceptation[[fn:1952]]; but rather, in employing such a name, they have regard only to a certain etymology." Thus, for example, from [[t:4]]makkel[[t:5]] [[t:6]]SCHAKÉD[[t:7]] (a staff of almond wood), one deduces [[t:8]]SCHÖKED[[t:9]] (vigilant, attentive)[[fn:1953]], as we shall explain in the chapters on prophecy[[fn:1954]]. It is from the same idea that, in the narrative of the [[t:10]]char[[t:11]], the word ’[[t:12]]HASCHMAL[[t:13]] (Ezekiel, I, 4) is employed, as has been explained; similarly [[t:14]]REGHEL ’EGHEL[[t:15]] and [[t:16]]NE’HOSCHES KALAL[[t:17]] (ibid., v. 7)[[fn:1955]]; similarly what is said by Zechariah (6, 1): [[t:20]]And the mountains were of [[t:21]] N[[t:22]]E’HOSCHES[[t:23]] (brass)[[fn:1956]], and other expressions of a similar nature.
root.text.Part 2..28.29: After these two propositions, I deliver the chapter which I have promised.
root.text.Part 2..29.0: Know thou that there is a difference between first and principle. For the principle exists either in the thing of which it serves as principle, or (simultaneously) with it, albeit it does not precede it in time[[fn:1957]]; it is said, for instance, that the heart is the principle of the animal, and that the element is the principle of that of which it is an element. Men also sometimes apply to this idea the word first. At other times, however[[fn:1958]], first is said of that which is merely anterior in time, without such anteriority being the cause of that which is posterior to it; as when it is said, “the first who dwelt in this house was such a one, and after him was such another,” without the one being called the principle of the other. The word which, in our (Hebrew) tongue, signifies priority, is TE’HILLA (תחלה); as for example: The beginning (תחלת) of the word of the Lord by Hosea (Hos. i. 2). That which designats the principle is RÉSCHÎTH (ראשית); for it is derived from RÔSCH (ראש), the head, which is the principle (beginning) of the animal, by its position[[fn:1959]].
root.text.Part 2..29.1: Now, the world was not created in a temporal beginning, as we have set forth, forasmuch as time is (itself) of the number of created things[[fn:1960]]; wherefore it is said BE–RÉSCHÎTH (בראשית, Gen. i. 1), in which the particle BE (ב) has the sense of in[[fn:1961]]. The true translation of this verse is therefore this: In the principle God created the upper and the lower (of the universe); this being the only explanation which accords with the creation (of the world)[[fn:1962]].
root.text.Part 2..29.2: — As for what you find reported on the part of some of the doctors, tending to establish that time existed before the creation of the world, it is very obscure; for that would be, as I have explained to you, the opinion of Aristotle, who thinks that one cannot imagine a beginning for time, which is absurd. What led them to profess such an opinion is that they encountered[[fn:1963]] (the expressions) one day, second day (Gen., I, 5, 8). He who professed this opinion took the matter literally: since, he said to himself, there was as yet no sphere that turned, nor sun, by what thing then would the first day have been measured? Here is the textual passage[[fn:1964]]: 'First day[[fn:1965]]: It follows from this, says R. Judah, son of R. Simon, that the order of times had existed previously. R. Abbahu says: it follows from this that the Holy One had already created worlds which He had then destroyed[[fn:1966]].' This latter opinion is even more blameworthy than the first[[fn:1967]]. You understand what seemed difficult to both of them, namely, that time existed before the existence of this sun; but the solution to what may have seemed obscure to both of them will be explained to you shortly[[fn:1968]]. Unless, by God! these (two doctors) intended to maintain that the order of times must necessarily have existed from all eternity[[fn:1969]]; — but then that would be to admit the eternity (of the world), a thing that every religious man must reject far away. This passage seems to me entirely similar to that of R. Eliezer: From where were the heavens created, etc.[[fn:1970]]. In short, one must not regard, in these subjects, what such a person may have said. I have already informed you that it is the fundamental principle of the entire religion that God produced the world from absolute nothingness, and not in a temporal beginning; time, on the contrary, is a created thing, for it accompanies the movement of the celestial sphere, and the latter is created.
root.text.Part 2..29.3: Furthermore, it behoves us to know that, regarding the particle ETH (אאת) in the verse את השמים ואת הארץ (Gen. I, 1), the Sages have declared in divers places that it signifies with. They mean thereby that God created with the heaven all that is within the heaven, and with the earth all that appertains to the earth[[fn:1971]]. Thou art also aware that they explicitly state that the heaven and the earth were created at once, citing this passage: I call unto them, they stand up together (Isaiah xlviii. 13)[[fn:1972]]. All things, therefore, were created simultaneously, and thereafter did they become distinct from one another in succession[[fn:1973]]. It is, according to their view, as with a husbandman[[fn:1974]] who has sown in the ground, at the same instant, various seeds, of which some have sprouted after one day, some after two days, and others after three days, although the entire sowing took place at the same moment. By this opinion, which is indubitably true, that doubt is dispelled which led R. Judah, son of R. Simon, to say what he said, because it was difficult for him to understand by what means the first, the second, and the third day were measured. The Sages declare themselves clearly upon this in the Bereshith Rabba; in speaking of the light which is said, in the Pentateuch, to have been created on the first day (Gen. I, 3), they express themselves thus: “These are the luminaries (ibid., v. 14) which were created from the first day, but which He did not suspend until the fourth day[[fn:1975]].” This subject is thus clearly set forth.
root.text.Part 2..29.4: It must further be observed that ארץ (earth) is a homonym, which is employed both in a general and a special sense. It applies, in general, to all that is beneath the sphere of the moon, that is to say, to the four elements; and is also used, in particular, of the last among them alone, which is the earth. The proof thereof is found in the words: And the earth was without form and void, darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the spirit of God, etc. (Gen. I, 2). Thus, they are all called ארץ (earth)[[fn:1976]]; thereafter it is said: And God called the dry land ארץ Earth (ibid., v. 10).
root.text.Part 2..29.5: —This is also one of the great mysteries; (I wish to say) that every time you find the expression [[t:0]]and God called such a thing thus[[t:1]], one has the purpose of separating it from the other idea (general), in which the name is common to both things[[fn:1977]]. This is why I have translated the (first) verse: [[t:2]]In the beginning God created the[[t:3]] [[t:4]]HAUT[[t:5]] [[t:6]]and the[[t:7]] [[t:8]]BAS[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]of the universe[[t:11]]); so that the word [[t:12]]ארץ[[t:13]] (earth) signifies, the first time, the [[t:14]]lower world[[t:15]], I wish to say the four elements, whereas in saying: [[t:16]]And God called the dry portion[[t:17]] [[t:18]]ארץ[[t:19]] [[t:20]]earth[[t:21]], one wishes to speak of the [[t:22]]earth[[t:23]] alone. This is therefore clear.
root.text.Part 2..29.6: Furthermore, it should be noted that the four elements are mentioned immediately after the heaven; for, as we have said, they are designated by the first name ארץ, earth[[fn:1978]]. In effect, there are enumerated: ארץ (earth), מים (water), רוח (spirit or air)[[fn:1979]] and חשך (darkness).—As for the word חשך (darkness), it signifies the elementary fire, and one must not think otherwise; (Moses, for example,) having said: And thou heardest His words out of the midst of the fire האש (Deut. iv. 36), says thereafter: When ye heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness החשך (ibid., v. 20); and elsewhere it is said: All darkness (calamities) shall be hid in his secret places, a fire not blown shall consume him (Job xx. 26)[[fn:1980]]. If the elementary fire has been designated by this name (of darkness), it is because it is not luminous, but only transparent[[fn:1981]]; for, were the elementary fire luminous, we should behold the entire atmosphere inflamed during the night.
root.text.Part 2..29.7: —These elements have been enumerated according to their natural positions: the earth (first), above it the water, the air adheres to the water, and fire is above the air; for, since air is designated as being [[t:0]]upon the face of the waters[[t:1]] (Gen., I, 2)[[fn:1982]], the [[t:2]]darkness[[t:3]] which is [[t:4]]upon the face of the deep[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]ibid.[[t:7]]) is indubitably situated above the [[t:8]]air[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]רוח[[t:11]]) [[t:12]][[fn:1983]][[t:13]]. That which motivated the expression [[t:16]]רוח אלהים[[t:17]], [[t:18]]the breath[[t:19]] or [[t:20]]the wind of God[[t:21]] (to designate [[t:14]]the air[[t:15]]), is that it was supposed [[t:22]]in motion[[t:23]], [[t:24]]מרחפת[[t:25]], and the movement of the wind is always attributed to God; for instance: [[t:26]]And there went forth a wind from the LORD[[t:27]] (Numb., 11, 31); [[t:28]]Thou didst blow with thy wind[[t:29]] (Exodus, 15, 10); [[t:30]]The LORD caused a west wind to turn[[t:31]] ([[t:32]]ibid.[[t:33]], X, 19), and many other passages. —Since the word ’[[t:34]]HOSCHEKH[[t:35]] ([[t:36]]חשך[[t:37]]), when first employed (v. 5) as the name of the element (of [[t:38]]fire[[t:39]]), is distinct from the ’[[t:40]]HOSCHEKH[[t:41]] subsequently mentioned, which designates [[t:42]]darkness[[t:43]], it is explained and distinguished by stating: [[t:44]]and he called the darkness Night[[t:45]] (v. 5), in accordance with what we have expounded. This is therefore equally clear.
root.text.Part 2..29.8: Furthermore, it is to be understood that in the passage: [[t:0]]And he made a division between the waters etc[[t:1]]. (v. 7), there is no mere local separation implied, such that one portion (of the waters) would have been above and another below, both possessing the same nature; the sense, on the contrary, is that He separated them one from another by a physical distinction, that is to say, by [[t:2]]form[[t:3]], and that He made of that part which He had first designated by the name of [[t:4]]water[[t:5]][[fn:1984]] a distinct entity, by means of the physical form with which He invested it, whilst He imparted to the other part a different form. This latter is the water (properly so called)[[fn:1985]]; for this reason He also stated: [[t:6]]And the gathering together of the waters called he Seas[[t:7]] (v. 10), thereby revealing to thee that the primordial [[t:8]]water[[t:9]], which is referred to in the words [[t:10]]upon the face of the waters[[t:11]] (v. 2), is not that which is in the seas, but that one part, above the atmosphere[[fn:1986]], was distinguished by a (particular) form, and that another part constitutes this (lower) water. Thus, the expression: [[t:12]]And he made a division between the waters which were under the firmament etc[[t:13]]. (v. 7), is to be understood similarly to that other: [[t:14]]And God divided the light from the darkness[[t:15]] (v. 4), where a distinction by [[t:16]]form[[t:17]] is in question.
root.text.Part 2..29.9: The firmament (רקיע) itself was formed of water, as it has been said: "The middle drop became solidified[[fn:1987]]."
root.text.Part 2..29.10: — [The expression And God called the firmament Heaven (v. 8) has furthermore the purpose which I have set forth unto thee[[fn:1988]], namely, to make manifest the homonymy and (to make it understood) that the heaven which is first mentioned in the words the heaven and the earth (v. 1) is not that which we (vulgarly) call heaven, which has been confirmed by the words in the open firmament of heaven (v. 20), declaring thus that the firmament is a different thing from the heaven. It is because of this homonymy that the true heaven is also sometimes called firmament, even as the true firmament is called heaven; thus, it is said: And God set them (the stars) in the firmament of heaven (v. 17).
root.text.Part 2..29.11: It is also clear from these words, — a point already demonstrated, — that all the stars, and (even) the sun and the moon, are fixed [[t:0]]dans[[t:1]] the sphere[[fn:1989]], because there is no void in the world[[fn:1990]]; they are not situated at the surface (inferior) of the sphere, as the common folk imagine, since we say [[t:2]]DANS[[t:3]] [[t:4]]the firmament of the heavens[[t:5]], and not [[t:6]]SUR[[t:7]] [[t:8]]the firmament of the heavens[[t:9]].
root.text.Part 2..29.12: — It is therefore clear that there was at first a certain common matter, called water, which was subsequently distinguished by three forms: one part formed the seas, another the firmament, and a third remained above this firmament; this last is entirely outside the earth[[fn:1991]]. Another method[[fn:1992]] has therefore been adopted for this subject, to (indicate) extraordinary mysteries. — That this thing which is above the firmament has been designated as water by name alone, and that it is not this specific water (of here below), is what the Doctors have also said in that passage: "Four entered into the garden (of knowledge), etc.[[fn:1993]]. Rabbi ‘Akiba said unto them: When ye arrive at the stones of pure marble, say not Water! water! for it is written: He that tells lies shall not tarry in my sight (Ps. 101, 7)[[fn:1994]]." Reflect then, if thou art of those who reflect, what light he (R. ‘Akiba) has shed by this passage, and how he has revealed the whole subject, provided that thou hast well examined it, that thou hast understood all that has been demonstrated in the Meteorology, and that thou hast perused all that has been said upon every point[[fn:1995]].
root.text.Part 2..29.13: What further merits thy attention is the reason wherefore, on the second day, it is not said כי טוב, that it was good[[fn:1996]]. Thou art acquainted with the opinions which the Doctors have expressed in this regard, according to their method of interpretation[[fn:1997]]; the best that they have said is: “that the work of the water was not completed[[fn:1998]].” According to my view also, the reason thereof is right clear: it is that, whenever mention is made of one of the works of creation[[fn:1999]] whose existence is prolonged and perpetuated and which have attained their definitive state, it is said thereof that it was good. But this firmament (רקיע) and the thing which is above it, called water, are, as thou seest, enveloped in obscurity. Verily, if one takes the matter literally and considers it but superficially[[fn:2000]], it is something which exists not at all; for, between us and the inferior heaven, there is no other body than the elements, and there is no water above the atmosphere[[fn:2001]]. And what would it be, if someone imagined that the firmament in question, with what is upon it, is above the heaven[[fn:2002]]? for then the matter would be most impossible and most incomprehensible. But (on the other hand), if one takes the matter in its esoteric sense and according to what was intended (in truth), it is extremely obscure; for it was necessary to make of it one of the occult mysteries[[fn:2003]], so that the vulgar should not know it. Now, how could it be permitted to say of such a thing that it was good? The words that it was good have no other meaning, save that the thing is of manifest and evident utility for the existence and the prolongation of this universe. But the thing whose (true) meaning is hidden, and which outwardly presents not itself as it is, what utility is there manifest therein unto men, that one might say thereof that it was good? — I must yet give thee another explanation thereof: it is that, although this thing[[fn:2004]] forms a most important part of creation, it is not however a purpose which was intended for the prolongation of the duration of the universe[[fn:2005]], so that one might have said thereof that it was good; but (it was made) for a certain urgent necessity, (that is to say) in order that the earth might be uncovered. Thou must well penetrate thyself with this.
root.text.Part 2..29.14: Thou must further know that, according to the explanation of the Doctors, the herbs and the trees, God caused them not to spring forth from the earth until He had watered it with rain[[fn:2006]], so that the passage: And a mist went up from the earth (Genesis, ii. 6) speaks of a prior circumstance, which preceded (this command:) Let the earth bring forth grass (ibid., i. 11). Wherefore Onkelos renders: ועננא הוה סליק מן ארעא “and a mist had gone up from the earth.” Moreover, this results clearly from the text itself: No plant of the field was yet in the earth (ibid., ii. 5). Thus the matter is clear.
root.text.Part 2..29.15: —Thou knowest, O reader! that the principal causes of generation and corruption, after the forces of the celestial spheres[[fn:2007]], are light and darkness, by reason of the heat and the cold which they have as a consequence[[fn:2008]]. It is in consequence of the movement of the celestial sphere that the elements mingle together, and their mixture varies by reason of light and darkness. The first mixture which springs therefrom consists of the two species of exhalations[[fn:2009]] which are the primary cause of all superior phenomena, among which is rain, and which are also the causes of minerals, and thereafter, of the composition of plants, which is followed by that of animals and finally that of man[[fn:2010]]. Darkness[[fn:2011]] is the nature of the being of the whole inferior world, and light supervens thereunto (as an accident)[[fn:2012]]; it suffices thee (to see) that, in the absence of light, all remains in a state of immobility. — The Scripture, in the account of the Creation, follows absolutely the same order, omitting naught of all this[[fn:2013]].
root.text.Part 2..29.16: What must further be known is that they (the Doctors) say[[fn:2014]]: “All the works of creation were created in their (perfect) stature, with all their intellect[[fn:2015]] and in all their beauty”; which is to say that everything which was created was so in its quantitative perfection, with its perfect form and with its fairest qualities[[fn:2016]]. It is these latter which the word לצביונם (in their beauty) indicats, which comes from צב׳, beauty, ornament, for example: the glory (צבי) of all lands (Ezek., xx. 6). Know this well; for it is an important principle, perfectly true and clear.
root.text.Part 2..29.17: What ought to be a subject of serious meditation is that, after having spoken of the creation of man, in the six days of creation, saying: male and female created He them (Gen., i. 27), and after having entirely concluded (the account of) the creation, saying: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them (ibid., ii. 1), a new chapter is opened, (to relate) how Eve was created from Adam. Therein is mentioned the tree of life and the tree of knowledge, the adventure of the serpent and what befell therefrom, and all this is presented as having taken place after Adam had been placed in the Garden of Eden. All the Doctors are agreed that this whole event took place on the Friday, and that naught was changed, in any wise, after the six days of creation. One must therefore see naught perplexing in any of these things; for, as we have said, there was as yet until then no fixed nature[[fn:2017]].
root.text.Part 2..29.18: Moreover, they have uttered other matters which I must cause thee to understand, gathering them from diverse places, and I must likewise direct thy attention unto certain points, even as they themselves have done toward us[[fn:2018]]. It must be known that all which I shall here cite from the discourses of the Sages are words of extreme perfection, the interpretation of which was clear unto those to whom they were addressed, and which are of a very great precision. Wherefore I shall not push the explanation thereof too far, nor shall I expound them at length[[fn:2019]], lest I reveal a secret[[fn:2020]]; but it shall suffice, to make them understood by a man such as thou art, that I cite them in a certain order and with a passing observation.
root.text.Part 2..29.19: Thus they say[[fn:2021]] that Adam and Eve were created together, joined back to back; (this double being) having been divided, He (God) took the half thereof, which was Eve, and she was given unto the other (unto Adam) for a companion[[fn:2022]]. The words אחת מצלעותיו (Gen., II, 21) signify (it is said) one of his two sides[[fn:2023]], and there has been cited as proof צלע המשכן (Exodus, 26, 20, etc.), which the Targum renders as סטרא דמשכנא, side of the tabernacle, so that here, they say, (one should translate): מן סטרוהי, from his sides. Understand well how it has been clearly stated that they were in some wise two and yet formed but one, according to these words: a member of my members and flesh of my flesh (Gen., II, 23), which has been further confirmed by saying that the two together were designated by a single name: She shall be called ISHA, because she was taken out of ISCH (ibid.); and, to make their union yet more manifest, it is said: He shall cleave unto his wife, and they shall be one flesh (ibid., v. 25). — How great is the ignorance of those who understand not that there is necessarily at the root of all this a certain idea! Behold then, this is clear[[fn:2024]].
root.text.Part 2..29.20: Another subject which they have set forth in the Midrash and which it behoovs thee to know is this: The serpent, they say, was ridden by a rider, and it was as great as a camel; it was his rider who seduced Eve, and this rider was Sammael[[fn:2025]]. This name they apply unto Satan: they say, for example, in several places, that Satan desired to make our father Abraham fail, so that he would not consent to offer Isaac (as a burnt-offering), and likewise he desired to make Isaac fail, so that he would not obey his father; and, upon this occasion, I mean, concerning the sacrifice of Isaac, they express themselves thus: "Sammael went unto our father Abraham and said unto him: What now, old man, hast thou then lost thy reason, etc.[[fn:2026]]" It is therefore clear that Sammael is Satan. This name, even as that of the nachash (serpent), indicats a certain idea; in relating how the latter came to deceive Eve, they say: "Sammael was riding upon him; but the Holy One laughed at the camel and his rider[[fn:2027]]."
root.text.Part 2..29.21: That which further merits thy attention is that the serpent had no manner of relation with Adam and addressed him not, but conversed and had communication only with Eve; it was through the mediation of Eve that evil befell Adam and that the serpent caused his ruin. Perfect enmity exists only between the serpent and Eve, and between the seed of the one and the seed of the other, although her seed (זרעה) be indubitably that of Adam[[fn:2028]]. What is yet more remarkable is that what chains the serpent unto Eve, that is to say, the seed of the one unto the seed of the other, is (on the one hand) the head and (on the other) the heel, so that she subdus him by the head[[fn:2029]], whilst he subdus her by the heel[[fn:2030]]. Behold then, this is likewise clear.
root.text.Part 2..29.22: Here is yet another of those wondrous passages, the literal sense of which is exceeding absurd, but in which, so soon as thou shalt have perfectly understood the chapters of this treatise, thou wilt admire the allegory, full of wisdom and in conformity with the nature of being<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:2031]]</sup>. "At the moment," say they, "when the serpent approached Eve, he infused into her impurity. The Israelites having presented themselves at Mount Sinai, their impurity was removed; as for the Gentiles, who presented not themselves at Mount Sinai, their impurity was not removed<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:2032]]</sup>." Meditate also upon this<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:2033]]</sup>.
root.text.Part 2..29.23: Another passage which it behoovs us to know is this: “The tree of life has (an extent of) five hundred years’ journey, and all the waters of creation flow forth from beneath it[[fn:2034]].” Therein it has been declared that the intent of this measure is to designate the thickness of its trunk, and not the extent of its branches: “The purpose of this saying,” say they, “is not its foliage, but its trunk (קורתו) [[fn:2035]] which has (an extent of) five hundred years’ journey.” By קורתו is understood its thick upright timber; they added this supplementary phrase[[fn:2036]] to complete the explanation of the matter and to bestow upon it greater clarity. This, then, is likewise manifest[[fn:2037]].
root.text.Part 2..29.24: It is also necessary to know the following passage: “As for the tree of knowledge, the Holy One has never revealed that tree to any man, nor will He ever reveal it[[fn:2038]].” And this is true; for the nature of existence so requirs[[fn:2039]].
root.text.Part 2..29.25: The following passage likewise merits that thou shouldst learn it: “And the Lord God took the man” (Genesis, 2, 15), that is to say, He exalted him; “and He placed him” (ויניחהו) “in the garden of Eden,” that is, He gave him rest (הניח לו) [[fn:2040]]. Thus, the text was not understood[[fn:2041]] in the sense that He (God) had removed him from one place and set him in another, but in the allegorical sense that He exalted the rank of his being amidst those creatures which are subject to generation and corruption, and established him in a certain station[[fn:2042]].
root.text.Part 2..29.26: Another point that it is essential to draw to your attention is the wisdom with which the two sons of Adam were designated by the names of [[t:0]]Kaïn[[t:1]] and [[t:2]]Hebel[[t:3]] (Abel), that it was Kaïn who slew Hebel [[t:4]]in the field[[t:5]] (Genesis, 4, 8), that both perished, although he who had exercised violence was treated with leniency[[fn:2043]], and finally that there existed only a durable existence for [[t:6]]Sches: For God has established me[[t:7]] (S[[t:8]]CHATH[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]another posterity[[t:11]] (Genesis, 4, 25). All of this is justified[[fn:2044]].
root.text.Part 2..29.27: That which merits further attention is the passage: [[t:0]]And man imposed names[[t:1]], [[t:2]]etc[[t:3]]. ([[t:4]]ibid.[[t:5]], II, 20), which informs us that languages are [[t:6]]conventional[[t:7]] and not [[t:8]]natural[[t:9]][[fn:2045]], as was previously believed[[fn:2046]].
root.text.Part 2..29.28.sub_0: That which, in fine, still merits thy meditation, are the four words employed to designate the relation between the heaven[[fn:2047]] and God, to wit: ברא to create, עשה to make, קנה to acquire, to possess, and אל God. It is said, for example: God created (ברא) the heaven and the earth (Gen., I, 1); in the day that the Lord made (עשות) earth and heaven (ibid., II, 4); author or possessor (קֹנה) of heaven and earth (ibid., XIV, 19 and 22); the God (אל) of the universe (ibid., XXI, 33)[[fn:2048]]; God (אלהי) of heaven and God of the earth (ibid, XXIV, 3). As for the expressions: אשר כוננתה (the moon and the stars) which thou hast ORDAINED (Ps. 8, 4), טפחה שמים (and my right hand) has METED OUT the heavens with spans, נוטה שמים, who STRETCHES OUT the heavens (Ps. 104, 2), they are all comprised within עשה, to make. As concerns the verb יצר, to form, it is not met with (in this sense)[[fn:2049]]. It seems to me, indeed, that this verb is applied to the formation of figure and lineaments, or to one of the other accidents; for figure and lineaments are likewise accidents. Wherefore it is said: יוצר אור, who forms the light (Isaiah, 45, 7), for the latter is an accident; יוצר הרים, who forms the mountains (Amos, 4, 13), signifies who fashions their figure; and it is the same with וייצר יי׳ אלהים, the Lord God formed, etc. (Genesis, 2, 7 and 19). But, in speaking of that Being which comprehends the whole of the universe, that is to say, the heaven and the earth, the verb ברא, to create, is employed, which, according to our view, signifies to produce from nothingness.
root.text.Part 2..29.28.sub_1: We also say עשה, to make, (which is applied) to the specific forms[[fn:2050]] that have been bestowed upon them, I mean to their physical characters. The verb קנה, to possess, has been applied to them, because God holds dominion over them, even as a master over his slaves; wherefore He is called the Lord of all the earth (Joshua, 3, 11, 13) and (simply) האדון, the Lord (Exodus, 23, 17; XXXIV, 23). But, since[[fn:2051]] there is no Lord without there being at the same time a possession, which would seem to presuppose a certain pre-existent matter[[fn:2052]], the verbs ברא, to create, and עשה, to make have (rather) been employed. When one says אלהי השמים, God of heaven, and אל עולם, God of the universe, it is from the point of view of the perfection of God and the perfection of the latter; He is ELOHÎM, that is to say, governing, and they are governed[[fn:2053]]. One must not perceive therein the idea of dominion, for that is the sense of קונה, possessor; (in saying ELOHÎM) it is from the point of view of the rank[[fn:2054]] which God occupies in being and of their own rank[[fn:2055]]; for it is He, and not the heaven, who is God. Thou must well impress this upon thy mind.
root.text.Part 2..29.29: These summary observations[[fn:2056]], together with what has preceded and what shall yet be said upon this subject, are sufficient in regard to the object proposed in this treatise and in respect of the reader[[fn:2057]].
root.text.Part 2..30.0: Thou hast perchance already discerned the reason wherefore such stress has been laid upon the law of the Sabbath, and wherefore it has for its penalty stoning, so that the prince of prophets did indeed inflict death because of it[[fn:2058]]. It occupies the third rank after the existence of God and the negation of dualism [for the prohibition against worshipping any other being than Him has no other end than to affirm Unity][[fn:2059]]. Thou knowest already, from my words[[fn:2060]], that ideas are not preserved if they be not accompanied by actions that may fix, publish, and perpetuate them among the vulgar. Wherefore it has been prescribed unto us to honor this day, in order that the principle of the novelty of the world might be established and published in the universe by the rest in which everyone should indulge[[fn:2061]] upon the same day; for, if it were asked what is the cause thereof, the answer would be: For in six days the Lord made etc. (Exodus, 20, 11).
root.text.Part 2..30.1: However, two different causes have been assigned to this law, which were to have two different consequences: in the first Decalogue (Exodus, ch. XX), it is stated, to justify the glorification of the Sabbath: For in six days the Lord made etc., while in Deuteronomy (5:15) it is stated: And you shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt[[fn:2062]]...; therefore the Lord your God commanded you to celebrate the Sabbath day. And this is correct[[fn:2063]]. Indeed, the consequence (indicated) in the first passage is the exaltation and glorification of this day, as it is said: Therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and hallowed it (Exodus 20:11), which is the consequence resulting from the cause (indicated by these words): For in six days etc. But, if it was made a law for us, and if we were commanded to observe this day, it is a consequence (resulting) from this other cause: that we were slaves in Egypt, where we did not work according to our own choice and when we wished, and where we were not free to rest.
root.text.Part 2..30.2: Rest and cessation from labour were therefore prescribed unto us, in order to combine two things: 1st, the adoption of a true opinion, namely, that of the creation of the world de novo, which, at the first glance and by the slightest reflection, leads to the acknowledgment of the existence of God; 2ndly, that we might remember the benefit which God has bestowed upon us by granting us rest from under the burdens of Egypt (Exodus vi. 6, 7). It is, as it were, a benefit which serves at once to confirm a speculative opinion and to produce the well-being of the body[[fn:2064]].
root.text.Part 2..31.0: The opinions of men concerning prophecy are like unto their opinions regarding the eternity or the novelty of the world; I mean to say that, even as those for whom the existence of God is proven profess three diverse opinions touching the eternity or the novelty of the world, as we have already set forth, so also the opinions concerning prophecy are three in number[[fn:2065]]. I shall not tarry over the opinion of the Epicurean—for he believs not in the existence of a God, and how, a fortiori, should he believe in prophecy?—but my purpose is only to relate the opinions of those who believe in God[[fn:2066]].
root.text.Part 2..31.1: I. The first opinion, professed by those among the heathen nations[[fn:2067]] who believed in prophecy, is likewise admitted by certain of the vulgar belonging to our religion[[fn:2068]]. God (say they), choosing whomsoever He wills among men, makes him a prophet and entrusts him with a mission; and it matters little, according to them, whether that man be wise or ignorant, aged or young. Nevertheless, they also lay down as a condition that he be a good man and of fair character; for no one has hitherto contended that, according to this opinion, God grants at times the gift of prophecy to a wicked man, unless He has first brought him back to the way of goodness.
root.text.Part 2..31.2: II. The second opinion is that of the philosophers[[fn:2069]]; namely, that prophecy is a certain perfection existing in human nature; but that the human individual obtains not this perfection save by means of exercise, which brings into actuality that which the species possesses potentially[[fn:2070]], unless it be hindered by some obstacle arising from the temperament or by some external cause. For, whenever the existence of a perfection is only possible in a certain species, it cannot exist to the ultimate degree in every individual of that species[[fn:2071]], but it must necessarily exist at least in some one individual[[fn:2072]]; and if this perfection be of a nature to require a determining cause for its realisation, such a cause is requisite[[fn:2073]]. According to this opinion, it is not possible that an ignorant man should become a prophet, nor that a man, without having been a prophet on the eve, should suddenly be one on the morrow, as one who finds a treasure. But the case is, on the contrary, as follows: if the superior man, perfect in his rational and moral qualities, possesses at the same time the most perfect imaginative faculty, and has prepared himself in the manner of which thou shalt hear further on, he will necessarily be a prophet; for this is a perfection which we possess naturally. It is therefore impossible, according to this opinion, that an individual, being fit for prophecy and having prepared himself therefor, should not be a prophet, no more than it is possible for an individual of sound temperament to be nourished with good food without there being produced therefrom good blood and other like things.
root.text.Part 2..31.3: III. The third opinion, which is that of our Law and a fundamental principle of our religion, is altogether similar to this philosophical opinion, with the exception of a single point[[fn:2074]]. For we believe that he who is fit for prophecy and prepared therefor may nevertheless not be a prophet, which thing depends upon the Divine Will. In my judgment, this is like unto all miracles, and belongs to the same category[[fn:2075]]; for nature requirs that every man who, by his natural constitution, is fit for prophecy and has exercised himself by education and study, should actually become a prophet; and if this be denied him, it is as when one is hindered from moving his hand, after the example of Jeroboam (I Kings xiii. 4), or as when one is hindered from seeing, like the army of the King of Syria when seeking[[fn:2076]] Elisha (II Kings vi. 18).
root.text.Part 2..31.4: — As touching what I have said, that it is our fundamental principle that one must be prepared and have attained perfection in the moral and rational virtues, this is what the Sages have said: “Prophecy resids only in the man who is wise, mighty, and rich[[fn:2077]]”. We have already set this forth in the Commentary on the Mishnah[[fn:2078]] and in the Great Work[[fn:2079]], and we have made it known that the disciples of the prophets were constantly occupied with preparation. But that he who is prepared may nevertheless suffer a hindrance and not become a prophet, is what thou mayest learn from the history of Baruch, the son of Neriah: for he had become the attendant of Jeremiah, who trained him[[fn:2080]], instructed him, and prepared him; yet, however much he was animated by the desire to become a prophet, this was nevertheless denied him, as he says: I fainted in my sighing, and I find no rest (Jeremiah xlv. 3), and it was answered him through the mediation of Jeremiah: Thus shalt thou say unto him: Thus says the Lord etc. And seekest thou great things for thyself? Seek them not (ibid., vv. 4 and 5). Verily, one would be at liberty to say that it was intended to declare thereby that prophecy, in respect of Baruch, was too much of a greatness[[fn:2081]]; likewise might it be said that in the passage of Lamentations (ii. 9): Her prophets also find no vision from the Lord, (it must be understood) because they were in exile[[fn:2082]], as we shall set forth. But we find numerous passages, as well in the biblical texts as in the words of the Sages, all of which insist upon this fundamental principle, to wit, that God makes whomsoever He wills and whenever He wills a prophet, provided it be a man of exceeding perfection and truly superior; for as to the ignorant among the vulgar, that seems not possible unto us, — I mean that God should make one of them a prophet[[fn:2083]], — no more than it would be possible for Him to make a prophet of an ass or a frog. Such is our principle: (I mean) that it is indispensable to exercise oneself and to attain perfection, and that thereby alone ariss the possibility to which the Divine power attaches itself[[fn:2084]].
root.text.Part 2..31.5: Suffer not thyself to be led into error by this passage: Before I formed thee in the belly (of thy mother), I knew thee, and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee (Jerem. i. 5)[[fn:2085]]; for this is the condition of every prophet, (I mean) that he must have a natural disposition from his primary constitution, as shall be set forth. As for these words: I am a child, NA’AR (ibid., v. 6)[[fn:2086]], thou knowest that the Hebrew tongue calls the pious Joseph NA’AR (a youth), though he was thirty years of age[[fn:2087]], and that Joshua also is called NA’AR, though he then approached his sixtieth year. In fact, it is said (of the latter), at the time of the matter of the golden calf: And his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man (NA’AR), departed not etc. (Exodus xxxiii. 11). Now Moses, our master, was then eighty-one years old[[fn:2088]], and his whole life was an hundred and twenty years; but Joshua, who lived yet fourteen years after him, attained the age of an hundred and ten years. It is therefore clear that Joshua was, at the time in question, fifty-seven years old at the least, and yet he is called NA’AR.
root.text.Part 2..31.6: Neither must thou suffer thyself to be led into error by what is found in the (prophetic) promises, where it is said: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy (Joel ii. 28); for he (the prophet) has explained this and made known what manner of prophecy this should be, saying: Your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions (ibid.). In truth, whosoever foretells an unknown thing[[fn:2089]], whether by means of magic and divination, or by means of a true dream[[fn:2090]], is likewise called a prophet; wherefore the prophets of Baal and those of Asherah are called prophets. Seest thou not that God has said: If there arise among you a prophet, or a DREAMER (Deut. xiii. 1)?
root.text.Part 2..31.7: As touching the scene of Mount Sinai, although all (the Israelites), by way of miracle, saw the great fire and heard the awesome and terrifying sounds, yet there attained to the rank of prophecy only those who were fit for it, and that in different degrees. Thou seest it well by this passage: Come up unto the Lord, thou, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel (Exodus xxiv. 1). He (Moses) occupies the highest degree, as it is said: And Moses alone shall come near the Lord: but they shall not come nigh (ibid., v. 2); Aaron is placed beneath him, Nadab and Abihu are beneath Aaron, the seventy elders beneath Nadab and Abihu, and the others beneath these latter, according to their degrees of perfection. A passage of the Sages says: “Moses forms a partition by himself and Aaron a partition by himself[[fn:2091]]”.
root.text.Part 2..31.8: Since we have been led to speak of the scene of Mount Sinai, we shall call attention, in a separate chapter, to the elucidations which the (biblical) texts, when rightly examined, as well as the discourses of the Sages, provide concerning this scene.
root.text.Part 2..32.0: It is manifest unto me that, in the scene of Mount Sinai, all which reached Moses reached not in its entirety the whole of Israel[[fn:2092]]. The word, on the contrary, was addressed to Moses alone [wherefore the allocution, in the Decalogue, is made in the second person singular], and he, having descended to the foot of the mountain, made known unto the people that which he had heard. The text of the Pentateuch (says): I stood between the Lord and you at that time, to shew you the word of the Lord (Deut. v. 5), and it is further said: Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice (Exodus xix. 19); it is expressly stated in the Mekhilthâ that he repeated unto them each commandment as he had heard it[[fn:2093]]. Another passage of the Pentateuch says: That the people may hear when I speak with thee, etc. (ibid., v. 9), which proves that the speech was addressed unto him; they heard the mighty voice, but they distinguished not the words[[fn:2094]], and it is of this mighty voice, heard (by them), that it was said: When ye heard the voice (Deut. v. 20). It is further said: Ye heard the VOICE of words, but saw no similitude; only ye heard a VOICE (ibid., iv. 12); but it was not said ye heard words. Whenever, therefore, mention is made of words being heard, it is intended only of the voice which was heard; it was Moses who heard the words and who reported them unto them. This is what is evident from the text of the Pentateuch and from many discourses of the Sages.
root.text.Part 2..32.1: Nevertheless, (I must cite) from the latter an assertion reported in several places of the Midraschîm and which is found also in the Talmud; it is this: “I AM and THOU SHALT HAVE NO OTHER, they heard them from the mouth of the Omnipotence[[fn:2095]].” They mean thereby that these words reached them (directly), even as they reached Moses our Master, and that it was not Moses who caused them to reach them. Verily, these two principles, I mean the existence of God and His unity, are conceived by (simple) human speculation[[fn:2096]]; and everything that can be known by demonstration is known in the same absolute degree by the prophet and by every other who knows it, without there being therein any superiority of the one over the other. These two principles, then, are not known solely by prophecy, (as says) the text of the Pentateuch: Unto thee it was shewed, that thou mightest know, etc. (Deut. iv. 35)[[fn:2097]]. As for the other commandments, they belong to the category of probable opinions and of things accepted by tradition, and not to the category of intelligibles[[fn:2098]].
root.text.Part 2..32.2: But, whatsoever they may have said in this regard, that which the (biblical) texts and the words of the Sages imply[[fn:2099]] is that all the Israelites heard in this scene but a single sound, at one time[[fn:2100]]; and it is the sound whereby Moses and all Israel heard (the two commandments) I AM and THOU SHALT HAVE NO OTHER, which Moses caused them to hear (anew) in his own language, by pronouncing distinctly intelligible letters[[fn:2101]]. The Sages have declared themselves in this sense, supporting it by these words[[fn:2102]]: ONCE God has spoken, twice have I heard this (Ps. lxii. 12), and they have clearly said, at the commencement of the Midrasch ’Hazêtha, that they heard no other voice emanating (directly) from God[[fn:2103]], which is also indicated by the text of the Pentateuch: ... with a great voice, and he added no more (Deut. v. 19). It was after having heard this first voice that there occurred that which is recounted of the terror they experienced and of their violent fear, and (that they uttered) the words reported: And ye said, Behold, the Lord our God has shewed us, etc. And now why should we die, etc.? Go thou near, and hear, etc. (ibid., vv. 21-24). He then advanced, he, the most illustrious of mortals, a second time, received the remainder of the commandments one by one[[fn:2104]], descended to the foot of the mountain, and caused them to hear them in the midst of this grandiose spectacle. They saw the fires and heard the voices, I mean those voices[[fn:2105]] which are (designated by the words) thunders and lightnings (Exodus xix. 16), such as the thunder and the loud sounding of the horn; and wheresoever mention is made (upon this occasion) of several voices being heard, as for example: And all the people perceived[[fn:2106]] the voices (ibid., xx. 15), it signifies naught but the sounding of the horn, the thunder, etc. But the voice of the Lord, I mean the created voice[[fn:2107]], whereby the word (of God) was communicated, they heard but once only, as the Pentateuch textually says and as the Sages have expounded in the place which I have pointed out to thee. It is of this voice (that it was said) that “their soul departed upon hearing it[[fn:2108]],” and by means of which the first two commandments were perceived.
root.text.Part 2..32.3: It must be known, however, that even for this voice, their degree (of perception) was by no means equal to that of Moses our Master. I must call thy attention to this mystery and inform thee that it is a thing traditionally admitted by our nation and known by its learned men. Verily, all the passages where thou findest (the words): And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, Onkelos translats them (literally) by ומלל יי, And the Lord spake, etc. And likewise (he translats the words): And God spake all these words (Exodus xx. 1) by ומלל יי יה כל פתגמיא. But these words of the Israelites (addressed) to Moses: And let not God speak with us (ibid., v. 16), he translats by ולא יתמלל עמנא מן קדם יי, and let it not be spoken with us from before the Lord. He has therefore revealed unto thee thereby the distinction which we have established[[fn:2109]]. Thou knowest that these remarkable and important things Onkelos, as it has been expressly said, learned from the mouth of R. Eliezer and R. Joshua[[fn:2110]], who are the Sages of Israel par excellence[[fn:2111]].
root.text.Part 2..32.4: It behoves thee to know all this and to bear it in mind; for it is impossible to penetrate into the scene of Mount Sinai more deeply than has been done[[fn:2112]], (this scene) being of the number of the secrets of the Law. The true nature of this perception and the circumstances that accompanied it are for us a thing right obscure[[fn:2113]]; for there has never been anything similar thereto aforetime, nor shall there be in the future. Know this well.
root.text.Part 2..33.0: As touching that passage which is met with in the Pentateuch, and which says: Behold, I send an angel before thee, etc. (Exodus, xxiii, 20), the sense of this passage has been explained in Deuteronomy (xviii, 18), where we read that God said unto Moses, during the scene at Mount Sinai: I will raise them up a prophet, etc.[[fn:2114]]. The proof of which[[fn:2115]] is that it is said (concerning) this angel: Beware of him and obey his voice, etc. (Exodus, xxiii, 21), an injunction which is indubitably addressed unto the multitude; but the angel did not manifest himself unto the multitude, unto whom he communicated (directly) neither commandment nor prohibition, that they should be warned not to be rebellious against him. The meaning of these words can therefore be naught but this: that God made known unto them that there should be among them a prophet, unto whom an angel should come, who should speak unto him, and who should communicate unto him commandments and prohibitions; God therefore commands us not to be rebellious against that angel whose word the prophet would cause to reach us, as has been clearly stated in Deuteronomy (xviii, 15): Unto him ye shall hearken, and again: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak IN MY NAME etc. (ibid., v. 19), which explains the words for MY NAME is in him (Exodus, xxiii, 21)[[fn:2116]].
root.text.Part 2..33.1: All this (was said unto them) only to give them the following admonition[[fn:2117]]: This grand spectacle which ye have seen, that is to say the scene[[fn:2118]] at Mount Sinai, is not a thing which is to continue for you; there shall be naught like unto it in the future, nor shall there always be fire or cloud, as there is now continually upon the tabernacle[[fn:2119]]. But an angel whom I shall send unto your prophets shall conquer the lands for you, shall lay open[[fn:2120]] the earth before you, and shall make known unto you what ye ought to do[[fn:2121]]; it is he who shall make known unto you what things are to be pursued and what are to be eschewed.
root.text.Part 2..33.2: — Hereby also has been given the principle which I have not ceased to set forth[[fn:2122]], to wit, that unto every prophet other than Moses, our Master, revelation came through the mediation of an angel. Know this well.
root.text.Part 2..34.0: I have already set forth to all[[fn:2123]], in the Commentary on the Mishnah and in the Mishneh Torah, the four differences whereby the prophecy of Moses, our Master, was distinguished from that of other prophets; and I have given proofs thereof and shown the evidence of them[[fn:2124]]. It is therefore not necessary to repeat this, and it is moreover outside the scope of this treatise.
root.text.Part 2..34.1: I must inform thee that all that I say concerning prophecy, in the chapters of this treatise, relats only to the prophetic quality of all the prophets who were before Moses and of those who were to come after him; but, as for the prophecy of Moses, our Master, I shall not touch upon it in these chapters, not even by a single word, neither expressly nor by allusion. Verily, according to my view, it is only by homonymity[[fn:2125]] that the name prophet is applied at once to Moses and to the others; and it is the same, in my opinion, regarding his miracles and those of the others, for his miracles are not of the same category as those of other prophets.
root.text.Part 2..34.2: The proof derived from the Law, (to establish) that his prophecy was distinct from that of all his predecessors, is found in these words: I appeared unto Abraham, etc., but by my name of ETERNAL I was not known to them (Exodus, vi. 3); for we are thereby informed that his perception was not like unto that of the patriarchs, but greater, nor, for a stronger reason, (like unto) those of other (prophets) who were before him[[fn:2126]]. But, that his prophecy was also distinct from that of all his successors, is what has been said, in the form of a simple statement[[fn:2127]]: And there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom God knew face to face (Deut., xxxiv. 10): it is thus clearly stated that his perception was distinct from the perception of all those who should succeed him among the Israelites, — who (notwithstanding) were a kingdom of priests and an holy nation (Exodus, xix. 6), and in the midst of whom was the Eternal (Numbers, xvi. 3), — and, with greater reason, among the other nations[[fn:2128]].
root.text.Part 2..34.3: That which generally distinguishes his miracles from those of any other prophet whatsoever, is that all the miracles wrought by the prophets, or wrought in their favour, were known only to a few persons, as for instance the miracles of Elijah and Elisha; seest thou not that the King of Israel inquirs concerning them[[fn:2129]], and requests Gehazi to make them known unto him, as it is said: Tell me, I pray thee, all the great things that Elisha has done; and he told, etc. And Gehazi said: My lord, O king, this is the woman and this is her son whom Elisha restored to life (II Kings, viii. 4 and 5). Thus it is with the miracles of every prophet, save for Moses, our master; wherefore the Scripture declars concerning the latter, likewise in the form of a statement[[fn:2130]], that there shall never arise a prophet who shall work miracles publicly, before both friend and adversary[[fn:2131]], as did Moses. This is what is said: And there arose not a prophet etc., in all the signs and the wonders etc., in the sight of all Israel (Deut., xxxiv. 10-12); here, then, are linked and joined together at once[[fn:2132]] two things: that there shall no more arise (a prophet) who shall have the same perception as he, nor who shall do that which he did. Thereafter it is declared that these miracles were wrought before Pharaoh, and all his servants, and all his land, his adversaries, as also in the presence of all the Israelites, his partisans: in the sight of all Israel; this is a thing which had not occurred with any prophet before him[[fn:2133]], and his true prediction has foretold that it should occur with no other.
root.text.Part 2..34.4: Be not misled by that which has been stated concerning the sun's light, which stood still for Joshua for several hours: [[t:0]]And he said in the sight of Israel[[t:1]] (Josh., X, 12); for it was not stated [[t:2]]of[[t:3]] [[t:4]]ALL[[t:5]] [[t:6]]Israel[[t:7]], as was done concerning Moses. Similarly, Elijah, upon Mount Carmel, acted only before a small company of men[[fn:2134]]. Should I state [[t:8]]for several hours[[t:9]], it is because the words [[t:10]]כיום תמים[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]about a whole day[[t:13]], Joshua, 10, 13) appear to me to signify [[t:14]]as the longest possible day;[[t:15]] for [[t:16]]תמים[[t:17]] denotes [[t:18]]complete[[t:19]]. It is therefore as if it had been declared that this day in Gibeon was for them as the longest of summer days in those regions[[fn:2135]].
root.text.Part 2..34.5: After thou shalt have set apart in thy mind the prophecy of Moses and his miracles, — for these pertain to a perception and to acts equally extraordinary[[fn:2136]], — and when thou shalt be convinced that this is a degree which we are unable to comprehend in all its reality, thou shalt hear what I shall say, in all these (following) chapters, concerning prophecy and the different degrees occupied therein by the prophets, setting aside this first degree (of Moses)[[fn:2137]]. Such is what I had to say in this chapter.
root.text.Part 2..35.0: Know that prophecy, in reality[[fn:2138]], is an emanation from God, which is shed forth, through the medium of the Active Intellect, first upon the rational faculty, and then upon the imaginative faculty; it is the highest degree of man and the term of perfection to which his species may attain, and this state is the highest perfection of the imaginative faculty. It is a thing which can in no wise exist in every man, and it is not a thing unto which one may arrive by perfecting oneself in the speculative sciences and by the improvement of morals, should they all be of the best and the most beautiful, without there being joined thereto the greatest possible perfection of the imaginative faculty in its original formation. Thou knowest that the perfection of these corporeal faculties, among which is the imaginative faculty, depends upon the best possible temperament of the organ bearing such faculty, upon its fairest proportion and the greatest purity of its matter[[fn:2139]]; this is a thing of which it is in no wise possible to repair the loss[[fn:2140]], or to supply the defect, by means of regimen. For an organ whose temperament has been ill-disposed from the beginning of its formation, the restorative regimen can at most preserve it in a certain degree of health, without being able to restore it to the best possible constitution; but, if its infirmity proceeds from its disproportion[[fn:2141]], from its position, or from its substance, I mean from the very matter of which it was formed, then is there no means of remedy[[fn:2142]]. Thou knowest all this well; it would therefore be useless to enter upon long explanations on this matter.
root.text.Part 2..35.1.sub_0: You also know the actions of this imaginative faculty, which consist in preserving the memory of sensible things, in combining them[[fn:2143]], and—what is (particularly) in its nature—in tracing (images); its greatest and most noble activity[[fn:2144]] occurs only when the senses are at rest and cease to function, and it is then that a certain inspiration comes to it, which is according to its disposition, and which is the cause of true dreams[[fn:2145]] and also that of prophecy. It differs only by degree, and not by species[[fn:2146]]. You know that they (the Sages) said on various occasions: "a dream is a sixtieth part of prophecy[[fn:2147]]"; but one cannot establish a proportion between two specifically different things, and it would not be permissible to say, for example, that the perfection of man is so many times the double of the perfection of a horse. They repeated this idea in Bereshith Rabbah, saying: "The unripe fruit of prophecy is the dream[[fn:2148]]." This is a remarkable comparison: for the unripe fruit (נובלת) is identically the fruit itself, except that it has fallen before its perfect maturity[[fn:2149]]; likewise, the action of the imaginative faculty during sleep is the same as in the state of prophecy, except that it is still insufficient and has not reached its end. — But why should we instruct you through the words of the Sages and leave aside the texts of the Pentateuch? (As for example:) If there be a prophet among you, I the Lord will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream (Numbers 12:6). Here God has made known to us the true being of prophecy, and has informed us that it is a perfection that occurs in a dream or in a vision. The word vision (מראה) is derived from to see (ראה); for it happens that the imaginative faculty acts so perfectly that it sees the object as if it existed externally, and the object which has its origin only within it[[fn:2150]] seems to have come to it through the channel of external sensation. In these two parts, I mean in the vision and in the dream, are contained all the degrees of prophecy.
root.text.Part 2..35.1.sub_1: It is well known that the matter wherewith a man is much occupied in his waking state, whilst employing his senses, and to which he applies himself and which is the object of his desire, is also that wherewith the imaginative faculty busies itself during sleep, when the Active Intellect overflows upon it, according as it is prepared thereunto. It would be superfluous to cite examples for this or to say more thereof; for it is a manifest thing which everyone knows, and it is even as the perception of the senses, against which no man of sound mind raiss an objection.
root.text.Part 2..35.2.sub_0: After these preliminaries, it must be known that we here treat of a human individual[[fn:2151]] whose cerebral substance, in its primitive formation, should be exceedingly well proportioned, by the purity of its matter and the temperament peculiar to each of its parts, by its quantity and by its position, and should suffer no derangement of temperament from any other organ.
