Furthermore, it behoovs that this individual should have acquired science and wisdom, so as to pass from potentiality to actuality[[fn:2152]]; that he should possess an all-perfect human intelligence and pure and equable human morals[[fn:2153]]; that all his desires should be directed towards the science of the mysteries of this universe and the knowledge of their causes; that his thought should ever be fixed upon noble things; that he should occupy himself only with the knowledge of God, the contemplation of His works, and that which must be believed in this regard; and finally, that his thought and his desire should be detached from animal things[[fn:2154]], such as the pursuit of those pleasures afforded by eating, drinking, cohabitation, and, in general, the sense of touch, which sense Aristotle has expressly declared, in the Ethics, to be a reproach unto us[[fn:2155]]. — [And how well has he spoken! and how true it is that this sense is a reproach unto us! for we possess it only in so far as we are animals, like the other brute beasts, and it contains nothing that pertains to the idea of humanity. As for the other sensual enjoyments, such as those of smell, hearing, and sight, although they be corporeal, there is sometimes found therein a pleasure for man as man, as Aristotle has set forth.
root.text.Part 2..35.2.sub_1: We have been led here to speak of that which is not our present aim, yet was this necessary; for too often the thoughts of distinguished scholars are preoccupied with the pleasures of the sense in question and desire them, and nevertheless they marvel that they are not prophets[[fn:2156]], since, (say they) prophecy is something which is in the nature of man.] — It would also be necessary that the thought and desire of this individual be detached from vain ambitions[[fn:2157]], I mean the desire to dominate or to be exalted by the common people and to win their homage and obedience without any other end[[fn:2158]] [for one ought rather to consider all men according to their stations[[fn:2159]], in respect of which they are assuredly similar, some to domestic cattle, others to wild beasts, upon whom the perfect and solitary man[[fn:2160]] bestows not his thought — if indeed he thinks of them at all — save to preserve himself from the evil they might do him, if perchance he has to do with them, or to derive profit from the advantages they may offer, when he finds himself reduced thereto for some necessity]. — If therefore, in an individual such as we have just described, the imaginative faculty, as perfect as possible, were in full activity, and the Active Intellect overflowed upon it by reason of the speculative perfection of the individual, such a one would indubitably perceive naught but most extraordinary divine things, would see naught but God and His angels, and the science he would acquire would have for its object only true opinions and rules of conduct embracing the goodly relations of men one with another.
root.text.Part 2..35.3: It is well known that in the three things we have laid down as conditions — to wit, the perfection of the rational faculty by means of study, that of the imaginative faculty in its primitive formation, and that of morals which is obtained when one detaches his thought from all corporeal pleasures and silenced the desire for every kind of foolish and pernicious grandeur — perfect men possess a great superiority over one another, and it is by reason of the superiority in each of these three things that all prophets are superior in rank one to another.
root.text.Part 2..35.4: Thou art aware that every bodily faculty is at times blunted, weakened, and impaired, and at other times strengthened. Now, this imaginative faculty is indubitably a bodily faculty; wherefore thou wilt find that the prophets, during times of sadness, anger, and such-like feelings, cease to prophesy. Thou knowest that the Sages say: «Prophecy comes neither during sadness nor during dejection[[fn:2161]]»; that our patriarch Jacob had no revelation during the days of his mourning, because his imaginative faculty was occupied with the loss of Joseph[[fn:2162]], and that Moses had no revelation, as heretofore, from the time of the unhappy event[[fn:2163]] of the spies until the generation of the wilderness had utterly perished[[fn:2164]], because he was overwhelmed by the enormity of their crime [although, for the rest, the imaginative faculty had no part in his prophecy, and the Intellect (Active) was poured out upon him without the mediation of that faculty[[fn:2165]]; for, as we have several times observed, he did not prophesy, like the other prophets, through parables[[fn:2166]], a matter which shall yet be explained elsewhere and is not the object of this chapter].
root.text.Part 2..35.5: Likewise, thou wilt find that certain prophets, after having prophesied for a certain time, were divested of prophecy, which, by reason of some accident that occurred, could not continue[[fn:2167]]. This is, indubitably, the essential and immediate cause wherefore prophecy ceased in the time of the Captivity; can there exist for a man, in any circumstance whatsoever, a weightier cause for dejection or sorrow[[fn:2168]], than to be a slave, the property of another, and subject to ignorant and impious men, who join the absence of true reason to the fullness of animal concupiscences, and to be able to do naught against it[[fn:2169]]? It is this wherewith we have been threatened, and it is this which was meant by these words: They shall wander to seek the word of the Lord, and shall not find it (Amos, viii, 12); and it is further said: Her king and her princes are among the nations, without law; her prophets also find no vision from the Lord (Lam., ii, 9). This is true, and the reason thereof is manifest; for the instrument has ceased to function[[fn:2170]]. It is for this same reason also that prophecy shall return to us in the days of the Messiah [may he be speedily revealed!], as has been promised unto us.
root.text.Part 2..36.0: It is necessary to call your attention to the nature of the being of this divine emanation[[fn:2171]] which arrives to us, by which we think and (by which) our intelligences are superior to one another. For sometimes it arrives to an individual in a measure sufficient to perfect it itself, without going beyond[[fn:2172]], sometimes what arrives to the individual suffices beyond its own perfection[[fn:2173]], (so that there remains) for the perfection of others. The same is true for all beings: there are some who have enough perfection to govern others (beings), while there are others who have perfection only to the extent that it is necessary for them to be governed by others[[fn:2174]], as we have expounded.
root.text.Part 2..36.1: This being so, thou must know that, if this emanation from the Intellect (Active) be shed only upon the rational faculty of man, without any of it being shed upon the imaginative faculty [whether because the emanation itself is insufficient[[fn:2175]], or because the imaginative faculty is defective in its original formation, so that it is incapable of receiving the emanation of the Intellect], this constituts the class of learned men who devote themselves to speculation. But if this emanation be shed at once upon both faculties, I mean upon the rational and upon the imaginative [as we have set forth and as others among the philosophers have also set forth][[fn:2176]], and the imaginative faculty has been originally created in all its perfection, this constituts the class of prophets. If, finally, the emanation be shed only upon the imaginative faculty, and the rational faculty remain behind, whether by reason of its original formation or by reason of lack of exercise, this constituts the class of statesmen who make laws[[fn:2177]], of diviners, of augurs, and of those who have true dreams; and likewise, those who perform miracles by extraordinary artifices and occult arts, without being nevertheless learned men, are all of this third class.
root.text.Part 2..36.2: What thou must be convinced of is that, to certain men of this third class, there occur, even when they are awake, wondrous chimerical visions, dreams and agitations, similar to prophetic visions, so that they believe themselves to be prophets; they take much delight, therefore, in what they perceive of these chimerical visions, believing that they have acquired sciences without having pursued studies, and they bring great confusion into grave and speculative matters, mingling together, in a wondrous manner, true things and chimeras. All this is because the imaginative faculty is strong in them, while the rational faculty is weak and has obtained absolutely nothing; I mean to say that it has not passed into action.
root.text.Part 2..36.3: It is known that in each of these three classes there are many gradations[[fn:2178]]. Each of the first two classes is divided into two parts, as we have set forth. For the emanation which reaches each of these two classes is either sufficient only for the perfection of the individual and no more, or it is sufficiently puissant that there remains unto that individual enough wherewith to perfect others[[fn:2179]]. As touching the first class, that of the learned, sometimes that which is poured out upon the rational faculty[[fn:2180]] of the individual is sufficient to make of him a man of study and intelligence, possessing knowledge and discernment, yet who feels not himself moved to instruct others, nor to compose works, having for this neither the inclination nor the (requisite) capacity; at other times, that which is poured out upon him is of a force sufficient to stimulate him necessarily to the composition of works and to the office of teaching. It is likewise with the second class: sometimes a prophet has inspirations which serve only for his own perfection; at other times he is inspired in such wise as to be compelled to make an appeal unto men, to instruct them, and to shed upon them (a portion) of his perfection.
root.text.Part 2..36.4: It is therefore manifest that, without this superabundant perfection, books on the sciences would not have been composed, nor would the prophets have called men to the knowledge of the truth. Verily, a learned man writs nothing for himself, to the end of teaching himself what he already knows; but it is in the nature of this (active) intellect[[fn:2181]] to communicate itself perpetually and to extend successively its emanation from one individual to another[[fn:2182]], until it reaches an individual beyond whom its influence cannot spread[[fn:2183]], and whom it only perfects (personally), as we have explained, by a comparison, in one of the chapters of this treatise[[fn:2184]].
root.text.Part 2..36.5: The nature of this matter is such that he who has received this superabundant overflow necessarily preaches unto men, whether he be hearkened to or no, even should he expose his person[[fn:2185]]; so that we find prophets who preached unto men even unto being slain, stimulated by this divine inspiration which left them neither quiet nor rest[[fn:2186]], even when they were smitten by great misfortunes. Wherefore thou seest Jeremiah declare[[fn:2187]] that, by reason of the contempt which he endured from those rebellious and incredulous men who lived in his time, he desired to conceal[[fn:2188]] his prophetic mission and no longer call them to the truth which they had rejected, but that this was impossible for him: For the word of the Lord, says he, was made a reproach unto me, and a derision, daily. Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay (Jeremiah xx. 8, 9). It is in the same sense that another prophet has said: The Lord God has spoken, who can but prophesy (Amos iii. 8)? — Thou must well consider this.
root.text.Part 2..37.0: Know that every man necessarily possesses a faculty of courage[[fn:2189]]; without this, he would not be moved by thought to avert that which is harmful to him. This faculty, in my judgment, is among the faculties of the soul what the expulsive[[fn:2190]] faculty is among the physical faculties. This faculty of courage varies in strength and weakness, even as do the other faculties: so that thou findest such a man as advancs against a lion, and another who fles before a mouse; one who advancs alone against an army to do battle, and another who trembls and is afraid when a woman utters a cry. There must also be possessed, from one's primitive formation, a certain predisposition of temperament, which, with a certain manner of thinking, shall increase [so that what is in potentiality shall come forth by the effort made to bring it forth], and which, with another manner of thinking[[fn:2191]], shall diminish through lack of exercise. From the earliest age, one recogniss in children whether this faculty[[fn:2192]] be strong or weak within them.
root.text.Part 2..37.1: Likewise, this faculty of divination (which is found in prophets) exists in all men, but varies in degree; (it exists) particularly concerning those things wherewith man is strongly preoccupied and in which he exerciss his thought. Thou divinest, for example[[fn:2193]], that such a one has spoken or acted in such a manner in such a circumstance, and it is in truth so. Thou findest such a man in whom the faculty of conjecture and divination[[fn:2194]] is so strong and just, that well-nigh everything which, in his imagination, he believs to be, is (really) such as he has imagined it, or is (at least) so in part[[fn:2195]]. The causes thereof are many, (and this occurrs) through a concatenation of many circumstances[[fn:2196]], anterior, posterior, and present; but, by the power of this (faculty of) divination, the mind traverss all these premises and draws the conclusions therefrom in so short a time that one would say it was the work of an instant[[fn:2197]]. It is by this faculty that certain men give warning[[fn:2198]] of grave things which are to come to pass.
root.text.Part 2..37.2: These two faculties, I mean, the faculty of boldness and the faculty of divination, must necessarily be very powerful in prophets. When the (Active) Intellect emanats upon them, these two faculties assume an exceeding great force, and thou knowest to what extent the effect produced thereby has reached; to wit, that a solitary man should boldly present himself[[fn:2199]], with his staff, before a great king, to deliver a nation from the thraldom imposed by him, and that he should feel neither terror[[fn:2200]] nor fear, because it had been said unto him (by God): For I will be with thee (Exodus, iii, 12). This is a state which varies greatly amongst them (the prophets), yet which is indispensable unto them[[fn:2201]]. Thus it was said unto Jeremiah: Be not afraid of them, etc. Be not dismayed at them, etc. Behold, I have made thee this day a defenced city, etc. (Jeremiah, i, 8, 17, 18); and unto Ezekiel it was said: Be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words (Ezek., ii, 6). Thus thou shalt find them all endowed with a mighty boldness. Likewise, by the great development of their faculties of divination, they promptly foretell the future; but, in this respect also, there is amongst them a variation (of degrees), as thou knowest.
root.text.Part 2..37.3: It must be known that true prophets undoubtedly possess also speculative perceptions, (but of such a nature) that man, by speculation alone, could not grasp the causes which may lead to such knowledge; even as when they foretell things which man could not foretell by means of mere conjecture and vulgar divination[[fn:2202]]. Indeed, that same inspiration[[fn:2203]] which is shed upon the imaginative faculty, so as to perfect it to such a degree that its action reaches even to the foretelling of the future and the perceiving of it as though it were concerning things perceived by the senses and which had reached that imaginative faculty by the way of the senses, (this same inspiration, I say) perfects also the action of the rational faculty to such a degree that it attains by this action to the knowledge of the real essence of things[[fn:2204]] and possesses the perception thereof as though it had obtained it through speculative propositions.
root.text.Part 2..37.4: Such is the truth which must be admitted by whosoever loves to render an impartial judgment[[fn:2205]]; for all things serve as testimony and proof unto one another. This befitts even much more the rational faculty[[fn:2206]]. Indeed, it is only upon it, in reality, that the Active Intellect (directly) emanats, which brings it into actuality, and it is through the rational faculty that the emanation reaches the imaginative faculty; how then could it be that the imaginative power were perfect to the point of perceiving what comes not to it by way of the senses, without the same being true for the rational faculty, that is to say (without its being perfect to the point) of perceiving what it could not perceive by means of premises, logical conclusion, and reflection? — Such is the true idea of prophecy, and such are the opinions which serve to characterize the prophetic teaching. If, in what I have just said concerning prophets,
root.text.Part 2..37.5: I have made it a condition that they be true prophets, it has been to make my reservations regarding the folk of the third class[[fn:2207]], who possess neither rational notions nor science, but only chimeras and erroneous opinions. It may also be that what those men perceive is nothing other than (true) ideas which they (formerly) held, and of which their (present) chimeras have preserved the traces[[fn:2208]], alongside all that is in their imaginative faculty; so that, after many of their chimeras have been annihilated and made to disappear, the traces[[fn:2209]] of these (ancient) ideas alone remained and appeared unto them as a novelty[[fn:2210]] and as a thing coming from without[[fn:2211]]. I deem it possible to compare them to a man who had with him, in his house, thousands of animals; these having all withdrawn from the house, save for a single individual from among the number of those that were there, the man, remaining alone with this individual, would imagine that the latter had just entered into the house unto him, whereas it is not so, and on the contrary, it is that very one which has not gone out.
root.text.Part 2..37.6: This it is which has given rise to the most pernicious errors and which has caused the ruin of many men who claimed to possess discernment[[fn:2212]].
root.text.Part 2..37.7: Thus[[fn:2213]], thou shalt find folk who base the truth of their notions upon dreams which they have had, imagining that what they beheld in sleep is aught else than the idea which they themselves conceived or heard whilst in a waking state.
root.text.Part 2..37.8: Wherefore, no attention must be paid unto those whose rational faculty is not perfect, and who have not attained unto the highest speculative perfection; for he alone who has reached speculative perfection can thereafter obtain other (superior) knowledge, when[[fn:2214]] the divine intellect is poured out upon him. It is such a one who is truly a prophet, and this was clearly expressed (by the words) ונביא לבב חכמה (Ps. xc. 12), that is to say, that the true prophet[[fn:2215]] is (he who possesses) a heart full of wisdom. This also is a matter with which one must be thoroughly impressed.
root.text.Part 2..38.0.sub_0: Having spoken of the essence of prophecy, which we have made known in all its reality, and having set forth that the prophecy of Moses, our Master, is distinguished from that of others, we say that it is this perception alone (that of Moses) which had for its necessary consequence the calling of us unto the Law. Indeed, a call similar to that which Moses made unto us had never been made by any of those whom we know[[fn:2216]], from Adam until him, nor was any such call made after him by any of our prophets. Likewise, it is a fundamental principle of our Law that there shall never be another; wherefore, in our opinion, there has never been, nor shall there ever be, but one single Law, even that of Moses, our Master. Herein follows a (more ample) explanation, according to what has been expressly stated in the prophetic books and what is found in the traditions. It is that, of all the prophets who preceded Moses, our Master, such as the Patriarchs, Shem, Eber, Noah, Methuselah, and Enoch, none ever said unto a class of men: “God[[fn:2217]] has sent me unto you and has commanded me to tell you such and such a thing; He forbidds you to do this thing and commands you to do that other.” This is a thing which is attested by no text of the Pentateuch and which no true tradition relats. Those, on the contrary, received no divine revelation[[fn:2218]] save in the sense which we have already set forth[[fn:2219]]; and if any among them were more powerfully inspired, as, for example, Abraham, he gathered men together and called them, by way of instruction and guidance, unto the truth which he himself had perceived. Thus it was that Abraham instructed men, showing them, by speculative proofs, that the universe had but one God, that it was He who had created all that is outside of Him, and that one must not worship these figures (of the stars), nor any created thing. This is what he inculcated upon men, drawing them by fair discourse and by benevolence; but never did he say unto them: “God has sent me unto you and has commanded or forbidden me (such or such a thing).” This is so true that, when circumcision was commanded unto him, for himself, his children, and those who belonged unto him, he circumcised them, but invited not (other) men, by a prophetic call, to do the like.
root.text.Part 2..38.0.sub_1: Seest thou not that the text of Scripture says concerning him: For I have known him, etc. (Gen. xviii. 19)? whence it clearly follows that he proceeded only by way of commandment[[fn:2220]]; and it was in the same form that Isaac, Jacob, Levi, Kohath, and Amram addressed their calls unto men. Thou findest likewise that the Doctors, speaking of the prophets prior (to Moses), say: The tribunal of Eber, the tribunal of Methuselah, the school of Methuselah[[fn:2221]]; for all these prophets did but instruct men, after the manner of preceptors, teachers, and guides, but never said: the Lord said unto me: Speak unto the sons of such a one[[fn:2222]].
root.text.Part 2..38.1: Thus did the matter pass before Moses, our Master. As for Moses, thou knowest what was said unto him and what he said, and (thou knowest) that word which all the people addressed unto him: This day we have seen that God does talk with man, etc. (Deut. v. 24). As for all those of our prophets who came after Moses, our Master, thou knowest in what manner they express themselves in all their relations and that they present themselves as preachers who invite men to follow the Law of Moses, threatening those who should prove rebellious and making promises unto those who should strive to follow it[[fn:2223]]. And we believe likewise that it shall ever be thus[[fn:2224]], as it has been said: It is not in heaven, etc. (ibid., xxx. 12); unto us and to our children for ever (ibid., xxix. 29). And so it must needs be; for, so soon as a thing is the most perfect possible of its kind, any other thing of the same kind cannot but be of a lesser perfection, whether by exceeding the just measure or by falling below it. If, for example, an equal temperament is the most equal possible in a species, any temperament which should be outside of this equality would err by deficiency or by excess. It is the same with this Law, which has been declared to be equal (i.e., equitable or just), saying: statutes and judgments RIGHTEOUS צדיקים (ibid., iv. 8); for thou knowest that צדיקים (righteous) signifies equal (or equitable)[[fn:2225]]. Verily, these are religious practices in which there is neither burden nor excess, such as (exist) in monachism, in the life of the pilgrim[[fn:2226]], etc., nor any deficiency (vice) which leads to gluttony and debauchery, so as to diminish the perfection of man in respect of morals and study, as (do) all the (religious) laws of the ancient peoples[[fn:2227]].
root.text.Part 2..38.2: Whenever we shall discourse, in this treatise, upon the reasons which may be assigned for the laws (of Moses[[fn:2228]]), thou shalt receive all necessary enlightenment touching their equability[[fn:2229]] and their wisdom; wherefore it has been said of them: The law of the Lord is perfect (Ps. xix. 8). When any man claims that they impose great and heavy burdens and that they cause torments, 'tis verily an error of judgment. I shall demonstrate that, for perfect men, they are easy; wherefore it was said: What does the Lord thy God require of thee? etc. (Deut. x. 12); and again: Have I been a wilderness unto Israel, etc. (Jer. ii. 31)[[fn:2230]]? All this, certes, (has been said) in respect of virtuous men. As for the impious, the violent, and the despotic, they consider it as the most hurtful and grievous thing that there should be a judge to hinder their despotism; and likewise, for men of ignoble passions, 'tis the most grievous thing to be prevented from abandoning themselves freely to debauchery and to incur punishment for having indulged therein[[fn:2231]]. And thus it is that every vicious man considers the hindrance of the evil he loves to commit, by reason of his moral corruption, as a heavy burden[[fn:2232]]. It behoves us not, therefore, to measure the facility or difficulty of the law according to the passion of every wicked, vile, and depraved man; but we must consider this law from the point of view of the perfect man whom it seeks to set as a model for all men[[fn:2233]]. This law alone do we call Divine Law; but all that exists outside of it in the way of political regimes, such as the laws of the Greeks and the follies of the Sabians and of other (nations), is the work of political men and not of prophets, as I have several times set forth.
root.text.Part 2..39.0: It has been right clearly set forth that man is by nature a social being[[fn:2234]], and that his nature (requirs) that he live in society[[fn:2235]]; he is not like the other animals, for whom the gathering into society is not a necessity. On account of the manifold composition of this (human) species, — for, as thou knowest, it is the most composite of all things[[fn:2236]], — there exists, amongst its individuals, such a varied difference that one scarce finds two individuals in harmony under any moral respect whatsoever, no more than one could find two figures perfectly alike[[fn:2237]]. The cause thereof is the difference of temperament, which produces a difference in the (respective) matters and also in the accidents which accompany the form; for every physical form has certain particular accidents which accompany it, besides the accidents which accompany the matter. Such great variation from individual to individual is not met with in any species of animals; on the contrary, the difference between the individuals of each species is but little sensible[[fn:2238]], save in man. Indeed, one may find two individuals who differ so greatly in every moral quality, that one would say they belong to two (different) species, so that thou shalt find (e.g.) such an individual who has cruelty even to the point[[fn:2239]] of slaying his young son in the violence of wrath, whilst another is moved (at the thought) of killing a gnat or a reptile, having a soul too tender for such an act; and it is the same in most accidents[[fn:2240]].
root.text.Part 2..39.1: Now, whereas the human species, by its nature, admitts of this variation amongst its individuals[[fn:2241]], and whereas social life is necessary to its nature, it is altogether impossible that society should be perfect unless it possess a guide who can regulate the actions of the individuals, remedying that which is defective and moderating that which is in excess[[fn:2242]], and who can prescribe actions and morals that all must continually practice, according to the same rule, so that the natural variation may be concealed by the great conventional harmony and that society may be in good order.
root.text.Part 2..39.2: Wherefore I say that the law, albeit it be not natural, yet enters, in certain respects, into the category of the natural[[fn:2243]]; for it was of the Divine wisdom, for the preservation of this species whose existence He willed, to implant in its nature (the condition) that its individuals should possess a faculty of governance. Sometimes the individual is he himself unto whom this governance has been inspired, and such is the prophet or the lawgiver; sometimes he is one who has the power to constrain (men) to practice what those two[[fn:2244]] have prescribed, to follow it and to bring it into action, and such are the sovereign who adopts this law (of the lawgiver) and the pretended prophet who adopts the law of the (true) prophet, either in its entirety or in part. If (the latter) adopts a part and abandons another part[[fn:2245]], it is either because it is easier for him, or because, through jealousy, he wishes to make it believed that these things came to him by (Divine) revelation and that he has not borrowed them from another; for there is such a man as delights in a certain perfection, finds it excellent and loves it, and who wishes that men should imagine that he is himself endowed with this perfection, although he well knows that he possesses no perfection whatsoever. Thus thou seest many men who boast of the poem of another and attribute it to themselves; and this is also what has been done for certain works of the learned and for many scientific details, (I mean) that a jealous and slothful person, having lighted (by chance) upon a thing invented by another, pretended to have invented it. This is also what has happened for this prophetic perfection; for we find that certain men, pretending to be prophets, spake things which had never been revealed by God[[fn:2246]], as (did), for example, Zedekiah, son of Chenaanah[[fn:2247]], and we find others who, arrogating to themselves the prophetic office, spake things which, doubtless, God had spoken, I mean that they had been revealed, but to others, as (did), for example, Hananiah, son of Azur[[fn:2248]], — so that they attributed them to themselves and adorned themselves therewith.
root.text.Part 2..39.3: All this is recognized and distinguished right clearly; but I shall expound it unto thee, that naught obscure may remain for thee, and that thou mayest possess a criterion whereby thou mayest distinguish between the regimes of conventional laws[[fn:2249]], those of the Divine Law, and those emanating from men who have borrowed from the words of the prophets, boasting thereof and attributing the same unto themselves. As for the laws which their authors have expressly declared to be the work of their own reflection[[fn:2250]], thou hast need[[fn:2251]] for them of no argument, the confession of the adversary rendering all proof unnecessary. I desire, therefore, to make known unto thee only the regimes which are proclaimed as prophetic, and which, in part, are truly prophetic, I mean Divine, in part legislative, and in part plagiarisms[[fn:2252]].
root.text.Part 2..39.4: If, then, thou findest a law of which the sole end and whose author, in calculating the effects thereof, had no other aim than to establish good order in the State and its affairs, and to remove therefrom injustice and violence—without insistence being laid, in any wise, upon speculative matters, and without regard being had[[fn:2253]] to the perfection of the rational faculty, or any concern for opinions, whether they be sound or infirm, the whole purpose being, on the contrary, to regulate in all respects the mutual relations of men and (to ensure) that they obtain a certain presumed felicity[[fn:2254]] according to the opinion of the legislator—(if, I say, thou findest such a law,) thou shalt know that this law is (purely) legislative, and that its author, as we have said, belongs to the third class, I mean those who possess no other perfection than that of the imaginative faculty[[fn:2255]].
root.text.Part 2..39.5: But, if thou findest a law of which all the provisions tend[[fn:2256]] (not only) to the improvement of corporeal interests, of which mention has just been made, but also to the improvement of faith, endeavouring first of all to spread sound opinions concerning God and concerning the angels, and tending to render man wise, understanding, and attentive, so that he may know the whole of being according to its true condition, then shalt thou know that this governance emanats from God and that this law is divine.
root.text.Part 2..39.6: But it will yet remain for thee to know whether he who proclaims it be himself the perfect man unto whom it was revealed, or whether it be a person who has boasted of these discourses and falsely attributed them unto himself. — To make trial thereof, one must examine (the extent of) the perfection of that person, watch[[fn:2257]] his actions, and consider his conduct. The most important criterion which thou canst have is the repulsion and contempt (which that person would have) for corporeal pleasures; for therein lies the first step of men of science, and, with even greater reason, of prophets; particularly regarding that of the senses which is a disgrace unto us, as Aristotle says[[fn:2258]], and notably the pollution of cohabitation which derivs therefrom. Wherefore God has confounded[[fn:2259]] by this latter anyone who arrogated (unto himself prophecy), so that the truth might be known to those who sought it and that they might not be led astray and into error. Thou seest an example thereof[[fn:2260]] in Zedekiah, son of Maaseiah, and Ahab, son of Kolaiah, who arrogated prophecy and drew men after them by delivering prophetic discourses revealed to others[[fn:2261]], but who (at the same time) gave themselves up to the ignoble pleasure of lust, even to the committing of adultery with the wives of their friends and followers, until at last God unveiled them, as He had confounded others, so that the king of Babylon caused them to be roasted in the fire, as Jeremiah clearly says: And of them shall be taken up a curse by all the captivity of Judah which are in Babylon, saying, The Lord make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire; because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours' wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them; even I know, and am a witness, says the Lord (Jerem. XXIX, 22 and 23). Understand well the intent of this[[fn:2262]].
root.text.Part 2..40.0: I need not explain what a dream is. As for the vision (מראה), — for example, I will make myself known unto him in a vision (Numb. 12, 6), — which is designated by the name of מַרְאֵה הַנְּבוּאָה, prophetic vision[[fn:2263]], which (in Scripture) is also called יַד יְיָ, hand of the Lord[[fn:2264]], and which also bears the name of MA'HAZÉ (מחזה) [[fn:2265]], it is a state of agitation and terror which seizes the prophet whilst he is awake, as is set forth concerning Daniel in these words: I saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me: for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength; and he continus: Then was I in a deep sleep on my face, and my face toward the ground (Daniel 10, 8, 9). When subsequently the angel speaks unto him and causs him to stand, this still occurrs within the prophetic vision. In such a state, the senses cease to function; that emanation (of which I have spoken) spreads over the rational faculty, and thence over the imaginative faculty, so that the latter is perfected and functions[[fn:2266]]. Sometimes the revelation beginns with a prophetic vision; then this agitation and strong emotion, following the perfect action of the imagination, go on increasing, and then the (true) revelation arrivs. This is what took place for Abraham; for (in speaking) of that revelation, it beginns by saying: The word of the Lord came unto Abram in a vision (Genesis 15, 1), and at the end (it is said), and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him (ibid., v. 12); and thereafter: And he said unto Abram, etc. (ibid., v. 13-16).
root.text.Part 2..40.1: Know thou that those amongst the prophets who recount having had a revelation, sometimes attribute it (expressly) to an angel, and sometimes to God, albeit it undoubtedly took place through the mediation of an angel; the Doctors have pronounced thereupon, saying: "And the Lord said unto her (ibid. XXV, 23), through the mediation of an angel[[fn:2267]]." — It must be known that whenever a passage (of Scripture) says of someone that an angel spoke unto him, or that the word of God was addressed unto him, this could not have taken place otherwise than in a dream or in a prophetic vision.
root.text.Part 2..40.2: The terms employed in the prophetic books exhibit four modes of expression regarding the word addressed to the prophets[[fn:2268]]: The first mode is when the prophet expressly relats[[fn:2269]] that this speech came from an angel, in a dream or in a vision. The second mode is when he merely reports the discourse addressed unto him by the angel, without expressly declaring it to have been in a dream or a vision, being assured that it is a matter generally known that no revelation exists save in one of two ways: In a vision do I make myself known unto him, in a dream do I speak with him (Numbers xii. 6). The third mode is when he mentions not an angel, but ascribs the speech unto God, as if He Himself had addressed it unto him, yet declaring that this word came unto him in a vision or in a dream. The fourth mode is when the prophet simply says that God has spoken to him, or commanded him to act[[fn:2270]], to do such a thing, or to speak in such a manner, without expressly mentioning either angel or dream, relying upon that which is known and established as a principle[[fn:2271]], namely, that no prophecy nor revelation comes otherwise than in a dream or a vision, and through the mediation of an angel.
root.text.Part 2..40.3: The first mode is employed in the following passages: And the angel of God said unto me in a dream (Genesis xxxi. 11); And God spake unto Israel in the visions of the night (ibid. xlvi. 2); And God came unto Balaam; And God said unto Balaam (Num. xxii. 9 and 12)[[fn:2272]]. — Concerning the second mode, the following examples may be cited: And God said unto Jacob: Arise, go up to Bethel (Genesis xxxv. 1); And God said unto him: thy name is Jacob (ibid., v. 10); And an angel of the Lord called unto him out of heaven; And the angel of the Lord called unto him a second time, etc. (ibid., xxii. 11 and 15); And God said unto Noah (ibid., vi. 13); And God spake unto Noah (ibid., viii. 15). — An example of the third mode is found in this passage: The word of the Lord came unto Abram in a vision, etc. (ibid., xv. 1). — For the fourth mode, the following examples are found: And the Lord said unto Abram (ibid., xii. 1); The Lord said unto Jacob: Return into the land of thy fathers (ibid., xxxi. 3); And the Lord said unto Joshua (Joshua iii. 7); And the Lord said unto Gideon (Judges vii. 2)[[fn:2273]]. And thus it is that they (the prophets) for the most part express themselves: And the Lord said unto me (Isaiah viii. 1); And the word of the Lord came unto me (Ezekiel xxiv. 1); And the word of the Lord came (II Sam. xxiv. 11; I Kings xviii. 1); And behold, the word of the Lord came to him (I Kings xix. 9)[[fn:2274]]; The word of the Lord came (Ezek. i. 3); The beginning of the word of the Lord by Hosea (Hos. i. 2); The hand of the Lord was upon me (Ezek. xxxvii. 1; xl. 1). There be many examples of this kind.
root.text.Part 2..40.4: All that is presented according to one of these four modes constitutes prophecy, and he who utters it is a prophet. But when it is said: "God [[t:0]]came[[t:1]] unto such a one in a [[t:2]]dream[[t:3]] of the night," it does not there concern prophecy, nor is that person a prophet. For it is intended (merely) that an admonition from God came to that person, and it is subsequently declared unto us that this admonition occurred by means of a dream; for, just as God causes one person to set himself in motion to save another person or to destroy him, so likewise does He bring forth, by means of what is seen in a dream, certain things which it is His will to bring forth. Assuredly, one doubts not that the Aramean Laban was a perfect villain and at the same time an idolater; and, as for Abimelech, albeit amongst his people he was a pious man, our father Abraham said of his city and his kingdom: [[t:4]]Surely there is no fear of God in this place[[t:5]] (Genesis, 20, 11); and yet, of each of the two, one means to say of Laban and of Abimelech, it is said (that God appeared unto him in a dream): [[t:6]]And God came unto Abimelech in a dream of the night[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]ibid.[[t:9]], [[t:10]]V[[t:11]]. 3), and likewise (it is said) of Laban: [[t:12]]In a dream of the night[[t:13]] ([[t:14]]ibid.[[t:15]], XXXI, 24)[[fn:2275]]. One must, therefore, impress this upon one's mind and attend to the difference that obtains between the expressions: [[t:16]]God came[[t:17]] and [[t:18]]God said[[t:19]], and between the expressions [[t:20]]in a dream of the night[[t:21]] and [[t:22]]in the visions of the night;[[t:23]] for of Jacob it is said: [[t:24]]God[[t:25]] [[t:26]]SAID[[t:27]] [[t:28]]unto Israel in the visions of the night[[t:29]] ([[t:30]]ibid.[[t:31]], XLVI, 2), whereas of Laban and Abimelech (it is said): [[t:32]]And God[[t:33]] [[t:34]]CAME[[t:35]] [[t:36]]etc. in a dream of the night;[[t:37]] wherefore[[fn:2276]] Onkelos translates it by [[t:38]]ואתא מימר מן קדם י״י[[t:39]], [[t:40]]and there came a[[t:41]] [[t:42]]WORD[[t:43]] [[t:44]]from before God[[t:45]], and he does not say (speaking) of the latter two: [[t:46]]ואתגלי י״י[[t:47]], [[t:48]]and God revealed himself[[t:49]].
root.text.Part 2..40.5: It is also to be known that it is sometimes said: the Lord said unto such an one, without it being (directly) concerning that person[[fn:2277]], and without his ever having received a revelation, but where the communication was made through the mediation of a prophet. Thus, for example, regarding this passage: And she went to enquire of the Lord (ibid., xxv. 22), it has been expressly said (that she addressed herself) 'to the school of Eber[[fn:2278]]'; it was he who answered her, so that it is of him it was spoken when it is said: And the LORD said unto her (ibid., v. 23)[[fn:2279]]. If it be true that it has also been said: 'And the LORD said unto her, by the mediation of a MALAKH (angel or messenger)[[fn:2280]],' this may be interpreted (in the sense) that it is Eber who is the MALAKH; for the prophet also is called MALAKH, as we shall set forth[[fn:2281]]. It may also be that it was intended to indicate the angel[[t:34]] who brought this prophecy unto Eber; or else (it may be) that it was intended to declare thereby that, wherever a discourse is found simply attributed unto God, the mediation of an angel must be admitted, (and that) for all[[fn:2282]] the prophets (in general), as we have set forth.
root.text.Part 2..41.0: We have already set forth that, wheresoever mention is made of the appearance of an angel, or of a speech made by him, it can only be a question of a prophetic vision, or of a dream[[fn:2283]], whether or not it be expressly declared, as has been said before. This thou must know and be well persuaded thereof. It matters not whether it be said at first of someone that he saw the angel, or whether it seems to be said that he took him at first for a human individual, and that at the end it became manifest unto him that it was an angel[[fn:2284]]; as soon as thou findest in the conclusion that he who was seen and who spake was an angel, thou shalt know and be certain that from the beginning it was a prophetic vision, or a prophetic dream. For, in the prophetic vision or in the prophetic dream, at one time the prophet ses God who speaks unto him, as we shall set forth, at another time he ses an angel who speaks unto him, at another he hears someone speaking unto him without seeing the person who speaks, and finally, at another time, he ses a human individual who addresses him, and afterwards it becoms manifest unto him that he who spake was an angel[[fn:2285]]. In prophecy of this last kind, he relats that he saw a man acting or speaking, and that thereafter he knew it to be an angel.
root.text.Part 2..41.1: It is this important principle[[fn:2286]] which has been professed by one of the doctors, and verily one of the greatest among them, to wit, R. 'Hayya the Great, concerning that passage of the Pentateuch: And the Lord appeared unto him in the plains of Mamre, etc. (Genesis, xviii. 1); for, after having first stated summarily that God appeared unto him, the text beginns to explain under what form this appearance took place, and says that he saw first three men, that he ran (to meet them), that they spake and that it was spoken unto them[[fn:2287]]. He, therefore, who offers this interpretation, says that these words of Abraham: My Lord, if now I have found favour in thy sight, pass not away, I pray thee, from thy servant (ibid., v. 3) are likewise a relation of that which, in the prophetic vision, he spake unto one of them: 'It was,' says he, 'unto the greatest among them that he addressed his speech[[fn:2288]].' Thou must also well penetrate this subject, for it contains a profound mystery[[fn:2289]].
root.text.Part 2..41.2: I say likewise that, in the history of Jacob, when it is said: And there wrestled a man with him (ibid., XXXII, 25), it treats of a prophetic revelation, since it is clearly stated at the end (verses 29 et seq.) that it was an angel. It is exactly as with the history of Abraham, in which it is first related summarily that God appeared unto him, etc., and thereafter the text beginns to explain how this came to pass. Likewise, concerning Jacob, it is said (first): The angels of God met him (ibid., V. 2); then it beginns to set forth what happened until the moment when they met him, and it is said that he sent messengers (unto Esau), and that after having acted and done (such and such a thing), Jacob was left alone, etc. (ibid., V. 25); for here it treats of those same angels of God of whom it was said at first the angels of God met him[[fn:2290]], and this struggle, as well as the whole dialogue (which follows), took place in a prophetic vision. Likewise, all that happened with Balaam in the way (Numbers, 22, 22 et seq.), as well as the speaking of the ass, (all this, I say,) took place in a prophetic vision[[fn:2291]], since it is expressly said at the end (verse 32) that the angel of the Lord spake unto him[[fn:2292]]. In like manner also, concerning these words (of the book) of Joshua (5, 13), he lifted up his eyes and looked, and, behold, there stood a MAN over against him, I say that this took place in the prophetic vision, since it is clearly said thereafter (V. 14 and 15) that it was a prince of the host of the Lord. — [As for this passage And a MALAKH (messenger) of the Lord came up from Gilgal, etc. And when the MALAKH of the Lord spake these words unto all Israel (Judges, 2, 1 and 4), the doctors have written that the MALAKH of the Lord spoken of here is Phinehas; they express themselves thus: 'it is Phinehas, who, at the moment when the Divine Majesty rested upon him, resembled a malakh (angel) of the Lord[[fn:2293]].']
root.text.Part 2..41.3: [We have already set forth that the name malakh is homonymous, and that the prophet also is called malakh[[fn:2294]], as, for example, in the following passages: He sent a MALAKH and has brought us forth out of Egypt (Numb., 20, 16); And Haggai, the Lord's MALAKH, spake in the Lord's message (Hag., I, 13); And they mocked the MALAKHIM (messengers) of God (II Chron., XXXVI, 16).] — When Daniel says: And Gabriel, the man whom I had seen at the first in a vision, came to me in a swift flight, about the time of the evening oblation (Dan., IX, 21), all this also took place in a prophetic vision; and it must by no means occur to thy mind that an angel could be seen, or the words of an angel heard, otherwise than in a prophetic vision or in a prophetic dream, as it has been laid down as a principle (in this passage): I will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream (Numb., 12, 6). From that which I have cited, thou shalt derive proof for other passages which I have not mentioned.
root.text.Part 2..41.4: By that which we have previously said concerning the necessity of a preparation for prophecy[[fn:2295]], and by that which we have said of the homonymy of the name malakh, thou shalt know that Hagar the Egyptian was not a prophetess, and that Manoah and his wife were likewise not prophets[[fn:2296]]; for the word which they heard, or which struck their mind, was something similar to that sound of a voice of which the doctors constantly speak, and which designats a certain situation in which an unprepared person may find himself[[fn:2297]]. That which has given rise to error hereupon is solely the homonymy[[fn:2298]]; but it is there (precisely) the principle which removs[[fn:2299]] most of the difficulties of the Pentateuch.
root.text.Part 2..41.5: — Observe well that the expression: [[t:0]]And the angel found her[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]וימצאה[[t:3]]) [[t:4]]near the source of water etc.[[t:5]] (Genesis, 16, 7) resembles that employed in the case of Joseph: [[t:6]]And a man found him[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]וימצאהו[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]wandering in the field[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]ibid.[[t:13]], XXXVII, 15), where all the [[t:14]]Midrashic[[t:15]] commentaries say that it was an [[t:16]]angel[[t:17]][[fn:2300]].
root.text.Part 2..42.0: We have already set forth, in our works, that the prophets sometimes present their prophecies in the form of parables[[fn:2301]]; this is because at times the prophet beholds a thing by way of a parable, and thereafter the meaning of the parable is explained unto him in that same prophetic vision. It is as[[fn:2302]] unto a man who has a dream, and who, in that very dream, imagins that he has awakened, that he has related the dream to another, and that the latter has explained its meaning to him, whilst the whole was naught but a dream. This is what is termed: 'a dream which has been interpreted in a dream[[fn:2303]],' whereas there be also dreams whose meaning is known only after one has awakened. In like manner, the sense of the prophetic parables is sometimes explained within the prophetic vision, as is manifest regarding Zechariah, who says, after having first presented certain parables: And the angel that talked with me came again, and waked me, as a man that is wakened out of his sleep; and said unto me, What seest thou? etc. (Zech. IV, 1 and 2); then he (the angel) explains to him the (new) parable[[fn:2304]].
root.text.Part 2..42.1: And the same is likewise manifest in the case of Daniel; for it is first said: Daniel saw a dream, and upon his couch (he had) visions of his head (Dan. VII, 1); and after having related all the parables and having expressed how much he was grieved at not knowing the explanation thereof, he finally inquirs of the angel, and the latter makes known unto him the explanation in that same vision: I came near, says he, unto one of them that stood by, and asked him the truth of all this. So he told me, and made me know the interpretation of the things (ibid., V. 16). After having said that he saw a dream, he calls the whole event ’HAZÔN (a vision), because, as he says, it was an angel who explained it to him in a prophetic dream. He says, therefore, after that: A vision (’HAZÔN) appeared unto me, even unto me Daniel, after that which appeared unto me at the first (ibid., VIII, 1). This is clear[[fn:2305]]; for ’HAZÔN is derived from the verb ’HAZA, even as MAREA (vision) is derived from RAA, and both verbs have the same meaning (that of seeing), so that there is no difference between the words MAREA, MA’HAZÉ and ’HAZÔN. There is no third way (of prophecy) besides those two ways of which the Pentateuch speaks: I will make myself known unto him in a VISION, and will speak unto him in a DREAM (Numbers, 12, 6)[[fn:2306]]; but there be in this certain gradations, as shall be set forth[[fn:2307]].
root.text.Part 2..42.2: — Nevertheless, among the prophetic parables, there be also many whose meaning is in no wise explained in the prophetic vision, but whose intent the prophet knows after having awakened, as is the case, for instance, with the staves which Zechariah took in a prophetic vision[[fn:2308]].
root.text.Part 2..42.3: It must be understood that, even as the prophets behold things which have a parabolical sense, — as, for example, the lamps of Zechariah (Zech. 4, 2), the horses and the mountains (ibid., VI, 1-7), the roll of Ezekiel (II, 9), the wall made by a plumb-line which Amos beheld[[fn:2309]] (7, 7), the beasts which Daniel beheld (ch. VII and VIII), the seething pot which Jeremiah beheld (1, 13), and other similar parables, whereby it is intended to represent certain ideas, — even so they also behold things whereby it is intended to indicate what the name of the thing seen suggests by its etymology or by its homonymy, in such wise that the action of the imaginative faculty consists, as it were, in causing a thing to be seen bearing a homonymous name, by one of the meanings of which one is guided toward another, which also is one of the species of allegory[[fn:2310]]. When, for instance, Jeremiah says: (that he saw) MAKKEL SCHAKED, a rod of an almond tree, his intention is to deduce something from the homonymy of the word SCHAKED[[fn:2311]], and he says thereafter: For I am SCHÔKED, watchful, etc. (Jer. I, 11 and 12); for it concerns neither the idea of the rod, nor that of the almond tree. Likewise, when Amos beholds KELOUB KAÏÇ, a basket of summer fruit, it is to deduce therefrom the fulfillment of the time; and he says: For the KÈÇ (or the end) is come (Amos, 8, 2).
root.text.Part 2..42.4: — That which is yet more astonishing occurs when attention is awakened by means of a certain name, the letters of which are also those of another name, albeit in an inverted order, [[fn:2312]] though there exist between these two names no etymological connection, nor any commonality of sense, as is found (for example) in the parables of Zechariah, when, in a prophetic vision, he takes the two [[t:0]]staves[[t:1]][[fn:2313]] for pasturing the flock, and designates the one by the name of N[[t:2]]O[[t:3]]’[[t:4]]AM[[t:5]] (grace, favour), and the other, by that of ’H[[t:6]]ÔBELÎM[[t:7]] (destroyers). [[fn:2314]] In this parable, the aim is (to indicate): that the nation, in its primitive state, enjoyed the [[t:8]]favour of the Eternal[[t:9]] who guided and directed it; that it was joyful in obeying God and derived pleasure therefrom, [[fn:2315]] and that God was propitious unto it and loved it — [as it is said: [[t:10]]Thou hast this day magnified the Lord, etc., and the Lord has magnified thee, etc.[[t:11]] (Deut. XXVI, 17 and 18)[[fn:2316]]] — when it was guided and directed by Moses and by the Prophets who succeeded him; but that subsequently it so altered its disposition as to conceive an aversion for obedience to God, with the result that God conceived an aversion for it, and made of its leaders [[t:12]]destroyers[[t:13]], such as Jeroboam and Manasseh. This is (the sense) according to etymology; for ’[[t:14]]HOBELÎM[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]חובלים[[t:17]]) is from (the same root as) [[t:18]]ME[[t:19]]’[[t:20]]HABBELÎM[[t:21]], [[t:22]]מחבלים כרמים[[t:23]] ([[t:24]]which[[t:25]] [[t:26]]DESTROY[[t:27]] [[t:28]]the vineyards[[t:29]], Song of Sol., II, 15). Subsequently, he deduces likewise — that is to say, from the name of ’[[t:30]]HOBELÎM[[t:31]] — that they held the Law in [[t:32]]aversion[[t:33]] and that God held them in aversion. But this sense can only be derived from ’[[t:34]]HOBELÎM[[t:35]] by means of the transposition of the letters ’H, B, L; he therefore states, concerning the idea of [[t:36]]aversion[[t:37]] and [[t:38]]abomination[[t:39]] encompassed within this parable: [[t:40]]My soul loathed them,[[t:41]][[fn:2317]] [[t:42]]and their soul also abhorred[[t:43]] ([[t:44]]BA[[t:45]]’[[t:46]]HALA[[t:47]]) [[t:48]]me[[t:49]] (Zech., XI, 8), and he transposes the letters ’H B L ([[t:50]]חבל[[t:51]]) to form B ’H L ([[t:52]]בחל[[t:53]]).
root.text.Part 2..42.5: According to this method[[fn:2318]], extraordinary things, which are likewise mysteries, are found in the words NE-’HOSCHES (נחשת), KALAL (קלל), RÉGHEL (רגל), ’ÉGHEL (עגל), and ’HASCHMAL (חשמל) employed in the Mercabâ[[fn:2319]]. In various passages, there are found other words which, after this observation, shall become clear unto thee by the context of the discourse, if thou examinest them well in every passage[[fn:2320]].
root.text.Part 2..43.0: Prophecy takes not place save by means of a vision or a dream, as we have set forth several times, so that we need no longer repeat it. We shall now say that, when the prophet is inspired, he sometimes ses a parable, as we have frequently explained. At times he believs he ses[[fn:2321]] God speaking unto him in a prophetic vision, as Isaiah said (6, 8): And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? At other times he hears an angel speaking unto him whom he ses, which is very frequent, as in these passages: And the angel of God said unto me etc. (Genesis, 31, 11)[[fn:2322]]; And he said unto me: Knowest thou not what these things mean? And the angel that talked with me answered etc. (Zech., IV, 5)[[fn:2323]]; Then I heard one saint speaking (Daniel, 8, 13); this is too frequent for one to enumerate all the examples. At other times the prophet ses a human personage who speaks unto him, as it is said in Ezekiel (XL, 3 and 4): And, behold, there was a man, whose appearance was like the appearance of brass, etc.; and the man said unto me, Son of man, etc., after it had been said at first (v. 1): The hand of the Lord was upon me[[fn:2324]]. Finally, at other times, the prophet, in the prophetic vision, ses no figure, but hears only words addressed unto him, as Daniel said: And I heard a man's voice between the banks of (the river) Ulai (Dan., VIII, 16), and as Eliphaz said: There was silence, and I heard a voice (Job, 4, 16), and as Ezekiel also said: And I heard him that spake unto me (Ezek., 2, 2); for that which spake unto him was not that thing which he had perceived in the prophetic vision; but, after having related in detail that wondrous and extraordinary thing which he declars to have perceived, he beginns to set forth the subject and the form of the revelation, and he says: I heard one that spake unto me[[fn:2325]].
root.text.Part 2..43.1: Having first spoken of this division of prophetic revelations, which is justified by the texts, I shall say that those words which the prophet hears in the prophetic vision, his imagination sometimes presents them unto him as being exceeding loud, as when a man dreams that he hears a great thunder, or that he ses an earthquake or a fire from heaven[[fn:2326]]; for often one has such dreams.
root.text.Part 2..43.2: At other times, the words which he hears in the prophetic vision are similar to habitual and familiar language, so that he finds therein naught that is strange. This shall become manifest unto thee by the history of the prophet Samuel, who, when God called him in a moment of inspiration, believed that it was the priest Eli who had called him thrice successively; thereafter Scripture explains the cause thereof, and it is said that what produced this effect upon him, so that he believed it to be Eli, was that he knew not then that the word of God was addressed unto the prophets in this form, this mystery having not yet been revealed unto him. It is therefore said, to give the reason thereof[[fn:2327]]: Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord, neither was the word of the Lord yet revealed unto him (I Sam., 3, 7), which means that he knew not yet, and it had not yet been revealed unto him, that it was thus that the word of the Lord was manifested. When it is said[[fn:2328]] that he did not yet know the Lord, it signifies that he had previously had no prophetic inspiration; for it has been said of him who prophesies: I will make myself known unto him in a vision (Num., 12, 6). The translation of the verse, if regard be had only to the sense, would therefore be this: 'Samuel had not prophesied before, and he knew not even[[fn:2329]] that such was the form of prophetic inspiration.' Thou must needs impress this upon thy mind.
root.text.Part 2..44.0: Having previously set forth the true sense of prophecy, according to what is required by speculation combined with what has been explained in our Law, I must needs enumerate for thee the degrees[[fn:2330]] of prophecy according to these two bases[[fn:2331]]. If I call them degrees of prophecy, it is not that he who occupies any degree whatever is a prophet; for, on the contrary, the first and the second degrees are but steps whereby to arrive at prophecy, and he who has reached one of these steps is not numbered among the prophets of whom we have spoken heretofore. If at times he be called a prophet, it is only by a species of generalization, because he is very nigh unto the prophets.
root.text.Part 2..44.1: Thou must not be led into error concerning these degrees, if thou findest in the prophetic books that a prophet[[fn:2332]] was inspired under the form of one of these degrees, and that it is afterwards declared of this same prophet that he had a revelation under the form of another degree; for it may happen that such a prophet, after having had a revelation under the form of one of the degrees which I shall enumerate[[fn:2333]], may thereafter, at another moment, have another revelation, at a degree inferior to that of the first revelation[[fn:2334]]. Indeed, just as the prophet does not prophesy throughout his whole life, without intermission, and as, on the contrary, after having prophesied at one moment, the prophetic inspiration forsaks him at other moments, even so may it be[[fn:2335]] that he prophesies at a certain moment under the form of a superior degree, and that afterwards, at another moment, he prophesies under the form of a degree inferior to the first. It may therefore be that he attains this superior degree but once in his life, and that thereafter he be deprived thereof (forever)[[fn:2336]], as it may also be that he retains an inferior degree (of inspiration), until the moment when his prophetic inspiration ceass entirely; for the prophetic inspiration necessarily forsaks all prophets[[fn:2337]] more or less time before their death, as has been declared concerning Jeremiah, saying: When the word of the Lord had ceased (to go forth) from the mouth of Jeremiah (Ezra, i. 1)[[fn:2338]], and as has been declared concerning David, saying: Now these be the last words of David (II Sam., xxiii. 1). And thenceforth one may conclude for all (others).
root.text.Part 2..44.2: After having made the preceding preliminary observation[[fn:2339]], I begin to enumerate the degrees in question[[fn:2340]], and I say:
root.text.Part 2..44.3.sub_0: I. FIRST DEGREE: The first step toward prophecy is when a divine assistance accompanies the individual, which setts him in motion and encourags him unto a virtuous action, great and of high importance[[fn:2341]], as, for example, to deliver a company of virtuous men from a company of wicked men, or to save a great and virtuous man, or to diffuse good upon a multitude of folk, so that (this individual) finds within himself something which impells and invits him to act. This is what is called the spirit of the Lord, and it is said of the individual who finds himself in this state: that the spirit of the Lord entered into him[[fn:2342]], or that the spirit of the Lord clothed him[[fn:2343]], or that the spirit of the Lord rests upon him[[fn:2344]], or the Lord is with him[[fn:2345]], and other like expressions[[fn:2346]]. Such was the degree of all the judges of Israel, of whom it has been said in general: And when the Lord raised up judges for them, then the Lord was with the judge, and delivered them etc. (Judges, ii. 18); and such also was the degree of all the virtuous kings[[fn:2347]] of Israel. This has been declared particularly regarding several judges and kings, e.g.: Then the spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah (ibid., xi. 29); of Samson it is said: The spirit of the Lord came mightily upon him (ibid., xiv. 19); it has been further said: And the spirit of God came upon Saul when he heard those tidings (I Sam., xi. 6); likewise, finally, it was said of Amasa, moved by the holy spirit to go to the aid of David: Then the spirit came upon Amasai, who was chief of the captains; thine are we (said he), O David! and on thy side, thou son of Jesse: peace! etc. (I Chron., xii. 18)[[fn:2348]].—Know thou that this kind of power remained inseparable from Moses, from the moment he had reached man's estate[[fn:2349]]; wherefore he felt himself moved to slay the Egyptian and to rebuff him of the two quarrellers who was in the wrong[[fn:2350]]. This power was so violent within him that[[fn:2351]], even after having been afraid and having taken to flight, when, having arrived[[fn:2352]] at Midian a stranger and fearful, he saw some injustice, he could not prevail upon himself not to make it cease and had not the strength to endure it, as it is said: But Moses stood up and helped them (Exodus, ii. 17).
root.text.Part 2..44.3.sub_1: In like manner, a similar power had attached itself to David since he had been anointed with the oil of unction, as the Scripture says: And the spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward (I Sam., xvi. 13); wherefore he courageously encountered the lion, the bear, and the Philistine. But such a spirit of the Lord never inspired, in any of those, any (prophetic) word whatsoever; this power, on the contrary, leads only to impelling the strengthened man to a certain action, not unto just any action, but to succouring an oppressed one, whether it be a great individual or a society, or at least (it impells) unto that which leads thereto. For, just as all those who dream a true dream are not for that reason prophets, even so could one not say of each of those whom a (divine) help assists for any thing whatsoever, as, for example, to acquire a fortune, or to attain a personal end, that the spirit of the Lord accompanies him, or that the Lord is with him, and that it is by the holy spirit that he has done what he has done. We say this, on the contrary, only of him who has accomplished a noble work, of high importance[[fn:2353]], or at least (who has done) that which may lead thereto, as, for example, the prosperous action[[fn:2354]] of Joseph in the house of the Egyptian, which was the first cause of the important events which followed thereafter, as is evident.
root.text.Part 2..44.4.sub_0: II. The SECOND DEGREE is when it seems to an individual that something has entered into him and that there has come upon him a new power which makes him speak, so that he utters maxims of wisdom, or a song of praise (unto God)[[fn:2355]], or salutary warnings, or discourses relative to political government or metaphysics, and all this in a state of waking, whilst the senses function according to their wont. It is of such a man that it is said that he speaks by the holy spirit. It was by this kind of holy spirit that David composed the Psalms and that Solomon composed the Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Likewise, it was by this kind of holy spirit that Daniel, Job, the Chronicles, and the other Hagiographa were composed; wherefore they are called KETHOUBÎM (Hagiographa), meaning that they are written by means of the holy spirit. It has been expressly said: “The book of Esther was dictated by the holy spirit[[fn:2356]].” It is in speaking of this kind of holy spirit that David said: The spirit of the Lord spake by me, and his word was in my tongue (II Sam., xxiii. 2), which is to say that it was He who made him utter these words. Of this class were also the seventy elders, of whom it is said: And it came to pass, that, when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied, and did not cease (Numbers, xi. 25); and likewise Eldad and Medad (Ibid., v. 26). In like manner, every high priest, when questioned by means of the Urim and Thummim[[fn:2357]], belongs to this class, that is to say—as the doctors express it—: “the divine majesty rests upon him, and he speaks by the holy spirit[[fn:2358]].” To this class belongs also Jahaziel, son of Zechariah, of whom it is said in the Chronicles: The spirit of the Lord came upon him, in the midst of the congregation. And he said, Hearken ye, all (ye men) of Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat! Thus says the Lord unto you, etc. (II Chron., xx. 14 and 15).
root.text.Part 2..44.4.sub_1: In like manner, Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada the priest, appertains unto this class; for it is said of him: And the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada the priest, and he stood above the people, and said unto them: Thus says God, etc. (Ibid., 24:20). Likewise, Azariah, the son of Oded, of whom it is said: “The Spirit of God was upon Azariah, the son of Oded; and he went out to meet Asa, etc.” (Ibid., 15:1-2). The same holds true of all those concerning whom the like expression is used. It must be understood that Balaam also, whilst he was yet pious, belonged to this category. This is what was intended by the words: And the Lord put a word in Balaam’s mouth (Numbers 23:5), for it is as though it were said that he spake by the Spirit of the Lord; and it is in this sense that he says of himself: he who hears the words of God (Ibid., 24:4).
root.text.Part 2..44.5.sub_0: — We must further observe that David, Solomon, and Daniel are likewise of this class, and that they belong not to the class of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Nathan the prophet, Ahijah the Shilonite[[fn:2359]], and their peers; for these—I mean David, Solomon, and Daniel—did not speak or utter all that they said save by the Holy Spirit[[fn:2360]]. As touching those words of David: the God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spake to me (II Sam. 23:3), they must be understood in the sense that He had made promises unto him through a prophet, whether it were Nathan or another; it is even as this passage: And the Lord said unto her (Genesis 25:23[[fn:2361]]), and as this other: And the Lord said unto Solomon: Forasmuch as this is done of thee, and thou hast not kept my covenant (I Kings 11:11), which undoubtedly is a threat addressed unto him through the mediation of Ahijah the Shilonite, or of another prophet. Likewise, when it is said regarding Solomon: In Gibeon the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, etc. (Ibid., 3:5), this concerns not a true prophecy. It is not at all like this passage: The word of the Lord came unto Abram in a vision (Genesis 15:1), nor like this other: And God spake unto Israel in the visions of the night (Ibid., 46:2), nor like the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah; for, although it was by a dream that each of these[[fn:2362]] received his revelation, the revelation itself made known unto him that it was a prophecy and that a revelation (from God) had come unto him. But, in this narrative concerning Solomon, it is (expressly) said at the end: And Solomon awoke, and, behold, it was a dream (I Kings 3:15); and likewise, it is said in the second narrative: The Lord appeared to Solomon the second time, as he had appeared unto him at Gibeon (Ibid., 9:2), where it had been expressly stated that it was a dream. This is a degree inferior to that of which it is said: I will speak unto him in a dream (Numbers 12:6); for those who possess a (true) prophetic inspiration in a dream do by no means call a dream that in which the prophecy came unto them, but declare positively that it was a (divine) revelation.
root.text.Part 2..44.5.sub_1: It is in this sense that our father Jacob expressed himself; for, having awakened from his prophetic dream, he said not that it was a dream, but declared positively: Surely the Lord is in this place, etc. (Genesis 28:16), and (further on) he says: God Almighty appeared unto me at Luz, in the land of Canaan (Ibid., 48:3), thus declaring that it was a revelation, whereas concerning Solomon, it is said: And Solomon awoke; and, behold, it was a dream. And likewise, thou seest Daniel declaring simply[[fn:2363]] that he had dreams; and, albeit he had there seen an angel whose words he had heard, he called them dreams, even after having derived from them the (sublime) instructions he had received: Then, says he, was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a vision of the night (Dan. 2:19). Further on he says: Then he wrote the dream, etc. I saw in my vision by night, etc. (Ibid., 7:1-2); And the visions of my head troubled me (Ibid., v. 15); and he says again: I was astonished at the vision, which none understood (Ibid., 8:27). This is undoubtedly a degree inferior to the degrees of those concerning whom it is said: I will speak unto him in a dream (Numbers 12:6). Wherefore it has been agreed[[fn:2364]], in our communion, to range the book of Daniel among the Hagiographa, and not among the Prophets. I was therefore bound to observe unto thee that, although in this kind of prophetic vision which Daniel and Solomon had, they saw[[fn:2365]] an angel in a dream, they nevertheless did not themselves take it for a true prophecy, but for a dream which was to make known the truth of certain things, which falls within the category of those who speak by the Holy Spirit, and forms the second degree. Thus it is that, in the classification of the Hagiographa, no distinction is made between Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Daniel, the Psalms, and the books of Ruth and Esther, all of which were written by means of the Holy Spirit and (the authors of which) are all called prophets by a general term.
root.text.Part 2..44.6: III. The [[t:0]]THIRD DEGREE[[t:1]] [which is the first degree of those who say: [[t:2]]The word of the Eternal was addressed unto me,[[t:3]] or who employ other expressions having a similar sense], it is when the prophet beholds a [[t:4]]parable[[t:5]] in a [[t:6]]dream[[t:7]], with all the conditions previously posited for true prophecy, and that in the very same [[t:8]]prophetic dream[[t:9]] it is explained to him the sense which was intended to be indicated by the parable, as occurs in the majority of the parables of Zachariah[[fn:2366]].
root.text.Part 2..44.7: IV. The [[t:0]]FOURTH DEGREE[[t:1]], that is to say, when he hears, in a [[t:2]]prophetic dream[[t:3]], clear and distinct words, without seeing the one who pronounces them; which occurred to Samuel when he received his first revelation, as we have explained in the treatise concerning him[[fn:2367]].
root.text.Part 2..44.8: V. The FIFTH DEGREE is when a personage speaks unto him in a dream, as it is said in one of the prophecies of Ezekiel: And the man said unto me, Son of man, etc. (Ezek. xl. 4)[[fn:2368]].
root.text.Part 2..44.9: VI. The SIXTH DEGREE is when an angel speaks unto him in a dream; and such is the condition of the greater part of the prophets, as it is said: And the angel of God spake unto me in a dream, etc. (Gen. xxxi. 11)[[fn:2369]].
root.text.Part 2..44.10: VII. The SEVENTH DEGREE is when it seems unto him, in a prophetic dream, that God speaks unto him[[fn:2370]], as when Isaiah says: I saw the Lord, etc., and He said, Whom shall I send? etc. (Isa. vi. 1 and 8)[[fn:2371]], and as when Micaiah, the son of Imlah, said: I saw the Lord, etc. (1 Kings xxii. 19; 2 Chron. xviii. 18).
root.text.Part 2..44.11: VIII. The [[t:0]]EIGHTH DEGREE[[t:1]], it is when he has a revelation in a [[t:2]]prophetic vision[[t:3]] and when he sees [[t:4]]parables[[t:5]], as, for example, Abraham in the [[t:6]]vision between the pieces[[t:7]] (of the slaughtered animals)[[fn:2372]]; for these parabolic visions took place during the day[[fn:2373]], as it has been declared[[fn:2374]].
root.text.Part 2..44.12: IX. The [[t:0]]NINTH DEGREE[[t:1]], it is when he hears [[t:2]]words[[t:3]] in a [[t:4]]vision[[t:5]], as has been said concerning Abraham: [[t:6]]And lo, the word of the Eternal came unto him, saying: This one shall not inherit thee[[t:7]] (Genesis, 15, 4).
root.text.Part 2..44.13: X. The TENTH DEGREE is when, in a prophetic vision, he ses a personage who speaks unto him, as, for instance, Abraham at the Oaks of Mamre, and Joshua at Jericho[[fn:2375]].
root.text.Part 2..44.14: XI. The ELEVENTH DEGREE is when, in a vision, he ses an angel who speaks unto him, as, for instance, Abraham at the time of the sacrifice of Isaac. This is, in my opinion, the highest degree reached by the prophets proclaimed in the (Holy) Books[[fn:2376]], provided it be assumed as a fact, as has been established, that the perfection of the rational qualities of the individual is obtained through speculation, and that Moses our Master be excepted from the common rule[[fn:2377]]. As to (the question of) whether it be possible that, in a prophetic vision also, the prophet believs himself to hear the speech of God[[fn:2378]], (I confess that) according to my view, this is somewhat improbable, and the active power of the imaginative faculty[[fn:2379]] extends not so far; for verily, we have not encountered such a state of affairs amongst the ordinary prophets[[fn:2380]]. Therefore it has been expressly said in the Pentateuch: I make MYSELF KNOWN unto him in a vision, I SPEAK unto him in a dream (Numbers xii. 6); thus has speech been placed in the dream only, whilst in the vision has been placed the union[[fn:2381]] and the emanation of the (Active) Intellect, which has been expressed by אתודע, I make myself known, which is a reflexive verb[[fn:2382]] (derived) from ידע, to know[[fn:2383]]. But it has not been clearly stated that, in a vision, one may hear[[fn:2384]] words coming from God.
root.text.Part 2..44.15: Having encountered texts which bear witness to words that the prophet might have heard, and in which (nevertheless) it is clear that the matter concerns a [[t:0]]vision[[t:1]], I submitted, by mere conjecture[[fn:2385]], that perhaps, where it is stated that words can be heard (only) in a dream and that it cannot be so in a [[t:2]]vision[[t:3]], this implies (the hypothesis) that the prophet imagines God Himself addressing him[[fn:2386]]; and all this I stated by adhering to the literal sense[[fn:2387]].
