Nevertheless, it might be argued that every [[t:4]]vision[[t:5]] in which mention is made of [[t:6]]words[[t:7]] heard was indeed, in the first instance, a [[t:8]]vision,[[t:9]] but that it subsequently culminated in a profound slumber and became a dream, as we have expounded concerning these words: [[t:10]]And a deep slumber fell upon Abram[[t:11]] (Genesis, 15, 12)[[fn:2388]], of which they (the doctors) have said: “It is the slumber of prophecy[[fn:2389]].” Thus, whenever words were heard, in whatsoever manner, it was in a [[t:12]]dream[[t:13]], as the text states: [[t:14]]I speak unto him in a dream[[t:15]] (Numbers, 12, 6), whereas in the [[t:16]]prophetic vision[[t:17]], only [[t:18]]parables[[t:19]] were perceived, or communications from the intellect[[fn:2390]] making known scientific matters similar to those obtained by means of speculation, as we have set forth, and this is what was intended to be conveyed (by the words) [[t:20]]I make myself known unto him in a vision[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]ibid.[[t:23]]). According to this latter interpretation, therefore, the degrees of prophecy would number [[t:24]]eight[[t:25]][[fn:2391]], the most elevated and perfect of which would generally be that in which the prophet is inspired [[t:26]]by a vision[[t:27]], even though it were but a [[t:28]]personage[[t:29]] speaking unto him[[fn:2392]], as has been stated.
root.text.Part 2..44.16: Thou wilt perhaps raise an objection against me, saying: “Thou hast counted, amongst the degrees of prophecy, that in which the prophet would hear words addressed unto him (directly) by God, as, for instance, Isaiah and Micaiah. But how can this be, since we hold as a principle that every prophet hears the word (of God) only through the mediation of an angel, except Moses our Master, of whom it has been said: With him will I speak mouth to mouth (Numbers xii. 8)?” Know then that it is indeed so, and that that which serves here as a mediator is the imaginative faculty; for it is only in the prophetic dream that the prophet hears God speaking unto him[[fn:2393]], whilst Moses our Master heard Him from above the mercy-seat, from between the two cherubim (Exodus xxv. 22)[[fn:2394]], without employing the imaginative faculty. We have already set forth in the Mishneh Torah the differences of this prophecy (of Moses), and we have explained the meaning of the words mouth to mouth (Numbers xii. 8), of the words as a man speaks unto his friend (Exodus xxxiii. 11), and of other expressions[[fn:2395]]. It is thence, therefore, that thou mayest draw thy understanding, and it is not necessary to repeat what has already been said.
root.text.Part 2..45.0: From a single individual one may conclude regarding all individuals of the same species, and learn that each of its individuals has such a form[[fn:2396]]. In saying this, my purpose is (to establish) that, from the form of one of the relations of the prophets[[fn:2397]], thou mayest conclude regarding all other relations of the same species.
root.text.Part 2..45.1: Following this preliminary observation, it must be known that, even as a man may seem to see, in a dream, that he has performed a journey into such a country, that he has married there, and that after remaining there a certain space of time, there was born unto him a son whom he named so-and-so, and who was in such a state and in such a circumstance[[fn:2398]], even so those prophetic parables which appear (to the prophet), or which, in the prophetic vision, are translated into action[[fn:2399]] [when the parable requirs[[fn:2400]] any act whatsoever], as well as certain things which the prophet executs, the intervals of time mentioned parabolically between the different actions and the translations from one place to another—all this (I say) exists only in the prophetic vision, and these are not real actions (existing) for the outward senses[[fn:2401]]. Some of these (matters) are related, in the prophetic books, in an absolute manner[[fn:2402]]; for, as soon as it is known that the whole was a prophetic vision, it were superfluous to reiterate at every detail of the parable that it had occurred in the prophetic vision.
root.text.Part 2..45.2: Thus, when the prophet has said: And the Lord said unto me, he has no need to declare that it was in a dream[[fn:2403]]; but the vulgar imagine that these actions, these removals, these questions and answers—that all this (I say) took place in the state of sense-perception[[fn:2404]], and not in the prophetic vision.
root.text.Part 2..45.3.sub_0: I shall now cite unto thee an example concerning which no man can be mistaken, and I shall connect therewith some other examples of the same kind; from these few instances, thou mayest conclude concerning those which I shall not have cited. That which is clear and whereon no man can err, is when Ezekiel says: I sat in mine house, and the elders of Judah sat before me, etc. A spirit lifted me up between the earth and the heaven, and brought me to Jerusalem, in the VISIONS OF GOD (Ezek., 8, 1 and 3). Likewise when he says: I arose and went forth into the plain (Ibid., 3, 23), this also was but in the visions of God, even as it is also said regarding Abraham: And he brought him forth abroad (Genesis, 15, 5), which took place in a vision (Ibid., v. 1). Likewise when he says: And set me down in the midst of the valley (Ezekiel, XXXVII, 1), it was again in the visions of God. Ezekiel, in that vision in which he was brought into Jerusalem, expresses himself[[fn:2405]] in these terms: I beheld, and lo, a hole in the wall. Then said he unto me: Son of man, dig now in the wall; and when I had digged in the wall, behold a door (Ibid., 8, 7-8). Even as, therefore, it had appeared unto him in the visions of God that he was commanded to dig through the wall in order to enter therein and see what was being done there, and as he subsequently digged, as he says, in those same visions of God, entered by the opening and saw what he saw—all this in a prophetic vision—likewise, when God says unto him: Take thee a tile, etc., lie upon thy left side, etc. Take thou also wheat, and barley, etc. (Ibid. 4, 1, 4 and 9), and likewise again, when He says unto him: And cause (the razor) to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard, etc. (Ibid., 5, 1), all this (signifies that), in a prophetic vision, it appeared unto him that he performed the actions which he had been commanded to do. Far be it from God to render His prophets a laughing-stock unto fools and an object of mockery[[fn:2406]], and to command them to perform acts of madness[[fn:2407]]!
root.text.Part 2..45.3.sub_1: Let us add to this that he would have been commanded to disobey (the Law); for, as he was a priest, he would have rendered himself guilty of two transgressions for every corner of the beard or of the hair (that he might have cut)[[fn:2408]]. But all this took place only in a prophetic vision. In like manner, when it is said: Like as my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot (Isaiah, 20, 3), this occurred only in the visions of God. None but men of weak understanding believe that in all these passages the prophet relats that it had (really) been commanded him to do such a thing, and that he did it; it is thus that he would relate that it had been commanded him to dig through the wall which was on the mountain of the temple (at Jerusalem), although he was then in Babylon, and he would add that he (really) digged it, as he says: And I digged in the wall (Ezek., 8, 8). Nevertheless, he says expressly that this occurred in the visions of God.
root.text.Part 2..45.4: It is even as we read concerning Abraham: The word of the Lord came unto Abram in a vision, saying (Genesis, 15, 1), and it is said in this same prophetic vision: And he brought him forth abroad and said: Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars (Ibid., v. 5); it is therefore clear that it was in the prophetic vision[[fn:2409]] that it seemed unto him to be led forth from the place where he was, so that he saw the heaven, and that subsequently it was said unto him: Tell the stars. Such is the narrative, as thou seest. I shall say as much of the command which was given unto Jeremiah to hide the girdle in the Euphrates; having hidden it, he went to seek it after a long space of time and found it marred and corrupted[[fn:2410]]. All these are parables of the prophetic vision[[fn:2411]]; for Jeremiah had not departed from the land of Israel for Babylon, and had not seen the Euphrates. Likewise, those words addressed unto Hosea: Take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and (have of her) children (born) of whoredoms (Hos., I, 2), and all this narrative of the birth of the children and of the names so-and-so which were given unto them, all this took place in a prophetic vision. Verily, as soon as it has been declared that these are but parables, there is no longer any reason to suspect that any detail therein had any reality[[fn:2412]], unless there be applied unto us that which has been said[[fn:2413]]: And the vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed (Isaiah, 29, 11). — In like manner, it seems unto me that what is related, concerning Gideon, of the fleece and of the other (miraculous) thing[[fn:2414]], took place only in a vision. Nevertheless, I shall not call this a prophetic vision, in the absolute sense; for Gideon had not attained unto the rank of the prophets, and how then should he have gone so far as to perform miracles[[fn:2415]]? His greatest merit was to be included among the judges of Israel[[fn:2416]] [for they (the doctors) have even placed him among the men of least account in the world[[fn:2417]]], as we have set forth[[fn:2418]]. But all this took place only in a dream, similar unto the dream of Laban and (unto that) of Abimelech, of which we have spoken[[fn:2419]].
root.text.Part 2..45.5: — Even so likewise[[fn:2420]], that which Zechariah says: I fed the flock of slaughter, even, the poor of the flock, and I took unto me two staves (Zech. xi. 7)[[fn:2421]], together with the sequel of the narrative, to wit: the wage demanded with gentleness, the acceptance of the wage, and the silver told out and cast into the treasury (Ibid., vv. 12 and 13); all this, it appeared unto him in a prophetic vision that he was commanded to do, and he performed it in the prophetic vision or in the prophetic dream.
root.text.Part 2..45.6: This is a matter of which one cannot doubt, and which can be unknown only to him who confounds together the possible and the impossible.
root.text.Part 2..45.7: From that which I have cited, thou mayest conclude concerning that which I have not cited; for all is of the same kind and follows the same method; all is a prophetic vision. Whenever, therefore, it is said that, in such a vision, he acted[[fn:2422]], or he heard, or he went out, or he entered, or he spake, or it was spoken unto him, or he arose, or he sat, or he ascended, or he descended, or he journeyed, or he questioned, or he was questioned, all this took place in the prophetic vision. Even though the actions designated should have endured for a long season, and should relate to certain specified times, to particular individuals, and to certain places, so soon as it shall be manifest unto thee that such action is a parable[[fn:2423]], thou shalt know with certainty that it occurred in the prophetic vision.
root.text.Part 2..46.0: It is indubitably clear and manifest that the prophets, for the most part, prophesy by parables[[fn:2424]]; for that which serves as an instrument thereto, I mean the imaginative faculty, produces this effect. It behoves us, likewise, to know something of metaphors and hyperboles[[fn:2425]]; for such are sometimes found in the texts of the prophetic books. If one were to take a given expression literally[[fn:2426]], without knowing it to be a hyperbole and an exaggeration, or if one were to take another expression in the sense which the words indicate according to their primitive acceptation, without knowing it to be a metaphor, there would thence arise divers absurdities. The Sages have said plainly: «The Scripture employs exaggerated language», that is to say hyperbole, and they have cited as proof these words: cities great and walled up to heaven (Deut. i. 28)[[fn:2427]], which is just. To the category of hyperbole belong also these words: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice (Eccl. x. 20). In like manner it is said: … whose height was like the height of the cedars, etc. (Amos ii. 9). This manner of speech is frequently met with in the utterances of all the prophets; I mean expressions employed by way of hyperbole and exaggeration, and not for the purpose of speaking with precision and exactness.
root.text.Part 2..46.1: Of this category is not that which the Pentateuch says concerning Og: הנה ערשו ערשׂ ברזל וגו׳, his bedstead, a bedstead of iron, etc. (Deut. iii. 11); for ערש signifies bedstead, as in אף ערשנו רעננה, our BED is green (Cant. i. 16). Now, the bed of a man has not the exact measure of the man himself; for it is not a garment wherewith he cloths himself. On the contrary, a bed is always larger than the person who lies therein, and it is customary, as is well known, that it exceeds the length of the person by about one third. If, therefore, the length of this bed be nine cubits, the length of him who lies therein shall be, according to the usual proportion of beds, six cubits, or somewhat more. The words באמת איש, after the cubit of a man (Deut. loc. cit.), signify: according to the cubit of an ordinary person amongst us, I mean, amongst the rest of men, and not according to the cubit of Og; for every individual has ordinarily his limbs proportioned[[fn:2428]]. It was therefore intended to say that the stature of Og was twice[[fn:2429]] that of an ordinary person amongst other men, or a little more[[fn:2430]]. Doubtless, this is an anomaly for individuals of the species; yet is it in no wise impossible.
root.text.Part 2..46.2: As touching that which the Pentateuch relats concerning the number[[fn:2431]] of the years of certain persons, I say, for my part, that the individual (in each case) specified alone attained that age (which is ascribed unto him), whilst other men reached only the natural and accustomed terms of life. The anomaly in such an individual either proceeded from diverse causes (subsisting) in his manner of nourishment and in his regimen, or else it must be regarded as the effect of a miracle[[fn:2432]]. There is no means of reasoning thereupon in any other wise.
root.text.Part 2..46.3: Likewise, moreover, great attention must be paid unto those things which have been spoken by metaphor. There be some which are clear and manifest, and which possess no obscurity for any man, as, for example, when it is said: The mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands (Isaiah, lv. 12), which thing is evidently a metaphor. It is the same when it is said: Yea, the fir-trees rejoice at thee, etc. (Ibid., xiv. 8), which Jonathan ben-Uziel has paraphrased thus: 'even the sovereigns have rejoiced because of thee, those who are rich in possessions,' seeing therein an allegory as (in this passage): Butter of kine, and milk of sheep, etc. (Deut. xxxii. 14)[[fn:2433]].
root.text.Part 2..46.4: These metaphors are exceeding numerous in the prophetic books; there be some in which even the vulgar recognize metaphors, but there be others which they take not for such. Indeed, no man could doubt that these words: the Lord shall open unto thee His good treasure, etc. (Deut. xxviii. 12) are a metaphor, since God has no treasure which contains the rain. Likewise, when it is said: He opened the doors of heaven, and rained down manna upon them (Ps. lxxviii. 23-24), no man will believe that there be in heaven a gate and doors; but this (is spoken) after the manner of similitude, which is a species of metaphor. In this wise must we understand these expressions: The heavens were opened (Ezek. i. 1); if not, blot me, I pray Thee, out of Thy book which Thou hast written (Exodus, xxxii. 32); him will I blot out of My book (Ibid., v. 33); let them be blotted out of the book of the living (Ps. lxix. 29). All this (is spoken) after the manner of similitude; not that God has a book, in which He writs and blotts out, as the vulgar believe, perceiving not that here is a metaphor.
root.text.Part 2..46.5: All (that I have said) belongs unto the same category. All that I have not cited, thou shalt compare with what I have cited in this chapter; separate and distinguish things by thy reason, and thou shalt understand what has been spoken by allegory, what has been spoken by metaphor, what has been spoken by hyperbole, and what has been spoken exactly according to that which the primary acceptation (of the terms) indicats. Then all the prophecies shall become clear and manifest unto thee; thou shalt have reasonable beliefs, well-ordered and pleasing unto God, for truth alone is pleasing unto God, and falsehood alone is odious unto Him. Let not thy ideas and thy thoughts become confused, so that thou shouldst admit unsound opinions, far removed from the truth, and take them for religion! Religious precepts are but pure truth, if they be understood as they ought to be; it is said: Thy testimonies are righteous for ever, etc. (Ps. cxix. 144), and it is said again: I the Lord speak righteousness (Isaiah, xlv. 19). By these reflections, thou shalt also escape from the imagination of a world which God created not[[fn:2434]] and from those corrupt ideas, some of which may lead to irreligion and to the admission of defect in God, such as the circumstances of corporeality, of attributes, and of passions, as we have set forth[[fn:2435]], unless thou believest that these prophetic discourses be a lie[[fn:2436]]. All the evil which leads to this is that men neglect[[fn:2437]] those things unto which we have called attention; but these are also subjects (which pertain to) the secrets of the Law, and, although we have spoken thereupon but in a summary manner, it will be easy, from what has preceded, to know the details thereof.
root.text.Part 2..47.0: It is most manifest that every thing produced has necessarily a proximate cause which caused it to be; this cause (in its turn) has a cause, until one reaches the First Cause of all things, that is to say, the free will of God[[fn:2438]]. For this reason, there are sometimes omitted, in the discourses of the prophets[[fn:2439]], all these intermediate causes, and there is attributed directly unto God such individual act as occurrs, by saying that it was God who did it. All this is known; we have already spoken thereof ourselves, as have others among the true philosophers[[fn:2440]], and it is the opinion of all our theologians[[fn:2441]].
root.text.Part 2..47.1: After this preliminary observation, hearken unto that which I shall set forth in this chapter, and bestow thereupon a right singular attention, over and above the attention which thou owest unto every chapter of this treatise. The matter which I desire to manifest unto thee is this:
root.text.Part 2..47.2: Know that all proximate causes, wherefrom springs that which is brought into being, whether these causes be essential and natural, or arbitrary, or accidental and due to chance[[fn:2442]] [by arbitrary, I mean that the cause of that which ariss is the free-will of a man], and even should the cause be naught but the will of any animal whatsoever[[fn:2443]], — all these causes (I say) are, in the books of the prophets, attributed unto God; and, in their modes of expression, it is simply said of such an event, that God has done it, or has commanded it, or has spoken it. For all these things, they employ the verbs to say, to speak, to command, to call, to send, and this is the subject unto which I have desired to summon thy attention in this chapter. Indeed, as it is God [even as it has been established[[fn:2444]]] who has stirred such a will in such an irrational animal, as it is He who has caused the rational animal to possess free-will, and as it is He, finally, who has determined the course of natural things [for chance is but an excess of the natural, as has been explained, and for the most part it participats in nature, in free-will and in will[[fn:2445]]], one must, by reason of all this, say of that which results from these causes, that God has commanded to do such a thing, or that He has said: “Let such a thing be.”
root.text.Part 2..47.3: I shall cite unto thee examples of all this, whereunto thou mayest compare all that which I shall not have mentioned (expressly). In speaking of natural things which ever follow their course, as (for example) of snow which melts when the air is warm, and of the waters of the sea which are agitated when the wind blows, it is thus expressed: He SENDS his word and melts them (Ps. 147, 18); he SPEAKS and raiss a stormy wind which lifts up the waves (Ps. 107, 25); of the rain which falls, it is said: And I WILL COMMAND the clouds that they rain no rain etc. (Isaiah, 5, 6).
root.text.Part 2..47.4: When speaking of that which has for its cause the free will of man, such as (for example) a war waged by a powerful nation against another nation[[fn:2446]], or an individual setting himself in motion to inflict harm upon another individual, even if he should have done no more than insult him, it is expressed thus: [[t:0]]I have[[t:1]] [[t:2]]COMMANDED[[t:3]] [[t:4]]my sanctified ones[[t:5]], [[t:6]]and I have[[t:7]] [[t:8]]CALLED[[t:9]] [[t:10]]my mighty ones for[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]to execute[[t:13]]) [[t:14]]my wrath[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]Isaiah[[t:17]], 13, 3), — where the tyranny of the impious Nebuchadnezzar and his armies is in question[[fn:2447]]; — and elsewhere: [[t:18]]I will[[t:19]] [[t:20]]SEND HIM[[t:21]] [[t:22]]against a hypocritical nation[[t:23]] ([[t:24]]Ibid[[t:25]]., X, 6). In the matter of Shimei, the son of Gera, it is said: [[t:26]]For the LORD has[[t:27]] [[t:28]]SAID[[t:29]] unto him: [[t:30]]Curse David[[t:31]] (II Sam., 16, 10). Concerning the pious Joseph delivered from the dungeon, it is said: [[t:32]]He[[t:33]] [[t:34]]SENT[[t:35]] [[t:36]]a king who released him[[t:37]] (Ps. 105, 20). Concerning the victory of the Persians and Medes over the Chaldeans, it is said: [[t:38]]And[[t:39]] [[t:40]]I will SEND[[t:41]] [[t:42]]against Babylon barbarians who will scatter her[[t:43]] (Jer., LI, 2). In the history of Elijah, when God commissions a woman to nourish him[[fn:2448]], He says to her: [[t:44]]I have[[t:45]] [[t:46]]COMMANDED[[t:47]] [[t:48]]there a widow woman to nourish thee[[t:49]] (I Kings, 17, 9). The pious Joseph says: [[t:50]]It was not you who[[t:51]] [[t:52]]SENT[[t:53]] [[t:54]]me hither, but God[[t:55]] (Genesis, 45, 8)[[fn:2449]].
root.text.Part 2..47.5: In speaking of that which has for its cause the will of an animal, which is moved by its animal needs (it is said, for example): And the Lord SPAKE unto the fish (Jonah, 2, 11); for (it is meant that) it was God who stirred in it this will, and not that He made of it a prophet or revealed Himself unto it. Likewise, it is said concerning the locusts which came in the days of Joel, son of Pethuel: For he is strong that executs his WORD (Joel, II, 11). In like manner also, it is said concerning the wild beasts which took possession of the land of Edom, when it was laid waste in the days of Sennacherib: And he has cast the lot for them, and his hand has divided it unto them by line (Isaiah, 34, 17). Although none of the expressions to say, to command, to send, have been employed here, the sense is evidently analogous; and thou shalt judge likewise of all phrases which have a similar turn of expression[[fn:2450]].
root.text.Part 2..47.6: Concerning accidental things, of mere chance, it is said, for example, in the history of Rebekah: And let her be (given) for a wife unto thy master's son, as the Lord has SPOKEN (Genesis xxiv. 51)[[fn:2451]]. In the history of David and Jonathan, it is said: Go thy way; for the Lord has SENT THEE AWAY (1 Sam. xx. 22)[[fn:2452]]. In the history of Joseph (it is said): And God SENT me before you (Genesis xlv. 7). Thou seest therefore clearly that, to designate the disposition of causes—in whatever manner they be disposed, whether they be causes by essence[[fn:2453]], or by accident, or by free choice, or by (animal) will—one employs these five expressions, namely: to command, to say, to speak, to send, and to call. Know this well, and reflect thereon[[fn:2454]] in each passage so as to explain it as it behoves; then many absurdities shall vanish, and thou shalt recognize the true sense of such passages as might be deemed remote from the truth[[fn:2455]].
root.text.Part 2..47.7: I have now reached the term of what I had to say[[fn:2456]] concerning prophecy, its parables, and its expressions. This is all that I shall tell thee upon this subject in the present treatise[[fn:2457]]; we shall therefore proceed to other matters with the help of the Almighty.
root.text.Part 2..47.8:
END OF THE SECOND PART
OF THE GUIDE FOR THE PERPLEXED.
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.0: IN THE NAME OF THE LORD, THE GOD OF THE UNIVERSE
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.1: The propositions which are needed to establish the existence of God, and to demonstrate that He is neither a body nor a force in a body, and that He is One [may His name be glorified!], are twenty-five in number, which, being generally demonstrated, contain naught that is doubtful; for Aristotle and the Peripatetics who succeeded him have already undertaken the demonstration of each of them[[fn:1267]]. There is, moreover, one proposition which we grant unto them as a concession[[fn:1268]], because it will be the means of demonstrating the matters in question, as I shall set forth; this proposition is the eternity of the world.
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.2: F<small>IRST PROPOSITION</small>. — The existence of any infinite magnitude whatsoever is inadmissible[[fn:1269]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.3: S<small>ECOND PROPOSITION</small>. — The existence of an infinite number of magnitudes is inadmissible[[fn:1270]], if they are to exist (all) simultaneously[[fn:1271]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.4: T<small>HIRD PROPOSITION</small>. — The existence of an infinite number of causes and effects is inadmissible, even though they be not magnitudes; thus, for example, it is manifestly inadmissible that a certain intelligence should have for its cause a second intelligence, this second a third, this third a fourth, and so on to infinity[[fn:1272]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.5: Q[[t:0]]UARTIÈME PROPOSITION[[t:1]]. — Change is found in four [[t:2]]categories[[t:3]]
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.6: 1° in the category of the [[t:0]]substance[[t:1]], and the change to which the substance is susceptible, namely, birth and corruption;
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.7: 2nd in the category of the [[t:0]]quantity[[t:1]], and here it is the growth and diminution;
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.8: 3rd in the category of the [[t:0]]quality[[t:1]], which is the transformation;
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.9: 4° in the category of the [[t:0]]lieu[[t:1]], that which is the movement of translation[[fn:1273]]; it is to this change in the place that the term [[t:2]]mouvement[[t:3]][[fn:1274]] is particularly applied.
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.10: CINQUÈME PROPOSITION. — Every movement is a change and a passage from [[t:0]]power[[t:1]] to [[t:2]]act[[t:3]][[fn:1275]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.11: SIXTH PROPOSITION[[t:0]]. — Movements[[fn:1276]] are sometimes essential (or inherent in the thing itself), sometimes accidental, sometimes due to violence, sometimes partial, and (in the latter case) a species of (movement) accidental. Essential, as the translation of the body from one place to another; accidental, as we would say (for example) of the blackness in some body, that it has transported itself from one place to another; due to violence, as when the stone moves upwards by something that forces it; partial, as the movement of the nail in the ship: for when the ship moves, we also say that the nail moves. And thus, every time a composite thing moves as a whole, we also say that its part moves[[fn:1277]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.12: SEPTIÈME PROPOSITION[[t:1]]. — All that undergoes change is divisible[[fn:1278]]; it is for this reason that all that is moved is divisible and is necessarily a body[[fn:1279]]. All that is not divisible is not moved[[fn:1280]], and, consequently, cannot in any manner be a body.
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.13: E<small>IGHTH PROPOSITION</small>. — Everything that is moved accidentally shall of necessity come to rest, forasmuch as its motion is not in its essence; wherefore it is impossible that it should perpetually perform this accidental motion[[fn:1281]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.14: N[[t:0]]EITHER[[t:1]]. PROPOSITION[[t:1]]. — Every body that movs another does not move, except inasmuch as it is moved itself at the moment when it movs[[fn:1282]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.15: T<small>ENTH PROPOSITION</small>. — Everything of which it is said that it is in a body belongs to one of these two classes[[fn:1283]]: it is either something that subsists by the body, as the accidents, or something by which the body subsists, as the physical form[[fn:1284]]; in both cases, it is a force (which is) in a body[[fn:1285]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.16: E<small>LEVENTH</small>[[fn:1286]] <small>PROPOSITION.</small> — Certain things which subsist by the body are divided by the division of the body, and are, consequently, accidentally divisible, as, for example, colours and in general the forces diffused throughout the whole body. Likewise, certain things which constitute the being of the body are in no wise divided, as the soul and the intellect[[fn:1287]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.17: T<small>WELFTH PROPOSITION</small>. — Every force which is diffused within a body is finite, forasmuch as the body (itself) is finite[[fn:1288]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.18: T[[t:0]]HE TENTH PROPOSITION[[t:1]]. — Nothing in the various species of [[t:2]]change[[t:3]][[fn:1289]] can be continuous, if it is not the motion of translation[[fn:1290]], and in this the (sole) circular motion[[fn:1291]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.19: F<small>OURTEENTH PROPOSITION</small>. — The motion of locomotion is anterior to all other motions and is the first of them[[fn:1292]] according to nature; for (even) generation and corruption are preceded by alteration; and alteration (in its turn) is preceded by the approach of that which alters toward that which is to be altered; finally, there is neither growth nor diminution, without there being first generation and corruption[[fn:1293]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.20: Q[[t:0]]UINTIES PROPOSITION[[t:1]]. — Time is an accident which accompanies motion and is inherent to it[[fn:1294]], and neither of the two exists without the other; a motion exists only in time, and one cannot think of time without motion. Consequently, everything for which there is no motion[[fn:1295]] does not fall under time.
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.21: S[[t:0]]EIZIÈME PROPOSITION[[t:1]]. — All that is incorporeal does not admit the idea of [[t:2]]number[[t:3]][[fn:1296]]; except in the case of a force within a body, whereby one may number the individual forces by numbering their matters or subjects[[fn:1297]]. This is why things [[t:4]]separated[[t:5]], which are neither a body nor a force within a body, do not admit the idea of number, except in the sense that they are causes and effects (one of the other)[[fn:1298]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.22: SEVENTEENTH PROPOSITION. — Whatsoever is moved has necessarily a mover[[fn:1299]]. Either it has a mover without itself, as the stone which the hand does move; or else it has its mover within itself, as the body of the animal[[fn:1300]]. This latter is composed of a mover and a thing moved; wherefore, when the animal dies, and is deprived of the mover, which is the soul, the thing moved, which is the body[[fn:1301]], albeit remaining such as it was, straightway ceass to have that motion[[fn:1302]]. But, since the mover which exists in the thing moved is hidden and manifests not itself unto the senses, it has been imagined that the animal movs without a mover. Everything moved, which has its mover within itself, is said to move by itself[[fn:1303]]; which signifies that the force which essentially movs that which is moved therefrom is found within its whole[[fn:1304]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.23: E<small>IGHTEENTH PROPOSITION</small>. — Whenever aught passes from potentiality to actuality, that which causs it to pass is other than itself, and necessarily is without it[[fn:1305]]: for, if that which causs it to pass (unto actuality) were within it, and there were no hindrance therein, it would not remain for an instant in potentiality, but would ever be in actuality[[fn:1306]]. If, however, that which causs a thing to pass (unto actuality) were within it, but there had existed a hindrance which was removed, there is no doubt that that which caused the hindrance to cease is that which caused this potentiality to pass into actuality[[fn:1307]]. Endeavour to understand this well[[fn:1308]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.24: NINETEENTH PROPOSITION. — Everything of which the existence has a cause is, in respect of its own essence, of a possible existence[[fn:1309]]: for, if its causes be present, it shall exist[[fn:1310]]; but if they have never been present, or if they have vanished, or finally, if the relation[[fn:1311]] which rendered necessary the existence of the thing be changed, it shall not exist.
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.25: T<small>WENTIES PROPOSITION</small>. — Everything which is of a necessary existence, in respect of its own essence, derivs not its existence, in any wise, from any cause whatsoever[[fn:1312]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.26: T<small>WENTY-FIRST PROPOSITION</small>. — Everything which is a compound of two different ideas has necessarily, in this very composition, the (immediate) cause of its existence such as it is, and, consequently, is not of a necessary existence in itself: for it exists by the existence of its two parts and of their composition[[fn:1313]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.27: T<small>WENTY-SECOND PROPOSITION</small>. — Every body is necessarily composed of two distinct notions, and is necessarily affected by accidents. The two notions which constitute its being are its matter and its form[[fn:1314]]; the accidents which affect it are quantity, figure, and position[[fn:1315]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.28: VIII-THIRD PROPOSITION[[t:1]]. — All that is in potency, in such a manner as to have within its very essence a certain [[t:2]]possibilité[[t:3]], may, at a certain moment, not exist in act[[fn:1316]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.29: V[[t:0]]INGT-QUATRIÈME PROPOSITION[[t:1]]. — All that is a thing of any sort[[fn:1317]] [[t:2]]en puissance[[t:3]] necessarily has a matter: for the [[t:4]]possibilité[[t:5]] is always in the matter[[fn:1318]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.30: T<small>WENTY-FIFTH PROPOSITION</small>. — The principles of the composite and individual substance are matter and form[[fn:1319]], and there must necessarily be an agent, that is to say, a mover, which has moved the substratum in order to dispose it to receive the form[[fn:1320]]; and this is the proximate mover, which disposs any individual matter whatsoever[[fn:1321]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.31: This is necessarily the point of departure for the inquiry concerning motion, the mover, and that which is moved. All necessary explanations have been given upon this subject[[fn:1322]] and Aristotle says expressly: «Matter does not move itself[[fn:1323]].» Herein lies the important proposition which leads to the inquiry concerning the existence of the First Mover.
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.32: Of these five-and-twenty propositions which I have placed at the head, some are manifest upon the slightest examination, being demonstrative propositions and primary notions[[fn:1324]], or nearly so, (intelligible) by the simple exposition which we have made of them[[fn:1325]]; others require numerous demonstrations and premisses, yet have all been already demonstrated in a manner that leavs no doubt, (and this) partly in the book of the Acroasis[[fn:1326]] and in its commentaries, and partly in the book of the Metaphysics and in its commentary[[fn:1327]]. I have already made it known unto thee that my purpose in this treatise is not to transcribe the books of the philosophers, nor to set forth the most remote propositions[[fn:1328]], but to record those propositions which are within our reach and necessary for our subject.
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.33: To the preceding propositions I shall add one which involvs the eternity (of the world), and which Aristotle maintains to be true and the most admissible of all; we grant it unto him by way of hypothesis[[fn:1329]], until such time as we shall be able to set forth our own ideas in this regard[[fn:1330]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.34: This proposition, which is <small>THE TWENTY-SIXTH,</small> says that time and motion are eternal, perpetual, and ever existent in act[[fn:1331]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.35: From this proposition, therefore, it necessarily follows, according to him, that there is a body having an eternal motion, ever in act, and this is the fifth body[[fn:1332]]. Wherefore he says that the heaven neither comes into being nor perishes: for motion, according to him, neither comes into being nor perishes. Indeed, says he, every motion is necessarily preceded by another motion, either of the same species or of another species[[fn:1333]]; and when it is imagined that the local motion of an animal is preceded by no other motion whatsoever, it is not true; for the cause which makes it (the animal) to move after having been at rest, goes back to certain things which bring about this local motion: it is either a change of temperament producing (in the animal) the desire to seek what is convenient for it, or to flee what is contrary to it, or else an imagination, or finally an opinion that occurrs to it, so that one of these three things setts it in motion, each of them being in its turn brought about by other motions[[fn:1334]]. He says likewise that in everything which occurrs, the possibility of occurring preceds in time that which occurrs, and he draws thence various conclusions to confirm his proposition[[fn:1335]]. — According to this proposition, the mobile which is finite[[fn:1336]] must move over a finite extent an infinite number of times, returning ever upon the same extent, which is possible only in circular motion, as is demonstrated by the thirteenth of these propositions. It follows that the infinite may exist by way of succession and provided there be no simultaneity[[fn:1337]].
root.text.Part 2.Introduction.36: This proposition Aristotle endeavours ever to confirm. As for me, it seems to me that he by no means claims to attribute a demonstrative force to the proofs wherewith he supports it[[fn:1338]]; but it is, according to him, that which is most admissible. Nevertheless, his followers and the commentators of his writings maintain that it is necessary and not merely possible, and that it has been demonstrated[[fn:1339]]. Each of the Motécallemîn (on the contrary) endeavours to establish that it is impossible: for, say they, one cannot conceive that there could occur, even successively, infinite facts (in number); and they consider this, in sum, as a primary notion[[fn:1340]]. That which seems to me is that the said proposition is possible, (and that it is) neither necessary, as the commentators on the words of Aristotle say, nor impossible, as the Motécallemîn maintain. It is not my purpose, at this moment, to set forth the proofs of Aristotle, nor to produce my doubts against him, nor to set forth my opinion upon the creation of the world; but my purpose, in this place, has been to enumerate the propositions of which we have need for our three questions[[fn:1341]]. Having placed these propositions at the head and having granted them, I begin to set forth that which results therefrom.
root.text.Part 3..0.0: It is well known that there exist human individuals whose faces possess forms similar unto those appertaining to one of the other animals, so that thou beholdest such an individual whose face resembls in some wise the face of a lion, and another who has, as it were, the face of an ox, and so forth[[fn:2473]]; it is according to these figures approaching those of the faces of animals that men receive surnames[[fn:2474]]. Thus the words face of an ox, face of a lion, face of an eagle (Ezekiel, i. 10), designate nought else than a human face, inclining toward the figures of those species. Two proofs support this: the first is that after having said of the ’hayyôth (figures of animals) in general: And this was their appearance; they had the likeness of a man (ibid., v. 5), he says of each of the ’hayyôth that it had a human face, an eagle's face, a lion's face, and an ox's face. The second proof is the explanation he gives in the second mercabâ, aiming to explain certain things which had remained obscure[[fn:2475]] in the first; for in the second mercabâ, he says: every one had[[fn:2476]] four faces, 1° the face of a cherub, 2° the face of a man, 3° the face of a lion, 4° the face of an eagle (Ezekiel, x. 14). He has thus clearly stated that what he had first called the face of an ox is the face of a cherub; but the word כרוב (cherub) signifies a man of tender age[[fn:2477]]. Thence may one likewise conclude concerning the two other faces[[fn:2478]]. If he has here omitted[[fn:2479]] the face of an ox, it is also to call attention to a certain etymology, a matter whereunto we have already alluded[[fn:2480]]. It would not be permissible to say that perhaps the perception of other figures is here intended; for, at the end of this second description, he says: This was the ’HAYYA (the living creature) that I saw under the God of Israel by the river of Chebar (Ibid., x. 20). — Thus is elucidated that which we deemed it necessary to explain in the first place[[fn:2481]].
root.text.Part 3..1.0: He (the prophet) relats having seen four ’HAYYÔTH (figures of animals) each of which had four faces, four wings, and two hands; the whole configuration of each ’hayyâ was the figure of a man, as he says: they had the likeness of a man (Ezekiel, i. 5)[[fn:2482]]. He likewise says that the hands were hands of a man (v. 8), for it is known that the hands of man are so formed as to be able to perform works of art, a matter of which one cannot doubt[[fn:2483]]. Further, he says that their feet were straight, which signifies that they had no joints; such is the literal sense of the words straight feet (v. 7)[[fn:2484]]. The doctors likewise say: “Their feet were straight feet; this signifies that the superior beings do not sit down[[fn:2485]].” Thou must also well understand this. — He says further that the soles of the feet, the organs of walking, were not like (those) of a human foot; the hands alone resembled the hands of man, but the feet were rounded like the sole of a calf's foot (v. 7)[[fn:2486]]. Then he says that between each pair[[fn:2487]] of these four ’hayyôth there was neither interstice nor space, and that, on the contrary, they were joined one to another, as it is said: joined one to another (v. 9)[[fn:2488]]. But, he adds, although they were joined one to another[[fn:2489]], their faces and their wings were separated above, as it is said: their faces and their wings were stretched upward (v. 11). Mark well the expression upward; for the bodies alone were joined one to another, whilst their faces and their wings were separated, yet only from above[[fn:2490]]. Wherefore he says: ופניהם וכנפיהם פרדות מלמעלה[[fn:2491]]. He says again that they were sparkling like the colour of burnished brass (v. 7), and finally that they were also luminous, as it is said: their appearance was like burning coals of fire (v. 13)[[fn:2492]]. This, in sum, is what he says of the configuration of the ’hayyôth, to wit, of their figure, their substance[[fn:2493]], their form, their wings, their hands, and their feet.
root.text.Part 3..1.1.sub_0: Beginning thenceforth to describe after what manner are the movements of these ’hayyôth, he expresses himself in this regard as follows: In the movements of the ’hayyôth, says he, there was neither turning, nor deviation, nor curvature; it was, on the contrary, a uniform movement, as he says: They turned not when they went (v. 12)[[fn:2494]]. — He says then that each of the ’hayyôth followed the direction of its face, which he expresses by these words: every one went straight forward (v. 9). Thus, he clearly says that each ’hayyâ walked only (on the side) whither its face was directed[[fn:2495]]; but would that I knew which face is intended, since each ’hayyâ had several faces[[fn:2496]]! Howsoever it may be, the four did not walk in the same direction, for otherwise he would not have attributed to each a particular movement by saying: every one went straight forward[[fn:2497]]. — He says further that the manner of moving of these ’hayyôth was a (rapid) running, and that it was likewise by running that they returned upon their steps[[fn:2498]]. This is what he expresses by the words: And the ’hayyôth ran and returned, רצוא ושוב (v. 14); for רצוא is the infinitive of the verb רָץ, he ran, and שוב, is the infinitive of the verb שָׁב, he returned. He employs not the verbs הלוך ובוא, to go and to come, but he says that their movement was a running and a returning upon their steps, which he explains by a simile, saying: as the appearance of a flash of lightning, BAZAK (ibid.), for bazak has the same meaning as barak (lightning). He says therefore: like unto lightning, whose movement seems the swiftest that exists, and which extends with rapidity, darting from a certain place, and thereafter instantly withdraws and returns with the same speed to its point of departure.
root.text.Part 3..1.1.sub_1: Jonathan ben Uziel explains the words ran and returned in these terms: “They went round the world and returned (upon their steps), like a single creature[[fn:2499]], swift as the appearance of lightning.” He (the prophet) then adds that, if the ’hayyâ performs this movement of running (forward) and backward toward a certain side, it is a movement[[fn:2500]] which proceeds not from itself, but from another thing, I mean from the divine intention. He says therefore that the side toward which, according to the divine intention, the ’hayyâ was to move, was that[[fn:2501]] toward which it performed this rapid movement designated by the words ran and returned. This is what he says in speaking of the ’hayyôth: Whither the spirit (divine), HA-RUAH, was to go, they went; they turned not when they went (v. 12). The word RUAH (רוח) signifies not here the wind, but has the sense of intention, as we have set forth concerning the word RUAH[[fn:2502]]. Thus, he means that the ’hayyâ followed in its course the direction given to it by the divine intention[[fn:2503]]. It is in the same sense that Jonathan ben Uziel has explained this passage: “Whither the will (רעוא) was that they should go, they went; they turned not when they went.” But as the words אל אשר יהיה שמה הרוח וגו׳, whither the intention was etc. might be understood in the sense that, in the future, sometimes God will will that the ’hayyâ take such a direction, and sometimes He will will that it walk in such another direction, opposite to the first[[fn:2504]], he (Ezekiel) returns to explain what is therein obscure, and he informs us that it is not so, and that (the aorist) יהיה, it is, it shall be, has here the sense of היה, it was, it had been, which frequently occurrs in Hebrew. The direction, says he, in which God willed that the ’hayyâ should walk was determined; the ’hayyâ walked in the direction in which God had willed that it should walk, and the (divine) will was stable with regard to that direction.
root.text.Part 3..1.1.sub_2: In order to explain this idea and to complete his discourse, he says in another verse: [[t:104]]Where it was the intention that they should go, there they went[[t:105]], [[t:106]]AND THE INTENTION WAS[[t:107]] ([[t:108]]ALWAYS[[t:109]]) [[t:110]]THAT THEY SHOULD GO THERE[[t:111]] ([[t:112]]v[[t:113]]. 20). Thou must thoroughly penetrate this remarkable explanation. — Thus he describes the manner of motion of the four [[t:114]]’hayyôth[[t:115]], after having described their figures.
root.text.Part 3..1.2.sub_0: One then proceeds to another description, and it is stated that, beneath the [[t:0]]’hayyôth[[t:1]], one perceived another body which was attached thereto. This body conjoined with the earth and likewise constituted four bodies, also possessing four faces[[fn:2505]]. No specific figure is attributed to it, neither that of man, nor that of any other animal[[fn:2506]]; but it is merely stated that these are bodies of great magnitude, formidable and terrifying, no figure being assigned to them, and their bodies being declared full of eyes[[fn:2507]]. These are designated by him as [[t:2]]OPHANNÎM[[t:3]], or [[t:4]]wheels: 'I beheld the ’hayyôth[[t:5]],' he states, '[[t:6]]and behold there was an[[t:7]] [[t:8]]OPHAN[[t:9]] (a wheel), [[t:10]]upon the earth, beside the[[t:11]] [[t:12]]’HAYYÔTH[[t:13]], [[t:14]]with its four faces[[t:15]]' ([[t:16]]v[[t:17]]. 15). He thus distinctly declares that it constituted a single body, one extremity of which rested nigh the [[t:18]]’hayyôth[[t:19]], whilst the other was situated upon the earth, and that this [[t:20]]ophan[[t:21]] possessed four faces. He proceeds: '[[t:22]]The appearance of the[[t:23]] [[t:24]]OPHANNÎM[[t:25]] [[t:26]]and their work was like unto the colour of a[[t:27]] [[t:28]]TARSCHISCH[[t:29]][[fn:2508]], [[t:30]]and all four had one likeness[[t:31]]' ([[t:32]]v[[t:33]]. 16). Thus, having initially referred to [[t:34]]an ophan[[t:35]], he subsequently speaks of [[t:36]]four[[t:37]], thereby distinctly indicating that the four faces possessed by the [[t:38]]ophan[[t:39]] are, in fact, the four [[t:40]]ophannîm[[t:41]][[fn:2509]]; and he further states that these four [[t:42]]ophannîm[[t:43]] presented one and the same form, a point conveyed by the words: '[[t:44]]and all four had one likeness[[t:45]]'[[fn:2510]]. He thereupon declares concerning these [[t:46]]ophannîm[[t:47]] that they were conjoined one with another[[fn:2511]], a concept expressed by the words: '[[t:48]]their appearance and their work was as it were a[[t:49]] [[t:50]]OPHAN[[t:51]] [[t:52]]in the midst of a[[t:53]] [[t:54]]OPHAN[[t:55]]' ([[t:56]]v[[t:57]]. 16). This is an expression which is not in any wise employed with respect to the [[t:58]]’hayyôth;[[t:59]] for, when speaking of the [[t:60]]’hayyôth[[t:61]], the term [[t:62]]תוך[[t:63]] (within) is not utilised, but rather it is stated that these were contiguous[[fn:2512]] one to another, employing the phrase [[t:64]]joined one to another[[t:65]] ([[t:66]]v[[t:67]].
root.text.Part 3..1.2.sub_1: 9); whilst he says of the ophannîm that they were interlaced one with another, as if an OPHAN were in the midst of another OPHAN. As touching that which he says, that the whole body of the ophannîm was full of eyes, it may be that he means (verily) that they were filled with eyes[[fn:2513]]. But it may also be (that this signifies) that they have manifold colours, (as in this passage) and the colour thereof, ועינו, was as the colour of Bdellium (Numbers xi. 7); or perchance he intended (by eyes) to signify likeness[[fn:2514]], according to the expression which we find in the language of the ancient doctors[[fn:2515]] כעין שגזל ,כעין שגנב, meaning like unto that which has been stolen, like unto that which has been taken by force; or lastly, it signifies various circumstances and qualities[[fn:2516]], as in this passage: It may be that the Lord will look בעיני, that is to say: on mine affliction[[fn:2517]]. Such then is the description which he gives of the form of the ophannîm.
root.text.Part 3..1.3.sub_0: Regarding the movement of the [[t:0]]ophannîm[[t:1]], he states that there likewise was neither curvature, nor turning, nor deviation, but that these were straight movements which did not vary[[fn:2518]]. He states as follows: [[t:2]]When walking, they directed themselves toward their four sides[[t:3]][[fn:2519]], [[t:4]]without swerving in their progress[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]v[[t:7]]. 17). He then states that these four [[t:8]]ophannîm[[t:9]] did not move of themselves, as did the [[t:10]]’hayyôth[[t:11]], but that, on the contrary[[fn:2520]], they possessed within them no other movement than that which was imparted to them by an impulse from without[[fn:2521]]. He insists upon the repetition of this idea, bringing it forth on several occasions. He declares that that which set the [[t:12]]ophannîm[[t:13]] in motion was none other than the [[t:14]]’hayyôth[[t:15]][[fn:2522]], so that, to employ an illustration, the relation of the [[t:16]]ophan[[t:17]] to the [[t:18]]’hayyâ[[t:19]] was as when one attaches a lifeless body to the fore or hind feet of an animal; whenever that animal is in movement, the wood or stone which one has attached to its limb will likewise be in movement. He states therefore: [[t:20]]When the[[t:21]] [[t:22]]’HAYYÔTH[[t:23]] [[t:24]]walked, the ophannîm walked beside them, and when the[[t:25]] [[t:26]]’HAYYÔTH[[t:27]] [[t:28]]rose from off the earth, the[[t:29]] [[t:30]]OPHANNÎM[[t:31]] [[t:32]]likewise rose[[t:33]] ([[t:34]]v[[t:35]]. 19); and he states further: [[t:36]]And the[[t:37]] [[t:38]]OPHANNÎM[[t:39]] [[t:40]]rose over against them[[t:41]] ([[t:42]]v[[t:43]]. 20), the cause of which he explains by stating: [[t:44]]for the spirit[[t:45]] ([[t:46]]ROUA’H[[t:47]]) [[t:48]]of the[[t:49]] ’[[t:50]]HAYYA[[t:51]] [[t:52]]was in the[[t:53]] [[t:54]]OPHANNÎM[[t:55]]. He repeats this idea once more to confirm it and to render it more perspicuous, and states: [[t:56]]When they walked, these likewise walked, and when they stood still, these stood still[[t:57]][[fn:2523]], [[t:58]]and when they rose from off the earth, the ophannîm likewise rose over against them, for the spirit of the ’hayyâ was in the[[t:59]] [[t:60]]OPHANNÎM[[t:61]] ([[t:62]]v[[t:63]]. 21).
root.text.Part 3..1.3.sub_1: The order of these motions is therefore as follows: The [[t:64]]’hayyôth[[t:65]] moved in the direction towards which, according to the divine intention, they were destined to move; and by the motion of the [[t:66]]’hayyôth[[t:67]], the [[t:68]]ophannîm[[t:69]] also were set in motion, following them because they were attached thereto, for the [[t:70]]ophannîm[[t:71]] did not move spontaneously towards the [[t:72]]’hayyôth[[t:73]]. This order, he describes by stating: [[t:74]]Whithersoever the intention was for them to go, thither they went, and the intention was[[t:75]] ([[t:76]]always[[t:77]]) [[t:78]]for them to go thither; and the[[t:79]] [[t:80]]OPHANNÎM[[t:81]] [[t:82]]rose up over against them, for the spirit[[t:83]] ([[t:84]]ROUA’H[[t:85]]) [[t:86]]of the ’hayyâ was in the ophannîm[[t:87]] ([[t:88]]v[[t:89]]. 20). I have already acquainted thee with the paraphrase of Jonathan ben Uziel, who states: “Whithersoever the will ([[t:90]]רעוא[[t:91]]) was for them to go [Lat.: etc.].”
root.text.Part 3..1.4: After having completed the description of the [[t:0]]'hayyôth[[t:1]], their figures and movements, and having spoken of the [[t:2]]ophannîm[[t:3]] situated below the [[t:4]]'hayyôth[[t:5]] to which they are attached and follow the movement, he approaches a third perception and returns to another description[[fn:2524]], namely, that which is above the [[t:6]]'hayyôth[[t:7]]. Above the four [[t:8]]'hayyôth[[t:9]], he says, there was [[t:10]]a firmament[[t:11]] ([Lat.: 2nd V. 22]); upon this firmament there was the [[t:14]]ressemblance d'un trône[[t:15]], and upon the throne [[t:16]]something resembling the aspect of a man[[t:17]] ([Lat.: 2nd V. 26)[[fn:2525]].
root.text.Part 3..1.5: Such is the sum of the description which he affords of the vision which he first beheld by the river of Chaboras.
root.text.Part 3..2.0.sub_0: Ezekiel, after having furnished the description of the [[t:0]]Merkabah[[t:1]], as presented at the commencement of the book, had, upon a second occasion, the self-same perception, when, in a prophetic vision, he was transported to Jerusalem; and here he expounds to us matters which had not been explained the first time. He substitutes, for instance, for the word [[t:2]]’hayyôth[[t:3]] (animals) the word [[t:4]]kheroubîm[[t:5]] (cherubim), and thus apprises us that the [[t:6]]’hayyôth[[t:7]] of which he first spoke are likewise angels, namely the [[t:8]]cherubim[[t:9]][[fn:2526]]. He says, therefore: [[t:10]]When the cherubim walked[[t:11]], [[t:12]]the[[t:13]] [[t:14]]OPHANNÎM[[t:15]] [[t:16]]walked beside them, and when the cherubim lifted their wings to mount up from the earth[[t:17]], [[t:18]]the ophannîm also turned not from beside them[[t:19]] (Ezekiel, X, 16); and thus he confirms the nexus of the two movements, as one has already stated[[fn:2527]]. Thereafter he says: [[t:20]]This was the[[t:21]] [[t:22]]’HAYYA[[t:23]] [[t:24]]that I had seen beneath the God of Israel, by the river Chebar[[t:25]], [[t:26]]and I knew that they were cherubim[[t:27]] ([[t:28]]v.[[t:29]] 20), so that, having again described the self-same figures and the self-same movements, he declares that the [[t:30]]’hayyôth[[t:31]] are the cherubim and that the cherubim are the [[t:32]]’hayyôth.[[t:33]] He sets forth, in this second description, yet another idea, namely, that the [[t:34]]ophannîm[[t:35]] are [[t:36]]galgallîm[[t:37]] (spheres)[[fn:2528]]: [[t:38]]The[[t:39]] [[t:40]]OPHANNÎM[[t:41]], he says, [[t:42]]I heard them called[[t:43]] [[t:44]]GALGAL[[t:45]] ([[t:46]]v.[[t:47]] 13). Then he expounds, concerning the [[t:48]]ophannîm[[t:49]], a third idea, by saying of them: [[t:50]]for they went whithersoever the head was turned[[t:51]], [[t:52]]they turned not as they went[[t:53]] ([[t:54]]v.[[t:55]] 11); he states clearly, therefore, that the constrained movement of the [[t:56]]ophannîm[[t:57]] occurred [[t:58]]whithersoever the head was turned[[t:59]], that is to say, as he has explained: [[t:60]]wherever it was the intention[[t:61]] (divine) [[t:62]]that they should go[[t:63]][[fn:2529]].
root.text.Part 3..2.0.sub_1: He subsequently adds a fourth notion concerning the [[t:64]]ophannîm[[t:65]], stating: [[t:66]]the[[t:67]] [[t:68]]OPHANNÎM[[t:69]] [[t:70]]were full of eyes round about[[t:71]], [[t:72]]their four[[t:73]] [[t:74]]OPHANNÎM[[t:75]] ([[t:76]]v.[[t:77]] 12), which he had not stated previously[[fn:2530]]. He further states in this second vision, speaking of the [[t:78]]ophannîm: their flesh[[t:79]], [[t:80]]their body[[t:81]], [[t:82]]their hands and their wings[[t:83]] ([[t:84]]ibid.[[t:85]])[[t:86]];[[t:87]] thus, after having at first spoken neither of [[t:88]]flesh[[t:89]] of the [[t:90]]ophannîm[[t:91]], nor of [[t:92]]hands[[t:93]], nor of [[t:94]]wings[[t:95]], but simply of their bodies, he ultimately declares that they possessed flesh, hands, and wings[[fn:2531]], without, however, attributing to them any specific form[[fn:2532]]. Moreover, he sets forth in this second vision that each [[t:96]]ophan[[t:97]] bears relation to a cherub[[fn:2533]], and he states: [[t:98]]an ophan beside each cherub[[t:99]] ([[t:100]]v.[[t:101]] 9). Finally, he further sets forth here that the four [[t:102]]’hayyôth[[t:103]] constitute but a single entity, being attached one to another[[fn:2534]]: [[t:104]]This was[[t:105]], he states, [[t:106]]the[[t:107]] [[t:108]]’HAYYA[[t:109]] [[t:110]]that I had seen beneath the God of Israel, by the river of Chaboras[[t:111]] ([[t:112]]v.[[t:113]] 20). It is thus that he designates the [[t:114]]ophannîm[[t:115]] by these words: [[t:116]]and behold there was an[[t:117]] [[t:118]]OPHAN[[t:119]] [[t:120]]upon the earth[[t:121]] (I, 15), even though there were, as he states[[fn:2535]], [[t:122]]four[[t:123]] [[t:124]]OPHANNÎM[[t:125]] (I, 16; X, 9); and this was because they were attached one to another, and that [[t:126]]all four had one likeness[[t:127]] (I, 16)[[fn:2536]]. Such are the elucidations he adds, in this second vision, concerning the form of the [[t:128]]’hayyôth[[t:129]] and the [[t:130]]ophannîm.[[t:131]]
root.text.Part 3..3.0.sub_0: I must needs call thy attention to an opinion adopted by Jonathan ben Uziel. Having seen that it is clearly said[[fn:2537]] (Ezekiel, X, 13): The OPHANNIM, I heard them called GALGAL (wheel or sphere), he affirmed that the ophannim are the heavens; he translated therefore every time ophan by גַּלְגַּלָּא, the sphere, and OPHANNIM by גַּלְגַּלַּיָּא, the spheres. That which doubtless seemed unto him to confirm this interpretation is that Ezekiel (I, 16) says concerning the ophannim that they were like unto the colour of tarshish, a colour which, as is known, is attributed unto the heaven. But having found this passage: I beheld the ’HAYYÔTH, and behold, one OPHAN upon the earth, which indicats indubitably that the ophannim are upon the earth, he saw therein a difficulty for this interpretation. Persisting nevertheless in his interpretation, he explains here the word earth as designating the surface of the heaven, which is a floor in respect of that which is above this surface, and he translats (the words) one OPHAN upon the EARTH by מִלְּרַע לְרוּם שְׁמַיָּא, beneath the height of the heaven; it behoves to understand what his interpretation is (of the whole)[[fn:2538]]. It seems unto me that what provoked this interpretation is that Jonathan believed that GALGAL was a name which primarily designats the heaven. But behold, in mine opinion, the truth of the matter[[fn:2539]]: the word GALGAL (גַּלְגַּל) expresses the idea of rolling; for example: And I will roll thee down (וְגִלְגַּלְתִּיךָ) from the rocks (Jeremiah, 51, 25); and he rolled (וַיָּגֶל) the stone (Genesis, 29, 10). Wherefore it has been said: And like a rolling thing (וּכְגַלְגַּל) before the whirlwind (Isaiah, 17, 13), because it is rolled, and for this cause also the skull is called GULGOLS (גֻּלְגֹּלֶת), because it is well-nigh round[[fn:2540]].
root.text.Part 3..3.0.sub_1: Now, as every sphere revolves swiftly, every spherical object has been designated [[t:88]]GALGAL[[t:89]][[fn:2541]]; it is for this reason that the heavens have been denominated [[t:90]]GALGALLÎM[[t:91]], inasmuch as they are [[t:92]]round[[t:93]], that is to say, because they are [[t:94]]spherical[[t:95]]; and (figuratively) the doctors aver (concerning fate): «It is a [[t:96]]galgal[[t:97]] (a sphere), which revolves[[fn:2542]].» For this same reason is the pulley termed [[t:98]]GALGAL[[t:99]][[fn:2543]]. Thus, when Ezekiel states: [[t:100]]The[[t:101]] [[t:102]]OPHANNÎM[[t:103]], [[t:104]]I heard them called[[t:105]] [[t:106]]GALGAL[[t:107]], it is to apprise us of their (spherical) figure, for no other shape or form is ascribed to them; (and it is said) merely that they are [[t:108]]GALGALLÎM[[t:109]] (spheres)[[fn:2544]]. As for his assertion that they were like the [[t:110]]Tarschisch[[t:111]] (I, 16), he likewise explains it in the second description, saying of the [[t:112]]ophannîm: And the appearance of the[[t:113]] [[t:114]]OPHANNÎM[[t:115]] [[t:116]]was as the colour of a stone of[[t:117]] T[[t:118]]ARSCHISCH[[t:119]] (X, 9), which Jonathan ben Uziel translates: [[t:120]]כעין אבן טבא[[t:121]], [[t:122]]resembling a precious stone.[[t:123]] Now, thou knowest that it is by this same expression that Onkelos renders the words: [[t:124]]like the work of the whiteness of sapphire[[t:125]] (Exodus, 24, 10), and he states: [[t:126]]כעובד אבן טבא[[t:127]], [[t:128]]like the work of a precious stone;[[t:129]] there is consequently no distinction between the words [[t:130]]as the colour of a stone of[[t:131]] [[t:132]]TARSCHISCH[[t:133]] and the words [[t:134]]as the work of the whiteness of sapphire[[t:135]][[fn:2545]]. Thou must thoroughly apprehend this.
root.text.Part 3..3.1: Thou shalt not deem it amiss that I cite the interpretation of Jonathan ben Uziel, whilst I myself have given an interpretation quite contrary. For thou shalt find that many among the Doctors, and even among the (modern) commentators, contradict his interpretation in regard to certain expressions and numerous subjects treated by the prophets. And how should it be otherwise in these profound matters? Furthermore, I do not tell thee to prefer my interpretation[[fn:2546]]; endeavour to understand his interpretation by the observations I have made to thee, and to understand mine also. God alone knows which of the two interpretations has attained the truth[[fn:2547]].
root.text.Part 3..4.0.sub_0: That which further merits attention is that the prophet speaks [[t:0]]of the visions of God[[t:1]] (Ezekiel, I, 1); he does not say [[t:2]]a vision[[t:3]], in the singular, but [[t:4]]visions[[t:5]][[fn:2548]], because these were several perceptions of diverse kinds, namely three perceptions: that of the [[t:6]]ophannîm[[t:7]], that of the [[t:8]]’hayyôth[[t:9]], and that of the [[t:10]]man[[t:11]] who was above the [[t:12]]’hayyôth.[[t:13]] For each of these perceptions, he says: [[t:14]]I saw[[t:15]][[fn:2549]]. He says for that of the [[t:16]]’hayyôth: I saw[[t:17]], [[t:18]]and, behold, a tempestuous wind, etc.[[t:19]] ([[t:20]]ibid., v.[[t:21]] 4); for that of the [[t:22]]ophannîm[[t:23]], he says: [[t:24]]I saw the[[t:25]] [[t:26]]’hayyôth, and behold there was an ophan upon the earth[[t:27]] ([[t:28]]v.[[t:29]] 15); finally, for the perception of the [[t:30]]man[[t:31]][[fn:2550]], who was above the [[t:32]]’hayyôth[[t:33]] in rank, he says: [[t:34]]I saw as the colour of the[[t:35]] [[t:36]]HASCHMAL[[t:37]] [[t:38]]etc.[[t:39]][[fn:2551]], [[t:40]]from the appearance of his loins, etc.[[t:41]] ([[t:42]]v.[[t:43]] 27). Except for these three instances, he does not repeat the expression [[t:46]]I saw[[t:47]] in the description of the [[t:44]]Mercabâ.[[t:45]] The Doctors of the [[t:48]]Mischnâ[[t:49]] have already expounded upon this subject, and it is they who have called my attention thereto. The first two perceptions, they say, that is to say, only that of the [[t:50]]’hayyôth[[t:51]] and of the [[t:52]]ophannîm[[t:53]], it is permissible to teach; but the third perception, namely the [[t:54]]’haschmal[[t:55]] and that which appertains thereto, one must teach only the [[t:56]]first principles[[t:57]] thereof. Nevertheless, our holy Doctor[[fn:2552]] opines that it is all three perceptions together that are called [[t:58]]Ma’asé mercabâ[[t:59]], and of which only the first principles should be taught. This is how they express themselves in this regard[[fn:2553]]: "How far (may one teach)[[fn:2554]] the [[t:60]]ma’asé mercabâ?[[t:61]] Rabbi Meir says[[fn:2555]]: Unto the last [[t:62]]וארא[[t:63]], [Lat.: I saw] ([[t:66]]v.[[t:67]] 27). Rabbi Isaac says: Unto the word [[t:68]]’haschmal:[[t:69]] from (the first) [[t:70]]וארא[[t:71]], [Lat.: I saw], ([[t:74]]v.[[t:75]] 4), unto the word [[t:76]]’haschmal[[t:77]][[fn:2556]], it is permissible to teach (the disciple); thenceforth, one transmits to him the first principles.
root.text.Part 3..4.0.sub_1: «There be some who say: from (the first) וארא unto the word ’haschmal, one imparts the first elements; from thenceforth, if he be a sage discerning by his own understanding, he may (study it), otherwise, not[[fn:2557]].» It is therefore clear from their expressions that it concerns diverse perceptions, indicated by the word וארא, I saw, thrice repeated, that these are different degrees of perception, and that the last perception, of which it is said: I saw as the colour of ’HASCHMAL (v. 27), — I mean the figure of the man divided in twain[[fn:2558]], of which it is said: from the appearance of his loins and upward, and from the appearance of his loins and downward (ibid.), — is the end of the perceptions and the highest among them. The Doctors are likewise divided (upon the question) whether it be permitted to teach it by any allusion whatsoever, I mean by imparting the first elements, or whether it be absolutely forbidden to indicate, even by the first elements, the teaching of this third perception, which may only be approached by the sage discerning by his own understanding. Likewise, the Doctors are divided, as thou seest, concerning the first two perceptions, those of the ’hayyôth and of the ophannîm, (to wit) whether it be permitted to teach the meaning thereof in plain terms, or whether it be permitted to teach only the first elements thereof, by allusion and in an enigmatical manner.
root.text.Part 3..4.1: Thy attention must also be fixed upon the order of these three perceptions. If he has placed at the head the perception of the ’hayyôth, it is because these take the first place by their nobility, by causality[[fn:2559]] [as he has said: for the spirit of the ’HAYYA was in the OPHANNÎM (i, 20)], and by other things besides[[fn:2560]]. After the ophannîm comes the third perception, which occupies a higher rank than the ’hayyôth, as has been expounded. The cause (of this order) is that the two preceding perceptions[[fn:2561]] necessarily precede, in study, the third perception, which draws its arguments from them.
root.text.Part 3..5.0: Know thou that this grave and important subject which Ezekiel undertook to teach us in describing the Mercabâ (or the Celestial Chariot), the prophetic inspiration having impelled him to teach it to us, this same subject Isaiah also has taught us summarily, without deeming it necessary to enter into the same details. I saw the Lord, says he, sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple; above it stood the seraphim (Isaiah, vi, 1, 2). Already have the Doctors expounded all this to us, and have made the same remark, saying that the perception which Ezekiel had was absolutely the same as that which Isaiah had. They have compared the matter to two men, the one a townsman and the other a countryman, who have beheld[[fn:2562]] the sovereign mounted on horseback: the townsman, knowing that the inhabitants of the city are acquainted with the manner in which the sovereign rids, dispenss with the description thereof, and says only: I have seen the sovereign; the other, desiring to describe it to the people of the country, who know nothing at all of his equipage, expounds to them in detail the manner in which he rids, the state of his troops[[fn:2563]], of his servants, and of those[[fn:2564]] who execute his commands. This is an observation of exceeding utility. Thus do they express themselves in ’Haghigâ[[fn:2565]]: «All that Ezekiel saw, Isaiah also saw; but Isaiah resembls a townsman who has seen the king, whilst Ezekiel resembls a villager who has seen the king.» The author of this text perhaps understood it[[fn:2566]] as I have said at the beginning (of the chapter), to wit, that the contemporaries of Isaiah had no need that all these details should be set forth to them, and that it sufficed him to say to them: I saw the Lord etc., whilst the people of the captivity had need of these details. But it may also be that the author intended to say that Isaiah was more perfect than Ezekiel, and that this perception, which disquieted Ezekiel and appeared to him so formidable, was to Isaiah a thing so familiar that it required not to be related in an extraordinary manner, being a thing well known to perfect men[[fn:2567]].
root.text.Part 3..6.0: One of the points which merit being examined is that the perception of the Mercabah is specified by the year, the month, and the day, and that the place is likewise specified.[[fn:2568]] It behoves us, therefore, to seek the reason thereof, and we must not believe that this is a matter which enfolds no idea.[[fn:2569]]
root.text.Part 3..6.1: That which it further behoves us to consider, and which is the key to the whole, are the words: the heavens were opened (Ezekiel, I, 1)[[fn:2570]]; for it is a thing which is frequently encountered in the prophets, I mean to employ figuratively the expressions opening and opening the gates; as for example: Open ye the gates (Isaiah, 26, 2), And he opened the doors of heaven (Ps., 78, 23), Lift up your heads, ye everlasting doors (Ps., 24, 9), Open to me the gates of righteousness (Ps., 118, 19), and many other passages.
root.text.Part 3..6.2: Another matter to which one's attention must be drawn is that, although this entire description be a prophetical vision — as it is stated: [[t:0]]And the hand of the LORD was upon him[[t:1]] (Ezekiel, I, 3)[[fn:2571]], — the manner of expression, in the diverse parts of this narrative, nevertheless presents a very significant difference. Indeed, in speaking of the [[t:2]]’hayyôth[[t:3]], it is said [[t:4]]a[[t:5]] [[t:6]]LIKENESS[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]דמות[[t:9]]) [[t:10]]of four ’hayyôth[[t:11]] ([[t:12]]ibid[[t:13]]., [[t:14]]v.[[t:15]] 5), and not simply [[t:16]]four ’hayyôth[[t:19]]; likewise, it states, [[t:20]]and above the ’hayya there was the[[t:21]] [[t:22]]LIKENESS[[t:23]] of [[t:24]]a firmament[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]v.[[t:27]] 22); in like manner, [[t:28]]there was as the appearance of a sapphire stone[[t:29]], [[t:30]]the[[t:31]] [[t:32]]LIKENESS[[t:33]] [[t:34]]of a throne[[t:35]] ([[t:36]]v[[t:37]]. 26), and yet again, [[t:38]]something which[[t:39]] [[t:40]]RESEMBLED[[t:41]] [[t:42]]the appearance of a man[[t:43]] ([[t:44]]ibid.[[t:45]]]). In all these passages, therefore, the word [[t:46]]likeness[[t:47]] ([[t:48]]דמות[[t:49]]) is employed; but, in speaking of the [[t:50]]ophannîm[[t:51]], it does not state, "the [[t:52]]likeness[[t:53]] of an [[t:54]]ophan[[t:55]]," nor "the [[t:56]]likeness of[[t:57]] OPHANNÎM," but rather distinctly enunciates a form actually existing[[fn:2572]]. Let one not be misled by the words: [[t:59]]They four had one manner of[[t:60]] [[t:61]]LIKENESS[[t:62]] ([[t:63]]v[[t:64]]. 16); for this passage bears not the same construction and contains not the sense to which one has alluded[[fn:2573]]. In the latter vision, this idea is confirmed and elucidated[[fn:2574]]. Commencing with the firmament, the details of which are enumerated, it is spoken of in an absolute manner[[fn:2575]]. [[t:65]]I saw[[t:66]], it states, [[t:67]]and behold[[t:68]], [[t:69]]in the firmament that was above the cherubims, there appeared over them as a sapphire stone[[t:70]], [[t:71]]as the appearance of the[[t:72]] [[t:73]]LIKENESS[[t:74]] [[t:75]]of a throne[[t:76]] (X, 1). Here, then, the firmament is spoken of in an absolute manner, and it is not stated, "likeness of a firmament," as had been done when assigning its place [[t:77]]above the likeness of the[[t:78]] [[t:79]]’HAYYÔTH[[t:80]][[fn:2576]]. But as for the throne, it is said that [[t:81]]the[[t:82]] [[t:83]]LIKENESS[[t:84]] [[t:85]]of a throne appeared above them[[t:86]] (the cherubim), which indicates that the firmament had first been perceived, and that subsequently there was manifested to him, above it, [[t:87]]the likeness of a throne[[t:88]][[fn:2577]]. One must thoroughly apprehend this.
root.text.Part 3..6.3: What should further fix thy attention is that in the first vision he relats that the ’hayyoth had at once wings and the hands of a man, whilst in this second vision, in which he setts forth that the ’hayyoth were cherubim, he perceived at first only their wings, and thereafter, in his vision, there appeared unto them hands of a man: And there appeared, says he, in the cherubims the form of a man’s hand under their wings (Ezekiel, X, 8), where the word form (תבנית) is taken in the same sense as the word likeness (דמות). The place which he assigns unto them[[fn:2578]] is under their wings. Thou must well penetrate thyself with this[[fn:2579]].
root.text.Part 3..6.4: — Remark well also how, in speaking of the ophannim[[fn:2580]], he says clearly over against them (X, 19), albeit he has attributed unto them no form[[fn:2581]].
root.text.Part 3..6.5: He says further: As the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness round about; such was the LIKENESS of the glory of the Lord (I, 28). The matter of the aforementioned rainbow and its true essence are well known[[fn:2582]]. This is indeed most extraordinary in point of comparison and allegory, and it must indubitably be attributed to a prophetic power[[fn:2583]]. Thou must well consider this and let it sink into thy mind.
root.text.Part 3..6.6: That which also merits thy fixed attention is that the human form which[[fn:2584]] is above the throne, he divids into two parts, of which the upper part was as the colour of ’haschmal, and of which the lower part was as the appearance of fire[[fn:2585]]. As touching the word ’haschmal, they (the Sages) have explained it as a compound word containing two ideas, ’HASCH (חש) and MAL (מל), that is to say, the idea of haste, signified by ’hasch, and that of cutting, signified by mal[[fn:2586]]; the intent was to combine two different ideas, by making allusion, in an allegorical manner, unto two sides, the upper and the lower. They give us a second indication, saying that it is derived from (two words signifying) to speak and to be silent; «they (the ’haschmallîm), say they, are sometimes silent and sometimes they speak» — whence they derive the idea of being silent (’hasch) from החשיתי מעולם, I have long time holden my peace (Isaiah, xlii. 14), — making allusion to the two ideas by attributing to them a wordless speech. In saying: «sometimes they are silent, sometimes they speak,» they indubitably had in view nought but a created thing. Thou shalt therefore recognize that they have declared unto us thereby that this human form above the throne, which is divided in twain, is not the image of God, who is above all composition[[fn:2587]], but the image of a created thing. Thus the prophet himself says: such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord (I, 28); but the glory of the Lord is not the Lord (Himself), as we have many times explained[[fn:2588]]. Consequently, all that which he presents allegorically in all these perceptions is nothing else than the glory of the Lord, that is to say, the chariot (mercabâ), and not He who rids thereon[[fn:2589]]; for God cannot be represented. Thou must well consider this and let it sink into thy mind.
root.text.Part 3..6.7: We have thus given thee also, in this chapter, some first elements; and if thou collectest[[fn:2590]] these elements, they shall form a useful whole for this subject. If thou readest attentively all that we have said in the chapters of this treatise even unto the present chapter, thou shalt understand the greater part of this subject, or even the subject in its entirety, with the exception of a small number of details and certain repetitions, the sense of which is obscure; but it may be that a more profound study shall shed light thereon, and that nothing thereof shall remain obscure.
root.text.Part 3..6.8: Hope not, after this chapter, to hear from me a single word upon this subject, neither clearly nor by allusion; for all that it was possible to say thereupon has been said, and I have therein even engaged myself too temerariously[[fn:2591]].
root.text.Part 3..6.9: Let us now proceed to other subjects among those which I hope to set forth in this treatise.
