root.text.Part 3..7.0: All bodies that are born and perish are subject to corruption only on the side of their matter alone; on the side of the form, and considering the form in itself[[fn:2592]], they are not subject to corruption, but are permanent. You see, in fact, that all specific forms [[t:0]]are[[t:1]] eternal and permanent; corruption only affects the form accidentally, I mean insofar as it is joined to matter. It is in the true nature of matter that it is never separated from [[t:2]]privation;[[t:3]] this is why it does not conserve any individual form, and it does not cease to strip itself of one form in order to take on another[[fn:2593]].
root.text.Part 3..7.1: Solomon therefore, in his wisdom, has expressed himself in a most remarkable manner by comparing matter to an adulterous woman[[fn:2594]]; for matter, being unable in any wise to exist without form, is ever like unto a married woman, who is never loosed from the bonds of her husband and is never found free[[fn:2595]]. But the unfaithful woman, albeit married, seeks unceasingly another man to take him in the stead of her husband, and she employs all manner of wiles to entice him, until he obtains from her that which her husband was wont to obtain. And such also is the condition of matter; for, whatsoever form it may possess, that form does but prepare it for the reception of another form, and it (the matter) ceass not to move in order to put off the form it possesses and to obtain another. When it has obtained it, the case is yet the same.
root.text.Part 3..7.2: It is manifest that all destruction, corruption, or imperfection has no cause save matter. Thus, for example, the deformity of a man, his members fashioned contrary to nature, the weakening, the interruption, or the derangement of his (corporeal) functions—no matter whether all this be innate in him or be the effect of an accident—all this (I say) is an effect of his corruptible matter, and not of his form. Likewise, every animal is subject to death or to sickness only because of its matter, not because of its form. All the faults, all the sins of man, have their cause solely in his matter, and not in his form, whilst all his virtues proceed from his form. If, for instance, man perceivs his Creator, if he has the conception of intelligible things, if he knows how to moderate his passion and his anger, if he reflects upon what must be done[[fn:2596]] and what must be avoided, all this is the effect of his form. But the passion for eating, for drinking, for giving himself up to love, and likewise anger and all the moral vices of man, all these are the effect of his matter. Now, as it is clear that such is the case, since divine wisdom willed that there should be no matter without form, and that none of these forms[[fn:2597]] should exist without matter, and as this most noble human form [which, as we have already set forth, is the image of God and His likeness[[fn:2598]]] is necessarily bound to this earthly matter, turbid[[fn:2599]] and dark, which causs in man all that is imperfect and corruptible, it has been granted unto this human form to exercise a power over matter, to make itself master thereof, to govern[[fn:2600]] and to dominate it, so as to subjugate it, to repress its exigencies, and to render it perfect and equal as far as possible.
root.text.Part 3..7.3.sub_0: In this respect, men are divided into several classes. There be certain men who strive ever to choose that which is most noble, and to seek immortality, as their noble form demands, and who consequently think only of the conception of intelligible things, of holding a true opinion concerning all things, and of uniting themselves with the divine intellect[[fn:2601]], which is poured out upon them and from which this form draws its existence. Whenever the exigencies of matter[[fn:2602]] invite them to that which it has of foul and notoriously shameful, they experience pain and shame for having abandoned themselves thereto, blushing to have been thus tarnished, and they use all their efforts to diminish this shame and to preserve themselves therefrom in every way. It is as a man unto whom the sovereign, in his wrath, has commanded, in order to abase him, to transport dung from one place to another; this man will use all his efforts to hide himself at the moment of this abasement, and will endeavour to transport but little a short distance, so that he may not soil his hands and his garments, and so that no other may see him. Thus will free men act. But the slave will feel contentment therein and will not think that a great penalty has thereby been laid upon him; he will cast his whole body into the dung and the filth, will soil his face and his hands, and will carry (his burden) publicly, laughing, rejoicing, and clapping his hands. Such also are the (different) conditions of men. As we have said, there be men in whose eyes all the exigencies of matter are a shame, an ugliness, and imperfections under the necessity of which they must pass, and particularly the sense of touch, which, as Aristotle has said, is a disgrace unto us[[fn:2603]], and by virtue of which we desire to eat, to drink, and to give ourselves up to love. It behoovs us, therefore[[fn:2604]], to restrain these things as much as possible, to hide ourselves from them[[fn:2605]], to perform them with sorrow, not to make them a subject of conversation[[fn:2606]], and not to form assemblies for such things; nay more, man must dominate all these exigencies (of matter), reduce them as much as he can, and admit only that which is indispensable.
root.text.Part 3..7.3.sub_1: He must take for his aim that which is the (true) aim of man, in so far as he is man, to wit, the sole conception of intelligible things, of which the most important and noble object is to understand, as far as possible, God, His angels, and His other works. Such men cease not to be with God, and it is of them that it has been said: Ye are all divine beings and sons of the Most High (Ps. lxxxii. 6). This is what is required of man, I mean to say that this is his final cause. For the others, whom a veil separats from God[[fn:2607]], that is to say, for the multitude of the ignorant, it is the contrary: they abstain from all thought and all reflection upon intelligible things, and consider as their final end (to satisfy) this sense which is our greatest shame, I mean the sense of touch, so that their thoughts and reflections have for their sole object good cheer and love. Thus it has been plainly said of those wretched beings given over to eating, drinking, and love: These also have erred through wine, they are out of the way through strong drink (Isaiah xxviii. 7); for all tables are full of vomit and filthiness, so that there is no place clean (ibid., v. 8); and women rule over them (ibid., iii. 12), contrary to that which was in the divine intention[[fn:2608]] from the creation: Thy desire (shall be) to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee (Genesis iii. 16). The prophet also depicts their violent passion, saying: Every one neighed after his neighbour's wife (Jeremiah v. 8); for they be all adulterers (ibid., ix. 1). Wherefore Solomon has devoted the whole book of Proverbs to warnings concerning unchastity and strong drink; for in these two vices are plunged those who are the objects of divine wrath and are far from God, of whom it has been said: For they belong not unto the Lord (ibid., v. 10); cast them out of my sight, and let them go forth (ibid., xv. 1).
root.text.Part 3..7.4: As touching this passage: A virtuous woman, who can find her, etc. (Proverbs, xxxi. 10), the whole of this allegory is right manifest. If one possesses a matter good and fitting, which does not prevail over him nor disturb the equilibrium within him, verily this is a divine gift. In general, it is easy to govern a fitting matter, as we have aforetime observed[[fn:2609]]; yet, if it be not fitting, it is nonetheless not impossible to subdue it by dint of discipline. It is unto this that all the moral sentences of Solomon and others are applied[[fn:2610]]; likewise, the prescriptions of the Law and its prohibitions[[fn:2611]] have no other end than to reform all these exigencies of matter. It behoves him, therefore, who desirs to be a true man, and not a beast having the figure and lineaments of a man, to use all his efforts to diminish all the exigencies of matter concerning feasting, physical love, anger, and all the vices resulting from concupiscence and wrath; he must needs blush thereat and impose limits upon them[[fn:2612]]. As for that which is indispensable, such as eating and drinking, he must restrict himself unto that which is most useful and have in view solely the need of sustenance, but never enjoyment. He must also eschew making them an object of conversation or social gathering. Thou knowest how greatly our doctors held in aversion “feasts not consecrated to a religious act,”[[fn:2613]] and that virtuous men, such as Phinehas ben Jair, never ate at the table of any man[[fn:2614]]: our Holy Doctor[[fn:2615]] having desired that the latter should accept a meal at his house, he refused. It is the same with drinking as with food, both having the same end[[fn:2616]]. To form a gathering for the purpose of taking intoxicating drinks ought to be, in thine eyes, a thing more shameful than a gathering of naked persons who, displaying all their nakedness, should satisfy their natural needs in open day and in one and the same place. Indeed, the satisfaction of one's need is a necessary thing which man has no means of avoiding, whilst to become intoxicated is an act which the vicious man committs of his own free will. If it be deemed unseemly to uncover the shameful parts, this is but a matter of mere convention, which pertains not to the domain of reason[[fn:2617]]; but to corrupt the intelligence and the body is a thing reprobated[[fn:2618]] by reason; wherefore he who truly desirs to be a man must hold such a thing in aversion and not even draw the conversation thereto.
root.text.Part 3..7.5: As for physical love, I need add naught to that which I have delivered in the Commentary on Aboth[[fn:2619]], (in which I have shown) how greatly our wise and pure Law holds it in aversion, how it forbidds to speak thereof, or to make it, in any fashion or under any pretext whatsoever, a subject of conversation. Thou knowest that the doctors say that Elisha was called holy[[fn:2620]] because he abstained from thinking on this thing, so that no impure accident ever befell him; and thou knowest likewise what they say of Jacob, to wit, “that he was never defiled by an impure accident before begetting Reuben.”[[fn:2621]] These are traditions spread among our coreligionists, in order to cause them to acquire human manners. Thou art acquainted with that sentence of the doctors: “The thoughts of sin are worse than the sin itself,”[[fn:2622]] and I have thereupon an explanation right remarkable. It is that the man who committs a sin only sinns by reason of the accidents which attach unto his matter, as we have expounded—I mean to say, he sinns by his animality; but thought is one of the properties of man which belong unto his form. If, therefore, he directs his thought unto sin, he sinns by the most noble of his two parts. Now, he who, by injustice, makes an ignorant slave to labour is not so culpable as he who exacts service from a free and distinguished man; for this human form and all the properties which belong unto it[[fn:2623]] ought not to be employed save for that which is worthy of them, that is to say, for attaching oneself unto that which is most exalted, and not for descending to the lowest degree[[fn:2624]].
root.text.Part 3..7.6: Thou knowest also with what severity obscenity of language is forbidden amongst us[[fn:2625]], and thus it ought to be; for language is one of the properties of man and a boon granted unto him whereby he is distinguished[[fn:2626]], as it is said: Who has made man's mouth? (Exodus, iv. 11); and the prophet has said: The Lord God has given me the tongue of the learned (Isaiah, l. 4). This boon, then, which has been granted us for our perfection, for learning and teaching, must not be employed for the greatest vice and for the most shameful thing, in such wise that we should say all that the ignorant and impious Gentiles say in their poems and in their narratives[[fn:2627]], which are well-suited unto them, but not unto those regarding whom it has been said: Ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exodus, xix. 6). And if any man applies his thought and his speech unto a thing relative to this sense which is a shame unto us, in such wise as to think, more than is necessary, on drinking or on physical love, or to recite verses thereupon, he abuss the boon which has been granted him and uss it to revolt against the Benefactor and to disobey His commandments, so that he resembls those of whom it was said: The silver and gold which I multiplied unto her, they prepared for Baal (Hosea, ii. 10).
root.text.Part 3..7.7: I deem it also possible to assign the reason why our (Hebrew) tongue is called the Holy Tongue; for it must not be believed that this is on our part a vain word[[fn:2628]] or an error, but it is a verity. It is that, in this sacred tongue, there has been created no word to (designate) the sexual organ of men or of women, nor for the act itself which leads to generation, nor for the sperm, nor for the urine[[fn:2629]], nor for the excrements. For all these things, no primitive term has been created in the Hebrew tongue, but they are designated by words taken figuratively and by allusions. It was intended thereby to indicate that one ought not to speak of these things, nor consequently to give them names, but that they are, on the contrary, things upon which one must keep silence, and that, when there is necessity to speak of them, one must extricate oneself by the use of other expressions, even as, when there is necessity to do them, one must surround oneself with the greatest secrecy. As for the organ of man, it has been called גיד, nerve[[fn:2630]], a name employed by similitude, as it is said: Thy neck is (stiff) as an iron sinew (Isaiah, xlviii. 4). It has been called also שָׁפְכָה[[fn:2631]], instrument for pouring (effusorium), because of its action. For the organ of the woman, (one finds) קֳבָתָהּ, her belly or her stomach, קֵבָה being the name of the stomach[[fn:2632]]. As for רֶחֶם (employed for vulva), it is the name of the part of the entrails in which the foetus is formed. The name of the excrements is צוֹאָה, a word derived from יצא, to go out; that of urine is מימי רגלים, waters of the feet[[fn:2633]], and that of sperm, שכבת זרע, layer of seed. The act itself which leads to generation has no name, and one uss, to designate it, the verbs ישגכב, he lies, יבעל, he marries, יקח, he takes (a woman), or יגלה ערוה, he uncovers the nakedness; no other expression is employed. Let not thyself be led into error by the verb ישגל, which thou mightest take for the proper term for the act; it is not so, for SHEGHAL (שֵׁגָל) is only the name of the young woman ready to give herself to love—for example: the consort (SHEGHAL) is placed at thy right hand (Ps. xlv. 10),—and the verb ישגלנה (Deuter. xxviii. 30), according to the Kethib[[fn:2634]], signifies: he shall take her as a woman for the thing in question.
root.text.Part 3..7.8: In the greater part of this chapter[[fn:2635]], we have departed from the purpose of this treatise, to discourse upon moral and religious matters; yet, albeit these things do not wholly enter into the plan of this work, we have been led thereto by a natural sequence of discourse.
root.text.Part 3..8.0.sub_0: Matter is a great veil[[fn:2636]] which prevents the perception of the separate Intelligence[[fn:2637]] as it is in its true essence, even were it the most noble and pure matter, I mean the matter of the spheres[[fn:2638]], and how much more so this dark and turbid matter which is ours. Wherefore, whenever our intelligence desirs to perceive the Deity, or any of the Intelligences (separate)[[fn:2639]], this great veil comes to interpose itself. To this allusion is made in all the books of the prophets, (when it is said) that a veil separats us from the Divinity, and that He is hidden from us by a cloud, by darkness, by a mist, or by clouds, and other such expressions, alluding to the fact that, by reason of matter, we are unable to perceive God. This is what was intended when it was said: Clouds and darkness are round about him (Ps. xcvii. 2), in which it is intimated that the obstacle lies in the opacity of our substance, and it is not meant that God is a body surrounded by mist and clouds which prevent Him from being seen, as the literal sense of the words of the allegory conveys. The same allegory is again repeated in the words: He made darkness his secret place (Ps. xviii. 12). Likewise, when (it is said that) God manifested Himself in a thick cloud, in darkness, the cloud and the thick darkness[[fn:2640]], one must likewise behold therein an indication of this idea; for all that is perceived in a prophetic vision is but an allegory to indicate a certain idea. Although this grandiose scene (of Sinai) was greater than any other prophetic vision and beyond all analogy[[fn:2641]], it is not, however, without indicating an idea, notably when God manifests Himself in a thick cloud (Exodus xix. 9); for it is intended to point out that the perception of His true being is impossible for us, by reason of the dark matter which surrounds our being, and not His; for He, the Most High, is not a body. It is known, moreover, and it is a thing well-known in our community, that the day of the scene at Mount Sinai was a day of cloud, of thick darkness, and of small rain, as it is said: O Lord!
root.text.Part 3..8.0.sub_1: When thou didst go forth from Seir[[t:23]], [[t:24]]when thou didst advance from the field of Edom[[t:25]], [[t:26]]the earth trembled[[t:27]], [[t:28]]the heavens poured forth and the clouds distilled water[[t:29]] (Judges, 5, 4). It is therefore possible that this is what was intended by the words [[t:30]]ténèbres[[t:31]], [[t:32]]nuée[[t:33]] and [[t:34]]brouillard[[t:35]] (Deuteronomy, 4, 11), and not that the ténèbres surrounded the Divinity; for near God there are no ténèbres, but rather the resplendent and permanent light, the effusion of which illuminates all ténèbres[[fn:2643]], as it is said in the prophetic allegories: [[t:36]]And the earth was illuminated by His glory[[t:37]] (Ezekiel, 43, 2).
root.text.Part 3..9.0: The [[t:0]]Motecallemin[[t:1]], as I have apprised you, conceive of [[t:2]]non-being[[t:3]] (or [[t:4]]privation[[t:5]]) solely as absolute non-existence; but all [[t:6]]privations of capacities[[t:7]][[fn:2644]] they do not regard as [[t:8]]privations[[t:9]], believing, on the contrary, that [[t:10]]privation[[t:11]] and [[t:12]]capacity[[t:13]], such as blindness and sight, death and life, must be considered as two opposing entities[[fn:2645]]; for in this, according to them, the case is analogous to heat and cold[[fn:2646]]. Hence they declare, in an absolute sense, that non-being requires no agent, for only action itself necessarily necessitates an agent[[fn:2647]]; which is true from a certain standpoint[[fn:2648]]. Nevertheless, although they assert that non-being needs no agent, they declare, in accordance with their principle, that God renders blind and deaf, and brings to repose that which is in motion[[fn:2649]]; for these privations are, in their estimation, things which exist (positively).
root.text.Part 3..9.1.sub_0: It is now necessary that we should make known to thee what is our own opinion in this regard, according to that which philosophical speculation requirs. Thou knowest already that he who removs the impediment (to motion) is in a manner the mover[[fn:2650]]; if any one, for example, removs a pillar from beneath a beam, so that the latter falls by its natural weight, we say that he who has removed the pillar has moved the beam, as it has been said in the Acroasis[[fn:2651]]. In this manner also, we say of him who has caused a certain faculty[[fn:2652]] to cease, that he is the author of such privation, although privation be not an existing thing. Thus we say of him who has extinguished the lamp during the night, that he has produced darkness, and of him who has destroyed the sight, that he has produced blindness, albeit darkness and blindness be privations and require no agent. It is in accordance with this exposition that one must explain the words of Isaiah: I form the light, and create darkness, I make peace, and create evil (Isaiah xlv. 7); for darkness and evil are privations. Observe well that he says not: עושה חשך, "who makes darkness," nor עושה רע, "who makes evil"; for these are not things of a positive existence, to which the verb עשה, to make; can be applied; but he employs for these two things the word בורא, creating, a word which in the Hebrew language relats to non-existence, as it is said: In the beginning God created (ברא) etc., which means: (he brought forth) out of nothingness. Whenever, therefore, non-existence is related to the action of an agent, it is in the manner which we have set forth. It is in this manner also that we must understand these words: Who has made man's mouth? or who makes the dumb, or deaf, or the seeing, or the blind (Exodus iv. 11)[[fn:2653]]?
root.text.Part 3..9.1.sub_1: But one may also interpret this passage in another manner, to wit: "Who is he that has created man speaking, or who has created him deprived of speech?" And it would then refer to the production of a matter unfit to receive such or such a faculty; for, if any one produces a matter incapable of receiving such (determined) faculty, it may be said of him that he has produced such a privation[[fn:2654]]; just as, if any one had been able to save a person from death, but had abstained and had not saved him, it might be said of him that he has killed him. Be that as it may, it is clear unto thee that, in no wise, can the action of an agent relate to a privation, and that producing a privation can only be said in the sense of an indirect action[[fn:2655]], as we have set forth. But that which an agent performs directly[[fn:2656]] is necessarily a thing of a positive existence; for, whatever the action may be, it can relate only to something existent[[fn:2657]].
root.text.Part 3..9.2: After this preamble, recall unto thyself that it has been demonstrated that evils are only such relatively to a certain thing[[fn:2658]], and that all evil, in relation to any being whatsoever, consists in the non-being of that thing or in the privation of one of its conditions of good. Wherefore it has been said, as a general thesis, that all evils are privations. In man, for instance, death is an evil, and it is his non-existence; likewise, his sickness, his poverty, and his ignorance are evils in relation to him, and all of these are privations of capacity. If thou shouldst pursue all the particular cases of this general thesis, thou shalt find that it never fails[[fn:2659]], save for him who knows not how to distinguish between privation and capacity, nor between two contraries, or who is totally ignorant of the nature of things, as, for example, he who knows not that health in general is a species of symmetry[[fn:2660]], that the latter belongs to the category of relation and that the absence of this proportion is in general sickness[[fn:2661]]. Death is, in relation to every living being, the privation of form; and likewise, for all that perishes among other beings, destruction is nothing else than the privation of its form.
root.text.Part 3..9.3: After these premises, it shall be acknowledged with certainty that it could in no wise be affirmed of God that He does evil directly; I mean to say, that God has primarily the intention of doing evil. This cannot be; all His actions, on the contrary, are pure good; for He does naught but being, and all being is good. All evils are privations, to which no action is attached, save in the manner we have set forth, (that is to say) inasmuch as God produces matter with the nature proper to it, to wit, to be always associated with privation, as is already known[[fn:2662]], the which renders it the cause of all corruption and of all evil. Wherefore everything, unto which God has not given this matter[[fn:2663]], perishes not and is subject to none of the (various) evils. Thus, the true action of God is good, for it is being. For this cause, the book which has illumined the darkness of the world has stated textually: And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good (Genesis, i, 31); for even the being of this inferior matter, which nevertheless by its nature is associated with privation, the source of death and of all evils, is notwithstanding a good, in view of the perpetuity of birth and the continual and successive reproduction of being[[fn:2664]]. Wherefore Rabbi Meir interprets the words: And, behold, it was very good, by these: And death is a good[[fn:2665]], according to the idea we have indicated.
root.text.Part 3..9.4: Keep well in mind what I have told thee in this chapter and endeavour to comprehend it. Then shalt thou find clear all that the prophets and the doctors have said (on this subject), to wit, that all good (alone) comes from the direct action of God. We read in Bereshith Rabba: «Nothing evil descends from above[[fn:2666]].»
root.text.Part 3..10.0: Those great[[fn:2667]] evils which men inflict upon one another, by reason of tendencies, passions, opinions, and beliefs, all flow from a privation; for they all result from ignorance, that is to say, from the privation of knowledge. Even as the blind man, by reason of the absence of sight, ceass not to stumble, to wound himself and to wound others also, when he has no one to lead him in the way, so do the parties among men, each[[fn:2668]] according to the measure of his ignorance, inflict upon themselves and upon others evils which weigh heavily upon the individuals of the (human) species[[fn:2669]]. Had they possessed knowledge, which is to the human form what the visual faculty is to the eye[[fn:2670]], they would be prevented from doing any harm to themselves and to others; for the knowledge of truth causs enmity and hatred to cease, and prevents men from doing evil to one another, as (the prophet) has announced, saying: The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid, etc.; and the cow and the bear shall feed, etc., and the sucking child shall play, etc. (Isaiah, xi, 6-8). He thereafter indicats the cause thereof, saying that that which shall cause these enmities, these discords, and these tyrannies to cease, is that men shall then possess the true knowledge of God. He says therefore: They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea (ibid., v. 9). Know this well.
root.text.Part 3..11.0: Ofttimes the vulgar are prone to imagine that there are, in the world, more evils than goods; so that all nations express this idea in many of their discourses[[fn:2671]] and of their poems, saying that it is rare to find good in this world[[fn:2672]], whilst its evils are numerous and perpetual. This error exists not only among the vulgar, but also with such a one as believs himself to possess some knowledge.
root.text.Part 3..11.1: There is a celebrated book of Al-Rāzī[[fn:2673]], which he has entitled Al-Ilāhiyyāt (Divine Things or Metaphysics), and in which, amidst a multitude of follies and absurdities, he has propounded this thesis: that evil in the world is more frequent than good, and that if the well-being of man and the pleasures which this well-being affords him be compared with the pains, the grievous sufferings, the infirmities, the paralyses[[fn:2674]], the adversities, the sorrows, and the calamities which befall him, one shall find that his existence—I mean that of man—is a punishment and a great evil inflicted upon him. He seeks to confirm this opinion by reviewing all these misfortunes, that he may combat all that the friends of truth believe concerning the benevolence of God and His manifest goodness[[fn:2675]], affirming that He is absolute Good, and that all that proceeds from Him is indubitably pure good.
root.text.Part 3..11.2.sub_0: The cause of all this error is that this ignorant man, as well as his fellows among the multitude, judged the universe only by the human individual alone. Every ignorant person imagins that the whole universe exists only for his own person, as if there were no other being but himself alone. If, therefore, that which befalls him be contrary to his desires, he decids that the whole of existence is evil; but if man were to consider and conceive the universe, and if he knew how small a place he occupies therein, the truth would become clear and manifest unto him. Indeed, this notable folly which men proclaim touching the multitude of evils alleged to be in the universe, they profess it neither with regard to the angels, nor with regard to the spheres and the stars, nor with regard to the elements and the minerals or plants composed thereof, nor with regard to the various species of animals; but their thoughts are directed only toward certain individuals of the human species. If someone, for example, having nourished himself with unwholesome food, becoms leprous, they marvel that he should be smitten with this great misfortune, and ask how such evil exists; likewise, they marvel if someone, by dint of debauchery, has become blind, and they find it cruel that this man should be stricken with blindness. I might cite yet other examples. But the true manner of viewing the matter is that all individuals of the human species who exist, and a fortiori those of other species of animals, are a thing of no value in relation to the immutable whole of the universe[[fn:2676]], as it is clearly said: Man is like unto vanity, &c. (Ps. cxliv. 4); the mortal who is but a worm, and the son of man who is but a maggot (Job xxv. 6); how much more them that dwell in houses of clay, &c. (ibid., iv. 19); Behold, the nations are as a drop (that falls) of a bucket, &c. (Isaiah xl. 15); and many other passages from the prophetic books speak of this important subject, which is of great utility[[fn:2677]] in making known to man his little worth. He must not err and believe that the universe exists only for his person; on the contrary, according to us, the universe exists by reason of the will of its Creator, and the human species is a very small thing therein in relation to the superior world, I mean, to the spheres and the stars.
root.text.Part 3..11.2.sub_1: As for the angels, there exists no true relation between them and man[[fn:2678]]. Man is but the most noble among the beings subject to contingency[[fn:2679]], that is to say, among those of our lower world; I mean that he is more noble than all that has been composed of the elements. Withal, his existence is a great good for him and a benefit from God, by reason of the properties and perfections which He has granted him. The greater part of the evils which smite individuals proceed from themselves, I mean from human individuals who are imperfect. It is our own vices that give us cause to lament and to cry for help. If we suffer, it is through evils which we inflict upon ourselves of our own free will, yet which we attribute to God;—far be such a thing from Him!—This is what God has declared in His book, saying: Is destruction His (that it should be attributed to Him)? No, to His children, to their own faults (Deut. xxxii. 5)[[fn:2680]]. Solomon has expressed the same idea, saying: The foolishness of man perverts his way, and his heart fretts against the Lord (Proverbs xix. 3).
root.text.Part 3..11.3: To explain myself more clearly, I shall say that all the evils which smite man may be reduced to one of the three following kinds:
root.text.Part 3..11.4.sub_0: The evils of the first kind are those which happen to man by the very nature of that which is subject to genesis and corruption, I mean because he is a material being. It is because of this that certain individuals are afflicted with infirmities and paralyses, which are innate[[fn:2681]] in them or which befall them through alterations occurring in the elements, such as the corruption of the air[[fn:2682]], the fires of heaven[[fn:2683]], the subsidences of the soil[[fn:2684]]. As we have already set forth, the divine wisdom willed that genesis should take place only as a consequence of corruption[[fn:2685]]; and, without individual corruption, there would be no permanent specific genesis[[fn:2686]]. It is clear thereby that all is pure goodness and benevolence, and that naught proceeds from God but good. He who, while being of flesh and bone, desirs at the same time to be shielded from every impression and not to be subject to any of the accidents of matter, desirs nothing else, though he perceive it not, than to unite two contraries together; for he desirs at once to be subject to impressions and not to be so. Indeed, were there anything that was not susceptible to impression, it would not be the product of genesis, and that which exists of it would be one (single) individual, and not individuals of a species[[fn:2687]]. How true is that which Galen has said in the third book of The Uses of the Parts[[fn:2688]]! "Give not thyself up to this vain illusion," says he, "that from the menstrual blood and the semen there could be formed an animal that dies not, or suffers not, or which has a perpetual motion, or which is resplendent like the sun." This passage from Galen calls attention to a particular case of a general proposition, which is this: "All that can be formed from any matter whatsoever is formed in the most perfect manner possible that this specific matter allows, and the imperfection wherewith the individuals of the species are tainted is in proportion to the imperfection of the (particular) matter of the individual." Now, the most eminently perfect thing that can be formed from blood and semen is the human species, with its well-known nature of being a living, rational, and mortal being; consequently, this latter kind of evil must necessarily exist[[fn:2689]].
root.text.Part 3..11.4.sub_1: Notwithstanding this, thou shalt find that the evils of this kind which befall men are very few in number and happen but rarely[[fn:2690]]. Verily, thou shalt find cities which for thousands of years have been neither submerged nor consumed by fire; likewise, thousands of men are born perfectly sound, and a man born infirm is an anomaly[[fn:2691]], or at least—should any one cavil at the word anomaly—he is a very rare exception, and forms not the hundredth nor even the thousandth part of those who are born in a sound state.
root.text.Part 3..11.5: The evils of the second species are those which men inflict upon one another, as, for example, the tyranny which they exercise over each other. These evils are more numerous than those of the first species, and the causes thereof are manifold and well known; they likewise proceed from ourselves, yet he who suffers therefrom[[fn:2692]] is powerless against them. Nevertheless, in no city whatsoever in the whole world are evils of this sort widespread or frequent[[fn:2693]] among individuals; on the contrary, they are encountered but rarely, as when one individual surpriss another by night to slay him or to rob him. It is only in great wars that evils of this kind embrace a multitude of people; but even this is not frequent in relation to the whole earth.
root.text.Part 3..11.6.sub_0: The evils of the third species are those which happen to each of us by his own act, and this occurrs frequently[[fn:2694]]. These evils are far more numerous than those of the second species. All men lament evils of this kind, and very few will be found who do not render themselves guilty thereof toward themselves. They who are smitten by them verily deserve to be blamed[[fn:2695]], and to them may be addressed these words (of the prophet): This has been by your means (Malachi i. 9). Concerning this matter it has been said: He that does it destroys his own soul (Proverbs vi. 32), and it is likewise of the evils of this species that Solomon said: The foolishness of man perverts his way (ibid., xix. 3). Elsewhere he has clearly stated, speaking of evils of this kind, that man brings them upon himself: lo, this only have I found, that God has made man upright; but they have sought out many devices (guilty) (Ecclesiastes vii. 29)[[fn:2696]]; it is these devices that have brought these evils upon them. It is also in respect of this species (of evils) that it has been said: Although affliction comes not forth of the dust, neither does trouble spring out of the ground (Job v. 6). Then, it is declared immediately after that it is man who gives birth to this sort of evils, and it is said: Yet man is born unto trouble (ibid., ver. 7)[[fn:2697]].—This species (of evils) follows in the train of all vices; I speak especially of the passion for gluttony, wine-bibbing, and carnal love, when these things are enjoyed to excess or without order, or when the food is of an evil quality; for therein lies the cause of all the pernicious maladies of the body and of the soul[[fn:2698]]. As for the maladies of the body, it is evident. The maladies of the soul (which result) from this evil regimen have two causes. The first is that the alteration which the body undergoes necessarily influencs the soul, inasmuch as the latter is a bodily faculty[[fn:2699]], and it is in this sense that it has been said that the character of the soul follows the temperament of the body[[fn:2700]]. The second cause is that the soul becoms familiarized with things unnecessary and accustoms itself thereto, so that it acquirs the habit[[fn:2701]] of desiring what is necessary neither for the preservation of the individual nor for that of the species.
root.text.Part 3..11.6.sub_1: Now, this desire is a thing which has no limit; for, whilst necessary things are all restricted and bounded, the superfluous, on the contrary, is unlimited. Dost thou desire, for example, to possess vessels of silver, it is more beautiful to have them of gold; some there are even who have them of crystal, and perhaps they are also made of emerald and ruby, in so far as these materials are attainable[[fn:2702]]. Thus, every man who is ignorant and of a false reasoning is constantly in pain and in sorrow because he cannot indulge in luxury as another has done; and often he casts himself into great perils, such as voyaging by sea and the service of kings, aiming to procure this useless luxury. But when, having entered upon these paths, he is smitten by misfortunes, he complains of the divine decree and of destiny, murmurs against fortune, and marvells at its lack of justice, because it has not helped him to obtain great riches, by means of which he might procure wine in abundance to make himself drunken and a great number of concubines decked with gold and precious stones to incite him to the enjoyment of love beyond his capacity, as if the pleasure of this base man were alone the end of the universe. To such a point has the error of the vulgar reached; they have gone so far as to accuse the Creator of impotence for having created the universe with this nature which, as they imagine, necessarily produces these evils, because it helps not every vicious man to satiate his ignoble passion and to bring his perverse soul to the term of its desires, which, as we have set forth, are without end. But virtuous and instructed men know the wisdom that presids over the universe and understand it, as David declared, saying: All the paths of the Lord are mercy and truth unto such as keep his covenant and his testimonies (Ps. xxv. 10), which means that they who have regard for the nature of existence and for the precepts of the Law, and who know the aim thereof, understand the mercy and the truth which preside over all; wherefore they propose for their aim the thing for which they were destined as men, that is to say, perception. Constrained by the needs of the body, they seek what is necessary for it: bread to eat, and raiment to put on[[fn:2703]], without aiming at the superfluous. If one limits oneself to the necessary, the matter is very easy and is obtained with little toil.
root.text.Part 3..11.6.sub_2: Whenever thou perceivest therein difficulty and toil, it is because, in striving to seek what is not necessary, it becoms difficult for us to find even the necessary; for, in proportion as our desires are directed too much toward the superfluous, the matter becoms more painful; we expend our strength and our substance[[fn:2704]] for that which is not necessary, and we find even the necessary no more.
root.text.Part 3..11.7: It behoves us to consider the conditions in which we stand in regard to that which is to be found[[fn:2705]]. Verily, according as a thing is more necessary to the animal, it is found more frequently and at a more trifling price; and in proportion as a thing is less necessary, it is found less frequently and is exceeding costly[[fn:2706]]. That which, for instance, is necessary to man, is air, water, and nourishment. Nevertheless, that which is most necessary of all is air, for one cannot be deprived thereof for a single moment without perishing, whilst one may dispense with water for a day or two[[fn:2707]]; wherefore air is indubitably that which is easiest to find and most gratuitous. But water is of a more urgent necessity than is nourishment; for certain men, provided they drink[[fn:2708]], can remain four or five days without food. Thus it is that water is found, in every city, more abundantly and at a more trifling price than nourishment. The same holds true of diverse aliments; those which are more necessary are found more easily and at a lower cost, in the same place, than those which are less necessary. But as for musk, amber, rubies, and emeralds, I do not believe that a man of sound sense can deem them very necessary to man, unless it be for a medical treatment[[fn:2709]]; and even then, they may be replaced, as well as other similar things, by several kinds of herbs and earths.
root.text.Part 3..11.8: It is herein that the bounty and the goodness[[fn:2710]] which God exerciss even toward this frail creature are manifest. But that which above all is most evident is His signal justice and the equality which He has established among animals[[fn:2711]]. In effect, the laws of nature[[fn:2712]] do not permit that an individual of any species of animals[[fn:2713]] should be distinguished from other individuals of the same species by a faculty peculiar to himself, or by a limb which he might possess in addition. On the contrary, all physical, animal (or psychic), and vital faculties[[fn:2714]], as well as the members possessed by one individual, are essentially the same as those possessed by another; and if there exists anywhere a defect, it is accidentally and by reason of some occurrence which is not according to nature, a thing which is rare, as we have already set forth. Between individuals who follow the course of nature, there is absolutely no difference of more or less, save that which results from the diverse disposition of (individual) matters[[fn:2715]]; and this is a necessary consequence of the nature proper to the matter of the species, a thing which concerns not one individual more than another[[fn:2716]]. But, that one should possess many bags of musk[[fn:2717]] and garments adorned with gold, whilst another lacks these superfluities of life, there is therein neither injustice nor violence. He who has obtained this superfluity has gained thereby no prerogative in his substance, and possesses but a lying illusion or a plaything; and he who lacks the superfluities of life is not necessarily diminished thereby[[fn:2718]]: He that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack; they gathered every man according to his eating (Exodus, 16, 18). This is what occurrs most frequently in all times and in all places, and we must not have regard to the exception, as we have already set forth.
root.text.Part 3..11.9: Thou shalt recognize therefore, by the two preceding reflections, the goodness which God exerciss toward His creatures, (on the one hand) in making them find what is necessary according to its relative importance[[fn:2719]], and (on the other hand) in establishing equality, from their very creation, between the individuals of the same species. It is from this true point of view that the prince of the learned[[fn:2720]] has said: For all His ways are judgment (Deut. 32, 4), and that David has said: All the paths of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 25, 10), as we have already set forth. David further said expressly: The Lord is good to all: and His tender mercies are over all His works (Ps. 145, 9); for the great good in the absolute sense is that He has caused us to exist, and in creating the governing faculty[[fn:2721]] in the animal, He has shewn it His mercy, as we have already set forth.
root.text.Part 3..12.0: Ofttimes the minds[[fn:2722]] of perfect men have been perplexed by the question of knowing what is the final end of this universe; but I shall show that, according to all systems, it is an idle question[[fn:2723]].
root.text.Part 3..12.1: Whenever, I say, an agent acts with intention, the thing done by him must necessarily have a final end for which he has made it; this is clear from the point of view of philosophical speculation and needs not to be demonstrated. Likewise, it is clear that the thing thus made with intention was brought into being after not having existed[[fn:2724]]. Finally, what is equally clear and admitted by common accord, is that the necessary Being, who has never been non-existent and who shall never be so, has no need of an efficient cause, as we have already set forth[[fn:2725]]. Now, as He has not been made, one cannot seek the final end thereof[[fn:2726]]. Wherefore one cannot ask "what is the final end of the existence of the Creator?" for He is not a created thing. It is therefore clear, according to these propositions, that one cannot seek a final end save for a thing brought into being, which has been made with intention by a being endowed with intelligence[[fn:2727]]; I mean to say that, for all that has taken its origin in an intelligence, one must necessarily seek what is the final cause thereof; but when it is not a thing brought into being, one cannot seek for it a final cause, as we have said.
root.text.Part 3..12.2: After this exposition, thou shalt understand that one cannot seek a final purpose for the whole of the universe, neither according to our own view, who profess the novelty of the world, nor according to the opinion of Aristotle, who believs it to be eternal. Indeed, according to his opinion concerning the eternity of the world, one cannot seek an ultimate final cause for any of the (principal) parts of the universe; for, according to this opinion, it is not permitted to ask what is the final purpose of the existence of the heavens, nor why they have such measure and such number, nor why the prime matter is of such a nature, nor what is the final purpose of such a species of animals or of plants; all things emanating, according to him, from an eternal necessity, for ever immutable[[fn:2728]]. Albeit physical science seeks the final purpose of every being in nature, this is not the ultimate end of which we speak in this chapter. Indeed, it has been set forth in physical science that every being in nature must necessarily have a certain end[[fn:2729]], but that this final cause, which is the most noble of the four causes, is hidden in most of the species[[fn:2730]]. Aristotle constantly declars that nature does nothing in vain[[fn:2731]]; which is to say that every work of nature has necessarily a certain end. He says expressly that plants were created for the sake of animals[[fn:2732]]. Likewise, he has set forth, concerning certain other things, that they exist for the sake of one another, which particularly applies to the members of animals[[fn:2733]].
root.text.Part 3..12.3: Know that the existence of this end in physical things has necessarily led the philosophers to admit a principle other than nature, which Aristotle calls the intelligent or divine principle, and it is this which does such a thing for the sake of another[[fn:2734]]. It must also be known that in the eyes of the impartial man, one of the strongest proofs for the novelty of the world is that it has been demonstrated, concerning physical things, that each of them has a certain end, and that such a thing exists for the sake of another, which proves the design of a being acting with intention; but one cannot conceive of design without it being a matter of a new production[[fn:2735]].
root.text.Part 3..12.4: I return now to the subject of this chapter, which treats of the final cause. I say then: Aristotle has set forth that, in physical things, the efficient, the form, and the end are but one and the same thing, I mean to say they are specifically one. Indeed, it is the form of Zeid, for example, which makes the form of the individual ’Amr his son; what it does is to give a form of its species to the matter of ’Amr, and the final purpose of ’Amr is to have a human form. It is the same, according to him, with each of the individuals of the physical species which have need to propagate[[fn:2736]]; for the three causes, in these, form but one. But all this is naught but the first end[[fn:2737]]. Nevertheless, all naturalists think that there necessarily exists, for every species, an ultimate end, albeit it be passing difficult to know it; and with greater reason (to know) the final cause of the entire universe. That which seems to emerge from the words of Aristotle is that, according to him, the ultimate end of these species consists in the permanence of generation and corruption, which is indispensable[[fn:2738]] to perpetuate becoming in this (inferior) matter, from which no permanent individual can come forth, and from which nevertheless must be born, in the last resort, all that is possible to be born therefrom, I mean to say the most perfect thing possible; for the ultimate goal is to arrive at perfection[[fn:2739]]. It is clear that the most perfect thing possible which can be born of this matter is man, and that he is the last and most perfect of these composite beings. If therefore one were to say that all sublunary beings exist because of him, it would be true from this point of view, I mean to say (granting) that the movement of variable things takes place in view of (perpetual) generation, so as to arrive at the most perfect degree. But one could not ask of Aristotle, given his doctrine of the eternity (of the world), what is the final cause of the existence of man. Indeed, the first end of every individual born being, according to him, the perfection of the specific form, every individual, in whom the actions resulting from this form are perfect, has perfectly and completely attained his final purpose; and the ultimate end of the species is to perpetuate this form by means of a continual succession of generations and corruptions, so that there always occurrs a new birth having for its goal[[fn:2740]] a greater perfection. It is therefore clear that, according to the doctrine of eternity, there is no occasion to seek the ultimate end of the whole of the universe.
root.text.Part 3..12.5.sub_0: But there be some who think that, according to our own opinion, who profess that the whole universe was created after not having existed, it is fitting to pose this question, that is to say, to seek the final cause of all this universe. Consequently, it is believed that the entire universe has for its end only the existence of the human species destined to worship God, and that all that has been made was made only for her, so that the celestial spheres themselves would accomplish their circular motion only to be useful unto her and to produce all that she requirs[[fn:2741]]. Certain passages of the prophetic books, taken in their literal sense, serve as a great support to this opinion: He formed it (the earth) to be inhabited (Isaiah, 45, 18); If it were not for my covenant (subsisting) day and night, I should not have appointed the laws of heaven and earth (Jeremiah, 33, 25)[[fn:2742]]; He has stretched them out as a tent to dwell in (Isaiah, 40, 22). Now, if the celestial spheres exist for the sake of man, with greater reason do all[[fn:2743]] the species of animals and plants. But, in examining this opinion as befitts men of understanding, one shall recognize how much it is subject to doubt. Indeed, one might ask of him who professes this opinion: Since the final purpose is the existence of man[[fn:2744]], could the Creator have produced man without all these preparations, or could he only be created following them? If one were to answer that the thing was possible[[fn:2745]] and that God, for example, could have produced man without there being a heaven, one might ask: of what use unto Him[[fn:2746]] were all those things which were not themselves the final purpose, and (which were created) only for the sake of a thing which could exist without them? But, even admitting that the whole was born for the sake of man, and that the final purpose of man, as has been said, is to worship God, one might yet ask: To what end must God be worshipped, since His perfection cannot increase, even should all creatures worship Him and perceive Him in the most perfect manner, and that even though there should exist absolutely nothing besides Him, He would not thereby be tainted with imperfection?
root.text.Part 3..12.5.sub_1: For if one should answer that it concerns not His own perfection, but ours [for it is our perfection which forms our greatest good], one would yet come to pose this question: To what end must we exist with this perfection? — This question of the final cause will therefore necessarily lead us to (answer in the last resort): “God has thus willed it[[fn:2747]],” or “His wisdom has thus required it”; and that is the truth. Thou findest, indeed, that the Sages of Israel, in their liturgical rituals, have expressed themselves thus: “Thou hast distinguished man from the beginning (of creation) and Thou hast destined him to present himself before Thee. Who could ask Thee for what purpose Thou actest? If man be righteous, what profit accrus unto Thee therefrom[[fn:2748]]?” They have therefore declared thereby that there is no other final cause of the universe than the Will alone. — But, if it be so[[fn:2749]], then the belief in the novelty of the world forcing us to admit that this universe could have been created differently as concerns its (respective) causes and effects[[fn:2750]], there would ensue[[fn:2751]] this absurdity that all beings, except man, would exist without any purpose, since the only end that was in view, and which is man, could exist without all these beings.
root.text.Part 3..12.6: Wherefore the only true opinion in my judgment, which is at once consonant with religious beliefs and in agreement with speculative opinions, is this: That it must by no means be believed that all beings exist for the sake of man; but on the contrary, all other beings likewise were created for their own sakes, and not for the sake of aught else. Thus, even according to our opinion which admitts the creation of the world, one cannot seek the final cause of all species of beings; for we maintain that it is by His Will that God has created all parts of the universe, and that some have their end in themselves, whilst others exist for the sake of another thing which has its end in itself. Even as He willed that the human species should exist, so likewise He willed that the celestial spheres and their stars should exist, and so again He willed that the angels[[fn:2752]] should exist. In every being, He has intended that being itself; and whenever the existence of a thing was impossible without being preceded by another thing, He produced the latter first, as for example, sensibility which preceds reason. This opinion has likewise been expressed in the prophetic books, as for example: the Lord has made all things for Himself, למענהו (Proverbs, XVI, 4), where the pronoun Himself may refer to the object (all things). If, however, the suffix הו referred to the subject (the Lord), the sense (of למענהו) would be: because of the essence of God, that is to say, because of His Will, which is His essence, as has been set forth in this treatise[[fn:2753]]. We have explained that the essence of God is also called glory, as in this passage: I beseech Thee, show me Thy glory (Exodus, xxxiii, 18)[[fn:2754]]. According to this, the passage "the Lord has made all things for Himself (or because of His essence)" would resemble this other passage: Even every one that is called by My name: for MY GLORY I have created him, I have formed him; yea, I have made him (Isaiah, xliii, 7); which signifies that, all things whose creation is attributed to Me[[fn:2755]], I have made only because of My Will alone. The words I have formed him; yea, I have made him refer to that which I have set forth, (to wit) that there are beings whose existence is possible only after that of another thing; He would therefore say: I have created this first thing which must necessarily precede, as for example matter (which must precede) every material being; then I have made, within this prior thing, or after it, all that I intended to bring into existence, yet without there being aught else (to guide Me) but the simple Will.
root.text.Part 3..12.7.sub_0: If thou examinest the book which is an infallible guide for those who desire to be guided, and which for this reason has been called Torah[[fn:2756]], thou shalt recognize therein, from the beginning of the account of creation until the end, the idea which we have in view. For it is in no wise declared therein that any thing whatsoever[[fn:2757]] was made for the sake of another thing; but it is said of each of the parts of the universe that God having produced it, its existence answered the purpose. Such is the sense of these words: And God saw that it was good; for thou knowest what we have set forth concerning this maxim: "The Scripture speaks according to the language of men[[fn:2758]]," and טוב, good, is an expression whereby we designate that which is conformable to our purpose[[fn:2759]]. Of the whole it is said: And God saw every thing that He had made, and, behold, it was VERY GOOD (Genesis, i, 31); for everything that was brought forth was so in accordance with the purpose (which was intended), without any defect therein[[fn:2760]], and this is what is expressed by the word מאד, very. Verily, it may be that a thing is good and answers momentarily to our purpose, but that afterwards the purpose fails. We are therefore taught that all these works answered the intention and the purpose of the Creator, and ceased not to remain conformable to that which He had intended. — Suffer not thyself to be led into error by what is said of the stars: to give light upon the earth, and to rule over the day and over the night (Genesis, i, 17 and 18), and believe not that this signifies: in order that they (the stars) might accomplish this action[[fn:2761]]; on the contrary, it was intended only to make known their nature such as it pleased the Creator to give them, I mean, to be luminous and to govern (this lower world). Even so it is said in speaking of man: And have dominion over the fish of the sea, etc. (ibid., v. 28), which does not mean that man was created for that purpose, but merely indicats the nature wherewith God has impressed him. If it be said of the plants that God gave them to men and to other animals (ibid., v. 29), this is what Aristotle and others have also declared[[fn:2762]], and it is manifest that plants were created only for the sake of animals, which cannot dispense with food.
root.text.Part 3..12.7.sub_1: But it is not so with the stars, I mean that they do not exist for our sake, and in order that benefits may come to us therefrom; for, as we have set forth, the words to give light, to rule, do but state the utility which results therefrom and which spreads over this lower world, in accordance with what I have already explained to thee of the nature of the benefits which are continually communicated from one thing to another[[fn:2763]]. If this good which perpetually occurrs be considered in relation to the thing to which it happens, it might seem that this thing, being the object of the benefit, is the final cause of that which has communicated to it its goodness and excellence. Even so any citizen might imagine that the final end of the sovereign is to preserve his house from thieves during the night, which is true up to a certain point; for, his house being guarded and this benefit coming to him from the sovereign, it might seem that the final end of the sovereign is to guard the house of that man. It is in this sense that we must explain every text whose literal meaning would indicate that an exalted thing was made for the sake of that which is inferior to it, which signifies only that this latter thing is a necessary consequence of the nature of the other.
root.text.Part 3..12.8: Thus, we must believe that the creation of all this universe was determined only by the Divine Will; one must seek for it no other cause, nor any other end. Even as we could not seek the final cause of the existence of God, so we could not seek the final cause of His Will, by virtue of which all that has been born and shall be born is such as it is.
root.text.Part 3..12.9.sub_0: One must not therefore hold this erroneous opinion that the celestial spheres and the angels exist only because of us. Already (the Prophet) has declared to us of what value we are[[fn:2764]]: Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket (Isaiah, xl, 15); and indeed, if thou considerest thy substance and that of the celestial spheres, of the stars, and of the Separate Intelligences, thou shalt recognize the truth and thou shalt know that man is indeed the most perfect and noble being that is born of this (inferior) matter, but that, if one compars his being to that of the spheres, and still more to that of the Separate Intelligences, he is but a very small thing, as it is said: Behold, He put no trust in His servants; and His angels He charged with folly: how much less in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust (Job, iv, 18 and 19)? It must be known that the servants (עבדיו) spoken of in this verse are not of the human species. The proof thereof is that it is said thereafter: How much less in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust? But the servants mentioned in this verse are the angels; and likewise the angels intended in this verse are undoubtedly the celestial spheres. Eliphaz himself setts forth this idea in another discourse, in other terms: Behold, says he, He putts no trust in His saints; yea, the heavens are not clean in His sight. How much more abominable and filthy is man (איש), which drinks iniquity (עַוְלָה) like water (ibid., xv, 15 and 16)! It is therefore clear that His saints are the same as His servants and that they are not of the human species; His angels, of whom mention is made in the other verse, are the heavens, and the word תֳּהֳלָה (folly/defect) has the same sense as the words: are not clean in His sight, I mean that they are material beings. But, although they be of the purest and most brilliant matter, they are nevertheless, relatively to the Separate Intelligences, turbid, dark, and without clarity.
root.text.Part 3..12.9.sub_1: If it be said, in speaking of the angels: Behold, He putts no trust in His servants, this signifies that they possess no stable existence; for, according to our opinion, they are created, and even, according to the opinion of those who admit the eternity of the world, they are the effects of a cause, and their role in the universe has neither stability nor fixity, in relation to God, the Necessary Being in the absolute sense[[fn:2765]]. The words how much less (this being) abominable and corrupt correspond to the words how much less them that dwell in houses of clay; it is as though one said: How much less this abominable and corrupt being, man, whom iniquity[[fn:2766]] spread through all his members does infect, that is to say, who is conjoined with privation[[fn:2767]]. The word עולה signifies crookedness (or iniquity), as in בארץ נכחוח יעול, in the land of uprightness he deals unjustly (Isaiah, 26, 10). The word איש, vir, has here the sense of the word אדם, homo; for the human species is sometimes designated by the word איש, vir; as for example מכה איש ומת, he that smits a man (virum) so that he die (Exodus, 21, 10).
root.text.Part 3..12.10: This, then, is what must be believed; for as soon as man knows himself, and is not deceived[[fn:2768]] concerning his own self, and understands every being even as it (truly) is, he finds peace and his thoughts are not troubled in seeking such an end for a thing that has not that end[[fn:2769]], or (in general) in seeking an end for that which has no other end than its existence dependent upon the Divine Will, or, if thou preferrest, upon the Divine Wisdom.
root.text.Part 3..13.0: That which man must likewise consider, in order to know what he himself is worth and not to suffer himself to be misled, is that which has been set forth concerning the dimensions of the spheres and the stars, and the immense distances which separate us therefrom. Verily, since there has been set forth the manner of measuring all distances in relation to the semi-diameter of the earth[[fn:2770]], (it follows that), the measure of the circumference of the earth, and consequently that of its semi-diameter, being known, all distances shall likewise be known. It has therefore been demonstrated that the distance between the centre of the earth and the summit of the sphere of Saturn is a journey of about eight thousand seven hundred years, of three hundred and sixty-five days each, reckoning for each day's journey forty of our statute miles, of which each has two thousand common cubits[[fn:2771]]. Consider this great and formidable distance; of it the Scripture says: Is not God in the height of heaven? and behold the height of the stars, how high they are! (Job, 22, 12). This signifies: Seest thou not that the height of heaven proves how far we are from conceiving the Divinity? For, whereas we find ourselves at this immense distance from that body from which so great a space divids us, so that its substance and most of the effects which it produces are unknown to us, how much more shall this be the case regarding the perception of its Author, who is no body at all?
root.text.Part 3..13.1: — This great distance which has been demonstrated is taken only at the minimum; for between the centre of the earth and the concavity[[fn:2772]] of the sphere of the fixed stars, the distance can in no wise be less, but it is possible that it be several times as much. Indeed, the thickness of the bodies of the spheres has only been determined by demonstration at its minimum, as follows from the treatises On the Distances[[fn:2773]]; and likewise one could not determine exactly the thickness of the (intermediate) bodies which, according to Thabit[[fn:2774]], reason constrains us to admit between each pair of spheres, these bodies having no stars by means of which a demonstration might be made. As for the sphere of the fixed stars, its thickness would form a journey of at least four years' march, as may be concluded from the measure of some[[fn:2775]] of its stars, each of which has a volume exceeding ninety times and more that of the terrestrial globe[[fn:2776]]; but it may be that the thickness of this sphere is yet greater. Regarding the ninth sphere, which causs the whole assembly (of the spheres) to accomplish the diurnal motion[[fn:2777]], its measure is not known at all; for, as it has no stars, we have no means whereby to know its magnitude.
root.text.Part 3..13.2: One must therefore consider how immense are the dimensions of these corporeal beings, and how numerous they are! Now, if the whole earth be but an imperceptible point[[fn:2778]] in relation to the sphere of the (fixed) stars, what shall be the proportion of the human species to the whole of created things? And how then could any one of us imagine that they exist in his favour and for his sake, and that they should serve him as instruments? But this is yet only a comparison between bodies; and what shall it be if thou considerest the being of the (separate) Intelligences?
root.text.Part 3..13.3: However, one might in this regard raise an objection against the opinion of the philosophers. If we were to contend, it might be said, that the final end of these spheres were, for example, to govern a single human individual or several individuals, it would be absurd from the point of view of philosophical speculation; but as we believe that they have for their final end the government of the human species, there is no absurdity (in supposing) that these great individual bodies are destined to bring into existence individuals belonging to species, whose number, according to the doctrine of the philosophers, is infinite. This might be compared to iron instruments of a hundredweight which the craftsman fashions to manufacture a small needle weighing a grain. Now, if it were a question of a single needle, it would indeed be, from a certain point of view[[fn:2779]], a matter of ill economy, although it be not so in an absolute sense; but if one considers that he manufacturs, by means of these heavy instruments, a great quantity of needles of the weight of several hundredweights, the fabrication of these instruments is, in any case, an act of wisdom and good economy. In like manner, the final end of the spheres is to perpetuate birth and corruption, and the final end of these latter is, as has already been said, the existence of the human species. We find Biblical texts and traditions which may serve as support for this idea. Nevertheless, the philosopher might answer this objection by saying: If the difference between the celestial bodies and the individuals of the species subject to birth and corruption consisted only in greatness and smallness, the objection would be well-founded; but as the former are distinguished from the latter by the nobleness of the substance, it would be highly absurd (to suppose) that the more noble should serve as an instrument for the existence of that which is basest and most vile.
root.text.Part 3..13.4: In sum, however, this objection may offer some succour to our belief in the creation of the world[[fn:2780]], and it is this subject which I have principally aimed at in this chapter. Furthermore[[fn:2781]], it is that I have ever heard those who have occupied themselves somewhat with astronomy tax with exaggeration[[fn:2782]] that which the doctors have said regarding distances; for they say clearly that the thickness of each sphere forms a journey of five hundred years, and that between each couple of spheres there is likewise five hundred years of journeying[[fn:2783]]. Now, as there are seven spheres[[fn:2784]], the distance between the seventh sphere — I mean to say its convex part — and the centre of the earth, will form a journey of seven thousand years. Whosoever shall hear this will imagine that there is in these words a great exaggeration and that the distance reaches not that measure. But by the demonstration which has been made concerning distances, thou shalt recognize that the distance between the centre of the earth and the lower part of the sphere of Saturn, which is the seventh, forms a journey of about seven thousand and twenty-four years. As for the distance of which we have spoken (above) and which would form a journey of eight thousand seven hundred years, it reaches unto the concavity of the eighth sphere. If the doctors say that between each couple of spheres there is such a distance, this must be understood of the thickness of the bodies which exist between the spheres[[fn:2785]], and not that there is there a vacuum.
root.text.Part 3..13.5: One must not require that all they have said relative to astronomy be in accord with reality; for the mathematical sciences were imperfect in those times, and if they spoke of these things, it is not that they had received thereon a tradition proceeding from the prophets, but rather because they were the sages of those times in these matters, or because they had heard them from the sages of the epoch. Wherefore, if we find in their writings words conformable to the truth, I shall say neither that they are not true, nor that they are due to chance; on the contrary, the man of a noble character who loves to be just must always hold, as far as possible, to interpreting the words of others in such wise as to reconcile them with that which has been demonstrated of the sublime truths of being[[fn:2786]].
root.text.Part 3..14.0.sub_0: The impossible has a stable and constant nature which is not the work of an agent and which is variable under no condition; wherefore one cannot attribute to God any power in this regard[[fn:2787]]. This is what none of the thinkers[[fn:2788]] in any wise contest, and it is ignored only by those who understand not intelligible notions. If there be dissent among thinkers, it is only with respect to certain imaginable things which, according to some thinkers, are in the category of the impossible which God Himself has not the power to change[[fn:2789]], and which, according to others, are in the domain of the possible, which it depends upon the Divine omnipotence to bring into existence at will. Thus, for example, the union of contraries at the same instant and in the same subject, the transformation of essentials[[fn:2790]], I mean the change of substance into accident and of accident into substance, or the existence of a corporeal substance without accident, all this is, for every thinker, of the category of the impossible. Likewise, it is impossible that God should call into existence His like, or that He should render Himself non-existent, or that He should become corporeal, or that He should change, and one cannot attribute to Him the power to do aught of all this. As for the question of knowing whether He can produce an accident alone which be not in a substance, a sect of thinkers, namely the Mutazilites, have imagined this and believed it to be in the domain of the possible[[fn:2791]], whilst others have judged it impossible. It is true that those who have professed the existence of an accident without a substratum were not led thereto by simple speculation, but by their regard for certain religious doctrines which speculation violently rejects, so that they had recourse to this hypothesis[[fn:2792]]. Likewise, to produce a corporeal thing without making use for that purpose of any pre-existing matter, is, according to us, in the category of the possible; but, according to the philosophers, it is impossible[[fn:2793]]. Likewise, the philosophers will say that it is in the domain of the impossible to produce a square whose diagonal be equal to the side, or a solid angle which be surrounded by four plane right angles[[fn:2794]], or other like things. But many a man who is ignorant of mathematics and who knows of these things only the simple words, without conceiving the idea thereof, will believe them possible.
root.text.Part 3..14.0.sub_1: Would that I knew[[fn:2795]] whether this be a door set open at the pleasure of every man, so that it be permitted to each to maintain, concerning everything that should come into his mind, that it is possible, whilst another should maintain that, by its very nature, the thing is impossible! Or else, is there something which closs this door and which defends the entry thereof, so that man be obliged to declare decidedly that such a thing is impossible by its nature[[fn:2796]]? The touchstone by which one must examine this, is it the imaginative faculty or the intellect? and how shall one distinguish between the things of the imagination and the intelligible? In effect, man is often at variance with another or with himself upon a thing which seems to him to be possible, and which he maintains to be possible[[fn:2797]] by its very nature, whilst it may be objected[[fn:2798]] that it is the imagination, and not the intellect, which makes this thing to appear possible. Is there consequently something which may serve as a criterion between the imaginative faculty and the intellect? and is this something outside of the one and the other, or is it by the intellect itself that one distinguishes between the intellect and that which is of the domain of the imagination? All this may give rise to researches which would merit being well deepened[[fn:2799]]; but this is not the aim of our chapter.
root.text.Part 3..14.1: Nevertheless, it is manifest that, according to all opinions and systems, there exist impossible things the existence of which is inadmissible, and in respect of which no power can be attributed unto God; yet, if it be true that God cannot change them, there is therein on His part neither weakness nor lack of power, and consequently they are necessary[[fn:2800]] (in themselves) and are not the work of an agent. It is manifest also that divergence can only exist in respect of those things which might, by hypothesis, be placed in either of the two categories[[fn:2801]], whether in that of the impossible or in that of the possible. Thou must well possess thy mind of this truth.
root.text.Part 3..15.0: The philosophers have professed concerning God a most grievous heresy[[fn:2802]], touching the knowledge He may possess of that which is without Him, and they have suffered a fall from which neither they nor those who have embraced their opinion shall be able to arise[[fn:2803]]. I will cause thee to understand the doubts which have cast them into this heresy, as well as the doctrine which our religion professes in this regard, and that which we oppose unto the evil and absurd opinions which they maintain concerning the divine omniscience.
root.text.Part 3..15.1: That which above all caused them to fall therein, and which led them thither at the first, is the lack of goodly order which seems at first sight to be remarked in the circumstances of human individuals; for, whilst certain virtuous men lead a life full of evils and sorrows, there are wicked men who lead a life happy and pleasant. They were therefore brought to pose the dilemma which thou shalt hear. It must necessarily be admitted, said they, one of two things: either that God knows naught of these individual conditions and perceivs them not, or that He perceivs and knows them. This is a rigorous dilemma. If, they continued, He perceivs and knows them, one must necessarily admit one of these three cases: either that He orders them and establishes therein the best, the most perfect, and the most complete order; or that He is unable to order them and has no power therein; or finally that, while knowing them and being able to introduce rule and goodly order, He neglects it, either because He disdains and despiss them, or because He is envious of them.
