Thus find we such a one among men who is able to do good unto another and knows the need of the latter to receive his benefit; but yet, through an evil disposition, through passion or jealousy, he envies him this good and does it not. One is evidently constrained to admit one of these diverse cases[[fn:2804]]. Indeed, every man who knows a certain thing either takes care of the governance of that thing of which he has knowledge, or he neglects it, as one neglects, for example, in his house the governance of cats or of things yet more base; but even he who occupies himself with a thing is sometimes incapable of governing it, even should he so desire. Having enumerated these different cases, they judged peremptorily that, of the three hypotheses admissible in respect of him who has knowledge of a thing, two are impossible[[fn:2805]] in respect of God: to wit, (to admit) that He be powerless, or that, being all-powerful, He should not concern Himself (with the things He knows); for this would be to suppose in Him vice or impotence. Far be both from Him! Of all the cases enumerated, there remain therefore but two (admissible in relation to God): either He knows absolutely naught of these conditions of men, or He knows them and orders them in the best manner. But, since we find them without order, without rule, and without a rigorous sequence, this proves that He knows them in no wise. Behold then what caused them to fall at the first into this great heresy.—All that I have just summarized of their different hypotheses, whilst bringing into relief[[fn:2806]] that which gave rise to their error, thou shalt find set forth and commented upon in the treatise of Alexander of Aphrodisias (entitled) On Governance[[fn:2807]].
root.text.Part 3..15.2: Thou shalt be astonished to see how they have fallen into something worse than that which they sought to avoid, and how they themselves were ignorant of a thing unto which they constantly called our attention and which they incessantly pretended to explain to us. If I say that they have fallen into something worse than that which they sought to avoid, it is because, in wishing to avoid attributing unto God heedlessness (of human affairs), they have declared that He is ignorant (of these things) and that all which passes in this world is for Him a mystery which He perceivs not. If, furthermore, I say that they were themselves ignorant of the thing unto which they were constantly calling our attention, it is because they considered being from the point of view of the conditions of human individuals, who themselves cause the evils wherewith they are afflicted, or receive them from the fatal nature of matter, as (these philosophers) cease not to say and to develop[[fn:2808]]. We have already set forth in this regard that which was necessary[[fn:2809]]. Having established themselves upon a foundation which destroys all goodly principles and which disfigurs the beauty of every true opinion[[fn:2810]], they have endeavoured to put away the absurdity which it presents[[fn:2811]], by pretending that it is impossible, for several reasons, to attribute unto God the knowledge of these individual things. First (say they), particular things are perceived only by the senses and not by the intellect; but God perceivs not by means of a sense. Next, particular things are infinite, whilst science consists in encompassing; but that which is infinite cannot be encompassed by science. Finally, the knowledge of things which happen, and which without contradiction are particular, would cause God to undergo a species of change; for it would be a successive renewal of knowledge. As for that which we maintain, we who are believers, that God knows these things before they are born, they say that we profess therein two absurdities: first, that science can have for its object pure non-being; secondly, that the knowledge of that which is in potentiality and the knowledge of that which is in act are one and the same thing[[fn:2812]]. There has been among them a conflict of opinions[[fn:2813]]: some have said that God knows only the species and not the individuals, whilst others have maintained that He knows absolutely naught outside of His essence, so that, according to this latter opinion, there would not be in Him a multiplicity of knowledges[[fn:2814]].
root.text.Part 3..15.3: Finally, there have been philosophers who believed as we do, that God knows all things and that absolutely naught is hidden from Him. These are certain great men prior to Aristotle, whom Alexander also mentions in the said treatise, but whose opinion he rejects, saying that what above all refuts it is that we see virtuous men smitten with evils, whilst the wicked enjoy all manner of happiness.
root.text.Part 3..15.4: In sum, it is manifest that all the philosophers, had they found the circumstances of human individuals so ordered that even the vulgar might discern therein a proper harmony, would have refrained from embarking upon all this speculation[[fn:2815]], and would not have refuted one another. But that which gave the first occasion for this speculation was the consideration of the respective conditions of virtuous and wicked men, which conditions, in their opinion, were not rightly ordered, as the ignorant among us were wont to say: The way of the Lord is not equal (Ezek. xxxiii. 17).
root.text.Part 3..15.5: Having shown that the theory of divine omniscience and that of providence are interconnected, I shall proceed to set forth the opinions of thinkers concerning Providence; and thereafter I shall endeavour to resolve[[fn:2816]] the difficulties raised against the knowledge which God is said to possess of particulars.
root.text.Part 3..16.0: The opinions of men touching Providence are five in number. All these are ancient; I mean to say, they are opinions which were heard expressed in the time of the prophets, from the first appearance of the True Law, which illuminats all this darkness.
root.text.Part 3..16.1: I. The first opinion is that which maintains that there exists no Providence whatsoever occupying itself with anything in all this universe; that all which therein exists, as well the heavens as other things[[fn:2817]], is due to chance and to certain dispositions[[fn:2818]], and that there is no being who regulats, governs, or cars for anything. Such is the opinion of Epicurus, who likewise professes the doctrine of atoms, believing that these intermingle according to chance, and that whatever springs therefrom is the work of hazard[[fn:2819]]. The infidels in Israel have likewise professed this opinion, and it is of them that it has been said: They have belied the Lord, and said, It is not he (Jer. v. 12). Aristotle has demonstrated that this opinion is untenable, and that the existence of things cannot be due to chance, but that, on the contrary, there is a being who ordains and governs them[[fn:2820]]. We have already touched upon this question in what has preceded[[fn:2821]].
root.text.Part 3..16.2.sub_0: II. The second opinion belongs to those who believe that certain things pertain to a Providence and are under the government of a being who ruls and ordains them, whilst others are abandoned to chance. Such is the opinion of Aristotle; I shall here set forth unto thee in summary what he thinks concerning Providence. He believs that divine Providence extends over the spheres and over that which they contain, and that by reason thereof their individual bodies (the stars) remain ever as they are[[fn:2822]]. Alexander says expressly that, according to the opinion of Aristotle, divine Providence ends at the sphere of the moon[[fn:2823]], and this is a branch which is attached to the fundamental doctrine of the eternity of the world. Verily, he believs that Providence corresponds to the nature of beings; consequently, the celestial spheres and the bodies which they contain being permanent, that which constituts Providence in their regard is to remain ever invariably in the same state; but, even as these beings give existence to other beings whose species alone, but not the individuals, exist perpetually[[fn:2824]], so there emanats from the Providence in question something which has for its effect the preservation and perpetuation of species, whilst the permanence of individuals is impossible. Nevertheless, the individuals of each species are not destined to an absolute abandonment; on the contrary, as soon as this (sublunary) matter is sufficiently pure to receive the form of growth[[fn:2825]], it is also endowed with forces which preserve it for a certain time, by attracting to itself that which is suitable and by expelling that which can be of no utility[[fn:2826]]. If it be more pure, so as to receive the form of sensibility, it is endowed with other forces which preserve and keep it, and with another faculty which gives it movement to direct itself toward what is suitable and to flee from what is contrary; moreover, each individual is endowed according to the needs of the species. If, finally, it has a purity yet greater, so as to receive the form of Intelligence, then it is endowed with another force, by means of which every man, according to his degree of perfection, governs, thinks, and reflects upon that which may serve to prolong the duration of the individual and to preserve the species[[fn:2827]].
root.text.Part 3..16.2.sub_1: As touching the other motions which betide all individuals[[fn:2828]] of a species, they are, according to Aristotle, the result of chance, and not the work of a Being who governs and ordains. Thus, for example, if there blows a wind more or less violent, it shall indubitably cause leaves to fall from a certain tree, shall break the branches of another, shall hurl down stones from a certain wall[[fn:2829]], shall cover with dust a certain plant so as to destroy it, and shall agitate certain waters[[fn:2830]] in such wise that a vessel found therein shall perish and all the crew, or a part thereof, shall be drowned. According unto him (Aristotle), there is no distinction between the falling of a leaf or a stone and the submersion of those virtuous and distinguished men who were within the ship; likewise, he makes no distinction between an ox which causs the death of a host of ants by depositing its excrements thereon, and a building whose foundations give way and which, in its collapse, causs the death of all those who are praying therein. Neither is there any distinction, according to him, between a cat that meets a mouse and tears it, a spider that devours a fly, and a hungry lion that meets a prophet and tears him[[fn:2831]]. In sum, here is the substance of his opinion: All that which he beheld continuing with sequence, without interruption and without its course undergoing any change, such as the conditions of the celestial spheres, or that which follows a certain rule and fails therein only by exception[[fn:2832]], as do physical things, he attributed to a governance, that is to say (he believed) that Divine Providence accompanied it; but that which he beheld not following any rules and not being subject to a certain law, such as the conditions of the individuals of each species, whether plant, or animal, or man[[fn:2833]], he said was the effect of chance and not of a governance, that is to say, that Divine Providence did not accompany it. He even deemed it impossible that these conditions should depend upon Providence, which connects with his opinion concerning the eternity of the world, and according to which it is impossible that all that which is should be otherwise than it is. Amongst us also, there were heretics who admitted this opinion, and they are those who said: The Lord has forsaken the earth (Ezek. ix. 9).
root.text.Part 3..16.3.sub_0: III. The third opinion is the contrary of the second. It is the opinion of those who believe that there is in the universe absolutely nothing, neither in details nor in the whole[[fn:2834]], which happens by chance, and that all, on the contrary, is the effect of a will, of an intention, and of a governance. Now, it is manifest that all that which is governed is the object of a knowledge[[fn:2835]]. This is what is professed by the Muslim sect of the Ash’arites[[fn:2836]]; and from this opinion there result great absurdities whose burden they have accepted and whose necessity they have endured. Indeed, they agree with Aristotle when he claims that there is equality between the falling of a leaf and the death of a human individual: even so it is, say they; nevertheless, it is not by chance that the wind has blown, it is God, on the contrary, who has set it in motion. Neither is it the wind which has caused the leaves to fall; but each leaf has fallen in consequence of a judgment and a decree of God, and it is He who has caused it to fall at this moment and in this place, so that the time of its fall could be neither hastened nor delayed, and that it could not fall in another place, all this having been decreed from all eternity. According to this opinion, they were constrained to admit that every motion and rest of animals is predestined, and that man has absolutely no power to do or not to do a thing. It follows likewise from this opinion that the nature of the possible is lacking to things of this sort, and that they are all either necessary or impossible; and indeed, they were forced to admit this, and they said that what we call possible, as, for example, that Zeid be standing and that Amr arrive, is possible only in relation to us, but that, in relation to God, there is absolutely nothing possible, and all is either necessary or impossible. It follows further from this opinion that religious laws possess no utility, since the man for whom every religious law was made has not the power to do anything whatsoever, and that he can neither fulfill that which was commanded him, nor abstain from that which was forbidden him.
root.text.Part 3..16.3.sub_1: The people of this sect pretend that it has pleased God to send (prophets), to command, to forbid, to inspire terror[[fn:2837]], to cause hope or fear, although we have no power to act; He can therefore impose upon us even things impossible, and it may be that, whilst obeying the commandment, we be punished, or that, whilst disobeying, we be rewarded. Finally, it follows from this opinion that the actions of God have no final end. They bear the burden of all these absurdities to safeguard this opinion, and they go so far as to maintain that, if we behold an individual born blind or leprous, to whom we cannot attribute any prior sin whereby he might have deserved this, we must say: God has willed it so. And if we behold the virtuous and religious man suffer death in tortures, we must say: "God has willed it so," and there is in this no injustice; for, according to them, it is permitted unto God to inflict punishments upon him who has not sinned and to do good unto the sinner. Their discourses concerning these things are well known[[fn:2838]].
root.text.Part 3..16.4: IV. The fourth opinion is the opinion of those who believe that man has the power (to act); wherefore, according to them, the commandments and the prohibitions, the rewards and the punishments, of which the Law speaks, are altogether in order[[fn:2839]]. They believe that all the actions of God derive from a wisdom, that one could not attribute injustice unto Him, and that He punishes not the man of good. The Mu’tazilites also admit this opinion, although, according to them, the power of man is not absolute[[fn:2840]]. They also admit that God has knowledge of the falling of this leaf and of the motion of this ant, and that Providence extends over all beings. This opinion also contains absurdities and contradictions. As for the absurd, here it is: If a man be infirm from birth, although he has not yet sinned, they say that this is the effect of divine wisdom and that it is better for this individual to be thus fashioned rather than to be well-constituted. We know not (in what consists) this benefit, although this has befallen him, not to punish him, but to do him good. They answer in like manner[[fn:2841]], when the virtuous man perishes, that it is in order that his reward be so much the greater in the world to come. They have even gone further: when it was asked of them why God is just toward man without being so also toward other creatures, and for what sin a certain animal is slaughtered, they had recourse to this absurd answer[[fn:2842]], that it is better for it (the animal), in order that God may reward it in another life[[fn:2843]]. Yea (say they), even the flea and the louse which have been killed must find for this a reward with God; and likewise, if this mouse, which is innocent, has been torn by a cat or by a kite, it is divine wisdom, say they, which required that it should be so with this mouse, and God will reward it in another life for that which has befallen it.
root.text.Part 3..16.5: I do not believe I ought to blame any of the partisans of these three opinions on Providence, for each of them was led by a grave necessity to the opinion which he professed. Aristotle held to that which seems manifest by the nature of being. The Ash’arites desired to avoid attributing to God ignorance in any matter whatsoever, for it is not fitting to say that He knows one particularity and is ignorant of another. They therefore had recourse to these absurdities (of which we have spoken) and accepted them. The Mu’tazilites, for their part, desired to avoid attributing unto God iniquity and injustice; but they did not think it fitting to set themselves in opposition to common sense, in such wise as to maintain that there is no iniquity in inflicting pains upon him who has not sinned. Neither did they believe they could admit that the mission of all the prophets and the revelation of the Law had no comprehensible reason; they therefore likewise bore the burden of these absurdities (of which we have spoken), and they were involved in contradictions; for they admit at once that God knows all things and that man has the faculty (to act freely), which, as is easily understood, leads to a manifest contradiction.
root.text.Part 3..16.6: V. The fifth opinion is our own, I mean that of our Law. I shall make known unto thee what the books of our prophets say concerning this matter, and it is likewise that which our doctors have generally admitted. I shall also inform thee of what some of our modern (scholars) have thought, and finally, I shall declare unto thee mine own opinion. I say then, that it is a fundamental principle of the Law of Moses, our master, admitted by all who follow it, that man possesses an absolute power of action; that is to say, that by his nature, by his choice, and by his will, he does all that a man is capable of doing, without there intervening any newly created thing[[fn:2844]]. Likewise (according to this opinion), all species of animals move by their own will alone; for God has so willed it, I mean that it is by the effect of His eternal and primitive will that all animals move according to their free-will, and that man has the power to do all that he wills, or all that he preferrs among the actions of which he is capable. This is a fundamental principle which, thanks be to God, has never been, within our communion[[fn:2845]], the object of any contradiction.
root.text.Part 3..16.7: In like manner, it is one of the fundamental principles of the Law of Moses, our master, that one cannot, in any wise, ascribe injustice to God, and that all the misfortunes that fall upon men, or the benefits that come unto them, whether individually or to many in common, are, according to what these have deserved, the effect of an equitable judgment, in which there is absolutely no injustice. If, therefore, an individual had his hand wounded by a thorn which he should immediately remove, it would be the effect of a punishment; and if there should happen to him the smallest enjoyment, it would be the effect of a reward. All this would be well-deserved, as the Scripture says, for all His ways are judgment (Deut. xxxii. 4), although we be ignorant of the manner in which it was deserved.
root.text.Part 3..16.8.sub_0: Behold then the succinct summary of these different opinions: Of all the varied conditions in which we see human individuals, Aristotle recogniss naught but pure chance; the Ascharites see therein the effect of the divine will alone; the Mo’tazales, the effect of divine wisdom; and we (Israelites) see therein the effect of what the individual has deserved according to his works. Wherefore it might be, according to the Ascharites, that God should cause the good and virtuous man to suffer in this lower world, and condemn him forever to that fire which is said to be in the other world; for, they would say, God has so willed it[[fn:2846]]. But the Mo’tazales think that this would be an injustice, and that the being that has suffered[[fn:2847]], were it even an ant, as I have said, shall have a compensation; for it is divine wisdom that has caused it to suffer, so that it might have a compensation. Finally, we ourselves admit that all that happens to man is the effect of what he has deserved[[fn:2848]], that God is above injustice, and that He punishes only him amongst us who has deserved the punishment. This is what the Law of Moses, our master, says textually, (to wit) that all depends upon merit; and it is also in accordance with this opinion that our doctors generally express themselves. These, indeed, say expressly: “No death without sin, no punishment without crime[[fn:2849]]”; and they say again: “Man is measured according to the measure which he has himself employed,” which is the text of the Mischnâ[[fn:2850]]. Everywhere they say clearly that, for God, justice is an absolutely necessary thing; that is to say, that He rewards the pious man for all his acts of piety[[fn:2851]] and uprightness, even if they had not been commanded him by a prophet, and that He punishes every evil action that an individual has committed, even if it had not been forbidden him by a prophet; for it is forbidden him by the natural sentiment which prohibits injustice and iniquity[[fn:2852]].
root.text.Part 3..16.8.sub_1: “The Holy One,” say they, “withholds from no creature that which it has merited[[fn:2853]].” They say further: “Whosoever says that God is prodigal (in His pardon) deservs to have his bowels torn out; it is true that God is long-suffering, but He reclaims that which is His due[[fn:2854]].” Elsewhere it is said: “He who performs a duty which is prescribed to him (by religion) is not comparable to him who performs it without it being prescribed unto him[[fn:2855]];” they say then clearly that even he upon whom the thing is not imposed (by religion) is rewarded therefor. This principle is constantly reproduced in their words; but there is found in the words of the doctors something more which is not found in the text of the Law, namely the chastisements of love[[fn:2856]], of which some speak. According to this opinion, man would sometimes be smitten with misfortunes, not for having sinned beforehand, but in order that his (future) reward might be all the greater. This is also the opinion of the Mo’tazales; but no text of the Law expresses this idea[[fn:2857]]. Thou must not allow thyself to be led into error by the idea of the trial, when it is said: God did prove Abraham (Gen. xxii. 1); He afflicted thee and suffered thee to hunger, etc. (Deut. viii. 3). Thou shalt hear further on what we have to say upon this subject[[fn:2858]]. Our Law occupies itself only with the conditions of human individuals; but never, in ancient times, had one heard mention in our communion of this compensation (which would be reserved) for animals. Never did any of the doctors make mention thereof; but some moderns among the Guéônim, having heard this from the Mo’tazales, approved it and made it a matter of belief[[fn:2859]].
root.text.Part 3..16.9: I shall now set forth unto thee what I myself think concerning this fundamental principle, to wit, concerning divine Providence. In this belief of which I am about to speak, I do not rely upon demonstrative proofs, but rather upon what has appeared to me to be the manifest intention of the Book of God and of the writings of our prophets. But the opinion which I admit offers less improbability than the preceding opinions and approaches more nearly to the reasoning of the Intellect. It is that I believe that in this lower world, I mean below the sphere of the moon, divine Providence has for its object, as regards individuals, only those of the human species alone; and that it is in this species alone that all the conditions of individuals, as well as the good and evil that happens unto them, are in accordance with merit, as it is said: for all His ways are judgment (Deut. xxxii. 4). As concerns other animals and, with even greater reason, plants, I share the opinion of Aristotle. I believe in no wise that such a leaf has fallen by the effect of a Providence, nor that such a spider has devoured such a fly by reason of a decree of God and by His momentary and particular will, nor that this spittle cast by Zeid fell upon such a midge, in a particular place, and killed it by reason of a judgment and a decree (of God), nor that it is by a particular divine will that such a fish has snatched such a worm from the surface of the water; on the contrary, all this is, in my view, the effect of pure chance, as Aristotle thinks. But, according to my manner of viewing it, divine Providence follows the divine overflow[[fn:2860]]; and the species to which this emanation of the (divine) Intellect is attached, in such a manner as to make of it a being endowed with Intellect and unto whom is manifested all that is manifested unto an intelligent being, (this species, I say) is accompanied by divine Providence, which measurs all its actions, so as to reward or to punish them. Verily[[fn:2861]], if it be true, as he (Aristotle) says, that the foundering of the ship with its crew and the falling of the roof upon the folk in the house were the effect of pure chance, it was nevertheless not, according to our opinion, by the effect of chance that the former entered into the ship and that the latter sat in the house; on the contrary, (this happened) by the effect of the divine will, according to what these people had deserved according to the judgments of God, whose rules are inaccessible to our intellects[[fn:2862]].
root.text.Part 3..16.10.sub_0: That which has led me unto this belief is that I have found no text in the prophetic books which speaks of Divine Providence as extending over any individual animal whatsoever, other than the human individual. The prophets even marvel that Providence should extend over human individuals; for man, and a fortiori any other animal, is too insignificant for God to concern Himself with him: What is man, that Thou takest knowledge of him? etc. (Ps. cxliv, 3); what is the mortal, that Thou art mindful of him? etc. (Ps. viii, 5). Nevertheless, there are found texts which manifestly proclaim that Providence extends over all human individuals and watches over all their actions; for example: He that fashions their hearts alike, who considers all their works (Ps. xxxiii, 15); Thou whose eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of men, to give every one according to his ways (Jeremiah, xxxii, 19); His eyes are upon the ways of man, and He ses all his goings (Job, xxxiv, 21). The Pentateuch also speaks of Providence in regard to human individuals and of the examination to which their actions are subjected; for example: in the day when I visit, I will visit their sin upon them (Exodus, xxxii, 34); whosoever has sinned against Me, him will I blot out of My book (ibid., v. 33); I will destroy that soul (Levit., xxiii, 30); I will set My face (My anger) against that soul (ibid., xx, 6)[[fn:2863]], and many other passages. All the events related of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are an evident proof of individual Providence[[fn:2864]]. As for the individuals of (irrational) animals, the matter is undoubtedly as Aristotle thinks; wherefore it is permitted, and even commanded, to slaughter them and to employ them for our use as it pleass us. That which proves that the care of Providence extends unto animals only in the sense indicated by Aristotle[[fn:2865]], is that the prophet, having seen the tyranny of Nebuchadnezzar and the great carnage which he made of men, says: «O Lord,» says he, «thou makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them,» indicating by these words that these species are abandoned.
root.text.Part 3..16.10.sub_1: Thus does he express himself: Thou makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them; he takes up all of them with the angle, etc. (Habac., i, 14, 15). Yet the prophet declars that it is not so (with men); it is not that they have been abandoned and that Providence has withdrawn from them, but rather that they were to be punished, having deserved that which befell them: O Eternal, says he, Thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O mighty God, Thou hast established them for correction (ibid., v. 12).
root.text.Part 3..16.11: One must not believe that this opinion[[fn:2866]] is refuted by such passages as these: He gives to the beast his food, etc. (Ps. cxlvii, 9); the young lions roar after their prey, etc. (Ps. ciii, 21); Thou openest Thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing (Ps. cxlv, 16); and likewise by this passage of the Doctors: «Sitting (upon His throne), He feeds all, from the horns of the unicorns even unto the eggs of insects[[fn:2867]].» Thou shalt find many similar passages, yet there is naught therein which refuts my opinion; for in all these passages, it is a question of a Providence watching over the species and not over the individuals, and therein is described, as it were, the Divine goodness[[fn:2868]], which prepars for every species the food necessary for it and the means of subsistence. This is clear and evident, and Aristotle likewise thinks that this kind of Providence necessarily exists. At least, this is what Alexander reports in the name of Aristotle, to wit, that the sustenance of each species is placed at the disposal of the individuals; for otherwise, the species would undoubtedly perish, which is clear to any who reflects thereon. — If the Doctors say that «to cause pain unto animals is a thing forbidden by the Law[[fn:2869]],» — which they connect with this passage: wherefore hast thou smitten thine ass (Numbers, xxii, 32)[[fn:2870]], — it is for the sake of our moral perfection, lest we should contract harsh habits, and lest we should cause (animals) to suffer in vain and without any utility, but that, on the contrary, we should apply ourselves to pity and mercy for any animal individual whatsoever, except in case of necessity, when thy soul longs to eat flesh (Deuter., xii, 20); but we must not slaughter through cruelty or for pleasure. Neither can one oppose unto my opinion this other question: «wherefore does God take care of human individuals, without taking the same care of every other animal individual?» for he who should ask this question might as well ask: «wherefore has God granted Intelligence unto man and has not likewise granted it unto all other species of animals?» Verily, one would answer this latter question, in accordance with one of the three preceding opinions: «God has so willed it,» or «His wisdom has so required it,» or «nature has so required it.» But the same answers may be made unto the first question.
root.text.Part 3..16.12: It behoovs thee to understand my opinion thoroughly. Verily, I am far from believing that anything whatsoever can be unknown unto God, or from attributing unto Him impotence; but I believe that Providence depends upon Intelligence, whereunto it is intimately bound. Indeed, Providence can emanate only from an intelligent being, and particularly from Him who is a perfect Intelligence in the highest degree of perfection; whence it follows that he alone unto whom there is attached aught of this emanation (of the Divine Intelligence) shall participate in Providence according to the measure wherewith he participats in Intelligence[[fn:2871]]. Such is, in my view, the opinion which accords with reason[[fn:2872]] and with the texts of the Law. As for the preceding opinions, they admit too much or too little: at times it is an exaggeration which results in a veritable confusion[[fn:2873]], in denying the intelligible and in contesting the sensible[[fn:2874]]; at other times it is too great a reserve[[fn:2875]] which produces most pernicious beliefs concerning the Divinity, destroys the good order in human existence[[fn:2876]], and effacs all the moral and intellectual qualities of man; and here I speak of the opinion of those who refuse to admit Providence for human individuals and who place these upon the same level as the individuals of other animal species.
root.text.Part 3..17.0: Having established that among all species of animals the human species alone is the object of the special care of Providence, this is what I have to add: It is a known thing that there exists no species outside the mind, but that, on the contrary, the species and other universals are things belonging unto the understanding, and that all which exists outside the mind is an individual being, or a collection of individuals[[fn:2877]]. This being known, it will also be known that the Divine emanation which we find united unto the human species, I mean the human intellect, is a thing which has its existence only through individual Intelligences, to wit, through that which has flowed (from the Divine Intelligence) upon Zeid, upon ’Amr, upon Khâled, and upon Becr.
root.text.Part 3..17.1: Such being the case, it follows, according to what I have said in the preceding chapter, that the more a human individual participats in this emanation by reason of his matter being better or worse predisposed, and by his exercise[[fn:2878]], the more shall he be protected by Providence, if it be true, as I have asserted, that Providence depends upon the Intellect. Wherefore Divine Providence shall not watch over all individuals of the human species in an equal manner; on the contrary, it shall protect some more than others, in proportion as their human perfection is greater or less. From this reflection it necessarily follows that Providence shall watch with exceeding care over the prophets, and shall vary according to the rank which they hold in prophecy[[fn:2879]]; and likewise, it shall watch over superior and virtuous men, according to their degree of superiority and virtue; for it is such a degree of the emanation of the Divine Intellect that has caused the prophets to speak, that has guided the actions of virtuous men, or has perfected by science the knowledge of superior men. As for the ignorant and sinful, being deprived of this emanation, they abide in a contemptible state and are ranked with the other species of animals: He is like the beasts that are void of speech (Ps. xlix. 13 and 21)[[fn:2880]]; wherefore it has been accounted a light thing to slay them, and it has even been commanded for the public good[[fn:2881]]. That which has just been said is one of the foundations of religion; I mean to say that it is based upon this principle[[fn:2882]], that Providence watches over every human individual in particular, according to his merit.
root.text.Part 3..17.2: Fix thy attention upon the manner in which Scripture expresses itself regarding Providence protecting the conditions of the patriarchs even unto the smallest details of their occupations and their possessions, as also upon the promises made unto them concerning this protection of Providence. To Abraham it was said: I am thy shield (Gen. xv. 1); to Isaac: I will be with thee, and will bless thee (ibid., xxvi. 3); to Jacob: I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest (ibid., xxviii. 15); to the prince of the prophets: Certainly I will be with thee (Exod. iii. 12); to Joshua: As I was with Moses, so I will be with thee (Josh. i. 5). By all these expressions it is declared that Providence watched over them according to the measure of their perfection. — Concerning Providence watching over superior men and neglecting the ignorant, it is said: He will keep the feet of His holy ones, but the wicked shall be silent in darkness; for by strength shall no man prevail (1 Sam. ii. 9). This means that if certain individuals be preserved from misfortunes, whilst others fall thereinto, it is not by reason of their bodily strength and physical dispositions: for by strength shall no man prevail; but it is, on the contrary, by reason of perfection and (moral) imperfection, that is to say, according as they approach or remove themselves from God. Wherefore they that are near unto Him enjoy a perfect protection: He will keep the feet of His holy ones, whilst they that are far from Him are exposed to all the strokes of chance, nothing protecting them against accidents, as happens unto him that walks in darkness and whose destruction is certain. It is said again concerning Providence watching over superior men: He keeps all his bones (Ps. xxxiv. 21); the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous (ibid., v. 16); when he calls upon Me, I will answer him (Ps. xci. 15). The texts that treat of this subject, I mean of Providence watching over human individuals according to the measure of their perfection and their superiority, are too numerous to be enumerated. The philosophers likewise have spoken in this sense. Abu-Nasr (Al-Farabi), in the introduction to his commentary on the Nicomachean Ethics of Aristotle, expresses himself in these terms: “Those who possess the faculty of causing their souls to pass from one moral quality to another[[fn:2883]] are, as Plato has said, those whom Divine Providence protects the most[[fn:2884]].”
root.text.Part 3..17.3: Thou seest now how this manner of reasoning has led us to recognize the truth of what all the prophets have said in this regard, namely, that Providence protects every individual in particular, according to the measure of his perfection, and how this is necessary from the viewpoint of speculation, if it be true, as we have said, that Providence depends upon the Intellect. It would not, therefore, be fitting to profess the opinion put forth by some philosophical sects, namely, that Providence exists for the species (human) and not for individuals; for individuals alone having a real existence outside the understanding[[fn:2885]], it is to these individuals that the Divine Intellect is attached, and consequently Providence also exists for these individuals.
root.text.Part 3..17.4: Examine this chapter with the greatest care; then all the fundamental principles of religion shall appear unto thee perfect and conformable[[fn:2886]] to speculative and philosophical opinions; the improbabilities shall vanish, and thou shalt have a clear and true idea of Providence.
root.text.Part 3..17.5: Having related the opinion of thinkers concerning Providence and the manner in which God governs the universe, I shall now also summarize the opinion of our communion concerning omniscience, and what I myself have to say in this regard.
root.text.Part 3..18.0: It is undoubtedly a primary notion[[fn:2887]] that God must unite within Himself all perfections, and that all imperfections must be removed from Him. It is also well-nigh a primary notion that ignorance of aught whatsoever is an imperfection, and that God can be ignorant of nothing. But that which has led certain thinkers, as I have said, to maintain boldly that He knows one thing and knows not another, is their imagination that the conditions of human individuals lack good order; and yet these conditions, for the most part, are not merely natural conditions, but depend at the same time upon man, who possesses free will and reflection[[fn:2888]].
root.text.Part 3..18.1: Already have the prophets declared that the ignorant, in order to prove that God has no knowledge of our actions, base themselves upon the well-being and tranquility which we behold the wicked enjoy, which may lead the pious man to believe that it is of no utility that he applies himself to good and endurs the pains caused him by the opposition of others[[fn:2889]].
root.text.Part 3..18.3: All that I purposed in this chapter was to show that this is a very ancient way of thinking, I mean to say this error of the ignorant who deny that God has knowledge (of human things), because the conditions of human individuals, which by their nature are in the category of the possible, lack good order: And the children of Israel, it is said, did secretly those things that were not right against the Lord (II Kings, xvii. 9). In the Midrash (it is said on this subject): “What did they say? This pillar, said they, neither ses, nor hears, nor speaks,[[fn:2897]]” that is to say: they imagined that God knows not these (human) conditions and that He addresses to the prophets neither commandment nor prohibition. The cause of all this, and what, according to them, is a proof thereof, is that the conditions of human individuals are not as each of us believs they ought to be. Seeing therefore that things did not come to pass according to their desire, they said: The Lord ses us not (Ezek. viii. 12), and Zephaniah says in speaking of them: Those who say in their heart, The Lord will not do good, neither will He do evil (Zeph. i. 12).
root.text.Part 3..18.4: As touching that which is (verily) to be thought concerning the omniscience of God, I shall declare unto thee mine opinion thereon, after having made known unto thee the principles whereon there is general agreement, and which no intelligent man can in any wise contest.
root.text.Part 3..19.0: One matter whereon there is agreement, is that no new knowledge can accrue to God, in such wise that He should know now that which He knew not aforetime[[fn:2898]]. Neither can He, even according to the opinion of those who admit the attributes, possess manifold and numerous knowledges[[fn:2899]]. This being demonstrated, we, the followers of the Law[[fn:2900]], do say that, by a single knowledge, He knows manifold and numerous things, and that, in respect of God, the variety of things known implies not a variety of knowledges, as is the case in respect of ourselves. Likewise, we say that all these things newly occurred, God knew them before they existed, and He has known them from all eternity. Consequently, no new knowledge has accrued to Him; for, when He knows that such a one, who exists not now, shall exist at such a time and shall return into nothingness after having existed for a certain season, His knowledge receivs no increase when that person comes into existence as He knew beforehand. There is then naught come into being which was unknown to Him; but there is come into being something whose future birth was known to Him from all eternity, even as it has been realized.
root.text.Part 3..19.1: But, from this belief (it may be objected), it would follow that (Divine) knowledge has for its very object things which exist not, and that it encompasses the infinite[[fn:2901]]. And this is indeed what we believe. We maintain that it is in no wise impossible that the knowledge of God should have for its object things which exist not yet, but whose future existence He knows beforehand and which He is able to bring into being; only that which never exists, that is what is, in regard to the knowledge of God, absolute non-being, which this knowledge cannot have for its object, even as our own knowledge cannot have for its object that which for us has no existence[[fn:2902]]. But that which presents a (real) difficulty, is to admit that it (Divine knowledge) encompasses the infinite. Certain thinkers have had recourse to this assertion: that, in a certain sense, Divine knowledge attaches to the species and extends thereby over all the individuals of the species[[fn:2903]]; such is the opinion to which all theologians have perforce been led by speculation[[fn:2904]]. However, the philosophers have maintained in an absolute manner that Divine knowledge cannot have non-being for its object, and that no knowledge can encompass the infinite; now (said they), as no new knowledge can accrue to God, it is inadmissible that He should learn any of the things newly occurred, and, consequently, He knows only things stable and invariable[[fn:2905]]. Unto some among them, another doubt arose: even though, said they, He should know only stable things, His knowledge would be manifold; for the multitude of things known implies the multiplicity of knowledges, each thing known supposing a special knowledge. Consequently (they concluded), He knows only His own essence[[fn:2906]].
root.text.Part 3..19.2: For my part, I deem the cause of all these perplexities to be that men have established a relation between our knowledge and that of God, so that each party, considering all that is impossible for our own knowledge, has imagined that it is necessarily the same[[fn:2907]] for Divine knowledge, or at least has found therein difficulties. In sum, the philosophers are in this matter to be blamed far more than any other party; for it is they who have demonstrated that, in the essence of God, there is no multiplicity, that God has no attribute outside His essence, and that, on the contrary, His knowledge and His essence are one and the same thing. It is they also who have demonstrated that our intellects are incapable of grasping His essence in all its reality, as we have set forth; how then can they have the pretension to comprehend His knowledge, since this latter is not a thing outside His essence? When we say that our intellects are incapable of comprehending His essence, do we not say thereby that they are incapable of comprehending how He has knowledge of things?[[fn:2908]] Verily, this knowledge is not of the same species as ours, that we might judge thereof by analogy. It is, on the contrary, a thing totally different; and even as there is there an essence of a necessary existence, an essence wherefrom, according to the opinion of the philosophers, all beings have emanated by necessity, or which, according to our opinion, has produced from nothingness all that is outside itself, in like manner do we say that this essence perceivs all that is outside itself, and that naught of that which exists[[fn:2909]] is unknown to it, but that there is nothing in common between our knowledge and His, even as there is naught in common between our essence and His. It is only the homonymy of the word knowledge which has given rise to the error; for there is therein but community of names, whilst for the real sense there is complete divergence. This, then, is what has led to the absurd, because it was imagined that all that pertains to our knowledge, pertains also to that of God[[fn:2910]].
root.text.Part 3..19.3: That which, for me, results likewise from the texts of the Law, is that, when God knows that any possible being whatsoever shall come into existence, this in no wise removs that possible being from the nature of the possible; on the contrary, it preservs that nature, and the (anticipated) knowledge of that which shall arise from possible things does not necessarily require that they should subsequently be realized in one of the two possible manners[[fn:2911]]. This is also one of the fundamental principles of the Law of Moses, whereon there is neither doubt nor division of opinions[[fn:2912]]. Were it not so, it would not have been said[[fn:2913]]: When thou buildest a new house, then thou shalt make a battlement for thy roof, etc. (Deuter. xxii. 8), and likewise: Lest he die in the battle, and another man take her (ibid., xx. 7). All the sacred legislation, that which it commands and that which it forbidds, supposs this principle, to wit, that Divine foreknowledge does not remove the possible from its nature; but for our weak intellects, this is right difficult to comprehend.
root.text.Part 3..19.4: Observe now in how many points, according to the adherents of the Law, the science of God differs from our own: 1st, In that this science, which is one, embraces a multitude of objects of diverse species. 2nd, In that it relats to that which exists not yet. 3rd, In that it relats to that which is infinite. 4th, In that it undergoes no change by the perception of things newly arisen; and yet it might seem that to know a thing shall exist is not the same as to know it has already come into existence, for in the latter case there would be this further circumstance, that what was only in potentiality has passed into act[[fn:2914]]. 5th, In that, according to the opinion of our Law, the divine prescience decids not[[fn:2915]] for one of the two possible cases, although God knows in a precise manner which of the two shall come to pass[[fn:2916]]. — I would fain know in what respect, even according to the opinion of those who consider (divine) science as an attribute added (unto the essence of God), our science resembls His! Is there here aught else than a simple community of names? But certes, according to our own opinion, who say that His science is in no wise a thing added to His essence, there must needs be between His science and our own a substantial difference, such as that which exists between the substance of heaven and that of the earth. This is also what the prophets have clearly stated: My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, says the Lord; for, as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts (Isaiah, 55, 8-9).
root.text.Part 3..19.5: In sum, thus do I resume my thought: Even as, without comprehending the true essence of God, we nevertheless know that His being is the most perfect being, that He is affected, in no wise, by imperfection, nor change, nor passion; even so, without comprehending what His science is in reality, since it is His essence, we nevertheless know that He cannot now know and now be ignorant; I mean to say that no new science can come unto Him, that His science can have neither multiplicity nor end, that none of the things which exist can be unknown to Him, and that the knowledge He has of these things leavs their nature intact, the possible preserving the nature of possibility. If in the whole of these propositions there be some which seem to involve contradiction, it is because we judge of them by our own science, which has nothing in common with the science of God, save the name. Likewise, the word intention is applied, by simple homonymy, to that which we ourselves have in view, and to that which God is said to have in view. Finally, in like manner, the word providence[[fn:2917]] is used by homonymy of that wherewith we ourselves are preoccupied, and of that wherewith God is said to be preoccupied. The truth is, consequently, that science, intention, and providence, attributed to us, have not the same sense as when they are attributed to God. It is therefore when one takes in one and the same sense the two providences, the two sciences or the two intentions, that the difficulties arise and the doubts of which we have spoken are born[[fn:2918]]; but when it is known that all which is attributed to us differs from that which is attributed to God, the truth becoms manifest. The difference that exists between these things attributed to God and the same things attributed to us has been clearly enunciated by these words: Your ways are not my ways, as we have previously stated.
root.text.Part 3..20.0: There is a great difference between the knowledge which the artificer possesses of the work he has produced and that which another possesses of this same work. Indeed, if the work has been executed conformably to the science of the artificer[[fn:2919]], then the latter, in executing his work, has but followed his science[[fn:2920]]; but for any other who contemplats this work and acquirs a perfect knowledge thereof, the science follows the work[[fn:2921]]. Thus, for example, the artificer who has made this box, in which, by the flowing of water, weights are moved, so as to indicate the hours which have passed of the day or of the night, knows and understands perfectly the whole quantity of water that must flow, the change of position of this flow, every thread that is pulled and every ball[[fn:2922]] that descends. If he knows all these movements, it is not because he considers the movements which are happening at this moment; it is the contrary which occurrs, for the movements which take place at this moment happen only conformably to his science. But it is not so for him who contemplats this machine; for the latter, at every movement he ses, acquirs a new knowledge, and his knowledge ceass not to increase and to be renewed successively by observation, until he acquirs thereby the knowledge of the whole machine. Wert thou to suppose the movements of this machine infinite, the observer could never acquire a perfect knowledge thereof. It is impossible also that the observer should know any of these movements before it takes place; for what he knows, he knows only in consequence of that which occurrs.
root.text.Part 3..20.1: Even so it is with the whole of the universe and its relation to our science and to that of God. Verily, what we know, we know only in consequence of the contemplation of beings; wherefore our science extends neither over future things, nor over that which is infinite; but our knowledge is renewed and multiplied according to the things of which we acquire knowledge. It is not so with God; I mean to say that it is not from things that the knowledge He has of them comes to Him, so that there would be therein multiplicity and renewal (of sciences); on the contrary, these things depend upon His science, which has preceded them and has established them as they are, whether separate beings, or material and permanent individuals, or material beings, individually variable, but which (in their whole) follow an imperishable and unalterable order[[fn:2923]]. For God, therefore, there is no multiple science, and nothing new can occur in His science, which is unalterable[[fn:2924]]; for, in knowing the whole reality of His unalterable essence, He knows by that very fact all that must necessarily result from His actions[[fn:2925]]. To put forth efforts to understand how this is done would be as though we put forth efforts that we might be He (God) and that our perception might be His[[fn:2926]]. Thus, therefore, he who sincerely seeks the truth must believe that nothing whatsoever is unknown to God, and that, on the contrary, all is manifest to His science, which is His essence, but that it is absolutely impossible for us to know this kind of perception[[fn:2927]]. If we knew how to account for it, we should ourselves possess the intelligence which gives this kind of perception[[fn:2928]]; but that is a thing which no being, save God, possesses, and which is itself the divine essence. Thou must well penetrate thyself with this; for I affirm that this is a very profound thought and a true opinion, in which, if one goes deep into it, one will find neither error nor false appearance, (an opinion) which offers no improbability, and by which one attributs to God no imperfection. Certes, these sublime and grave questions could in no wise be the object of a demonstration, neither according to the opinion we profess, we the followers of the Law, nor according to the opinion of the philosophers, however much they may be divided elsewhere upon the problem (which occupies us). For all subjects, therefore, which are not susceptible of being demonstrated, one must follow the method we have followed for the problem in question, I mean the problem of the omniscience of God[[fn:2929]]. Understand this well.
root.text.Part 3..21.0: The history of Job, so strange and so astonishing[[fn:2930]], relats to the subject wherewith we are occupied; I mean that it is a parable which has for its aim to set forth the opinions of men concerning Providence. Thou knowest that certain doctors say expressly: “Job never existed, and this is but a parable[[fn:2931]].” Even those who believe that he existed and that it is a history which (really) happened, know not how to assign to him[[fn:2932]] either time or place. Some doctors say that he existed in the time of the patriarchs; others say, in the time of Moses; others again, in the time of David; others finally say that he was of those who returned from Babylon. But all this does but confirm the opinion of those who say that he never existed. In sum, whether he existed or not, the fact remains that all readers have been cast into perplexity by his history such as it is related to us[[fn:2933]]; so that there have been objected against the science and the Providence of God what I have already mentioned[[fn:2934]], to wit, that the virtuous and perfect man, full of probity in his actions, and who has the greatest care to avoid sins, is yet smitten, stroke upon stroke, with great misfortunes, in his fortune, in his children, and in his person, without having deserved it by any sin whatsoever. According to both opinions again, whether Job existed or not, the prologue of the book, I mean the discourse of Satan, the words which God addresses to Satan, Job delivered into the power of the latter, all this (say I), for every intelligent man, is indubitably a parable. Nevertheless, this is not a parable such as there are many, but a parable to which are attached profound thoughts, things which form the mystery of the universe[[fn:2935]], and which serves to clear up great obscurities and to manifest the highest truths[[fn:2936]]. I shall tell thee of it all that can be told[[fn:2937]], and I shall relate the words of the doctors who have awakened my attention to all that I have been able to understand of this important parable.
root.text.Part 3..21.1: The first thing that must engage thy attention are the words: There was in the land of 'OUZ (Hus) a man (Job, I. 1), in which a homonym is employed, to wit, Uz (עוץ); for it is at once the name of a man: his first-born Uz (Genesis, 22, 21), and the imperative of a verb (expressing the idea of) to reflect, to meditate, as for example עוצו עצה, take counsel (Isaiah, 8, 10). It is therefore as if one said: Meditate upon this parable[[fn:2938]], reflect thereon, seek to penetrate its meaning, and behold what the true opinion is[[fn:2939]]. Afterward it is related that the sons of God (the angels) came to present themselves before the Lord, and that Satan presented himself in the midst of them[[fn:2940]]. It is not said “the sons of God and Satan came to present themselves before the Lord,” so that all would have been there by the same title[[fn:2941]]; but the expression used is: The sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan also came in the midst of them (Job, 1, 6; II, 1). By this manner of expression is designated one who came without being intended or his presence sought, but who rather, upon the occasion of the arrival of those whose presence was intended, presented himself in the midst of the newcomers[[fn:2942]]. — Then it is said that this Satan was roaming upon the earth and walking through it; there is therefore no relation between him and the superior world, to which he has no access. Such is the meaning of the words: (I come) from roaming upon the earth and from walking through it (ibid., I, 7; II, 2); for he roams and walks only upon the earth[[fn:2943]]. — Afterward it is related that this upright and perfect man was delivered into the hands of Satan, and that the latter was the cause of all the misfortunes that befell him in his fortune, in his children, and in his person[[fn:2944]].
root.text.Part 3..21.2: After having thus indicated the underlying idea[[fn:2945]], the exposition beginns of what the thinkers[[fn:2946]] have said upon this subject; first, an opinion is related which is attributed to Job, then other opinions (are attributed) to his friends. I shall clearly set forth these various opinions, which caused among them so great a conflict of ideas[[fn:2947]] concerning this event of which Satan alone was the cause, whilst they all believed, Job as well as his friends, that God Himself had acted, without the mediation of Satan. That which is most astonishing and most remarkable in this narrative is that science is not attributed to Job, nor is he called a wise, or intelligent, or learned man; for, on the contrary, naught is attributed to him but excellent morals and uprightness in actions. Indeed, had he been a wise man, his situation would have held nothing obscure for him, as shall be explained further on.
root.text.Part 3..21.3: I will further observe that the misfortunes of Job are presented in a certain gradation, according to the different characters of men[[fn:2948]]. Indeed, there be men who are not affrighted[[fn:2949]] by the loss of their fortune, of which they make little account, but who are seized with terror by the death of their children and die thereof from grief. There be others who bear with resignation[[fn:2950]] even the loss of children; but no being that has sensation[[fn:2951]] can endure pains. All men, I mean the vulgar, glorify God with their tongue, and call Him just and beneficent when they are happy and at ease, or even in a state of supportable suffering. But when those misfortunes arrive which are related of Job, then there be some who, in losing only their fortune, blaspheme and believe that the whole universe lacks good order; others, although afflicted by the loss of fortune, continue to believe in (divine) justice and in the good order (of the universe), but if they be tried by the loss of children, they cannot resign themselves; others finally resign themselves and are not troubled in their faith, even when they lose their children, but none of them endurs the pains of the body without complaining and without blaspheming, either with his tongue or in his thought.
root.text.Part 3..21.4: In speaking of the sons of God, it is said both times that they came to present themselves before the Lord (ibid., I, 6; II, 1). But as for Satan, although he came in the midst of them the first and the second time, the expression להתיצב, to present oneself, is not used regarding him the first time, whereas the second time it is said (II, 1): “And Satan also came in the midst of them to present himself before the Lord.” It is necessary well to understand this idea, and thou shalt recognize how remarkable it is[[fn:2952]]; thou shalt then be convinced that it is as it were by a divine inspiration that I have found all these ideas[[fn:2953]]. Indeed, the words to present oneself before the Lord signify that they stood there subject to the order proceeding from His will[[fn:2954]]. It is thus that Zechariah[[fn:2955]], speaking of the four chariots coming out etc., says: The angel answered and said unto me: These are the four winds which go forth from where they presented themselves מהתיצב before the Lord of all the earth (Zechariah, 6, 5)[[fn:2956]]. — It is therefore clear that the sons of God and Satan do not occupy the same rank in the universe; on the contrary, the sons of God are more stable and more durable, but he too (Satan) occupies in the universe a certain rank below theirs[[fn:2957]].
root.text.Part 3..21.5: What is further remarkable in this parable is that, after having said that Satan roamed particularly upon the earth and having spoken of the acts to which he gave himself, it is declared that he is forbidden to take possession of the soul, that all these earthly things are placed in his power, but that there is a barrier between him and the human soul[[fn:2958]]; such is the meaning of these words: אך את נפשו שמור, only take heed of his soul (Job, 2, 6). I have already explained to thee that, in our language, the word נפש, soul, is a homonym, and that it applies to that thing which remains of man after death[[fn:2959]]; it is over this thing that Satan has no power[[fn:2960]].
root.text.Part 3..21.6: After these observations, hearken unto this word so instructive emanating from the sages, unto whom one may with justice apply the name of sages, (a word) which has enlightened all that is obscure, laid bare all that was veiled, and revealed most of the mysteries of the Law; I speak of that which they say in the Talmud[[fn:2961]]: «Rabbi Simeon, son of Lakish, says: Satan, the evil inclination, and the angel of death are one and the same thing.» All that we have said, this passage reveals in a manner which shall have naught of obscurity for him who has understanding[[fn:2962]]. It is therefore manifest that these three names designate one and the same idea, and that all the actions attributed unto each of these three things are the action of one and the same thing. This is likewise what the ancient doctors of the Mishnah have expressed: «It has been taught as follows: he descends and seducs, then ascends and accuss, and finally, having obtained permission, he takes away life[[fn:2963]].» Thou shalt now understand that what David beheld in a prophetic vision at the time of the pestilence,—the angel having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem (I Chron., 21, 16), — appeared unto him only to indicate a certain idea, which idea is the same[[fn:2964]] as that of which mention is also made in a prophetic vision, concerning the sin committed by the sons of the high priest Joshua: And Satan stood at his right hand to resist him (Zechariah, 3, 1)[[fn:2965]]. Following (this latter passage), it is declared how far Satan is removed from God[[fn:2966]]: The Lord rebuke thee, O Satan; even the Lord that has chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee (ibid., v. 2). It is he also whom Balaam, in a prophetic vision, beheld upon his way, and who said unto him: Behold, I went out to withstand thee (Numbers, 22, 52).
root.text.Part 3..21.7: [It must be known that the word SATAN (שׂטן) is derived from the verb SATA (שׂטה, to turn aside), for example turn from (שְׂטֵה) it, and pass away (Prov., 4, 15), I mean to say that this word contains the sense of turning aside, departing; for Satan is indubitably he who turns aside from the ways of truth and causs one to be lost in the ways of error[[fn:2967]]]. — This same idea[[fn:2968]] is expressed also by these words: for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth (Genesis, 8, 21). Thou knowest how widespread in our religion is the idea of the good and the evil inclination, and thou art acquainted with this word of the doctors: «with both thy inclinations[[fn:2969]]». Elsewhere they say that the evil inclination ariss in the human individual from birth: sin lies at the door (Genesis, 4, 7), and as the Scripture says: from his youth (ibid., VIII, 21), whilst the good inclination comes not unto him until after the perfecting of his intelligence[[fn:2970]]. Wherefore, say they, in the parable concerning the human body and its various faculties, contained in this passage: a little city, and few men within it, etc. (Eccles., IX, 14), the evil inclination is called a great king and the good inclination is called a poor wise man[[fn:2971]]. All these things are found in well-known texts, emanating from the doctors. — Now, as they have declared unto us that the evil inclination is Satan, who indubitably is an angel, — and who indeed is designated as an angel, since he is found among the number of the sons of God, — the good inclination also is in reality an angel[[fn:2972]]. Thus, when the doctors say, as all the world knows[[fn:2973]], that every man is accompanied by two angels, the one at his right hand and the other at his left, they refer to the good inclination and the evil inclination; and indeed they say expressly in the Gemara of Shabbath: «the one good, the other evil[[fn:2974]].» — Thou seest therefore how many wonderful things are revealed unto us by this word[[fn:2975]], and how many false ideas it causs to vanish.
root.text.Part 3..21.8: I believe that I have now set forth and thoroughly elucidated the history of Job[[fn:2976]]. But I desire also to set forth unto thee what is the opinion attributed unto Job and what is that which is attributed unto each of his friends, by alleging proofs which I shall collect from their respective discourses. One must not pay heed unto other words[[fn:2977]], necessitated by the whole of the discourse[[fn:2978]], as I have explained unto thee at the commencement of this treatise.
root.text.Part 3..22.0: This history of Job being admitted (as true), the matter upon which from the first[[fn:2979]] the five personages, that is to say Job and his friends, were in agreement, was that God had knowledge of all that had befallen Job, and that it was God who had smitten him with all these misfortunes. All likewise agreed in recognizing that God could not be charged with injustice and that one could not attribute iniquity unto Him. These are ideas which are frequently found repeated even in the words of Job[[fn:2980]]. If one considers the words which the five men exchange in their dialogue, one would be tempted to believe that what one says, all the others say likewise, and that the same ideas are repeated and cross one another. On the part of Job, they are interrupted only by the description which he makes of the violent pains and sufferings which he endurs despite his uprightness, by the painting of his righteousness, of his noble character and of the goodness of his actions. On their part, his friends mingle, in the discourses which they address unto him, exhortations to patience, consolations and gentle words, saying that he ought to be silent and not give rein unto his words, like one who contends with his fellow, but rather submit in silence[[fn:2981]] to the decrees of the Divinity. To which he replies that violent pains prevent one from being patient and steadfast, and from expressing oneself as is meet. All his friends agree in maintaining that they who do good are rewarded for it, and that they who do evil are punished for it. If, say they, one ses a sinner in happiness, one may be certain that the contrary shall take place in the future; he shall perish, and misfortunes shall fall upon him, upon his children[[fn:2982]] and upon his race. If, on the contrary, one ses a pious man in adversity, he cannot fail to obtain a reparation[[fn:2983]]. This idea thou shalt find repeated in the discourses of Eliphaz, of Bildad and of Zophar, and the three are in agreement upon this opinion. But this is not the aim of this whole history, in which it was intended rather to make known what each of them professed in particular and the opinion which he held upon an event where we see the man most upright and of the most perfect integrity smitten with the greatest and most violent calamities.
root.text.Part 3..22.1.sub_0: According to the opinion of Job, this event proved that the virtuous man and the impious are equal before God, who despiss the human species and abandons it[[fn:2984]]. It is thus that he says among other things: It is all one; therefore I said it, He destroys the perfect and the wicked; if the scourge slay suddenly, He will laugh at the trial of the innocent (Job, 9, 22-23); that is to say, if the torrent[[fn:2985]] arrivs suddenly, causs to perish and carries away all whom it encounters, He (God) laughs at the calamity of the innocent. He thereafter confirms this opinion by saying: One dies in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet; his vessels are full of milk, etc. And another dies in the bitterness of his soul, and never eats with pleasure. They shall lie down alike in the dust, and the worms shall cover them (XXI, 23-26). He further allegs for proof the prosperous state of the wicked and their happiness, and he dwells much thereupon: Even when I remember, says he, I am afraid, and trembling takes hold on my flesh. Wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power? Their seed is established in their sight, etc. (ibid., v. 6-8). After having described this perfect happiness, he says unto his interlocutors: Let us admit that it be as ye pretend, that the children of this happy miscreant perish when he is no more and that their trace disappear, what injury results for this happy man from that which shall happen unto his family when he shall be no more? For what pleasure has he in his house (which he leavs) after him, when the number of his months is cut off in the midst (ibid., v. 21)? Elsewhere he declars that naught is to be hoped for after death, so that there remains naught else to say, save only that there is abandonment[[fn:2986]]. He expresses therefore his astonishment that God, having not neglected, in the beginning, the creation of the human individual, should yet neglect to govern him[[fn:2987]], and he says: Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese, etc. (X, 10)? — This is one of the opinions professed concerning Providence[[fn:2988]]. The doctors, as thou knowest, declare this opinion of Job to be extremely blameworthy[[fn:2989]], making use of expressions such as the following[[fn:2990]]: «Dust in the mouth of Job[[fn:2991]]. — Job sought to turn the dish upside down[[fn:2992]].
root.text.Part 3..22.1.sub_1: —Job denied the resurrection of the dead. —Job had set himself to utter blasphemies.” Yet if God says unto Eliphaz[[fn:2993]]: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has (42, 7), the doctors, to justify this[[fn:2994]], say: “A man is not held responsible in the hour of his suffering[[fn:2995]]”, which is to say that he (Job) was excusable by reason of his grievous sufferings. Nevertheless, such words accord not with the whole of this parable[[fn:2996]]. The cause (of the discourse in question) is none other than that which I shall set before thee[[fn:2997]]: it is that Job had returned from that most erroneous opinion and had himself demonstrated its falsity. This was but an opinion which arose at the first, especially in a man smitten by calamities and inwardly convinced of his own innocence, and this no man shall dispute; wherefore this opinion is attributed unto Job. However, he uttered all these discourses only so long as he remained in ignorance and knew God only by tradition, even as the multitude of religious men knows Him; but as soon as he attained a certain knowledge of God, he acknowledged that true felicity, which consists in the knowledge of God, is reserved for all those who know Him[[fn:2998]], and that none of all these calamities can disturb it in man. These imaginary felicities, such as health, wealth, and children, Job had regarded as the end, so long as he knew God only by tradition and not by reflection; wherefore he fell into all these wanderings and uttered these (blameworthy) discourses. Such is the meaning of these words: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear; but now mine eye ses thee. Wherefore I abhor (all this) and repent in dust and ashes (XLII, 5, 6). These words must be completed thus according to the sense: “Wherefore I despise all that I had formerly desired, and I repent of having been in dust and ashes[[fn:2999]];” for it is this situation which is attributed unto him (in saying): And he sat down among the ashes (II, 8). It is therefore because of this final discourse, which indicats true perception, that it is said of him immediately thereafter: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.
root.text.Part 3..22.2: Eliphaz’s opinion concerning this occurrence is likewise one of the doctrines espoused regarding Providence. According to him, indeed, all the calamities which had befallen Job, he had merited; for he had committed sins which had deserved this fate[[fn:3000]]. This is what he says to Job: [[t:0]]Is not thy wickedness great[[t:1]], [[t:2]]and thine iniquities infinite[[t:3]] (XXII, 5)? Elsewhere he says to Job: “The good deeds and virtuous conduct upon which thou dost rely[[fn:3001]] do not render thee necessarily a perfect man before God, in such wise that thou canst not be punished: [[t:4]]Assuredly[[t:5]], [[t:6]]He places no confidence in His servants, He finds defects even in His angels[[t:7]]. [[t:8]]What then shall become of those who dwell in houses of clay, who have their foundation in the dust[[t:9]] (IV, 18-19)?” Eliphaz ceases not to reiterate this thought[[fn:3002]]; I mean to say that he believes all that befalls man must have been merited by him, but that the faults by which we earn chastisement elude our perception, and (that we are ignorant) in what manner they have brought us the punishment.
root.text.Part 3..22.3: The opinion of Bildad the Shuhite upon this question is that which admitts compensation[[fn:3003]]. Verily, he says unto Job: “These great misfortunes, if so be that thou art pure and hast committed no sin, have for their reason to make thee deserve a reward so much the greater; and certes thou shalt have the fairest compensation[[fn:3004]]. All this, therefore, is for thy good, to the end that the happiness which thou shalt enjoy in the future may be so much the greater.” Such is the sense of those words which he addresses to Job: If thou wert pure and upright; surely now he would awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous. Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase (VIII, 6 and 7). Thou knowest that this opinion concerning Providence is very widespread, and we have already set it forth.
root.text.Part 3..22.4: The opinion of Zophar the Naamathite is that which admitts that all depends upon the sole will of God, that one must seek no reason in the divine actions, and that one must in no wise ask why He has done this thing or that thing[[fn:3005]]. Wherefore, in all that God does, one must seek neither a reason of justice nor a requirement of His wisdom, for it pertains to His greatness[[fn:3006]] and to His true essence to do that which He wills, whilst we are incapable of penetrating into the secrets of His wisdom, which requirs that He act according to His will and without any other reason[[fn:3007]]. This is what he says unto Job: But oh that God would speak, and open his lips against thee; and that he would shew thee the secrets of wisdom, for they are double to that which is[[fn:3008]]! Canst thou by searching find out God (the secret)? Canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection (XI, 5, 6, 7)?
root.text.Part 3..22.5: Thou seest, consequently, if thou reflectest thereon, how this history, which has so much disquieted men, has been (wisely) disposed, so as to bring forward the different opinions concerning Providence which we have previously set forth[[fn:3009]]. Each of these opinions is there presented apart[[fn:3010]], and is attributed to one of the men of antiquity, renowned for virtue and science[[fn:3011]], if so be that it is a parable; or else they may indeed have spoken thus in reality, if it be a true history. Thus, the opinion attributed unto Job is conformable to that of Aristotle; the opinion of Eliphaz to that of our religion; the opinion of Bildad corresponds to the doctrine of the Mutazilites; and lastly, the opinion of Zophar corresponds to the doctrine of the Asharites. These are the ancient opinions concerning Providence.
root.text.Part 3..22.6.sub_0: Thou perceivest then a new opinion, which is that attributed to Elihu.
