For this reason[[fn:3012]] is the latter deemed superior to those others[[fn:3013]], and it is declared that, albeit he was the youngest amongst them, he surpassed them in knowledge. He beginns by reprimanding[[fn:3014]] Job, whom he taxes with folly for having displayed pride and for being astonished at the misfortunes which befell him, although he had done naught but good; for he had long boasted of his deeds. Then he likewise taxes with dotage[[fn:3015]] the opinion of the three friends of Job concerning Providence, and he employs expressions so singularly enigmatic, that the reader, in considering his words, is at first astonished, believing that he adds absolutely nothing to that which Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar had said, and that, on the contrary, he does but repeat their ideas in other terms and with greater development. Verily, he does naught else but reprimand[[fn:3016]] Job, describe the divine justice and the wonders of the universe, and (proclaim) that God is affected neither by the virtue of the pious man, nor by the sin of the impious[[fn:3017]]; yet all these things the friends of Job had already spoken. Nevertheless, by reflecting thereon, thou shalt understand the new idea which he has introduced and which was his aim, an idea which none of them had expressed aforetime. With this idea, however, he has repeated all that those others had said, even as all of them, Job and his three friends, each repeats the idea expressed by the others, as I have already told thee; and this has for its purpose to conceal that which is peculiar to the personal opinion of each, so that it seems to the vulgar that they all meet in one and the same opinion, although it be not so. The idea which Elihu adds and which none of them had expressed, is that which he presents allegorically by the intercession of an angel. It is, says he, a thing attested and well known, that when a man is sick unto death and when he is despaired of, if he has an angel, no matter which, to intercede for him[[fn:3018]], the intercession of the latter shall be accepted, the sick man shall recover[[fn:3019]], shall be saved, and shall return to the best possible state. Nevertheless, this cannot continue alway, and there can be no continual intercession for evermore, but only twice or thrice[[fn:3020]]. This is what he says: If there be a messenger with him, an interpreter, etc.
root.text.Part 3..22.6.sub_1: (XXXIII, 23); and, after describing the progressive state of the convalescent and the joy occasioned by his return to perfect health[[fn:3021]], he adds: [[t:4]]All this[[t:5]], [[t:6]]God does twice or thrice for man[[t:7]] ([[t:8]]ibid.[[t:9]], [[t:10]]v.[[t:11]] 29).— This is an idea which is expounded by Elihu alone; but what he further adds, before (expressing) this idea, is that he commences by describing[[fn:3022]] how prophetic inspiration arises, saying: [[t:12]]For God speaks once, yea twice, though man perceive it not. In a dream[[t:13]], [[t:14]]a vision of the night[[t:15]], [[t:16]]when deep sleep falls upon men etc.[[t:17]] ([[t:18]]ibid.[[t:19]], [[t:20]]v.[[t:21]] 14 and 15). Subsequently, he confirms this opinion[[fn:3023]], and to demonstrate in what manner it must be understood, he describes a series of physical phenomena, such as thunder, lightning, rain, the breath of the winds. He also intermingles therewith many matters concerning living beings, speaking, for example, of the outbreak of pestilence; [[t:22]]in a moment they die in the midst of the night etc.[[t:23]] (XXXIV, 20), of great wars which erupt: [[t:24]]He breaks in pieces mighty men without number, and setts others in their stead[[t:25]] ([[t:26]]ibid.[[t:27]], [[t:28]]v.[[t:29]] 24), and of many other similar matters[[fn:3024]].
root.text.Part 3..22.7: Thou shalt find likewise that, in the revelation which Job had[[fn:3025]], and whereby it became clear unto him that he had been mistaken in all that he had imagined, there is naught but a constant description of physical things, whether they be elements, or meteors, or the nature of different species of animals, and naught else. If mention be there made of the ethereal regions, of the heavens, of Orion, and of the Pleiades, it is because of their influence upon our atmosphere; for all the objects unto which God calls the attention of Job belong only to the sublunary world. Thus Elihu also draws his admonitions from the different species of animals: Who teaches us, says he, more than the beasts of the earth, and makes us wiser than the fowls of heaven (XXXV, 11). In this discourse (of God), the description of the Leviathan is mainly dwelt upon, which is an assemblage of various corporeal properties belonging to animals that walk, swim, or fly[[fn:3026]] — By all these things it is intended to signify that our intelligences arrive not at the understanding of how these physical things came to be, which exist in the world of generation and corruption[[fn:3027]], nor at the conception of the origin of the physical force existing within them. These are not things which resemble that which we ourselves do; and how could we desire to establish a comparison between the manner in which God governs and cars for them, and the manner in which we govern and care for that which is committed to our government and care? Verily, it behoves us to stay our steps at this little (which we know thereof) and to believe that nothing can be hidden from God, as Elihu says: For his eyes are upon the ways of man, and he ses all his goings. There is no darkness, nor shadow of death, where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves (XXXIV, 21-22). But the idea of the Providence of God is not the same as our own[[fn:3028]], and the idea of the government of which creatures are the object on the part of God is not the same as the government which we exercise; these two (respective things) fall not under one and the same definition, as is believed through error, and have nothing in common save the mere name, even as our action and that of God resemble not each other and fall not under one and the same definition. Just as the works of nature differ from the works of art, so does the divine government, the divine Providence, and the divine intention, of which these physical things are the object, differ from our human government, from our foresight and our intention regarding the things which are the object thereof.
root.text.Part 3..22.8: The whole book of Job has for its purpose to establish this article of faith and to call attention to the proofs which may be deduced from physical things, so that thou mayest not err and desire, in thy imagination, to establish a comparison between the knowledge of God and our own, or (to believe) that the intention, the Providence, and the government of God resemble our intention, our foresight, and our government. The man who shall have been penetrated with this shall easily endure every calamity. Misfortunes shall no longer cause him to doubt concerning God, nor (shall he ask himself) whether God has knowledge thereof or not, whether He cars (for man) or whether He forsaks him; on the contrary, they shall inspire him with more love, as is said at the end of this revelation: Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes[[fn:3029]], and as the doctors express it: «Those who act from the love of God and rejoice in sufferings, etc.[[fn:3030]]»
root.text.Part 3..22.9: If thou considerest all that I have just said with the attention which the reading of this treatise requirs, and if thou then examinest the book of Job, thou shalt understand the sense thereof, and thou shalt find that I have summarized all its ideas, leaving aside only that which is a mere ornament of style and serves only to complete the allegory[[fn:3031]], as I have expounded unto thee several times in this Treatise.
root.text.Part 3..23.0: The conception of trial[[fn:3032]] is likewise most obscure, and constituts one of the greatest difficulties of religion. The Law speaks thereof in six passages, as I shall set forth unto thee in this chapter[[fn:3033]].
root.text.Part 3..23.1: As for the manner in which the vulgar generally understand the notion of trial—to wit, that God sends calamities upon a man, although he has committed no sin, and for the purpose of granting him a reward all the greater—this is a principle which is nowhere expressly mentioned by any text of the Law; and, among the six passages of the Pentateuch, there is but one alone which, taken literally, might lead one to believe such a thing[[fn:3034]]; I shall explain the sense thereof further on. This opinion is even in opposition to that which the Law lays down as a principle; for it is said: a God of truth and without iniquity (Deut. xxxii. 4).
root.text.Part 3..23.2: Neither is this vulgar opinion admitted by all the doctors; for there be some who say: “No death without sin, and no punishment without transgression[[fn:3035]].” Verily, it is this latter opinion that every religious man endowed with intelligence must admit; nor ought he to attribute injustice unto God, so as to believe that Zeid is pure from all sin, that he is a perfect man, and that he has in no wise deserved that which has befallen him.
root.text.Part 3..23.3: As touching the trials which the Pentateuch mentions in the passages in question, their object, in appearance, is to make an experiment and an inquiry, in order to know the degree[[fn:3036]] of faith of such a man or such a nation, or the degree of his piety. But herein lies precisely the great difficulty[[fn:3037]], and particularly in the history of the sacrifice of Isaac, which was known only to God and to the two personages[[fn:3038]], to one of whom it was said[[fn:3039]]: for now I know that thou fearest God (Gen. xxii. 12). It is the same with this passage: for the Lord your God proves you, to know whether ye love etc. (Deut. xiii. 4), and with this other passage: to know what was in thine heart (ibid., viii. 2). I shall now resolve for thee all these difficulties.
root.text.Part 3..23.4: Know that whenever, in the Pentateuch, mention is made of a trial, it has no other end and no other object than to make known unto men what they ought to do or what they ought to believe. Consequently, the trial consists, so to speak, in the performance of a certain act in which one has not in view the act itself, which, on the contrary, is proposed only as an example that men should follow and take for a model. Thus, when it is said: to know whether ye love etc. (Deut. xiii. 4), it signifies not: that God might know it, for He already knew it; but it is similar[[fn:3040]] to this other passage: that ye may know that I am the Lord that does sanctify you (Exod. xxxi. 13). There[[fn:3041]], the meaning is: that the nations may know; and likewise He says here: “If there arise a man who arrogats to himself prophecy, and ye see his wonders[[fn:3042]] which cause men to believe that he speaks truly, ye shall know that this is a thing whereby God wills to make known unto the nations to what degree ye are imbued with His Law, how far ye are capable of understanding the true being of God, that ye suffer not yourselves to be deceived by the guile of an impostor, and that your faith in God is not shaken; and this shall serve as a support for all those who aspire unto the truth, so that they shall seek beliefs which are sufficiently firm that, in their presence, no further regard be paid to the worker of miracles[[fn:3043]]. Indeed, such a one would invite belief in that which is impossible[[fn:3044]]; but it can only be of use to have recourse to miracles when that which is proclaimed is possible, as we have set forth in the Mishneh Torah[[fn:3045]].
root.text.Part 3..23.5: — Since, therefore, it is manifest that the expression לדעת, to know, signifies here: that men may know, it shall be likewise with that which is said concerning the manna: to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no (Deut. viii. 2); that is to say, that nations may know it, and that it may be published throughout the whole world that they who devote themselves to the service of God receive their sustenance in an unexpected manner. It is in exactly the same sense that, where the fall of the manna is first spoken of, it is said: that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no (Exodus xvi. 4); which is to say, that every man may draw therefrom a lesson and see whether it be profitable to devote oneself to the service of God, and whether this be sufficient, or no. As touching that which is said concerning the manna for a third time: Who fed thee in the wilderness with manna, which thy fathers knew not, that he might humble thee, and that he might prove thee, to do thee good at thy latter end (Deut. viii. 16), this passage might lead one to believe that God sometimes afflicts man that he may subsequently obtain a reward so much the greater; but, in reality, it is not so. This passage expresses rather one of the two following ideas: 1st, the idea repeated concerning the manna in the first and second passages, that is to say, that it may be known whether it suffices, or no, to be devoted to God in order to have food and to be sheltered from fatigues and pains; or else 2nd, the word הסותך would here signify to accustom thee, a sense which the same verb has in this passage: Who had not been accustomed (נִסְּתָה) to adventure to set the sole of her foot, etc. (ibid., xxviii. 56), so that it would have been said here: God first accustomed you to hardship in the wilderness that you might enjoy a greater well-being when you should have entered the land (of Canaan); and this is true, for it is sweeter to pass from hardship unto rest than to be always at rest. It is also known that, had they not suffered misery and hardship in the wilderness, they would not have been able to conquer the land, nor to fight; which the Pentateuch says expressly: for God said, Lest perhaps the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt: But God led the people about, through the way of the wilderness of the Red Sea (Exodus xiii. 17 and 18). Indeed, ease and prosperity do cause valiancy to vanish, whilst privations and fatigues do engender it, and therein lies the good which the passage in question promiss them at their latter end.
root.text.Part 3..23.6: As for this passage: for God has come to test you (Exodus 20:20), it has the same meaning as that of Deuteronomy, where it is said, concerning the one who prophesies in the name of a false god: for the Lord your God is testing you (Deut. 13:4), the meaning of which we have already explained. Here then, in the scene at Mount Sinai, he says to them: Fear not, for this great spectacle you have seen took place solely so that you might, by your own sight, acquire a certain conviction, and so that, if the Lord your God, to manifest your great faith, should test you by a false prophet who would invite you to overturn what you have heard, you would remain firm, without wavering[[fn:3046]]; for if I had presented myself to you as a prophet, as you wished[[fn:3047]], and if I had reported to you what had been said to me, without you having heard it yourselves, it might be that you would deem true what was reported to you by another, even if he came to overturn what I had announced, since you would not have heard it yourselves in this spectacle.
root.text.Part 3..23.7: As for the story of Abraham regarding the sacrifice of Isaac, it contains two great ideas that are fundamental to religion. The first is to inform us to what limit the love and fear of God must extend. He was commanded (Abraham) to do something to which neither the sacrifice of wealth nor even the sacrifice of life can be compared; it was indeed the most extraordinary thing[[fn:3048]] that can happen in the world, one of those things that human nature cannot be believed capable of accepting. Imagine a childless man[[fn:3049]], animated by an extreme desire to have children, possessing great fortune and status, and desiring that his lineage become a nation: if he has a son, after having despaired of having one, what love, what passion he will have for this son! However, fearing God and desiring to obey His command, he sets little store[[fn:3050]] by this beloved son, renounces all he had hoped for from him, and consents to sacrifice him after several days of travel. And indeed, if he had hastened to do it at the very moment he received the command, it would have been an act of recklessness and haste, without much reflection; but to do such a thing several days after having received the command was an act that presupposed thought and mature reflection, the respect that the command of God deserved, as well as the love and fear of God. Certainly, one must not assume other circumstances, nor suppose (in Abraham) any impression whatsoever[[fn:3051]]; for if our father Abraham hastened to sacrifice Isaac, it was not out of fear that God would put him to death or make him poor, but solely because it is the duty[[fn:3052]] of mortals to love and fear God, independent of any hope of reward or any fear of punishment, as we have explained in several places. Thus, if the angel says to him: for now I know that thou fearest God (Genesis 22:12), it means: this act, by which you merit, in the absolute sense, (the epithet of) ירא אלהים, God-fearing, will make known to all mortals how far the fear of God must go.
root.text.Part 3..23.8: Thou shalt know that this idea has been confirmed and set forth in the Law, where it is said that the sum of the whole Law, all that it contains in the way of commands, prohibitions, promises, and narrations, has but one single object, which is the fear of God. These are the terms: If thou wilt not observe to do all the words of this law that are written in this book, that thou mayest fear this glorious and fearful name, etc. (Deut. xxviii. 58). — Such is one of the two ideas which were intended in the (narrative of the) sacrifice of Isaac.
root.text.Part 3..23.9: The second idea is to let us know that prophets must accept as real what revelation brings them from God; for one must not imagine that, because this revelation takes place—as we have explained—in a dream or in a vision, and by means of the imaginative faculty, it follows that what the prophets hear or what is presented to them in a parable might not be certain, or at least that some element of doubt is mixed therein. It was therefore intended to let us know that everything the prophet sees in the prophetic vision is real and certain to him, that he doubts none of it, and that he considers it in the same manner as all real things perceived by the senses or the intellect. The proof of this is that Abraham hastened to sacrifice his only son whom he loved[[fn:3053]], as he had been commanded, although this command had reached him in a dream or in a vision. But if the prophetic dream had been obscure to the prophets, if some doubt or uncertainty[[fn:3054]] had remained in them regarding what they perceived in the prophetic vision, they would not have hastened to do what is repugnant to human nature, and Abraham would not have consented to perform, in doubt, an act of such high gravity[[fn:3055]].
root.text.Part 3..23.10: Verily, it was meet that this event—I mean the sacrifice in question—should occur through the mediation of Abraham and unto a man such as Isaac[[fn:3056]]; for our father Abraham was the first to make known the unity of God and to establish prophecy[[fn:3057]], so as to perpetuate this belief and to draw men towards it, even as it is said: For I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of the Lord, to do righteousness and justice (Genesis, xviii. 19). Even as they followed the true and profitable opinions which they had heard from him, so ought one to follow the opinions derived from his acts[[fn:3058]], and notably from this act whereby he established the fundamental principle of the truth of prophecy[[fn:3059]], and whereby he has made known unto us the measure to which the fear and love of God must extend.
root.text.Part 3..23.11: Such are the notions that one must form concerning trials, and it must not be believed that God wills to try and to test a thing[[fn:3060]], in order to know that which He knew not before. How far is He exalted above that which ignorant and foolish men imagine in their perverse thoughts! Thou must well possess thyself of this truth.
root.text.Part 3..24.0: Actions, with respect to their end, may be divided into four kinds: the idle action, the frivolous action, the vain action, and the good and useful action. That which is called a vain action is that which is performed for a certain end, which end, however, is not attained, because certain hindrances oppose it. Ofttimes wilt thou hear one say: “I have laboured in vain[[fn:3061]]”, when he has wearied himself in seeking a person whom he has not found, or when he has undertaken a toilsome journey without having made a gainful traffic. It is likewise said: “Our trouble for this sick man has been vain”, when the latter has not returned to health. It is the same with all actions whereby one seeks to attain an end; (they are called vain) when the end is not reached. — The idle action is that whereby one aims at no end whatsoever[[fn:3062]], even as certain folk, whilst meditating, play with their hands, and as do the distracted and the heedless. — The frivolous action is that in which one has in view an insignificant end, I mean, whereby one aims at a thing which is not necessary and which has not even any great utility; thus, for instance, when one dancs without having for his end the taking of exercise, or when one does things which aim at provoking laughter, these are indubitably things that shall be called frivolous. But herein a distinction must be made, according to the purpose and the worth of those who act; for there be many things which, in the eyes of some, are necessary or very useful, whereas, according to others, there is no need of them. Thus, for example, in the eyes of those who understand medicine, the different kinds of bodily exercise are necessary for the preservation of health; and, in the eyes of the learned, writing is a very useful thing. He, therefore, who, for the sake of his health, betaks himself to exercises, such as the game of ball, wrestling, boxing, or the holding of the breath, or who, for the sake of writing, mends the kalam (reed) or prepars paper, performs in the eyes of the ignorant a frivolous act, which yet is not frivolous in the eyes of the learned. — The good and useful action is that which is performed for a noble end, I mean necessary or useful, and which causs that end to be attained.
root.text.Part 3..24.1: — This, methinks, is a classification against which no objection can be raised. Verily, he who performs any act whatever, at one time aims at a certain end, and at another has no end; and the end in view is sometimes noble, sometimes insignificant, and sometimes it is attained, and sometimes it is not. This classification is therefore of absolute necessity.
root.text.Part 3..24.2: After this exposition, I say: An intelligent man could not maintain that any action of God can be vain, or idle, or frivolous. According to the opinion of all of us who follow[[fn:3063]] the Law of Moses our master, all His actions are good and useful, even as it is said: And God saw every thing that He had made, and, behold, it was very good (Genesis, i. 31). Consequently, all that God does for the sake of aught is either necessary or very useful for the existence of that thing which He has in view. Thus, for instance, food is necessary to the animal for its preservation, and eyes are very useful to it for that purpose; wherefore food has no other end than to preserve the animal for a certain time, and the senses have no other end than the utility which their perceptions afford to the animal. Such is also the opinion of the philosophers, to wit, that there is nothing idle[[fn:3064]] in any of the physical things; that is to say, that all things which are not artificial presuppose actions having a certain end, whether we know that end or be ignorant of it. But according to that sect among the thinkers[[fn:3065]] which claims that God does nothing for the sake of another thing, that there are neither causes nor effects, but that, on the contrary, all the actions of God are but the result of His will alone, that one must not seek an end for them, nor ask why He has done such a thing, that He does what pleass Him and that it is not the result of wisdom—according to those (I say), the actions of God would enter into the category of idle things, or rather they would be below the idle action; for, if it be true that the author of such an action aims at no end, at least he cars not for what he does; whereas God, according to them, knows well what He does, and yet He does it without any end, nor for any utility.
root.text.Part 3..24.3: But, that which appears inadmissible from the very outset, is that there should be in the actions of God aught that is frivolous; and one must pay no heed to the folly of those who have contended that the ape was created for the diversion of man. That which has given rise to such notions, is that they were ignorant of the nature of generation and of corruption, and that they forgat a fundamental principle, to wit, that it is with intention that God has brought into being all possible things such as we behold them; His wisdom willed not that they should be otherwise; and, consequently, that would be impossible, for things must be such as His wisdom has required.
root.text.Part 3..24.4.sub_0: As for those who have said that God, in all that He has wrought, had in view no end, they were necessarily led thereto by considering the whole of being from the standpoint of their opinion[[fn:3066]]; for having asked themselves what might be the end of the existence of the world in its entirety, they necessarily answered, as do all those who maintain the novelty of the world: “Even so has He willed it, without having any other reason.” Thereafter they continued this reasoning with respect to all the details of the universe, so that, for example, far from agreeing that the perforation of the uvea and the transparency of the cornea had for their end to give passage to the visual spirit[[fn:3067]] in order to produce perception, they denied on the contrary that such was the cause of vision. It is not, said they, in view of vision that this membrane was perforated and that which is above was rendered transparent, but it is thus that God willed it, although vision were possible had it been otherwise. We have certain biblical passages whose literal sense, at first sight, might give rise to such a notion. It is said, for instance: The Lord has done whatsoever He pleased (Ps. 135, 6); and what His soul desirs, even that He does (Job 23, 13); and elsewhere: and who shall say unto Him, What doest Thou? (Eccles. VIII, 4.) But the sense of these passages and other like ones is this: That which God wills is necessarily done, and there is naught that can hinder the accomplishment of His will. [However, God wills only that which is possible; not all that is possible, but only that which is required by His wisdom[[fn:3068]]]. Likewise, the absolutely good work which God wills to perform cannot be stayed by any obstacle, and naught can prevent it[[fn:3069]]. Such is the opinion of every theologian and that of the philosophers, and such also is our own; for, although we believe that the world was created, all our doctors and all our sages admit that this event took place not by the sole will of God; but they say that divine wisdom, which we are unable to comprehend, necessitated the existence of this whole universe at the moment when it came into being, and that this same invariable wisdom had necessitated non-existence before the world existed.
root.text.Part 3..24.4.sub_1: Thou shalt find this idea often repeated[[fn:3070]] among the doctors, for example in the explanation of this passage: He has made every thing beautiful in his time (Ecclesiastes 3, 11)[[fn:3071]]. By all this, they sought to avoid that which it is indeed meet to avoid, to wit, (admitting) that the Agent (that is to say, God) might accomplish an act, without having in view any end whatsoever. Such is the belief of the doctors of our Law, and it is this also which our prophets have declared, namely, that the actions of nature, even unto the smallest details, are wisely ordered and are linked one to another, that they are all causes and effects (of one another), and that none of them is either idle, or frivolous, or vain, but that on the contrary they are actions of a perfect wisdom, as it is said: O Lord, how manifold are Thy works! in wisdom hast Thou made them all (Ps. 104, 24); and elsewhere: And all His works are solid (Ps. 33, 4); and yet elsewhere: The Lord by wisdom has founded the earth (Prov. 3, 19). Such expressions are frequent, and the contrary opinion cannot be admitted. Philosophical speculation likewise decids that, in all the works of nature, there is naught idle, nor frivolous, nor vain, and with even greater reason in the nature of the celestial spheres; for these, by reason of their noble matter, are more solid and more regular.
root.text.Part 3..24.5: It must be known that the greater part of the false opinions which have brought such perplexity into the researches concerning the final cause, whether of the whole universe or of each of its parts, have no other source[[fn:3072]] than, on the one hand, the error in which man was concerning himself, imagining that the whole universe exists only for him, and, on the other hand, his ignorance both as touching the nature of this inferior matter and as touching the primary end of the Creator, which was to bring into existence all that whose existence was possible, existence being indubitably the good[[fn:3073]]. It is from this error and from the ignorance of these two things that doubts and perplexity arise, so that one imagins that, among the actions of God, there be some that are frivolous, or idle, or vain. Know that those who have resigned themselves to this absurdity, so that for them the divine actions resemble idle actions which have absolutely no end, have sought thereby only to avoid making them depend upon a wisdom, fearing lest that should lead to professing the eternity of the world[[fn:3074]]; they have therefore closed the door to this opinion. But I have already informed thee what is in this regard the opinion of our Law, and that it is this opinion which must be admitted; for we say naught absurd in maintaining that the being and non-being of all these acts depend upon the divine wisdom, but that we are often ignorant how this wisdom manifests itself in the works of God. It is upon this opinion that the whole Law of Moses, our master, is based. It says at the beginning: And God saw every thing that He had made, and, behold, it was very good (Genesis 1, 31), and it says toward the end: The Rock (the Creator), His work is perfect (Deut. 32, 4.) Thou must well penetrate thyself with this. If thou examinest this opinion, as well as the philosophical opinion, by studying all the preceding chapters of this treatise which relate to this subject, thou shalt find that the two opinions differ in respect of none of the smallest details of the universe[[fn:3075]]. Thou shalt find only the single difference which we have already set forth[[fn:3076]], to wit, that, according to them (the philosophers), the world is eternal, whereas, according to us, it is created. Understand this well.
root.text.Part 3..25.0.sub_0: Even as the speculative theologians differ upon the question of whether the actions of God depend upon His wisdom or whether they depend solely upon His will without having absolutely any end, likewise they differ in the manner of considering the laws which He has prescribed for us. In effect, there be those who attribute to these latter no reason and who maintain that all laws depend upon the sole will (of God), whilst others maintain that all that is prescribed or forbidden depends upon divine wisdom and aims at a certain end, that all laws have a reason and that they have been prescribed in view of some utility. However, we (Israelites), all of us, whether of the common people or of the learned, believe that they all have a reason, but that in part we are ignorant of the reasons, not knowing in what manner they are conformable to the divine wisdom[[fn:3077]]. Passages of Scripture say this clearly: statutes and judgments righteous (Deut. IV, 8); the judgments of the Lord are truth, they are righteous altogether (Ps. 19, 10). The statutes or regulations called חֻקּׅים, for example those relating to garments of heterogeneous materials, to meat seethed in milk, to the scapegoat[[fn:3078]], and concerning which the doctors express themselves in these terms: “Things which I have prescribed for thee, upon which thou art not permitted to reflect, of which Satan makes the object of his criticism, and which the gentiles refute[[fn:3079]],” — (these regulations, I say), the doctors in general do not consider them as things which are absolutely without reason and for which an end must not be sought; for that would lead us to (attribute to God) idle actions, as we have said. All the doctors believe on the contrary that they necessarily have a reason, I mean an end of utility; but this reason escaps us because of the weakness of our intelligence or our lack of instruction. According to them, therefore, all the commandments have a reason, I mean that every prescription or prohibition has an end of utility; sometimes the utility thereof is evident to us, as that of the prohibition of murder and theft; sometimes the utility thereof is not so evident[[fn:3080]], as for example when one forbidds the use of the first products of trees[[fn:3081]] or the mixing of the vineyard (with other plants[[fn:3082]]).
root.text.Part 3..25.0.sub_1: Those commandments, the utility of which is evident to all, are termed [[t:10]]משפטים[[t:11]], [[t:12]]laws[[t:13]] or [[t:14]]ordinances[[t:15]], and those, the utility of which is not generally manifest, are styled [[t:16]]חקים[[t:17]], [[t:18]]statutes[[t:19]] or [[t:20]]regulations[[t:21]]. They frequently declare: «[[t:22]]for it is not a vain thing for you[[t:23]] (Deut., XXXII, 47), and if it be vain, it is of your own accord[[fn:3083]];» signifying thereby: This legislation is not a vain enactment devoid of useful purpose, and should it appear thus to you regarding certain precepts, the fault lies with your own apprehension. You are acquainted with that widely prevalent tradition amongst us, that Solomon comprehended the reason for all the commandments, with the exception of those pertaining to the [[t:24]]red heifer[[t:25]][[fn:3084]]; and similarly with this opinion of the doctors, namely, that God concealed the reason for the commandments, lest they should be neglected, as befell Solomon in the case of the three commandments whose reason is expressly indicated[[fn:3085]].
root.text.Part 3..25.1: This principle they do constantly proclaim in all their discourses, and the texts of the Sacred Books do likewise indicate it. Nevertheless, I have found a passage of the Doctors in Bereshith Rabba which seems at first sight to say that certain commandments had no other reason than that of prescribing something[[fn:3086]], without any other end or real utility being in view. Thus it is there said: «What matters it to the Holy One whether one slays animals by the throat or by the nape of the neck? Thou mayest therefore infer thence that the commandments have no other purpose than that of refining men[[fn:3087]], as it is said: The word of the Lord is pure (Ps., 18, 31)[[fn:3088]].» Albeit these words be passing strange, the Doctors nowhere else pronouncing in a like sense, I have interpreted them, as thou shalt hear, in such wise as not to abandon the doctrine which they have constantly proclaimed[[fn:3089]], and not to depart from the principle upon which all are agreed, to wit, that all commandments have a truly useful end: for it is not a vain thing (Deut., XXXII, 47), and as it is said elsewhere: I have not said unto the seed of Jacob: Seek ye Me in vain; I am the Lord, speaking righteousness, declaring things that are right (Isaiah, 45, 19). That which every man of sound reason ought to believe in this regard is as follows: the general enactments of the commandments[[fn:3090]] have necessarily a reason and have been prescribed in view of a certain utility; but the particular details, it has been said, have no other end than to prescribe something[[fn:3091]]. Thus, for example, the precept of slaying animals for the need of good nourishment is of manifest utility, as we shall set forth[[fn:3092]]. But, if it be said that they must be slain by the upper part of the throat, and not by the lower[[fn:3093]], and that the gullet and the windpipe must be cut in a determined place, these and similar regulations have no other end than that of refining men[[fn:3094]]. This is what results from their manner of expression: «Whether one slays by the throat or by the nape.» Verily, I have only cited this example because we read in the passage of the Doctors these words: «Whether one slays by the throat or by the nape;» but if the matter be well examined, the truth is this[[fn:3095]]: As there is a necessity to feed upon the flesh of animals, the intention was to inflict the easiest death upon them and at once to obtain this in the simplest manner [for, to decapitate, a sword or other similar instrument would be required, whereas one may slay with any instrument whatsoever], and to bring about death more easily, it was made a condition that the knife be passing sharp.
root.text.Part 3..25.2: A more exact example of the particular details is found in the sacrifices. Indeed, the precept of offering sacrifices has a great and manifest utility, as I shall expound[[fn:3096]]. But, whether the victim be now a lamb, now a ram, and that the victims be of a fixed number, these are things for which no reason can ever be given. In my judgment, all those who take the trouble to seek reasons for any of these particular details betray a great folly; and so far from removing thereby any absurdity they might possess, they do but increase the absurdities. He who imagins that these details can be motivated is as far from the truth as he who believs that the general precept has no real utility.
root.text.Part 3..25.3: It must be known that it is the Divine Wisdom that willed,—or, if thou preferest, thou shalt say it is necessity that required,—that there should be particular details for which no reason could be assigned; and it was in some wise impossible that there should not be in the Law things of this nature. I say that this was impossible; for if thou shouldst ask, for example, why (one must offer) a lamb and not a ram, the very same question might be asked if ram had been said instead of lamb, since some species was necessary. Likewise, if thou shouldst ask why seven lambs and not eight, the same question might be asked if eight, or ten, or twenty had been said, since some number was necessarily required. This resembls in some wise the nature of the possible[[fn:3097]], where it must needs be that one of the possible things should happen,
root.text.Part 3..25.4: without one having the right to demand why this one among those things took place and not another among the possible things; for the same question might be asked if another possible thing had been realised instead of that one. Thou must well imbibe this notion. If the Doctors say often that all the commandments have their reasons, and likewise (if it be said) that these reasons were known to Solomon, it pertains to the utility of such a commandment considered in its generality, without pursuing all the details thereof.
root.text.Part 3..25.5: This being so, I have deemed it right to divide the six hundred and thirteen commandments into several classes, of which each contains a certain number of commandments of the same kind, or at least of a like nature. I shall make known unto thee the rationale of each of these classes, by demonstrating that it has an indubitable and incontestable utility. Thereupon I shall return to each of the commandments comprised in that class, and explain the reason thereof, so that there shall remain but a very small number of commandments<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3098]]</sup>, the motive of which is hitherto unknown to me. I have also been able to explain the particular ordinances and conditions pertaining to certain commandments, of which it is possible to give the reason. Thou shalt hear all this hereafter.
root.text.Part 3..25.6: But all these motives (of the commandments), I shall be unable to set forth until I have first provided several chapters containing useful preliminaries to serve as preparation for the subject I have in view; these be the chapters which I shall now begin.
root.text.Part 3..26.0: The Law as a whole aims at two things, to wit: the well-being of the soul and the well-being of the body.
root.text.Part 3..26.1: As for the well-being of the soul, it consists in this: that all men should possess sound ideas according to their respective faculties<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3099]]</sup>. Regarding this, the Scripture speaks sometimes in plain terms, and sometimes by way of allegories<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3100]]</sup>; for it is not in the nature of the vulgar sort to possess the capacity requisite for comprehending such a subject in its full reality.
root.text.Part 3..26.2: As for the well-being of the body, it is attained through the improvement of the manner of life of men one with another. This result is achieved by two means: first, by removing mutual violence from among men, so that the individual may not permit himself to act according to his own pleasure and the power he possesses<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3101]]</sup>, but shall be constrained<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3102]]</sup> to do that which is profitable unto all; secondly, by causing each individual to acquire morals useful for social life<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3103]]</sup>, in order that the interests of society may be well ordered.
root.text.Part 3..26.3: It must be known that, of these two aims (of the Law), the one is indubitably of a more exalted order, to wit, the well-being of the soul, or the acquisition of sound notions. But the second preceds it in the order of nature and of time; it is the well-being of the body, which consists in the society being well governed and in the condition of all the individuals composing it being improved as far as possible. The second aim is the more urgent, and it has been set forth with exceeding precision even in its smallest details; for it is only after having attained this second aim that one can reach the first. Verily, it has been demonstrated that man is capable of a double perfection, to wit, a first perfection, which is that of the body, and an ultimate perfection, which is that of the soul. The first consists in his enjoying perfect health throughout the whole bodily economy[[fn:3104]], which he can only obtain by always finding what is necessary when he seeks it, namely, his food as well as the other things which pertain to the regimen of the body, such as raiment[[fn:3105]], the bath, and the like. Man, alone and isolated, could not achieve this, and the individual can only reach this point through the union of society, for it is a well-known maxim that man is by nature a sociable being[[fn:3106]].
root.text.Part 3..26.4: The second perfection is to become rational in actu, that is to say, to possess intellect in actu[[fn:3107]], so that, by this second perfection, he may have of all that exists such knowledge as man is capable of. It is evident that in this second perfection there is no question of actions nor of manners, but solely of notions, unto which one is led by speculation and which are the fruit of reflection.
root.text.Part 3..26.5: It is evident likewise that one cannot attain to this ultimate and sublime perfection until after having obtained the first; for it is impossible that man, whilst harassed by pain, by hunger, thirst, heat, or cold, should even grasp the ideas that one would have him understand[[fn:3108]]; and how much less, for a stronger reason, could he form them of his own motion? But, after having arrived at the first perfection, it is possible to reach the second, which is indubitably the most noble, for it is by it alone that man is immortal.
root.text.Part 3..26.6: The true Law, which, as we have said, is unique[[fn:3109]]—I mean the Law of Moses, our Master—has come unto us only to bring us this double perfection. It regulats, on the one hand, the mutual relations of men, by making reciprocal violence to cease among them and by refining them with noble and generous manners, so that the peoples may endure, that a stable order may be established among them, and that thereby each individual may reach the first perfection; on the other hand, it improvs beliefs and produces sound notions, whereby one may attain the ultimate perfection. The Torah speaks of both, and it teaches us that the aim of the whole Law[[fn:3110]] is to cause us to reach these two perfections. It is there said: The Lord commanded us to do all these statutes, to fear the Lord our God, for our good always, that He might preserve us alive, as it is at this day (Deut. vi. 24). Here the ultimate perfection is spoken of first, because it is the most noble; for, as we have explained, it is the final aim. It is indicated by the words: For our good always; for thou knowest that the Sages explain these words of Scripture: That it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days (ibid. xxii. 7), as follows: "That it may be well with thee in a world of perfect bliss, and that thou mayest prolong thy days in a world of eternal duration[[fn:3111]]." Likewise, in our passage, the words for our good always express absolutely the same idea, that is to say, that we should attain to a world entirely of bliss and duration, which signifies perpetual permanence (immortality); but the words that He might preserve us alive, as it is at this day relate to the first corporeal existence, which is prolonged for a certain time, and whose perfect order can only be established by social union, as we have explained.
root.text.Part 3..27.0: One thing whereon it is necessary to call thy attention is that the (metaphysical) truths whereby one reaches the ultimate perfection, the Law has communicated to us only the most important points thereof, whilst inviting us in a general manner to believe therein. These points are: the existence of God, His unity, His omniscience, His power, His will, and His eternity. All these notions are the ultimate ends (of science), which can only be understood in detail and in a very clear manner[[fn:3112]] after the knowledge of many other ideas[[fn:3113]]. The Law has likewise invited us to believe certain things the belief in which is necessary for the good organization of the social state, as for example the belief that God is exceedingly wroth against those who disobey Him, and that for this reason one must fear Him, respect Him, and beware of disobeying Him[[fn:3114]]. As for the other truths relative to all that exists[[fn:3115]], which form the numerous branches of the speculative sciences and whereby the notions which are the ultimate end are consolidated, the Law, without proclaiming them clearly as it has proclaimed the former[[fn:3116]], has summarized them in these words: To love the Lord[[fn:3117]]. Thou knowest with what energy this love is expressed: With all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might (Deut. vi. 5). We have already explained, in the Mishneh Torah, that this love can only take place through a profound understanding of the whole of being and through the contemplation of the divine wisdom manifested therein, and we have said there also that the Sages have called attention to this subject[[fn:3118]].
root.text.Part 3..27.1: From all that we have hitherto stated concerning this matter, it results that, whenever a commandment, whether affirmative or negative, has for its object to put an end to mutual violence, or to inculcate good morals conducing to right social relations, or to inspire a true idea which must be accepted, either for its own sake or because it is necessary for the cessation of violence or for the acquisition of good morals, such a commandment has an evident reason and a manifest utility, and there is no occasion to ask what its end may be. Indeed, no person has ever been so perplexed as to inquire why we have been commanded to believe[[fn:3119]] that God is One, or why we have been forbidden to slay and to steal, or why we have been forbidden to exercise vengeance and retaliation, or why we have been commanded to love one another. But the commandments which have perplexed men and concerning which they have held divers opinions [so that some have said they possessed no utility other than that of prescribing something[[fn:3120]], whilst others have maintained that they possessed an utility unknown to us], these are they which, taken literally, appear not to be useful for any of the three things of which we have spoken; I mean those which neither inspire any idea, nor ennoble the morals, nor put an end to violence. It would seem, in truth, that these commandments have no relation either to the welfare of the soul, since they inculcate no belief, or to the well-being of the body, since they provide no useful rules for politics or economics; such are the precepts which forbid garments of divers materials, heterogeneous seeds, meat seethed in milk[[fn:3121]], and those which command the covering of blood, the breaking of the neck of a heifer, the redeeming of the firstborn of an ass[[fn:3122]], and others of like nature.
root.text.Part 3..27.2: But thou shalt hear further on my explanation of all these precepts, for which I shall give the true and well-demonstrated reasons, save for certain precepts of detail, as I have said. I shall show that all these precepts and others of like nature must necessarily relate to one of the three things of which we have spoken, and that they must either rectify a belief, or improve the conditions of society, which is attained by two things: the cessation of mutual violence and the acquisition of good morals.
root.text.Part 3..27.3: —One must be imbued with that which we have said concerning beliefs: sometimes the commandment inculcats a true belief which is in itself the sole end, as for example the belief in the unity, the eternity, and the incorporeality of God; at other times it is a belief necessary for the cessation of mutual violence, or for the acquisition of good morals, as for example the belief that God is greatly wroth against him who has committed violence, as it is said: My wrath shall wax hot, and I will kill you etc. (Exodus, 22, 24), and the belief that God hearkens instantly to the prayer of him who has suffered violence or has been frustrated: And it shall come to pass, when he cries unto me, that I will hear; for I am gracious (ibid., v. 26).
root.text.Part 3..28.0: It is well known that our father Abraham [peace be upon him!] was brought up in the religion of the Sabians[[fn:3123]], who believe that there is no God but the stars[[fn:3124]]. When, in this chapter, I shall have made known to thee their books which, being translated into Arabic, are now in our hands, as well as their ancient annals[[fn:3125]], and when by means of these documents I shall have revealed to thee their doctrine and their chronicles, thou shalt recognize that they therein[[fn:3126]] expressly declare that the stars are (that which constituts) the divinity[[fn:3127]], and that the sun is the supreme god[[fn:3128]]. All the seven planets[[fn:3129]], they say elsewhere, are gods; but the two luminaries (the sun and the moon) are the greatest among them. Thou shalt see that they say clearly that it is the sun which governs the upper and the lower world; such is what they state textually.
root.text.Part 3..28.1: In their books and annals, thou shalt find the history of our father Abraham which they recount in these terms: Abraham, who was brought up in Cutha[[fn:3130]], having set himself in opposition to all the world by maintaining that there exists an efficient cause (of the universe) other than the sun, divers arguments were alleged against him, and there were cited to him, among other proofs, the manifest and evident action which the sun exerts upon the universe. “Ye are right,” Abraham answered them: “it is as the axe in the hand of the carpenter.” Some of his arguments against them are then reported, and, at the end of the narrative, it is related that the king caused our father Abraham to be imprisoned, and that he, even in prison, persisted long in assailing their opinions. Finally the king, fearing lest Abraham should prejudice his government and turn the people from their religious beliefs, exiled him to Syria[[fn:3131]], after having confiscated all his substance.
root.text.Part 3..28.2: Such are the tales they recount[[fn:3132]], and thou shalt find this narrative with fuller developments in the Nabataean Agriculture[[fn:3133]]. They make no mention of that which our true traditions[[fn:3134]] relate concerning Abraham, nor of the revelation that came unto him; for they accused him of falsehood because he combated their pernicious opinion. Since he stood in opposition to the belief of all the world, there can be no doubt, I think, but that he was for those erring men an object of malediction, of reprobation, and of contempt. Now, as he endured this for the love of God, choosing rather to profess the truth than to be held in honour[[fn:3135]], it was said unto him: I will bless them that bless thee, and him that curss thee will I curse, and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed (Genesis, xii, 3); and, in sooth, we see in this day[[fn:3136]] the greater part of the inhabitants of the earth glorifying him with one accord and blessing themselves by his memory, so much so that even they who are not of his race claim descent from him. He has no longer any adversaries, and none remains ignorant of his greatness, save only the last sectaries of that extinct religion[[fn:3137]] who yet abide at the extremities of the earth, such as the infidel Turks in the far north, and the Hindus in the far south; for these remain attached to the religion of the Sabians, a religion which once embraced the whole earth.
root.text.Part 3..28.3: The loftiest degree[[fn:3138]] reached by the speculation of the philosophers in those times was to imagine that God is the spirit of the celestial sphere; that is to say, that the celestial sphere and the stars are the body of which God is the spirit[[fn:3139]]. This is what Abu Bakr ibn al-Sayigh says in his commentary upon the Acroasis[[fn:3140]].
root.text.Part 3..28.4: Wherefore all the Sabians admitted the eternity of the world; for, according to them, the heavens are God.
root.text.Part 3..28.5: They maintain that Adam was a person born of a man and a woman, like other human individuals[[fn:3141]]; yet they glorify him, saying that he was a prophet, an apostle of the Moon, who invited men to the worship of the Moon, and that he composed books upon agriculture[[fn:3142]]. The Sabians likewise say that Noah was a husbandman, and that he approved not the worship of idols; wherefore thou shalt find that Noah was an object of reprobation unto all the Sabians, who say that he never worshipped any idol[[fn:3143]]. They say also in their books that he was smitten and incarcerated because he devoted himself to the worship of God, and they recount yet other like tales. They maintain that Seth combated the opinion of his father Adam concerning the worship of the Moon[[fn:3144]], and they put forth lies exceedingly ridiculous, which denote a great defect of reasoning and show that they were further removed from philosophy than all other men; and verily[[fn:3145]] they were in a state of extreme ignorance. They recount, for example, that Adam, having come forth from the clime of the sun[[fn:3146]], near unto India, and penetrating into the region of Babylon, brought with him marvelous things; amongst others, a tree of gold which flourished and had leaves and branches, a similar tree of stone, and a green leaf of a tree which the fire could not consume. He (Adam) spake also of a tree which could shelter ten thousand persons, albeit it had but the height of a man[[fn:3147]]; he brought with him two leaves thereof, of which each could enwrap two persons. They recount yet a multitude of other such fables; and it is a matter of wonder that people who believe the world to be eternal should nevertheless admit the existence of these things, acknowledged as naturally impossible by those who apply themselves to physical studies[[fn:3148]]. That which they say of Adam, and all that they attribute unto him, has no other purpose than to fortify their opinion concerning the eternity of the world, in order to draw the conclusion that the stars and the celestial sphere are the divinity[[fn:3149]].
root.text.Part 3..28.6: But when he grew up who was the pillar of the world[[fn:3150]], having recognized that there exists a separate God[[fn:3151]], who is neither a body nor a force in a body, and that all these stars and all these spheres were His works, and having understood the absurdity of all those tales wherewith he had been reared, he began to refute their doctrine and to show the falsity of their opinions; he declared himself publicly their adversary, and proclaimed the name of the Eternal, the God of the universe[[fn:3152]], a proclamation which embraced at once the existence of God and the creation of the world by that same God.
root.text.Part 3..28.7: In accordance with these Sabian opinions, they erected statues unto the planets, statues of gold unto the sun and statues of silver unto the moon[[fn:3153]], and they allotted the metals and the regions unto the planets[[fn:3154]], saying that such a planet is the God of such a region. They built temples in which they placed statues, and they asserted that the forces of the planets were poured forth upon these statues, so that the latter spoke[[fn:3155]], understood, thought, and inspired men, making known unto them that which is of use. They speak in the same wise of the trees which fell to the lot of these planets: if (say they), one consecrate such a tree to such a planet, planting it in the name of the latter, and employing for it and with it[[fn:3156]] this or that procedure, the spiritual force[[fn:3157]] of that planet is poured forth upon that tree, inspires men and speaks unto them in their sleep. Thou shalt find all this textually in their writings, unto which I shall call thy attention. Such were the prophets of Baal and the prophets of Asherah, of whom it is spoken amongst us[[fn:3158]] and in whom these ideas had become so fortified that they forsook the Eternal[[fn:3159]] and cried out: O Baal, hear us! (I Kings, 18, 26.) The cause thereof was that these opinions were most common, that ignorance was widespread, and that the world was then generally plunged into foolish imaginations of this kind; thus there arose among them (the Hebrews) ideas which gave birth to soothsayers, augurs, sorcerers, enchanters, evocators, magicians, and necromancers[[fn:3160]].
root.text.Part 3..28.8.sub_0: We have already expounded, in our great work Mishneh Torah[[fn:3161]], that our father Abraham began to refute these opinions by arguments and by a preaching full of gentleness which won men over, and that he drew them unto the worship of God by treating them with benevolence. When subsequently the prince of the prophets appeared[[fn:3162]], he fulfilled the intention (of Abraham), by commanding that these men (idolaters) should be slain, that their traces be made to disappear and their root be destroyed [Ye shall demolish their altars, etc.[[fn:3163]]], and by forbidding to follow in any wise their customs: and ye shall not walk in the manners of the nation, etc. (Levit., XX, 23). Thou knowest by many passages of the Pentateuch that the Law had principally for its aim the cessation of idolatry, the effacement of its trace, (the removal of) all that is connected therewith, even unto the very memory thereof, and all that may lead to one of its practices [such as evocation, magic, passing through the fire[[fn:3164]], divination, the art of soothsaying and augury, sorcery, incantation, and necromancy], and finally to warn that one must beware of performing even the semblance of these practices, and a fortiori of imitating them themselves. It is expressly declared, in the Pentateuch, that all things whereby they believed they rendered worship unto their divinities and approached them were in hatred and abomination unto God; it is this which this passage says: for every abomination to the Eternal, which he hats, have they done unto their gods (Deut., XII, 31). It is related, as thou shalt find in their books which I shall make known unto thee, that, under certain circumstances, they offered to the sun, their supreme god, seven beetles, seven mice, and seven bats. Verily, this alone suffices to inspire disgust in human nature.
root.text.Part 3..28.8.sub_1: — All the commandments, therefore, which have for their object the prohibition of idolatry and all that depends therefrom, which may lead thereto, or which is in relation therewith, are of a manifest utility; for they all aim at preserving us from these pernicious opinions, which turn us aside from all that is useful for attaining the two perfections[[fn:3165]], by giving us those foolish preoccupations in which our ancestors were reared, — Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor, and they served other gods (Joshua, 24, 2), — and of which the veracious prophets have spoken, saying: They followed after vain things which profit not[[fn:3166]]. Great, therefore, is the utility of every commandment which preservs us from this grave error and which leads us back to the true belief, namely, that there is a God, the Creator of all these things, that it is He who must be worshipped, loved, and feared, and not these imaginary divinities, and that, to approach the true God and to conciliate His benevolence, one has no need of all these painful practices, but that it suffices to love Him and to fear Him, two things which are the true object of divine worship, as we shall set forth: And now, Israel, what does the Eternal thy God require of thee, etc.? (Deuter., 10, 12.) Further on, I shall enlarge more upon this idea.
root.text.Part 3..28.9: — Returning now to my theme, I say that what has enabled me to understand the meaning of a great number of commandments and what has made known unto me the reason thereof, is the study I have made of the doctrines of the Sabians, of their opinions, their practices, and the ceremonies of their worship. This is what thou shalt see, when I shall expound what has motivated these commandments, which are believed to be without any reason whatsoever. I shall therefore speak unto thee of the books[[fn:3167]] whereby thou mayest learn all that I myself know of the doctrines and opinions of the Sabians, in order that thou mayest acquire the certainty that all that I shall say to motivate these commandments is the truth.
root.text.Part 3..28.10: The greatest work upon this subject is the Nabatean Agriculture, a work translated by Ibn-Wa’hshiyya[[fn:3168]]. I shall inform thee, in the following chapter, why the Sabians have inscribed their religious doctrines in treatises on agriculture. Thus, the book in question is filled with the foolish conceits of idolaters and with that which may entice and captivate the minds of the multitude; therein they speak of talismans, of the cooperation of spirits (of the stars)[[fn:3169]], of magic, of demons, and of ghouls that inhabit the deserts. Therein are related incidentally great follies, which move intelligent men to laughter and by which they pretended to insult the manifest miracles, which made known to the inhabitants of the earth that there is a God who governs them all, as it is said: To the end thou mayest know that the earth is the Eternal's (Exodus, 9, 29), and in another passage: That, I am the Eternal, in the midst of the earth (ibid., VIII, 18).
root.text.Part 3..28.11: It is likewise related therein that Adam, the first man[[fn:3170]], recorded in his book that there existed in India a tree of which the branches, if taken and cast upon the ground, move each like unto creeping serpents; that another tree, the root of which has a human form, gives forth a hoarse sound and utters distinct words; that a man, by taking the leaves of a certain herb [of which a description is given], and placing them in his bosom, renders himself invisible, so that it is not seen whither he enters nor whence he departs; and finally that if, with this selfsame herb, fumigations be made in the open air, there is heard in the atmosphere, so long as the smoke ascends, a noise and sounds most terrifying. Divers fables of a like nature are therein recounted at great length in the style[[fn:3171]] of a simple exposition[[fn:3172]] concerning the remarkable qualities of plants and the peculiarities of nature, so that they seem to offer an insult unto miracles and to induce the belief that these latter were accomplished by means of artifices[[fn:3173]].
root.text.Part 3..28.12: One of the fables of this book (of the Nabataean Agriculture) is that relating to the shrub of the Althæa, one of those plants which were employed as Asheroth[[fn:3174]], even as I have informed thee. It is related that this shrub, after having been stationed for twelve thousand years at Nineveh, had a quarrel with the mandrake, which sought to take its place, and that the person whom this shrub (the Althæa) inspired remained for some time deprived of his revelations; thereafter, when inspiring him anew, it recounted unto him that it had been occupied in pleading with the mandrake, and it commanded him to write unto the Chaldeans[[fn:3175]], that they might judge their cause and declare which of the two plants, the Althæa or the mandrake, is preferable for their magic and of more frequent employment. 'Tis a right long fable[[fn:3176]], and if thou readest it, thou shalt thereby be able to judge of the intelligence of the men of those times and of the state of their sciences. Such were in those days of darkness the sages of Babylon unto whom allusion is made[[fn:3177]]; for such were the religious beliefs in which they had been nurtured. Had not the belief in the existence of God been so generally acknowledged in present religions, there would be in our days a darkness yet thicker than that which reigned in those times; nevertheless, there is such in other respects[[fn:3178]]. But let us return to our subject.
root.text.Part 3..28.13: In the book in question, it is related concerning a personage from among the prophets of idolatry, who was called Thammuz, that he invited a certain king to worship the seven planets and the twelve signs of the Zodiac. This king put him to death in a cruel manner[[fn:3179]]; and it is related that, on the night of his death, all the idols from the different regions of the earth assembled in the temple of Babylon, before the great golden statue, which is that of the sun. This statue, which was suspended between heaven and earth, came to station itself[[fn:3180]] in the midst of the temple, and all the other statues placed themselves around it. It began to pronounce the funeral oration of Thammuz and to recount that which had befallen him; all the idols wept and lamented throughout that whole night, and at morn they flew away and returned unto their temples in the different regions of the earth. Thenceforth comes that perpetual custom of lamenting and weeping for Thammuz, on the first day of the month of Thammuz (July); it is the women[[fn:3181]] who weep for him and who recite his funeral eulogy[[fn:3182]].
root.text.Part 3..28.14: — Direct thy attention unto all this, and thou shalt understand what were the ideas of the men of those times; for this legend of Thammuz is of a most high antiquity among the Sabians. By the book in question, thou mayest know the greater part of the foolish notions of the Sabians, as well as their practices and their festivals.
root.text.Part 3..28.15: As for that which they relate concerning the adventure of Adam, the serpent, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, in which allusion is also made to an unaccustomed manner of clothing[[fn:3183]], thou must be well on thy guard lest thy mind be troubled and lest thou imagine that what they say ever happened unto Adam or unto any other. It is by no means a real history, and the slightest reflection will cause thee to perceive that all which they have related in this fable is naught but falsehood. Thou shalt perceive that it is a story which they have copied from the Pentateuch. When that book had spread among the religious sects[[fn:3184]], and when these, having heard the text of the narrative of the creation, took it entirely in its literal sense, they (the Sabians) forged[[fn:3185]] this story in question, to the end that the inexperienced men who should hear it might be led to believe that the world is eternal and that this history, related in the Pentateuch, had actually occurred even as they recounted it[[fn:3186]].
root.text.Part 3..28.16: Albeit a man such as thou hast no need of this observation[[fn:3187]], — for thou art possessed of sufficient science to prevent thy mind from cleaving unto the fables of the Sabians and unto the follies of the Casdeans and the Chaldeans[[fn:3188]], who are devoid of all science truly deserving of that name, — yet have I deemed it my duty to offer a warning for the preservation of others; for the vulgar are but too prone to give credence unto fables.
root.text.Part 3..28.17: Amongst the number of these (pagan) books is likewise the book Istimakhis[[fn:3189]], which is attributed unto Aristotle, though it be passing far from being his work; likewise the writings relating unto talismans, such as the book of Tomtom[[fn:3190]], the book Al-Sarb[[fn:3191]], the book “Of the Degrees of the Celestial Sphere and of the Figures appearing in each Degree[[fn:3192]]”, another book on talismans attributed unto Aristotle, another attributed unto Hermes[[fn:3193]], and finally a book of the Sabian Is’hâk for the defense of the religion of the Sabians[[fn:3194]], and his great work upon the laws of the Sabians, upon various details of their religion, their festivals, their sacrifices, their prayers, and other religious subjects.
root.text.Part 3..28.18: All the books which I have just enumerated are books of idolatry which have been translated into Arabic. It is indubitable that they form but a small portion (of that literature), in comparison with those which have not been translated or which no longer even exist, but have been lost and have perished in the course of years. Those which still exist amongst us at this day contain the greater part of the opinions of the Sabians, as well as their practices, which, in part, are still spread throughout the world; I speak of the construction of temples, of the statues of metal and stone which are erected therein, of the construction of altars, of what is offered there in the way of sacrifices or different kinds of food, of the institution of festivals, of gatherings for prayers or for other ceremonies performed in these temples, [in which are reserved places which they hold in great honour and which they call the chapels of the intelligible forms[[fn:3195]]], of the images which they place upon the high mountains (Deut. xii. 2), of the honours rendered unto the Asheroth[[fn:3196]], of the erection of monumental stones[[fn:3197]], and finally of other matters which thou mayest read in the books whereunto I have called thy attention.
root.text.Part 3..28.19: The knowledge of these opinions and practices is of the utmost importance for the understanding of the reasons of the (divine) commandments; for the foundation of our whole Law and the pivot upon which it turns, is the effacing of these opinions from minds and the destruction of their monuments; “to efface them from minds,” as it is said: Lest your heart be deceived (Deut. xi. 16),… whose heart turns away this day etc. (ibid., XXIX, 17), “and to destroy their monuments,” as it is said: Ye shall destroy their altars… and cut down their Asheroth (Deut. vii. 5)[[fn:3198]], and destroy the names of them out of that place (ibid., XII, 3). These two points are found repeated in several passages; for such is the principal end of the whole Law, even as the doctors have informed us by their traditional explanation of these words: All that the Lord has commanded you by the hand of Moses (Numbers, xv. 23); “Whence thou mayest learn, say they[[fn:3199]], that he who professes idolatry denies the whole Law, and he who denies idolatry acknowledges the whole Law.” Thou must well possess thyself of this truth.
root.text.Part 3..29.0: By considering these antiquated and unreasonable opinions, thou shalt recognize that it was a notion generally prevalent among men, that the worship of the stars resulted in the prosperity of the earth and the fertility of lands. The learned, as well as the virtuous and pious men of those times, preached in this sense and taught that agriculture, whereby alone man subsisted, could not be accomplished and succeed according to desire save by means of the worship[[fn:3200]] of the sun and the (other) planets, and that, if they were provoked by disobedience, the lands would become desert and be laid waste. They (the Sabians) relate in their books, that Jupiter[[fn:3201]] had smitten with his wrath the desert and uncultivated places, which, for that cause, are deprived of water and trees and inhabited by ghouls. They held in great honour husbandmen and tilers of the soil, because these occupy themselves with the cultivation of the earth, which responds unto the will of the stars and is[[fn:3202]] well-pleasing unto them. The reason why the idolaters esteemed oxen so highly is none other than because these are useful for agriculture. They even said that it is not permitted to slaughter them[[fn:3203]], because, albeit being endowed with strength, they yield themselves unto man for agriculture[[fn:3204]]. If they act thus, if they submit unto man despite their strength, it is solely (they say) because their service in agriculture is pleasing unto the gods. As these opinions were widely spread, they linked idolatry unto agriculture, the latter being a thing necessary for the subsistence of man and of most animals; the idolatrous priests preached unto the men assembled in the temples and confirmed them in this notion, that by means of this worship (of the stars), the rains would descend, the trees would bear fruit, and the lands would be fertile and populous. One must read what is said in the Nabatean Agriculture in the place where the vine is spoken of; thou shalt find there these very words of the Sabians: “All the ancient sages and prophets have prescribed it as a duty to play musical instruments, on festival days, before the idols; they said with reason that the gods take pleasure therein and grant the fairest reward unto those who do so. They have made many goodly promises for this act, promising amongst others the prolongation of life, the removal of calamities, the disappearance of infirmities, the fertility of seeds, and the abundance of fruits[[fn:3205]].” Such are the literal words of the Sabians.
root.text.Part 3..29.1: Now, as these opinions were so generally diffused that they were believed to be true, and as God, in His mercy towards us, desired to efface this error from our minds and to relieve our bodies of these toils, by bringing to an end these wearisome and profitless ceremonies and by giving us His laws through Moses, the latter announced to us in the name of God that, if these stars and idols were worshipped[[fn:3206]], their cult would result in the failure of rain, that the soil would be desolate and yield nothing, that the fruits of the trees would fall, that calamities would befall social relations[[fn:3207]], and infirmities would afflict the person, and that human life would be shortened. Such is the object of the words of the covenant which the Lord has made[[fn:3208]]. Thou shalt find this same subject repeated throughout the whole Pentateuch, to wit: that the worship of the stars brings about the cessation of rain, the devastation of the soil, the destruction of social relations, diseases of the body, and brevity of life; whilst by forsaking their worship and embracing the service of God, one obtains the descent of rain, the fertility of the soil, the improvement of social relations, health of body, and length of days. This is the contrary of that which the worshippers of false gods preached, in order to propagate their cult[[fn:3209]]; for the principal aim of the Law is to cause this belief to cease and to efface every trace thereof, as we have set forth.
root.text.Part 3..30.0: There be certain persons who are loath to perceive a motive in any of the (divine) laws; they prefer to find no rational sense in the commandments and prohibitions[[fn:3210]]. That which leads them to this is a certain weakness which they experience in their souls, but upon which they cannot reason, and of which they could not well give an account. This is what they think: If the laws were intended to profit us in this (temporal) existence, and if they had been given to us for such or such a motive, it might well be that they were the product of the reflection and thought of a man of genius; if, on the contrary, a thing has no comprehensible sense and produces no advantage, it emanats from the Divinity, for human reflection would not lead to such a thing. It would seem that, according to these weak minds, man is more perfect than his Creator; for man (according to them) would speak and act with a view to a certain end, whilst God, far from acting likewise, would command us, on the contrary, to do that which is of no utility to us, and would forbid us actions which can bring us no harm. Far from Him be such a thought! The contrary is the case, and it is always our good that the Divinity has in view, as we have shewn by the words of Scripture: That we might be happy always, and that He might preserve us alive, as it is at this day (Deuter., vi. 24)[[fn:3211]]. Elsewhere it is said: Surely they that shall hear all these statutes will say, this great nation is a wise and understanding people (Ibid., iv. 6). Here it is clearly stated that even all the statutes (or ordinances)[[fn:3212]] shall appear to the nations as emanating from wisdom and intelligence. But if a thing[[fn:3213]] has no discernable motive, if it produces no advantage, nor averts any evil, why should it be said of him whose object of belief or rule of conduct it is, that he is wise and intelligent and that he occupies an exalted rank?
