What would there be in that which could astonish the peoples?
root.text.Part 3..30.1: But nay; the matter is indubitably as we have said, namely, that each of the six hundred and thirteen commandments must either produce a sound opinion, or destroy an erroneous opinion, or establish a rule of justice, or cause injustice to cease, or train man in good morals, or preserve him from depraved morals. The whole of the commandments, therefore, relats to three things: to opinions, to morals, and to the practice of social duties. If we do not here include speech, it is because the words which Scripture commands or forbidds to be uttered[[fn:3214]], sometimes enter into the class of social duties, and sometimes cause certain opinions or certain morals to be contracted. Wherefore here, where the question is to indicate the motive of each commandment, we confine ourselves to the three classes which we have just indicated.
root.text.Part 3..31.0: If thou considerest the divine works, I mean the works of nature, thou shalt understand what providence, what wisdom God has manifested in the creation of living beings, in the arrangement of the movements of the members, and in the position of these latter in respect to one another; likewise, thou shalt acknowledge the wisdom and providence of God in the different conditions through which He causs the whole of the individual (animal) successively to pass[[fn:3215]]. As for the arrangement of its movements and the relative position of the organs, I shall cite the following example: The anterior part of the brain is extremely soft, whilst the posterior part has more consistency; the spinal marrow is yet more consistent, and, as it extends, it becoms firmer. The nerves are the organs of sensation and motion; consequently, the nerves which serve for simple sensory perception or for a movement of little difficulty, such as that of the eyelid and the jaw, proceed from the brain, whilst those which are necessary for the movement of the limbs issue from the spinal marrow. Now, as the nerves, even those which issue from the spinal marrow, could not, by reason of their softness, set the joints in motion, it has been skillfully remedied in the following manner: the nerves are ramified into fibres, which, being filled with flesh, have become muscles; then the nerve, having passed beyond the extremity of the muscle[[fn:3216]] and having become firm by fragments of the ligaments which are mingled therewith, has become a tendon[[fn:3217]]. The tendon joins the bone[[fn:3218]] and is attached thereto: only then can the nerve, in consequence of this gradual transformation, set the limb in motion. I cite but this single example, because it is the most manifest among the marvels set forth in the treatise on the Utility of the Parts[[fn:3219]], all of which are clear, manifest, and well known to him who examins them with a penetrating mind. Likewise, God has used providence toward the individuals of the mammals; for, as these are born with extreme delicacy and cannot nourish themselves with dry food, there have been prepared for them teats which give them milk, that they may be able to nourish themselves with a succulent food, appropriate to the constitution of their members, until these latter become little by little and gradually firm and solid.
root.text.Part 3..31.1: Many things in our Law have been thus ordained by the Supreme Disposer. Indeed, as it is impossible to pass suddenly from one extreme to the other, man, according to his nature, cannot abruptly quit all his habits. When, therefore, God sent Moses, our master, in order to make of us, by the knowledge of God, a kingdom of priests and an holy nation (Exodus, xix. 6) [as He declared by saying: Unto thee it was shewed that thou mightest know, etc. (Deuteron., iv. 35), Know therefore this day, and consider it in thine heart, etc. (Ib., v. 39)], and in order to make us devoted to His worship, as it is said: and to serve him with all your heart (Ib., xi. 13), ye shall serve the Lord your God (Exodus, xxiii. 25), and him shall ye serve (Deuteron., xiii. 5), then (I say)[[fn:3220]] it was a widespread custom, familiar to the whole world,—and we ourselves had been reared in this universal cult,—to offer diverse species of animals in those temples where the idols were placed, to worship these latter and to burn incense before them. Religious men and ascetics were the only ones who devoted themselves to the service of these temples consecrated to the stars[[fn:3221]], as we have set forth. In consequence, the wisdom of God, whose providence is manifested in all His creatures, did not judge it fitting to command us to reject all these species of worship, their abandonment and their suppression; for that would have appeared then inadmissible to human nature, which always affects that which is habitual to it. To demand then such a thing would have been as if a prophet in these times, in exhorting to the worship of God, should come to tell us: “God forbidds you to address prayers to Him, to fast, and to invoke His help in misfortune; but your worship shall be a simple meditation, without any practice.”
root.text.Part 3..31.2: This is why God allowed these various kinds of worship to remain; but, instead of being directed toward created objects and imaginary things without reality, He transferred them to His name and commanded us to practice them toward Himself. He thus commanded us to build Him a temple: Let them make Me a sanctuary (Exodus 25:8), to raise the altar in His name: An altar of earth thou shalt make unto Me (Ib., XX, 21), to offer sacrifices to Him: If any man of you bring an offering unto the Lord (Leviticus I, 2), to prostrate oneself before Him, and to burn incense before Him. He forbade the performance of any of these actions for any other than Himself: He that sacrifics unto any god shall be utterly destroyed (Exodus 22:19); for thou shalt worship no other god (Ib., XXXIV, 14). He designated priests for the service of the sanctuary, saying: That they may minister unto Me in the priest's office (Ib., XXVIII, 41); and, as they were occupied with the temple and its sacrifices, it was necessary to establish for them revenues that would suffice for them, which are called the dues of the Levites and the priests. The result of this divine providence[[fn:3222]] was to erase the memory of idolatrous worship and to consolidate the great and true principle of our belief[[fn:3223]], namely, the existence and unity of God, without human minds being repulsed and startled by the abolition of ceremonies that were familiar to them and outside of which none were known.
root.text.Part 3..31.3.sub_0: I know that at first glance your mind will refuse to admit this idea and that you will feel a sense of repugnance toward it. You will mentally pose these questions to me: How can one suppose precepts, prohibitions[[fn:3224]], and important acts, minutely detailed and prescribed for fixed times, which yet would not have their purpose in themselves, but in something else, as if this were merely an expedient devised by God to achieve His primary goal? What, then, prevented Him from revealing to us (directly) what His primary goal was and making us capable of conceiving this goal, without needing these means that you suppose to be only a secondary goal? But listen to the answer I have to give you[[fn:3225]]; it will remove this anxiety from your heart and manifest to you the truth of what I have observed. Indeed, the very text of the Pentateuch presents us with something analogous, saying: God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near, etc. But God led the people about, through the way of the wilderness, by the Sea of Reeds (Exodus 13:17 and 18). Just as God, for fear of an obstacle that their bodies naturally could not overcome, caused them to deviate from the direct path[[fn:3226]] that had first been intended, toward another path, so that the primary goal might be attained, so too, fearing (to reveal directly to them) what the soul naturally could not conceive, He prescribed for them these laws of which we have spoken, so that the primary goal might be reached, namely, the conception of the true God and the abolition of idolatry. For just as it is not in the nature of man that, after having been raised in servile labor, that of clay and bricks, etc., he should suddenly wash the stain from his hands and immediately fight the descendants of Anak[[fn:3227]], so it is not in his nature that, after having been raised in very diverse kinds of worship and in habitual practices with which minds become so familiar that they become, as it were, a primary notion, he should abandon them all at once.
root.text.Part 3..31.3.sub_1: On the one hand, God employed providence by making these men wander in the desert until they had become valiant [for it is known that the life of the desert and physical privations[[fn:3228]] produce valor, while the opposite engenders cowardice], and, moreover, there were also born men who were not accustomed to degradation and servitude; all this was done by divine orders given through the mediation of Moses, our teacher: At the commandment of the Lord they rested, and at the commandment of the Lord they journeyed; they kept the charge of the Lord, at the commandment of the Lord by the hand of Moses (Numbers 9:23). On the other hand, the laws of this class[[fn:3229]] were given to them by divine providence so that they might maintain that kind of practice to which they were accustomed, and that thereby faith—which was the primary goal—might be strengthened. You will ask (secondly): "What then prevented God from revealing to us (directly) what His primary goal was and making us capable of conceiving this goal?" But this second question can be retorted against you, saying: What then prevented God from making them take the path of the land of the Philistines and making them capable of engaging in wars, without needing to make them take this detour with the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night (Exodus 13:21, 22)? Similarly, a third question could be addressed to you regarding the details of promises and threats relating to the entire law[[fn:3230]], and one could say to you: "Since the primary goal and intention of God were that we should believe in this law and observe the practices it prescribes[[fn:3231]], why did He not give us the faculty to always conceive this goal[[fn:3232]] and to act accordingly, rather than using an indirect means, (by warning us) that He would reward us for our obedience and punish us for our disobedience? And why realize all these rewards and all these punishments? For[[fn:3233]] this is yet another indirect means employed toward us to obtain from us what was His primary goal. What then would have prevented Him from fixing in us a natural inclination to perform[[fn:3234]] the acts of piety He desired and to repudiate the sins He detested?"
root.text.Part 3..31.4: To these three questions and all other similar ones, a single general answer can be given, which is as follows: Although all miracles consist in the change of the nature of any being among existing things[[fn:3235]], God does not change the nature of human individuals by miracle. It is because of this important principle that it is said: O that there were such an heart in them, etc. (Deuteron. 5:26)[[fn:3236]]. This[[fn:3237]] is the reason for the precepts, the prohibitions, the rewards, and the punishments. We have already, in several places in our works, expounded this fundamental principle, supporting it with proofs[[fn:3238]]. If we profess this principle, it is not because we believe that changing the nature of any human individual is difficult for God; on the contrary, it is possible and depends upon the power (of God). However, according to the principles contained in the Law of the Pentateuch[[fn:3239]], He never willed to do so and never will; for if it were His will to change the nature of the human individual each time because of what He wants to obtain from that individual, the mission of the prophets and the entire legislation would be useless[[fn:3240]].
root.text.Part 3..31.5: Returning now to my subject, I observe: As this species of worship, — by which I refer to sacrifices, — possessed but a secondary aim, whilst invocations, prayers, and other religious observances approximate more closely to the principal end and are requisite for its attainment, God instituted a marked distinction between the two classes (of worship). Indeed, the worship of the former species, — I mean that of sacrifices, — though directed towards God, was nevertheless not enjoined upon us as it had initially been, that is to say, to offer sacrifices in every place and at every time. Temples could not be erected everywhere, nor could any casual individual be appointed as a sacrificer, permitting [[t:0]]whosoever would to officiate[[t:1]] (I Kings, XIII, 33). All this, on the contrary, He (God) prohibited, and He established[[fn:3241]] a single temple: [[t:2]]in the place which the LORD shall choose[[t:3]] (Deuteronomy, 12, 26); sacrifices could not be offered elsewhere: [[t:4]]Take heed to thyself that thou offer not thy burnt offerings in every place that thou seest[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]Ib.[[t:7]], [[t:8]]v.[[t:9]] 13), and only a particular family was permitted to exercise the priesthood. All this was intended to restrict this species of worship, and to permit only such portions thereof to subsist as divine wisdom deemed not to be wholly relinquished. But invocations and prayers are performed in every place and by whomsoever; the same applies to the [[t:10]]tzitzit[[t:11]][[fn:3242]], the [[t:12]]mezuzot[[t:13]][[fn:3243]], the [[t:14]]tefillin[[t:15]][[fn:3244]] and other similar objects of worship.
root.text.Part 3..31.6: By reason of this notion which I have revealed unto thee, there are oftentimes found in the books of the prophets reproaches addressed unto men concerning their great assiduity[[fn:3245]] in offering sacrifices, and it is declared unto them that these latter have no end which is essential in itself[[fn:3246]], and that God has no need of them. Samuel said: Has the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord (I Sam. xv. 22)? Isaiah says: To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me, says the Lord, etc. (i. 11). Jeremiah says: For I spake not unto your fathers, nor commanded them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices: but this thing commanded I them, saying, Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and ye shall be my people (Jer. vii. 22, 23). This passage has appeared difficult unto all those whose discourses I have seen or heard. How, said they, could Jeremiah say of God that He prescribed nothing unto us concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices, seeing that a great number of commandments relate only to that? But the sense of this passage accords with what I have set forth unto thee: “That which I have principally for my object,” says He, “is that ye should perceive Me and that ye should worship none other than Me: I will be your God, and ye shall be my people. The prescription to offer sacrifices and to repair to the temple had no other end than to establish this fundamental principle, and it is for this reason that I have transferred these ceremonies unto My name, so that the trace of idolatry might be blotted out and the principle of My unity firmly established. But ye have neglected this end and have attached yourselves to the means[[fn:3247]]; for ye have doubted My existence: They have belied the Lord, and said, It is not he (Jer. v. 12); ye have given yourselves up to idolatry: …. to burn incense unto Baal, and walk after other gods... and come and stand before me in this house (Ib., vii. 9, 10)[[fn:3248]]; ye continue to repair to the temple and to offer sacrifices, which were not the end primarily held in view.”
root.text.Part 3..31.7: I have yet another manner of interpreting this verse, which likewise leads unto the idea that we have just set forth. For indeed, the biblical text and tradition agree in declaring that in the first laws which were prescribed unto us, there was no question whatever of burnt offerings and sacrifices; for thou must not occupy thyself with the Passover lamb in Egypt[[fn:3249]], which had a clear and manifest reason, as we shall set forth[[fn:3250]], and which, moreover, was prescribed in Egypt itself, whereas the legislation alluded to in the verse (of Jeremiah) concerns that which was prescribed unto us after the departure from Egypt. This is why there is made in this verse this express restriction: In the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt; for the first precepts given after the departure from Egypt were those prescribed at Marah, where He says unto us: If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the Lord thy God, etc. (Exod. xv. 26); there he made for them a statute and an ordinance, etc. (Ib., v. 25). The true tradition says: “At Marah, there were prescribed the Sabbath and the civil laws[[fn:3251]]”; therefore, by statute, allusion is made to the Sabbath, and by ordinance, to the civil laws, which have for their object the cessation of injustice. Here, then, it is a question of the primary object, as we have explained, I mean to say (that it concerns) firstly the highest truths of faith, such as the newness of the world[[fn:3252]]; for thou knowest that the law of the Sabbath was prescribed unto us especially to consolidate this fundamental principle, as we have set forth in this treatise[[fn:3253]]. Besides true ideas, it was also intended to cause injustice to cease among men. It is therefore clear that, in the first laws, there was no question of burnt offerings and sacrifices, for these have but a secondary object, as we have stated.
root.text.Part 3..31.8: The same idea which Jeremiah expressed is also set forth in the Psalms in the form of an exhortation unto the whole nation, which then ignored the primary object, and distinguished it not from the secondary object: Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify against thee: I am God, even thy God. I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices or thy burnt offerings, to have been continually before me. I will take no bullock out of thy house, nor he-goats out of thy folds (Ps. l. 7-9). Wheresoever this idea has been repeated, the end which I have indicated was intended. It behoves thee to be well penetrated with this and to reflect upon it.
root.text.Part 3..32.0: That which, among other things, the perfect Law had furthermore for its object, was to make us repress and despise our appetites, and to restrict them as much as possible, so as to satisfy them only in that which is necessary. Thou knowest that the passion unto which the multitude most frequently gives itself up[[fn:3254]] is intemperance in food, drink, and physical love. It is this which destroys the ultimate perfection of man, and which is also detrimental to his primary[[fn:3255]] perfection, by corrupting the majority of social and domestic relations. For, by following only one’s passion, as do the ignorant, one destroys one’s speculative aspirations, the body is corrupted, and man perishes before his physical constitution demands it[[fn:3256]]; cares and sorrows multiply, mutual jealousy and hatred increase, and men come to blows to despoil one another. That which brings all this about is that the ignorant man considers pleasure as the only essential end to be sought. Therefore God (blessed be His name) has used foresight in giving us laws proper to destroy this end and to turn our thoughts from it in every manner. He has forbidden us all that leads to greed and to mere pleasure, and this is one of the most pronounced tendencies of this Law. Seest thou not that the textual words of the Law command to put to death him who manifests an excessive leaning for the pleasure of good cheer and drink? This is the stubborn and rebellious son (Deut. xxi. 18) whom they call a glutton and a drunkard (Ib., v. 20). It is commanded to stone him and to cut him off promptly (from society), before the matter[[fn:3257]] takes on more gravity and he can cause many people to perish and destroy the position of virtuous men by his violent greed[[fn:3258]].
root.text.Part 3..32.1: That which the Law furthermore had in view was (to inspire us with) gentleness and docility[[fn:3259]]; it wills that man, far from being harsh and coarse, should on the contrary show himself flexible, obedient, and condescending[[fn:3260]]. Thou knowest this divine precept: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked (Deut. x. 16); Take heed, and hearken, O Israel (Ib., xxvii. 9); If ye be willing and obedient, etc. (Isaiah i. 19). In speaking of the docility to accept that which is obligatory, the expression is employed: We will hear it, and do it. The same idea is expressed allegorically by the words: Draw me, we will run after thee (Song of Sol. i. 4)[[fn:3261]].
root.text.Part 3..32.2: Another object which the Law had in view was purity and holiness, which consists in the repression of physical love, in eschewing it, and in indulging therein as little as possible, as I shall hereafter set forth[[fn:3262]]. When God commanded the sanctification of the nation for the reception of the Law, as it is said: Sanctify them to-day and to-morrow (Exodus xix. 10), He said[[fn:3263]]: Come not at your wives (Ib., v. 15), declaring thereby that holiness consists in the repression of physical love. Likewise, it has been declared that abstinence from wine is holiness, for it is said of the Nazirite: He shall be holy (Numbers vi. 5). In the Siphra, we read: “Ye shall sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy (Lev. xi. 44); this is the sanctification by the commandments[[fn:3264]].” Even as the Law calls obedience to the commandments holiness and purity, so does it designate the transgression of the commandments and shameful actions by the name of impurity, as I shall set forth.
root.text.Part 3..32.3: Cleanliness of garments, the washing of the body, and the removal of its defilements, are likewise matters which the Law has had in view; yet these follow only after the purification of actions and after the heart has been cleansed of impure ideas and morals[[fn:3265]]. To content oneself with keeping the exterior clean by washing and wearing clean garments, whilst remaining eager for pleasures and indulging in gluttony and physical love, would be exceedingly blameworthy. Isaiah has said concerning this: They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens, behind one in the midst[[fn:3266]], eating swine's flesh, etc. (Isaiah lxvi. 17); by which is meant that they show themselves pure and holy in open and public places, but thereafter, when they are alone in their chambers and in the interior of their houses, they persist in their sins, permitting themselves to eat forbidden things, such as the swine, the mouse, and other abominations. It may also be that, by the words אחר אחת בתוך, behind one that is within, it was intended to indicate that, in seclusion, they give themselves up to forbidden love. In short, it was meant that their exterior is clean and shows neatness and purity[[fn:3267]], but that within they persist in indulging their passions and the enjoyments of the body. Such, however, was not the intent of the Law, which, on the contrary, has had as its chief object the restraint of passion, and willed that the purification of the exterior should only take place after that of the interior. Solomon has already called attention to those who take care to wash their bodies and purify their garments, whilst their actions are impure and their morals depraved: There is a generation, says he, that are pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness; there is a generation, O how lofty are their eyes! and their eyelids are lifted up (Prov. xxx. 12, 13). By considering the intentions of the Law which we have mentioned in this chapter, thou wilt understand the reasons for a great number of commandments, which had remained unknown before the knowledge of these intentions, as I shall hereafter set forth.
root.text.Part 3..33.0: Furthermore, it must be known that the Law has no regard for that which is exceptional. Legislation has not been made with a view to that which happens but rarely; but in all that it has sought to inculcate in the way of ideas, morals, and useful actions, it has had in view only the most frequent cases, without regard to that which occurrs but seldom, nor to the harm that might result from such a legal provision and regime for a single individual. Verily, the Law is a divine thing; yet we must consider the things of nature, which embrace those general advantages existing in the Law, and from which nevertheless individual harms result, as has been set forth by ourselves and by others[[fn:3268]]. Upon this reflection[[fn:3269]], thou wilt no longer marvel that the purpose of the Law is not accomplished in every individual. On the contrary, there must necessarily exist individuals whom this regime of the Law does not render perfect, since the physical forms of the species do not produce, in every individual, all that is necessary[[fn:3270]]; for all these things have emanated from one God, from one agent[[fn:3271]], and were given from one shepherd[[fn:3272]]. The contrary would be impossible[[fn:3273]], and we have already set forth that the impossible has a stable nature that never varies[[fn:3274]]. It further follows from this reflection that laws cannot adapt themselves exactly[[fn:3275]] to the diverse circumstances of individuals and of times, like medical treatment, which, for each individual in particular, must be in conformity with his present temperament. It is necessary, on the contrary, that the legal regime be absolute and embrace the generality of men, although it may, while suiting certain individuals, not suit others; for, if it were to conform to individuals, the generality would suffer, and “thou wouldst make of it something relative[[fn:3276]].” Wherefore that which the Law has chiefly aimed at is independent of the circumstances of time and place; the legal provisions are absolute and general, as it is said: One ordinance shall be both for you of the congregation (Numbers xv. 15), and they have in view only that which is useful generally and in the most frequent cases, as we have set forth.
root.text.Part 3..33.1: After these preliminary observations, I proceed to the exposition which I had in view[[fn:3277]].
root.text.Part 3..34.0: To this end, I have divided all the commandments into fourteen classes[[fn:3278]].
root.text.Part 3..34.1: The Ist class compriss those commandments which relate to fundamental principles; these are they which we have enumerated in the treatise Yesode ha-Torah (of the Foundations of the Law). To this class also appertain repentance and fasts, as I shall hereafter set forth. In the matter of inculcating these sublime truths, which are to inspire in us belief in the Law, there is no occasion to inquire into their utility, even as we have already declared.
root.text.Part 3..34.2: The IInd class compriss the commandments pertaining to the prohibition of idolatry, and these are they which we have enumerated in the treatise Abodah Zarah (of Idolatry). It behoves one to know that the commandments relating to garments of diverse materials, to the first-fruits of trees, and to the mixture in the vineyard (with other plants)[[fn:3279]] belong likewise unto this class, as shall be explained. The motive of this class also is easily discerned; for its general purpose is to establish true ideas and to perpetuate them among the people during the course of years.
root.text.Part 3..34.3: The IIIrd class compriss the commandments relating to the improvement of moral qualities; these are they which we have enumerated in the treatise De’oth (of Ethics). It is well known that by good morals the intercourse of men and their society are brought to perfection, which is a thing necessary for the proper regulation of the social state.
root.text.Part 3..34.4: The IVth class compriss the commandments relating to alms, to loans, to gifts, and to all that appertains thereto; such are the valuations and consecrations[[fn:3280]], the ordinances concerning loans and slaves, and all the commandments which we have enumerated in the book Zera‘im (of Seeds), with the exception of diverse mixtures and the first-fruits of trees. The reason for all these commandments is manifest; for all men, in their turn, derive benefit therefrom. Indeed, if a man be rich to-day, he may be poor to-morrow, either he or his seed; and if he be poor to-day, to-morrow he or his son may be rich.
root.text.Part 3..34.5: The Vth class comprehends the commandments which aim at the prevention of violence and injustice. These are they which, in our work, form the subject of the book Nezikin (of Damages). The utility of this class is self-evident.
root.text.Part 3..34.6: The VIth class comprises the commandments relating to criminal punishments[[fn:3281]], such as the penalties of the thief, the robber, false witnesses, and in general all that we have enumerated in the book Schofetim (of Judges). The utility thereof is manifest and evident; for, should the offender not be punished, crime would never cease, and those who breathe only violence would not be restrained. There are only weak-minded persons who contend[[fn:3282]] that the abolition of punishments would be mercy towards men; whereas it would rather be true cruelty towards them and the destruction of society. Mercy, on the contrary, resides in this order given by God: Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates. (Deut., XVI, 18.)
root.text.Part 3..34.7: The VIIth class comprises the property rights which pertain to the mutual transactions of men, such as lending[[fn:3283]], hiring for wages, deposits, sales, purchases, etc.; inheritances also belong to this category. These are the commandments which we have enumerated in the books Kinyân (of Acquisition) and Mischpatim (of Rights). This class is of manifest and evident utility; for these pecuniary relations are necessary for men in every State, and it is essential to establish equitable rules in these transactions and to subject them to a useful appraisal.
root.text.Part 3..34.8: The VIII<sup>th</sup> class comprises the commandments relating to sacred days[[fn:3284]], I mean to the Sabbaths and the festivals[[fn:3285]]. Scripture has already assigned the motive for each of these days and indicated the reason thereof, which is either to give rise to a certain idea[[fn:3286]], or to procure for us the rest of the body, or to produce both these effects at once, as we shall subsequently set forth.
root.text.Part 3..34.9: The IXth class comprises the other religious practices imposed upon all[[fn:3287]], such as prayer, the reading of the Schema, and the other matters which we have enumerated in the book Ahabâ (of Love), with the exception of Circumcision. The utility of this class is evident; for all these practices serve to confirm the ideas relating to the love of God, to that which must be believed concerning Him, and to that which must be attributed unto Him.
root.text.Part 3..34.10: The Xth class comprises the commandments relating to the sanctuary, to its (sacred) utensils, and to its ministers. These are the commandments which we have enumerated in a part[[fn:3288]] of the book ’Abôdâ (of Worship). We have previously spoken of the utility of this class[[fn:3289]].
root.text.Part 3..34.11: The XIth class compriss the commandments relative to sacrifices; these be, for the most part, the commandments which we have enumerated in the book Abôdâh (of Service) and in the book Korbanôth (of Sacrifices). We have already stated in the preceding chapter (ch. xxxii) what utility lay in the ordaining of sacrifices in general, and what was the necessity thereof in those times.
root.text.Part 3..34.12: The XII<sup>th</sup> class compriss the commandments relative to cases of cleanness or uncleanness. The general object of all these commandments was that one should abstain, whilst in a state of uncleanness, from visiting the Sanctuary, to the end that one might be impressed with its grandeur, and that it might be an object of fear and reverence, as I shall hereafter set forth.
root.text.Part 3..34.13: The XIIIth class compriss the commandments relative to the prohibition of certain foods and that which appertains thereto; these are the commandments which we have enumerated in the treatise Maakhalôth Assurôth (of Forbidden Foods); but the ordinances concerning vows and Naziriteship likewise belong unto this class. All these have for their object to subdue the passion which leads us to seek after delicacies, and to prevent feasting and drinking from being regarded as the end of life[[fn:3290]], even as we have set forth in the Commentary on the Mishnah, in the introduction to the treatise Abôth[[fn:3291]].
root.text.Part 3..34.14: The XIVth class compriss the commandments relative to the prohibition of certain kinds of intercourse. These be they which we have enumerated in the book Nashim (of Women), and in the treatise Issure Biâh (of Forbidden Unions); the hybridizing of animals (of two species) likewise belongs unto this class. These commandments also have for their object to diminish carnal intercourse with women, to restrain, so far as possible, the unbridled desire for cohabitation, and to prevent its being regarded, as is done by the ignorant, as the end (of human existence), even as we have set forth in the Commentary on the treatise Abôth[[fn:3292]]. Circumcision likewise belongs unto this class.
root.text.Part 3..34.15: It is well known that the whole of the commandments may be divided into two parts, the one concerning the relations between man and man, the other concerning the relations between man and God[[fn:3293]]. In our division, the classes of which we have just enumerated, the fifth, sixth, seventh, and a portion of the third class, relate to the relations between man and man; the other classes concern the relations between man and God. For every commandment, whether positive or negative, which has for its object to endow us with a certain moral quality, or idea, or to correct our actions, and which concerns[[fn:3294]] only the individual himself whom it serves to perfect, has been called by the Sages the relation between man and God, although in reality it may sometimes lead unto relations between man and man; but this latter case only occurrs after many intermediate steps and from general points of view, and at first sight naught is perceived therein which might affect other men. Thou must well understand this.
root.text.Part 3..34.16: Having made known the reasons for these several classes of commandments, I shall proceed to treat of the precepts comprised within each of them, especially those which are deemed to be of no utility, or which are taken for ordinances lacking any rational principle; I shall set forth the reasons for them and the instances of their utility, save for a small number of which, until this present hour, I have not yet grasped the purpose[[fn:3295]].
root.text.Part 3..35.0: The commandments comprised in the first class, to wit, the doctrines, and which we have enumerated in the treatise Yesode ha-Torah (of the Foundations of the Law), are all clearly reasoned. If thou dost examine them one by one, thou shalt ever find therein a true notion susceptible of demonstration. Likewise, everything which serves as an incentive and encouragement to study and teaching is of manifest utility; for if one has not acquired knowledge, one shall possess neither practical virtues nor sound notions[[fn:3296]]. It is equally of manifest utility to honour those who are the supporters of the Law[[fn:3297]]; for if they be not an object of high consideration[[fn:3298]], their words will not be hearkened to when they seek to direct our thoughts and our actions. In the commandment expressed by the words: Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head (Levit. xix. 32)[[fn:3299]], is also contained the duty of deporting oneself with modesty[[fn:3300]].
root.text.Part 3..35.1: Unto this first class belong also the precepts which command us to swear by His name and which forbid us to violate an oath, or to swear in vain[[fn:3301]]. All this has a manifest reason, and has for its object the reverence due unto the Divinity; for these are actions which strengthen the belief in His greatness.
root.text.Part 3..35.2: To this class belongs furthermore the precept to invoke God in moments of distress, as it is said: Ye shall blow an alarm with the trumpets (Numbers x. 9)[[fn:3302]]; for this is an act which serves to strengthen a true notion, namely, that God perceivs our condition, that it depends upon Him to improve it if we obey Him, and to make it evil if we disobey Him, and that we must not regard this as the effect of chance or of a mere accident. Such is the import of these words: If ye walk with Me קרי, contrary unto Me (Leviticus xxvi. 21)[[fn:3303]], which must be understood thus: “If ye consider these calamities which I bring upon you for your punishment as a mere chance, I shall increase for you this pretended chance in that which is most grave and most cruel,” as it is said: And if ye walk with Me contrary unto Me, then I will walk contrary unto you also in fury (Ib. v. 27-28). Verily, their belief that it was but a pure chance must have the effect of leaving them, without return, to persist in their pernicious opinions and in their impious actions, as it is said: Thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved (Jeremiah v. 3). Wherefore God has commanded us to invoke Him, to have recourse unto Him[[fn:3304]] and to address our supplications unto Him in every calamity.
root.text.Part 3..35.3: It is evident that repentance likewise belongs to this class; I mean to say that it forms part of those notions which must be admitted so that there may exist a well-ordered religious society. Indeed, it is impossible that man should not sin and stumble, whether by adopting through ignorance an opinion or a conduct which cannot be approved, or by suffering himself to be overcome by concupiscence or passion. If, therefore, man could believe that this evil is for ever past remedy[[fn:3305]], he would persist in his error, and perhaps would he sin yet more, having no means of reparation; but, by believing in repentance, he will amend himself and become better once more, and even more perfect than he had been before he sinned. Wherefore the acts which are to strengthen this true and most useful notion are numerous; I refer to confessions[[fn:3306]], sacrifices for error[[fn:3307]] and for certain sins committed with intent, and fasts. That which characteriss repentance in general for every sin is the forsaking thereof; and it is this which this notion has ultimately for its object. All these things, therefore[[fn:3308]], are of manifest utility.
root.text.Part 3..36.0: The commandments contained in the second class are all those which we have enumerated in the treatise Aboda Zarâ (concerning idolatry). It is manifest that they all aim at preserving us from the errors of idolatry and from other false conceits which idolatry brings in its train, such as prognostications, auguries, sorcery, incantation[[fn:3309]], and other like things. When thou shalt have read all the books of which I have spoken unto thee, thou wilt see clearly that what thou hearest called magic consists of practices exercised by the Kasdim and the Chaldeans[[fn:3310]], and which were especially frequent among the Egyptians and the Canaanites. They desired to make it believed, or believed themselves, that these practices exercised a miraculous or extraordinary influence in the world, whether upon an individual or upon the inhabitants of a city; whilst logic and reason cannot admit that the practices exercised by magicians produce any effect whatsoever[[fn:3311]], as, for example, when they seek to gather such a plant at such a moment, or when they take such a quantity of one thing and such a quantity of another. These are very varied procedures, which I shall summarize into three kinds: 1st, those which relate to some being, whether plant, animal, or mineral; 2nd, those which relate to a determined time in which such practices must be exercised; 3rd, certain actions performed by men, as for example dancing, clapping the hands, shouting, laughing, hopping upon one leg[[fn:3312]], lying upon the ground, burning a certain thing, or making a certain fumigation, or pronouncing certain words, whether intelligible or unintelligible. Such are the different species of magical operations.
root.text.Part 3..36.1: There be certain magical operations which are not accomplished save by the conjunction of all these acts at once. They say, for instance: One shall take such or such a quantity of leaves of such a plant, at the moment when the moon is found under such a sign of the zodiac, in the east or at one of the other cardinal points[[fn:3313]]; one shall also take the horns of such an animal, or its excrements, or its hair, or its blood, in such a quantity, when the sun shall be found, for example, in the midst of heaven, or at another determined place; finally, one shall take such a metal, or several metals, which one shall melt under the ascendant of such a sign, at the moment when the stars shall be found in such a situation[[fn:3314]]; thereafter, one shall speak, saying such a thing, and one shall make with these leaves, etc., a fumigation unto this figure of metal, and, as a consequence of all this, such a thing shall come to pass. But there are other magical operations which, as they believe, are accomplished by means of but one of these three kinds of acts. In the most part of these magical operations, they lay down as a necessary condition that they be executed by women. Thus, for example, they say that, to obtain that water should gush forth, it is needful that ten virgin women, adorned with jewels and clad in red robes, should dance and approach one another, going now forward, now backward, and pointing to the sun, etc., etc.[[fn:3315]]; by this means, as they imagine, the water will gush forth.
root.text.Part 3..36.2: They further assert that if four women, lying upon their backs, should lift their legs and spread them asunder[[fn:3316]], and if, in this unseemly posture, they should utter such words and perform such an act, the hail would cease to fall in those places. There are yet many other of these absurdities and follies, the practice of which, according to their express condition, belongs only unto women. In all magical operations, it is also necessary to observe the state of the stars; for they pretend that such a plant has fallen as a portion to such a star, and likewise they attribute every animal and every mineral to a certain star[[fn:3317]]. According to their opinion also, the practices exercised by magicians[[fn:3318]] are a species of worship rendered to such or such a star, which, finding pleasure in such a practice, in such words, or in such a fumigation, does for us that which we desire.
root.text.Part 3..36.3.sub_0: After this preliminary observation, which thou mayest verify by reading their books which are now in our hands and which I have made known unto thee, hearken to what I shall say: That which formed the aim and, as it were, the centre of the Law, was the destruction of idolatry, the trace of which it desired to make disappear; it willed not that one should imagine that any star whatsoever could exercise an influence, whether harmful or beneficent, upon anything concerning human individuals, for it is this opinion which has led to the worship of the stars. In consequence, every magician was to be put to death[[fn:3319]]; for the magician is indubitably devoted to idolatry, although he follows particular and strange ways, different from those which the multitude follows for the worship of false gods. Now, as they have laid down as a principal condition, in all these magical operations, or at least in the most part, that they should be exercised by women, it is said: Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live (Exodus, xxii. 17). Furthermore, as a natural pity prevents men from slaying women, it is expressly said, in speaking of idolatry: a man or a woman (Deut., xvii. 2), and the words that man or that woman are repeated (ibid., v. 5), an expression which is employed neither concerning the profanation of the Sabbath, nor concerning any other commandment. The reason thereof is the great pity which women naturally inspire. — The magicians attributed to their art such efficacy, that they pretended, by their operations, to be able to expel dangerous animals from the fields[[fn:3320]], such as lions, serpents, and the like. They also pretended to be able, by their magic, to guarantee plants against all manner of dangers, and they had, for example, operations by which they pretended to prevent the hail from falling, and others which, they said, caused the worms in the vineyards to die, so that these should not be destroyed. The Sabeans, in the book of Nabataean Agriculture, have even entered into long details upon the manner of killing the worms of the vineyards by means of those Amorite usages[[fn:3321]] of which we have spoken. Likewise, they pretended to possess operations to prevent the leaves of trees and the fruits from falling.
root.text.Part 3..36.3.sub_1: It is by reason of all these superstitions, then widely prevalent, that in the words of the Covenant[[fn:3322]] it is declared, among other things, that the worship of false gods and those magical operations, whereby it was believed[[fn:3323]] these dangers might be averted, would on the contrary become the cause of these misfortunes. It is said, for example: I will also send wild beasts among you, which shall rob you of your children (Levit., xxvi. 22); I will also send the teeth of beasts upon them, with the poison of serpents of the dust (Deut., xxxii. 24); All thy trees and fruit of thy land shall the locust consume (ibid., xxviii. 42); Thou shalt plant vineyards, and dress them, but shalt neither drink of the wine, nor gather the grapes, for the worms shall eat them (ibid., v. 39); Thou shalt have olive trees throughout all thy coasts, but thou shalt not anoint thyself with the oil; for thine olive shall cast his fruit (ibid., v. 40). In short, in the presence of all the artifices invented[[fn:3324]] by the worshippers of false gods to perpetuate the worship thereof, by making men believe that, by these means, one may avert certain misfortunes and obtain certain advantages, it has been declared in the words of the Covenant that, as a result of the worship of these gods, these advantages shall be wanting and these misfortunes shall arrive. — Thou wilt now understand, O reader! wherefore the Scripture has insisted upon these particular curses and blessings, contained in the words of the Covenant, and has made them stand forth more than the others; thou shalt therefore know how to appreciate the great utility thereof.
root.text.Part 3..36.4.sub_0: To the end that we might be kept far from all magical operations, we are forbidden (in general) from practicing any of the customs of the idolaters, even those which pertain to agricultural and pastoral practices[[fn:3325]] and others of a similar nature; I refer to all things which they allege to be profitable, and which, in their opinion, belong solely to the domain of certain occult forces[[fn:3326]], without being required by the study of physical science. It is of this that the Scripture says: Ye shall not walk in the customs of the nation, etc. (Levit. xx. 23), and this is what the Doctors term ways of the Amorites. Verily, these are but the branches of certain practices of magicians; for they are things which proceed not from physical reasoning, and which lead unto magical operations, which, relying necessarily upon astrology, result in the glorification of the stars and the rendering of worship unto them[[fn:3327]]. The Doctors expressly declare: “Whatever is practiced as a medicinal remedy is not considered a way of the Amorites;”[[fn:3328]] signifying thereby: whatsoever the study of physics requirs is permitted, but other practices are forbidden. Wherefore, after having said: “An tree whose fruits fall off, men load it with stones and mark it with red chalk,” this practice is met with the following objection: “As for loading it with stones, it is in order that its sap may diminish[[fn:3329]]; but wherefore mark it with red chalk? etc.” It is therefore manifest therefrom that it would be forbidden to mark it with red chalk, or to do any other such thing devoid of reason[[fn:3330]], because these would be ways of the Amorites. Likewise, concerning the “foetus of sacred animals which must be buried,”[[fn:3331]] it is said: “It is not permitted to hang it upon a tree, nor to bury it at a cross-road, because these are ways of the Amorites.” Thence one may conclude regarding other analogous cases[[fn:3332]]. Thou shalt not be scandalized by certain things which have been permitted, as for example the nail of one hanged and the tooth of a fox[[fn:3333]]; for in those times these things were considered as proven by experience.
root.text.Part 3..36.4.sub_1: They fell, therefore, into the category of medicines, in the same manner as, amongst us, peony is suspended over an epileptic, or as the excrements of a dog are employed against swellings of the throat, and fumigations of vinegar and marcasite[[fn:3334]] against hard tumors of the tendons[[fn:3335]]; for all remedies which, like these, are proven by experience, albeit they be not rational, it is permitted to employ them, and they enter the category of medicines by the same title as purgative remedies[[fn:3336]]. Thou must well imbue thyself, O reader! with the remarkable observations I have just made, and keep them in thy memory: for they shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck (Proverbs i. 9).
root.text.Part 3..36.5: As touching the prohibition against rounding the corners of the hair and the beard, we have already set forth in our great work that this was a custom of idolatrous priests[[fn:3337]]. It is for the same reason that fabrics of heterogeneous materials were forbidden; for it was the custom of idolatrous priests to join together, in the stuffs which served them for raiment, vegetable and animal matters, and to carry at the same time in their hand a seal made of some mineral. Thou shalt find this textually in their writings.
root.text.Part 3..36.6: It is further for the same reason (of idolatry) that it is said: The woman shall not wear that which pertains unto a man, neither shall a man put on a woman's garment (Deut. xxii. 5). Thou shalt find this in the book of Tomtom[[fn:3338]], which prescribs that a man, when appearing before the planet Venus, should be clad in a variegated female garment, and that a woman should cover herself with a breastplate and weapons of war when appearing before Mars. This prohibition, I believe, has yet another reason: namely, that such an action excits the passions and leads unto all manner of debaucheries.
root.text.Part 3..36.7: As to the prohibition of deriving any profit whatsoever from idols, the reason thereof is right clear; for sometimes, in taking them to break them, one might preserve them and they might become a snare. Even when they had been broken and melted, or sold unto a pagan, it would be forbidden to make use of the price received therefrom. The reason for this is that often the vulgar see in accidental things essential causes; thus, for example, thou shalt often find such a man who says that, since he has dwelt[[fn:3339]] in such a house, or since he has bought such a beast of burden, or such a piece of furniture, he has grown rich and has acquired a great fortune, and that these objects have been for him a cause of blessing. It might therefore happen that a person, whose commerce, by chance, had become flourishing, or who had gained much money by this price (of the idols), should see in the latter a cause, imagining that the blessing attached to the price of that sold statue has produced this result. He would, consequently, profess a belief which the Law in its entirety has endeavored to combat, as results from all the texts of the Pentateuch. It is further for the same reason that it is forbidden to derive profit from the ornaments which cover an object of worship[[fn:3340]], as well as from the offerings or the vessels of idolatry[[fn:3341]], so that we may be preserved from this erroneous opinion; for, great in those times was the belief in the stars; it was believed that they gave life or death, and that all good and all evil proceeded from them. Wherefore the Law, to be more sure of causing such an opinion to cease, has employed the symbols of the Covenant[[fn:3342]], the invocation of witnesses[[fn:3343]], the vehement adjurations and the imprecations of which we have spoken[[fn:3344]]; and God has warned us to take nothing of that which belongs unto idols, nor to derive any profit therefrom, and He has made known unto us that, if the least thing of the price received therefrom were mixed with the fortune of a man, it would bring about the loss and the ruin of that fortune. Such is the sense of these words: Neither shalt thou bring an abomination into thine house, lest thou be a cursed thing like it, etc. (Deut. vii. 26); with all the more reason, one must not believe that there is in such a thing a blessing. If therefore thou pursuest in detail all the commandments relating unto idolatry, thou shalt find that they evidently have for their reason the cessation of these pernicious opinions and the directing of our thoughts elsewhere[[fn:3345]].
root.text.Part 3..36.8: What we must further observe is that the authors of these false opinions, which are devoid of foundation or utility, seek[[fn:3346]] to procure their acceptance and to establish them by spreading abroad among men the notion that whosoever should fail to perform a certain act serving to perpetuate a particular belief, should be smitten with such or such a calamity. It may perchance happen one day by accident to some individual, so that he will thereafter desire to perform the act in question and will admit the belief of which it treats. It is well known that it is in the nature of men, in general, to experience the greatest dread, the most violent terror, concerning the loss of their fortune and their children. Wherefore, in those times, the fire-worshippers proclaimed that he who did not cause his son and his daughter to pass through the fire[[fn:3347]], would behold the death of his children. This absurd belief undoubtedly had the effect of making everyone hasten to perform the act in question, because of the great commiseration and the fear which he felt for the fate of his children; the more so as this act was a small thing and very easy, for they required naught else but to make them pass through the fire[[fn:3348]]. Let us add thereto that the care of young children is committed unto women, and it is known how readily these latter allow themselves to be impressed[[fn:3349]], and what is generally the weakness of their understanding. Wherefore the Law rose up strongly against this act and branded it with more energy than other species of idolatry, (employing these words): To defile my sanctuary and to profane my holy name (Levit., 20, 3); thereafter the truthful (prophet) made known, in the name of God, that although by performing this act they believe they prolong the life of their children[[fn:3350]], God will cause those who so act to perish and will destroy their race: I, says He, will set[[fn:3351]] my face against that man and against his family, etc. (ibid., v. 5). Know that the traces of this act, once so widespread in the world, have been preserved even unto this day. Thou mayest behold the midwives taking small children in their swaddling-clothes, casting into the fire incense of an unpleasant odour, and waving the infants over this incense, (holding them) above the fire. This is undoubtedly a manner of passing through the fire, the practice of which is by no means permitted. Thou seest, consequently, how much malice the authors of this idea have employed in perpetuating it by means of a chimera[[fn:3352]], so that, despite the opposition made to it by the Law for thousands of years, its trace is not yet effaced.
root.text.Part 3..36.9: The partisans of idolatry acted in like manner with respect to property[[fn:3353]]. They prescribed that there should be consecrated to the object of their worship[[fn:3354]] a certain tree, to wit, the aschérâ[[fn:3355]], and that its fruits should be taken, of which a part would be used as offerings, and the remainder would be eaten in the temple of idolatry, as they have set forth in the rites of the aschérâ. They prescribed the like for the firstfruits of every tree whose fruits serve for food, I mean that a part thereof should be used as offerings, and another part consumed in the temple of idolatry; and they also spread this belief that every tree, whose first produce had not been employed for this purpose, would wither away, or cast its fruit, or produce but little, or be smitten with some other calamity, even as they spread the notion that every child who was not made to pass through the fire would die. Men, therefore, fearing for their goods, hastened to act thus. But the (divine) Law rose up against such a notion, and God commanded that all which the fruit-tree should produce in the space of three years should be burned[[fn:3356]]; for there be trees that produce at the end of one year, others that bear their first fruits after two years, and others finally that produce only after three years. This is what most frequently occurrs when one plants, as is generally the custom, in one of the three known ways, which are planting, layering, and grafting[[fn:3357]]. No provision was made for the case where one might have sown a stone or a pip; for the ordinances of the Law relate only to the most frequent cases[[fn:3358]], and planting, in Palestine, gives the first products, at the latest, at the end of three years. God has therefore promised us that, in consequence of the loss and the corruption of this first product, the tree would produce all the more, as it is said: That it may yield unto you the increase thereof (Levit., 19, 25); and He commanded us to consume the fruit of the fourth year before the Lord[[fn:3359]], in opposition to the custom of consuming the firstfruits[[fn:3360]] in the temple of idolatry, as we have set forth.
root.text.Part 3..36.10: The ancient idolaters further relate, in the Nabatean Agriculture, that they suffered certain substances which they enumerate to fall into putrefaction, observing the entry of the sun into certain signs of the ecliptic and engaging in numerous magical operations. They pretended that everyone ought to make these preparations, and that whenever a fruit-tree was planted, a portion of this putrefied mixture should be scattered around the tree, or in the very place it was to occupy; by this means (they said), the tree would sprout promptly and bear fruit in a much shorter period than is customary. This, they add, is a marvelous process, of the talismanic kind[[fn:3361]], and one of the most efficacious magical devices for hastening the production of fruit in all things that can produce it. I have already explained to thee how much the Law held in abhorrence all these magical operations; wherefore it has forbidden all that fruit-trees produce during three years, from the day of their planting. It is therefore not necessary to hasten their production, as they pretend; for, in Syria, most fruit-trees, according to the course of nature, produce their fruits perfectly at the end of three years, without it being necessary to have recourse to that famous magical operation which they employed. Imprint well also upon thy mind this remarkable observation.
root.text.Part 3..36.11: Another opinion, very widespread in those times and which the Sabians have perpetuated, is that concerning the grafting of trees of different species; they pretended that by operating under the ascendant of a certain constellation, by making a certain fumigation and pronouncing a certain invocation, at the moment of grafting, the product of this graft would be very useful in diverse respects. What is most notorious in this regard is what they have said, at the commencement of the Agriculture, concerning the grafting of the olive upon the citron-tree. For my part, I doubt not that the Book of Medicines, suppressed by Hezekiah[[fn:3362]], contained similar things. — They say further that, if one wishes to graft one species upon another species, it is necessary that a young damsel, holding in her hand the branch which one wishes to graft, should surrender herself to a man in a shameful manner of which they give the description, and that at the moment they accomplish this act, the woman should graft the branch upon the tree[[fn:3363]]. This custom was doubtless very widespread, so that no one acted otherwise; the more so as therein was found the sensual pleasure of love joined with the lure of gain[[fn:3364]]. Wherefore the mixture of two species was forbidden, that is to say, the grafting of one tree upon a tree of another species[[fn:3365]], in order to keep us far removed from everything that might give occasion[[fn:3366]] to idolatry, as well as from their abominable and unnatural amours. It is because of grafting[[fn:3367]] that it is forbidden to join together two species, of whatever plant it may be, and even to bring them near to one another. If thou examinest what the Talmudic tradition says upon this commandment[[fn:3368]], thou wilt find that, according to the written law, grafting is in every place punishable by corporal chastisement[[fn:3369]], for it is this which the prohibition chiefly had in view, whilst the mixtures of heterogeneous seeds, I mean their juxtaposition, is forbidden only in the Holy Land[[fn:3370]].
root.text.Part 3..36.12: It is also expressly stated, in that Agriculture, that it was the custom to sow together barley and grapes; for it was believed that this process alone could make the vine prosper. Wherefore the Law has forbidden the mixture of the vineyard (with other plants), and has commanded that the whole be burned[[fn:3371]]; for all the customs of the gentiles, to which certain occult properties were attributed, were forbidden, even when they contained no trace of idolatry, as we have explained concerning that passage of the doctors: "It is not permitted to suspend it from a tree, etc.[[fn:3372]]" All these customs, called ways of the Amorites, were forbidden because they lead unto idolatry. If thou examinest their customs relating to agriculture, thou wilt find that in such cultivation they turn toward such stars, and in such other toward the two luminaries (the sun and the moon). Often they fix, for the sowing, the moment of the ascendants (of certain constellations), perform fumigations, and he who plants or sows walks in a circle; there be those who believe they must make five turns for the five planets[[fn:3373]], others believe they must make seven for the five planets[[fn:3374]] and the two luminaries. They pretend that there are in all this particular virtues, very useful for agriculture, in order to bind men to the worship of the stars. Wherefore all these customs of the gentiles were generally forbidden, as it is said: Ye shall not walk in the manners of the nation, etc. (Levit., 20, 23); and that which was very well known or very widespread, or which was expressly designated as a species of idolatrous worship, was the object of a particular prohibition, such as for example the firstfruits of trees, the mixture of heterogeneous seeds, and the mixture of the vineyard (with other plants). What is astonishing is the opinion of Rabbi Josiah relative to the mixture of the vineyard, and which is accepted as a doctrinal decision, to wit "that one is only guilty on condition of having sown, with a single cast, wheat, barley, and grape-stones[[fn:3375]]." Doubtless, he had read somewhere that this process had its origin in the ways of the Amorites.
root.text.Part 3..36.13: It is therefore manifest and beyond all doubt that the weaving of heterogeneous materials, the first-fruits of trees, and the commingling of diverse seeds, were forbidden only by reason of paganism; and that the said heathen customs were prohibited because they lead unto idolatry, even as we have set forth.
root.text.Part 3..37.0: The commandments comprised within the third class are those which we have enumerated in the treatise De’oth (of Ethical rules). They are all of an evident and manifest utility; for they generally concern those morals which serve to improve social relations, a matter which is so[[fn:3376]] clear that I need not dwell thereon.
root.text.Part 3..37.1: It must be known that there are likewise certain commandments which, whilst having for their object the purification of morals, yet prescribe acts seemingly without purpose, and which might be taken for mere caprices of the Law. These we shall set forth, each separately, in their proper places[[fn:3377]]; but those which we have enumerated[[fn:3378]] in the treatise De’oth do expressly declare themselves as having for their aim these noble (social) morals.
root.text.Part 3..38.0: The commandments comprised within the fourth class are those which we have enumerated in the book Zera‘im (of Seeds) of our work, with the exception of heterogeneous seeds; it further contains the laws relating to estimations and consecrations[[fn:3379]], as well as the commandments which we have enumerated in the treatise Malwe-we-lowe (of the lender and the borrower), and in the treatise ‘Abadim (of Slaves). If thou shalt examine all these commandments one by one, thou wilt find them of an evident utility for (inspiring us with) sentiments of commiseration toward the wretched and the poor, and (for engaging us) to afford the indigent succour of every kind, that we may not oppress him who is in need, nor afflict the heart of those who find themselves in an unhappy condition[[fn:3380]].
root.text.Part 3..38.1: The duty of giving unto the poor is a matter which is self-explanatory. The motive for the heave-offerings (for the priests) and the tithes has been clearly indicated: For he (the Levite) has no part, nor inheritance with thee (Deut. xiv. 29); and thou knowest the reason thereof: namely, that this entire tribe (of the Levites) might devote itself unto the Divine service and the study of the Law, and that it should have no need to occupy itself with either ploughing or harvesting[[fn:3381]], but should belong unto God alone, as it is said: They shall teach Thy judgments unto Jacob, and Thy Law unto Israel (ibid., xxxiii. 10). Thou findest in several passages of the Pentateuch these words: the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow; for the Levite, having no possession, is ever reckoned among the number of the poor.
root.text.Part 3..38.2: —As touching the second tithe, it was merely commanded to expend the same in feasts at Jerusalem[[fn:3382]], the which must needs have led to the bestowing of alms; for, inasmuch as it could only be employed for feasts, it was an easy matter for each man to distribute it[[fn:3383]] by little and little. This gathering together in a single place was likewise intended to have the effect[[fn:3384]] of establishing amongst men firm bonds of brotherhood and love.
root.text.Part 3..38.3: As for the precept concerning the fruit of the fourth year[[fn:3385]], although by its connection with the law regarding the first-fruits it be related to an idolatrous custom[[fn:3386]], as we have aforementioned, it nevertheless enters into the category of those ordinances relative to the heave-offering of the produce of the earth and the dough, the first ripe fruits, and the first of the fleece[[fn:3387]]; for the first-fruits in general were consecrated unto God in order to confirm generosity within us, and to diminish intemperance and the greed of lucre. For the same reason the priest receivs the shoulder, the jaws, and the stomach[[fn:3388]]; for the jaws constitute one of the principal parts of the animal body; the shoulder, to wit the right one, is the first of the members that issue from the trunk, and the stomach is the first of all the entrails.
root.text.Part 3..38.4: In the recitation which must accompany the presentation of the first-fruits[[fn:3389]], there is likewise a manifestation of humility; for it is performed by him who bears the basket upon his shoulders[[fn:3390]]. Therein is expressed gratitude for the goodness of God and for His benefits, to the end that man may know it is a religious duty for him, when he finds himself in prosperity, to recall his seasons of distress. The Law insists right often upon this: Remember that thou wast a bondman, etc. (Deut. v. 15; xvi. 12); for it was feared lest those habits so common to all who have been reared in affluence should prevail, namely, self-sufficiency, vanity, and the neglect of true ideas: Lest when thou hast eaten and art full, etc., thine heart be lifted up (ibid., viii. 12-14); Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked (ibid., xxxii. 15). It was in this fear that it was commanded to perform the recitation of the first-fruits each year before God and in the presence of His Majesty. Thou knowest also that the Law strongly enjoins to remember ever the plagues that fell upon the Egyptians: That thou mayest remember the day when thou camest forth, etc. (ibid., xvi. 3); And that thou mayest tell in the ears of thy son, etc. (Exodus x. 2). And there were just reasons for so doing; for these are events which confirm the truth of prophecy, as well as the doctrine of retribution[[fn:3391]]. Thus, every commandment that serves to recall the memory of one of the miracles, or to perpetuate a certain belief, is of recognized utility.
root.text.Part 3..38.5: It is expressly said concerning the sanctification of the first-born of man and of beasts: And it came to pass, when Pharaoh would hardly let us go, etc., that I sacrifice to the Lord (Exodus xiii. 15). The reason why the ox, the small cattle, and the ass are particularly designated is right clear[[fn:3392]], for these are domestic animals which are reared and found in most places, especially in Syria, and above all amongst us Israelites, who were all shepherds, from father to grandsire: Thy servants are shepherds (Genesis xlvii. 3)[[fn:3393]]. But horses and camels are not habitually found with shepherds, nor do they exist everywhere; if thou readest, for example, of the expedition against Midian[[fn:3394]], thou findest there mentioned, in the matter of animals, only the ox, the small cattle, and the ass. Verily, the species of the ass is necessary to all men, and particularly to those occupied with the labors of the field: I have oxen and asses (Genesis xxxii. 6), whereas camels and horses are ordinarily found only with certain persons and in certain localities. — As for the prescription to break the neck of the first-born of an ass (Exodus xiii. 13), the reason thereof is that it shall necessarily constrain the owner to redeem it; wherefore it is said: “The commandment which enjoins to redeem it has the preference over that which enjoins to break its neck[[fn:3395]].”
root.text.Part 3..38.6: The various commandments that we have enumerated in the treatise Shemitah we-Yobel (of the Sabbatical year and the Jubilee) have for their object, at times to prescribe commiseration and liberality toward men in general, — as it is written: That the poor of thy people may eat: and what they leave the beasts of the field shall eat (Exodus xxiii. 11), — and to cause the earth to become more fertile by strengthening itself through rest[[fn:3396]]; at other times to inspire benevolence toward slaves and the poor, I mean the release of debts and the manumission of Hebrew slaves; and at yet other times to provide in perpetuity for the necessaries of life, by making the land an inalienable estate, so that it cannot be sold absolutely[[fn:3397]], — The land shall not be sold for ever (Levit. xxv. 23), — so that consequently the fortune of each man remains as a fund reserved for him and his heirs, and he can enjoy only the usufruct thereof[[fn:3398]]. Thus, then, have we assigned the reasons for all that is contained in the Book of Zera’im of our work, with the exception of the mingling of heterogeneous animals, the reason of which shall be set forth hereafter[[fn:3399]].
root.text.Part 3..38.7: The commandments which we have enumerated in the treatise 'Arkhin wa-Ḥaramim (concerning Valuations and Vows of Devotion) likewise have for their object acts of liberality. Some of these (gifts) belong unto the priests; others are destined for the repair of the Temple. By all these, man accustoms himself to generosity and learns to despise wealth and not to be niggardly in matters pertaining to God; for most of the evils which disturb human societies[[fn:3400]] arise only from the thirst for riches, the desire to increase them, and the greed for gain.
root.text.Part 3..38.8: — In like manner, all the commandments which we have enumerated in the treatise Malveh ve-Loveh (concerning Lender and Borrower), if thou examine them one by one, thou shalt find that they breathe forth benevolence, mercy, and clemency toward the unfortunate; it is forbidden to deprive any man of an object of utility necessary for his subsistence; for instance, no man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge (Deut. xxiv. 6).
root.text.Part 3..38.9.sub_0: Likewise, the commandments which we have enumerated in the treatise ‘Abadim (concerning Slaves) breathe forth mercy and benevolence for the unfortunate. That which especially denots a great humanity is that the Canaanite slave must be set at liberty when he is deprived of one of his members[[fn:3401]], so that his servitude be not aggravated by any mutilation[[fn:3402]], even were one but to cause him the loss of a tooth, and with even greater reason if another injury be caused him[[fn:3403]]. Moreover, it is not permitted (to the master) to strike him otherwise than with a whip or a rod, or with other such things, as we have explained in the Mishneh Torah; and furthermore, if he strike him violently so as to kill him, he is punished with death like any other man (who should have struck him)[[fn:3404]]. — The words thou shalt not deliver unto his master the servant (Deut. xxiii. 16), besides recommending pity (for slaves), contain another precept of great utility, namely, that we ought to possess the generosity to protect him who implors our protection, to defend him, and not to deliver him up to him from whom he has fled. It suffices not even that thou accordest him thy simple protection, but thou hast towards him the obligation[[fn:3405]] of providing for his needs and of doing him good, and thou must not, by a single word, afflict his heart. It is this which God has said: He shall dwell with thee, even among you, ... in that place which he shall choose in one of thy gates, where it liks him best: thou shalt not oppress him (ibid., v. 17). If this duty has been imposed upon us toward the lowest and most base of men, that is to say, the slave, what shall it be if a man of high worth implors thy protection? what must thou not do in his regard[[fn:3406]]? — But also, on the other hand, the criminal, the impious man, who implors our protection, must be neither protected, nor pitied, nor relieved in any wise from the penalty which he has deserved, even should he place himself under the protection of the most illustrious[[fn:3407]] and most eminent of men.
root.text.Part 3..38.9.sub_1: It is this which the Scripture indicats by these words: Thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die (Exodus xxi. 14); for, although such a one has put himself under the protection of God and has taken refuge near an object consecrated to His name, God protects him not, but commands, on the contrary, to deliver him to him who is the master to do himself justice[[fn:3408]] and before whom he has fled. And with much greater reason, (the culprit) who implors the help of a man ought to find with him neither protection nor pity; for pity for impious and criminal men is but harshness toward the whole world. These are, without contradiction, equitable manners, which ought to be numbered among the statutes and righteous judgments[[fn:3409]]; they resemble in no wise the manners of the heathens[[fn:3410]], among whom it was considered as a virtue worthy of praise to be proud and to become the passionate champion of the first comer[[fn:3411]], whether he were an oppressor or oppressed, as is everywhere found in their chronicles and in their poems[[fn:3412]].
root.text.Part 3..38.10: Thus, then, all the commandments which belong unto this class are clearly motivated and of manifest utility.
root.text.Part 3..39.0: The commandments contained in the fifth class are those which we have enumerated in the Book of Nezikin (of Damages); their common object is to cause injustices to cease and to prevent the infliction of injury upon others. To the end that men might avoid with the utmost care the causing of damage, man is held responsible for every injury proceeding from his property, or occasioned by his own act, provided it was possible for him to be circumspect and to use precautions[[fn:3413]] so as not to do harm. Wherefore are we held responsible for the damages proceeding from our beasts, that we may watch over them; as also for those caused by fire or the pit[[fn:3414]], which are the work of man and may be guarded and watched by him, lest any harm result therefrom. Nevertheless, these provisions impose upon us a certain equity[[fn:3415]] whereunto I must call attention. Thus, one is not responsible for the tooth and the foot in the public thoroughfare[[fn:3416]]; for it is a thing against which no precaution can be taken, and moreover it is rare[[fn:3417]] that any damage should happen in such a place. He, furthermore, who placs aught upon the public way is guilty against himself and exposs his property to loss; wherefore one is responsible for tooth and foot only within the property of him who suffers the damage[[fn:3418]]. — But the damage caused by the horn or any similar thing, which may be foreseen everywhere and against which those who walk in the public way can take no precaution, is subject in every place to the same law[[fn:3419]]. Here, however, a distinction must be made between the docile animal and that which is notoriously dangerous[[fn:3420]]. If the act be exceptional, one is responsible for but half the damage; but if the animal which causs the damage has made a habit thereof and be known for it, one is responsible for the whole damage[[fn:3421]].
root.text.Part 3..39.1: The price of a slave is generally fixed at the half of that which a free man is generally worth[[fn:3422]]; for thou findest that, for the estimations of men, the maximum is sixty shekels[[fn:3423]], whilst the average value of a slave is thirty shekels of silver (Exodus, 21, 32).
