root.text.Part 3..39.2: If it has been commanded to put to death the beast which shall have killed a man[[fn:3424]], it is not to inflict a punishment upon the animal, — an absurd opinion which the heretics attribute to us[[fn:3425]], — but to punish its master. For this reason has it been forbidden to derive any profit from the flesh of the animal, so that its master may watch it with care, knowing full well that, if the beast killed a child or an adult, free man or slave, he would inevitably lose the price thereof, and that, if it were a notoriously dangerous animal, he would even be obliged to pay a ransom over and above the loss of the price. It is for the same reason that the beast must be put to death which has served for bestiality[[fn:3426]], in order that the master may take heed to his animal and watch over it as over his own family, lest he lose it[[fn:3427]]. Verily, men are as anxious for their property as for their persons; there are even some who set their property above their persons, but the most part attach an equal value to both: to take us for bondmen, and (to take also) our asses (Genesis, 43, 18).
root.text.Part 3..39.3: That which further belongs to this class is the commandment to put to death the pursuer[[fn:3428]]. This commandment, I mean to kill him who meditats a crime before he has executed it, applies to these two cases only, namely, if any one pursue his neighbour to kill him, or if he pursue a person to violate her chastity; for these are crimes which it is impossible to repair when they are accomplished[[fn:3429]]. As for other transgressions which entail a capital sentence, such as, for example, idolatry and the profanation of the Sabbath, they do no wrong to other persons, and affect only ideas; wherefore the transgressor is not put to death for the mere intent, but only for the accomplished deed.
root.text.Part 3..39.4: Desire, as is well known, is forbidden, because it leads to covetousness, and this, because it leads to rapine; thus the doctors have expounded[[fn:3430]].
root.text.Part 3..39.5: The duty of restoring a lost thing[[fn:3431]] is self-explanatory. Not only is it an excellent virtue beneficial to society[[fn:3432]], but it is also a thing of reciprocal utility; if thou dost not restore what another has lost, thou shalt not be restored what thou shalt have lost, just as he who does not honour his father shall not be honoured by his son. There are many similar cases.
root.text.Part 3..39.6: If he who committs an involuntary homicide be condemned to exile[[fn:3433]], it is in order to appease the mind of the avenger of blood[[fn:3434]], by withdrawing from his sight the person by whom this misfortune has occurred. His return (from exile) depends upon the death of the man who is the greatest and most beloved in Israel, an event which must needs calm the unfortunate man[[fn:3435]] whose kinsman has been slain. For it is in human nature that he who has been smitten by a calamity finds consolation in a similar or greater misfortune wherewith another has been struck; and, among the instances of death which may befall us, none is a greater calamity than the death of the High Priest.
root.text.Part 3..39.7: As for the precept of breaking the neck of a heifer[[fn:3436]], its utility is manifest; for this duty devolvs upon the city nearest to (the place where) the murdered person was found, and most frequently the murderer is from among its inhabitants. The elders of that city, therefore, invoke God as a witness that they have neglected naught in the maintenance and safety of the highways and in the protection of travellers[[fn:3437]], as the (traditional) explanation[[fn:3438]] says. If, then (say they), this man has been murdered, it is not because we have neglected the public interests; moreover, we know not who has slain him. Necessarily, in most cases, the investigation, the departure of the elders, the measuring (of distances), and the presentation of the heifer[[fn:3439]] will give rise to much discourse and conversation; the matter being thus bruited abroad, one may come to know the murderer, for anyone who knows him, or who has heard of him, or who by certain circumstances[[fn:3440]] has some inkling thereof, will come and say: The murderer is such a one. Indeed, as soon as any person, were it even a woman or a slave, declars that such a one is the murderer, the neck of the heifer is not broken[[fn:3441]]. It is certain that if the murderer were known (to any person whatsoever) and silence were kept regarding him, whilst God was taken to witness that he is not known[[fn:3442]], there would be therein great temerity and a grievous sin. Consequently, even a woman who should know him must declare it. As soon as he is known, the object is attained; for even should the tribunal not condemn him to death[[fn:3443]], the sovereign, who has the power to condemn upon probability, would have him put to death; and if the king does it not, it will be the avenger of blood who will seek to slay him, and he will employ ruses to surprise him in order to put him to death. It is therefore clear that the precept of breaking the heifer's neck has for its object the discovery of the murderer. That which confirms this idea is that the place where this ceremony[[fn:3444]] is accomplished must never be tilled nor sown[[fn:3445]]; the owner of this land will therefore employ all manner of ruses and make researches to know the murderer, so that this ceremony may not take place and his field may not be forbidden unto him forever.
root.text.Part 3..40.0: The commandments contained in the sixth class concern criminal punishments[[fn:3446]]. Their utility in general is well known, and we have already spoken thereof. Hearken now unto the details and the manner of judging the extraordinary cases[[fn:3447]] which present themselves therein.
root.text.Part 3..40.1: In general, the penalty to be inflicted upon whosoever committs a crime against his neighbour is to act towards him exactly as he has acted; if he has caused a bodily injury, he shall suffer a bodily injury, and if he has attacked the fortune of another, he shall suffer a pecuniary penalty, albeit it be permitted unto the owner to be generous and to forgive. The murderer alone, by reason of the enormity of his crime, can by no means obtain pardon, and no ransom must be accepted from him: And the land cannot be cleansed of the blood that is shed therein, but by the blood of him that shed it (Numbers, xxxv. 33). Wherefore, even should the victim survive for an hour or for some days, speaking and having all his presence of mind, and should he say: “I desire that my murderer be released, I have forgiven and pardoned him,” he would not be hearkened unto. On the contrary, life must needs be given for life, regarding as equal the child and the adult, the slave and the freeman, the sage and the ignorant; for, among all the crimes of man, there is none greater than that. He who has deprived another of a limb shall be deprived of the same limb: As he has caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him again (Leviticus, xxiv. 20). Thou must not be troubled by the fact that, in this case, we inflict only a pecuniary penalty; for my present purpose is to assign reasons for the Biblical texts and not to assign reasons for the traditional explanation[[fn:3448]]. Moreover, I have also regarding the tradition in question an opinion which must be delivered orally[[fn:3449]]. For wounds where it was impossible to return exactly the like, one was condemned to a pecuniary fine: He shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed (Exodus, xxi. 19).
root.text.Part 3..40.2: He (we have said) who makes an attempt upon the fortune of any man shall suffer a pecuniary penalty in a measure exactly similar: Whom the judges shall condemn, he shall pay double unto the other (Exodus, xxii, 8), (to wit) the amount of that which he has taken, whereunto shall be added as much from the fortune of the thief. — It must be known that, the more frequent a kind of crime[[fn:3450]] is and the more easy to perpetrate, the more severe must the penalty be, in order that men may abstain (from committing it); and the more rare it is, the lighter must be the penalty. It is for this reason that the fine paid by him who steals sheep is double that which is paid for other moveable objects, I mean to say (that it is) fourfold, provided however that he has parted with them by sale or has slaughtered them[[fn:3451]]. For at all times they are frequently stolen[[fn:3452]], because they are in the fields, where they cannot be watched as one watches things that are within the cities; wherefore also those who steal them are wont to sell them promptly, so that they may not be recognised in their possession, or to slaughter them, so that their appearance may vanish. Thus, therefore, the fine for the most frequent cases (of theft) is the heaviest. The fine to be paid for the theft of an ox is further increased by one more, because this theft is yet far more easy. Verily, sheep graze together (in flocks), so that the shepherd may encompass them with his sight, and they can scarce be stolen save during the night; but oxen, as is observed in the book of Agriculture, graze very far apart from one another, wherefore the herdsman cannot encompass them with his sight, and they are very frequently stolen.
root.text.Part 3..40.3: Likewise, the law concerning false witnesses[[fn:3453]] wills that there be done unto them exactly as they intended to do; if they intended to cause a sentence of death, they shall be put to death; if they intended to cause the infliction of stripes, they shall be scourged; if they intended to cause a fine to be imposed, they shall be punished with a like fine. All this has for its object to render the punishment equal to the crime, and it is in this sense also that the laws are called just[[fn:3454]].
root.text.Part 3..40.4: The reason wherefore the [[t:0]]highwayman[[t:1]] is not compelled to pay anything in addition, by way of fine [for the fifth part is but an expiation for the false oath[[fn:3455]]], is that brigandage occurs but rarely. Indeed, the act of theft is more frequent than brigandage: 1[[t:2]]st[[t:3]], because theft may be committed in any locality, whereas brigandage can but with difficulty be executed within the precincts of towns; 2nd, because theft may be perpetrated both upon objects in plain sight and upon those surrounded by secrecy and surveillance, whereas brigandage is only practicable upon objects manifest and evident[[fn:3456]], so that one may take precautions against the highwayman, put oneself on guard, and offer him resistance[[fn:3457]], which cannot be done in regard to the thief; 3rd, because the highwayman is known, so that he may be summoned (to justice) and one may seek to reclaim that which he has taken, whereas the thief is unknown. For all these reasons, the thief is condemned to a fine, whereas a similar condemnation does not apply to the highwayman.
root.text.Part 3..40.5: Preliminary observation[[fn:3458]]. — Know thou that for the penality, whether it be grave and very painful, or lesser and easy to endure, four things are taken into consideration:
root.text.Part 3..40.6: 1<sup>o</sup> The gravity of the crime; for those actions from which a great injury results entail a heavier penalty, whereas those which cause but an inconsiderable injury are punished more lightly.
root.text.Part 3..40.7: 2ndly, the frequency of the occurrence; for that which transpirs more frequently must be restrained by a more severe penalty, whereas a lighter punishment suffices to repress a crime which presents itself but seldom[[fn:3459]].
root.text.Part 3..40.8: 3rdly, the strength of the temptation; for a thing unto which man is impelled, whether by a passion that violently excits him, or by the force of habit, or lastly, by the great grief he feels in abstaining therefrom, nothing can cause him to renounce it save the dread of a grievous chastisement.
root.text.Part 3..40.9: 4thly, the facility of perpetrating the deed in secret and with mystery, so that others perceive it not; for such an action can only be repressed by the fear of a punishment both grave and rigorous.
root.text.Part 3..40.10: After this observation, it must be known that the classification, according to the punishments of which the Pentateuch speaks, compriss four categories[[fn:3460]]: 1st, that which causs the offender to be condemned to the penalty of death inflicted by the tribunal[[fn:3461]]; 2ndly, that which entails excision, consisting (for us) merely in stripes, assuming however that the crime in question is one of the most heinous[[fn:3462]]; 3rdly, that which entails the penalty of stripes [and in which the sin, far from being accounted among the most heinous, is but a simple transgression], or else the penalty of death inflicted by God[[fn:3463]]; 4thly, that which contains simple prohibitions giving no occasion even to the penalty of stripes. Of this latter class are all transgressions in which there is no act, with the exception however of the following[[fn:3464]]: a) a vain oath[[fn:3465]], because of the high idea which must be entertained of the reverence due to the Divinity; b) the exchange (of animals designated for sacrifices)[[fn:3466]], lest one be led thereby to despise the sacrifices consecrated unto God; c) the curse which one might pronounce against his neighbour by invoking the name of God[[fn:3467]], because men are generally far more sensitive to a curse than to a bodily injury. Save for these exceptions, all transgressions in which there is no act can cause but a trifling injury; moreover, one can hardly guard against them, since they consist but in words, and if they were to be punished[[fn:3468]], men would be continually smitten. Furthermore, admonition, in these cases, is scarcely possible[[fn:3469]]. — In the number of stripes there is likewise wisdom, for they are fixed at a maximum, but are indeterminate with respect to the persons. Indeed, each individual can only be smitten according to what he can endure; but the maximum of stripes is forty, even though he might be able to endure a hundred[[fn:3470]].
root.text.Part 3..40.11: As for capital punishment, thou shalt find it in none of the cases relating to prohibited foods; for there results therefrom no great evil, nor are men strongly impelled thereto as they are to the pleasures of love. One incurrs the penalty of excision for the use of certain foods: for the use of blood (for example)[[fn:3471]] which men were, in those times, very eager to eat, practicing thereby a certain idolatrous rite, as is set forth in the book of Tomtom[[fn:3472]]; wherefore it was so severely forbidden. In like manner, the use of fat[[fn:3473]] is punished by excision, because men delight therein; it has also a distinct role in the sacrifice, which it was intended thereby to honour[[fn:3474]]. Likewise again, the penalty of excision applies to him who uss leavened bread during the Passover and to him who takes food on the day of the Great Fast[[fn:3475]], (things forbidden) as much to impose upon us a painful privation as to lead us unto faith; for these are acts serving to consolidate beliefs which are the foundations of religion, namely (on the one hand) the belief in the Exodus from Egypt and in its miracles, and (on the other hand) that relating to repentance: for on this day shall he make an atonement for you (Levit. xvi. 30). Finally, one incurrs the penalty of excision, for having eaten the remnant of the sacrifice, or the abominated sacrifice, or for having, in a state of impurity, eaten holy things[[fn:3476]], which is as reprehensible as eating fat. The purpose is to give importance to the sacrifice, as shall be set forth hereafter.
root.text.Part 3..40.12: Capital punishment thou shalt find only in grievous cases, such as the subversion of faith, or a (social) crime of extreme gravity; I refer to idolatry, adulterous or incestuous intercourse, the shedding of blood, and all that leads unto these crimes (such as the following instances): 1st, the Sabbath (the profanation of which is punished with death), because it serves to establish the belief in the creation of the world[[fn:3477]]; 2nd, the false prophet and the rebellious elder[[fn:3478]], (who are punished with death) by reason of the great corruption which they spread; 3rd, he that smits or curss his father or his mother[[fn:3479]], forasmuch as this betokens great effrontery and destroys the organization of families, which is the principal basis of the State; 4th, the stubborn and rebellious son[[fn:3480]], because of what he may hereafter become, for he will of necessity become a murderer[[fn:3481]]; 5th, he that steals a person[[fn:3482]], because he exposs him to death; likewise, lastly, 6th, he that comes to steal by breaking in, forasmuch as he disposs himself to murder, as the doctors have explained[[fn:3483]]. The three last, I mean the stubborn and rebellious son, he that steals a person and sells him, and he that steals by breaking in, will certainly end by becoming murderers. Thou shalt find capital punishment in no other case save these grievous crimes. Not all incests are punished with death, but only those which are more easily committed, or which are most shameful, or towards which one is more strongly impelled; those which meet not these conditions are punished only with excision. Likewise, not all kinds of idolatry are punished with death, but only the principal acts of such worship, as, for instance, the adoring of idols, prophesying in their name, causing (children) to pass through the fire, the practice of necromancy, magic, or sorcery.
root.text.Part 3..40.13: It is manifest also that, since punishments cannot be dispensed with, it is likewise indispensable to appoint judges, distributed throughout all the cities. There is also need of the testimony of witnesses. Finally, there must be a sovereign who is feared and respected, who may exercise all manner of restraints, strengthen the authority of the judges, and be (in turn) strengthened by them[[fn:3484]].
root.text.Part 3..40.14: Having set forth the reasons for all the commandments which we have enumerated in the book Shophetim (of Judges), we must, according to the purpose of this treatise, direct the attention to certain provisions mentioned therein,
root.text.Part 3..40.15: and notably to those which relate to the rebellious elder[[fn:3485]]. I say then: As the Almighty knew that the provisions of the Law, in all times and in all places[[fn:3486]], would require, according to the diversity of places, events, and circumstances[[fn:3487]], sometimes to be extended and sometimes to be restricted, it was forbidden to add anything thereto or to diminish anything therefrom, and it was said: Thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it (Deut. xiii. 1); for this might have led to the corruption of the legal ordinances and to the belief that they proceeded not from God. Nevertheless, God permitted the learned of every age, I mean the Great Tribunal, to take care for the strengthening of these legal provisions by means of new regulations which should prevent their alteration[[fn:3488]], and to perpetuate these preservative cares, even as the doctors say: “Make a hedge about the Law[[fn:3489]].” Likewise, it was granted unto them, under certain circumstances or in consideration of certain events, to suspend certain practices prescribed by the Law, or to permit certain things which it had forbidden[[fn:3490]]; yet such a suspension was not to be made perpetual, as we have explained in the Introduction to the Commentary upon the Mishnah, concerning the temporary ruling[[fn:3491]]. By this method, the unity of the Law was preserved, and at the same time the circumstances of the moment could always be taken as rules of conduct[[fn:3492]]. But, had it been permitted unto every one of the learned to indulge in these partial considerations[[fn:3493]], men would have been exposed to numerous divisions and schisms. Wherefore God has forbidden all the learned, save the Great Tribunal alone, to undertake such a thing, and He commanded that whosoever should oppose this tribunal be put to death; for, if every thinker had been able to revolt against it, the object in view would have been frustrated and the benefit (of these provisions) would have been destroyed.
root.text.Part 3..40.16: It must further be known that, for the transgression of the prohibitions of the Law, four categories may be established: 1<sup>st</sup> that which is under compulsion, 2nd that which is committed through inadvertence, 3rd that which is committed with premeditation, 4th that which is committed with effrontery[[fn:3494]].
root.text.Part 3..40.17: As for him who is [[t:0]]compelled[[t:1]] (to sin), it is explicitly stated that he will not be punished and that he bears no fault. God has said: [[t:2]]and to the young woman thou shalt do nothing[[t:3]], [[t:4]]the young woman has not committed a sin worthy of death[[t:5]] (Deutér., 22, 26).
root.text.Part 3..40.18: He who sinns unwittingly is culpable, for had he taken due heed to remain tranquil and to watch over himself, he would not have fallen into error. Nevertheless, he can by no means be punished, albeit he requirs an atonement, which consists in the offering of a sacrifice. Herein the law has made a distinction between the private person, the king, the high priest, and the teacher of the law[[fn:3495]]. We learn thereby that he who acts, or who renders a doctrinal decision, according to his individual doctrine—unless it be the Great Sanhedrin or the high priest—is of the class of those who sin with premeditation, and is not numbered among those who sin unwittingly[[fn:3496]]; wherefore the rebellious teacher is put to death, although he acted or rendered decisions according to his personal doctrine[[fn:3497]]. To the members of the Great Sanhedrin alone it appertains to decide according to their own doctrine[[fn:3498]]; therefore, if they have erred, they are considered as having sinned unwittingly, even as it is said: if the whole congregation of Israel sin through ignorance (Lev. iv. 13). It is by reason of this principle that the Sages have said: “An error in doctrine is accounted as a wilful sin[[fn:3499]]”, which signifies that he whose knowledge is circumscribed, and who yet acts or gives decisions according to that circumscribed knowledge, is regarded as sinning with premeditation. Verily, it is not the same with him who eats a portion of the fat of the kidneys, believing it to be the fat of the tail[[fn:3500]], as with him who eats the fat of the kidneys wittingly, but ignorant that such fat is forbidden; for the latter, although an expiatory sacrifice suffices for him, comms nigh unto a voluntary sin. Yet this is only so when he alone committs the sin[[fn:3501]]; but he who renders decisions (erroneous) proceeding from his ignorance[[fn:3502]] must indubitably be regarded as sinning with premeditation, for the text (of the law) excuss an erroneous decision only in the case of the Great Sanhedrin alone.
root.text.Part 3..40.19: He who sinns with premeditation shall undergo the prescribed punishment, whether it be the capital penalty, or the legal stripes[[fn:3503]], or the stripes for rebellion[[fn:3504]] in cases of transgressions where legal stripes are not applicable, or finally a pecuniary penalty. If, for certain transgressions, premeditation has been assimilated unto ignorance, it is because they are committed frequently and with ease, consisting solely in words and not in deeds, as, for example, the oath of testimony[[fn:3505]] and the oath of deposit[[fn:3506]]. The same holds for intercourse with a betrothed bondwoman[[fn:3507]], which (sin) is regarded as lighter because it frequently occurrs, seeing that she (the bondwoman) yields herself up[[fn:3508]], being neither entirely a slave, nor entirely free, nor entirely under the power of a husband, as the tradition says in explaining this commandment[[fn:3509]].
root.text.Part 3..40.20: The insolent sinner is he who not only acts with premeditation, but who is sufficiently impudent and audacious to transgress the law in public. Such a one sinns not out of mere passion, nor because his perverse inclinations make him seek pleasures which the law has forbidden, but to resist the law and to rise in rebellion against it. Therefore is it said of him: he reproaches the Lord (Num. xv. 30), and he indubitably deservs death. He who so acts does it only because he has formed an opinion of his own, in consequence of which he rersists the law. Wherefore the traditional interpretation says that Scripture here speaks of idolatry[[fn:3510]], a system which undermins the very foundation of the law; for no man will ever worship a star without believing it to be eternal, as we have several times explained in our works. The same, in my judgment, applies to every transgression whereby one manifests the intention to overthrow the law and to rebel against it. According to my view, if an Israelite should eat meat cooked in milk, or clothe himself in garments of diverse materials[[fn:3511]], or shave the corners of his hair[[fn:3512]], with the intent to show his contempt for these prohibitions and to demonstrate that he believs not in the truth of this legislation, he would be guilty of blasphemy against the Lord and would deserve death, not as a punishment (for his sin), but for his infidelity; even as the inhabitants of a seduced city are put to death for their infidelity, and not as a punishment for their crime, which is the reason why their goods are delivered to the flames and pass not to their heirs, as do those of others condemned to death[[fn:3513]]. I would say the same of any community of Israelites who by common consent[[fn:3514]] transgress any commandment whatsoever and who act insolently. They all deserve death, as thou mayest learn from the history of the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad, concerning whom it is said: And the whole congregation decided to go up to war against them[[fn:3515]]. In the warning given unto them, it was set forth that, having committed this sin by common consent, they were guilty of infidelity and had shown themselves rebellious against the whole religion, and it was said unto them... turning away this day from following the Lord, etc. (Josh. xxii. 16), whereunto they replied on their part: God, the Lord God knows... if it be in rebellion, etc. (ibid., v. 22). Thou must also well possess thyself of these principles concerning criminal punishments.
root.text.Part 3..40.21: Furthermore, the book Schophetim (of Judges) contains also the commandment to destroy the race of Amalek[[fn:3516]]. Verily, even as the individual is punished, so must a whole tribe or nation be punished, to the end that all tribes may be intimidated and may not mutually assist one another in doing evil, and that they may say: “One might deal with us as they dealt with such a tribe[[fn:3517]]”. In this manner, if there should arise in their midst a wicked and destructive man, having a soul so depraved as not to care for the evil he does and not to reflect thereon, he would find no one to assist him in executing the evil designs he desirs to accomplish. Amalek, then, having been eager to draw the sword, it was commanded to exterminate him by the sword; but Ammon and Moab, who had acted with baseness and had employed craft to do harm, suffered no other punishment than to be excluded from Israelitish marriages, and to see their friendship rejected with contempt. All these provisions show that God has proportioned the punishments, to the end that they should be neither too severe nor too lenient, but as God has expressly said: according to his fault (Deut. xsv. 2).
root.text.Part 3..40.22: This book (Schophetim) contains furthermore the commandment to prepare a place apart (without the camp) and a paddle[[fn:3518]]; for one of the objects which the law aims at, as I have erst made known unto thee[[fn:3519]], is cleanliness and the removal of defilements and impurities, to the end that men should not be as the beasts. By this commandment[[fn:3520]], it was also intended to strengthen in the warriors, by the prescription of these acts, the confidence that the Divine Majesty dwells in their midst, as it is set forth in assigning the motive for this commandment: For the Lord thy God walks in the midst of thy camp (ibid., XXIII, 15). This leads further to this other idea: That He see no unclean thing in thee, and turn away from thee (ibid.), which is an admonition not to give oneself over to debauchery, which, as is well known, prevails in a camp of war when soldiers remain too long absent from their homes. God therefore, to preserve us from such conduct, has prescribed acts which should remind us that the Divine Majesty dwells among us, and He has said: Therefore shall thy camp be holy: that He see no unclean thing in thee. Even he that has been defiled only by a nocturnal accident must go abroad out of the camp, whereinto he may not return until after the going down of the sun[[fn:3521]], so that every man may be well imbued with this thought, that the camp is as a sanctuary of the Lord, and that its mission is not, like the armies of the heathen, to destroy, to ravage, to do evil unto others, and to take their goods; for we, on the contrary, aim to prepare men for the worship of God and to establish order among them. I have already made known unto thee that I indicate the motives of the commandments only according to the literal sense of the text[[fn:3522]].
root.text.Part 3..40.23: Finally, this same book (Schophetim) contains also the law concerning the beautiful captive woman[[fn:3523]]. The doctors say, as thou knowest: “The Law has herein spoken only in respect of human passion[[fn:3524]].” Nevertheless, I must observe that this commandment also contains noble moral lessons which virtuous men ought to take as rules of conduct. Thus, although under the dominion of an indomitable passion, he (the warrior) must be alone with this woman in a retired place, as it is said: within thine house (Deuter., XXI, 12), and he must not violate her during the war[[fn:3525]], as the doctors have explained. Furthermore, it is not permitted unto him to have commerce with her a second time, until her affliction be calmed and her grief assuaged; and he must not hinder her from yielding herself up to sorrow, from neglecting her raiment, and from weeping, as it is written: she shall bewail her father and her mother (ibid., v. 13). For indeed, those who are overwhelmed with sadness find relief in weeping and in exciting their grief, until their physical powers be too much enfeebled to bear this agitation of the soul, even as those who are transported with joy are calmed by all manner of diversions. Wherefore the Law, full of benevolence towards her, grants her in this regard full liberty[[fn:3526]], until she be weary of weeping and of giving herself over to sadness. Thou knowest that he may have commerce with her a first time while she is yet a heathen[[fn:3527]]. Likewise, for thirty days, she may publicly profess her religion, and even give herself to idolatry, without any man being able, during all that time[[fn:3528]], to seek a quarrel with her concerning her belief. After this, if he succeeds not in converting her to the precepts of the Law, it is not permitted unto him to sell her, nor to use her as a slave. The law has therefore respected this woman who has become inviolable in consequence of cohabitation, and, although the act was in some sort a sin[[fn:3529]],—for she was then a heathen,—it is nevertheless said: Thou shalt not make merchandise of her, because thou hast humbled her (ibid., v. 14). Thou seest what noble morality is contained in this commandment[[fn:3530]]. And now the motives of all the commandments of this book are sufficiently elucidated.
root.text.Part 3..41.0: The commandments comprised in the seventh class, relating to the rights of property, are those which we have enumerated in certain portions of the book Mischpâtim (of Judgments) and of the book Kinyân (of Acquisition). They all possess a manifest motive; for they contain provisions of equity for the transactions which of necessity take place among men, and (they recommend them) to yield unto one another a succour profitable to both parties[[fn:3531]], in such wise that neither of the two interested parties should desire to have the larger share in the whole and to be alone advantaged in every respect.
root.text.Part 3..41.1: Before all things, one must abstain from all fraud in buying and selling, and be content with the customary profits of an acknowledged legitimacy[[fn:3532]]. Certain conditions have been established for the validity of the transaction, and fraud has been forbidden, even should it consist but in words[[fn:3533]], as is well known.
root.text.Part 3..41.2: Next comes the law relating to the four guardians[[fn:3534]], which is of manifest equity and justice. Verily, he who keeps a deposit without fee, having absolutely no interest in this matter and acting out of pure kindness, is responsible for naught, and every damage which occurrs must be borne by the owner[[fn:3535]]. The borrower, who alone has all the profit, while the owner does him a kindness, is responsible for everything and must bear all the damages which arise[[fn:3536]]. If any man chargs himself with a deposit for a wage, or takes a thing on hire, both of them—I mean the depositary and the owner—have a common interest therein, and consequently the damages must be divided between them; those which arise from a lack of care in supervision must be borne by the depositary, as, for example, if the object has been stolen or lost, for theft and loss show that he has neglected to bestow upon it great care and extreme foresight[[fn:3537]]; but the damages which it is impossible to prevent,—as, for example, if the animal (lent) has been maimed, or driven away, or if it be dead, which are cases of vis major,—must be borne by the owner.
root.text.Part 3..41.3: Stress is further laid upon the benevolence due to the hireling, by reason of his poverty; and it is prescribed to pay him his hire promptly, and in no wise to defraud him of that which is his due, that is to say, to recompense him according to the value of his labor[[fn:3538]]. Benevolence toward him proceeds so far that one ought not to prevent him, nor even the beast (whilst engaged in labor), from eating of the food which is the object of their toil, according as the (traditional) ordinances relating to this law require[[fn:3539]].
root.text.Part 3..41.4: The laws concerning property encompass likewise the matter of inheritances. Sound morality requirs that a man should not refuse to do good unto him who is worthy thereof. He ought not, therefore, at the moment of his departure, to be envious of his (natural) heir, nor should he squander his fortune, but leave it unto him among men who has the greatest right thereto, namely, unto the next of kin: unto his kinsman that is next to him of his family (Numbers, xxvii. 11). It has been expressly stated, as is well known, that this is first the child[[fn:3540]], then the brother, and thereafter the uncle (ibid., v. 8-10). He must give preference to the first-born of his sons, the first object of his love, and must not suffer himself to be led by his passion: he may not make the son of the beloved first-born (Deut., xxi. 16). The equitable Law has desired to preserve and fortify within us this virtue, I mean that of having regard for kinsmen and protecting them. Thou knowest the word of the prophet: He that is cruel troubls his own flesh (Prov., xi. 17); the Law, in speaking of alms, says: Unto thy brother, to thy poor, etc. (Deut., xv. 11), and the doctors greatly extol the virtue of the man “who is attached to his kinsfolk and who marries his sister’s daughter[[fn:3541]].”
root.text.Part 3..41.5: The Law has taught us that we must proceed to the utmost degree in the practice of this virtue, that is to say, that a man must ever have regard for his kinsman and hold the ties of family in high esteem; and though his kinsman should have shown himself hostile and malicious toward him, and should have manifested an exceedingly vicious character, he must nevertheless treat him with all the regard due to kinship[[fn:3542]]. God has said: Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite, for he is thy brother (Deut., xxiii. 8). Likewise, he of whom thou hast one day stood in need, from whom thou hast derived benefit and whom thou hast found in a moment of distress, even should he have done thee evil thereafter, thou art bound to take account of the past. God has said: Thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian, because thou wast a stranger in his land (ibid.). Nevertheless, it is well known how much evil the Egyptians did unto us thereafter[[fn:3543]]. — Thou seest how many noble virtues we learn by these commandments. The two last-cited passages, it is true, do not belong at all to this seventh class; but having spoken of the regard due to kinsmen in inheritances, we were led to say a word concerning the Egyptians and the Edomites.
root.text.Part 3..42.0: The commandments comprised in the eighth class are those which we have enumerated in the book Zemannim (of Times or Seasons). All, save a small number, are clearly justified by their motives in the (Biblical) text.
root.text.Part 3..42.1: As touching the institution of the Sabbath, the reason thereof is too well known to require exposition. It is understood that, on the one hand, it is for rest; it was desired that every person might devote the seventh part of his life to pleasure, and rest from the toils and troubles from which no one, neither small nor great, can escape. On the other hand, it was intended to perpetuate throughout the generations a great and most important doctrine, namely, that of the creation of the world in time[[fn:3544]].
root.text.Part 3..42.2: The institution of the fast of the Day of Atonement is likewise well-grounded, for it serves to establish the idea of repentance[[fn:3545]]. It is the day whereon the Prince of the Prophets brought down from Sinai the second tables unto the Israelites and announced unto them the pardon of their great sins[[fn:3546]]. This day became, therefore, in perpetuity a day of penitence uniquely consecrated to Divine worship. For this reason must one abstain on this day from all bodily gratification and from all occupation relating to material interests—I speak of industrial labors. One must confine himself (on that day) to confessions, that is to say, to confessing his sins and repenting of them.
root.text.Part 3..42.3: The festivals are all intended for rejoicings and for pleasant assemblies, which generally are necessary unto man, and have also the advantage of cementing the friendships which ought to be established among men in civil societies. Each of these days is particularly grounded.
root.text.Part 3..42.4: The subject of the Passover is well known; if it lasts seven days, it is because the period of seven days is a mean period between the natural day and the lunar month[[fn:3547]]. Thou knowest also that this period plays a great part in physical things[[fn:3548]]. Wherefore it is the same in religious matters; for religion ever imitats nature and, in a manner, complets physical things. Verily, nature has neither thought nor reflection, whereas religion is the rule and the regimen emanating from God, from whom every intelligent being derivs his intelligence. But this is not the subject of this chapter; we return, therefore, to the matters wherewith we are here occupied.
root.text.Part 3..42.5: The Feast of Weeks is the day of the Revelation of the Law[[fn:3549]]. To glorify and honor this day, one counts[[fn:3550]] the days from the first of the festivals until then, even as one who awaits the arrival of his best friend and counts the days and the hours. Such is the reason why one counts the ’omer[[fn:3551]] from the day of the departure from Egypt until the day of the revelation of the Law, which was the true object of that departure: And I brought you unto myself (Exodus xix. 4). This great spectacle lasted but one day, and likewise is the memory thereof celebrated each year during one day. But if one ate unleavened bread only for one day, it would not be perceived, and the thing which it is intended to recall would not become manifest; for it often happens that one partaks of the same kind of food for two or three days. It is only by continuing to eat it during a complete period that the matter which it has for its object becoms clear and the signification manifest.
root.text.Part 3..42.6: Likewise, the feast of the New Year[[fn:3552]] lasts but one day; for it is a day whereon men must do penance and awaken from their indolence. It is for this reason that the shofar (horn) is sounded on this day, as we have explained in the Mishneh Torah[[fn:3553]]; it is, as it were, a preparation and an opening for the day of fasting; thus thou seest that it is a traditional custom, very widespread in our communion, to observe the ten days from the commencement of the year until the Day of Atonement.
root.text.Part 3..42.7: The Feast of Tabernacles, being dedicated unto mirth and rejoicing, endurs seven days, to the end that the object thereof be well understood. The reason why it is celebrated in this season[[fn:3554]] is set forth in the Law: When thou hast gathered in thy labours out of the field (Exodus xxiii. 16); that is to say, at the time when, being free from care, thou restest from necessary toils. Aristotle has already remarked in the ninth book of the Ethics that such, it would seem[[fn:3555]], was a custom most widely diffused among the nations of antiquity. Thus he expresses himself: “The sacrifices and the (solemn) assemblies, among the ancients, took place after the ingathering of the fruits; they were, as it were, sacrifices of thanksgiving for the leisure[[fn:3556]].” Such are his words. Furthermore, one may easily dwell in the succah (booth) during this season, in which there is neither oppressive heat nor troublesome rain.
root.text.Part 3..42.8: The two festivals of Tabernacles and of the Passover have each for their object a religious belief and a moral thought. As touching belief, the Passover is intended to recall the miracles of Egypt and to perpetuate the memory thereof throughout all generations; and the Feast of Tabernacles is to perpetuate for ever the memory of the miracles of the wilderness. The moral thought is that man, in his prosperity, ought to remember the days of distress, so that he may manifest unto God his full gratitude and derive therefrom lessons of submission and humility. Therefore must we eat unleavened bread and bitter herbs during the feast of Passover, in order to remind ourselves of what befell us. Even so, we must quit our houses and dwell in booths, as do the unhappy inhabitants of the fields and deserts, to the end that we may remember that such was formerly our condition—(that your generations may know) that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths (Leviticus xxiii. 43)—and that, through the goodness of God, we were brought forth thence to dwell in splendid houses in one of the fairest and most fertile regions of the earth, by virtue of the promises which He had made unto our ancestors, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, men perfect in their beliefs and their virtues. Indeed, this is also one of the pivots of religion; I mean (the belief) that every benefit which God bestows or has bestowed upon us is due only to the merit of the patriarchs who kept the way of the Lord to do justice and judgment[[fn:3557]].
root.text.Part 3..42.9: The reason why the Festival of Cabanes terminates in a second festival, which is the [[t:0]]eighth day of closing[[t:1]], is so that on this day one may complete the rejoicings to which one cannot give oneself over in the huts, but only in spacious habitations and in grand edifices.
root.text.Part 3..42.10: As for the four species (of plants) constituting the lulab[[fn:3558]], the doctors have assigned a reason for them after the manner of the drashoth[[fn:3559]], the method of which is known unto all who understand the words of the Rabbins; for these are with them as mere poetic allegories, and they mean not that such is the actual sense of the text[[fn:3560]]. Men have regarded the drashoth in two different ways: some have imagined that what the doctors have therein stated is the explanation of the true meaning of the texts; others, despising these explanations, have made them a subject of mockery, since it is most manifest that such is not the sense of the text. The former[[fn:3561]] have obstinately contended to defend, according to their own opinion, the truth of the drashoth[[fn:3562]], believing that this was the true sense of the (biblical) text, and that one should attribute to the drashoth the same authority as to the traditional laws. But neither of these two parties has been willing to understand that these were but poetic allegories, the meaning of which is by no means obscure to the intelligent man. This method was very prevalent in those times, and everyone employed it, even as poets use poetical locutions. Thus, for example, the doctors say: “Bar-Kappara taught that where it is said: thou shalt have a paddle upon thy weapon, אזנך (Deut. xxiii. 14), we should not read AZENEKA (thy weapon), but OZNEKA (thine ear); and this teaches us that a man, when he hears an unseemly thing, should put his finger in his ear[[fn:3563]].” Now, I would fain know whether, in the opinion of the ignorant, the doctor in question truly believed that this passage should be so explained, that such was the object of this commandment, and that by YATHED (paddle), one must understand the finger, and by AZENEKA, the ears. I do not think that a single man of sound sense could believe this. Rather is it a very beautiful poetic allegory whereby he wished to inculcate a noble moral, to wit, that it is forbidden to hear obscene words, even as it is forbidden to utter them; and he has attached this unto a biblical passage, after the manner of poetic allegories. Likewise, whenever it is said in the drashoth: “thou must not read in such a manner, but in such another,” it must be understood in this sense.—I have wandered from my subject; yet is this a useful observation, of which all intelligent theologians and Rabbins may have need. I now resume the continuation of our subject.
root.text.Part 3..42.11: In my opinion, the four species constituting the lulab indicate the mirth and joy which the Hebrews felt when they left the wilderness, which was no place of seed, or of figs, or of vines, or of pomegranates; neither was there any water to drink (Numbers xx. 5), to go unto places where there were fruit trees and rivers. To celebrate the memory thereof, they took the fairest and most fragrant fruit of those places[[fn:3564]], their foliage[[fn:3565]] and their most beautiful verdure, to wit, willows of the brook. These four species are distinguished by three peculiarities: 1st, they were in those times very frequent in the land of Israel, so that everyone could procure them. 2ndly, they are of a beautiful appearance, full of freshness, and have in part a goodly odour, such as the citron and the myrtle; as for the branches of the palm-tree and the willow, they have no odour, neither bad nor good. 3rdly, they keep their freshness for a week, a quality which peaches, pomegranates, quinces, pears, etc., possess not.
root.text.Part 3..43.0: The commandments comprised within the ninth class are those which we have enumerated in the book Ahabâ (Of the Love of God). They are all clearly motivated, and the reason for them is manifest[[fn:3566]]; for all these religious practices (which they prescribe for us) have for their object to cause us ever to think of God, to cause us to love and fear Him, to the end that we may obey His commandments in general, and believe concerning God that which every religious man must of necessity believe. These practices are: prayer[[fn:3567]], the reading of the Schema’[[fn:3568]], the blessing of the meal[[fn:3569]] and their appurtenances, the blessing of the priests[[fn:3570]], the phylacteries[[fn:3571]], the inscription upon the door-posts[[fn:3572]], the acquisition of the book of the Law and the reading thereof at certain seasons[[fn:3573]]. All these practices are of a nature to give rise to profitable thoughts; this is clear and evident, and it would be bootless to say a word more, for I could but repeat myself.
root.text.Part 3..44.0: The commandments comprised within the tenth class are those which we have enumerated in the treatises On the Chosen House (or of the central sanctuary), in that On the Utensils of the Sanctuary and its Ministers, and in that On the Entrance into the Sanctuary[[fn:3574]]; we have already made known, in general, the utility of this class.
root.text.Part 3..44.1.sub_0: It is well known that the idolaters sought to build their temples and to erect their idols in the highest place they could find: upon the high mountains (Deut. xii. 2). Therefore did our father Abraham choose Mount Moriah, which was the highest mountain in those regions[[fn:3575]], and there proclaimed the unity of God, and designated the Kiblâ[[fn:3576]], fixing it exactly to the West. Verily, the Holy of Holies was in the West, and it is this which the doctors indicate when they say: “The Divine Majesty is in the West[[fn:3577]].” The doctors have already explained in the Gemara of the treatise Yômâ that it was our father Abraham who determined the Kiblâ, that is to say, the site of the Holy of Holies[[fn:3578]]; and here, in my opinion, is the reason: Since it was then a very widespread opinion that worship should be rendered to the sun, which passed for God, and as doubtless all the world turned, in praying, towards the East[[fn:3579]], our father Abraham took for his Kiblâ, upon Mount Moriah, that is to say, upon the place of the sanctuary, the western side, in order to turn his back upon the sun. Dost thou not see what the Israelites did, when their defection[[fn:3580]] and their infidelity caused them to return to those ancient perverse opinions? They turned their backs against the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the East, prostrating themselves toward the East before the sun (Ezekiel viii. 16). Thou must well ponder this remarkable observation. I doubt not, moreover,
root.text.Part 3..44.1.sub_1: that this place chosen by Abraham in a prophetic vision was known to Moses our master and to many other persons; for Abraham had recommended that this place should be consecrated to worship, as the (Chaldean) translator expressly says[[fn:3581]]: “Abraham worshipped and prayed in this place and said before the Lord: Here future generations shall worship, etc.” If, in the Pentateuch, this is not expressly said in a positive manner, and if it is only alluded to by the words which God shall choose[[fn:3582]], there were for this, as it seems to me, three reasons: 1st, lest the (pagan) nations should seek to seize this place and wage violent war for its possession, knowing that it was the most important place upon earth for the religion (of the Israelites); 2nd, lest those who then possessed it should destroy it by devastating it as much as possible; 3rd, and this is the weightiest reason, lest each tribe should seek to have this place in the portion it was to possess, and to conquer it, which would have caused such disputes and troubles as there were concerning the priesthood. Wherefore it was commanded not to build the central sanctuary until after the establishment of the monarchy, so that it might belong to one alone to give orders[[fn:3583]], and that all strife might cease, as we have explained in the book Schophetim[[fn:3584]].
root.text.Part 3..44.2.sub_0: It is further known that those men (the idolaters) built temples to the planets[[fn:3585]] and that there was placed in each temple the statue which it was agreed to worship, that is to say, a statue consecrated to a certain planet forming part of a sphere[[fn:3586]]. We were therefore commanded to build a temple to the Most High and to deposit therein the holy Ark containing the two tables which comprised (these two commandments): I am the Lord, etc. and Thou shalt have no other gods, etc.— It is known that the article of faith concerning prophecy must precede the belief in the Law; for, without prophecy, there is no Law. The prophet receivs revelation only through the medium of an angel; for example: And the angel of the Lord called (Genesis xxii. 15), And the angel of the Lord said unto her (ibid., xvi. 9-11), and other passages innumerable. Moses himself was initiated into his prophetic mission by an angel: The angel of the Lord appeared unto him in the midst of the fire (Exodus iii. 2)[[fn:3587]]. It is therefore clear that the belief in the existence of angels must precede the belief in prophecy, and that the latter must precede the belief in the Law. Now, as the Sabians were ignorant of the existence of God and imagined that the Eternal Being, who could never not have existed, was the celestial sphere with its stars, whose forces were poured out upon idols and upon certain trees, such as the Aschêrôth[[fn:3588]], they believed that it was the idols and the trees that inspired the prophets, made revelations to them by speaking to them, and made known to them what was useful or harmful; and these opinions we have already set forth, in speaking of the prophets of Baal and of the prophets of Aschêrâ[[fn:3589]].
root.text.Part 3..44.2.sub_1: But when the truth was manifested to men, and it was known by means of demonstrations that there exists a Being who is neither a body nor a force within a body, to wit, the true and only God; that, furthermore, there exist other beings, separate[[fn:3590]] and incorporeal, upon whom is poured forth the divine being[[fn:3591]] and who are the angels, as we have set forth[[fn:3592]], and finally, that all these beings are without the celestial sphere and its stars, then were men convinced that it was these angels who in reality made revelations unto the prophets, and not the idols and the Aschérôth. Thus, it is manifest from the foregoing that the belief in the existence of angels is joined to that which has for its object the existence of God, and that it serves to establish the truth of prophetic revelation and of the Law. To confirm this article of faith, God commanded the placing above the ark the image of two angels[[fn:3593]], so as to consolidate the belief of the people in the existence of angels, a true belief, which is the second after the belief in the existence of God, as well as the principle of prophecy and of the Law, and the negation of idolatry, as we have set forth. Had there been but a single figure, I mean the figure of a single cherub, it might have given rise to error, and one might have believed that it was a figure under which God was worshipped, as the idolaters were wont to do, or also that there was but a single individual angel[[fn:3594]], which would have led to a kind of dualism. But, as two cherubim were made, alongside the express declaration that the Lord our God is one (Deut. vi. 4), the belief in the existence of angels was thereby confirmed, and it was established that they were several. One ran no risk, therefore, of being deceived and of taking them for God, since God is one and it is He who has created this plurality (of Intelligences).
root.text.Part 3..44.3: Before[[fn:3595]] it was placed the candlestick as a sign of honour and respect for the temple; for this temple, ever illumined by lamps and separated (from the Holy of Holies) by a vail[[fn:3596]], was intended to impress the soul mightily. Thou knowest what importance the Law attaches to our being struck with the majesty of the sanctuary and the respect which is due thereunto, so that in beholding it man may have the sentiment of his own frailty and become humble. It is said: Ye shall reverence my sanctuary (Levit. xix. 30); and, to give more force to this recommendation, it has been joined to that of the observance of the Sabbath.
root.text.Part 3..44.4: — The altar of incense, the altar of burnt offerings and their vessels were of an evident necessity[[fn:3597]]. As for the table and the bread which was to be continually set forth thereon[[fn:3598]], I know not the reason thereof, and until this moment I have found naught to which I might attribute this usage.
root.text.Part 3..44.5: As for the prohibition of hewing the stones of the altar[[fn:3599]], thou knowest the reason which the Doctors have given for it: “It is not fitting,” say they, “that that which shortens life should be lifted up upon that which prolongs it[[fn:3600]].” This is good after the manner of drashôth, as we have said; but this prohibition has another manifest reason. It is that the idolaters constructed their altars with polished stones; wherefore it was forbidden to do as they did, and, to avoid this imitation, it was commanded to make the altar of earth, as it is said: An altar of earth thou shalt make unto me (Exodus xx. 21). Nevertheless, if it became indispensable to make it of stone, these stones must at least have their natural form and be not polished. Thus was it also forbidden to erect stones adorned with figures and to plant trees near the altar[[fn:3601]]. All this has one and the same purpose, to wit, that we should not worship God under the individual forms of the cults[[fn:3602]] which they (the heathens) rendered unto their divinities, and this has been forbidden in a general manner in these terms: How did these nations serve their gods? even so will I do likewise (Deuter. xii. 30), which signifies that one must not act thus toward God, for the reason thereafter stated: Every abomination to the Lord, which he hats, have they done unto their gods (ibid., v. 31).
root.text.Part 3..44.6: Thou knowest also how widespread in those times was the worship of Pe’ôr, which was celebrated by uncovering one's shameful parts[[fn:3603]]. Wherefore it was commanded unto the priests to make for themselves breeches to cover their nakedness (Exodus xxviii. 42) during the service, and nevertheless they were not to go up to the altar by steps (as it is said): that thy nakedness be not discovered thereon (Exodus xx. 23).
root.text.Part 3..44.7: The Temple was to be continually guarded, and a watch maintained round about it, for the sake of its honor and that it might be held in reverence<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3604]]</sup>, and lest it should be encroached upon by the profane<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3605]]</sup>, the unclean, and those in a state of impurity<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3606]]</sup>, as shall be hereafter explained. That which, among other things, was intended to glorify the Sanctuary and to cause it to be honored in such wise as to ensure our respect, was the prohibition of entry unto men intoxicated<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3607]]</sup>, the unclean, and those of ill-kept appearance—to wit, having their hair in disarray or their garments rent—and the requirement that every officiating minister should sanctify his hands and his feet<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3608]]</sup>.
root.text.Part 3..44.8: It was further for the honor of the Temple that it was ordained to honor its ministers; the priests and Levites were specially designated (for the service), and the priests were provided with splendid vestments, of great beauty and elegance: holy garments for glory and for beauty[[fn:3609]]. No man who possessed a physical blemish was admitted to the service, and herein it is not only a question of one afflicted with an infirmity, for deformities likewise rendered the priests unfit (for service)[[fn:3610]], as has been set forth in the traditional explanation of this commandment[[fn:3611]]; for the vulgar do not esteem a man according to his true form[[fn:3612]], but rather by the perfection of his members and the beauty of his raiment. All this is designed to the end that the Temple be honored and respected by all people.
root.text.Part 3..44.9: — As for the Levite, who was not charged with the offering of sacrifices and was not deemed to make atonement for sins—as it is said of the priests: He shall make an atonement for him, or for her (Leviticus, iv. 26; xii. 8, and passim)—but had no other function than the recitation of hymns, he became unfit for service only upon the loss of his voice[[fn:3613]]. Verily, the purpose of song is to ensure that the words exert a more profound impression upon the soul; now, the soul is only so impressed by sweet melodies, with the accompaniment of musical instruments, as was ever the custom in the Sanctuary.
root.text.Part 3..44.10: — Even unto those priests fit for service who remained in the Sanctuary, it was not permitted to sit therein, nor to enter the interior of the Temple at all times, nor ever to enter the Holy of Holies, with the exception of the High Priest (who might enter it on the Day of Atonement four times, and no more)<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3614]]</sup>; and all this was out of reverence for the Sanctuary.
root.text.Part 3..44.11: Since, in this holy place, many animals were daily slaughtered, and flesh was therein cut up and consumed by fire, and the inwards were washed<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3615]]</sup>, it is certain that, had it been left in such a state, it would have yielded an odor like unto that of a shambles. Wherefore it was commanded to burn incense there twice daily, in the morning and in the afternoon, to diffuse a pleasant odor and to perfume the garments of all who performed the service. Thou knowest what the Sages say: “From Jericho the odor of the incense was perceived”<sup class="footnote-marker">[[fn:3616]]</sup>. This served equally to maintain the respect for the Sanctuary. But had it not possessed a pleasant odor, and still more so if the contrary had been the case, there would have resulted the opposite of respect; for the soul is cheered by goodly odors and is attracted thereby, whilst it is repelled by foul odors and fles from them.
root.text.Part 3..44.12: — As for the oil of anointing[[fn:3617]], it possessed a twofold advantage: on the one hand, it imparted a sweet savour unto that which was imbued therewith, and on the other, it inspired reverence for the object anointed, sanctifying it and distinguishing it from other things of like kind, whether it were a human individual, a garment, or a vessel. All this was intended to lead to the veneration of the Temple, which, in its turn, should inspire the fear of God; for, upon entering therein, one was deeply impressed, and hearts of stone were softened and rendered pliable. It is for the purpose of softening them and making them humble that God, by His remote decrees[[fn:3618]], has employed all this foreseeing wisdom, so that, by frequenting the Temple, they might become accessible unto the divine precepts, which serve us as guides, and might attain unto the fear of God, as is clearly set forth in the text of the Pentateuch: Thou shalt eat before the Lord thy God, in the place which He shall choose to place His name there, the tithe of thy corn, of thy wine, and of thine oil, and the firstlings of thy herds and of thy flocks; that thou mayest learn to fear the Lord thy God always (Deut. xiv. 23). Thou wilt now perceive what was the end in view in prescribing all these things. — The reason why it was forbidden to imitate the oil of anointing and the perfumes is right manifest: it was, on the one part, to the end that this odour should be perceived only in that holy place, and that the impression thereof might be the more profound; and, on the other part, lest it might be believed that all who were anointed with this oil, or with an oil similar thereto, were men of distinction, which might have given rise to grave inconveniences and contentions.
root.text.Part 3..44.13: If it was commanded to bear the Ark upon the shoulders, and not upon wagons, it is manifest that this was to show respect unto it[[fn:3619]]; nought was to be altered in its form, and the staves were not even to be removed from the rings[[fn:3620]]. In like manner, one was not to alter the form of the Ephod and of the Breastplate, nor even to separate them one from the other[[fn:3621]]. All the garments of the priests were to be woven of a single piece[[fn:3622]], being neither cut nor fashioned by division, to the end that the form of the fabric might not be altered.
root.text.Part 3..44.14: — It was also forbidden to each of the ministers of the Sanctuary to take upon himself the functions of others[[fn:3623]]; for when duties are entrusted unto several persons, without assigning unto each[[fn:3624]] a particular office, it comes to pass that all neglect them and become remiss.
root.text.Part 3..44.15: — It is evident also that this gradation established for the different places (of the Sanctuary)[[fn:3625]], by prescribing special ordinances for the Temple Mount, for the ḥēl or rampart[[fn:3626]], for the Court of the Women, for the Courtyard, and so forth even unto the Holy of Holies—all this, I say, had for its object to render greater homage unto the Temple and to inspire a deeper reverence in all who approached it.
root.text.Part 3..44.16: And now we have set forth the reasons for all the particular commandments which are comprised within this class.
root.text.Part 3..45.0: The commandments comprised in the eleventh class are those which we have enumerated in the remainder of the book ’Abôdâ (of Worship) and in the book Korbanôth (of Sacrifices). We have already treated of their general utility[[fn:3627]], and we shall now undertake to set forth the reasons thereof in detail, so far as we have been able to apprehend them. Thus, then, we say.
root.text.Part 3..45.1: It is related in the text of the Pentateuch, according to the exposition of Onkelos, that the ancient Egyptians worshipped the constellation of Aries; wherefore it was forbidden among them to slay sheep, and they held shepherds in abomination, as it is said: Lo, shall we sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians, etc. (Exodus, viii, 22)[[fn:3628]]; For every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians (Genesis, xlvi, 34). In like manner, certain sects of the Sabians who worshipped demons believed that these latter assumed the form of he-goats; for which reason they bestowed upon the demons the name of he-goats. This opinion was very prevalent in the days of Moses, our teacher: and that they no more offer their sacrifices unto he-goats (Levit., xvii, 7); wherefore these sects likewise abstained from the eating of he-goats[[fn:3629]]. As for the slaughtering of oxen, it was held in abomination by well-nigh all idolaters, and all held this species in great honour[[fn:3630]]. Hence thou wilt find that the Hindus even unto our own day never slaughter the bovine species, even in those lands where they sacrifice[[fn:3631]] other kinds of animals. It was, therefore, to obliterate the vestiges of these unwholesome opinions that we were commanded to sacrifice specifically these three kinds of quadrupeds: of the herd and of the flock ye shall bring your offering (Levit., i, 2), so that men might draw nigh unto God by the very act which they had deemed the most heinous of crimes, and that they might seek in that act the remission of their sins. Thus was it sought to heal these corrupt notions, which are the maladies of the human soul, by means of the contrary extreme.
root.text.Part 3..45.2: It was precisely for this same purpose that we were commanded to sacrifice the Paschal lamb, and, in Egypt, to sprinkle the blood thereof upon the exterior of the doors, that we might be delivered from those opinions, and that by proclaiming the contrary we might make (the Egyptians) share in the belief that the act which they regarded[[fn:3632]] as a cause of death was, on the contrary, that which saved from death: And the Lord will pass over the door, and will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses to smite you (Exodus, xii, 23), as a reward for having publicly performed their worship and rejected the follies professed by idolaters[[fn:3633]].
root.text.Part 3..45.3: — Such, then, is the reason for which these three species were particularly chosen for the sacrifices. Moreover, these species are domestic animals[[fn:3634]] which exist in great number; whereas the idolaters were wont to sacrifice[[fn:3635]] lions, bears, and other wild beasts, as is related in the book Tomtom.
root.text.Part 3..45.4: Inasmuch as the greater part of the people possess not the means to offer a quadruped, it was ordained to offer likewise as a sacrifice those birds which are most common in Syria, being the best and most easy to obtain: namely, turtledoves and young pigeons[[fn:3636]]. He that was unable to offer even a bird might offer baked oblations, prepared in any of the divers manners of cooking known in those times, whether in the oven, or upon the griddle, or in a frying-pan; and he who found it difficult to offer baked cakes might offer fine flour[[fn:3637]]. All these ordinances were directed unto those who had the voluntary desire (to offer sacrifices)[[fn:3638]]. — Furthermore, it is expressly stated that, if we did not perform this manner of worship, I mean that of sacrifices, we should not thereby be stained by any sin: But if thou shalt forbear to vow, it shall be no sin in thee (Deuter., xxiii, 23).
root.text.Part 3..45.5: Since the idolaters offered but leavened bread, and frequently offered sweet things and mingled honey in their offerings,—as is often seen in the books of which I have spoken to thee,—and since in none of their offerings did they make use of salt[[fn:3639]], God, on the one hand, forbade the offering of any manner of leaven or of honey (Levit. ii. 11), and, on the other hand, He commanded that salt should ever be offered: With all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt (ibid., v. 13).
root.text.Part 3..45.6: All sacrifices were to be without blemish and in the most excellent state, to the end that one should not come to disdain the sacrifice nor to hold in contempt that which was to be offered to the Divinity, as it is said: Offer it now unto thy governor; will he be pleased with thee, or accept thy person? (Malachi i. 8.) It is also for the same reason[[fn:3640]] that it was forbidden to offer in sacrifice an animal that has not yet accomplished seven full days[[fn:3641]], forasmuch as its species is not yet perfectly formed and it is found to be repulsive; it is indeed like unto an untimely birth. It is likewise for the same reason that it is forbidden to offer the hire of a harlot and the price of a dog[[fn:3642]], by reason of the turpitude of these two things. For the same reason also, full-grown turtle-doves and young pigeons were offered[[fn:3643]], both being the best of their kind, for full-grown pigeons possess no flavour. Finally, for the same reason, the offerings were to be kneaded with oil and composed of fine flour[[fn:3644]], for these are the things most perfect and sweet. The frankincense (which was placed therein) was chosen because of the goodly fragrance which its smoke diffused in places where there was an odour of burnt meat.
root.text.Part 3..45.7: It is further out of reverence for the sacrifice, and that it should not be regarded with aversion and loathing, that it was prescribed to flay the burnt-offering and to wash the inwards and the legs, although they were to be burnt in their entirety[[fn:3645]]. Thou wilt find that this was a matter of constant concern and from which they sought to preserve themselves: But ye have profaned it, in that ye say, The table of the Lord is polluted; and (ye disparage it) saying,[[fn:3646]] the fruit thereof, even His meat, is contemptible (Malachi i. 12). For the same reason also, an uncircumcised or unclean man[[fn:3647]] may not eat of the sacrifice; nor can it be eaten when it has been rendered unclean, nor after the prescribed delay, nor when it has been profaned by thought[[fn:3648]], and it must be eaten in a specified place[[fn:3649]]. The burnt-offering, which pertains wholly unto God, may in no wise be eaten; that which is offered in atonement for a fault, to wit, the sin-offering and the guilt-offering[[fn:3650]], must be eaten within the court, and only on the very day of the slaughtering and the night following. The peace-offerings, which are of a lower degree and of lesser holiness, must be eaten only within the whole city of Jerusalem and may yet be eaten on the morrow (of the slaughtering), but no later; for after that delay, they spoil and become corrupt.
root.text.Part 3..45.8: It is also to cause us to reverence the sacrifice and all that has been consecrated in the name of God, that the Law declars guilty whosoever shall have derived enjoyment from holy things; he must offer a trespass-offering and pay a fifth part more thereto[[fn:3651]], even though he should have committed the sin through inadvertence.
root.text.Part 3..45.9: In like manner, it was forbidden to work with sacred animals or to shear them[[fn:3652]]; all this, out of reverence for the sacrifices. The law relating to the exchange (of animals)[[fn:3653]] was given by way of precaution; for, had it been permitted to substitute a good animal for a bad one, men would also have substituted a bad one for a good one, pretending that it was better. The Law therefore pronounced that: both (the beast) itself and that which was put in its place should be holy (Leviticus xxvii. 10 and 33). — If it was prescribed that he who would redeem any of the things he had consecrated must add a fifth part of the value[[fn:3654]], the reason thereof is manifest. Verily, (as the proverb says) "the nearest kinsman to a man is himself"[[fn:3655]]; being therefore ever inclined by his nature to be parsimonious of his money, he would not inquire diligently[[fn:3656]] into the price of the consecrated thing, nor would he submit it to a rigorous estimation[[fn:3657]], in order to truly ascertain its value. Wherefore we have been secured against him by the requirement of an augmentation[[fn:3658]], to the end that the consecrated object might be sold to another for its true value[[fn:3659]]; all this, to preserve from contempt that which has been consecrated to God and that which is to serve in obtaining His favour[[fn:3660]].
root.text.Part 3..45.10: The reason wherefore the offering of the priest[[fn:3661]] was to be burnt, is that every priest was bound to present his offering with his own hand[[fn:3662]]; if, therefore, he had himself eaten the offering presented by him, it would have been as though he had offered nothing at all. Verily, of every offering of a private individual, there was offered upon the altar only the incense and a handful (of flour)[[fn:3663]]. If then, not content with the scantiness of this sacrifice, he who offered it had further been permitted to eat it, there would not have even remained a semblance of worship; for which cause this offering was to be burnt.
root.text.Part 3..45.11: The ordinances which particularly concern the paschal lamb, to wit, that it must be eaten only roasted with fire, in one house, and without breaking a single bone thereof (Exodus, xii, 8 and 46), have all an evident reason. Indeed, even as the unleavened bread is motivated by haste, so also the roasting had for its motive precipitancy[[fn:3664]]; for they had not leisure to make diverse dishes nor to prepare dainties. They would even have feared to tarry for the breaking of the bones and the taking out of the contents; for, to sum up all this[[fn:3665]], it is said: and ye shall eat it in haste (ibid., v. 11). Now, in haste, one cannot stop to break the bones, nor to send portions from one house to another and await the return of the messenger; for all such actions denote negligence and delay, whilst the object was to secure themselves by speed and precipitancy, lest any person should be late and miss the opportunity of departing with the multitude, so that harm might have befallen him by being taken unawares. These customs were thereafter perpetuated in commemoration of the event, as it is said: Thou shalt therefore keep this ordinance in his season from year to year (ibid., xiii, 10). If it was said that "the paschal lamb could only be eaten by those who had been numbered to partake of it[[fn:3666]]," it was to inculcate the duty of purchasing it, and so that no one should rely upon a kinsman, a friend, or the first comer who might have offered it to him, lest he should have failed to provide for it beforehand. As for the prohibition against giving it to be eaten by the uncircumcised[[fn:3667]], the doctors have already explained it[[fn:3668]], saying that the Hebrews, during their long sojourn in Egypt, had neglected the commandment of circumcision, in order to assimilate themselves unto the Egyptians[[fn:3669]]. When, therefore, the paschal lamb was ordained and it was made a condition that no one should slaughter it save after having practiced circumcision upon himself, upon his children, and upon the men of his house, and that only then he might come near and keep it (ibid., xii, 48), they all underwent circumcision. The multitude of the circumcised, say they, caused the blood of circumcision to be mingled with the blood of the paschal lamb, and it is to this that the prophet alludes when he says: weltering in thy blood (Ezekiel, xvi, 6), to wit, the blood of the paschal lamb and that of the circumcision[[fn:3670]].
root.text.Part 3..45.12.sub_0: It must be known that the Sabians regarded blood as a thing most unclean, and, despite this, they ate it, because they believed it to be the food of demons, and that, if any person ate thereof, he did thereby fraternize with these evil spirits, who would come unto him and make known to him future things, as the vulgar imagine concerning demons. There were, however, some people to whom it seemed hard to eat blood, for it is a thing repugnant to human nature. These, therefore, having slaughtered an animal, collected the blood into a vessel or into a pit, and ate the flesh of that animal near the blood; they imagined, in so doing, that the demons ate this blood, which was their food, whilst they themselves ate the flesh, and that, by this means, fraternization might be obtained, since they all ate at the same table and in the same gathering. According to their opinion, the demons would then appear unto them in a dream, make known to them hidden things[[fn:3671]] and render them services. These were the opinions followed in those times, accepted with eagerness and generally spread abroad, the truth of which was beyond doubt in the eyes of the vulgar[[fn:3672]]. The perfect Law undertook to bring to an end these inveterate maladies in those who acknowledge it, by forbidding the eating of blood; it insisted upon this prohibition as much as upon that of idolatry; God has said: I will set my face (My anger) against that soul that eats blood (Leviticus, xvii, 10), even as He said concerning him who gives of his seed unto Molech: I will set my face against that man (ibid., xx, 5)[[fn:3673]].
