There exists no third commandment concerning which one expresses himself in this manner, which is only employed toward those who give themselves up to idolatry or who eat blood; for by eating of the latter, one is led to a species of idolatry, which is the worship of demons. Nevertheless, it (the Law) declared blood to be pure and made of it a means of purification for him who should undergo contact with it: Thou shalt sprinkle it upon Aaron, and upon his garments, etc., and he shall be hallowed, and his garments (Exodus, xxix, 21).
root.text.Part 3..45.12.sub_1: It commanded the sprinkling thereof upon the altar, and made the whole ceremony consist in pouring it there, not in gathering it: And I, it is said, have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement, etc. (Levit., xvii, 11); it was poured there, as it is said: And he shall pour out all the blood (ibid., iv, 18), and elsewhere: The blood of thy sacrifices shall be poured out upon the altar of the Lord thy God (Deuter., xii, 27). Finally, it was even commanded to pour out the blood of every animal that one should slaughter, without it being a sacrifice, as it is said: Thou shalt pour it upon the earth as water (ibid., xii, 16 and 24; xv, 23). Next, it was forbidden to assemble around the blood and to eat there, as it is said: Ye shall not eat anything with the blood (Levit., xix, 26)[[fn:3674]]. As they persisted in sinning and in following the well-known custom in which they had been nurtured, of fraternizing with demons by eating around the blood, God absolutely forbade them to eat in the wilderness flesh of desire[[fn:3675]], but willed that every (animal intended for consumption) should be offered as a peace-offering[[fn:3676]], declaring unto us that the reason thereof was that the blood should be poured upon the altar and that they should not assemble around it; He said therefore: To the end that the children of Israel may bring, etc., and they shall no more offer their sacrifices unto devils, or demons (ibid., xvii, 5 and 7). But there yet remained (to prescribe a rule of conduct) concerning the wild beast and the fowl, for the wild beast could never serve as a sacrifice and the fowl could not be offered as a peace-offering[[fn:3677]]; God therefore prescribed, following this, that when one had slaughtered a wild beast or any fowl whatsoever of which it is permitted to eat the flesh, one should cover the blood thereof with dust[[fn:3678]], so that they should not assemble to eat around the blood. It was thus that the end of severing the fellowship[[fn:3679]] between those who were truly possessed and their demons was completely attained.
root.text.Part 3..45.13: — It must be known that this belief was well-nigh contemporary with Moses, our teacher, that it was much followed and that it led men astray. Thou findest this textually in the song HAAZINU: They sacrificed unto devils, not to God; to gods whom they knew not, etc. (Deuter., xxxii, 17). The doctors have thus explained the meaning of the words not to God: not content, say they, with worshipping real beings, they even worship imaginary beings. Thus it is expressed in the Sifri: "It suffices them not to worship the sun, the moon, the planets and the constellations, but they even worship the reflections thereof (בבואה)." The word בבואה is the name for the shadow (or the reflection)[[fn:3680]].
root.text.Part 3..45.14: — I now return to our subject. It must be known that meat of desire was prohibited in the wilderness alone; for it was one of those opinions then current that demons inhabited the deserts, and that there they did speak and appear, whilst in cities and inhabited places they did not manifest themselves; wherefore such of the inhabitants of cities as desired to practice any of those follies went forth from the city and betook themselves to desert and solitary places. Hence it was that meat of desire was permitted (unto the Hebrews) after their entry into the land (of Canaan). Moreover, this malady must then have lost its strength, and the adherents of such opinions must have diminished. Furthermore, it would have been passing difficult and well-nigh impossible for all who desired to eat of the flesh of a (domestic) animal to repair unto Jerusalem. For all these reasons, meat of desire had been forbidden only in the desert.
root.text.Part 3..45.15: Furthermore, it is to be known that the more grave a sin, the more does the sacrifice required for it diminish in value as touching its species[[fn:3681]]. For this reason, the sin of idolatry committed through inadvertence especially demands a she-goat[[fn:3682]], and the other sins of an individual require a ewe or a she-goat[[fn:3683]]; for in every species the female is of less account than the male, and there is no sin greater than idolatry, nor any species[[fn:3684]] lower than the she-goat. By reason of the distinguished rank occupied by the king, the sacrifice which he offers for a sin of inadvertence is a he-goat[[fn:3685]]; as for the high priest and the congregation, since their sin of inadvertence consists not in a mere (personal) act, but in a legal decision[[fn:3686]], their sacrifice was distinguished by prescribing for them the offering of bullocks[[fn:3687]], and, for the sin of idolatry, he-goats[[fn:3688]]. — Inasmuch as the sins for which an asham (trespass-offering) was offered are less grave than those for which a hattâth (sin-offering) was brought, the asham sacrifice was a ram or a young lamb[[fn:3689]]; thus was chosen a species and a sex more distinguished, and it was ordained to be a male from among the sheep. Perceivest thou not that for the burnt-offering likewise, which belongs entirely unto God, a more distinguished sex was chosen, and it can be naught but a male[[fn:3690]]? It is further by the same principle that the offering of the sinner and that of the unfaithful wife suspected of a sin[[fn:3691]] were deprived of embellishment and sweet savour, and neither oil nor frankincense was to be put with these offerings. This embellishment was suppressed therein because the person offering it had not followed a seemly conduct; and, as if there were a movement of repentance, it was said, as it were, unto him[[fn:3692]]: By reason of thy evil actions, thy offering shall be in an inferior state. As for the unfaithful wife, whose action is more shameful than a sin of inadvertence, her offering is of an inferior substance; for it consists of barley meal. These particulars which have just been reviewed[[fn:3693]] possess a most remarkable significance.
root.text.Part 3..45.16.sub_0: The Sages say that the reason why, on the eighth day of the consecration (of the priests), a young calf as a sin-offering was offered (Levit. ix. 2), was to make atonement for the golden calf; and that likewise the sin-offering of the Day of Atonement was a young bullock for sin (ibid., XVI, 3), to make atonement for the golden calf. In accordance with the idea they have expressed, it seems to me that the reason why all sin-offerings, as well for the individual as for the congregation, were he-goats, — I speak of the he-goats offered on the festivals, on the New Moons, and on the Day of Atonement, as well as the he-goats offered for the sin of idolatry[[fn:3694]], — the reason, I say, is that their principal sin at that time was to offer sacrifices unto the he-goats (demons), as the text of Scripture expressly says: and they shall no more offer their sacrifices unto he-goats (demons) after whom they have gone astray (Levit. xvii. 7). As for the Sages, they think that the reason why the atonement for the sins of the congregation was constantly made by the sacrifice of he-goats was that the he-goat is connected with the sin which the whole congregation of Israel had committed of old. They allude to the selling of Joseph the righteous, in whose history it is said: And they killed a kid of the goats, etc. (Genesis xxxvii. 31)[[fn:3695]]. This reason must by no means be considered weak; for the aim of all His actions is that every sinner should be convinced that he must ever remember his sin and confess it, as it is said: And my sin is ever before me (Ps. li. 5), and that he and his posterity must seek to obtain pardon for that sin by a religious act of the same kind as the sin itself. This is what I would say: If he has sinned in a matter of money, the reparative act must also consist in a sacrifice of money; if he has sinned by corporeal enjoyments, he must impose upon himself a religious act which fatigus and afflicts his body, by fasting and watching in the night; if he has committed a moral sin, he must repair it by an opposite moral act, as we have explained in the treatise De'ôth (of Morals) and elsewhere[[fn:3696]].
root.text.Part 3..45.16.sub_1: Finally, if he has committed a speculative error, that is to say if, through his incapacity or his negligence in betaking himself to research and speculation, he has admitted a false idea, he must combat it by banishing it from his mind and by preventing it from dwelling[[fn:3697]] upon aught worldly, to occupy himself only with matters of the intellect and the serious examination of things which ought to be believed. It is in this sense, well-nigh, that it was said: If my heart has been secretly enticed, my hand has been laid upon my mouth (Job xxxi. 27)[[fn:3698]], which is an allegorical expression signifying that one must abstain and halt before that which is obscure, as we have set forth in the first book of this treatise[[fn:3699]]. Thus, thou seest that when Aaron had failed in making the golden calf, it was imposed upon him, and upon all those of his race who were to succeed him, to offer a bullock and a young calf[[fn:3700]]. Likewise, where the sin is brought into relation with a he-goat, the religious act was accomplished by means of a he-goat[[fn:3701]]. If the soul be well penetrated with these ideas, man shall be led thereby to hold sin in abhorrence and to depart from it, that he may not be obliged, in falling therein, to submit himself to a long and painful atonement; sometimes even the atonement cannot be accomplished[[fn:3702]], so that man shall avoid sin in advance and flee from it, which evidently is of great utility. It behoovs thee to penetrate thy mind well with this subject.
root.text.Part 3..45.17: I deem it my duty here to call thy attention to a most remarkable thing, albeit it may seem foreign to the purpose of this treatise. The he-goat offered at the New Moons is alone called sin-offering UNTO THE LORD (Numbers xxviii. 15), an expression which is employed neither for any of the he-goats offered at the festivals, nor for the other sin-offerings; the reason of which, in my judgment, is very clear: it is that the sacrifices which the congregation offered at certain seasons, that is to say, the additional sacrifices (of the festivals), were all burnt-offerings, and there was each day a he-goat as a sin-offering. This he-goat was eaten, whilst the burnt-offerings were entirely consumed by fire; wherefore they are expressly called offering made by fire UNTO THE LORD[[fn:3703]], whilst it is never said either sin-offering UNTO THE LORD, nor peace-offering UNTO THE LORD, because these sacrifices were eaten. Even those sin-offerings which were burned[[fn:3704]] could not be called offerings made by fire unto the Lord, the reason of which I shall explain in this chapter. One could not, therefore, (all the more so) call the he-goats (of the festivals) sin-offerings unto the Lord, for they were eaten, and were not burned in their entirety. But, as it might be feared that the he-goat of the New Moons should be considered as a sacrifice offered unto the moon, after the example of the Egyptians, who offered sacrifices unto the moon at the beginnings of the months[[fn:3705]], it is expressly said in speaking of this he-goat that it is consecrated unto God, and not unto the moon. This fear could not be entertained concerning the he-goats offered at the festivals and on other solemn days[[fn:3706]], for these days were neither beginnings of months, nor marked by any phenomenon of nature, but had been instituted by the decrees of the Law. On the contrary, the beginnings of the lunar months were not instituted by the Law; but the nations offered on those days sacrifices unto the moon, even as they offered them unto the sun when he rose and when he entered into certain degrees (of the ecliptic), as is known from those books (of the Sabians). It is for this reason that there is used, in speaking of this he-goat (of the New Moons), a particular expression[[fn:3707]], saying unto the Lord, in order to destroy the errors which were rooted in the grievously sick hearts (of the Israelites). Penetrate thy mind well with this remarkable idea.
root.text.Part 3..45.18: It must also be known that every sin-offering, whereby it is believed that great sins are expiated, or even a single sin—as, for instance, the sacrifice for the sin of ignorance[[fn:3708]] and other like offerings[[fn:3709]]—is burnt entirely without the precincts, and not upon the altar; for naught was burnt upon the altar save the burnt-offering and that which resembls it[[fn:3710]], and for this cause is it called the altar of burnt-offering (Exodus, xxx, 28, and passim). Verily, the consumed burnt-offering was (accounted) a sweet savour unto God, and likewise every Azcarâ[[fn:3711]] offered a sweet savour unto God. It must indubitably have been thus, since this ceremony was intended to abolish idolatrous beliefs, as we have already set forth. But the custom of burning those sin-offerings (of which we have spoken) signifies naught else than that the trace of such sin was blotted out and had vanished even as that body which had just been consumed by fire, and that no vestige of that action remained, even as there remained no vestige of that sin-offering which had been destroyed by the flames. Consequently, the latter, when it was burnt, could not yield a sweet savour unto God; but, on the contrary, it was a smoke which God must needs detest and abhor; wherefore it was burnt entirely without the precincts. Dost thou not perceive that, concerning the offering of the woman suspected of adultery, it is said that it is an offering of memorial to bring iniquity to remembrance (Numbers, v, 15), and not that it is a thing favourably accepted?
root.text.Part 3..45.19: The scapegoat being ordained for the total expiation of great sins, so that there exists no public sin-offering which expiats so many as it, and that it, in a manner, bears away all sins, it was not to be slaughtered, nor burnt, nor offered as a sacrifice[[fn:3712]]; but it was to be removed as far as possible and cast into a land called GUEZÉRA (Levit., xvi, 22), that is to say, a place remote from habitations. It is indubitable to all that sins are not bodies[[fn:3713]] which can be transferred from the back of one individual unto that of another. But all these acts are but symbols intended to make an impression[[fn:3714]] upon the soul, to the end that this impression may lead to penitence; the meaning being: we are delivered from the burden of all our former actions, which we have cast behind us and hurled to a great distance.
root.text.Part 3..45.20: As regards the offering of wine, it has hitherto left me in perplexity. How is it that an offering of wine was prescribed, which was also presented by idolaters[[fn:3715]]; I have not been able to comprehend this; but another has given the reason, which is as follows: The faculty of [[t:0]]appétition[[t:1]], which has its source in the liver, finds nothing better than flesh; the faculty [[t:2]]vitale[[t:3]], which has its source in the heart, finds nothing better than wine; in like manner, the faculty which has its source in the brain, namely the faculty [[t:4]]psychique[[t:5]], delights in songs accompanied by instruments[[fn:3716]]. It is for this reason that each faculty endeavours to approach God by means of the thing it loves most, so that one offers (to God) flesh, wine, and sounds, that is to say, songs.
root.text.Part 3..45.21: The pilgrimage has a manifest utility; that which serves as its motive is that this assembly and the impression it produces result in a renewed zeal for the Law and in the fraternity which is established among men. It is thus especially with the commandment to assemble the people[[fn:3717]], the reason of which is clearly indicated: that they may hear, etc. The money given for the second tithe was destined to be expended there[[fn:3718]], as we have already set forth[[fn:3719]]. It was likewise thus with the fruit of the fourth year[[fn:3720]] and the tithe of the cattle. Thus, therefore, one had there the meat of the tithe, the wine of the fourth year, and the money of the second tithe, so that provisions were there in abundance; for it was permitted to sell naught of all these things, nor to defer them from one season to another; but, as God has said: Year by year (Deuter., xiv, 22). These things shall therefore of necessity be used for the giving of alms, and, in truth, it is strenuously enjoined to give alms during the festivals, saying: Thou shalt rejoice in thy feast, thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, etc., and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow (ibid., xvi, 14). Now, we have traversed the particular commandments belonging to this class, and we have touched upon many of their details.
root.text.Part 3..46.0: The commandments comprised in the twelfth class are those which we have enumerated in the book Tohorâ (of Purification). Although I have already briefly spoken of their utility[[fn:3721]], we must here give fuller explanations; and, after having justified this class as is meet, I shall give the reasons for these details, so far as they are clear unto myself.
root.text.Part 3..46.1: I say, then, that this Divine Law, which was given to Moses, our master, and which has been attributed unto him, had no other end than to render the ceremonies of worship more facile and to alleviate[[fn:3722]] the burden thereof; and if there be any that may appear to thee grievous and most heavy, this proceeds from the fact that thou art unacquainted with the usages and rites that existed in those times. Let a comparison, therefore, be made between a cult in which a man burns his child and that in which one burns a young pigeon[[fn:3723]]! It is said in the Pentateuch: for even their sons and their daughters they have burnt in the fire to their gods (Deuter., 12, 31); such was the worship they offered to their gods, and that which is analogous thereto, in our worship, is the burning of a young pigeon, or even a handful of fine flour. It was in this regard that our nation was rebuked in the time of its rebellion, and that it was said unto it: O my people, what have I done unto thee? and in which have I wearied thee? testify against me (Micah, VI, 5); it is said again, in the same sense: Have I been a wilderness unto Israel? a land of darkness? wherefore say my people, We are lords; we will come no more unto thee, etc. (Jeremiah, 2, 31), which signifies: what then is the grievous burden they have seen in this law, that they should forsake it[[fn:3724]]? Elsewhere God apostrophizes us, saying: What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me (ibid., v. 5)? All these passages have but one and the same end.
root.text.Part 3..46.2: After this preliminary observation, which is of great import and which thou must not lose from thy sight, I say: We have already set forth that all which was sought to be obtained through the sanctuary was that it should produce an impression upon him who came to visit it, and that it should inspire fear and reverence, as it is said: and ye shall reverence my sanctuary (Levit., 19, 30). But, when one continually approaches any object of respect, the effect which it produces upon the soul does diminish, and the impression received therefrom is lessened. The doctors have already called attention to this subject, saying that it is not well to enter at every moment into the sanctuary, and they cite in support these words: Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour's house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee (Prov., 25, 17)[[fn:3725]]. It was with this intention that God forbade the unclean to enter the sanctuary; and the cases of uncleanness being very numerous, one could but very rarely find a person who was pure. Indeed, even if one had preserved himself from the contact of a carcass, he might not have escaped contact with one of the eight creeping things[[fn:3726]] which often fall into the house, as well as into food and drink, and against which one often stumbls[[fn:3727]]. Having avoided that, one might still not have escaped contact with a woman in her courses or one afflicted with an issue of blood, a man afflicted with gonorrhœa, a leper, or their bed[[fn:3728]]; even had one escaped these, one could not always avoid cohabitation with his wife, or having a nocturnal accident[[fn:3729]]. Even when one had purified himself from these uncleannesses, it was not permitted to enter the temple before the setting of the sun[[fn:3730]]. Now, as one could not enter the temple during the night, as results from the treatises Middoth and Tamid[[fn:3731]], it might happen for the most part that he (who had purified himself) would cohabit that very night with his wife, or that there might come upon him one of the other causes of uncleanness, and he would find himself the next morning at the same point as the day before.
root.text.Part 3..46.4: In measure as the case of uncleanness might happen more frequently, the purification was more difficult and lasted longer. To be under the same roof with dead bodies, and especially with those of kinsmen and neighbours, is a case more frequent than any other uncleanness; one could not, therefore, become pure again except by means of the ashes of the red heifer, which are exceeding rare, and after seven days[[fn:3733]]. The flux (of blood or gonorrhœa) and the menses are more frequent than contact with an unclean thing; wherefore these uncleannesses required seven days (of purification)[[fn:3734]], and he who came into contact with them was unclean for a single day[[fn:3735]]. If the purification of the man afflicted with gonorrhœa, of the woman afflicted with an issue of blood, and of the woman in childbirth, is not completed but by a sacrifice, it is because these cases happen more rarely than the menses[[fn:3736]]. — All these uncleannesses, I mean those of the menses, gonorrhœa, issue of blood, leprosy, a dead body, a carcass, a creeping thing, and of semen, are things most foul. The legal dispositions relative thereto have, therefore, various ends: 1st, to remove from us all foulness; 2nd, to preserve the sanctuary; 3rd, to have regard for customs generally spread abroad, for thou shalt hear presently what grievous ceremonies the Sabians imposed upon themselves in these cases of uncleanness; 4th, to alleviate this heavy burden and to ensure that the question of what is pure or impure should not fetter man in any of his occupations, for this question concerns only the sanctuary and holy things: She shall touch no hallowed thing, nor come into the sanctuary (Levit., 12, 4). For the rest, one is guilty of no sin in remaining unclean as long as one wills, and in nourishing oneself as much as one wills with profane things tainted with uncleanness. According to the customs spread among the Sabians until our time in the countries of the Orient, I mean among the remnants of the Magi[[fn:3737]], the woman having her menses remains isolated in an apartment, the places upon which she walks are burnt[[fn:3738]], he who speaks to her becoms unclean, and if the wind that blows passes over the woman and over a pure man, the latter becoms unclean. Thou seest, consequently, how far these usages are from what we say: “All the works that a woman does for her husband, the woman having her menses may do likewise, except the washing of his face, etc.[[fn:3739]]”; one is only forbidden to cohabit with her during the days of her defilement and uncleanness. — Another custom spread among the Sabians until our time is that they repute as unclean all that is separated from the body, whether hair, or nail, or blood; wherefore every barber, among them, is unclean, because he touches the blood and the hair[[fn:3740]]. Whosoever has himself shaved must plunge into water springing from a fountain. They have many of these inconvenient usages, whilst we pay no attention to what is pure or impure save in regard to holy things and the sanctuary. However, if the Scripture says: Ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy (Levit., 11, 44), this is by no means said in regard to what is pure or impure; the Siphra says expressly that it referrs therein to a “sanctification by the commandments[[fn:3741]]”, and likewise the doctors say, concerning these words: Ye shall be holy (Levit., 19, 2), that it referrs to a sanctification by the commandments. Wherefore the transgression of the commandments is also called טומאה (defilement or uncleanness), an expression employed in regard to the fundamental commandments[[fn:3742]], which are idolatry, incest, and murder. In speaking, for example, of idolatry, it is said: because he has given of his seed unto Molech, to defile my sanctuary (Levit., 20, 3); of incest, it is said: defile not ye yourselves in any of these things (ibid., XVIII, 24); of murder, it is said: so ye shall not pollute the land, etc. (Numbers, 35, 34). It is seen, consequently, that the expression טומאה (defilement or uncleanness) is an homonymous term which is used in three different senses. It is said: 1st, of disobedience and the transgression of the commandments in matters of action or opinion; 2nd, of foulness and filth: her filthiness is in her skirts (Lamentations, I, 9); 3rd, of those things reputed (unclean), I mean when one touches or carries such a thing, or when one is found under the same roof with such a thing[[fn:3743]]. It is in this third sense that we say: “The words of the Law are not susceptible of uncleanness[[fn:3744]].” Likewise, the word קדושה, holiness, is said, as an homonym, in three senses, opposed to the three significations of which we have just spoken.
root.text.Part 3..46.5: Inasmuch as one cannot be purified from the uncleanness caused by a dead body except at the end of seven days, and for this purpose the ashes of the red heifer must be found; and since, on the other hand, the priests have constant need to enter the Sanctuary to offer the sacrifices, it has been particularly forbidden to every priest to expose himself to the impurity arising from a dead body, save in a case of extreme necessity, where it would be repugnant to human nature to abstain; I refer to contact with the bodies of father and mother, children and brethren[[fn:3745]]. As it is highly necessary that the High Priest be continually in the Sanctuary, even as it is said: it (the diadem) shall be always upon his forehead (Exodus, xxviii. 38), it has been absolutely forbidden unto him to defile himself by a dead body, were it even that of his own parents[[fn:3746]]. Perceivest thou not that this prohibition does not embrace the women? the sons of Aaron (it is said), and not the daughters of Aaron[[fn:3747]], because there is no need of women in the service of the sacrifices.
root.text.Part 3..46.6: As it is inevitable that persons tainted with impurity should enter the Sanctuary by error, or eat, in their state of uncleanness, of holy things, and since there be some who do this with premeditation—the most impious of men committing the gravest sins of deliberate purpose—it has been commanded to offer sacrifices to expiate the defilement of the Sanctuary and of the holy things; these are of divers kinds, some for premeditated sin, others for that committed through inadvertence. These are the goats of the festivals, those of the New Moons, and the scapegoat[[fn:3748]], as is set forth in its place, to the end that he who sinns of deliberate purpose may not believe that he has not committed a great sin in defiling the Sanctuary of the Eternal, but may know, on the contrary, that his sin has been expiated by the sacrifice of the goat; as it is said: and that they die not in their uncleanness (Levit., xv. 31); and Aaron shall bear the iniquity of the holy things, etc. (Exodus, xxviii. 38)[[fn:3749]], an idea which is frequently repeated.
root.text.Part 3..46.7: As touching the impurity of leprosy, we have already set forth its significance[[fn:3750]]. The doctors also have expounded it and have made us to know that it is established as a principle that this malady is a chastisement to punish evil-speaking[[fn:3751]]. At first, this alteration is remarked in the walls[[fn:3752]]; if the man repent, the end is attained; but if he continue to sin, the alteration extends to his bed and to the vessels of his house[[fn:3753]], and if he yet persist in his sin, it extends to his garments and thereafter to his body. This was a miracle which was perpetuated in the nation, like that of the bitter waters of the woman suspected of adultery[[fn:3754]]. It is manifest that this is a most profitable belief, especially if one reflects that leprosy is contagious and that all men feel toward it an almost instinctive loathing[[fn:3755]]. The reason why the purification was performed with cedar wood, hyssop, scarlet wool, and two birds[[fn:3756]], has been indicated in the Midraschôth; but it suits not our purpose, and hitherto I have been unable to account for any of these things. Neither know I for what reason cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool are employed in the ceremony of the red heifer, nor why a bunch of hyssop is used for the sprinkling with the blood of the Paschal lamb[[fn:3757]]; I find naught whereby to justify the preference given to these species.
root.text.Part 3..46.8: The reason why the red heifer is called ’hattath (sin-offering)[[fn:3758]], is because it complets the purification of him who has been defiled by a dead body, so that he may enter into the Sanctuary[[fn:3759]]; I mean that, from the moment one has defiled himself by a corpse, it would be for ever forbidden him to enter the Sanctuary or to eat of holy things, were there not this heifer to take away (symbolically) this sin[[fn:3760]]. It is even as the diadem (of the High Priest) which expiats defilement[[fn:3761]] and as the goats which are burnt[[fn:3762]]. Wherefore he who was occupied with the red heifer and the goats that were to be burnt rendered his garments unclean[[fn:3763]], even as he who was occupied with the scapegoat, which, by reason of the great sins it was supposed to carry away, rendered unclean those who touched it[[fn:3764]].
root.text.Part 3..46.9: — Thus have we assigned motives, in this class, to all the commandments of which we have deemed it possible to conjecture the reasons.
root.text.Part 3..47.0: The commandments comprised in the thirteenth class are those which we have enumerated in the treatises Maakhalôth assourôth (of forbidden foods), Sche’hîtâ (of the manner of slaughtering animals), Nedarim ou-nezirouth (of vows and the Nazirite state). We have already, in this treatise[[fn:3765]] and in the commentary upon Aboth, sufficiently and at large expounded the utility of this class; we shall here provide more ample explanations, whilst reviewing the particular commandments therein enumerated.
root.text.Part 3..47.1: I say, then, that all the foods which the Law has forbidden us constitute unwholesome nourishment. In all that has been forbidden us, there be only the swine and the fat which are not deemed injurious[[fn:3766]]; yet it is not so, for the swine is (a food) more humid than is meet, and of an exceeding superfluity[[fn:3767]]. The principal reason why the Law holds it in abomination is that it is right filthy and feeds upon unclean things. Thou knowest how much the Law cars to remove the sight of filth, even in the open field, in a camp of war[[fn:3768]], and much more so in the interior of cities; but if the flesh of swine were eaten, the streets and even the houses would be filthier than latrines, as is now to be seen in the land of the Franks[[fn:3769]]. Thou knowest the saying of the Sages: «The snout of the swine is as walking filth[[fn:3770]].»
root.text.Part 3..47.2: Likewise, the fat of the intestines[[fn:3771]] is over-nourishing, hinders digestion, and engenders cold and thick blood; wherefore it is more fitting that it be burned[[fn:3772]].
root.text.Part 3..47.3: In like manner, blood and the beast that dies of itself are difficult of digestion and provide base nourishment; and it is also known that the beast teréphâ is very nigh unto being a dead beast[[fn:3773]].
root.text.Part 3..47.4: — As for the characteristic signs (of a clean animal), to wit, for quadrupeds, the chewing of the cud and the cloven hoof, and for fishes, the possession of fins and scales[[fn:3774]], it must be known that the existence of these signs is not the cause why it is permitted to eat thereof, nor is the lack of these signs the cause why these animals are forbidden. They be merely signs whereby one may recognize the good species and distinguish it from the bad[[fn:3775]].
root.text.Part 3..47.5: — The reason for the commandment concerning the sciatic nerve is set forth in the text itself[[fn:3776]].
root.text.Part 3..47.6: — The prohibition of eating a limb of a living animal[[fn:3777]] is based upon the fact that such an act accustoms one to cruelty. The kings of the heathens were wont to do so in those times, and it was likewise an idolatrous practice to sever a certain limb from a quadruped and to devour it[[fn:3778]].
root.text.Part 3..47.7: Concerning the prohibition of eating meat cooked in milk, apart from the fact that it constituts a very gross food, generating a superfluity (of blood), it is not improbable that idolatry had some part therein. Perhaps it was eaten during some idolatrous ceremony, or at one of the festivals of the heathens; and what confirms me in this latter opinion is that where the Law twice forbidds the eating of meat cooked in milk[[fn:3779]], it mentions it beside the precept concerning the pilgrimage: Three times in the year, etc.[[fn:3780]]. It is as though it said: At the time of your pilgrimage, when ye enter the temple of the Lord your God, ye shall not cook anything after the manner aforesaid, as the idolaters were wont to do. This is, I believe, the most plausible reason for this prohibition; yet have I found no mention thereof in those books of the Sabians which I have perused.
root.text.Part 3..47.8: The precept regarding the slaughtering of animals is necessary. For the natural food of man consists only of vegetable substances and the flesh of animals, and the best of meats are those which are permitted unto us, a fact of which no physician is ignorant. Now, since the necessity of obtaining good nourishment requirs that the animal be slain, it was intended that it should die in the easiest manner, and it was forbidden to torment it, whether by an improper slaughter, or by piercing the lower part of the neck[[fn:3781]], or by severing a limb, as we have already explained.
root.text.Part 3..47.9: — In like manner was it forbidden to slaughter on the same day the mother and her young[[fn:3782]], to the end that we might take care not to slay the young before the eyes of the mother; for the animal would, in such a case, endure too great a grief. Verily, in this respect, there is no difference between the pain felt by man and that of other animals; for the love and tenderness of a mother for her offspring depend not upon reason, but upon the action of the imaginative faculty, which most animals possess as well as man. If this commandment has been given specifically regarding the bovine and ovine species, it is because these are the domestic animals which we are permitted to eat and which men are generally accustomed to consume, and these are also the species in which the mother and her young can be distinguished[[fn:3783]].
root.text.Part 3..47.10: — The precept of dismissing the mother from the bird’s nest[[fn:3784]] has an analogous reason. Verily, for the most part, eggs that have been sat upon and young birds that yet require the mother are not fit for food; if, therefore, one must dismiss the mother so that she flies away, not only shall she be spared the grief of seeing her young taken, but often even this shall lead to the leaving of the whole, since that which one might take is generally not good to eat[[fn:3785]].
root.text.Part 3..47.11: If the Law has had regard unto these sorrows of the soul in the case of quadrupeds and birds, how much more so in regard to all the individuals of the human race? One must by no means object to me that which the Doctors say: “He who says: Thy mercy extends unto the nests of birds, etc.[[fn:3786]]”; for that is one of the two opinions of which we have spoken, to wit, the opinion of those who think that the Law has no other motive than the mere will (of God), whilst we, for our part, follow the second opinion[[fn:3787]].
root.text.Part 3..47.12: We have already observed that the Law itself explains wherefore it is necessary to cover the blood, and that this precept concerns particularly the clean wild beast and the clean fowl[[fn:3788]].
root.text.Part 3..47.13: — Besides the precepts which have been given us to interdict the use of certain foods, there have been prescribed unto us precepts relating to vows of (voluntary) abstinence[[fn:3789]]. If any man say that this bread, or this meat, be for him a thing forbidden, he is prohibited from eating thereof. All this has for its end to exercise man in sobriety and to moderate his desire for eating and drinking. The Doctors have said: “Vows are a hedge around abstinence[[fn:3790]].” But as women, being easily impressionable and of a feeble soul, are prone to be moved by passion, there would be in the house grave difficulties, strifes, and disorder, if they were mistresses of making vows; for such kind of food would be permitted to the husband and forbidden to the wife, and another would be forbidden to the daughter and permitted to the mother. Therefore has the matter been entrusted to the head of the family, in all that which may concern him[[fn:3791]]. On the other hand, thou seest that the woman who governs herself, and who is not under the dependence of a head of family, is subject in respect of vows to the same rule as men; I speak of her who has neither husband nor father, or who has attained the age of puberty and is called boghers[[fn:3792]].
root.text.Part 3..47.14: The Nazirite vow has a motive very clearly indicated, which is that of abstaining from the drinking of wine[[fn:3793]], which in all times has made victims[[fn:3794]]: many and mighty were those whom it has slain[[fn:3795]]; and these also have erred through wine (Isaiah, xxviii. 7). The law of the Nazirite, as thou mayest see, forbidds among other things the use of all that proceeds from the vine[[fn:3796]], with much strictness, to the end that men should content themselves with that which is necessary. Indeed, he who abstains from wine is called holy and is placed in the same rank of holiness as the High Priest, so that, like the latter, he dars not even make himself unclean by contact with (the corpse of) his father or his mother[[fn:3797]]. All this greatness comes unto him from his abstinence from drink[[fn:3798]].
root.text.Part 3..48.0: The commandments comprised within the fourteenth class are those which we have enumerated in the book Nashim (of Women) and in the treatises Issure Biah (of Unlawful Unions) and Kil'e Behemah (of the Mixing of Animals of Two Species); the commandment of circumcision belongs likewise unto this class. We have already previously made known the object of this class[[fn:3799]]; now, I shall set forth the details thereof.
root.text.Part 3..48.1: I say then: It is well known that friends are a thing of which man has need throughout his whole life, as Aristotle has already set forth in the ninth book of the Ethics[[fn:3800]]. In seasons of health and prosperity, he enjoys their familiarity; in seasons of adversity, they serve him as a refuge; finally, in old age, when his body waxes weak, he seeks succour at their hands. These advantages man finds in a far higher degree in his children, and likewise in his parents. Fraternity, friendship, and reciprocal devotion exist in perfection only among kinsfolk descended from the same family, so that men of the same tribe having a common ancestor, even though remote, are imbued with love, devotion, and sympathy for one another, which is one of the principal tendencies of the Law.
root.text.Part 3..48.2: Wherefore the Law has forbidden prostitution, which is the destruction of the family[[fn:3801]]; for the child that is born thereof is a stranger unto all the world, no family is known unto him, and none of his kinsfolk[[fn:3802]] knows him, which is the most grievous condition for himself and for his father. There was yet another grave reason for prohibiting intercourse with a harlot: it was to prevent men from surrendering themselves too passionately and with too much persistence to carnal love. Verily, the diversity of prostituted persons augments passion; for man is not excited by one single person to whom he is continually accustomed as he is by persons ever new, differing in countenance and in manners. Finally, there is in the prohibition of the harlot another great utility, to wit, the avoidance of mischiefs; for, if it were permitted to have intercourse with a harlot, several men might, by chance, approach the same woman at the same time, which would inevitably cause strife, and, most often, they might slay one another, or slay the woman, which, as is well known, did frequently happen: And they assemble themselves by troops in the harlot's houses (Jeremiah v. 7). It is, therefore, to avoid these great mischiefs and to obtain the general advantage (already mentioned), which is the knowledge of the family, that the Law forbidds intercourse with the harlot and with the cinaedus,
root.text.Part 3..48.3: so that for the purpose of surrendering oneself in a lawful manner to carnal love, there is no other mean than to take a wife for oneself alone and to espouse her[[fn:3803]] publicly; for, if it sufficed to dwell alone with her, man would most often take a harlot into his house for a certain time, by agreement with her, and would say that she is his wife[[fn:3804]]. Wherefore a bond[[fn:3805]] and an act have been prescribed whereby he appropriats the woman, and these are the betrothal; then a public act, which is the marriage: And he (Boaz) took ten men, etc. (Ruth iv. 2).
root.text.Part 3..48.4: As it may sometimes happen that perfect concord reigns not in their union and that their household be not well-ordered, divorce has been permitted. But, if divorce could be accomplished by a mere word, or by the dismissal of the woman from the house, she would watch for a moment when she was not observed[[fn:3806]] and would go forth, pretending that she is repudiated; or else, if a man had had intercourse with her, she and the seducer would pretend that she had been repudiated beforehand. Wherefore the Law wills that divorce be valid only by means of a writing which attests it: and he shall write her a bill of divorcement (Deut. xxiv. 1).
root.text.Part 3..48.5: As the suspicion of infidelity and the doubts which may arise in this regard are frequent concerning a wife, the Law has prescribed unto us provisions touching the woman suspected of adultery[[fn:3807]]; and this procedure had perforce for its consequence that every married woman, fearing the terror of the bitter waters, observed herself with extreme care and took good heed[[fn:3808]] not to cause grief to the heart of her husband. Verily, if the woman were pure and could entirely reassure her husband concerning herself, most men would certes have given all they possessed to redeem her from the act to which she was to be subjected[[fn:3809]], and would even have preferred death to this great ignominy—to wit, to have the head of the woman bared, her hair dishevelled, her garments rent so that her bosom be exposed, and to make her go round the sanctuary in the presence of the public, both women and men, and in the presence of the Great Tribunal[[fn:3810]]. Thus, by inspiring this dread, great misfortunes have been prevented[[fn:3811]] which might trouble the order of many a household.
root.text.Part 3..48.6: Inasmuch as the young virgin may marry whomsoever she first encounters, there has been imposed upon her seducer naught but the duty to espouse her[[fn:3812]]; for he is the one who is most suitable for her, and this marriage is better calculated to rehabilitate her[[fn:3813]] than one which another might contract with her. But if she, or her father, refuss, he (the seducer) shall nevertheless pay the mohar[[fn:3814]]. For him who is guilty of violation[[fn:3815]], an additional punishment has been added: he may not put her away all his days (Deut. xxii. 29).
root.text.Part 3..48.7: As for the motive of the levirate, it is written (in the Pentateuch) that it was an ancient custom, prior to the revelation of the Law[[fn:3816]], and which the latter allowed to subsist[[fn:3817]]. Touching the ceremony of the drawing off of the shoe[[fn:3818]], the reason thereof is that these acts (of which it consisted) were deemed ignominious according to the manners of those times, and that thereby the brother-in-law, to avoid such acts, might be induced to perform the levirate. This results clearly from the text of the Pentateuch: So shall it be done unto that man, etc., and his name shall be called in Israel, etc. (Deut. xxv. 9-10).
root.text.Part 3..48.8: By the history of Judah[[fn:3819]] one may learn to maintain a decent conduct and to observe equity in one's dealings; I refer to those words (of Judah): let her take it to her, lest we be shamed (Gen. xxxviii. 23). The explanation thereof is as follows: Before the legislation (of Moses), intercourse with a harlot was what marriage has been since that legislation[[fn:3820]]; I mean to say that it was a permitted act, for which there was absolutely no repugnance. To pay a harlot the hire upon which one had agreed was then what the payment of a woman's dowry is now in case of divorce[[fn:3821]]; that is to say, it was a right of the woman which the man was bound to pay. When, therefore, Judah says: lest we be shamed, he teaches us thereby that it is shameful for us to speak in general of matters relating to cohabitation, even though it be permitted, and that one must, on the contrary, pass it over in silence and conceal it, even should this lead to a loss of money. This is, as thou seest, what Judah did when he said: It is better that we suffer a loss and that she keep what she has received, rather than reveal our search and reap shame therefrom. Such is the decent conduct which we learn from this history. As for the lesson of equity which we may derive from it, it is when he says, to assure that he is free from all violence toward the woman, that he did not retract and did not diminish the price whereon he had agreed with her: Behold, I sent this kid, etc. (ibid.); for there is no doubt that this kid was one of the best of its kind, and for that reason he employs the demonstrative הזה, this. Such is the equity of which Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham had set them the example—namely, that one must neither change his word (once pledged), nor alter his promise; that one must pay in full what is due; that there is no difference between that which has been entrusted to thee of another's fortune, by way of loan or deposit, and what thou owest him in any manner whatsoever, by way of hire or otherwise; finally, that the dowry of every woman is as the hire of any hireling, so that he who withholds what is due to his wife is as guilty as he who withholds the hire of a hireling; for it matters little whether one cavills with the hireling and seeks pretexts to dismiss him without hire, or whether one acts thus toward his wife to dismiss her without a dowry.
root.text.Part 3..48.9: I must here point out to thee the great equity of these righteous statutes and judgments (Deut. iv. 8), in the judgment pronounced against the slanderer of his wife[[fn:3822]]. Without doubt, this wicked man loved not his wife whom he has slandered, and found her unpleasing: if, therefore, he had desired to divorce her according to the manner of all those who repudiate their wives, naught would have prevented him; but, had he divorced her[[fn:3823]], he would have been obliged to pay her what was her rightful due. He therefore brought an evil name upon her, in order to rid himself of her without payment; he calumniated and slandered her with lies, in order to withhold from her the sum which she had the right to demand of him and which is fifty shekels of silver[[fn:3824]], for that is the mohar of virgins, fixed in the Law. Wherefore God has condemned him to pay an hundred shekels of silver (ibid., xxii. 19)[[fn:3825]], according to this principle: Whom the judges shall condemn, he shall pay double unto his neighbour (Exod. xxii. 8), and in conformity with the judgment of false witnesses, as we have already set forth[[fn:3826]]. It is the same with this slanderer, who, having desired to make her lose the fifty shekels which are due to her from him[[fn:3827]], is condemned to pay an hundred. Such is his punishment for having wished to withhold the indemnity imposed upon him and having sought to seize it; but his punishment for having assailed the honour of the woman and having accused her of fornication consisted in being himself dishonoured by scourging: and they shall chastise him (Deut. xxii. 18). Finally, his punishment for having obeyed his concupiscence and having sought only pleasure alone consisted in remaining perpetually bound to her: He may not put her away all his days (ibid., v. 19); for the cause of all that occurred was that he found her unpleasing.
root.text.Part 3..48.10: Thus are evil morals healed, if they have the Divine precept for their physician; and in all the dispositions of this Law, if thou examine them well, thou shalt not cease to behold on every side a manifest and resplendent equity. Observe well how equality has been established between the judgment of the slanderer who sought to withhold the indemnity imposed upon him, and the judgment of the thief who has seized the property of another, and how the false witness, who only sought to inflict an injury but did not succeed therein, has been treated as equal to him who has done harm and exercised violence, I mean (equal to) the thief and the slanderer; all three are judged according to one law and one statute[[fn:3828]]. The wisdom of the laws of God must inspire the same astonishment as that which He has displayed in His works: the Rock, it is said, His work is perfect, for all His ways are justice (Deuter., 32, 4). This signifies: even as His works are of an extreme perfection, so His laws are of an extreme justice; but our intelligences are too weak to grasp the perfection of all that He has made and the justice of all that He has decreed; and, even as we understand certain wonders of His works, in the members of animals and the movements of the celestial spheres, so we understand the justice of a part of His laws. But that which remains hidden from us, in both respects, is far more considerable than that which is manifest unto us. — But let us return to the subject of the chapter.
root.text.Part 3..48.11: The commandments relating to unlawful unions[[fn:3829]] have all for their object to render cohabitation more infrequent, and to cause one to feel a repugnance for it, and to seek it as rarely as possible. As for the prohibition of pederasty and bestiality, the motive thereof is evident; for if it be only with repugnance and by necessity that one yields to natural union, how much more (ought one to shun) that which is outside the course of nature and which has no other end than mere voluptuousness.
root.text.Part 3..48.12: The women whom it is forbidden to wed (by reason of kinship) are all found in the same position, that is to say, that for the most part, each of them is continually with the man[[fn:3830]] in the same house; she will easily yield to his desire, will be prompt to suffer herself to be taken, and he may cause her to come into his presence without difficulty, without any judge being able to reproach the man because she is found with him. If, therefore, it were with this familiar woman as with any other unmarried woman, I mean, if it were lawful to wed her and she were only forbidden (unto that man) because she is not his wife, the greater part of men would be constantly exposed to intimate commerce with such women. But since it is absolutely forbidden to cohabit with them, since we are prevented therefrom in the most energetic manner, being threatened with the penalty of death or that of excision[[fn:3831]], and since there is no means of union with these women, it might be assured that man would not seek to approach them and that he would turn away his thoughts from them.
root.text.Part 3..48.13: As for this facility (of intercourse), it is right manifest that it exists for each of the women whom it is forbidden to wed[[fn:3832]]. Verily, it is a thing well known that as soon as a man has taken a wife, her mother, her grandmother, her daughter, her granddaughter, and her sister are for the most part near unto this husband, who encounters them continually, in coming in, in going out, and in occupying himself with his affairs; likewise, the wife has frequent relations with her husband's brother, with his father, and with his son. It is also known that man is very frequently with his sisters, with his maternal and paternal aunts, with the wife of his uncle, and that often he has been brought up with them. These are all the kindred women whom it is forbidden to wed; and if thou reflectest thereon[[fn:3833]], thou shalt find that the reason indicated (to wit, intimacy) is one of those why marriage between kindred is forbidden.
root.text.Part 3..48.14: I find a second reason in considerations of modesty; for it is only in consequence of a very great immodesty that the act in question can take place between the root and the branch[[fn:3834]], I mean the cohabitation (of a man) with his mother or with his daughter[[fn:3835]]. Wherefore mutual commerce between the root and the branch has been forbidden, and it matters little whether it be the root that wedds the branch, or whether it be the branch that wedds the root[[fn:3836]], or whether the root and the branch wed the same third person[[fn:3837]], that is to say, that the same person yields to cohabitation with the root and the branch. Therefore is it forbidden to take at once a woman and her mother, and to wed the wife of one’s father or that of one’s son; for in all these cases, one and the same person would uncover his nakedness before that of the root and the branch. Brothers and sisters are assimilated to root and branch; now, as it is forbidden to wed one's sister, it is also forbidden to wed the sister of one's wife and the wife of one's brother; for in this manner two persons, who are as root and branch, would both wed the same third person.
root.text.Part 3..48.15: As the union between brothers and sisters is severely forbidden, and as they have been likened unto stock and branch—or rather, the brother and the sister[[fn:3838]] being as one soul—there was likewise forbidden the marrying of one's maternal aunt, who is in the stead of the mother, and one's paternal aunt, who is in the stead of the father. But, even as it has not been forbidden to marry the daughter of one's uncle or aunt, so, by analogy, it has not been forbidden to marry the daughter of one's brother, or the daughter of one's sister. If it be permitted for the uncle to marry the wife of his nephew, whilst it is forbidden for the nephew to marry the wife of his uncle, this is explained according to the first reason. Indeed, the nephew is frequently found in the house of his uncle, and he forms a bond with the wife of his uncle, even as he bonds with the wife of his brother; but the uncle is not so frequently found in the house of his nephew and has no such intimacy with the wife of the latter. Seest thou not that, the father being bonded with the wife of his son, even as is the son with the wife of the father, both marriages are equally forbidden[[fn:3839]] and punished with the same death[[fn:3840]]?
root.text.Part 3..48.16: As for the prohibition of having commerce with a woman during her courses or with a married woman, the reason thereof is too manifest for one to have need to seek it out.
root.text.Part 3..48.17: Thou knowest also that it is forbidden unto us to enjoy, in any manner whatsoever, a woman whom the Law interdicts unto us, were it even to look upon her with a view to pleasure, as we have set forth in the treatise Issuré Biâ (of illicit unions)[[fn:3841]]. Therein have we said that our Law in no wise permitts us to occupy our thoughts with carnal love[[fn:3842]], nor to excite concupiscence in any manner, and that man, if he feels himself excited against his will, must occupy his mind with other thoughts and reflect upon other matters, until this excitation shall have passed away. Behold what the Doctors say in their sentences, which serve to perfect even virtuous men: «If this hideous thing[[fn:3843]] encounters thee, drag it to the house of study; if it be of iron, it shall melt, and if it be of stone, it shall be shattered, as it is said: Is not my word like as fire? says the Lord, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces (Jeremiah, xxiii, 29)[[fn:3844]]?» The Doctor here gives unto his son this rule of conduct: If thou feelest thyself excited to concupiscence and if thou sufferest therefrom, go to the house of study, devote thyself to study and to reading, question and allow thyself to be questioned, and this suffering shall undoubtedly vanish. The expression this hideous thing is remarkable, and in truth, there is naught more hideous. This morality is not only prescribed by religion, but is also recommended by the philosophers. I have already quoted unto thee textually the words of Aristotle[[fn:3845]], who says: «this sense which is a shame unto us», meaning the sense of touch which invits us to seek after good cheer and carnal love. In his writings, he calls those people abject who give themselves up to carnal love and to good cheer, and he lavishes upon them blame and mockery, as thou shalt find in his treatise on Ethics and in that on Rhetoric[[fn:3846]].
root.text.Part 3..48.18: It is in view of this virtuous conduct, which we must propose unto ourselves as the goal of all our efforts, that the Doctors have forbidden us to look upon «the quadrupeds and the birds at the moment of their coupling[[fn:3847]].» According to my view, this is also the reason why it is forbidden to couple animals of different species[[fn:3848]]; for it is known that ordinarily an individual of one species is not inclined to couple with one of another species, unless it be driven thereto by force, as one ses continually practised by those abject men who desire to obtain the birth of mules. The Law therefore willed not that the Israelite should descend to such a practice, which reveals so much abjection and impudence, and that he should occupy himself[[fn:3849]] with things of which religion abhorrs the simple mention, and a fortiori the execution, unless it be by necessity; but there is no necessity to effect this coupling. It seems also to me that the prohibition of yoking together two species for any labor whatsoever has for its motive to distance us from the coupling of two species; if therefore it be said: thou shalt not plow with an ox and an ass together (Deut. xxii, 10), it is because, being joined together, they might sometimes couple one with another. The proof thereof is that this provision embraces also animals other than the ox and the ass: «Whether it be an ox and an ass, or other animals of two species; but the Scripture speaks of what is habitual[[fn:3850]].»
root.text.Part 3..48.19: I believe likewise that one of the motives for circumcision is to diminish cohabitation and to weaken the (sexual) organ, in order to restrain its action and to leave it at rest as much as possible[[fn:3851]]. It has been claimed that circumcision had for its purpose to complete what nature had left imperfect[[fn:3852]], which has given occasion to criticize (this precept); for, it was said, how could the things of nature be imperfect, so as to stand in need of a completion coming from without, the more so since it is known how useful the prepuce is to the member in question? But this precept has in no wise for its goal to supply a physical imperfection; on the contrary, it concerns only the remedying of a moral imperfection. The true goal is the bodily pain to be inflicted upon this member, which in no way derangs the functions necessary for the preservation of the individual, nor destroys procreation, but which diminishes passion[[fn:3853]] and excessive concupiscence[[fn:3854]]. That circumcision weakens concupiscence and sometimes diminishes voluptuousness is a thing of which one cannot doubt; for if, from birth, one causs this member to bleed by removing its covering, it shall undoubtedly be weakened. The Doctors have expressly said: «The woman who has given herself to love with an uncircumcised man finds it difficult to separate from him[[fn:3855]];» this is, according to me, the most important motive for circumcision. And who then first practised this act? Was it not Abraham, so renowned for his chastity? as the Doctors say concerning this passage: Behold now, I know that thou art a fair woman to look upon (Genesis xii, 11)[[fn:3856]].
root.text.Part 3..48.20: Circumcision has, in my judgment, another motive of great moment: it causs those who profess the idea of the Unity of God to be distinguished by a common bodily sign impressed upon them all, so that he who pertains not thereto, being a stranger, may not claim to belong to them[[fn:3857]]; for there might be men who would so act with the intent of deriving profit therefrom, or of deceiving those who profess this religion (of Unity). This act[[fn:3858]], no man would perform upon himself or upon his son, save by reason of a sincere conviction; for it is no mere incision in the leg, nor a cautery upon the arm, but a matter exceeding hard. It is known likewise how much men love and succour one another when they bear the same distinctive mark, which serves them as a species of covenant and pact; and in like manner, circumcision is a covenant concluded by Abraham our father for the belief in the Unity of God, so that all they who are circumcised alone enter into the covenant of Abraham. By this covenant, one is pledged[[fn:3859]] to believe in the Unity: to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee (Genesis, xvii. 7). This is yet another important motive which may be assigned for circumcision, and it is perchance of greater weight than the former.
root.text.Part 3..48.21: Religion cannot be truly accomplished, nor perpetuated, unless circumcision take place during the years of infancy; and for this there are three reasons[[fn:3860]]: 1. If the child were permitted to grow up, it might be that he would not perform it (circumcision). 2. He suffers not so much as a grown person would suffer, seeing that his membrane is tender and his imagination yet weak; for a grown person finds that thing terrible and cruel, before it occurrs, which his imagination figurs to him beforehand. 3. Parents have not yet a great affection for the child at the moment of its birth; for the imaginative form[[fn:3861]] which produces in parents the love for the child has not yet become consolidated within them. Verily, this imaginative form augments by habitual contact[[fn:3862]] and increass as the child grows, and it is only later that it beginns to decline and to fade away. Wherefore the father and the mother feel not for the new-born babe that love which they feel for a child of one year, nor do they love the child of one year as much as that of six years. If, therefore, the child were left for two or three years (without being circumcised), the consequence would be the neglect of circumcision, by reason of the affection and love which would be felt for the child. But at the time of its birth, this imaginative form is very weak, especially in the father, unto whom this commandment is enjoined[[fn:3863]]. The reason why circumcision takes place on the eighth day is that every animal, at the moment of its birth, is very weak and exceeding tender, as though it were still in its mother's womb; only after seven days is it numbered among those beings which are in contact with the air. Seest thou not that for quadrupeds also regard was had to this circumstance? Seven days it shall be with its dam, etc. (Exodus, xxii. 30). Before this term, it is considered as an abortion, and likewise man may not be circumcised until after the term of seven days. In this manner also the matter remains fixed, and "thou dost not make of it something variable[[fn:3864]]."
root.text.Part 3..48.22: That which also enters into this class is the prohibition against mutilating the organs of generation of any male among animals[[fn:3865]], a prohibition which is linked to this principle of righteous statutes and judgments (Deut. iv. 8)[[fn:3866]], that is to say, of the golden mean in all things; one must not indulge overmuch in physical love, as we have said, but neither must it be utterly annihilated. Has not God pronounced this command: Be fruitful and multiply (Genesis, i. 22)? This organ must therefore be weakened by circumcision, but not entirely uprooted; on the contrary, that which is natural must be left in its nature, yet one must guard against excesses. It is forbidden for the castrated and the eunuch to marry an Israelite woman[[fn:3867]]; for it would be a cohabitation lost and without purpose, and such a marriage would also become a stumbling-block for the woman and for him who seeks her[[fn:3868]], which is right manifest.
root.text.Part 3..48.23: To remove us from illicit unions, it is forbidden for the bastard to marry the daughter of an Israelite[[fn:3869]]. It was intended that the adulterous man and woman should well know that, by committing this act, they impress beforehand upon their children a stain forever irreparable[[fn:3870]]. Bastards being held in contempt according to the custom of all nations[[fn:3871]], the race of Israel has been judged too noble to unite with them. — Unto the priests it is forbidden, by reason of their nobility, to marry a harlot, a divorced woman, or a woman born of such a marriage[[fn:3872]]; unto the high priest, who is the noblest among the priests, it is forbidden even to marry a widow, or a woman who should not be a virgin[[fn:3873]]. The reason for all this is evident. — If it be forbidden to admit bastards into the congregation of the Lord (Deut. xxiii. 2), with much more reason, male and female slaves[[fn:3874]]. As for the prohibition against alliance with the Gentiles, it is motivated in the text of the Pentateuch: Lest... thou take of their daughters unto thy sons, etc. (Exodus, xxxiv. 16).
root.text.Part 3..48.24: The majority of the statutes (or ordinances)[[fn:3875]], the reason of which is unknown to us, have no other end than to remove us from idolatry. If for certain details the motives be unknown to me, and if I know not their utility, the reason is that it is not with things known only by tradition as it is with those which have been seen[[fn:3876]]. Therefore the little that I know of the opinions of the Sabians, having drawn it from books, cannot be compared to that which was known by those who knew their acts from having seen them, especially now that these opinions have vanished for two thousand years or more. If we knew all the particulars of these acts, and if we had heard all the details of these opinions, we should understand all the wisdom contained in the details of the practices relating to sacrifices, to impurities, etc., the reason of which does not appear easy to me (to comprehend)[[fn:3877]]. For my part, I doubt not but that all this had for its end the effacing from our minds of these false ideas and the cessation of these useless practices, which caused the time of life to be lost in vain and idle occupations. These ideas did but hinder the human mind from seeking the conceptions of the intellect, or useful actions, as our prophets have expounded to us, saying: They have followed after vain things, which cannot profit[[fn:3878]]; Jeremiah says: Our fathers have inherited nought but lies, vanity, and things in which there is no profit (Jeremiah, xvi. 19). Thou wilt understand how pernicious all this is, and whether it was not a thing that had to be brought to an end at any cost[[fn:3879]]. Thus, then, the majority of the commandments, as we have expounded, have no other end than to cause these opinions to cease, and to lighten the great and grievous burdens, the fatigues and the pains which those men imposed upon themselves for the celebration of worship[[fn:3880]]. Consequently, every precept of the Law, whether affirmative or negative, the reason of which thou art ignorant of, has no other end than to heal one of those maladies which, thanks be to God, we no longer know this day. This is what every perfect man must believe, who understands the true sense of this divine word: I said not unto the seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain (Isaiah, xlv. 19).
root.text.Part 3..48.25: Now, we have traversed, one by one, all the commandments comprised within these several classes[[fn:3881]], and we have indicated the reasons thereof. There remain but a few[[fn:3882]] for which I have not been able to assign a motive, as well as certain unimportant particulars; but in truth, we have virtually given the reason for them in a manner that lies within the reach of every studious and intelligent man[[fn:3883]].
root.text.Part 3..49.0: There are yet other matters which belong to the mysteries of the Law, and which, having perplexed many persons, stand in need of explanation. These are certain narratives related in the Pentateuch, in which no utility is apparent, such as, for instance, when there are enumerated the peoples descended from Noah, their names and the places of their habitations (Genesis, ch. X), the Horites, descendants of Seir, as also the kings that reigned in the land of Edom (Ibid., 36, 20, 31 et seq.), and other like accounts. The Doctors say, as thou knowest, that the impious Manasseh did naught but continually occupy[[fn:3884]] his ignoble council with the criticism of these passages: “He sat there,” say they, “interpreting the Haggadôth[[fn:3885]] in a mocking spirit; he would say, for example: Had Moses need to write, ‘And Lotan's sister was Timna’ (Ibid., v. 22)?” I shall first make known unto thee a general principle, and thereafter I shall return to the details, even as I did in assigning motives for the commandments.
root.text.Part 3..49.1: Know that, whenever thou findest in the Pentateuch any narrative whatsoever, it has of necessity a certain utility for religion, whether it confirms one of the fundamental ideas of religion, or whether it teaches us a certain rule of conduct, so that there be among men neither mutual violence nor injustice. I shall now pass through the different cases[[fn:3886]].
root.text.Part 3..49.2: Since it is a fundamental belief of religion that the world was created, that in the beginning there was created but a single individual of the human species, who is Adam, and that the ancient times from Adam until Moses our Master comprised but a space of about two thousand five hundred years, these facts, set forth in a plain and simple manner, would have been promptly called into doubt; for even then men were found scattered to all the ends of the earth, forming diverse nations, speaking diverse tongues, widely remote from one another. These doubts were therefore silenced by indicating the genealogy and extraction of them all, mentioning the names of the best known among them, “such an one, the son of such an one,” as also their ages, and making known the place of their habitation, as well as the reason why they were scattered to the ends of the earth and why their languages were so different, although they were all originally in the same place and spoke the same tongue, as it behooved them to do, seeing they were the children of a single individual. Likewise, the recital of the history of the Deluge and of that of Sodom and Gomorrah was intended to show the truth of this idea: Verily there is a reward for the righteous: verily he is a God that judges in the earth (Ps. lviii. 11).
root.text.Part 3..49.3: Likewise, the description of the war of the nine kings has for its object to make known that miracle, namely, the victory achieved by Abraham, with a small number of men having no king with them, over four powerful kings[[fn:3887]]. We are also informed how he defended[[fn:3888]] his kinsman (Lot), who held the same belief as he, and how he braved the perils of war to rescue him. Finally, we are shown how reserved[[fn:3889]] he was, moderating his desires, despising gain, and applying himself to noble conduct, as it is said: That I will not take from a thread even to a shoelatchet, etc. (Genesis xiv. 23).
root.text.Part 3..49.4: If the tribes of the Seirites be all enumerated, and their particular genealogy[[fn:3890]] set forth, it is solely by reason of one commandment: for God specifically ordained the extermination of the seed of Amalek. Now, Amalek was none other than the son of Eliphaz, whom he had by Timna, the sister of Lotan[[fn:3891]]. But God had not commanded the slaying of the other sons of Esau; and whereas Esau had allied himself with the Seirites, as the Scripture plainly says[[fn:3892]], he had children by that race. He reigned over them, and his progeny became mingled with theirs; whence it followed that the whole land of Seir, with its tribes, was attributed to the preponderant tribe, which was that of the descendants of Esau, and especially that of Amalek, the most noble amongst them. Had not all these families been designated in detail, they might perchance have been slain through error. Therefore does the Scripture expressly designate their tribes, as if to say: those whom ye behold this day in the land of Seir and in the kingdom of Amalek are not all the descendants of Amalek, but the descendants of such and such an one; and if they be traced back to Amalek, it is because his mother belonged to their race[[fn:3893]]. All this betokens the divine justice, which willed not that one tribe should be slain indiscriminately[[fn:3894]] with another; for the divine decree struck only the race of Amalek in particular. We have already set forth what wisdom there was in this measure[[fn:3895]].
root.text.Part 3..49.5: The reason wherefore are enumerated the kings that reigned in the land of Edom (Genesis, 36, 31), is that there is a commandment which says: Thou mayest not set a stranger over thee, which is not thy brother (Deuteron., 17, 15). Now, among the kings mentioned, there was not a single one who was a native of Edom[[fn:3896]]; seest thou not that their family is indicated as well as their country—such an one, from such a place; another, from another place? It appears to me right probable that their acts and their history were generally known—I mean the acts of these kings of Edom—and that they tyrannized over and humbled[[fn:3897]] the descendants of Esau; for which cause they are recalled[[fn:3898]] to the memory of the Israelites. It is as though it were said: «Take ye warning from your brethren, the descendants of Esau, who had for their king such or such an one [whose acts were then well known]; for never has a man of a strange race reigned over a nation without exercising over it a tyranny more or less grievous.»
root.text.Part 3..49.6: In sum, that which I have told thee concerning the interval which now separats us from the religious practices of the Sabeans[[fn:3899]] may also be applied to the history of those times which is now unknown to us; for, if we knew it, and if the events which then occurred were manifest to us, we should understand, in respect of many details, the ground which caused them to be mentioned in the Pentateuch.
root.text.Part 3..49.7: It must further be well understood that written narratives are not regarded in the same light as the events of which one is a witness; for in the latter, there are certain details having necessary consequences which cannot be related without prolixity[[fn:3900]]. Wherefore, in reading these narratives, the reader finds therein prolixity or repetitions; but had he been a witness of that which is related, he would understand that what has been said is necessary. Whenever, therefore, thou seest narratives in the non-legislative portion of the Pentateuch, it seems to thee at times that such or such a narrative had no need to be written, or that it contains either tedious lengths or repetitions[[fn:3901]]; the reason thereof is that thou hast not been a witness of the details which led the author to frame his narrative as he has done.
root.text.Part 3..49.8: Of this category is the enumeration of the stations[[fn:3902]]. It might appear at first sight that a thing altogether useless had been related; it is therefore by reason of this false notion which might be held that it is said: And Moses wrote their goings out according to their journeys by the commandment of the Lord (Numbers, 33, 2). And this was of a very great necessity; for all miracles are certain to him who has seen them, but for posterity, the account thereof becoms a mere tradition, and for him who hears it, it is easy to deny it[[fn:3903]]. It is known to be impossible and unimaginable that a miracle should be certified and attested by all men in the course of ages. Now, one of the miracles related in the Pentateuch, and even one of the greatest, is the sojourn of forty years which the Israelites made in the desert, where they found manna every day. In that desert, as the Pentateuch says, there were fiery serpents, and scorpions, and drought, where there was no water (Deuter., 8, 15). These were places very remote from a cultivated land and which were not suited to the nature of man: no place of seed, or of figs, or of vines, or of pomegranates, etc. (Numbers, 20, 5); these places are also called a land that no man passed through (Jeremiah, 2, 6); and the text of the Pentateuch says: Ye have not eaten bread, neither have ye drunk wine or strong drink (Deuter., 29, 5). All these miracles were manifest and visible. Now, God knew that in the future, it would befall these miracles as it befalls traditions, and that it would be thought they sojourned in a desert nigh unto inhabited places, where man can abide, and similar to those deserts which the Arabs inhabit this day, or that they were places where one might plow and reap, or sustain oneself by some plants found therein, or that it was in the nature of the manna to fall continually in those places[[fn:3904]], or that there were in those places cisterns with water.
