Wherefore, to remove all such doubts, the account of all these miracles has been confirmed by the enumeration of these stations, so that future generations might see them and recognize the magnitude of the miracle by which the human species was able to sojourn in those places for forty years.
root.text.Part 3..49.9: It is for the same reason that Joshua pronounced a perpetual anathema against whosoever should rebuild Jericho[[fn:3905]], to the end that the miracle might be certified and established; for whosoever should behold those walls sunken into the earth would perceive that it was not the wall of a demolished edifice, but that it had been engulfed by a miracle.
root.text.Part 3..49.10: Likewise, when it is said: at the commandment of the Lord they encamped, and at the commandment of the Lord they journeyed (Numbers ix. 20), this might have sufficed for the narrative; and it might appear at first sight that all which is subsequently related upon the same subject is but an unnecessary prolixity, as, for example, the words: And so it was, when the cloud abode from even unto the morning, etc. (v. 19), and so it was, when the cloud abode, etc. (v. 21), or whether it were two days, etc. (v. 22). I shall now impart unto thee that which has occasioned all these details: the reason thereof is that the Scripture desired to insist upon this account, in order to destroy the notion then held by foreign nations, and which they hold even unto this day, to wit, that the Israelites were lost upon the way and knew not whither they should go, as it is said: They are entangled in the land (Exodus xiv. 3). Even thus the Arabs unto this day call that desert Al-Tîh, and imagine that the Israelites were wandering astray (tâhou)[[fn:3906]] and were ignorant of the path. The Scripture, therefore, setts forth with emphasis that these irregular stations, the return to several among them, and the diverse duration of the stay in each—in such wise that they remained in one station eighteen years[[fn:3907]], in another a day, and in yet another but a single night[[fn:3908]]—that all this (I say) was decreed by God and was not a mere wandering upon the road, but depended upon the lifting of the pillar of cloud. For this cause are all these details given, after having declared, in the Pentateuch, that this interval of the way was short, well known, much frequented, and by no means unknown; I speak of the interval between Horeb [whither they had repaired with intent, according to that which God had commanded them: ye shall serve God upon this mountain (Exodus iii. 12)] and Kadesh-barnea, where the inhabited land beginns, as the Scripture says: Behold, we are in Kadesh, a city in the uttermost of thy border (Numbers xx. 16). This interval is traversed in eleven days, as it is said: There are eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of mount Seir, unto Kadesh-barnea (Deut. i. 2); it is not, therefore, a path in which one might wander for forty years, and this must be attributed solely to the causes expressly written in the Pentateuch.
root.text.Part 3..49.11: Thus it is that whenever thou art ignorant of the reason why any history whatsoever has been related (in the Pentateuch), there was for it a grave motive, and to all such cases may further be applied that principle which the Doctors have brought to our notice: «For it is not a vain thing for you (Deut. xxxii. 47); and if it be vain, it is because of you[[fn:3909]].»
root.text.Part 3..50.0: The chapter which we are now about to set forth adds no new subject to those contained in the other chapters of this treatise. It is, as it were, a conclusion, setting forth the worship to which he must devote himself who understands the true duties to be practiced toward God[[fn:3910]], after having rightly comprehended His true being; it is intended to guide man to that worship which is the true end of man, and to make him know how Providence watches over him in this world until the moment when he passes into life eternal[[fn:3911]].
root.text.Part 3..50.1: I commence my discourse, in this chapter, by presenting unto thee the following parable: The sovereign was in his palace, and his subjects were partly within the city and partly without. Of those who were in the city, some turned their backs upon the habitation of the sovereign and journeyed in another direction; others turned toward the habitation of the sovereign and directed their steps toward him, seeking to enter his dwelling and to present themselves before him, but hitherto they had not yet perceived the wall of the palace. Of those who were repairing thither, some, having reached the palace, went round about it seeking the entrance; others had entered and were walking in the vestibules; others, finally, had succeeded in entering the inner court of the palace and had arrived at the place where the king was, that is to say, at the sovereign's own habitation. These, however, although they had arrived in this habitation, could neither see the sovereign nor speak with him; but, after having penetrated into the interior of the dwelling, they had yet to perform other indispensable steps, and then only could they present themselves before the sovereign, see him from afar or from near, hear his word, or speak unto him. — I shall now explain unto thee this parable which I have devised:
root.text.Part 3..50.2: As for "those who were outside the city," these comprise all such men as possess no religious belief, neither speculative nor traditional, such as the furthest of the Turks in the extreme north[[fn:3912]], the Negroes in the extreme south, and those who resemble them in our climates. These are to be accounted as irrational animals; I place them not in the rank of men, for they occupy among beings a rank inferior to that of man and superior to that of the ape, since they possess the figure and lineaments of man and a discernment above that of the ape.
root.text.Part 3..50.3: "Those who were within the city, but turned their backs upon the habitation of the sovereign," are men who hold an opinion[[fn:3913]] and who think, but who have conceived ideas contrary to the truth, whether in consequence of some grave error that has befallen them in their speculation, or because they have followed those who were in error. These, by reason of their opinions, the more they walk, the further they recede from the habitation of the sovereign; they are far worse than the first, and there arrive moments when it even becoms necessary to slay them and to efface the traces of their opinions, lest they lead others astray.
root.text.Part 3..50.4: — "Those who turned towards the habitation of the sovereign and sought to enter therein, but who had not yet beheld the habitation of the sovereign," are the multitude of religious men, that is to say, the ignorant who occupy themselves with religious observances.
root.text.Part 3..50.5: — "Those who had arrived at the palace and went round about it," are the casuists[[fn:3914]] who admit, by tradition, true opinions, and who discourse upon the practices of worship, but who engage not in speculation concerning the fundamental principles of religion, nor seek in any wise to establish the truth of any belief whatsoever.
root.text.Part 3..50.6: — As for those who plunge into speculation on the fundamental principles of religion, they are 'those who had entered the vestibules', where men are undoubtedly admitted to varying degrees.
root.text.Part 3..50.7: They who have comprehended the demonstration of all that is demonstrable, who have attained unto certainty in metaphysical matters, wheresoever this be possible, or who have approached unto certainty where one can but approach it, these are they "who have arrived within the interior of the palace, in the presence of the Sovereign."
root.text.Part 3..50.8: Know, my son, that so long as thou occupiest thyself but with mathematical sciences and with logic, thou art of those who go round about the palace (of the Sovereign) and seek the entrance thereof, even as the Doctors say allegorically: «Ben-Zôma is still without[[fn:3915]]»; after having understood the objects of physics, thou hast entered the palace and walkest in its vestibules[[fn:3916]]; finally, after having completed the physical sciences and studied metaphysics, thou hast entered into the presence of the Sovereign, into the inner court, and thou findest thyself with Him in the same apartment. This latter degree is that of the (true) sages, but even here there are (to be distinguished) different degrees of perfection. They who, after having perfected themselves in metaphysics, occupy their thought with God alone, devoting themselves entirely unto Him, and withdrawing from all that is without Him, and who make the whole action of their intelligence to consist in reflecting upon the (created) beings, in order to draw from these latter the proof of the existence of God and to know in what manner He may govern them, these (I say) are found in the hall where the Sovereign sitts; such is the degree of the prophets. There was one whose perception was so powerful and who knew so well how to isolate himself from all that is without God, that it could be said of him: And he remained there with God (Exodus, 34, 28), questioning, receiving answers, speaking and receiving the word (of God), in that holy abode. By reason of his great contentment in that which he perceived, he did neither eat bread nor drink water (ibid.); for the intelligence so far prevailed, that it annihilated every material faculty in the body, I mean the various faculties of the sense of touch. There have been other prophets who beheld only, some from near at hand, others from afar, as it is said: From afar the Lord appeared unto me (Jeremiah, 31, 3). Having already spoken previously of the degrees of prophecy[[fn:3917]],
root.text.Part 3..50.9.sub_0: we return to the purpose of this chapter, the object of which is to encourage man to occupy his thought with God alone, after he has learned to know Him, as we have set forth. This is the true worship which befitts those who have perceived the transcendent truths; the more they meditate upon God and abide with Him, the more does He become the object of their worship. As for those who meditate upon God and who speak much of Him without possessing science, but rather attaching themselves to a mere being of their imagination, or to a belief which they have received by tradition, these, I say, finding themselves[[fn:3918]] without the palace and far removed from it, do not really think of God nor meditate upon Him. Verily, that being who exists only in their imagination and of whom their mouth speaks responds to naught that is real and is but an invention of their fancy, as we have set forth when speaking of the attributes[[fn:3919]]. One must not give oneself unto this species of worship save after having conceived (the idea of God) by means of the intellect; it is only after having understood God and His works, as far as the intelligence requirs[[fn:3920]], that thou canst entirely consecrate thyself unto Him, seek to draw nigh unto Him and strengthen the bond which exists between thee and Him, to wit, the intellect[[fn:3921]], even as it is said: Unto thee it was shewn to know that the Lord, etc. (Deuter., 4, 35); know therefore this day and consider it in thine heart, etc. (ibid., v. 39); know ye that the Lord He is God (Ps. 100, 3). Already the Pentateuch setts forth that this supreme worship, whereon we call attention in this chapter, can only take place following upon perception: To love the Lord your God, it is said, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul (Deuter., 11, 13). We have already set forth several times[[fn:3922]] that love (of God) is in proportion to perception; it is only following upon love that there can come this worship whereon the Doctors also have called attention, saying: «c’est le culte du cœur[[fn:3923]].» This consists, in my view, in applying the thought to the principal object of the intellect[[fn:3924]] and in devoting oneself unto Him as much as one is able.
root.text.Part 3..50.9.sub_1: Wherefore thou findest (in Scripture) that David, in dictating to Solomon his last wishes, recommends unto him especially these two things, namely, to strive to arrive at the knowledge of God and then to render unto Him a worship (worthy of that knowledge): And thou, says he, my son Solomon, know thou the God of thy father, and serve him, etc. If thou seek him, he will be found of thee, etc. (I Chron., 28, 9). This whole exhortation can have for its object naught but intelligible conceptions, and not the creations of the imagination; for thoughts relating to things of the imagination are not called דעה, knowledge, but are called העולה על רוחכם, that which comes into your mind (Ezekiel, XX, 32). It is therefore clear that after having acquired the knowledge of God, one must aim at devoting oneself unto Him and constantly occupy the thought and the intelligence[[fn:3925]] with the love which is His due. This is attained, for the most part, only through solitude and isolation; wherefore every superior man seeks often to isolate himself and joins with no one, save in case of necessity[[fn:3926]].
root.text.Part 3..50.10: [ANNOTATION. We have already set forth unto thee that this intellect which flows down upon us from God is the bond which exists between us and Him[[fn:3927]]. It depends upon thee, either to strengthen and consolidate this bond, or to weaken and relax it little by little, until it be undone[[fn:3928]]. This bond can only be strengthened when one makes use of it to love God and to draw nigh unto Him, as we have set forth; it is weakened and relaxed when thou occupiest thy thought with that which is without Him. Know thou that, even though thou wert the man most learned in true metaphysics, if thou turnest thy thought from God and occupiest thyself entirely[[fn:3929]] with thy food or other necessary affairs, thou hast severed this bond which exists between thee and God, and thou art no longer with Him, even as He is no longer with thee; for this relation which existed between thee and Him has ceased in fact in those moments. Wherefore superior men employed but rare moments in occupying themselves with other things than Him[[fn:3930]], from which they wished to preserve us by this warning: «Turn ye not unto that which comes of your own thought[[fn:3931]].» David said: I have set the Lord always before me, because He is at my right hand, I shall not be moved (Ps., 16, 8); that is to say: I never turn my thought from God, and He is as my right hand which I forget not for a moment by reason of the swiftness of its movements; wherefore I shall not be moved, that is to say, I shall not fall.
root.text.Part 3..50.11: — Ye must know that all the ceremonies of worship, such as the reading of the Law, prayer, and the practice of other commandments, have no other end than to train thee to occupy thyself with the commandments of God instead of occupying thyself with worldly matters, and, so to speak, to occupy thyself with God alone and none other. But, if thou prayest by moving thy lips and turning thy face toward the wall, whilst thou art thinking of what thou hast to sell or to buy, or if thou readest the Law with thy tongue, whilst thy heart is occupied with the building of thy house, without reflecting upon what thou readest; in fine, if thou performest any commandment whatsoever with thy limbs, like one who diggs a pit in the earth or who cutts wood in the forest, without reflecting either upon the meaning of this practice, nor upon Him who has ordained it, nor upon that which it has for its end, then thou must not believe that thou hast attained any end whatsoever; on the contrary, thou then drawest nigh unto those of whom it has been said: Thou art near in their mouth, and far from their reins (Jeremiah, xii, 2).
root.text.Part 3..50.12: Now, I shall indicate unto thee the manner of training thyself to arrive at this important end:
root.text.Part 3..50.13: The first thing to which thou must attach thyself is to keep thy mind free from all other things at the moment when thou devotest thyself to the reading of the Schemâ’ and to prayer, and that thou contentest not thyself with reciting with attention the first verse of the Schemâ’ and the first benediction of the prayer[[fn:3932]]. When thou shalt have succeeded therein and shalt have made it a habit for years, thou must endeavour, every time thou readest in the Pentateuch or hearest it read, to apply thy whole thought unceasingly to reflect upon that which thou shalt hear or that which thou shalt read. When thou shalt have likewise made this a habit, thou shalt endeavour to have thy mind always free in all that thou readest of the other discourses of the prophets and even in all the benedictions, and to apply thyself to reflect upon all that thou shalt pronounce and to understand the meaning thereof. When thou shalt have performed these religious acts and thy thought, at the moment of practicing them, shall have remained pure from all preoccupation with worldly things, then only shalt thou be able to begin to occupy thyself with the necessary things or the superfluities of life. In general, thou shouldst not apply thy thought to worldly things[[fn:3933]] save at the moment of eating and drinking, or when thou art in the bath, or when thou conversest with thy wife or thy young children, or when thou speakest with any man whomsoever. Thus, I leave thee sufficient and ample time to think of all that is necessary for thee in matters of business, of domestic economy, and of bodily needs; but, in the moments when thou occupiest thyself with religious things, thy thought must be entirely upon that which thou doest, even as we have set forth.
root.text.Part 3..50.14: When thou art quite alone, or when thou art awake in thy bed, beware well, in those precious moments, of thinking of anything else than of this intellectual worship which consists in drawing nigh unto God and in presenting thyself before Him in the true manner which I have made known unto thee, and not by the fantastic action of the imagination[[fn:3934]]. At this stage may arrive, according to my view, every man of science who has prepared himself therefor by this kind of exercise (of which we have spoken).
root.text.Part 3..50.15.sub_0: If a human individual could succeed in perceiving the high truths and in enjoying that which he has perceived, to such a degree as to be able to converse with men and to occupy himself with his bodily needs, whilst his whole intelligence were turned toward God and that, in his heart, he were always in the presence of God, albeit being externally with men,—much as it is said in the poetical allegories composed upon these subjects: I sleep, but my heart waks; it is the voice of my beloved that knocks, etc. (Canticles, V, 2),—that would be a degree (of perfection) which I would not attribute even to all the prophets, and I would rather say that it is the degree of Moses our master, of whom it is said: Moses alone shall come near the Eternal, but they shall not come near (Exodus, 24, 2), and he was there with God (ibid., XXXIV, 28); and to whom it was said: But as for thee, stand thou here by Me (Deuter., 5, 28), according to the sense that we have attributed to these verses[[fn:3935]]. This is also the degree attained by the patriarchs, who were to such a degree near unto God, that it was from them that was derived the denomination by which He was known in the world[[fn:3936]]: The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; ... this is my name for ever (Exodus, 3, 15). Their intelligence having perceived God even unto uniting with Him, it resulted therefrom that He concluded with each of them a perpetual covenant: Then will I remember my covenant with Jacob, etc. (Leviticus, XXVI, 42). Indeed, the sacred texts attest clearly that these four, I mean the patriarchs and Moses our master, were united with God, that is to say, they perceived Him and loved Him; likewise, Divine Providence watched with care over them and over their posterity after them. Notwithstanding this, they occupied themselves sometimes with the government of men, with the increase of their fortune, and with the seeking of possessions; and this proves, in my opinion, that while busying themselves with their affairs, they were occupied therewith only with their body, whilst their intelligence was unceasingly with God.
root.text.Part 3..50.20: The philosophers have likewise set forth that, in youth, the corporeal forces constitute an obstacle to the majority of moral virtues[[fn:3949]], and a fortiori to that pure meditation resulting from the perfection of ideas which leads man to love God passionately. It is impossible that this meditation should arise whilst the ebullition of the bodily humours persists; but in proportion as the forces of the body weaken and the fire of desire is quenched, the intellect is strengthened, its light increass, its comprehension gains in clarity, and it experiencs a greater delight in that which it has apprehended; so that, in the man bowed down under the weight of years and drawing nigh unto death, this comprehension receivs a vast increase, yields an exceeding great joy, and inspirs a true passion for Him who is its object, until at length, in the midst of this delight, the soul is sundered from the body.
root.text.Part 3..50.21: It is unto this state that the doctors have alluded when speaking of the death of Moses, of Aaron, and of Miriam, and saying that all three died by a kiss. This passage, say they, And Moses, the servant of the Eternal, died there in the land of Moab by the mouth (the command) of the Eternal (Deut. xxxiv. 5), teaches us that Moses died by a kiss; in like manner it is said of Aaron: … by the mouth (the command) of the Eternal, and he died there (Numbers, xxxiii. 38); likewise they say of Miriam that she also died by a kiss, but concerning her, it is not said: by the mouth of the Eternal, because she was a woman, and it was not seemly to employ, regarding her, this allegory[[fn:3950]]. They intend thereby that all three died in the delight which this comprehension caused them to experience and by the violence of love. The doctors have employed in this passage the well-known allegorical method, according to which this comprehension, resulting from the violent love which man feels for God, is called a kiss, as it is said: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, etc. (Song of Sol., i. 2). This manner of death, say they, whereby man escaps true death, befell none but Moses, Aaron, and Miriam; the other prophets and pious men are below this degree. But in all, the comprehension of the intellect is strengthened at the moment of parting (from the body), as it is said: Thy righteousness shall go before thee, and the glory of the Eternal shall follow thee (Isaiah, lviii. 8). After this, the intellect remains for evermore in the same state; for the obstacle which sometimes hid (its object)[[fn:3951]] has been removed; it then continually tasts this great delight, which is of a nature quite other than the delights of the body, as we have set forth in our works and as others have set forth before us.
root.text.Part 3..50.22: Apply thyself to understand this chapter, and exert thy whole endeavour to multiply the moments in which thou mayest be with God, or seek to rise towards Him, and to diminish the moments in which thou art occupied with other things, without seeking to reach Him. These counsels[[fn:3952]] suffice for the purpose I had in this treatise.
root.text.Part 3..51.0: A man alone in his house sitts, movs, and busies himself in a manner he would not do in the presence of a king; when he finds himself with his family or with his kinsfolk, he speaks freely and at his ease, as he would not speak in the king's hall. He, therefore, who desirs to attain human perfection and to be truly a man of God, will be well imbued with this idea[[fn:3953]], that the great King who accompanies him and who cleavs to him constantly is greater than any human person[[fn:3954]], though it were even David or Solomon. This King, who cleavs (unto man) and accompanies him, is the intellect which emanats upon us and which is the bond between us and God; and even as we perceive Him by means of this light which He pours upon us, as it is said: by Thy light do we see light (Ps. xxxvi. 10), so by means of this light does He observe us, and thereby is He ever with us, enveloping us with His gaze: Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him (Jeremiah, xxiii. 24)? This must be well understood,
root.text.Part 3..51.1: and it must be known that perfect men, so soon as they are imbued therewith, will attain, by the ways of truth and not of imagination[[fn:3955]], to such a degree of piety, humility, fear, and reverence for the Divinity, and will feel such shame before God, that they will conduct themselves in their private life, whether being with their wives or in the bath, as they would conduct themselves in public before all men. Thus, for example, it is said of the conduct of our celebrated doctors with their wives: “Uncovering a span and covering a span[[fn:3956]].” Elsewhere it is said: “Who is a modest man? He who performs his needs by night even as he would do in the broad day[[fn:3957]].” Thou knowest also that the doctors have forbidden “to walk with an upright stature, the whole earth being full of the glory of God (Isaiah, vi. 3)[[fn:3958]].” All this aims at confirming the idea of which I have spoken, to wit, that we find ourselves always before God, and that it is in the presence of His Majesty that we go and come. The greatest doctors even refrained from baring their heads, because the Divine Majesty envelops man[[fn:3959]]. It is for the same reason that they spoke little; in the treatise Aboth we have already sufficiently set forth why it is good to speak little[[fn:3960]]: For God is in heaven, and thou upon earth; therefore let thy words be few (Ecclesiastes, v. 1).
root.text.Part 3..51.2: The idea whereunto I have awakened thy attention contains likewise the design of all the practices prescribed by the Law; for, by applying themselves unto all these practical details and by repeating them, certain men of excellence shall exercise themselves to attain unto human perfection, so as to fear God, to respect and to revere Him, knowing Him who is with them, and in this manner they shall thereafter perform that which is necessary. God Himself has set forth that the end of all the practices prescribed by the Law is to receive thereby those impressions of which we have, in this chapter, demonstrated the necessity unto those who know the high truths, (which impressions consist) in fearing God and respecting His precepts. He says: If thou wilt not observe to do all the words of this law that are written in this book, that thou mayest fear this glorious and fearful name, THE LORD THY GOD (Deuter., 28, 58). Thou seest how clearly He says that all the words of this Law have but one single end, to wit, to cause one to fear this name, etc.; that this end must be obtained through the practices, this thou mayest recognize by the words of this verse: if thou wilt not observe to do, in which it is clearly stated that it is the result of the practices[[fn:3961]], (that is to say, of the performance) of the affirmative and negative precepts. As for the ideas which the Law teaches us, to wit, those of the existence of God and of His unity, they must inspire us with love (for God), as we have several times set forth, and thou knowest with what energy the Law insists upon this love: With all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might (Ibid., 6, 5). In truth, these two ends, to wit, the love and the fear of God, are attained by two things: unto love one arrivs by the ideas which the Law contains concerning the true doctrine of the existence of God[[fn:3962]]; unto fear one arrivs by means of all the practices of the Law, as we have set forth.—Thou must well understand this brief exposition.
root.text.Part 3..52.0: This chapter contains the exposition of the meaning of three words which it is necessary to explain; these are the words ’HÉSED (חסר), MISCHPAT (משפט), CEDAKA (צדקה).
root.text.Part 3..52.1: We have already set forth in the commentary upon Abôth that ’HÉSED signifies excess in all things, whatsoever they be[[fn:3963]]; but it is more often employed to express an excess of beneficence. It is known that to be liberal is said in two senses: it is, first, to do good unto him to whom one ows absolutely naught; and second, to do good unto him who has deserved it, beyond that which he has deserved. The prophetic books most often employ the word ’HÉSED in the sense of “doing good unto him to whom one ows absolutely naught”; wherefore every benefit which comes from God is called ’HÉSED, as it is said: I will mention the loving-kindnesses (חסדי) of the Lord (Isaiah, 63, 7). Wherefore also all this universe, I mean its production by God, is called ’HÉSED, as it is said: For I have said, Mercy (חסד) shall be built up for ever[[fn:3964]] (Ps. 89, 3), which is to say: the construction of the universe is a benefit. God says again in enumerating His attributes: ורב חסד, abundant in goodness (Exodus, 34, 6).
root.text.Part 3..52.2: —As for the word CEDAKA, it is derived from CÉDEK (צדק), which signifies equity. Equity consists in doing justice unto whomsoever may invoke a right, and in giving unto every being according to its merit. Nevertheless, in the prophetic books, the discharge of debts which are incumbent upon thee towards another is not called CEDAKA, according to the first sense; for if thou payest unto the hireling his wages, or if thou payest thy debt, that is not called CEDAKA. But that which is there called CEDAKA is the fulfillment of duties which are incumbent upon thee towards another from the standpoint of a good moral character, as, for example, to succour him who suffers from any evil whatsoever[[fn:3965]]. Wherefore it is said, concerning the duty of restoring the pledge (Deuter., 24, 13): ולך תהיה צדקה, “and it shall be righteousness unto thee;” for if thou walkest in the way of the moral virtues, thou art equitable toward thy rational soul, since thou fulfillest thy duty toward it. Every moral virtue being called CEDAKA[[fn:3966]], it is said (Genesis, 15, 6): And he believed in the Lord; and He counted it to him for CEDAKA (virtue), in which one means the virtue of faith. It is the same with this passage: And it shall be our CEDAKA (virtue), if we observe to do, etc. (Deuter., 6, 25).
root.text.Part 3..52.3: —As for that which concerns the word M<small>ISCHPAT</small>, it signifies the fit judgment pronounced in respect of him who is judged, whether it be to his advantage or to his detriment.
root.text.Part 3..52.4: In summary, the word ’H<small>ESED</small> is applied unto that which constitutes absolute liberality; C<small>EDAKA</small> is predicated of every good which thou performest from the standpoint of moral virtue, whereby thou dost perfect thy soul. Finally, that which is termed M<small>ISCHPAT</small> has for its result at times a punishment, and at times a benefit.
root.text.Part 3..52.5: We have already set forth, whilst treating of the negation of (divine) attributes, that every attribute ascribed unto God in the books of the prophets is an attribute of action[[fn:3967]]. Thus, inasmuch as He bestows existence upon all things, He is called ’HASSÎD[[fn:3968]] (beneficent); in respect of His tenderness toward weak beings[[fn:3969]], that is to say, in so far as He governs living beings by means of their faculties, He is called ÇADDÎK (equitable); finally, in respect of the relative benefits and the great relative calamities[[fn:3970]] which occur in the universe, and which are a result of the judgment emanating from (divine) wisdom, He is called SCHOPHET (judge). These three words are found in the text of the Pentateuch, for example: Shall not the JUDGE of all the earth, etc. (Genesis, 18, 25); He is EQUITABLE and just (Deut., 32, 4); abundant in LOVING-KINDNESS (Exodus, 34, 6).
root.text.Part 3..52.6: In explaining the signification of these words, our purpose was to prepare (the reader) for the succeeding chapter.
root.text.Part 3..53.0: The word ’H[[t:0]]OKHMA[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]חכמה[[t:3]]), in the Hebrew language, is employed in four senses[[fn:3971]]: 1st. It signifies the perception of truths (philosophical) which have for their ultimate aim the perception of God, (and in this sense) it is said: [[t:4]]But whence shall one draw the[[t:5]] [[t:6]]חכמה[[t:7]], [[t:8]]wisdom[[t:9]], [[t:10]]etc.[[t:11]] (Job, 28, 12); [[t:12]]if thou seekest her as silver, etc.[[t:13]] (Prov., 2, 4), and many other passages. 2nd. It refers to the possession of any art (or industry) whatsoever; for example: [[t:14]]All the artists[[t:15]] (or [[t:16]]industrious ones[[t:17]], [[t:18]]חכם לב[[t:19]]) [[t:20]]among you[[t:21]] (Exodus, 35, 10); [[t:22]]and all the industrious women[[t:23]] ([[t:24]]ibid[[t:25]]., [[t:26]]v.[[t:27]] 25). 3rd. It applies to the acquisition of moral virtues; for example: [[t:28]]and that he might make wise[[t:29]] (or [[t:30]]instruct[[t:31]], [[t:32]]יחכם[[t:33]]) [[t:34]]his elders[[t:35]] (Ps. 105, 22); [[t:36]]in the aged is wisdom[[t:37]] (Job, 12, 12), for that which is acquired by old age alone, is the disposition to receive moral virtues[[fn:3972]]. 4th. It is also employed in the sense of shrewdness and cunning; for example: [[t:38]]Come, let us deal shrewdly[[t:39]] ([[t:40]]נתחכמה[[t:41]]) [[t:42]]with him[[t:43]] (Exodus, 1, 10). It is in this sense that it is said: [[t:44]]And he sent thence for a wise woman[[t:45]], [[t:46]]אשה חכמה[[t:47]] (II Samuel, XIV, 2), which signifies: endowed with shrewdness and cunning. Similarly, in this passage: [[t:48]]they are wise[[t:49]], [[t:50]]חכמים[[t:51]], [[t:52]]to do evil[[t:53]] (Jeremiah, 4, 22). —It may be that the word ’H[[t:54]]OKHMA[[t:55]], in the Hebrew language, bears (originally) the sense of [[t:56]]shrewdness[[t:57]] and [[t:58]]application of thought[[t:59]], in such wise that this shrewdness or sagacity shall have for its object now the acquisition of intellectual qualities, now that of moral qualities, now that of a practical art, and anon evil designs and wickednesses. Thus it is clear that the adjective ’H[[t:60]]AKHAM[[t:61]] ([[t:62]]חכם[[t:63]]) is applied to him who possesses intellectual qualities, or moral qualities, or any practical art whatsoever, or cunning for wickednesses and evil designs.
root.text.Part 3..53.1: According to this explanation, he who is instructed in the whole Law, and who knows its true sense, is called ’HAKHAM from two points of view, because it embraces at once intellectual and moral qualities. But, as the intellectual truths of the Law are accepted by tradition, without being demonstrated by speculative methods, it happens that, in the books of the prophets and in the words of the Doctors, the science of the Law is made a thing apart and absolute science a thing apart. This absolute science is that which provids demonstrations for all those intellectual truths which we have traditionally learned through the Law; and whenever the (Holy) Scriptures speak of the greatness and wonder of science, and of the rarity of those who possess it, — for example: Great men are not always wise (or learned) (Job, 32, 9); where shall wisdom be found, (or science) (Ibid., XXVIII, 12)? and many other similar passages, — it always pertains to that science which provids us with the demonstration of the (philosophical) ideas contained in the Law. In the words of the Doctors, this also occurrs very frequently; I mean that they make the science of the Law a thing apart and philosophy a thing apart. Thus, for example, they say of Moses that he was “father of the Law, father of science, and father of the prophets[[fn:3973]]”; and when it is said of Solomon: For he was wiser (more learned) than all men (I Kings, 4, 31, or V, 11), the Doctors remark: “but not (wiser) than Moses[[fn:3974]]” [for in saying: than all men, one intends to speak only of his contemporaries; wherefore are mentioned Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, who were then celebrated as men of learning].
root.text.Part 3..53.2: The Doctors further declare that from man is first required the knowledge of the Law, thereafter (philosophical) science, and finally the knowledge of the tradition which is linked unto the Law, that is to say, the knowing how to derive thence rules for his conduct[[fn:3975]]. Such must be the successive order of studies: first, one must know the ideas in question traditionally, then one must know how to demonstrate them, and finally one must render an exact account of those actions which constitute good conduct[[fn:3976]]. Hearken how they express themselves concerning the questions which are successively addressed unto man regarding these three things: «When man appears before the (celestial) tribunal, he is first asked: Hast thou appointed set hours for the study of the Law? Hast thou engaged in the discussion of science? Hast thou learned to understand one thing from another[[fn:3977]]?» It is therefore manifest that, in their view, the knowledge of the Law is one thing and philosophy another; the latter consists in confirming the truths of the Law by means of true speculation.
root.text.Part 3..53.3: — Having premised these matters, hearken to that which we shall say. The philosophers, both ancient and modern, have set forth that there are found in man four species of perfections[[fn:3978]]:
root.text.Part 3..53.4: The first species, which is of the least value, yet unto which the inhabitants of the earth devote their entire lives, is perfection in the matter of possession; it embraces what man possesses in the way of goods, garments, furniture, slaves, lands, and the like; and even the attainment of regal dignity belongs to this species. This is a perfection which appertains in no wise to the person; it is but a certain relation which affords unto man, at the most, naught but an imaginary enjoyment, to wit, the saying: this house is mine, this slave is mine, this fortune is mine, these troops are mine. But if he considers his own person, he shall find that all this is external to his essence, and that each of his possessions is in itself what it is; wherefore, when this relation ceass, it is found[[fn:3979]] that there is no difference between him who was a great king and the meanest of men, without any of the things which were in relation with him undergoing a change. The philosophers have shown that he whose every effort tends to obtain this kind of perfection toils but for a thing purely imaginary; for it is a thing that has no stability, and should this possession even remain with him his whole life long, no perfection would thereby accrue to him in his essence.
root.text.Part 3..53.5: The second species appertains, more than the first, unto the essence of the person; it is the perfection in the conformation and the constitution of the body; I mean to say, that the temperament of the person be of a perfect equilibrium, and that his members be well-proportioned and possess the necessary strength. Neither can this species of perfection be adopted as the final end; for it is a bodily perfection which man possesses not in so far as he is man, but in so far as he is an animal, and which he has in common with the meanest of animals. Moreover, albeit the strength of a human individual should reach its utmost limit, it would not yet equal that of a vigorous mule, and, much less, that of a lion or an elephant. By this perfection, according to that which we have just said[[fn:3980]], one attains at most to the bearing of a heavy burden or the breaking of a hard bone, or the doing of other similar things, in which there is no great utility for the body; as for the advantages for the soul, this species (of perfection) has absolutely none.
root.text.Part 3..53.6: The third species is, more than the second, a perfection in the essence of man; it is the perfection of the moral qualities, which signifies that the morals of such a man are good in the highest degree. The greater part of the commandments have no other end than to bring us unto this species of perfection. Yet this itself is but a preparation for another perfection, and is not an end in itself. Indeed, all the moral virtues concern only the relations of men one with another, and the moral perfection which a man possesses does but, as it were, dispose him to be useful unto others, so that he becoms thereby an instrument for the service of others. If, for example, thou shouldst suppose a human individual isolated, having naught to do with any man, thou shalt find that all his moral virtues are vain and idle, that he has no need of them, and that they perfect his person in no wise; he has need of them and derivs profit therefrom only in respect of others[[fn:3981]].
root.text.Part 3..53.7: The fourth species is the true human perfection; it consists in the acquisition of the intellectual virtues, to wit, in the conception of intelligibles which may afford us sound notions regarding metaphysical subjects. This is the ultimate end (of man), which gives unto the human individual a true perfection; it belongs unto him alone, through it he attains immortality, and by it man is (truly) man. If thou considerest each of the three preceding perfections, thou shalt find that they profit others and not thyself[[fn:3982]], albeit, according to vulgar notions, they necessarily profit thee and others[[fn:3983]]; but this last perfection profits thee alone, and none other shars the benefit thereof with thee: let them be only thine own, etc. (Prov. v. 17)[[fn:3984]]. Wherefore it behoves thee to be desirous of obtaining this thing which remains thine own, and that thou shouldst bestow neither fatigue nor toil upon that which profits others, while neglecting thine own soul, so that its lustre be tarnished by the preponderance of the bodily faculties[[fn:3985]]. It is in this sense that it is said, at the commencement of those poetic allegories composed upon these subjects: My mother's children were angry with me, they made me the keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept (Song of Solomon, i. 6). It is in the same sense further said: lest thou give thine honour unto others, and thy years unto the cruel (Proverbs v. 9).
root.text.Part 3..53.8: The prophets likewise have set forth these same matters unto us and have explained them, even as the philosophers have explained them, by declaring that neither possession, nor health, nor morals, are perfections in which one should glory or which one ought to desire, and that the only perfection which may be the object of our pride and our desires is the knowledge of God, which is the true science. Jeremiah expresses himself thus concerning these four perfections: Thus says the Lord: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let him that glories glory in this, that he understands and knows me (Jeremiah ix. 22-23). Thou wilt observe how he has enumerated these things according to the degree of value attributed unto them by the vulgar[[fn:3986]]. In effect, that which, for the vulgar, is the greatest perfection, is to be rich; to be strong is a lesser quality, and that which is still less esteemed (by the multitude) is the wise man, that is to say, he who possesses good morals[[fn:3987]]. Nevertheless, the latter likewise is honoured by the vulgar, unto whom the discourse (of the prophet) is addressed. This is why he has enumerated them in this order.
root.text.Part 3..53.9: The doctors also have understood this verse in the sense of the ideas which we have just presented, and they have clearly stated what I have set before thee in this chapter, namely: that wheresoever mention is made of wisdom (’HOKHMA) par excellence, which is the ultimate end, it signifies the knowledge of God; that the treasures so ardently desired[[fn:3988]] which man possesses, and whereby he thinks to become perfect, are not perfection; and that, finally, all the practices of religion, to wit, the various ceremonies of worship, and likewise the morals which are useful unto men in general in their mutual relations—that all this (I say) is not connected with this ultimate end and has not the same value, but that these are merely preparatory things for the attainment of that end.
root.text.Part 3..53.10: Hearken unto their very words, whereby they express these ideas; ’tis a passage from Bereschith Rabbâ, in which we read as follows: “One text says (of wisdom): all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it (Prov. viii. 11), and another text says: all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her (Ibid., iii. 15); by desirable things is meant the practice of the commandments and good works; by things thou canst desire, precious stones and pearls; neither desirable things, nor the things thou canst desire, are equal unto wisdom. But let him that glories glory in this, that he understands and knows me (Jeremiah ix. 25)[[fn:3989]].” Thou wilt observe how concise these words are, and how perfect was their author, having omitted nothing of all that we have said and presented through a long exposition and long preliminaries.
root.text.Part 3..53.11: Having discussed this verse (from Jeremiah) and the notable ideas it encompasses, and having mentioned what the doctors have said upon this subject, we shall now complete its exposition: In expounding, in this verse, what constitutes the noblest of ends, the prophet did not confine himself merely to (indicating as such) the knowledge of God [for if such had been his intent, he would have said: [[t:0]]but in which one may glory[[t:1]], [[t:2]]is in understanding and knowing Me[[t:3]], and would have stopped there; or else, he would have said: [[t:4]]it is in understanding and knowing Me[[t:5]] ([[t:6]]knowing[[t:7]]) [[t:8]]that I am one[[t:9]], or [[t:10]]that I have no figure[[t:11]], or [[t:12]]that there is none like unto Me[[t:13]], or other similar expressions]; but he said: “in which one may glory, is in comprehending Me and knowing My [[t:14]]attributes[[t:15]],” by which he intended the [[t:16]]actions[[t:17]] of God, as we have expounded concerning those words: [[t:18]]Make known to me Thy ways[[t:19]], [[t:20]]etc.[[t:21]] (Exodus, 33, 13)[[fn:3990]]. He has therefore declared unto us in this verse that these actions, which one must know and take as a model, are ’H[[t:22]]ÉSED[[t:23]] (benevolence), M[[t:24]]ISCHPAT[[t:25]] (justice), and C[[t:26]]EDAKA[[t:27]] (equity).
root.text.Part 3..53.12: He then subjoins another essential idea, saying: בארץ, upon the earth, and this idea is the pivot of religion. For it is not as the unbelievers[[fn:3991]] maintain, who believe that Divine Providence stopps at the sphere of the moon and that the earth, with all that is found therein, is neglected by God: The Lord has forsaken the earth (Ezekiel, ix. 9)[[fn:3992]]; but on the contrary, even as it has been declared unto us by the Prince of Sages[[fn:3993]], the earth is the Lord's (Exodus, ix. 29), which signifies that the earth also, in certain respects, is the object of Providence, even as is the heaven in other respects[[fn:3994]]. Such is the sense of these words (of Jeremiah): for I am the Lord who exercise loving-kindness, judgment and righteousness UPON THE EARTH. Thereafter, he complets his thought, saying: for in these things I delight, says the Lord, which signifies: “it is my intention that loving-kindness, righteousness, and judgment should emanate from you upon the earth,” according to what we have set forth concerning the thirteen attributes of God[[fn:3995]], namely, that we must have for our aim to imitate them and to regulate our conduct after them. Thus, that which he had for his final purpose to express by this verse, was to declare that the perfection in which man may truly glory, is to have acquired[[fn:3996]], according to his faculty, the knowledge of God and to have recognized His Providence watching over His creatures and revealing itself in the manner in which He produces and governs them[[fn:3997]]. Such a man, after having acquired this knowledge, will ever conduct himself[[fn:3998]] in such wise as to aim at loving-kindness, equity, and justice, by imitating the actions of God, as we have set forth at divers times in this treatise.
root.text.Part 3..53.13: These are all the questions which I have deemed it necessary to approach in this treatise, and the development of which has appeared to me most profitable for men such as thou art. I trust that, with profound meditation, thou wilt well comprehend all the subjects I have treated therein with the help of God.
root.text.Part 3..53.14: May He fulfill for us and for all our brethren, the Israelites, that promise which He has made unto us: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped (Isaiah, xxxv. 5); The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light; they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them has the light shined (Ibid., ix. 1). Amen.
root.text.Part 3..53.15: God is nigh unto all them that call upon Him in sincerity, without turning aside. He suffers Himself to be found by all those who seek Him, and who walk straight before them without going astray.
root.text.Part 3..53.16: END OF THE THIRD AND LAST PART OF THE GUIDE FOR THE PERPLEXED.
root.text.Part 3.Introduction.0:
GOD OF THE UNIVERSE
PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION.[[fn:2458]]
We have already set forth many a time that the principal object we pursued in this treatise was to explain, so far as explanation is possible, the Ma’asé beréschith (the Account of the Creation) and the Ma’asé mercabâ (the Account of the Chariot)[[fn:2459]], out of consideration for those for whom this work was composed[[fn:2460]].
root.text.Part 3.Introduction.1: We have likewise set forth that these subjects belong to the secrets of the Law; and thou knowest how severely the Sages rebuke him who reveals these secrets, even declaring plainly that he who conceals the secrets of the Law, which are clear and manifest to speculative minds, shall receive a very great reward. At the end of the treatise Pesa’him, in interpreting these words: For her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the Lord, to eat sufficiently and for durable clothing, WE-LIMEKHASSÉ ATHÎK (Isaiah, xxiii. 18), they say: «And for him who covers (limekhassé) the things revealed by the Ancient (’attik) of Days, to wit, the secrets of the Law[[fn:2461]].» Thou must therefore understand, if thou possessest intelligence, what lesson they intended to impart to us thereby. They have explained elsewhere[[fn:2462]] how profound is the Ma’asé mercabâ, and how inaccessible it is to vulgar minds; and it has been declared that even that which is clear therein to him who has been admitted to understand it[[fn:2463]], is forbidden by religion to be taught or communicated to others, unless it be by word of mouth and to a single individual possessing certain qualities, and even then one shall only impart to him the first elements[[fn:2464]]. This is the reason why this science has entirely vanished from our community, so that not even the slightest trace thereof is to be found[[fn:2465]]. And indeed, so it must needs have been, for it was only transmitted by tradition from one sage to another[[fn:2466]], and was never committed to writing.
root.text.Part 3.Introduction.2: Since this is so, how shall I proceed to awaken attention to that which has appeared to me well-nigh clear, or to that which is for me of an indubitable evidence, according to what I have understood thereof[[fn:2467]]? Nevertheless, I should have deemed it a great cowardice towards thee and towards every perplexed man, to refrain from writing aught of that which is clear to me, so that my inevitable death would have caused its loss; it would have been, as it were, to rob of the truth him who is worthy of it, or to grudge the heir his inheritance[[fn:2468]], both of which things betoken a blameworthy character.
root.text.Part 3.Introduction.3: On the other hand, we have already stated that religion forbidds us to expound this subject clearly, to say nothing of what simple judgment imposs upon us[[fn:2469]]. Add to this that what I believe myself to possess thereof is but simple conjecture and a personal opinion[[fn:2470]]. I have had no divine revelation therein which might have made me know that this is indeed what was intended, nor have I learned[[fn:2471]] from any master that which I think of it; but it is the texts of the prophetic books and the discourses of the Sages, as well as those speculative propositions which I possess, that have led me to believe that the matter is indubitably thus. Nevertheless, it is possible that it may be otherwise, and that something quite different was intended.
root.text.Part 3.Introduction.4: Guided by a right thought and by divine assistance, I have taken in this regard the course of which I shall now speak: I shall give thee concerning the words of Ezekiel an explanation which, when heard by the first comer, might seem to him to add nothing to what the text expresses, as though I were merely translating words from one language into another, or summarizing the literal sense of the discourse; but if it be examined with perfect care by him for whom this treatise was composed and who has well understood every chapter thereof, the whole matter shall be clear to him, even as it is clear and manifest to me, so that naught therein shall any longer be a mystery to him. This is all that it has been possible to do to be useful to every one, whilst refraining from teaching clearly, and as it ought to be done, anything whatsoever concerning this subject.
root.text.Part 3.Introduction.5: After this preliminary observation, apply thy mind diligently unto those chapters which shall treat of this noble, sublime, and grand subject, which is a peg whereon all is suspended and a pillar whereon all is stayed[[fn:2472]].
root.text.Part 3..50.15.sub_1: It appears to me, furthermore, that which occasioned these four personages to remain in the most perfect communion with the Almighty, and that which procured for them the constant protection of His Providence, even in those moments when they were engaged in the augmentation of their worldly fortunes, that is to say, during the moments devoted to pastoral pursuits, to agriculture, and to the administration of their families, was that in all these actions they had as their objective the attainment of proximity to the Divine as far as possible; for the principal aim they sought in this life was to bring into being a nation that would know and worship the Almighty: for I have distinguished him, to the end that he may command (Genesis, 18, 19). Hence, it is patent that all their endeavours were directed towards this sole objective, namely, to disseminate throughout the world the belief in the unity of God and to lead mankind to the love of God. Wherefore, they attained to this lofty degree of perfection; for these occupations constituted a grand and veritable form of worship. This lofty degree, a person such as myself cannot pretend to guide men towards its attainment; but the degree previously alluded to, one may strive to attain by means of the exercise of which we have spoken. It is necessary to address to the Almighty our humble supplications, that He may remove the obstacles which separate us from Him, although the greater part of these obstacles arise from ourselves, as we have expounded in diverse chapters of this treatise[[fn:3937]]: Your iniquities have established a separation between you and your God (Isaiah, 59, 2).
root.text.Part 3..50.16: At present, a most singular reflection has occurred unto me, whereby certain doubts may be assuaged and by which various metaphysical enigmas are revealed. We have heretofore expounded, in the chapters of Providence, that Providence watches over every being endowed with intelligence, in accordance with the measure of its intelligence[[fn:3938]]. Consequently, the individual possessed of perfect perception, whose Intelligence never ceass to occupy itself with the contemplation of God, is ever under the guardianship of Providence; but the individual who, notwithstanding his perfect perception, permits his thought, at certain moments, to be unoccupied with the consideration of God, is under the guardianship of Providence solely during those moments in which his thought is directed towards God, whilst it abandons him during the moments of his preoccupations. Nevertheless, Providence does not abandon him in the manner it abandons one who never directs his thoughts towards God; it merely becoms less effective, owing to the fact that this individual, endowed with perfect perception, does not possess the intellect in actuality during the moments of his preoccupations, and who, in those moments, is intelligent only in proximate potentiality[[fn:3939]], resembling a skilled writer at the moment when he is not engaged in writing. Thus, the individual who never occupies his thoughts with the consideration of God is analogous to one who finds himself in darkness and who has never beheld the light, as we have expounded upon the words: And the wicked perish in the darkness (I Samuel, II, 9)[[fn:3940]]; the individual who perceivs God and dedicats his entire being to the consideration of this object of his thought is similar to one who finds himself surrounded by the radiance of the sun. Finally, the individual who thinks, yet is preoccupied, resembls, during the moments of his preoccupations, one who finds himself on a day of mist and who does not receive the rays of the sun owing to the clouds that intercept the light.
root.text.Part 3..50.17: It is for this reason that it appears unto me, that all those amongst the prophets, or amongst the pious and perfect men, who were afflicted with one of the evils of this world, were thus afflicted only in a moment in which they forgot God, and that the magnitude of the misfortune was in proportion to the duration of this forgetfulness, or to the unworthiness of the thing in which they were so preoccupied. If [[fn:3941]] it were indeed thus, this would resolve the great difficulty which has led philosophers to deny that Divine Providence watches over each individual man, and to assimilate, in this respect, human individuals to those of other species of animals; for the proof which they allege in support of this notion, is that pious and virtuous men are sometimes afflicted with great misfortunes. The mystery which lies beneath this, would thus be clarified, even according to the opinions of philosophers; for Divine Providence would perpetually watch over the man who is favoured with that outpouring of the Divine, which is bestowed upon all those who labour to attain it[[fn:3942]]. For, when the thought of man is perfectly pure, when he perceivs God, by employing the true means, and when he enjoys that which he perceivs, it is not possible for any kind of evil to ever afflict this man; for he is with God, and God is with him. But, when he turns away from God, and in some sort withdraws himself from His gaze, God withdraws Himself from him, and he then remains exposed to all the evils which may, by accident, come upon him; for that which calls forth Providence, and savs from the floods of chance, is that outpouring of the Divine Intelligence, which has, for a certain time, withdrawn itself from such a pious and virtuous man, or which has never come unto another, who is vicious and wicked, and it is for this reason that they have both been afflicted by the blows of chance.
root.text.Part 3..50.18: This conviction, I daresay, is further corroborated by the textual narrative of the Pentateuch, in which the Almighty has spoken thus: I shall hide My countenance from them; he (the people) shall be devoured, and numerous evils and calamities shall befall him, and he shall say on that day: Is it not because the Lord is not with me that these misfortunes have befallen me (Deut., 31, 17)? It is patently evident, my dear fellow, that if He hids His face, we ourselves are the causa causans, and that this veil (which serves to conceal Him from us) is the direct result of our own actions, as it is written: And I will hide My face on that day, because of all the evil which he has done (ibid., v. 18). There can be no doubt, nay, 'tis an absolute certainty, that that which is stated concerning the community applies equally to an individual; hence, it is crystal clear that if a human being is abandoned to chance and exposed to being devoured like the beasts of the field, the reason for this state of affairs is that he is separated from the Divine Presence by a veil. However, if his God is with him, no evil can befall him[[fn:3943]], as it is written: Fear not, for I am with thee[[fn:3944]], be not dismayed, for I am thy God (Isaiah, 41, 10), and as it is written again: When thou walkest through the waters, I will be with thee; the rivers, they shall not overflow thee (ibid., XLIII, 2), in which the sense is: "when thou walkest through the waters, accompanied by Me, the rivers shall not carry thee away[[fn:3945]]." Indeed, whosoever has rendered himself worthy of receiving the effusion of this Intelligence[[fn:3946]] finds himself under the guardianship of Providence and secure from all evils, as it is written: The Lord is with me, I fear not; what can man do unto me (Ps., 118, 6)? and as it is written again: Trust in Him and thou shalt be at peace (Job, 22, 21), that is to say: turn thyself towards Him and thou shalt be preserved from all evil.
root.text.Part 3..50.19: If thou dost peruse the Canticle of Misfortunes[[fn:3947]], thou shalt discover that it treats of that sublime Providence which watchfully presids over mankind and preservs it from all corporeal calamities[[fn:3948]], both those that are general and those that are particular to diverse individuals (in such a manner that no calamity befallenth them), neither those that are inherent to the nature of being in general, nor those that emanate from the malice of men. Behold, what is said therein: For He shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, from the noisome pestilence. He shall cover thee with His feathers, and thou shalt take refuge under His wings; His truth shall be thy shield and buckler. Thou shalt not be afraid of the terror by night, nor of the arrow that flies by day, nor of the pestilence that walks in darkness, nor of the destruction that wasts at noonday (Ps., 91, 3-7). Speaking thereafter of the protection (of God) against the malice of men, it is said: If it were to befall thee, whilst thou art journeying, to pass through a vast battlefield, in such a manner that a thousand dead were to fall on thy left and ten thousand on thy right, no evil would befall thee; but thou wouldst behold and observe with thine eyes how God has judged and punished these wicked men whom death has smitten, whilst thou hast been preserved. Such is the import of these words: A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand, but the evil shall not come nigh thee (ibid., v. 7 and 8). After having subsequently expounded in detail how the righteous man is preserved, it indicats the reason for this lofty protection, and says what is the cause whereby the sublime Providence watchfully presids over this man: Because he has set his passion (חשק) upon Me, I will deliver him; I will set him on high, because he has known My name (ibid., v. 14). — We have already expounded in preceding chapters that to know the name of God signifies to comprehend God; he (the Psalmist) says, therefore, in a manner of speaking: If such a man enjoys this protection, it is because he has learned to know Me and has thereafter set his passion upon Me. Thou art also acquainted with the difference that exists between אוהב (loving) and חושק (being passionate); for the love that is borne to such an excess that one cannot think of anything else but the beloved object, that is passion.
root.text.Part 2..18.15: That which renders yet more evident the existence of determination[[fn:1743]] in the celestial sphere, so that no man could find for it any other determining cause than the design of a being acting with intention, is the manner of existence of the stars. In effect, the sphere being always in motion and the star remaining always fixed[[fn:1744]], this proves that the matter of the stars is not the same as that of the spheres. Already Abu Nasr (Al-Farabi), in his glosses upon the Acroasis, has expressed himself in the following terms: «Between the sphere and the stars there is a difference; for the sphere is diaphanous, whilst the stars are not so. The cause thereof is that there is between the two matters and between the two forms a difference, though it be small.» Such are his expressions. I, however, do not say small, but (I say) that they differ greatly; for I derive the proof thereof, not from the transparency, but from the motions. It is therefore clear to me that there are three matters and three forms: 1st, bodies which, in themselves, are always at rest, and these are the bodies of the stars; 2nd, bodies which are always in motion, and these are the bodies of the spheres; 3rd, bodies which sometimes move and sometimes are at rest, and these are the elements. Now, I should like to know what could have joined together these two matters[[fn:1745]], — between which there is an extreme difference, as it seems to me, or (at the very least) a small difference[[fn:1746]], as Abu Nasr says, — and who is he that has prepared this union? In short, two diverse bodies, of which one is fixed in the other, without being mingled therein, and being, on the contrary, circumscribed in a particular place of the latter and strongly attached, (all this) without the design of a being acting with intention, would be an astonishing thing[[fn:1747]]. But, what is yet more astonishing, are those numerous stars which are found in the eighth (sphere), all of them globes, some small, others large, here a star, there another [apparently at the distance of a cubit], here ten (stars) clustered together, there a great space with nothing. What then is the cause which particularly distinguishes this space by ten stars and that other by the lack of stars? Finally, the body of the sphere is a single simple body, without diversity; for what cause, then, does such a part of the sphere suit the star located therein, rather than another? All this, like all things of the same kind, would be most improbable, or rather would border upon the impossible, were it admitted that all proceeds from God by necessity, as Aristotle supposs.
root.text.Part 3..18.2: But a prophet (Asaph) tells us that after having long reflected upon this subject, he understood that things must be considered by their final issue, and not by their beginning. Behold how he depicts the series of his reflections: They say: How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High? Behold, these are the ungodly, who prosper in the world; they increase in riches. Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency (Ps. lxxiii. 11-13). Then he says: When I thought to know this, it was too painful for me; until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end. Surely Thou didst set them in slippery places, etc. How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment! etc. (ibid., v. 16-19). Malachi makes precisely the same reflections: Your words have been stout against Me, etc. Ye have said, It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept His ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the Lord of hosts? And now we call the proud happy, etc. Then they that feared the Lord spake often one to another, etc. Then shall ye return, and discern, etc. (Malachi, iii. 13-18). David also speaks of this opinion[[fn:2890]] widespread in his time, and which necessarily resulted in injustice and the reciprocal violence of men[[fn:2891]]. He seeks to produce arguments to destroy this opinion and to establish that God has knowledge of all this: They slay, says he, the widow and the stranger, and murder the fatherless. Yet they say, The Lord shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard it. Understand, ye brutish among the people: and ye fools, when will ye be wise? He that planted the ear, shall He not hear? He that formed the eye, shall He not see? (Ps. xciv. 6-9). I shall explain to thee the sense of this last argument, after having first shown thee how little those who assail with their attacks the words of the prophets have understood these words (of David). Years ago, some physicians, men of wit of our own community, expressed to me their astonishment at these words of David. From his reasoning, said they, it would follow that He who created the mouth eats, that He who created the lungs cries out, and the same would hold for the other organs. But thou shalt see, O reader of this treatise, how far these persons were from understanding the import of this argument; harken to its meaning: It is clear that he who fashions any instrument whatever, if he possessed not the idea of the work which that instrument is to serve, would find it impossible to fashion an instrument for that use. If, for example, the smith did not form a just idea of sewing, he could not fashion the needle in a form which alone can make it serve for sewing, and the same is true of other instruments; for, as certain philosophers believed that God perceivs not individual things, which are things perceived by the senses, whilst God perceivs not by a sense, but by an intelligible perception, he (David) argus against them from the existence of the senses. If, says he, the manner in which the eye perceivs were for God a mystery which He were incapable of knowing, how could He have produced this organ, destined for visual perception? Was it pure chance that caused a limpid humor to be born, and then another similar humor, then a membrane which chance alone likewise would have perforated, and that finally before the opening there should be placed a transparent and hard membrane[[fn:2892]]? In short, can an intelligent man imagine that the humors, the membranes, and the nerves of the eye, which are so wisely organized[[fn:2893]] and whose whole has for its end this visual action, are a simple effect of chance? Assuredly not, and there is therein necessarily an intention of nature, as all physicians and all philosophers have declared. Now, nature has neither intelligence, nor (consequently) organizing faculty[[fn:2894]], whereupon the philosophers are agreed; but this artistic organization[[fn:2895]] emanats, according to the opinion of the philosophers, from an intellectual principle, and, according to us, it is the work of an intelligent Being who has impressed such faculties upon all that possesses a natural faculty. If, therefore, this Intelligence perceived not the object in question and knew it not, how, in that case, could it have produced or caused to emanate from itself a nature tending toward a goal which it knew not? It is therefore with reason that he (David) calls these men brutish and fools. Thereafter he setts forth that this is a defect of our perception. God (says he), who has given us this Intelligence by which we perceive, whilst our incapacity to grasp His true essence gives rise within us to these grave doubts, God knows this defect which exists in us, and we must not take account of the attacks which are the result of the weakness of our reflection[[fn:2896]]: He, says he, that teaches man knowledge, the Lord, knows the thoughts of man, that they are vanity (ibid., v. 10-11).
root.text.Part 3..46.3: All this, therefore, contributed to the end that one should keep far from the sanctuary and not enter therein at every instant. Thou knowest, moreover, what the doctors say: “No person, were he even pure, shall enter the court for the service until he has bathed[[fn:3732]].” These acts, then, maintained reverence and served to produce the impression which was to lead to the piety that was the aim.
root.text.Munk's Introduction.0: The work of Maimonides that is the subject of this publication is sufficiently well-known and appreciated. It is understood what importance it holds for biblical exegesis and theology, and how rich it is in information regarding the history of medieval philosophy, particularly among the Arabs. None of the questions that interest the theologian are passed over in silence; and, although the solutions to these questions are generally based on allegorical exegesis and a metaphysics that has had its time, they often offer us glimpses of light that can still guide our research today and serve as a beacon to penetrate the elevated regions that, for the human mind, are shrouded in mystery. As the true founder of a rational theology, in which philosophical thought maintains all its rights, Maimonides has exercised a decisive influence on his co-religionists, the consequences of which are still felt today; and the principles he laid down, eagerly embraced by some and passionately rejected by others, have given rise to a struggle in which human reason has emerged victorious, after having brought about a reconciliation between faith and thought that the great genius of Maimonides, anticipating the centuries, had set as the noblest goal of all his efforts. But the high reputation of this illustrious man was not confined to the synagogue, and this spirit of such incontestable superiority found appreciators among the elite men of all confessions. Muslim scholars did not disdain to read the Guide, and one of them even wrote a commentary on certain parts of this work, which we still possess and in which he lavishes praise on the author. In Egypt, where Maimonides lived, Coptic theologians studied his work and made it accessible to their community by having copies made in Arabic characters. It must have been known early on
root.text.Munk's Introduction.1: It is known in Europe through a Latin version; for it is often cited by the scholastics, and men such as Saint Thomas and Albert the Great invoke its authority. The fame enjoyed by Maimonides' work shows that there is more to it than just Jewish theology; and, indeed, although this theology was the author's primary goal, he dealt with a wide range of subjects, which he used to support his system, and his work, based on extensive reading and solid erudition, abounds in information of all kinds that would be sought in vain elsewhere. Without mentioning his exposition of the Arab Peripatetic system, drawn from the works of Ibn Sina, we must particularly highlight the precious details that the author provides at the end of the first part regarding the system of the Motécallemin or Muslim scholastics, and the curious information that, in the second part, he provides about the books of the Sabians, which are still so little known today and whose Arabic translation exists only very incompletely in a few European libraries. I must not anticipate here what I will have to say later in the Prolegomena that I intend to publish, regarding the era of Maimonides, the life of this illustrious man, his works, the manuscripts that exist, and the editions that have been published; but I wanted to draw attention to the great importance of his Guide for the Perplexed and the general interest that this work offers, which deserves, for so many reasons, to occupy one of the first places among the monuments of Arabic literature, and which, however, has not been the subject of any critical work by orientalists until now. While our century has seen the publication of so many other Arabic works, far less worthy of occupying minds, the original Arabic of the Guide has remained buried in a few libraries; the Hebrew version by Samuel ibn Tibbon has been the only one published in several editions, generally very faulty. It is on this version that two Latin translations have been made, one of which, attributed to the Jewish physician Jacob Mantino and published in Paris in 1520, is almost unknown, and the other, attributed to Jean Buxtorf the son (Basel, 1629, in-4), has been the only one to make Maimonides' masterpiece accessible to the European reader until now. It will be easily understood that Buxtorf's work, whatever its merit, cannot meet the requirements of criticism. Ibn Tibbon's version, which can be called a true copy of the original Arabic, can only be fully understood by one who possesses
root.text.Munk's Introduction.2: PREFACE. At the same time, knowledge of Arabic and that of rabbinic Hebrew, and who has acquired sufficient notions of Muslim philosophy and its terminology. Buxtorf, an excellent Hebraist, was completely foreign to the language and literature of the Arabs and lacked all the indispensable resources for the interpreter of a work of this nature. Thus, his translation, if it allows the reader to grasp the entirety of Maimonides' work, leaves much to be desired in the details, disfigured by numerous misinterpretations. Moreover, it is not accompanied by any commentary that could aid the reader in understanding the many details that were easily grasped by the author's contemporaries but are full of obscurity for us. Since Buxtorf, the Guide has been the subject of no work, except for a few modern commentaries written in Hebrew by authors who were far beneath such a task, and an edition of the second part of Ibn-Tibbon's version, accompanied by a German translation and explanatory notes, by M. Simon Scheyer (Frankfurt am Main, 1838, in-8). This partial publication, for which the Arabic text was consulted, is the only one that offers a truly scientific character and responds to some extent to the needs of the European reader. For more than twenty years, I had formed the project of publishing the Arabic text of the Guide, of accompanying it with a French translation, and of adding more or less developed annotations, which could provide the reader with all the necessary clarifications for understanding the text and by which he could be enabled to place himself always from the author's point of view and to judge him with perfect intelligence of the era that saw the birth of this work and the studies that served as its basis. I announced this project, as early as 1833, in my Reflections on the worship of the ancient Hebrews, p. 80 (t. IV of M. Cahen's Bible), where I gave as a specimen two chapters of the second part; but I found in Paris only incomplete manuscripts of the first and second parts of the Arabic text. Later, I was put in possession of a copy of the Hebrew version of the Venice edition, which had in the margin a partial copy of the Arabic text, notably of the first part, from chapter XXXIII to chapter LXXI. A trip I made to Oxford in 1835 allowed me to collate this fragment with six manuscripts from the Bodleian Library and to complete the first part; but I could not prolong-
root.text.Munk's Introduction.3: PREFACE. During my stay at Oxford, I was able to devote all the necessary care to this work and definitively establish all parts of my text. It was the liberality of the curators of the Leyden Library that generously came to my aid to complete my critical work on the Arabic text of the Guide.
