The late Mr. Weyers, whose premature loss is lamented by Oriental scholars and whose memory will be preserved with pious respect, spontaneously offered to put at my disposal the two manuscripts of the aforementioned library, which were sent to me in Paris. His learned successor, Professor Juynboll, was kind enough to continue this remarkable favour, without which it would have been impossible for me to execute my work with the meticulous exactness that the importance of the subject made a sacred duty for me. In making this acknowledgement, I feel the need to add an expression of the deepest gratitude. Finally, having obtained the most indispensable materials, I found myself hindered by the numerous material difficulties that oppose an undertaking of this importance. Unfortunately, I was only able to contemplate the execution of the work at the very moment when Providence subjected me to the most severe trial that could paralyse the efforts of a writer for whom the most meticulous readings and research are at once a need and an imperative duty. The total loss of sight seemed to render impossible the continuation of the work to which I had already devoted so many sleepless nights and from which it was hard for me to renounce forever. But, having recovered from my initial despondency and supported by the encouragement of friendship and generous protection, I saw in the new difficulties that I would have to overcome a diversion from the pain, and I hoped that, through perseverance, I could create a consolation for myself from the few literary fragments saved from the shipwreck. I must now render to the reader an account of the first fruits of my efforts, which I am permitted to present to him today. This first volume contains the first part of the Guide, which is entirely devoted to preliminary questions and is intended to prepare the reader for the solution of the lofty questions of theology and philosophy treated in the other two parts. The author first explains a certain number of homonymous words found in the Holy Scripture, sets forth their various meanings, and particularly insists on the figurative sense that must be attributed to them when they are applied to God.
root.text.Munk's Introduction.4: PREFACE. The author intermingles general observations on theological studies and the manner in which one ought to prepare oneself for them. Subsequently, he addresses the question of divine attributes, demonstrating that all manner of attributes must be removed from God, and he expounds upon the sense in which the various attributive terms employed by sacred writers and philosophers ought to be understood. Finally, he summarises the system of Muslim theologians, which was partly adopted by the Jewish theologians of the East, and, illustrating the paradoxical and arbitrary nature of this system, he reveals its impotence in providing a rational foundation for the most important dogmas of religion, particularly with regards to demonstrating the existence, unity, and incorporeality of God, as well as creation ex nihilo. It has been observed what resources were at my disposal for the publication of the Arabic text of this part. I had it printed in Hebrew characters: firstly, because the author himself, like all Jewish Arabic writers, employed the Hebrew script in writings related to Judaism, and this script has been preserved in all the manuscripts that remain to us of the Guide; secondly, to avoid the numerous typographical difficulties and the unappealing appearance presented by an Arabic text often bristling with Hebrew citations. The change in script cannot present any serious difficulty to the Arabist, provided that he has familiarised himself with the mode of transcription, which is all the more simple and natural given that the Hebrew and Arabic letters, belonging to languages of the same root, correspond exactly to one another and can easily be substituted for one another. Indeed, the conventional orthography of the manuscripts, which I have scrupulously preserved, presents nothing that could hinder the Arabist, except for the substitution of the punctuated càph (îp) for the khà (^) and the guimel without a point (3) for the ghaïn (p) (i), a substitution also commonly used by the Christians of Syria, who write Arabic in Syriac characters. I have merely followed the example set by Pococke in his Porta Mosis, and by Schnurrer in the extracts he published from several Jewish Arabic authors. Nevertheless, to avoid presenting the less practised reader with certain difficulties found in the publications of these two scholars, I deemed it necessary to introduce, with regards to grammatical forms,
root.text.Munk's Introduction.5: VI PREFACE. notably the desinences, a more regular orthography, by avoiding the irregularities and inconsistencies that most Jewish Arabic manuscripts and often even those of Muslims present. Thus, for example, I have often added the accusative termination, which is almost always lacking in manuscripts, and at other times I had to suppress this same termination that ignorant copyists often placed at random; in words derived from roots whose third radical is a weak letter, I have suppressed this letter whenever the grammatical rules required it, writing, for instance, ])îé (^) for ••y-IÛ, I^DO for "^I^DD, and I have made the same suppression in the future apocopes, adding Arabic vowels, which I have often used for clarity and which are also found here and there in the manuscripts of Jewish Arabs and Syrian Christians; in the hamzated verbs, which the copyists, in accordance with the usage of vulgar Arabic, frequently confuse with the verbs with quiescent letters, I have restored the hamzated letter, and I have written, for example, pnni"' for iirni"» (fol. 17 6), ^vin^ for pinS^ (fol. 97 6) (i). Nevertheless, I have preserved in my text a few slight inaccuracies that evidently emanate from the author himself and which may be considered as anomalies of the local dialect; thus, I have always written "•ît^, i<:x, although the more correct orthography is '^iîi^ (^')ï Ï<i3t< (^L')• The imperative n^< (for j or Tij) falls into the same category (2). — As for the variants of the different manuscripts, I have limited myself to indicating, in the notes accompanying the translation, all those that may offer some interest for the critique of the text or for the interpretation of certain passages; I have accepted in my edition the reading that seemed to me the best, and my choice has been guided by a conscientious examination of both the original text and the Hebrew versions. In the French translation, I have aimed above all at strict fidelity, without however allowing myself to be led into a servile literalness that could have harmed clarity. I have sought, as far as possible, to enable the reader, by means of my translation, to understand each word of the Arabic text, and.
root.text.Munk's Introduction.6: PREFACE. When the genius of the language absolutely refused the fidelity that I had imposed upon myself, I have given in a note the word for word of the original (*). It is all too easy, when it comes to the interpretation of profound and obscure passages, to conceal one's ignorance behind a vague translation with elegant turns of phrase, and it seemed to me that, in a work of the nature of this one, elegance must give way to the most precise expression of the author's thought. I had to make the greatest efforts to unite fidelity with clarity and to compensate for certain negligences of style that can be reproached in our author, as in all Arab writers in general, and I do not disguise from myself that, if on the one hand my translation can fully satisfy the need of one who seeks in it an aid for the study of the original text or of the Hebrew version of Ibn-Tibbon, on the other hand it will often require the indulgence of the French reader who neither wants nor can have recourse to the text, and who, uninterested in the philological part of my work, seeks only to become familiar in an easy manner with the subjects treated in this work. I must add, however, that as I advanced in my translation and could suppose the Arabist reader to be sufficiently familiar with certain turns of phrase of the original, I sought more and more to consider those who will read only the translation, and, without ceasing to be faithful, I departed a little from that literalness that will be particularly noticeable in the introduction and the first chapters. I have accompanied the translation with annotations, more or less numerous, more or less developed, according to what seemed to me to be required by the subjects treated in the various chapters and the terms more or less explicitly employed by the author. The latter, as he often declares, addressed himself to readers versed in the different branches of theological studies and in the relative literature, as well as in the philosophy of the time; the different classes of readers for whom this translation is intended will therefore necessarily require, in order to understand it in all its parts, information (1) Sometimes, to render the phrase clearer, I have added between ( ) explanatory words that are not found in the text; the parentheses of the text have been indicated by [ ].
root.text.Munk's Introduction.7: VII PREFACE. varied which may, as far as possible, enable them to place themselves at the author's point of view and follow him everywhere in his reasoning. To some, it was necessary to explain what is particularly within the domain of biblical exegesis and Jewish theology; to others, all that supposes a notion more than superficial of Aristotelian philosophy in the form it had taken in the Arab schools through the works of Al-Farabi and Ibn-Sina. Often it was necessary to recall certain opinions of Jewish theologians prior to the author, or even to quote in extenso unpublished passages. I believed it necessary to provide all literary and historical information that the reader could not easily find elsewhere, and which is indispensable for the prompt understanding of certain passages; therefore, I think that even in my most extensive notes, there will be no unnecessary digressions. Where it was sufficient to provide simple indications, I was sparing of textual citations. I have indicated, as far as possible, all passages, whether from the Talmud and the Midrashim, or from Aristotle and a few other authors, to which Maimonides alludes; these indications, of incontestable utility, have generally been neglected by commentators. A certain number of critical notes are devoted to the variants of the Arabic text and the divergences offered by the two Hebrew versions. With a view to those who will use my translation to study the Hebrew version of Ibn-Tibbon, I believed it necessary to rectify, with the help of manuscripts, the main errors that disfigure the editions of this version. One will read with interest several notes that Ibn-Tibbon added to his version, as well as a few others emanating from the author himself (ch. LXXIV), and which until now had remained unpublished. In short, I have desired to make (1) The importance I believed I had to attach to these indications did not allow me to shrink from the difficulties that my current situation opposes to such a task, and I have not hesitated in all my research, often taking some vague memories as a starting point, to undertake long readings to reach the desired goal. There are, I think, in this first volume, only three citations for which I could not indicate the location: page 14, a passage from Midrash or Haggadah (Exposing the power, etc.), which is also cited by R. Moses ben-Nachman, in his Commentary on Genesis, but which may no longer exist in our Midrashim; page 107, a passage from Alexander of Aphrodisias, which I did not have at my disposal; page 381, words attributed by the author to Galen and related to time.
root.text.Munk's Introduction.8: PREFACE. ix so that this work could serve as a repository for those seeking information on Jewish theology and Arabic philosophy; to the details given in the notes, I hope to add a more systematic exposition that I reserve for the Prolegomena. I must conclude this preface without expressing my deep gratitude to those who have kindly assisted me in the accomplishment of my difficult task. I shall not attempt to express all the sentiments that the warm devotion of a tried friend inspires in me, who has more than once supported my flagging courage. Mr. Albert Cohn has not only hastened the material execution of this publication through his zeal, but his profound knowledge of the Arabic language has also enabled him to actively cooperate in the revision of the text proofs and to spare me errors that could have escaped my notice during reading. Another friend, Rabbi Trénel, has kindly collated my translation with the Hebrew version of Ibn-Tibbon, and has often had occasion to draw my attention to the errors committed by the editors that needed to be rectified in the notes. Finally, a modest scholar, Mr. Clément-Mullet, who applies his solid knowledge of Oriental languages to important research related to the history of sciences, has assisted me, with devoted friendship, in the revision of the translation proofs and in the verification of numerous citations made in the notes. I must not forget those who, with unwavering devotion and patience, have written under my dictation and have made the long and laborious readings that my research required. I pay here a painful tribute of regrets to the memory of the young and studious Isidor Stillmann, who assisted me for the greater part of this volume, and who, suddenly taken away by premature death, has left me a successor equally devoted in his friend Mr. Joseph Mistowski, with whose help I have been able to continue and complete this part. I have had to struggle against very great difficulties in undertaking a task that may be beyond my strength, and I feel that I must arm myself with courage and patience to accomplish the mission that I have given myself, consulting rather my zeal than my physical and intellectual capacities. The gravity of this mission and the duties that the memory of the illustrious doctor imposes upon me, whose interpretation I dare to attempt,
root.text.Munk's Introduction.9: IX PREFACE. Thought does not permit me to abuse the rights that I may have to the indulgence of the learned world. It is my duty to invite serious and impartial criticism from competent men, and I shall welcome with sincere gratitude the critical observations and advice that will be addressed to me in public journals or that will be kindly sent to me directly. I shall be happy to profit from all warnings to rectify the errors I may have committed and to avoid new ones; and if this first part of my work can deserve, on some points, the approval of scholars, it will be for me a powerful encouragement to persevere, with the aid of Providence, in the long and difficult career that remains for me to pursue. S. MUNK. Paris, April 1856.
